review_text:
The quick TLDR is: it's a solid, but somewhat bland, horror, third-person shooter. A quick score would put it at a 6.5/10 (above average - good). 
If you like Survival Horror/Horror Action (it has difficulties picking which one it wants to be), then it's still worth a playthrough if you're hungering for a game and it's on sale. 

I did enjoy my time with it, but in my playthrough I was wishing it was better than actually it is, since the core movement and shooting felt great. The visuals are great. The enemies are basic, but felt nice to shoot. However in the end the overall package was just kinda by-the-numbers bland. 

This left me somewhat disappointed because it does the basics pretty damn well, but there's nothing too special to make it stand out from the other, more better acclaimed games in the genre. 
Also I had plenty of resources throughout the entire game. I've seen other people complain about the ammo count, but I basically had a small armoury throughout. No idea if the devs made the game easier or I'm just too used to these kind of games.

The real issue I have with the game is that the level design is incredibly linear, but the slower paced gameplay feels like it needs a more open/Resident Evil 1 type level design. 
Especially since it has a limited inventory, which does nothing other than be annoying. You're not making any meaningful decisions on route planning, or what items to take because the game is a line bar the odd optional offshoot for items. So it's restricting you just for the sake of it. There's nothing stopping you (most of the time) to run back down the line you ran up to put stuff away. It just adds needless travel time if you care about loot.

The shooting is your basic third-person style seen in many other modern survival horror games, but at a slower, more deliberate pace, with nothing else going for it outside of the focus on charged shots (the charged shots are quite nice, I do like them). 
Which is fine, I like the slower pace, but the game turns into a shooting gallery with explosive barrels galore, so what's the point of trying for the slower gameplay if you're constantly locking me into combat arenas with explosives everywhere?

The game seems to have an identity crisis on what kind of horror game it wanted to be. Survival horror, or action horror. And currently it sits in this awkward middle ground where it satisfies neither too well. This is where my disappointment comes from. 

The story is fine, it starts interesting but it did lose me as it went on. I feel like it tried too much and by the end I stopped caring. Interesting ideas, but the execution didn't fully land for me. 

Overall like I said at the start, if you're a horror fan it's worth a try on a good sale, and I do wish Bloober Team luck on their future projects. They had the basics down, but Cronos: The New Dawn wasn't quite there in closing it out.

review_text:
What a game!

The developers and writers managed to make, in my opinion, one of the scariest games in terms of feel. They aren't using cheap tricks like jump scares and exaggeratedly loud sudden noises like most other horror games do. Instead they rely on pure tension with incredible level design and sound.

You be walking down the hall of an apartment building and by the time you reach the end of it be sweating and breathing rapidly, only because of the background noises you can hear and the lightning. Even though nothing will have happened and nothing jumped you or attacked you. You still feel like it was a mission getting through that hallway. Thinking what is it that can make those noises? Why did the wood creak the way it did just now behind me? Did I just hear a door open?

The level design is stunning so far, everything seems to be placed appropriately to enhance the experience.
The music score is incredible and perfectly fits the setting and the calling of the travellers.

Don't forget to take your time and read every note you collect, they tell the story of what happened and really gets you thinking.

All in all, amazing game, 10/10. Bravo!

review_text:
Probably I’m writing this too late for most of you… the game has been out awhile.  I got this on Humble some time ago, and it sat there gathering dust until one day I decided to play JC3.  But I pressed the wrong install button and ended up playing JC4.  I am a JC newb.  I played JC2 once many years ago, but I won’t be comparing this game to previous entries in the series.

This game is super fun.  It’s an action movie in video game format.  The hero you play is named Rico because of course it is.  He has a perpetual 5 o’clock shadow, and confronts enemies with his signature leather jacket (sleeves rolled up… naturally...  Rico is a man who gets to work) and worn-in jeans.  He has holsters crisscrossing his torso.  He speaks in English but with a manly Spanish accent (which probably should have been Austrian in keeping with the action hero genre).   And with his wingsuit, grappling hook, and parachute, he can do all sorts of moves not permitted by physics.  He’s basically spider-man.  That’s one of his super-powers.  The other is that he is practically immune to bullets.

There’s plenty of gunplay to be had, and all that is really fun, but the game is really about movement.  Nothing beats using his grappling hook shoot him over the heads of his enemies while they voice their amazement.  It took me a little bit to get used to the movement mechanics.  Early on, the game introduces timed missions.  These were frustrating; it took me about 15 tries to complete the first one.  But once I had the hang of it, the timed missions were no big deal.  I do admit to nearly rage quitting on the second timed mission.

The game gives you about 10 mission types (+3 more with the DLC) on repeat.  There’s two variations of timed missions, defend the base, snipe the bad guys, find the right vehicle to gain entry into the stronghold, turn off the switches, destroy the McGuffin, etc..  Then there are a bunch of little missions like wingsuit through the rings within a time limit, drive really fast through a checkpoint, crash a car – those latter ones can be completely ignored without impacting the game in any meaningful way (which I did).  The DLC missions, particularly the one about the bugs, offer more challenge, but in a good way.  Once of the DLC is a racing mini-game – but I got motion sick playing it, so that was that.

I had a great time playing the action hero.  I loved Rico’s almost irritated grunts when perforated by shrapnel.  Rico and his allies have an army, but he always goes it alone, flying into heavily defended locales, murdering his enemies, and securing his objective.  Then, moving on to the next one.  Despite the repetitiveness of the missions, I never got bored.  I loved improving my skills around Rico’s movement --  I got a Serotonin jolt every time I executed a particularly slick move.

Highly recommend this for people who like the 3rd-person action genre, particularly if you prefer games that prioritize senseless violence over story.

review_text:
TL;DR This honestly would have been a more enjoyable experience if it was a VN like Friendsim.

Act 2 plays and feels like a product of significantly lower quality than Act 1. 
In short, it hardly feels like a sequel at all, at least in regards to gameplay. Act 1 was a pleasant surprise following its tumultuous conception and development. Charming and well polished, it gave me high hopes for the next in the series. That was a long wait, and unfortunately I can't rightly say Act 2 lived up to my hopes.

As I understand it, the original team that worked on Act 1 was majorly laid off after Viz acquired Homestuck. I was hoping this wouldn't result in too much turbulence when it came to continuing the Hiveswap series, but going from the first act to this game gave me whiplash. 

This game is presented as the sequel to Hiveswap: Act 1, obviously, but it plays more like a sequel to Hiveswap: Friendsim (The 0.99$ VN's that were released episodically after Act 1, and before this game).

Instead of playing like a point and click adventure game, like the previous game, [b]this plays a lot more like a VN[/b]. 

You retain your inventory from the first game if you carry your save over, but for the VAST majority of the game you don't use anything and you spend most of your time going through dialogues with characters from Friendsim. Each screen from the first game had plenty of objects that you could interact with in different ways with your items and abilities; In this game, there are hardly any items in the background to find or do anything with, and it makes them feel much hollower. You only interact with characters for the most part, and most screens consist of walking back and forth between characters until you exhaust their dialogue and the game lets you proceed to the next screen. 

Some of the longer sections of the game are just long because you have to walk all the way from the front of the train to the back, and then to the front again. At one point you have to walk from the VERY FRONT all the way to the back, just to have your character say "Well I didn't need to do this" and have you walk all the way up to the front again. And strangely enough, the walking mechanics are... spotty? You have to mash click to keep moving, and sometimes you will just... stop. It's a weird thing to mention but... This is the "core gameplay". so it's worth mentioning.

There are two significant sections of the game that I would say actually constitute "puzzles"; The trial, and the finale in the front car. Keep in mind this game is [i]very[/i] short. I think your mileage will vary when it comes to these; Personally, I did not think either event was very good by adventure game standards.

[spoiler]The outcome of the trial is apparently decided by an unrelated dialogue from an unrelated character BEFORE you board the train; If you don't select a certain option, you will not be able to access the "Good" ending to the trial. I'm not a big fan of that. The trial itself isn't exactly going to be putting Phoenix Wright out of business anyway. As mentioned below, keeping track of your items and the timeline in the trial is inconsistent and un-intuitive.[/spoiler]

The game falls short of Act 1 in other departments as well:
There is a real inconsistency to the quality of the assets in the game. Some backgrounds can be very quality, but others will have very obvious artifacting, or just be way lower resolution. 
Example: Moving from the indigo car to the purple car. The indigo background is very nice and high quality, but the transition between the cars and the purple car are much lower resolution, and some places have very harsh artifacting present.
One of the worst and most obvious discrepancies in quality is in the final sequence; Using Byers in the final sequence releases him and he has a flying animation, but when he lands again his sprite reverts to an asset from the previous game... But it's not properly cut out. The sprite is surrounded by a spotty white pixel halo from it not being prepared properly for transparency. This is very confusing because it's very obvious, and I'm pretty sure nearly anyone could fix this problem in under an hour in photoshop.
These are just some specific examples, these kind of discrepancies are present mostly throughout the length of the game.

There's also small general inconsistencies in miscellaneous areas of the game;
- Some items you acquire (Namely for the trial) go into your inventory, but some don't for whatever reason. It can be hard to keep track of what you actually have, because you can't even check the trial timeline/suspects/etc. until actually starting the trial. Sometimes you can't even check the timeline while questioning a witness, which is very annoying.
- Your interactions are commonly inconsistent: Some doors you just walk through by clicking, some open a little Look/Exit menu and you have to click again. 
- Some characters will talk very slowly, which makes me want to click to fill out their text box so I can read it. But when you are in a dialogue with multiple characters, sometimes one can speak VERY QUICKLY, which will cause you to skip over their text if you're in a rythm. The VNs avoid this problem by letting you go back through dialogue... And again, this basically plays like a VN. 

These are clearly very small criticisms, but you have to remember that these are basically the mechanics of the whole game. It gets annoying over time. The VNs were 90 cents, and also focused on dialogue... And they don't suffer from the same QoL problems.
You feel the minor annoyances a lot more because there's just not a lot else going on.

This is a very nitpicky example to mention, but even the achievements are arguably lower quality. The first game has unique little icons for each achievement, but this game uses the same icon for all of them. It might not mean much but to me it does illustrate a difference in the level of care this time around. 

I hate to say it, but this episode makes it harder to recommend Act 1, which is already a pretty niche title. I hope that the next installment makes some improvements, or at least reclaims some of the good aspects of the first game.

PS. The achievement for continuing your save still hasn't unlocked for me, which is really annoying me.

Overall 4/10

Setting: 10/10
Story: 3/10
Gameplay: 5/10

TL:DR Game's art is great. Gameplay is basic. Story sets itself up to be really interesting and upsettingly explores basically none of it.


The game is advertised as a mix or homage to a few classic survival horror games, but doesn't really deliver on any of the things that made those games exceptional. The survival part of the game is weakly fleshed out, being of a very basic "craft this thing when you need it and be economical" skein. There's some light RPG upgrade systems that are *very very basic* to the point of it just being raw numbers. It does make the difference when it comes to playing the game, but is so boring/uninteresting I felt cheated given the games they reference.

The gameplay is very weak though. It's THE MOST basic kind of survival horror that is more reminiscent of PS2 games than any kind of modern riff on them. Headshot the enemy or shoot the glowy spot, dodge enemy attacks by literally walking out of the way. You can inflate your gameplay to 20+ hours if you want by melee juking things to death if you really want. Not a fan of the basic nature of this, especially when other titles have already set a better standard. Then there's the fire/merge mechanic, severely limited in it's execution that it's seemingly pointless except on boss fights, and even then it's...the same as everything else.

The Setting is absolutely great though, a lot of mystery and questions, a lot of beautiful settings, a lot of visual horror - a visually great and interesting world...

...which is a shame because the story is so BASIC it's insulting. They hint at things bigger than we are, and then proceeds to NEVER explore them and instead focuses the story around a completely uninteresting *nothing* that doesn't even make sense in terms of the story they DO tell us.

Skip, wait for sale, your choice.

review_text:
A metroidvania that feels like it was made by a small team which has some truly awful combat.  You can equip one special item and two weapons, but early enemies are either slow and plodding or have ranged attacks that they let off in quick succession.  Many fights were 'hold shield to block projectile, move up, block projectile, move up, block projectile, strike, wait, block projectile, wait, block projectile, strike...'

Arial combat causes you to stop moving and drop as you swing.  You can equip a special item to slightly help, but this is in place of better options like a damage booster.  Other items are misleading, such as a 'slingshot' not being a weapon but instead an item that improves the damage of a limited number of consumable thrown grenades.  Magic is already powerful and if you have MP you can waste difficult enemies. 

The thing that made me end up refunding the game so early on is the save system.  You can save at a small number of computer stations and you automatically save when you encounter a statue.  But you can't autosave at the same statue until you've saved at another one.  This feels like an attempt to make a slower, more deliberate form of gameplay but it feels overly restrictive along with the other issues.  It seems average at best and even watching a few videos showing where the story will go did not make me want to continue.  The cadence of combat just isn't worth the frustration to me, but I'm dead certain that it will 'click' for the right people and be an enjoyable (but too short) experience.

review_text:
I have been a long time fan of the Just Cause games and thought the series peaked with Just Cause 3. The wing suit absolutely changed the game, adding a well needed way to traverse the map. Just cause 4 does add some new mechanics, but things feel less polished and complete with the fourth entry. I normally don't leave negative reviews unless I have enough problems with the game that it feels justified to actually say that it wasn't worth it in the end.

The overall performance feels like it isn't polished enough even after all this time, cut scenes stutter and graphics struggle to load in, the gameplay at times feels sluggish and controls hesitate, especially the grappling hook in times of need. vehicle controls were always bad, a signature of the just cause series, but when you are required to get vehicles through floating rings in annoying places, even using the grappling hooks many tools and abilities can only get you so far. some of them were a struggle not just because of the controls or challenge of ring location, but because things just don't feel like they work well enough. 

I never found myself caring about the characters or story, which to be fair doesn't need to be outstanding, because the gameplay has always been what shines. Though I found times where I really enjoyed flying around the map and tormenting citizens and militants alike with all my grapple tools, overall, the monotonous challenges and missions became pretty excessive near the end. when your mission design basically consists of: Go activate a few consoles... Go hack a few terminals...Go flip a few breakers... among other similar tasks across the entire game.

In the end, I spent more time fighting with the slow and imprecise controls, relentlessly annoying military forces (Prototype vibes sometimes) and wishing that the slapstick fun and laughter I had at times would be less few and far between. This game wasn't as fun as Just cause 3, it dumbed down missions and challenges too much, and felt like a sad experience considering what preceded it. 

It is a pretty map though...

review_text:
I've got more time in on PS4 but I wanted to quickly get this review up.

If you've played the previous entires then you know what you're in for here. This is a less than perfect MX simulator and it's far from a triple A game. However, having said that, this is the best entry into the series so far. There have been a lot of improvements over MXGP 3 and ME SX. The game has been copping some flak for the punishing ways in which your rider loses control of the bike, the tail sliding out excessively & frequently and the same old (well, worse) scrubs. Yes, those are all issues, but come on, we know what we're gonna get with a Milestone game. 
It's gonna be many years before we can call this series a true motocross sim, but this is not a bad game by any means and I'm sure the more serious issues will be patched.

The rider physics have been drastically improved and are inching their way closer to being realistic. The bike physics look genuinely good now as well. The AI are more difficult now but they still take the same lines and are predictable in every race. There's more variety this time around though, you'll see riders going off track and miscalculating their scrubs more often. 

The game looks great, the rain looks great (gone is that green rain from GP3), lighting is beautiful and the bikes are more detailed than ever before. It also looks much more real than previous entries, gone is the cartoony feel. 
The tracks have been rendered & scaled properly, the jumps, bumps, berms all look and feel the way they do in real life, which is something we haven't seen yet.  Wet tracks feel more realistic and are easier to race on now. Still though, ruts have no real impact and some of the corners are hard to take without sliding out when really there should be ruts that have developed to help. 

As for sound, the bikes sound better but still not amazing. The atmosphere sounds are pretty awful, the crowd cheering samples sound like they're coming from inside a stadium and not outdoors, same with the PA sound effects. The crowd still only cheer when your rider scrubs, and nobody else's, which is ridiculous. Besides the sounds of the bike though, this is all pretty irrelevant. 

Other minor improvements have been added as well, such as riders becoming transparent when they are immediately behind you in third person view, instead of blocking your screen (but if they've become transparent in game and you go to free cam, they'll be transparent there too, come on Milestone..). 

If you're a fan of the series or MX in general, picking this up should be a no brainer, just don't expect a perfect, polished game. 
7/10 for what it is.

I had high hopes for this game given the rave reviews and made sure to play it through to completion to discover whatever twist I'd been told "transcends art." Instead, I got a hamfisted, entirely predictable story interrupted by some clicking. For a game that is touted as handling autism in an enlightening and sympathetic manner, it really feels as though the authors have no firsthand experience with the subject matter.

Pacing was poor, I found myself waiting rather than being actively engaged. The story itself wasn't fleshed out, and didn't really offer any opportunity to connect with the characters. The attempted humour was seemingly disconnected references tossed in willy-nilly. Adventure/puzzle are my absolute favourite games and this left me very disappointed. Progression was entirely linear and didn't leave any room for thought. I think my biggest peeve is the dialogue can't be hurried or skipped. You have to wait for an entire bout of uninteresting bickering between the two playable characters (of which there is plenty) before you can move on with the story.

On the plus side, the music and visuals were worthwhile.

A decent game for when you need to turn off your brain. Its excellent to quench bloodlust.

[b] Pros [/b] 
- Guns are responsive and feel different
- Kills are satisfying, feel nice and meaty when the head flies off the body.
- Enemy variants and ammo variants feel nice
Thats about where the pros end because as much as the game is [i] fun [/i] it has its  "quirks"

[b] Cons [/b]
- Although stealth is very much promoted in this game, its practically non-existent, the moment you shoot a non silenced weapon, the AI in range INSTANTLY lock onto your current position and gun you down (if youre in the open). This breaks the immersion and sandbox feel as youre practically forced into slotting silenced weapons if you want to have the stealth feel
- The ragdolls can break and uh... fling across the map straight into an enemies field of view which naturally breaks the game (only happens with explosive ammo in my experience)
- Some guns are just better than others, if your playstyle is upgrade oriented rather than "use what you like" then youre locked into a single sniper
- Assault rifles are hot garbage. Do not even think about it.
-Sniper? what sniper. Just use the silenced pistol and you can clear the whole game 10x faster! :D

TLDR:
Good bit of fun, a bit janky in some parts but the levels are BIG and OPEN, the kills are MEATY and GOOD so it gets a pass.

I'm always down for something indie, especially when it leans on the horror or the meta genre. 

[b]IMSCARED[/b], is exactly a combo of both, not only it tries to manipulate you, but also your computer. This oldschool-esque video game does well in evoking a sense of dread, paranoia, and a sad haunting atmosphere. In my opinion, pixelated horror games are often the scariest to me than those with realistic graphics, so this hits the spot. It's scary that I got a lot of chills, even if I'm replaying for achievements, it still does not fail to startle and unsettle me. Really cool stuff.

This is, if not, one of the first ever video games involving fourth wall breaking, and for such a short game, it's pretty underrated, yet good! Really showing how simple graphics are enough to immerse in a setting. 

Nonetheless, if you like games such as OneShot, Undertale, and or The Witch's House because of the unbelievable lot of jumpscares it has prepared, then you should definitely give this a chance. But I must warn you to be careful, [b]because it's waiting for you to play, one more time.[/b]

review_text:
It pains me to mark this as not recommended, but I am just not feeling it.

The game is visually stunning and I can't name many other games that surpass it in terms of art style. Sadly that's where most of the praises end. Sure it has a fittingly oppressive atmosphere and it provides a niche horror experience, but they really aren't well experienced with gameplay design.

Where the game excels artistically, it falls short with giving the player a fun time alongside it. The combat is geniunely some of the worst I've seen. It's incredibly clunky, sluggish and not rewarding in the slightest. Enemies are more of a chore and annoyance, meant to frustrate the player, than they are a fun and integral part of the game. Honestly, you could've taken them out completely and probably be left with a better, more engaging experience overall. It also doesn't help that you can't tell the recharge on your basic weapon due to the color choice and that same recharge is incredibly slow as is everything else in this game. Not to mention the abhorrent range on that thing. I missed more stuff at near point blank and ended up getting hit back as a result because it's so absurdly short. It also doesn't help that there's little clutter everywhere on the ground that you can easily get stuck on resulting in getting hit more. It only leads to a more frustrating experience. 
And that's not where the shortcomings of the combat end. Switching weapons is also very slow and you can't dodge anything while doing it, so good luck switching to another weapon after running out of ammo mid fight. Also the reloads are slow as hell as is everything else and it's even worse since you can't reload cancel. Once you start reloading, you better believe you're putting every bullet you have into the mag even though you only needed one to finish off the enemy. It also doesn't help that enemies are inconsistent with their health. Sometimes they take 2 shots, sometimes 4. I know it's probably due to the crit spots, but I swear, sometimes I shoot them in the exact same places and they either survive or they just die. This only leads to more unpredictability which can be a detriment to the player and cause more health loss. It really doesn't help that the game is pretty stingy with giving the player healing and that the checkpoints are spaced apart quite a bit.

Apart from that it's also easy to get lost in some of these places. They tend to be quite large, although linear, but most of the areas look the same. Since the game requires quite a bit of backtracking at certain points, you'll be finding yourself blindly searching for where you're supposed to be going. The game doesn't tell the player anything at all. It won't hold your hand and that is completely fine. Sometimes it will leave a better impression if it allows player agency even if it is a linear game, however, it would help if some of the areas weren't so similar looking and maze-like.

The game is also kind of buggy. Sometimes the bullets phase through the enemies, leaving them unaffected. I'm pretty sure the enemies don't have some kind of i-frames, but I could be wrong. Either way it's really annoying missing a shot that clearly hit and then losing precious health because of it. Apart from that, I got stuck in place twice after certain cutscenes for seemingly no reason, resulting in me needing to restart to the latest checkpoint and one time the game didn't allow me to interact with anything even though it was giving me the prompts, leading to another soft lock and reset. It really took away from the overall experience, especially since these bugs were really only a waste of time.

(minor spoilers for the ending) The game is very ambiguous with its story. It doesn't tell you much and only poses more questions than it answers, but it definitely ends with a very negative ending that could be unsatisfying for some, especially because of what you have to go through only to end the game with it. I could bet everyone (myself included) were expecting something very grandiose, but were left disappointed with such a cruel outcome.

Overall, the game has tons of potential, but is too clunky and unsatisfying to play as is. I really do care about it, hence why I'm writing this much. I hope that the developers improve upon the annoyances of this game in their possible future titles and combine such an astounding visual style with good gameplay to form an extremely palatable horror experience.

review_text:
There were only a couple of things I liked about this game. The first was that I didn't have any technial issues with the game itself, no crashes and no dropped frames that I noticed, it ran smoothly, nothing to complain about there. The other was that most of the story was decent. 

As for the gameplay, overall, I did not find it enjoyable and close to zero replayability. Even though I purchased this during the summer sale, it was not worth the 5 and I am very unlikely to play anything else in this series. 

As in most action games, this game is centered around combat with some puzzles.  

The combat started to wear after only a few fights and this feeling only got reinforced the longer I played.  I believe the combat system is called "free flow", which appears to be a fancy way of saying  button masher with a timing element. To be fair, the variety of tools and moves available added some complexity.  While the combat may be superficially attractive it has very little real depth and is more cinematic than anything else.   Even perfect fights were oddly unsatisfying and often felt wrong on some level due to the somewhat clunky timing and occaisionally odd attack sequencing.  I can honestly say that I diskliked every character, sometimes for different reasons by the time I finished the game. 

The puzzles were ok at first, but after solving a few they did little other than stretch the game out and by the time I completed the main storyline finishing anything I missed was just a form of self flagellation.

review_text:
Luck-based scarcity of healing elixirs and a few terrible enemy designs essentially means that every run is a coin toss of how much fun you'll have. maybe you'll get fun enemies, well-placed traps, the like. or maybe you get bullet-sponge gravediggers swarming you, or a warden blocking you from moving somewhere.

I've always believed that using bullet sponges as a balancing measure isn't great. The calamity system is interesting, but red orb hitreg, lag, and a general sense of "a few mild mistakes have now led to my being screwed over in the middle of a fight with a near-invincible sepulcher" kinda ruins it for me.

Also, now i got to deal with gatekeepers. just why? invisible cretins that completely disrupt the otherwise clean and entertaining flow of the game, forcing you to go on a scavenger hunt so that you can pass through an area.

There's the "toxic gas cloud" thingamjig too. Barely get close to it ( "it" being released every two seconds), and you lose a third of your health. I believe there's a rosary bead that can cancel it, but it's so impossibly far down the progression path that you're still kinda screwed by it.

I know this game is still in early access. but it isn't really the lag spikes or occasional glitch that prompted me to leave a negative review. It's intentional designs that really shouldn't make it into the final release without some tweaking. This game is kinda going the "forever winter" route in that regard, but who knows, maybe they'll see this.

review_text:
I've played enough hours now I feel I can give an informed review.

Good:

- The art style and game mechanics are fun and engaging, and hit the right spot of nostalgia for NHL '94 fans

- The gameplay is fast paced and rewards good puck control

- Passing and shooting feel solid

- It is the best PC hockey game in recent memory

Bad:

- Your players lose control of the puck way too easily. Expert mode is ridiculous to the point of being unfun.

- The AI routinely scores goals from distance on shots that land less than 1/50 times for a human player, and that is not an exaggeration. Be prepared to lose your entire run because of the terrible AI of your goalie, repeatedly.

- Playing defense feels too much like a roll of the dice because the game is terrible at figuring out which player you are trying to switch to on defense. You will often lose the game (and consequently your entire run) solely because of it. 

Suggestions to devs:

- Audience animations would add a lot of color to the mix 

- When you go to start a new game you only have the option to choose from one of three randomly selected star teammates. This only leads to me restarting if I don't get to select the one I just bought or actually want to use. I'm not sure what the point is of limiting the options.

- The main changes in Expert mode seem to be a) making it incredibly easy to lose control of the puck if an opponent gets even remotely close to you and b) severely nerfing your goalie, who will suddenly let in a lot of terrible shots from outside. There is not much the player can do to shore up these disadvantages, which makes the increase in difficulty feel cheap.

Overall, worth the price of admission even though it needs some tweaks and worth rewarding the devs for having the cojones to put out a good hockey game on PC. However the game's terrible goalie AI and inability to effectively switch which player you are controlling often results in a very frustrating experience, and none of the updates have addressed these issues.

The reloading on the other hand made me die very often; you should definitely be able to cancel such a long  animation.

I am one of the ones that was very satisfied with the ending as it fits the theme extremely well and has many over/under tones.  I would've loved for this to be longer to maybe experience two more generations but maybe for other games.

review_text:
Let me say that while I don't feel as if I'd recommend this game, I'm not claiming it was a wholly unenjoyable experience. It just might not be what a lot of people are looking for, and the number of positive reviews are a bit misleading.

Positive:
-Some well-crafted storytelling, I'll admit.
-Good worldbuilding, some clever ideas.
-Positive representation of autistic characters, not a lot of misinformation that stood out to me that might have ruined that.

Negative:
-Short.
-While the story is inventive, it is also linear, and I hesitate to call To the Moon an "interactive storybook" at all, but that's the best description I can think of because it kind of falls short of being a game.
-Moving around is a chore. The characters are often slow, and you inexplicably bump into things on the map sometimes that are arbitrarily solid. (You can walk through cars, but not over flowers? Really?)
-Puzzles are simple and boring. Does not feel like much at stake. They don't really add much to the story by being there other than giving the player something active to do.
-Gameplay mostly consists of walking around and clicking things until you click on something "important." Click on enough important things and you can unlock the simple tile puzzle and move on to the next memory. There's nothing really fun about it.
-On that note it would have made sense for the game to be more passive. The components that were there seemingly just to make it "like a game" felt out of place.
-IF YOU USE THE INTENDED CONTROLS (the mouse) YOU'RE GONNA HAVE A BAD TIME. You click somewhere for the characters to go somewhere, but they often don't quite reach entirely, maybe because of an obstacle, and so it feels like the characters are never going where you want them to go. Getting to objects is exhausting. When I discovered you could use the traditional arrow keys to move and the space to interact it was a life saver.
-Too much dialogue, I hate to say. Wayyy too much bickering between the protagonists bogs down the whole game. Way too much melodramatic prosey monologuing at times, too, taking away from the impact of actually beautiful and important dialogue. Just too much. It's clumsy. You spend much of the game inundated in wooords.
-What's worse is the characterization is weak at best. Most of the characters don't have much in the way of personality, which you kind of expect from this kind of game especially if it's supposed to be carried by character interactions.
-A lot of it... was not funny. When it was trying to be funny. A lot of inward groans to be had at the unnecessary snark. (There were funny parts to be had, definitely. Most of the annoying stuff was in the dialogue between Watts and Rosalene, who as I already said, spend way too much time bickering.)
-This is a bit of a personal nitpick, but I wish, if they were going to make a game about asperger's, that they might just name it outright. I don't understand why everyone was so cagey and vague about River's "condition," it struck me as unnecessary.

Verdict: If you are going to get it, get it on sale. Then stick it out past Act 2, because that's where the story starts picking up and you don't have to put up with the puzzles and junk. Don't approach it expecting much in the way of a game, or much in the way of replay value. It's a decent story, not decent enough for me to wholly recommend the experience, but not bad enough for me to say there was nothing worthwhile about it, either.

review_text:
I want to preface this review by saying that I was familiar with the Shinsengumi and their role as cultural icons in Japanese media and extended culture as a whole, even before playing this game. Perhaps no other Japanese political group has been romanticized as much as they have, it is quite fascinating to me. The end of the Bakumatsu period signaled a big shift for Japan, after all. This game is a testament to all those ideas, attributes, and even exaggerations bestowed upon the group and their history together. Of course, you don't have to know about the Shinsengumi beforehand to enjoy this game. It does a good job at explaining the era's political climate, and the glossary feature is helpful if you want to learn more as well.

You should know that there is a fantasy element to the game too. It personally is what kept me so interested and wanting to come back for more each time, along with the political themes in some of the routes. It is also what sets it apart from other retellings of the history of the Shinsengumi. Each route has differences that make you want to keep playing through them and seeing how the story develops. I will say though, some are better written than others. I do not know if it is something to do with the localization, but the dialogue in certain routes did make me roll my eyes on a few ocassions. Still, each route has something that everyone can enjoy. 
Also, as other people have mentioned this particular Hakuoki game isn't as heavy on the romance as the next one (Edo Blossoms). There is ocassional romantic dialogue, but it is not the main focus.

All in all, there is a reason for why Hakuoki is one of the most popular otome franchises of them all. Kyoto Winds has a beautiful, emotional soundtrack, pretty illustrations, stellar voice acting, and a engaging rethreading of the narrative surrounding the Shinsengumi.

review_text:
Why do I have a faint feeling this was supposed to be Just Cause Mobile?

As a big fan of the series, with 100% achievements runs on JC2 and JC3,

The core gameplay simply isn't good. • Welcome to Panel Hacking©, Button Pressing™, Hold ya'& Position simulator, instead of the juicy firing at anything colored red like in Just Cause 3.

There's a serious lack of balancing on enemy quantity, how many resources you have for destruction, and damage dealt. The game is _maybe_ fun with infinite ammo mods and boosting hook range a bit, yet some objectives are still too hard. Absolutely go for quality of life mods like these if playing.

The frontline, manage your army mechanic simply doesn't matter for the average gameplay. If only enemy forces *obliterated* you inside their territory, and expanding ally forces yourself, truly managing attacks, securing weapons, vehicles and people were the core loop, then it might've been fun.

That being said, the game is more than a 5/10 to me, as it's at least consistent and kinda polished, but I don't recommend investing the time. I hate to take this position, it sinks further down a chance for a JC5 - if that is ever going to happen after the franchise situation in the past Years.

As a completionist, the challenges are often dull or with the most annoying restriction of performing a jump with 'this' specific vehicle. JC2 is the most repetitive in the series, but JC4 is the most boring and feels like a chore. I may or may not complete the achievements after finishing the story, or reset them to not hurt average game completion in the future.

The in-game graphics are decent, but with hard flickering issues on hair and kinda uncanny models. That can't be said for the cutscenes, they are abysmal. Seriously, aliasing issues (pre-rendered, SSAA it c'mon), too dark, too much compression artifacts. They should've been all in-game rendered, much less disk space and more quality on what's already bad. Some destruction models or cutscenes feels too basic, that's the source of that faint Mobile feeling I talked about.

As a standalone game, without looking at the great feats of JC3, it's an overall positive game, definitely better than JC1 and on par/slightly worse than JC2 fun-wise.

It's the first and only downstep of quality in the series, which questions the franchise for the future. It's worth it on a sale, and supporting the franchise *might* make a difference in the years to come.

(Funny things aside, we got another Tom Sheldon model remake 😂)

review_text:
Where Winds Meet is a beautifully crafted wuxia open-world RPG that mixes cinematic martial arts, exploration, and absolute chaos in the best way possible.

My first half hour vanished inside character customization, and the second half hour disappeared while I tried naming my hero. I tested more than fifty names, every single one was taken, and in the end I had to add a prefix just to start my journey. For my second hour, I spent most of it dying repeatedly to the Puppeteer’s spear. And somehow, the next five hours slipped away as I wandered through the beautiful wuxia world, completely absorbed by its landscapes and atmosphere.
The game is fully free-to-play and monetized only through cosmetics and battle passes—no pay-to-win, no predatory gacha. Performance can vary, and the menu system is so complicated it feels like the real final boss, but once you understand it, everything flows.

Combat is “Souls-light,” rewarding good timing without punishing you too hard. The world is packed with bosses, puzzles, treasures, side quests, and a surprisingly deep social system—raids, PvP, sects and more (I have to explore that). You also get odd but heroic jobs, like removing someone’s itchy back, immobilizing a molester, or healing ducks… though never fight the ducks. They are secretly boss-level enemies. And Elder Gongsun—please, Let me hit You. And there is some Shaming Prisoner Activity with Special Time Limit.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a stylish, chaotic, and surprisingly heartwarming wuxia adventure. Between the stunning open world, flexible playstyles, cinematic combat, and the absurd stories it creates, it’s easily one of the most memorable free RPG experiences available.

review_text:
[h2]SUMMARY[/h2]

Think Inception but with less gunfights and more melodrama.

Although To the Moon is laudable for its high concept and its willingness to explore themes of living with autism, its execution is weak due to general issues with storytelling pacing, writing, and gameplay.

[h2]STORYTELLING[/h2] 

The most glaring issue with the storytelling is the entire first act, which centers around the two point of view doctor characters stepping backwards through the memories of their patient. Unfortunately, during this portion of the game the doctors have very little active agency beyond serving as veritable exposition sponges. And at two hours (out of a total game runtime of three to four) the first act and its incremental episodes start to feel interminable. While some interesting ideas are explored during this portion (how to cope with an autistic partner), it is boring, and there is not sufficient payoff for everything introduced here.

That does not even touch upon the gameplay, which feels like barely justified busywork and makes the early pacing issues even worse.

The second and third acts work better as they are shorter and give the two player characters more to do in the story.

[h2]WRITING[/h2]

Dialog and writing are stilted and weak, and characters either are extremely bland or unbearably obnoxious. For instance, Kan Gao attempts to characterize female doctor as an acerbic hard-ass to contrast to male doctor's loveable goofball. The goal was clearly for the two doctors to have a buddy cop dynamic - catty but familiar. However, because neither female doctor or male doctor have any charisma, this falls flat, and both characters just read as insufferably lame.

[h2]TECHNICAL[/h2]

The use of the RPG Maker as a game engine does To the Moon no favors. The grid based movement is slow and stilted and results in some very odd collision detection with random scenery. Although graphically To the Moon is a very handsome game by RPG Maker standards, indie gaming culture has changed so much in the past decade that To the Moon's visual stylings feel quaint at best.

On the upside, music is pleasant and effectively used in game.

[h2]CONCLUSION[/h2]

To the Moon was widely decorated in its original release, but all of the problems the game has with story, writing, and gameplay suggest that it is a product of its time: fast forward almost a decade, and games that focus exclusively on story are no longer novel.

review_text:
I could have written this review ages ago if I still had access to my old Steam account. But better late than never.

As it is, I just played To The Moon for the second time since I was 13. I am now in my mid-twenties, and I could not be more surprised how charmed I am even today. It is a touching science-fiction drama about true love, loss, family, following your heart, and fulfilling someone's seemingly impossible dying wish. It also breaches into a few other sensitive topics, which I do not want to spoil here. Still, it is beautifully depicted with some unexpected humor that may or may not strike a nerve amid deep and introspective storytelling. The music is quite serene and enjoyable from a little indie studio like Freebird, as well.

For a 2011 work in 2025, this game is outdated, indeed. The controls are clunky, the graphics could be a bit clearer - yes, even for a pixel game - and the dialogue between Doctors Rosalene and Watts leaves something to be desired. But it is no less worth the $10 price tag. The writers put a lot of heart and soul into it, which radiates warmth you can feel. The first time I played this, it had me in shambles, and I have [b]never[/b] forgotten about it all these years. What I did forget, however, is the ending and how it will leave you questioning your own deepest desires and life choices. [i]What would you wish for, if you were on your deathbed and allowed the opportunity to live your life all over again?[/i]

Overall, it is an unexpectedly striking and creative game at its core that will undoubtedly leave you an emotional wreck if you can look past the negatives I have mentioned. I absolutely recommend To The Moon to anyone looking for an affordable indie game that explores a consistent theme of tragedy. This one will mark and encourage you to return to it again someday.

review_text:
The core combat in this game feels great: The movement and shooting feels smooth, and the looting is rewarding.
However, I have some grips with the gameplay of this game:

• The UI is cumbersome and sometimes annoying. Why can't I change characters while in the hub town? Why is the item inventory not just another tab in the menu? Why can't I claim all feats (achievements) at once? etc.

• The exploration in this game is honestly not fun. Some chests are locked behind some characters' abilities (why am I forced to pick Ace?), and having to stop the stage's mission to search for resource nodes or chests feels counter-intuitive and, unfortunately, annoying. Some chests are too well-hidden for a looter shooter, especially for their feeble rewards.

• The games forces you to use different characters too much. In addition to exploration, I'm being forced to constantly change characters for story quests, side-quests, feats. I honestly hate this. Let me use the characters that I want, give me more liberty.

• As you level up you unlock skill and stat points to spend. In my opinion, stat increases are too meager and the skill tree feels a little unimpactful. This is a trend with games like Borderlands I feel we could've escaped, but alas it stays with Relic Hunters.

Overall, I expected this game to be one I could binge and spend hours in, but these cons unfortunately bothered me more than I hoped. You can tell some features were added on top of the base game to increase its longevity (which is a great thing!), but the execution damaged the cohesion and flow of the game in general.

review_text:
This is a very entertaining game (or, rather, series of games)! It's appropriately challenging - I had to use a few hints - but overall, the gameplay is unlikely (not impossible, but unlikely) to frustrate you unless you're bad at puzzles. I really like puzzles, though, so maybe take that last part with a grain of salt.

I don't mind having to wait for keys, though I do find it a bit annoying that it caps off at just two. My biggest gripe with the game is that there's no chapter select: when going back to collect missed stars, I sometimes skip over them and I have to start the story over from the beginning AGAIN [i]just[/i] to go back to that part. It'd be nice if there was an option to go back to specific chapters once you've finished a story.

I'd say the Covenant purchase is worth it - for ~$7, it's a pretty quality game. It's a couple dollars more than buying 10 keys (for reference, each story requires 8 keys, one per chapter), but considering it's a whole new story AND skips/hints are completely free, I think the higher price is reasonable.

If you're looking for a nice point & click, I'd recommend this game! It's not for everyone, but I like it :)

review_text:
I remember the first time I played this: T'was the end of summer vacation and I was entering 7th grade in 2007. If there was one upside to having a birthday in September is that while school would always drool, the birthday presents would always rule. And in that most perilous gaming year of 07, that was the time I began to realize how my taste in games was truly being forged before my eyes. Playing games The Darkness, Gears of War, Call of Duty 2, Condemned and oh so much more were help defining what I love in video games and the next step in my journey was the tale of a destroyed Utopia in Irrational Games' seminal classic shooter Bioshock,

Even to this day, this thing still holds up really well: The chaotic combat that makes you act quick on your toes, the stellar sound design that heights the atmosphere to intoxicating levels, the dense level design that makes you look around every corner, the marvelous art direction that still holds your attention even if visually ir shows its age. But the thing that is the really big selling point here is it's story, a tale of madness, murder, obsession, cruelty, humanity, greed, deceit but maybe even hope...if you play your cards correctly. review_text:
When PSO2 first came to the west it was something special, something new, people had been waiting on the game to come to the west for 8 years and the wait was worth it. The game had come out with Episodes 1-3 with Episodes 4-6 being released later. The game even whilst being released in a technically incomplete state in the west was still filled with hundred of hours worth of content with the quality of said content ranging from standard MMO to just straight up mind boggling and there was always something to work towards. PSO2 wasn't perfect by any means, but is wasnt bad either and had  extremely strong foundations and additions that would make it very easy for SEGA to keep adding or improving upon for whatever would come next for Phantasy Star as a series or so you would think.

PSO2 NGS would get announced. SEGA showcases a complete refresh/new game using a whole new game engine, revamped Character customization, and the game is no longer separated by multiples maps with instances within them, NGS instead has and open world. NGS releases and its just okay, the first couple hours felt amazing, but the more you played the more empty the game felt and it just didn't feel as good as PSO2, sure the combat was more fluid, but its felt like it was missing something. it is now 2025 and while the game hasn't been abandoned i might as well be. Content roll out for NGS was always slow and too be honest i don't see a problem with it being slow, it's the contents of the updates that have absolutely killed this game for me and many others. For some reason SEGA has decided to take a page out of bungie's book and they consistently choose to release mediocre content updates and under deliver constantly. The game will not have a meaningful update for MONTHS and then when they do update it, they either release a small mediocre content drop that only lasts hours, give us another recycled seasonal event for the trillionth time or release another pay-to-win/ cosmetic gacha. The game as it is is a shadow of its former self and now shares more in common with Barbie Fashion Designer than the game it used to be. 

Until SEGA decides to open their eyes and actually take the development of this game seriously then i can't see myself recommending this game to ANYONE long-term or short-term unless they like throwing them selves into the empty hobby of whaling out on every gacha for "fun".

review_text:
Firm suggestion: REMAP YOUR KEYS. The default control scheme is... odd, to say the least. Somebody here on Steam helpfully wrote a guide for a more comfortable control scheme that you can utilize, or at least springboard off of, for your own comfort, so why not use it?

If you're bad at stealth games, like I am, then this is a game you want to play in small doses - maps are large and take time to complete, and even the easier missions can range into an hour or longer depending on how badly you do (in my case, it routinely takes me an hour or longer, because as I said, I'm bad at stealth games). This is also not a game where you can simply charge through and kill everything in sight - your characters are squishy, and even the strongest among you will quickly be torn apart; you will routinely be outnumbered, and if an alarm gets raised, reinforcements get called in to make things even worse; and you have to toggle your combat abilities every single time you want to attack anything, which takes precious seconds that will cost you your life.

However, the game has proven to be very engaging otherwise, and the diversity of each character's moveset strongly urges you to strategize on the fly, aided as well by the Shadow system which allows you to coordinate multiple characters' actions simultaneously. The game urges liberal use of quicksaves, and in fact has a built in function to remind you when you haven't quicksaved in a while. You can load quicksaves at the push of a button, even in the middle of being spotted by patrols, so don't worry about it if you get caught and start dying, just hit your quickload button and it magically never happened!

Mind the voice acting - it's British actors trying to affect Japanese accents. It, uh, it can be a bit touch-and-go in places.

Played this on hard difficulty and I loved it.

What makes this game stand out from the other metrovania-likes is the difficulty. Enemies hit hard but so do you. Your health don't get replenished at save points and it makes all your healing items so much more valuable. No more item hoarding problem! 

However, higher difficulty doesn't mean less fun! First of all, it really makes you think beforehand about your strategy of approaching a fight and use all the items, abilities, and environmental effect at your disposal. You also get insanely powerful items with unique effects to fight your way through and the game really encourages you to try out different combos. Being able to figure out your own strategy to survive is super satisfying.

Plus the character splash art looks super cute! The pixel sprites are also very well animated. And you get to fight all the waifu bosses (especially if you are a fellow gent who likes monster girls). All in all, highly recommend.

The game also has great replayability by offering special modes after you beating the game. These new modes completely changes how you approach fights and also adds new plots so it's very much worth the time.

KCD2 is the best game in 2025. 10/10 hope it wins GOTY

review_text: The concept of a young devilish child reaving havoc was one that definately piqued my interest, however, sadly dissapointed with the gameplay. One of the many problems I found with this game that I don't usually have with many others is that I have to constantly refer to other sources for help. You will find yourself looking for quest items that are often way too subtley hidden in a mansion where you will pace back and forth, room to room just looking for something to get by. The problem lies in the lack of the games ability to aid the player without necessarily giving anything away (Note: You are given a tool to find items but even this is given 6 limits and can only be used in a room so it is nontheless wasteful unless you know the item could be in a specific room). Even better yet this could be solved with a non-linear format, one which provides players the ability to use multiple killing methods. This would increase replayibility and ease the painfully dullness of searching items. Some of the game mechanics lacked sense, for instance why give certain abilities only to be limited. The game sacrifices player free reign with a linear story line which isn't that great to begin with. You'd think that with multiple deaths in one home would peak the interest of the media (besides the one journalist) and feds or perhaps even motivate the family or employees to move out, but the characters all lacked sense regardless of how "strange" or accidental the deaths are. It's no surprise that the sequel, (yes there's a sequel) didn't do well. Once the intial pique of the concept passes, theres hardly anything else that holds you there. The game needs to be rebooted, everything but the concept out the window.

review_text:
I'm hardly one for reviews, but I saw a lot of things that justify going this extra mile. The devs have been very upfront and clear about what they want with this game, and this deserves extra love.
Witchfire has a slow start, in my opinion. I know people have feelings about that, but this review is among other things to clear this out: this is a very good FPS/extraction game, but definitely much of it's goodies require some hours of investment. Right now, I don't know how they could make this work in any other way, given the game they want to build. Make first map extremely easy? Honestly, I think that would be deceiving. The first map (as of the writing of this review) is very fair to show what you should set yourself for the rest of the time. It's not a relax experience, that doesn't mean hard, but also doesn't mean you can doze off while playing.
The shooting itself is very satisfying and precise, the different weapons definitely cover a lot of ground in different play styles, and the magic, although still underwhelming for me, presents some options for interesting gameplay. That is to say, the devs are clearly very opinionated on what makes a good shooter, and good mechanics that complement and make this properly challenging.
Devs also have my regards for clearly stating they don't want to lower the game difficulty, admitting this will close doors for some players, but knowing the product they want to launch. This doesn't make the game niche in any way, but clearly a lot of people will prefer a simpler experience.
They also show a lot of concern for eventually doing proper elaboration on the story. Not gonna lie, I'm a bit too tired of the next new worldbuilding/lore dump, so it's definitely not a problem for me. Still, it shows again that they know where they want to go with this game. Buuuut, if this is a concern for you, Witchfire has mostly implicit storytelling for the time, but the studio stated they have the intention of working on this in proper time.
I have mixed feelings for early access games, but I got too many green flags to ignore Witchfire. This is building to be a very fun game, and I trust the 1.0 will be worth every penny when it's launched.

Overall, this game in it's stock state is worse than the original game BONEWORKS.

Main cons:
- The jankiest climbing system I've ever used in a VR game
- A basically non-existent and at times infuriating story
- Slightly dumbed down graphics/level scale because of the quest port
- Modding SDK over-reliance (see below)
- Game always chooses physics "realism" over player experience, which leads to a lot of janky interactions that are "correct" but feel awful as a player

The big selling point of this game was the modding support, which is cool and all, but skimping on the content of the main game and getting players to make actually good content for your game is kinda cheap. Also, this is improving over time as far as I know, but the modding SDK is currently super limiting in scope of what's possible to be made.

review_text:
tl;dr Great metroidvania that even if it's somewhat short, has good survival mechanics that tests the player's creativity and skills.

Lost Ruins, even though it's a metroidvania, it's sold as a survival experience, and as such, it should be tackled with a bit of patience. I see some people complaining about how the combat is slow, heavy and clunky, but I personally like it because you can feel the weight of the weapon you're trying to use, and it was done purposely so you build your character around such "flaws", like equipping a accessory that increases the attack speed of heavy weapons, or cast speed and/or cost of spells, and the game gives the player freedom to do any kind of build, as long you have the equipment to make it work. Early on that might be a problem tho, since you have to either buy the equipment or find it around the map.

You can't grind out of any situation in the game or increases the stats of your character through items, like other games in the genre do, because it doesn't have a level up system, but the game has lots of checkpoints and save points, so it doesn't ending up being too frustrating and whatnot. I personally think there's way too many checkpoints in the game tho. 

I just think that the existence of shields somewhat broke the difficulty down a lot, which enables you to defend yourself virtually against anything, but it's not just aimlessly guarding, since you have to time the guard action correctly to defend (which has a pretty forgivable timing window), and elemental attacks usually pierce the shield (which you can mitigate or nullify completely with the right accessory), so it involves a bit of skill.

Visual wise, Lost Ruins is beautiful. Every area has its own design and particularities, and the use of simulated pixels it's a shown of its own. I like how there's no reuse of enemy design, and how each enemy race suits the area which you encounter them perfectly, without feeling like out of place. The boss design is superb. A bit fanservicey, but it's great. I really like it.

Replay wise, it offers quite a bit of content actually. The main campaign, which is divided into 4 difficulty modes, has two endings, and 3 extra modes are unlocked after finishing it for the first time, which may not contain anything new per se, it offers diversified gameplay and more challenges.

Anyway, I really recommend Lost Ruins to the fans of the metroidvania genre. It may be somewhat slower early on, but keep pushing. It's really fun. It really is what I've expected, and a bit more.

review_text:
This game is really frustrating to play and the controls are generally counter intuitive, which paired with a style of level design that demands so much of the player while offering virtually no freedom of how to tackle a situation, is a recipe for disaster in my opinion. Shadow Tactics is excellent as a concept, has a passable story and great art direction, but the execution is possibly the worst I have ever seen in a game that demands so much of the player. 

I keep coming back to this game hoping to feel different and it just makes me wish I refunded it while I had the chance. The quick save feature, while brilliant in theory, just leads you to resent the game's level design even more. It makes it immediately clear that this game was designed in mind that even a single step outside of what exact action (or combination of actions) the game expects you to perform is immediate mission failure and having to quick load and try again. 

Expecting a player to bash their head against a wall over and over and clearly designing the game around that process is just not fun design. Overcoming challenging obstacles is a rewarding experience, I don't think anyone would challenge that claim. There are hundreds of games that exemplify this well. But when you finally succeed in Shadow Tactics, you're not left with euphoric celebration. You're left with a feeling of "Thank god that is finally over" only to watch a short, barely animated dialogue sequence and to be thrust into an even more absurdly designed level.

I really wanted to like this game but it's just not for me, I gave it several attempts and I will probably give it a few more because I have never left a game unfinished before, but I just don't think it's going to happen. Time and money are both precious and for CDN$ 47.99, plus paid DLC, there are thousands of better games to spend your time and money on.

review_text:
I originally bought this game because I thought it would maybe be an average horror game, but honestly it's bad enough that at some point I was playing it just to have a laugh.  There's a lot of issues with the game. 

- Shimmying through narrow spaces, crawling through vents, or even unlocking doors using the panel are all pointless non-gameplay for what I can only assume is padding. Even more funny is they try to make the vent crawling seem scary with all the scary noises as you crawl, but you literally can't do anything while in the vents so there's nothing scary about it at all. You can't even aim your gun.

-A lot of times there's two paths to go, one progresses the story and the other has treasure. So which is which? I don't know, better hope you chose the treasure path the first time because if not you're locked out of it forever. But it's not like it matters because you can't carry the treasure because you only have 6 inventory slots, it's awful. 

- The pacing is bad. I'm fairly far into the game and have not come across a single boss or even setpiece really. it's all just "run through space corridor, kill some guys" repeat. Every part of the space station looks the same. It might be realistic, but it's not memorable and doesn't create engaging enough visuals. At one point you go into a waste management facility and other than Jacob wading through and getting caked in sh*t there's nothing distinct or interesting about this level. There's not even a great big mutated sh*t monster or something for you to fight. It's just pointless. I'm not even sure if I could explain where in the game I am right now. The chapter is called "Habitat" but it's just a dark metal space station like the rest of the game.

-Most importantly, the core combat sucks. It's all melee focused and it's just hit twice, dodge once or twice, then hit twice again until the creature is dead. Not only that but the fighting feels like a series of QTE animations instead of you feeling in control. There's a gun too but it's clunky, weak, and obviously not what's intended to be used most of the time. Most enemies act the same when meleeing them too which makes it really unfun and tedious. God help you if you have to fight multiple enemies at once. You can block as well as dodge, but the game doesn't explain why you would do one over the other. In fact they don't explain the dodge at all, you will pick up on it eventually (and trivialize every encounter after) but until then it fees like stumbling in the dark, which you already do enough of in this game.

- It's just not scary. Being able to melee enemies means it becomes not a test to conserve ammo, but trying to stay awake during the game's repetitive combat. Melee therefore puts the control back in the player's hands both in terms of not needing to watch your ammo, and also as someone who can easily stand up to the threats, which kind of kills the whole horror aspect. In most horror games if an enemy comes too close to you, you're probably either going to take a huge chunk of damage or just straight up die, but this game insists on you getting up close and personal, which just doesn't work to a horror game's favor. The checkpoint system and linearity help ensure even if you do mess up you can immediately retry anyways. The game tries it best despite this to scare you, often to mixed results at best, but it does so using really overdone horror game tropes and jumpscares. Oh look you just got the power cell you needed to power up the door on the other side of the room, I hope some monsters you've seen a million times don't pop out of vents on your trek back.

- The QTEs are ridiculous. There's way too many monsters that just grab you and force you to mash the button until the enemy is dead or gets off you. You can't even avoid it or get better at them. You just have to watch the animation and mash the button as your health drains, over and over. Every combat encounter in this game feels like a QTE now that I think about it, whether you're doing melee or mashing buttons, it all boils down to the exact same finger dance that you'll tire of in the first hour. Is this 2010 where we need to explain to developers that QTEs aren't fun?

Ok, so what's good? Well, the graphics are honestly amazing and lifelike, and the enemy designs, what few there seem to be, are kinda cool. That's about it. Definitely skip this game.

[h1]In true samurai style, [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] is a perpetual trial of patience.[/h1]
[i]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/i] is a game I've had my eye on for an incredibly long time at this point, yet I never quite got around to until recently.  I loved the [b]art[/b], I loved the look of the [b]strategic gameplay[/b], I loved the [b]culture[/b], I loved the [b]price[/b], and I really loved that it seemed to always have [b]Overwhelmingly Positive[/b] reviews.  And while I tend to find it blasphemous to leave a review on a game you haven't completed, I'll attempt to be as blunt as possible- [b]I can't fucking bring myself to complete this game.[/b]

This is my first negative review and it breaks my heart to leave one, but I was so [b]immensely disappointed[/b] with [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] that I feel like I ended up with a completely different game than everyone else.  While there are some aforementioned, albeit it occasionally subjective, redeeming qualities of this game, there's one [b]massive negative[/b].  Above all else, [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] is an [b]inconsistent, perpetual trial of patience[/b], fueled by the somewhat controversial design decision to not include a pause button.  While it seems the massive majority of people adore this game, you'll find the massive majority of negative reviews and discussion surrounding this game will revolve around this design choice.

[i]Shadow Tactics[/i] is a [b]really inconsistent[/b] trial and error game, and while it tends to be really satisfying to pull off combos and sweep areas clean without things going disastrously wrong, it never quite feels worth it after an hour of fighting the control scheme, and on not that uncommon of an occasion, it's hard to pinpoint what exactly went [i]right[/i] that one time it worked.  [b]The challenge of [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] never feels like it comes from how you're going to approach a situation, but rather how you're going to get the controls to actually work enough to pull it off[/b]; an issue that's, again, exacerbated by the lack of a pause button.  All of this is further compounded by the really spotty, limited ability to barely queue up actions for multiple characters to execute at the same time.

[i]Shadow Tactics[/i] is a trial of patience above all else, and the control scheme doesn't even attempt to meet you halfway.  After 15 hours of busting my ass to give this game a fair shake, I got exhausted of the constant, cyclical sunk cost loop I found myself in.

Excellent 2D dungeon crawler but I think some people over-look the "crawler" aspect of it.
It's not a fast paced game and it tells you that right away, but think of it like Demon Souls first came out on the PS3; it was slow, methodical, and brutal and 'Lost Ruins' does the same.

The graphics are fun without being too distracting nor is it trying too hard which makes for an enjoyable world to explore filled with interesting characters and enemies.

One of my favorite aspects of this one is the environmental interactions. There were times when I was trying new strategies on bosses and enemies only to light myself on fire, freeze myself while half submerged in water, shocked to death, and none of them felt cheap because I brought it on myself and could have been avoided if I paid more attention.

Give it a shot; I think its a fantastic game. It's some-what difficult, but not the hardest game out there and gives a great feeling of satisfaction as you progress through it.

review_text:
Kyoto Winds is only Part 1. It's well-written and very fun to read, but I was disappointed in the lack of romance in half the routes since this is advertised as a romance themed story.

Still, it's an excellent visual novel and I totally recommend it if you love historical fiction based otome.

[b]Tip/piece of advice:[/b] 
[i]Don't read Kazama's route last.[/i] If you wait, you'll probably end up hating him. If you read his as one of the first few, his route gives quite a bit of good insight into who he is below the surface. I thought knowing more about him added some important details and depth to endings with the Shinsengumi men and helped me understand Kazama's behavior and actions much better. 

[b]Why this is an excellent visual novel:[/b]
-Has trope characters without them being annoyingly cliched
-Choices matter and there are a lot of them 
[i](I used a walkthrough because I spent 10 hours wandering around in my conversations and got nowhere even with a character in mind)[/i]
-Every character is important and has depth (you just need to read every route to see it)
-Story is consistent and full of twists
-Anime style battle scenes are designed well
-The translation is a little off in places but mostly fine, and it's very polished for a remastered game
-MC's behavior is appropriate for the culture, time period, and her age, so...slightly naive
-UI is easy to use and it has full controller support. 
-Rich with historical fiction, action, and dark fantasy themes
-Fantastic plot full of adventure and suspense
-Samurai characters always make for good stories
-Gorgeous art and beautiful men 
-Terrific voice acting (Kazama's voice actor is a fav of mine and he does not disappoint)
-Absolutely LOVE the music
-History plus the supernatural, always a great combination

[b]Why "romancing 12 men" seems like the wrong way to describe this:[/b]
I expected the romance to be woven within this story, in EVERY route. But, half of the routes don't have anything I'd call a love story in them. Although I suppose you could look at the duty and honor of a samurai as romantic.

Without spoilers I'll explain what I mean because I was a bit shocked honestly. Each route is written to fit the personality of the male love interest. The protagonist is just kinda along for the ride.

Flirty and cute and feel like the beginning of a dark fantasy based romance:
-Sakamoto & Hachiro Iba

Iba's is probably my favorite and the smoothest love journey for our MC.

Cutesy with subtle flirtations and romance woven around duty, honor, and sacrifice:
-Harada, Souma, & Heisuke

Sweet & shocking, developing into an intense friendship that made me want to cry:
-Souji

The mysterious guy chasing you trope, adding drama and suspense
-Kazama

"Sister zoned" or "that girl that just won't stop following me around":
Sanaan, Hijikata, Saito, Kamazaki & Nagakura

While there were many openings to slip in some romantic lines or scenes, all 5 focused more on the Shinsengumi, duty and honor as a samurai, the civil unrest, and ultimately, the brutality of war. 

As you can see, I did spend 100 hours reading and re-reading because it's a really fun read. Just don't have high expectations for the romance in each route. There is absolutely none in some of them. I only managed to do one bad ending though. I enjoyed the good endings far too much.

Starting as a ambitious tactical sniper shooter, Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts turns down to be an annoying, buggy game that ruins the experience of the game, regardless of file integrity verification and reinstalls.

With limited ammo and supplies, you start your missions and try to beat your objectives and try to achieve challenges for money and unlock points in beautiful open-area mission maps, opposed to the open world from Sniper Ghost Warrior 3, always in contact with your client. The missions and challenges at first were nice, actually challenging and made fun to beat.
