review_text:
Nearly a year later and we still have empty promises and no updates. 

The whole idea of bonelab was built around modding and we still haven't gotten the SDK update or workshop support. The whole selling point and main campaign idea was that you could mod the game. Even before bonelab released, the devs were hyping up the fact that this game could be the Gmod for VR. It's not like the developers are trying hard to save their game. They've been nearly radio silent since the game came out, relying on the communities false sense of hope and underdeveloped mods to keep the game going. 

Onto the actual game itself; It was disappointing. It was hardly a sequel to boneworks. Half of the campaign was just a tutorial for the new characters, while the other half is just linear. Boneworks' biggest selling point was that you could beat the game however you wanted. There wasn't one true way to beat a level. This is especially true on the level Warehouse. Furthermore nearly all the new enemies in bonelab are just reskinned boneworks NPC's. If there is a simple way to describe the gameplay of bonelab, it would be "Boneworks 0.5" as it felt like more of a downgrade than anything else.

I tried to love Bonelab more than anything, but seeing what it is now and the fact that the once respect Stress Level 0 developers have adopted the "Launch now, fix later" ideology and not make any improvements to the game for nearly a year hurts. I don't understand how this was the same company that made something as good as Boneworks. 

TL;DR: Don't buy this game. The gameplay isn't fun and the devs abanonded it. If you want an actual fun campaign try "Boneworks", "Vertigo 2", or "Half Life Alyx". If you want a fun sandbox try "Blade and Sorcery" or "Hot dogs Horseshoes and Hand Grenades".

A visually stunning game that offers little in terms of game play or mechanical engagement.

The puzzles are straight forward and almost boring. They exist to slow you down rather than draw you into the world. "Stick your hand in gross gooey hole and fiddle until it works" rinse and repeat. On that note, I wish they didn't give you a weapon at all. Why is there clunky pointless combat in a puzzle game? The weaponry and "combat" are an obvious afterthought to the aesthetic of the game. So why is it even here? Wouldn't a stealth mechanic suit the theme better?

Whenever those chicken monsters show up, I sigh, walk away and wait for them to leave the area and proceed. This is a stupidly tedious way to add monsters into the game. I'm not worried they will find me since they don't chase or track you, I turn a corner and presto combat is done. Several minutes later I'm back to what I bought the game for, which itself is becoming a mystery to me.

I'll watch a review or play through rather than finish the game. And I recommend you do the same. Zero reason to pay for this experience unless you like supporting toothless visuals with laborious game play.

review_text:
This game [i]used to be[/i] worth purchasing, but for now I would hold off. Heres why! ;

[b]Low Player Numbers -  [/b]
I haven't seen this game marketed beyond very small you-tubers, so now that its initial launch interest has died down its hard to impossible to find active servers. When you do find them[i] (and active is a bit of a stretch seeing servers can host 100 people and I see at max 30 now)[/i]  , they are either limited to you if you don't want to join another discord server (Which will be full of people who take pretending to be a lion online a little too seriously and often don't have the best attitude.) or are servers that are set up for people to mess around in - which is fine but doesn't leave much space for you to experience the game the way the rest of us could a few months ago! 

[b]No support for solo play -  [/b]
I understand this is a multiplayer concept, but its possible to spawn into a solo server. This should be a chance to experience the mechanics of each different animal and prepare for joining a multiplayer server, however with no AI it just means you are aimlessly walking around maps with almost nothing to do. Solo play is never a requirement for a multiplayer game, but if its broken/ boring solo then you put the pressure on other people to bring the fun instead of the product you purchased to entertain you. It turns the game very hit or miss in terms of fun, one night could be great and then next a total bore.

[b]The DLCs...[/b]
I get it, money makes the world go round  - But other games of this level and type allow players to unlock skins, or attend events for exclusive items or coats for free. (Beast or Bermuda for example) So I find it really hard to be able to justify paying more than I paid for the base game for some 'Halloween' coats and items when Im yet to see any marketing that could expand the playerbase that the game clearly needs to do well. 

TLDR I had a really good time with this game for a few months until it started to die down in numbers. I have seen first hand plenty of the 'toxic community' members other reviews mention but frankly I don't think they're worth getting upset over or even acknowledging, but I understand why they are mentioned in a lot of reviews as they're often friends of server owners who get away with rule breaks. Part of me wonders how much they could be to blame for this drop in player base, as a few bad apples defo cause me to stop joining certain servers.

I think the game itself is a 5/5 but the bugs in the port force me to give it a 4/5.

review_text:
43 Hours | 100% Achievements (The True Dawn)

Let me be clear: Cronos: The New Dawn is a superb survival horror experience, but it’s one that demands mastery and respect for its core mechanics. Hitting the 100% achievement mark felt like earning a degree in resource management and strategic combat, and if you’re looking for a title that rewards deep commitment, this is it.

The Atmosphere and World (10/10)
Bloober Team knocked the atmosphere out of the park. The grim, brutalist architecture of 1980s post-apocalypse Poland combined with the unsettling sci-fi aesthetic is truly unique. Exploring the ravaged wasteland as the Traveler, jumping between time periods to unravel the mystery of "The Change," is constantly intriguing. I spent hours hunting down every audio log and text file, and the lore here is dense, disturbing, and genuinely compelling.

Strategic Combat and the Merging Mechanic
This is where the game earns its survival horror stripes, and why the "Mixed" reviews don't understand the depth. Cronos isn't a fast-paced action game; it’s a constant tactical exercise.

    Charged Shots are King: Learning to prioritize charged blasts and headshots for ammo efficiency is essential. Normal shots are a waste of precious resources.

    The Merging Mechanic: This is the genius layer of difficulty. Every encounter is a puzzle: Do I spend my precious Pyre fuel to burn the corpse now, or risk a nearby Orphan merging with it to become a heavily armored, acid-spitting abomination? When you get deep into the game, failing to burn a body quickly means an immediate, terrifying difficulty spike, which is what made the hardest encounters so satisfying to overcome.

The 100% Journey
My 43 hours weren't just running through the story. Achieving all the cores, finding every collectible, and unlocking all the suit upgrades is a massive undertaking. The 37 Cores are expertly hidden, forcing you to use the time manipulation puzzles and Gravity Boots to fully explore every corner. If you are an achievement hunter, this game is perfectly paced to push you to the brink of your resources while rewarding your exploration with meaningful power progression.

Final Verdict
If you love strategic survival horror games like the modern Resident Evil remakes and Dead Space, and appreciate a punishing difficulty that you can eventually conquer through mastery and resourcefulness, buy this game. It is a slow, tense, and incredibly rewarding journey to the "New Dawn."

TL;DR: Strategic survival horror masterclass with fantastic atmosphere and lore. The merging mechanic ensures every fight is tense, and the collectibles/upgrades are essential for the full experience. A must-buy for genre fans.

A visually stunning and technically impressive game, but it’s ultimately bogged down by an ahistorical narrative and a story that feels more like something you'd see in a Netflix series than a true representation of the 15th century.

If you’ve ever read a book older than 100 years, you’d have a much better sense of how people actually thought and acted back in that time compared to what’s portrayed here. The dialogue, the characters’ motivations, and the overall tone are all designed to cater to a younger audience raised on Netflix dramas. Characters have become more likeable, more quippy, and are less grounded in the actual historical mindset of the period. It’s the same trend that’s ruining modern TV and film, where everything is made palatable for the masses at the cost of nuance and authenticity.

I'm not surprised, because if you want to create a successful modern brand, it has to sell well and appeal to as many people as possible. However, I'm not one of those people. 

I’d be more inclined to rate this game positively if it weren't for the fact that the main developers and producers lied about its content. They’ve marketed a product that doesn't live up to its promises, and frankly, I don’t think they deserve your money for it. That said, the artists, programmers, and everyone else who put real work into bringing this game to life absolutely deserve recognition for their talent and effort

review_text:
Se existe uma epopeia moderna nos videogames, esse game é Yakuza 5.

As ideias que não deram certo no quarto game voltam aqui com um aprimoramento massivo, são cinco protagonistas jogáveis, cinco narrativas que se interlaçam no decorrer de 70 horas de jogo. A qualidade aqui é impressionante: cada protagonista tem seus arcos secundários, coadjuvantes memoráveis, substories intrigantes e minigames variados. É espantosa a profundidade que encontramos em Y5, e fica bem evidente como esse jogo é o responsável por criar as fundações que tornaram Yakuza 0 tão popular.

A narrativa é a mais impactante desde o segundo jogo, principalmente porque ela realmente avança o status quo das organizações e desenvolve os personagens e suas motivações; ninguém termina Y5 da mesma forma que começa, e isso vale para praticamente todo mundo relevante. Saejima tem muito tempo para brilhar e mostrar as suas qualidades, Akiyama segue brilhando após sua estreia em Y4, Haruka passa por um grande arco e até mesmo o novato, Shinada, se destaca.

Mas em especial, preciso dizer: Kiryu é MONSTRUOSO em Yakuza 5. De longe é uma das melhores performances de um protagonista na história dos videogames, e não afirmo isso de forma leviana. O Dragão de Dojima entrega tudo nesse jogo, seus ideiais, suas inseguranças, seus sacrifícios e esperanças estão todos escancarados, e a história vai revelando isso de forma muito natural com o desenrolar dos eventos. É algo muito impressionante.

Apesar disso,o conflito principal está longe de ser perfeito, é muito dependente de plot twists e eventos convenientes para prosseguir, sem falar em algumas coisas extremamente dramáticas que ocorrem - bem pastelão, estilo novela - mas tudo fica aceitável se você não questionar muito. Nesse sentido, acho que Y0 continua a melhor história da franquia, ao menos é a melhor contada, mas não se deixe enganar, Y5 figura no Top 3 da série.

Agora, rumo ao Yakuza 6 e o encerramento do arco de Kiryu.

review_text:
The Callisto Protocol – A Visually Stunning Horror Game with Room for Improvement

Developer: Striking Distance Studios
Release Date: December 2, 2022
Platforms: PS5, Xbox Series X/S, PC

Overview

The Callisto Protocol is a third-person survival horror game set in the distant future, where you play as Jacob Lee, a prison guard caught in the middle of a deadly outbreak that transforms prisoners into terrifying monsters. Initially released in late 2022, the game received criticism for its combat mechanics and repetitive gameplay. However, a series of post-launch updates have enhanced the overall experience, improving combat fluidity and enemy variety. While The Callisto Protocol remains visually stunning and atmospheric, it still faces some challenges in terms of gameplay variety and story depth.

What Makes It Great?

✅ Visually Stunning & Atmospheric Design
The Callisto Protocol is still one of the best-looking horror games out there. The updated visuals in 2025 continue to impress, with incredible environmental detail and atmospheric lighting that perfectly sets the mood for its terrifying world. The game does an excellent job of creating a claustrophobic, oppressive environment that feels truly alive, with every hallway and dark corner evoking a sense of dread. Even now, the visuals are a highlight, immersing players in a gripping, unsettling world.

✅ Brutal Combat & Gore (Post-Launch Improvements)
The combat in The Callisto Protocol has seen several improvements since launch. The fighting mechanics now feel smoother and more responsive, with the brutal dismemberment system remaining a key draw. The violence and gore remain impactful, making every enemy encounter feel satisfying. Although still not perfect, the combat is more fluid than it was at launch, with the improvements making the brutal confrontations more engaging and less frustrating.

✅ Intense Horror Atmosphere
The game continues to excel in creating a spine-chilling atmosphere. With the dark, decaying setting of Black Iron Prison, the terror is palpable throughout. The sound design is a key contributor to the experience, keeping players on edge with its eerie audio cues, distant growls, and the unsettling ambiance of the prison. The combination of atmospheric visuals and sound design creates a feeling of constant fear that works well, even years after the game’s original release.

✅ Immersive Sound Design
Sound plays a huge role in the tension of The Callisto Protocol. From the creaking metal of the prison to the bone-chilling growls of monstrous enemies lurking around every corner, the sound design effectively enhances the horror experience. The use of ambient noise, the subtle but unnerving hum of machinery, and the sudden intensity of enemy sounds keep you on constant alert, making every encounter feel more terrifying. Even with the visuals being top-notch, it’s the sound that truly heightens the sense of dread in this world.

✅ Environmental Storytelling
While the main story leaves much to be desired, the environmental storytelling has always been one of the game’s strongest points. In 2025, the game’s world feels even more detailed and filled with lore, with remnants of the past scattered throughout the prison. These small, environmental clues help paint a picture of the chaos that unfolded before you arrived, adding depth and mystery to the experience. The setting remains a crucial element that elevates the atmosphere and offers a richer understanding of the world.

What Could Be Better?

❌ Combat Mechanics Still Feel Stiff
While post-launch updates have made combat more fluid, it’s still not without its issues. review_text:
8 years of waiting ... It's really just a puzzle game. Here's my main takeaways: 

- Interesting setting: it's probably the main selling point. Can't think of another game that pushes the 'biomechanical' look and feel as much or as well in the environment. Enemies just look like uncooked poultry, but the rest is good. Also, somehow, not very scary or creepy. I think that might be due to how the game is just moving from puzzle to puzzle, and ultimately makes me feel more frustrated than anxious.

-Lackluster shooting and combat: the 'guns' feel awful. Combat for the first half of the game is just about taking pot shots and then running for cover. The final weapon only needs to be fired 3 or 4 times. The enemies is this game are painfully uninteresting.

-Bare-bones story: there isn't really one. Why are we here? Why this red infection stuff? Why is biotech based entirely on solving puzzles? Does the ending only exist to cop out of an explanation as to why we did any of this? Lots of moments with little to no payoff. By the end I still know nothing to the point where even guessing is grasping at straws. Pretty disappointing. 

- The puzzles: the actual *meat* of the game. Only a few puzzles that were really just mind-numbing, fewer that were fun. Many of the puzzles were unintuitive, or force the player to walk mazes, or just take ages to wait for parts to move. Frankly, these felt like a waste of time, possibly unnecessary padding. Definitely the hardest part is just finding the will to backtrack and try to find objectives. You can end up running around on 1 hp for a lot of it due to the save/checkpoint system.

If you're interested in puzzles and HR Giger environments in a game that can be completed in less than 6 hours, maybe worth a try.  For me, however, I thought this game would have some more substance in terms of combat, suspense, or horror, so not much for myself to enjoy. Not a bad showing for a game ... but 8 years since announcement and all the hype was worth about 6 hours of play time, a few ooh's and ah's, and a lot of puzzles. If this game had instead better shooting sections (or none), less puzzles (or none), and more focus on the unique scenery, there might be a cool experience here. And the price?! Definitely not worth $40 USD. As is, it's just too slow for too little substance.

review_text:
ok, I'll keep it to list of pros and cons because mostly everything probably has been said about the game anyways.

pro:
· graphics & sound are some of the best I've seen. mostly graphics. (and at least now, after the patches it ran well and I had no issues whatsoever. on release this seemed to not have been the case. as seems to be the new normal for games in the 2020s.)
· there is (at least for the setting) a decent variety in locations.

con:
· the dumbest and dumbed down melee combat EVER in a video game. alternate pressing left and right and then hit the enemy. repeat. ad infinitum. that's it - that is what you do for 90% of the time.
· levels linear as hell, so the exploration is not as good as it could be. dead space's ishimura made sense and felt real, even if fictional. the callisto protocol may look "realistic" but feels very much like a game. don't get me wrong: it is still fun to "explore", but the rewards for doing so are rather slim: some audio-logs and resources. in the end there is very little that lies beyond the main path anyways.
· the game is just fully reliant on jumpscares. they get old quickly
· it's just a meanspirited game. a lot of the forementioned jumpscares give you no chance to avoid damage. in a game where you are trying to save resources and are careful this feels unfair and 'cheap'
· the constantly repeating canned animations are annoying rather soon
· not even variety in the progression of the story. it is always elevators failing, a platform breaking down, so we gotta find an alternative route. if I got a buck for each time jacobs falls from a platform while trying to hold on and then having to go through more monster-filled tunnels, then the game would have been free.
· boring and most uninspired characters. everything is just one note.
· all these points result in you having seen everything the game has to offer after one or two hours of playing.

tl;dr:
this one trick pony is a waste of time, money and talent, aping its origin and failing in every department but visuals.

review_text:
Impressive art direction, decent sound design and... nothing else.
The beginning was boring, when you do you-don't-know-what with you-don't-know-what because no other choice to progress.
And then you reach the point where you have enemies.

How to tell it while staying polite... they are a pain in the arse.
You can't dodge their attacks, they hurt like hell and you have a handful of health points.
For a relatively long time, your only weapon will just do melee attacks (remember, the enemies shoot you from a distance, and they aim well), and you can't strike more than twice until a cooldown is imposed.
But you don't know how long you have to wait until it's back ON, unless you right click. And when you right click, you walk at 1 meter per second (remember it's already very hard if not impossible to dodge at full speed, with right click, it's impossible).
And, of course, at close range you can't walk around the enemy to strike them, they do U-turns at light speed to kill you.

And when you finally get a ranged attack, it's with a very limited supply of ammo that does little more damage than a BB gun.

Add to that a level design meant for you to get lost and with those enemies you can't even explore.
What do you have at the end of this all?
A bad game.
I'm really sorry to say that, especially since I backed the game, but it's just bad.

review_text:
As a linear story-focused game it's very solid. Combat is fun as long as you keep the enemies at bay - guns are very fun and you will get to use them plenty, but there are almost no options for dodging attacks etc. The story itself is honestly a great take on the usual "zombie apocalypse" cliche. The atmosphere and art direction are brilliant.

Sadly, the game falls short on what it's advertised as - survival horror. On normal difficulty I was absolutely overflowing with resources and ammo so the feeling of having to "survive" was quite minimal. I also didn't feel even mildly stressed at any point during the game. There are very few psychologically heavy moments and almost no shock content. Jumpscares are pretty tame. It's more "gross" than "scary". 

However, it's still a very pleasant experience that takes a solid amount of time to complete. Easy 8/10

review_text:
There once was a game that I held dear to my heart called Phantasy Star online 2.
It was simple, clunky, some would even say dated, and yet as I played on the JP server and day one on Global servers, I loved every minute and it became the MMO I adored the most. A satisfying mission based loop with lots to do, systems to learn, people to see, and challenges to overcome. I remember my first 13 star, my first maxed out class of hunter, playing Hero when they just came out. I got hyped fighting Omega Masquerade, encountering FINAL FANTASY 14'S ODIN and dueling him 1 on 1, and getting to share that experience with friends who wanted to try the game I loved. PSO2 truly was an experience no MMO could replicate for me and I'm thankful for that games existence.

New Genesis however has taken that game I loved so much and turned into a lifeless husk of itself. A game that failed to see why the game reached the highs it did. The episode 6 director YSOK truly pushed PSO2 classic to it's limits, with the best gameplay possible and mission design, and for his reward he was replaced with the director that almost killed PSO2 classic before during episode 5, Hamazaki. Over the last few years of New Genesis, we've experienced extreme mismanagement of what the game needs and what it gets. Over centralization of character customization as a focus, open world design leading to a much more sluggish and just unsatisfying loop, constant reuse of content, an incredibly short story, and an aggressively over grindy system to keep investment into the game. I remember grinding out to unseal the sealed nodatchi in PSO2 classic due to variety and fun making the grind smooth, but NGS feels agonizing with the same DOLLs again and again.
The classes feel smoother but many feel like they lack the depth of PSO2 classic classes, not featuring as many photon arts or Techniques as before. The game lacks content to this very day, and feels incredibly short and lacking in replay value.

And all of this would still be fine if they didn't harm PSO2 classic in the process. No one will ever get to experience the version of PSO2 I fell in love with. It was put into maintenance mode, got it's graphics and lighting butchered, skyboxes broken, and got numerous bugs introduced into it, and nowadays most people don't even have it installed due to being a separate dlc, meaning they'll likely never be tempted to try it, which was already a pain in the neck regardless of that fact to access.

I miss Phantasy Star Online 2... And I always will. Thank you for every great memory you gave me, every friendship you helped me make. I hope that one day, you are saved from New Genesis and given your own game client, and get support again, cause New Genesis is not Phantasy Star Online.

At first i loved the game, good mechanics, nice people except for a server or 2 and most of the glitches had easy fixes. Now lets get to why i wouldn't recommend it, the developers don't seem to care about what we say, the lions are completely overpowered (ive seen a lion take down an Apex elephant by itself), all big cats can out run any herbivore, the new wild dogs are half developed, a lot of herbivores have needed updates for a long time and they are adding updates (that no one asked for) way to early that are causing more glitches with no fixes.

Btw the reason why lions are overpowered is because its one of the devs favorite animal. One of the "easy" fixes for something they have been saying they'll fix for a long time is drinking water, most of the time in order to drink you have to put your camera in the water which makes you unable to see around you and makes it even more difficult to dodge a croc. review_text:
I love style, design, graphics of this game, this is probably how people of 80s imagined future will look like. Nice future and actionmovie vibe.

Unfortunately game is full of poor gameplay-design choices. It probably was fine in the year when game was released, but modern games have advanced quite a lot since then, and Blood Dragon does not stand good near them. 
For example - a lot of unskippable animations which take a lot of time and are annoying when you see them for 100th time. You can't pull out gun and shoot, no, you have too some gun tricks at first. Start to reload shotgun in a bad time and sudden enemy appears - well, you are screwed because you either need to wait until character will load all shells into shotgun, or switch to different weapon and see another pointless guntrick animation while you are being killed. "Q" to heal sometines does not work because character is doing some another animation already.
In other words - controls are extremely unresponsive, you can't cancel some annoying animations and have to wait until you can shoot, heal, etc. Another example - really stupid AI companion who leeroyjenkins into enemy crowd and dies; instead of just sitting behind cover while I kill them all (that was 1st or 2nd mission). Another weird thing - can't toggle ads, and can't untoggle sprint and crouch, this is opposite of what I need.

Summary:
- This DLC was extremely awesome and amazing for its time.
- Quite bad controls comparing to modern games. It's cool that Ubisoft has released this DLC as separate game, but they could have adjusted controls to fit modern practices. Extremely annoying.

review_text:
As a massive fan of the Yakuza series, diving back into Yakuza 5: Remastered was nothing short of incredible, and it truly solidifies why this franchise holds such a special place in my heart. This game is an absolute epic, a sprawling masterpiece that perfectly encapsulates everything that makes Yakuza so uniquely brilliant.

What sets Yakuza 5 apart, even within this beloved series, is its sheer ambition. You're not just following one protagonist; you're immersed in the lives of five distinct characters, each with their own deeply compelling storylines that eventually intertwine in spectacular fashion. From Kazuma Kiryu's quiet life as a taxi driver to Taiga Saejima's desperate prison break, and the vibrant dreams of Haruka Sawamura, every narrative thread is handled with the series' signature blend of gritty drama, heartfelt emotion, and sudden, side-splitting humor. The storytelling here is absolutely top-tier, constantly evolving and keeping you hooked with its twists and turns.

Beyond the narrative, the scope of this game is astounding. You're not confined to just one district; you get to explore five incredibly detailed and lively Japanese cities, each bustling with unique side quests, minigames, and unforgettable characters. Whether you're mastering the art of taxi racing, becoming an idol, or hunting bears in the mountains, the sheer variety of activities means there's always something engaging to do. The combat remains incredibly satisfying, offering distinct fighting styles for each character that feel powerful and fluid.

Yakuza 5: Remastered is more than just a game; it's a monumental achievement in interactive storytelling and world-building. For any Yakuza devotee, or anyone looking to jump into one of gaming's most compelling sagas, this remaster is an essential experience. It’s a testament to the series' enduring quality and why it continues to be my absolute favorite series.

And based on how ineffective Bloober Team was when trying to write a cohesive storyline for The Medium, I didn't have any genuine faith they could write themselves out of this vague story either.

Refund! I do not recommend spending $60 on this game.

VIDEO REIVEW : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rF6JoEf8aCs

@BlooberTeam's  love letter to Dead Space. While it has a gorgeous world, eerie audio, and some heavy story beats… it doesn't really stick the landing....

You play a “Traveler” sent back in time to gather memories and stop a plague from wiping out humanity. The concept is great, and the final few hours hit hard. But most of the game feels disconnected.... like three stories struggling to become one.

Combat is sluggish, then again so was DeadSpace. You move like you're wading through molasses. Enemies are slow too, so you end up jogging past most threats. 
Survival mechanics feel shallow. Inventory is so tight you’re basically forced into buying upgrades to increase that. You also end up upgrading your early weapons so much the new weapons get ignored. They aren't good enough to hard swap too and using more currency to upgrade them just doesn't work.

As for the graphics and sound? Incredible. The game looks great and I love the soundtrack it has.

But is it worth yoru time? At $60, I’d hesitate. At $40? Solid pick for fans of moody sci-fi. It’s not the new Dead Space… but it’s a solid weekend ride.

Verdict: Worth wishlisting.

review_text:
[h1] OVERHATED GAME ALERT [/h1]

As a fan coming off of Just Cause 3, I can understand the frustration at release, especially with how the marketing material presented the game as far more than what it's worth.
As is typical for Western games, the game also released broken and unfinished.
I got it years after release for chump change, and with all patches and DLC.

Ultimately, this game isn't as good as the predecessor, but a lot of it is down to personal preference.

First,
[h2] The Cons [/h2]
Let's get the elephant out of the room: The downgrade in GRAPHICS and PHYSICS is laughable.
However, I think one needs to understand that, unlike the predecessor, this game wasn't made with Unreal Engine 4, but Avalanche's proprietary Apex tool. Which is to say, a lot of time and money that could have gone into development was siphoned by making this tool. I imagine they didn't use UE4 because of licensing fees.

The SOUNDTRACK suffered, too.
But again, Avalanche can't really be blamed. You can beat Henry Jackman, who composed Just Cause 3 alongside Zach Abramson, and I imagine Jackman doesn't charge pennies either.
However, Abramson has done as good of a job as he could to learn from working with Jackman, and I think the effort should be complimented. The adaptive mixing is also back and better.

Personal Issue: The WINGSUIT CONTROLS are easier.
It was quite fun to spend hours crashing in Just Cause 3, but now being able to look back at just how good I've gotten at daring wingsuit maneuvers. It seems that in Just Cause 4, your wingsuit loses momentum much slower, and thus, the experience is also not as kinetic, since the momentum simulates wind resistance, and you hardly feel any of that here.

Now,
[h2] The Pros [/h2]
The STORY is a mixed bag, but generally, I prefer it.
While Just Cause 1 and 2 were not to be taken seriously at all, 3 did have some important and personal beats, and generally communicated its theme rather well.
Di Ravello was also, while generic, a good dictator antagonist.
Here, both villains, Oscar Espinoza and Gabriela Morales, are eternally in the background and hardly interact with the characters. Especially Gabriela, being the sister of Rico's friend and sister in arms Mira, has so much missed potential.
However, Oscar Espinoza ties very well into both Rico's personal history, as well as that of the country of Solis, and is generally interesting because of that. I just wish we'd actually gotten to see him act like the crybaby which he looks like. I do like that he's an oligarch who uses a mercenary army, though, as both of those things are underexplored in ficiton inspired by contemporary politics. Like how Di Ravello served as a baseline example for fascism, Espinoza does for oligarchy.
The sci-fi tech is kind of out of the blue here, as, while it was already present in 3, there it had a coherent theme that suspended the audience's disbelief, that being the mineral Bavarium, which only existed in its ficitonal country of Medici.
Here, the Black Hand just have all sorts of insane sci-fi weapons, tools, vehicles etc., just 'cause Espinoza has unlimited money and can buy stuff from wherever he wants.

I really like the other CHARACTERS.
I found most characters in 3 to be pretty damn annoying (except for the radio propaganda guy, David Tennant), and I like how much of the personalities of 4's cast tie into your interactions with them.
The new radio propaganda isn't as funny as Tennant's was, but I like it being a talkshow where the hosts, Thiago and Santiago, legitimately believe the garbage their script says.
There's Sargento, the strategist of the Army of Chaos, who coordinates the army behind the back the one-man-army that is Rico. He's inexperienced, but he's got heart, and Rico inspiring and teaching him is cool.
Javi is an archaeologist who used to perpetuate the Espinoza dynasty's propaganda about how they were supposedly the ones who had been improving Solis in the centuries since the Conquistado Diego Espinoza de Malaga arrived, and who, after being locked up for getting sick of lying, now tasks Rico to help him uncover the relics of the last dynasty of indigenous ancient Solino rulers, in order to prove Espinoza a liar.
My favorite is Garland King, who is just female Michael Bay from New York and who wants to Rico to be her stuntman in what I can only assume to be the most idiotic movie since Morbius. I love her.

Many disagree, but I actually like that you take over BASES by completing certain tasks now, instead of just destroying all the chaos objects.
They are, of course, a staple of the series, and their meaning has now been reduced so much that they even respawn upon restarting the game, but the developers at least found some good use for them, which is that they make the arcade-style score counter relevant again, by essentially acting as experience points. Every time you fill the chaos meter, you get an additional squad of insurgents, which you need to take over more areas.

The new GRAPPLING HOOK is also cool.
Random tasks which you are given while exploring the map are nice, and they reward you by unlocking mods for your grapple, depending on which character gave you the task. It gives you a lot more to do while randomly exploring.

The DLC for this game is much better than the undercooked additons of 3.
While they added cool mechanics and expanded on the lore, 3's DLCs were really just tacked on.
4's three DLCs all add new missions all over the map which completely switch up your gameplay and have their own themes.

[h2] Verdict:
Some things better, some things worse, but generally overhated. Buy on sale if interested. Better with mods.
8/10 [/h2]

review_text:
Notes:
- .Hack//G.U. Last Recode covers the G.U. portion of the .Hack series and what happened after .Hack//Roots, which is an 26-episode anime series (Optional but not required to understand the story past Volume 1). 

- The first 4 installments where Kite is the protagonist (.Hack//Infection and so on) are not included and are NOT required to understand the full story of G.U.

- Other than that, there's complementary content and alternate versions of G.U. outside of the game but this game is the canon story of the G.U. portion and other games, mangas and animes are vaguely referenced in the game as a jig and not part of the main story.

Main Story: The game starts where the .Hack//Roots left off after the Twilight Brigade events where Haseo becomes a PKK (Player-killer killer) and hunts for Tri-edge to avenge his friend Shino. The game is divided into 3 acts where Volume 4 serves as a 3-hour long Epilogue to the whole G.U. Saga. Online Jack (on the News Capture) occurs at the same time as the G.U. events.

Gameplay: It's a 2007 JRPG where you smash Attacks to perform 1-2-3 combos and use skills as a mix-up. Combos change depending on the weapon and you gain more weapon-types later in Volume 2, a slight rework in Volume 3 and a full rework in Volume 4. It's a 2007 game, it can feel severly dated yet nostalgic- very similar to Tales of Games.
You gain increased EXP from enemies with higher level, Damage scales off Level disparity, between the range 1 to 10 and grinding for EXP isn't much of a thing unless you skip pass all the enemies on the field- but it doesn't take long to find a word combination outside the main story and start grinding 3 - 5 levels in 10mins.

Exploration: You use a 3-word system to generate an instance and walk around hallways with enemies located on specific areas, repeating the same combination of words will yield the same result and you can fine tune the enemy's level range and rewards with the 2nd and 3rd word- as well as area objective and location. It can feel quite repetitive.

Aesthetic: The game tries to replicate the feel of booting up your old PS2, XB360 or even Gamecube menu with functions like email, movies, forums and such to emulate the feeling of an old PC from the early 2000s. Every time you logout the game, it's as if you're done for the day and log in the next day, hence the gimmick of "logout > check email > login > repeat" model through the entire game's story.

Rating: As dated as the game is, it's a solid 6/10 for new people, 7/10 for those who ride on the nostalgia of old games and probably a 7.5 to 8/10 for the .hack fans- as it's the last game CyberConnect released since 2017 related to the .hack series. 
If Bandai allowed them, they would, willingly, make a sequel, with all of these traits updated to today's design philosophies and a modern twist to the .hack series.

review_text: Honestly, Yakuza 5 just doesn't cut it as a good Yakuza game. I tried it out because I had played 0 first, and this game inspired 0, so I expected much more from it, but this game feels so drag-on, tutorial-filled, and non-action-packed. By the time I got to Part 2 I just thought it was uninteresting, and returned to it after 2 years, and the story really didn't pick up until the Finale, apart from Haruka and Akiyama's part. I just thought this game was too packed with side stuff. This is usually where Yakuza games shine for most people but it can get repetitive and boring fast doing the same thing over and over again, and especially you'll have to do these things 5 times each because each character has something new for them to do. There also is no CP or unlockable abilities like earlier games so everything has to be done by constant trips and while walking, bottomless stomach, sprinting, or anything. This means that for each new character you play as there will be the same "Learn from Masters, Do Side Story, See all Revelations, Visit all Restaurants, Do Touring, Increase Weapon Skill, Play Minigames, Fight In Victory Road, Complete Hostess, repeat." for each character all while being hounded by the numerous fighting encounters that they can drag you into, as well as the countless backtracking and trips you'll have to do. The Level Ups also are so strange and disorganized. The fights also give out pretty cheap rewards, and also And the story? Ok but a bit underperforming in my opinion. Every time you get into the city there's always many things hounding you from progression, such as a substory or a revelation, or a certain enemy that sneaks up on you causing needless encounters, and there are far too many of these. And, even when it LOOKS like something interesting will happen, there are needless dialogue scenes between story events to make the game feel longer than it actually should be. The characters are also not bad, but a lot of them were a bit off to me, especially with the way they changed during the story, and some of the plot twists that occured for certain characters. There are returning ones like Yuya, Majima, Kamiyama, and Komaki, but everyone just feels so "meh". And I feel like the story just is poorly written, and replaying this to completion has showed me why I have stopped playing this, because it just is a long, gruelling journey with no satisfaction or reward. It's not a action-packed, immense story-telling game like the first 3 games (0,1,2) are. Instead, they were more content-hungry and less action and adventure here than ever. Maybe if you're a die-hard Yakuza fan you'll love this, but me, it wasn't as great just because it had the most content. I finished it but still my opinion hasn't changed. I don't know if i'd say I wish I never bought it, because I think this one is just ok, but it's nothing too special, although it's definitely better than Yakuza 3/4. After the Yakuza 0 Trilogy (0,K1,K2) it's the best of the remastered collection given it has 0 unnecessary changes from the original game unlike the other two games with an ok story and the biggest number of protagonists, but there are some other notable flaws that keep it from being as good.

review_text:
This is a review after ~3 hours of playing. For now, I'm really glad I got this in a Humble Monthly, since this obvious copy of Dead Space is absolutely not worth the asking price. Clunky controls, generic setting, bland story, uninspired enemy design, monotonous and boring combat, predictable jumpscares, and to top it all off, AMD sponsorship which means no DLSS, so all of those raytracing options are doing is killing the framerate (I could barely keep to 50-60 FPS on a 4070). 
It's clear that *some* effort went into making the game, and it's far from being outright bad, and can look really pretty at moments, but it's far from being Dead Space, the game it's obviously trying to impersonate.
It's one of those games that really make me wish for a "neutral" recommendation option.

*edit* after four more hours, I've decided to stop playing and simply watch through the story on Youtube. 

Also, just consider this situation:
The game heavily conditioned me to expect jumpscares literally all of the time. I call an elevator down, and aim my shotgun at it, fully expecting an enemy to jump out when it arrives. Sure enough, the door opens, there's an enemy inside, and I shoot it immediately. They forgot to remove the door hitbox, though, so my shot just bounces off thin air, leaving the enemy unharmed. This has to be like, *the* next level of clunky and anticlimactic.

review_text:
I'm not sure why the support for this game is so overwhelming. I'm having a lot of difficulty getting into it. The camera is annoying to deal with because there's an extra rotational element and it doesn't hard lock to characters, so I'm constantly clicking the camera reset and awkwardly rotating the environment to try and figure out where I am and what I'm looking at. 

The controls are really frustrating and I've had far more difficulty than I would have expected on normal mode. There are all kinds of objects that stop you dead in your tracks that really shouldn't do that. I can't count how many times I got caught by a guard because for some reason the idiot shinobi doesn't understand that he can walk OVER dead bodies or tiny little crates. I've also had quite a few instances of getting caught because I'm trying to do one thing and my character does something else instead. Some of the stuff you can interact with is just too close together for me to be able to quickly and accurately pick the right ones.

I tried using the shadow mode or whatever, that was frustrating because if you don't set everything up to be COMPLETELY IDIOT PROOF, your characters will end up stumbling over each other, or one of them will get caught before he can execute the action. Why I can't ask them to walk to a position with the pathing I used in shadow mode is beyond me. The morons just fucking BEELINE straight to the location you pointed to. Also, good luck having two characters complete actions that involve them going through the same tight spaces or the same door, because for some stupid reason, they have collision with each other. Can a skinny little shinobi really not fit through the same door as a samurai at the same time? why do they have to get stuck on each other?

I'm sure some of these problems could be solved by putting extra effort into planning, but I'm not interested in micromanaging every tiny little movement these characters make. Maybe give them a little bit more intelligence and less object collisions, but definitely give players the option to map out EXACT pathing in shadow mode, so that I don't have to spend 10 minutes getting them all into perfect positions manually before they inevitably fuck up their actions and get caught by a guard anyway.


There's just so much information to keep track of and less mobility than I would expect from a ninja. Why can't I do a little dodge roll? A Genji dash? Maybe a slide? Something to cover that last like, 2 meters quickly so that you don't alert the whole damn village because you tried to clear an open space just a little too late into the enemy patterns.

I often found myself shouting things like "Go!!!" and "What the fuck!?" and "Why are you doing this to me!?" at my tv.

Maybe it's me though. Maybe I'm just too used to the other games I've been playing lately having a large degree of immersion and ease of use. I can't help it. I like feeling like the controls are an extension of my body, instead of a clunky tool that kinda sorta gets the job done if you really want it to. It just feels like a lot of clunky stuff to keep track of, even after almost 2 hours of practice.

I don't know whether to recommend this game or not because I didn't get far enough into it to make a fair call. This frustration induced migraine is keeping me from continuing. Maybe I'll play more and edit this review later, but for now I'm just done with this game. I'm going to say not recommended unless you're super into top down RTS games. I've never been the biggest fan of the genre, but I really wanted to like this one with what people have been saying. Oh well.

Yeah it has all the flaws everyone already told you about (and more), and yeah it looks incredible. The combat sucks, the variety in general as well, and the level design mostly consists of straight corridors and a TON of crawling through vents (and other "seamless" loading screens). It can be absurdly punishing, too. And the saving/checkpoint system is just as bad as the menus. Don't even get me started on the stupid DLCs.

Still, it has a captivating atmosphere, bolstered by its stunning visuals, albeit basically a cheap copy of Dead Space (the game simply couldn't avoid that comparison). So if you take it for what it is, a simplistic good-looking survival-horror game with a few clever jumpscares, you might enjoy it. I still think it is overpriced, though, despite the visual quality.

I have to give it a negative review because the game simply won't work beyond a certain point in the story. An endless loading screen stops me from progressing after a cutscene; and if I skip said cutscene, the game simply sends me straight back to the main menu without saving. Thankfully, I have now managed to fix this issue, but the game was just broken from the beginning. Add to that the recurrent stuttering and you have a long list of things to fix for the devs.

All in all, it's not *good*, but it's not bad enough for me to quit it right away. And the story was pretty good, despite the amount of times you just fall off unstable ground an get separated from your partner -- that was quite repetitive.

Hopefully it is a lukewarm start to many better projects in the future by this team.

review_text:
I've tried this game a few times over the last 6 months since I've purchased it.

It has a great concept.   I like the idea.   However, it's just a total fail when it comes to implementation.   The root of the problem is the absolutely WONKY AI when it comes to your village people. (Y M C A)   Its been brought up and mentioned to the dev numerous times in the forum and the response is "it works fine."

Let me describe the scenario:

1) You have a water purifier near a lake.  You have water masters harvest from the pond and bring  it back to the water purifier.   Attempting to turn dirty buckets of water into clean water.   While they are doing that, the farmer decides his crops need water and go to the water purifier to steal the dirty water to water his crops.   The water master gets pissed, goes back to the farm and steals the water buckets back.   The farmer then goes to the water purifier and steals the dirty water again... Repeat for eternity.  So in the end, all your guys are doing is swapping materials back and forth between buildings.

Same thing with every other resource.  I've seen it happen to wood, stone, etc.

The more buildings you have, the more the problem rears its ugly head.  You have more buildings and more citizens fighting over the resources.  As the game proceeds and you have 30+ buildings, the economy starts to crawl, and you start to notice nothing is actually being built very fast.   You start using your "hand of god" and plucking trees and dumping them on buildings to create them faster...  You see citizens wandering around, but you are now getting less than 1 building built per day.  When the game first starts off, you can build 10 buildings in the first day without much trouble.

2) With the new trash update, it seems the trash men like to pick up the corruption's garbage.  They will leave my town, which is walled in, to pick up some garbage outside of town and get picked off from corruption towers, and what not.   While they are out there being attacked, it triggers your golems to come to the defense of the town because "Buck Rodgers" went to clean up outside of the walls.  They die... So now during the day you are constantly chugging away your magic/mana/essence reviving golems and now you have to micro manage the garbage men and keep picking them up with your "hand of god" and dumping them back into town.

All in all, the game is great for about the first 10 days on the map.  After that the system breaks down and you get a buggy mess of frustration.  For that reason I cannot recommend the game.  However, if we can get the dev to work on a few of these issues this game could really be a rockstar.

On the 10th day I say i had enough and even discovering the end of the story and any replay ability was not in question and I myself DO enjoy challenging punishing games but this one just annoyed me really. and spending all the time is not worth it in the end.

It's not often I drop a positive review for a game, and then change it to negative in hindsight (except that one tower defense game but we do not speak it's name here), but here we are.

The game is fun at first, like I got a good 20 hours of fun from it and if you think that's enough for you, go right ahead, you'll get your money back. My issue is that once you know how the game ticks, it's EXTREMELY easy to beat it. So much so that even the secret hard mode the stand-in of the dev says "this mode was too hard but this is my true vision B)" is also stupidly easy.

So what do you do once the main game is completely trivialized? PvP. And nothing BUT PvP. And even better? PvP against people who religiously play the game and try to exploit every single stat or line of code possible so they can maximize their side so they're quite literally unkillable, turning the battle into a war of attrition until you eventually die.

This is your life now. You HAVE to participate in it because the base game's difficulty DOES NOT go up anymore than the directors cut. I personally signed up to play an army builder and fight NPC battles, not fight "Xx_DespotL0v3r69_xX"'s unbeatable army of anime girls.

I actually REALLY enjoyed the game back when I didn't fully understand it, when I was learning the ropes and getting a little closer to winning each time, but now that I've learned the rules, I can't un-learn them, and at the end of run I do I gotta draft my ass up to the PvP Pit and watch my guys get clobbered by #26 on the leaderboard of Despot's Stinkiest.

Again, if 20 hours is a good time sink for you, go straight ahead because the game is good for those 20 hours. But once those 20 hours are up, you're gonna be just like me. In the pits.

review_text:
UPDATE AFTER BEATING THE GAME: My original review remains pretty much spot on, in fact, the game gets slightly worse as you progress further like most games these days where they dump most of their development time on the first part of the game to get people "hooked".

Added annoyances in addition to previous review:

1. Third person shooter with significant offset, there is no way to switch aim shoulders. Have fun making blind right hand turns.
2. The levels get so dark towards the end that the flashlight is almost literally useless, on top of it's hilariously short and unrealistic range already.
3. Every single boss in the game, sans the last one, are basically the same (some are literally the same, just in a slightly different arena).
3a. In fact: In the entire game there are less than half a dozen unique monsters.
4. You won't stop constantly fighting with the inventory until like four fifths of the way into the game when you finally max it out... on the second to last level.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:

Story is unique, game is visually acceptable, and that's largely what's carrying the reviews. Gamers these days are extremely shallow.

Otherwise the game is a mashup of various different horror games that have come in the past, but does not replicate any portion of what they did well below surface level.

In fact in some cases it borrows the concept but completely disregards the pieces that made it good.

We have Dead Space enemies, but no limbing system, just shoot them in the head. Shooting them in the leg will cause the smaller ones to fall over temporarily, but melee damage (Stomp, just like DS) does so little damage that spamming it on something won't kill it, and due to animation locking, doing it with more than one mob around is a death sentence.

We have brutal inventory management (as if anyone ever actually liked that), just so that "increasing inventory space" has value as an RPG mechanic, you will be forced repeatedly to drop at least one or two pieces of your gear just to carry story items that have zero value. As an example that means potentially having to drop your shotgun just so you can pick up a door key (they take the same space), dropping requires backtracking to the last checkpoint to put it in a box, and then running all the way back to the key, once you've used the key, you need to run all the way back to the previous checkpoint to pick up the gear you had to drop for the story item.

A lot of people complain about the slow character movements, this doesn't bother me, your basically stuck in a Big Daddy suit so it makes sense that the character is just going to be slow. What does bother me is the fact that collision modeling and movement in this game can be pretty bad. Your big character will get stuck on a whole bunch of stuff it shouldn't. Your character is also treated like it has no momentum. To give you an example, running away from something that hits you in the back, you will not keep moving in the direction you were going in and will "stun" in place instantly, monsters that are visually "less dense" than the player will flinch the player far more than seems believable.

Finally, the game designers seem to be in love with the completely cheese of just locking the player in an arena with a ton of mobs when you pick up a story item. "...and here we have the player pick up the key, which magically makes a dozen monsters angry, and the doors autolock until all the monsters are dead."

All in all it boils down to a game that is surface level unique, but actually extremely generic mechanically.

Cronos is a straight up arena shooter with a horror paint job and inventory management tacked on.

Would it be worth it? Yes, if it was maybe half of what it currently costs. Blame steam for the thumbs down because their system is binary, in reality it would probably be something like 6 or 7 out of 10.

Getting tired of these art house style games that are basically solely carried on the story and graphics and then just throw in game play mechanics they've seen other games do so they can call them games.

...actually Cronos could make a pretty decent movie.

Will update this review if my opinion appreciably changes the further I get, but I doubt it.

review_text:
Scorn is an absolutely gorgeous art piece that, at its best, is moody, immersive, and completely a visual marvel. However, Scorn is also not just an art piece - it's a game; and the game part of Scorn brings it so very low that I'm not sure I can recommend the actual product.

Barring the lack of story and context - which is a bit of a shame but not a dealbreaker - the levels are pretty poorly paced, puzzle mechanics are "introduce ---> reuse until any semblance of uniqueness in its design is lost ---> repeat", and the combat is at once unsatisfying and unfair. The weapons themselves are actually fine and I think feel pretty good in isolation, but they're just not in a sandbox where they can shine.

Ultimately, you can buy the art book and witness the artistry of these guys at a much better pace - that is, at your *own* pace - with no distractingly convoluted level design, annoying enemy encounters, or nonsensical mechanics to draw you out of the experience. And I do think you should support these developers one way or another, because art like this is once in a generation and I would hate to not see more like it. I just think the medium of art is sometimes as important to consider as the art itself.

I really wanted to love this game, but the gameplay is pretty fustrating. I have plenty of experience with 3rd person shooters and melee based games. Ive played thru dead space remake, jedi fallen order, jedi survivor and final fantasy 15. Easy mode in this game is what hard/hardcore mode would be in other games. You have to press left or right to dodge, and you cant press the same button during repeated attacks. Once you get the hang of things its not too bad till you get to the boss fights. So even if you think you have enough ammo there's a good chance you don't have enough and its very fustrating. The main villain of the game was pretty evil and there's lots of plot twists/having to trust bad people to get through the game. The graphics look pretty next gen, so you need a powerful computer to play the game. Its overall decently optimized I would say, it doesn't have the stuttering problem that dead space remake had.

I do hope the game studio still makes a sequel and they listen to the criticism of their poor combat mechanism and improve upon it in the sequel. If they make a sequel I will still buy it

review_text:
I can sort of see the appeal, but absolutely not for me.
My issues:
1. The gameplay/run-n-gun loop has too many flow breakers: your first gun has a cold/hot/overheated state, but if you drop ADS, that resets. So you have to keep ADS up and firing. But it's also a super weak assault rifle that has to be reloaded all the time, so again - balancing that "hot" state feels needlessly fiddly. It's not impossible, just not very fun - kind of like trying to remember a slightly confusing schedule of when you have to take your bins out.
2. Healing is garbage: one health item, that doesn't fully heal you, and ALSO takes you out of the combat flow state to use? No thanks... Estus Flasks this isn't.
3. In-level perks are almost all garbage with a few exceptions, and the "see a third" material drops seemingly at random with no way to get some before you've already gained some perks. I don't really understand why it's even there
4. Enemies are pretty basic with a lot of homing attacks that while they aren't impossible to dodge, add another layer of annoyance on top of the flow-breakers above: if I'm facing an aquabus guy, for example, I have to shoot him; then break LOS to dodge the magic bullet he fires, then rub marmalade on my gun to unlock a 12% damage buff, then fire a few more bullets, reload (which interups Dodge), then change the oil on a 1980 Ford Escort to trigger my Marzipan Spell buff... and I found after a while I really didn't care.
5. Bosses are just random hit-spam nonsense - doesn't feel like Dark Souls where I can go defensive for a few runs to learn a pattern, then juice up and counter punch them. In this I just sort of have to hope I don't die and that I've got enough bullets and cranberry poptarts
6. WAAAY too little ammo for a game where the melee is time locked AND I'm forced to use a crappy full-auto SMG. I was dry half the time because I went to punch a low health guy but I hadn't waited the requisite 4-6 weeks for my punch to go from Anaemic Slap With A Herring to Actual Punch.

It probably will get better, the art is lovely, and the Devs obviously seem to care, but I just didn't get into the flow or the gameplay loop at all. I had a few massively successful runs and a few stupid deaths and I felt like I played the same each time

review_text:
Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun - A Stealthy Symphony in Feudal Japan
Step into the vibrant yet perilous world of 17th-century Japan with Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. This tactical stealth masterpiece, crafted by Mimimi Games, throws you headfirst into the shoes of six unique ronin and kunoichi, each with their own skills and personalities, tasked with eliminating powerful enemies and navigating intricate levels amidst a backdrop of political intrigue and personal vendettas.

A Shadowy Ballet:

Shadow Tactics' brilliance lies in its meticulous blend of strategy and stealth. Every level unfolds like a meticulously choreographed dance, demanding calculated planning and precise execution. You'll spend hours studying enemy patrol patterns, strategically positioning your characters, and chaining their abilities together to overcome seemingly insurmountable odds.

A Gallery of Lethal Artists:

Your six operatives are more than just pixelated pawns; they're living, breathing individuals with distinct strengths and weaknesses. Hayato, the agile ninja, scales walls and eliminates lone guards with ease. Yuki, the cunning kunoichi, distracts enemies and lays deadly traps. Mugen, the hulking samurai, slices through foes in a whirlwind of steel. Each character demands careful consideration, and mastering their synergy is key to success.

A Feast for the Senses:

Shadow Tactics is a visual and auditory treat. The hand-drawn art style is breathtaking, with lush landscapes, detailed environments, and expressive character animations. The soundtrack is equally captivating, blending traditional Japanese instruments with haunting melodies and heart-pounding action cues. Every element immerses you deeper into the world, heightening the tension and the thrill of each successful maneuver.

A Glimmer in the Darkness:

Despite its unforgiving gameplay and punishing difficulty, Shadow Tactics never feels unfair. Each challenge, no matter how daunting, feels meticulously crafted, offering multiple solutions and rewarding experimentation. The satisfaction of pulling off a flawlessly executed plan, perfectly synchronizing your characters' abilities to eliminate an entire patrol without raising an alarm, is unparalleled.

Not Without Scars:

However, Shadow Tactics isn't without its blemishes. The camera controls can be clunky at times, and the occasional technical hiccup can disrupt the flow of gameplay. The story, while engaging, takes a backseat to the stellar mechanics, and the ending might leave some players wanting more.

A Must-Play for Stealth Aficionados:

Despite these minor flaws, Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun remains a masterclass in the stealth genre. Its innovative gameplay, breathtaking visuals, and unforgettable characters make it a must-play for any fan of strategic thinking and nail-biting tension. So, don your ninja garb, sharpen your katana, and prepare to enter the shadows – Shadow Tactics awaits.

Verdict:

Pros:
Innovative and rewarding tactical stealth gameplay
Diverse and well-developed characters with unique abilities
Stunning hand-drawn art style and immersive soundtrack
Satisfyingly challenging without feeling unfair
Cons:
Clunky camera controls and occasional technical issues
Story takes a backseat to the gameplay
Abrupt ending might leave some players wanting more
Score: 4.5 out of 5 shurikens. A near-flawless stealth masterpiece that will captivate and challenge you in equal measure.

Recommended for: Fans of tactical games, stealth enthusiasts, and lovers of beautiful art and captivating soundtracks.

Not recommended for: Players who prefer action-packed gameplay or dislike challenging difficulty levels.

I hope this review gives you a glimpse into the captivating world of Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. Whether you're a seasoned shinobi or a curious newcomer, this game is sure to leave you speechless. So, prepare to unleash your inner shadow warrior and dive into this unforgettable experience.

This game isn't scary...  It's just *boring*.  The combat is extraordinarily clunky - you are in apparently a glass tank that can be damaged by a passing mosquito but which stops you moving, you have one bullet, and the enemies are numerous and vastly outgun you.  Which is odd, what with them being diseased fleshbags and me having all this armour and all.

There's nothing about that that builds a sense of horror, it just builds incredulity. And while making combat awful is a well-worn trope to encourage the player to seek to avoid it in favour of stealth or intelligence - there is absolutely no stealth or intelligence to exploit.  It's a run and gun for someone who can't run and packs a peashooter.

Avoid.  Not even in the same league as Bloober's others, let alone the games it wishes it was.

Oh, and this is terribly optimised even for Bloober.  RTX4090 and it struggles - and not because it's a pretty game.

shadow tactics: blades of the shogun is a stealth-focused real-time strategy/tactics game developed by the now-defunct mimimi productions and published by daedalic entertainment. it released in december 2016 for PC and then july 2017 on consoles. players control a group of characters as they perform different kinds of stealth-oriented acts such as assassination, espionage, and even things like stealing important documents and rescuing other ally characters. the game is set in feudal japan and tells an interesting narrative that keeps players intrigued throughout. 

i am extremely pleased with this entry in mimimi's catalogue, as it's a giant improvement and complete change of pace from their first game that i played, the last tinker: city of colors. i would say they went from that game being a chikdish 5 or 6 out of 10 kind of game, to developing a superb entry in the tactical-stealth sub-genre that i wouldn't say is anything below a solid 7/10. im excited to potentially get around to playing the expansion, desperados III, & shadow gambit, the other stuff mimimi put out before closing in 2023.

review_text:
Gameplay is kinda meh... it’s just so clunky. You get somewhat used to it, but still. Overall, I can’t recommend the game. If it’s on sale (at least 40% off), you can give it a go if you’re just looking for some "horror" shooter to kill time.

The horror also falls completely flat. The only part that felt somewhat like a horror-game was the hospital area. Most of the time, though, the game just throws cheap jump scares at you.
About halfway through, it gets especially annoying. The screen flashes with random screaming faces or sudden images, over and over again. It’s not scary, it’s just loud and irritating.

Enemies are weak and boring. They just slowly walk towards you while you stand there shooting them, maybe "running" a few steps back if they get too close, turn around, and shoot again. That’s literally every fight in the game.

Bigger enemies (“arena enemies”) are a joke. You just circle around an obstacle, wait to shoot an explosive barrel, rinse and repeat until it dies. Every bigger fight is like this, maybe the last two bosses are different, but that’s about it.
And you can see an arena fight coming from miles away: there are some red barrels in the next room... you know exactly what’s about to happen. Every. Single. Time.

The “survival” part of all this basically comes down to having limited ammo...that’s it. Health is never really a problem. I died 11 times in my playthrough, and I believe all 11 of those deaths happened in the first area, because I was trapped in a room with just a few bullets left, 1 HP, and the enemy kept one-shotting me. At that point, I was still getting used to the extremely slow gameplay. After that, if I recall correctly, I never died again.

The story is just convoluted for the sake of it. You never know why you’re doing the things you’re doing for the first three-quarters of the game. What’s the meaning behind it all, what are the Essences why are they there, what is the Collective, why am i awaken... and in the end it’s all about one dude simping for one girl...and why? Nobody knows... or maybe I just don’t, because the game never managed to immerse me...everything was just so overblown.
After the Station B area, I just wanted it to end...fast. The last part was just so tiresome and, again, convoluted... just because.

The only fun thing about this game was looting and upgrading your weapons. That was the only thing keeping me going.

I even tried to refund the game after the first hour of gameplay because it was just so bad at first (though I kinda got used to it in the end). I bought it together with Silksong, played Silksong first, and Cronos just sat in my library for two weeks or longer, so I couldn’t get a refund anymore.

So I just played it...

review_text:
I've been a player since week 1 of early access. Here are my thoughts.

This is THE best Starship Troopers game out there.

The gameplay loop, gun physics, and overall combat with the arachnid forces is satisfying. The side missions are interesting and bring variety to the game. Many of the mutators to the missions are great, but some of them are severe pain points. Those I will talk about first:

Mutators:
-These generally enhance either the players or the arachnids, or change the environment. Such as sandstorms, infinite utilities, more of a specific kind of bug, etc. However, part of the issue is mutator combinations leading to fully unwinnable situations. Tactics and skill should be the determining factor in whether or not the players can scratch out a win, not luck with the parameters of the mission. For example, gunners that spawn all the time that have mountains of health can lead to troopers fighting just the gunners to stay alive, which leaves all the other bugs unchecked.

Cool Concept - Poor Execution
-Perhaps it is just me, but the persistent arachnid bodies, while a cool bit that reinforces the lore (and provides a ramp for the bugs to use, a tactical challenge) and is visually striking can lead to problems. Many players don't know that they can clear those bodies, and when the bodies pile up, the game begins to lag significantly. My ping sits around 14, and I've got Tigers rubber banding at me like a yoyo, which is frustrating. A potential solution for this is to have them only pile near player structures. 

Now for some of the good bits:

I hate this planet... in a good way -- Each planet provides its own unique challenges. Valaka has a bit of everything, corners, structures, rocky formations, vertical challenges, tunnels, open spaces. Agni Prime has a bit more of a valley feel and its lava pools and foliage can provide interesting challenges. The lack of rocky formations limits cover and safe spots. X-11's tunnels and crater are unique as well, creating a central location to hunker down in, and a variety of close quarters paths for side objectives. Boreas' verticality is interesting in itself.

Gun Physics: Knowing how iron sights works improves your experience. Leading your targets increases your accuracy, especially based on distance. These are enjoyable gun physics that reward your skill level.

Movement: Feels natural. I can climb stuff I think I should be able to climb.. usually. There are more cases where I can than I can't. 

This review will switch if the major issues of unwinnable mutator combinations, and too many persistent bodies is fixed.

I love this game, but they ruined it. 

So, it used to be one of the few MMOs with solid combat, and from what I've seen of New Genesis, combat was improved. Everything else was just decimated though.

- Cool new combat changes.
- The world looks cool. Kinda has a Kingdom Hearts vibe to it.
Cons of New Genesis
- The game is significantly harder to run despite looking the same
- The new plot is very poorly written in contrast to the old one. The pacing is just awful and uninteresting
- The Phantasy Star has been sucked dry. It's just Xenogears now. I mean, there wasn't much Phantasy Star left, but they sure folded that toothpaste tube as hard as they could.
- This used to be one of the few lobby based MMOs out there. The appeal of having a lobby is that it prevents the god-awful treks that MMOs are known for. In base PSO2, there was little to no busy work, and it was incredibly easy to connect with friends and hop on a mission together. That is no more.
- MUCH WORSE MONETIZATION
- Significantly worse level design. Original PS02 was like an actiony 3rd person shooter, better than any single player 3rd person shooter I'd played, primarily because of the solid map design that rewarded situational awareness and allowed verticality.

review_text:
[h1] UPDATING MY REVIEW AFTER 90 HOURS [/h1] 
I previously gave the game a thumbs up and noted that despite it's flaws, it was a good game. However, I've now lost interest in the desire to continue to play it. 

The first 50ish or so hours in the first region was pretty fun. It's challenging, the story is decent, and the game play feels fresh and different. However, upon entering the 2nd region, I've grown very tired of the repetitive time-wasting "quests" , overly drawn-out cut scenes, and the main character, Henry, gets so insanely overpowered, there's not a single fight that is fun. 

All quests are fetch, find, and talk-to quests. Quite literally. Wow, so much fun. Worse of all, every NPC encountered in the quest just drag on and on in their dialogue, it becomes mouth-droolingly boring. You can tell they attempted to design each quest as if each have their own backstory and conclusion, but you have to listen to an NPC spend 5 minutes telling you the backstory about his brother you're trying to find, only to be told you now need to go talk to other NPC's across the map to find out more. 

Once you experience this 3 or 4 times, you start to see the pattern and I started to not look forward to any of the main quest of side quests, as they're all the same. There is never anything exciting or fun in them. And worse of all, there is ABSOLUTELY NOTHING satisfying in the conclusion of the quest. EVER. You might get a few hundred coins or a cheap piece of gear. That's all you're going to get for your 1-2 hours of listening to long and drawn out NPCs yap away about characters you're not invested in. 

I think the huge main city duels is a PERFECT example and representation of how lackluster every quest is in this game. In the largest city in the game in the 2nd region, there's these -- what's supposed to be massive spectacles of dueling tournaments where the entire city comes together and watches knights duel each other in various tournaments. When I found out I could join, it was the first thing I was looking forward to do in the game so I joined it. 

The day of the tournament came and they even have a graphical cutscene as if you're about to watch a massive gladiatorial spectacle. And then the game starts and a whopping 10 or so NPCs are standing around "cheering" - which is just depicted by 3 or so voice actors randomly whistling and cheering on either you or your opponent. The duel starts and....I beat the opponent in 2 or 3 hits in the 1st round of 3 in less than 10 seconds. I did the same thing in the 2nd and final round, eventually winning the tournament. 

That was it. It was over. This entire tournament the devs attempted to conjure as a massive spectacle was nothing more than a tiny little street fight that lasted all but 3 minutes and the game pretends you just won like Spartacus in gladiator arena. THIS is a PERFECT representation of every single quest in this game. This is how it ALL feels. 

Just to make my point, in one other example - the devs defend their "Savior Schnapps" save potion saying "We once saw a suggestion from a player that it would be really cool if taverns are save points. Where you go to the tavern to hang out and drink a beer and that's how you save the game". 

Cool! Except that's not even CLOSE to what taverns are like in this game. The biggest tavern in this game never has more than 2 or 3 people actually in the tavern. You can't visually drink (you can only drink from your inventory), the audio cues for taverns make them literally dead places (with 1 or 2 people talking quietly in the background), there's no music, no band playing, no drinking parties, no yelling or bar fights, etc. Compare this to something like Skyrim or RDR2's bars. They were LIVE and fun to visit. Taverns in this game is like nearly abandoned buildings. There's nothing in them, no people in them, no action or life in them. They're boring dead places that you will never look forward to visiting. 

Everything about this game is like it was written down and sounded good on paper, but the execution was a complete failure. 

I really wish they fleshed out their ideas better as the ideas are great. But when you actually play it, you start to realize what their intention was and realize what your actual experience is an they are very far apart.

You will fail (a lot), but the gameplay loop is satisfying enough to encourage you to try again, think more critically, and discover new strategies.
