Reflect Studios has managed to capture lightning in a bottle with [b] Dead Signal. [/b] It's a must-play for fans of psychological horror and a perfect entry point for those new to the genre. The game's atmosphere and gameplay makes it worthwhile to return again and again after each failed attempt. It's a tough game, but it's tough in the best possible way. I give [b] Dead Signal [/b] five deliveries to 2C... out of five.

review_text:
One of the most fantastic but frustrating games I have ever played.

To start off, the game is fantastic in the sense that 2K & Irrational games have created a game that is truly unique and vastly different than any other game at the time.  Almost 10 years later, Bioshock has aged very well and can easily be played for many more years to come.  The weapons & combat system offer great variety and satisfaction.  Shooting an enemy with a pistol to taking photos of hideous splicers for damage buffs, each weapon offers something unique for every combat situation as well as enjoyability.  

Visually, Bioshock is beautiful; considering it's age, the graphic design really is ground breaking compared to many other games that were made of the same year.  There are many small details that Irrational games added to give a strong emotional feel towards Rapture - the environment and atmosphere in particular.  The water and fire effects are pleasing to look at.  I believe the graphics in Bioshock will withstand the test of time.

The story is very well done.  From beginning to end you will most definitely be engaged,  I don't want to put any spoilers on this review so I will keep this part short; the game's story is very good.

Now,  this is the kicker for this game - not the game in particular, but, STEAM's version of the game.  There are MAJOR MAJOR MAJOR bug issues with this game on STEAM.  First of all, you cannot play this game without a microphone plugged in; don't even bother starting it up because you're game is just going to crash before you even hit the main menu.  

The next part is where Bioshock on STEAM will make you drop to your knees and cry.  The game WILL CRASH ON YOU.  I have tried everything in my power to make this game fully operational but nothing worked.  I had to save this game EVERY 30 seconds to a minute.  Since Bioshock does NOT have autosave you have to do it yourself; guess what happens when you forget to save the game? That's correct! You lose all your progress! YAY!

I somehow managed to finish this game, considering how much I enjoyed it while it managed to run for 10-15 minutes at a time before I had to reboot it.  If you can withstand this kind of frustration and headache then you will love this game - otherwise, just buy an XBOX 360 and play this game on the console.

5/5 Gameplay, Graphics and Story

0/100 for STEAM's horrendous port version of this game.

A really cool game coded by one guy. I love building kingdoms and one way to keep your people safe is zigzag your walls with towers allowing you to make a tower defence system to play around with which is a lot of fun. It was initially a bit difficult for me to get into but then it clicked and the use of god powers helped too. Also love having different golems too.

Some new player tips:
- Walls block off your build-able range so place torches outside of your walls.
-  If your people are dying from dehydration, you need to filter dirty water to make clean water. And if its summer or your kingdom covers a large area then build a bottler.
- Your people can starve even if you have food, I think the food needs to be transported to their houses. You can always use your god hand to pick up and drop food from the map into houses. You can also pick up and drop resources onto buildings under construction too

review_text:
Do you want to relive the joys of Action Man comics you read when you were 5? The plot of Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts is for you! Join the devoted fandom, including all 45% of people who actually completed the first mission, according to achievements. Enjoy infinite replayability as the borked checkpoint system forces you to go back through areas you cleared out entirely before you were suddenly sniped by a black spot half a kilometer away! Live the thrill of starting missions from scratch when you inevitably hit "restart mission" instead of "restart from checkpoint" for the third time, because the menu has both tabs right next to each other.

Challenge yourself with in game additional tasks that push you past the bounds of what you feel you can accomplish and, indeed, what the developers can reasonably expect anybody to achieve with the moveset and ruleset afforded to you. I particularly love how these challenges contradict each other, with "kill the target from 300 metres away" and "complete the mission using only a knife" being afforded to you in the same mission. This brilliant decision gives you an opportunity to further appreciate the boring levels as you trudge through them multiple times to get the completion above 50%. 

I love how you can sometimes spend ages scouring the map to find your target, only to find that they haven't spawned in yet. It gives you ample time to appreciate the clumsy movement system, invisible walls, and climbing mechanics that will fail and drop you to your death as often as they work. Once, a target spawned right behind me inside a cloud of red smoke and gunned me down before I could even spot him. This was an incredible display of this game's incredible AI which, apart from this spot of physics-defying genius, largely involved ignoring me as I shoot their comrade in the head mid conversation, and they stand there gawking for several seconds waiting for their turn. Sometimes, I can crouch walk right through their line of sight without issue and other times I find them suddenly spotting me from across the map without warning and alerting the entire base. 



EDIT: So I didn't expect this salty little rant to blow up as it did and somehow end up as one of the highest rated reviews. In the interest of fairness, I should also comment on some things I liked because this game isn't as terrible as I made it out to be above. While there are many more little frustrations I have not yet mentioned, I will still list some of the pros below. The things it does well, it does REALLY well. If this sort of thing appeals to you then it may be worth your time if you can abide the frustrations.  

I like how some aspects of the mission can change when attempted a second time. I am sure that will keep things fresh for those going for 100%

The actual sniping is excellent, simulating realism while still being very accessible. It is very satisfying to curve a bullet around a barrier to hit an enemy who thinks they are hiding.

Levels are enormous and open. Huge compounds can be approached from a number of different viable positions.

Just want to preference this by saying I did not expect this to be like Dead Space, so that's not where my disappointment in it comes from.

Honestly the story and atmosphere was great, but that was the sole reason I even made it over 4 hours, stopping just past the pipe slide. The actual gameplay and combat in my opinion is some of the most dull, unengaging stuff I've seen in a game for a long time. Most of the time it felt more like I was just watching the game play itself rather than actually participating.

Your input in any combat gets boiled down to hold a dodge button, doesn't matter which, and it'll work. Then if they keep swinging, just keep changing dodging direction until they're done. Then you get to just click the mouse to attack until they stop you, and its back to dodging. They try to mix it up with using your gun to get extra hits in, or using your gravity glove to grab and throw enemies. The first few enemies seem scary and threatening, but then it all becomes pretty mundane when you realize this is the whole game.

This game would be good for someone who isn't really looking for a challenge, they just want simple mechanics. Like I said, the story seemed interesting, but if I want to see the rest of it I'll probably watch someone else play it, because the only difference is that I wont be the one alternating a dodge button left and right, again, and again, and again...-_-

Not every game needs to be a Doom Eternal level of engagment, but after playing that on Nightmare and coming to this, it's a real drag.

review_text:
The atmosphere is outstanding. It could have been a great horror walking simulator with puzzle aspects. I want to recommend with a thumbs up, but I can't.

Here is what kills it:
- The combat is frustratingly cumbersome. Everything is slow. That includes stashing ammo, reloading, switching weapons. Everything has an animation that prevents you from running. Fighting more than 1 enemy is challenging in an unrewarding way. I feel like given the setting and atmosphere, I would have preferred having no weapon and playing hide and avoid the monsters. You can skip most of the encounters, but when it is unavoidable, you'll wish you were playing any other game.
- The story's pace is slow and bucket shaped, meaning the high points are at the beginning and at the end. It has a very long middle part filled with linear puzzles, redundant environment and out of place combat. It's a linear game where areas become inaccessible the more you progress, so wandering and exploring is not on the menu. Nothing is said about the setting and the story. You have to imagine it yourself. I personally like that, but you may not.
- The game is ridiculously short for the price. Just check my play record. at least 2 hours is me getting lost in the beginning and dying to enemies. Don't get unless it drops to 5$.

That being said, I would keep an eye out for another game set in this universe.

review_text:
BioShock, released in 2007, stands as a landmark title in the first-person shooter genre, praised for its atmospheric setting, gripping narrative, and innovative gameplay mechanics. Set in the dystopian underwater city of Rapture, the game offers a unique blend of narrative-driven exploration and fast-paced combat. However, the progression system, currency mechanics with many vending machiens, and its repetitive combat are points of contention among players and that I particularly disliked.

BioShock's greatest strength lies in its atmospheric design and stunning graphics. The underwater city of Rapture is a visually captivating and immersive environment, filled with intricate details that showcase the downfall of a utopian dream. The art deco architecture, flickering neon lights, and murky underwater vistas contribute to an unparalleled sense of place, creating a world that feels both haunting and alluring.

While BioShock's narrative is often lauded for its depth and twists, the utilization of audio logs falls short when compared to its spiritual predecessor, System Shock. System Shock adeptly integrated audio logs to provide context, world-building, and character development. In BioShock, while audio logs exist, their impact feels diminished, failing to create the same level of engagement or emotional connection with the characters and the unfolding story. Sometimes they add to world-building, sometimes they are required to progression, but this lack of consistency makes its use ambiguous and not as impactful as it was in the past. The narrative tries to be smart, but fails at the beginning to make you care about the protagonist. It feels pushed down your throat from the first time you leave the bathysphere.

One of BioShock's divisive aspects is its progression system, particularly the myriad vending machines and multiple currencies. The game introduces various upgrade options scattered across different machines, leading to a fragmented and confusing experience for players. With separate currencies for weapons, plasmids, and health, the system feels unnecessarily convoluted, hindering the flow of gameplay and diminishing the sense of accomplishment when obtaining upgrades. The fact you can only change your upgrades on a fresh playthrough might be a reason for some players to experiment with different builds, but for me just means I missed on a lot of content based on my upgrade path.

BioShock attempts to diversify combat through the introduction of plasmids, genetic modifications that grant the protagonist unique abilities. While initially intriguing, the combat system falls victim to repetitiveness. The limited number of plasmids and their predictable combinations result in encounters that become formulaic and lose their excitement over time. Despite the promise of varied combat, players may find themselves resorting to the same tactics repeatedly, detracting from the overall experience, without mentioning the limited amount of enemy types and clunky mechanics like research that completely kill the combat flow.

In conclusion, BioShock, with its captivating atmosphere, compelling narrative, and innovative setting, stands as a landmark title in gaming history. However, the game falters in its progression system, convoluted currency mechanics, and the repetitive nature of its combat. While the graphics and atmospheric design contribute to an unforgettable gaming experience, the missed opportunities with audio logs and the flawed progression system prevent BioShock from reaching its full potential. Some might say BioShock remains a must-play for those who appreciate immersive storytelling and atmospheric world-building in the realm of first-person shooters. I say there are better ways of spending 12-18 hours gaming.

review_text:
If you are willing to endure suffering caused by truly awful combat mechanics and an excessive number of puzzles, just so you can enjoy the visuals, then perhaps the game is worth considering for a purchase at 25€ or less.

I genuinely wish the game were simply a walking simulator with some lore, but unfortunately, it is not.

Developers, I implore you not to incorporate combat mechanics into a video game if you do not possess the expertise to make them enjoyable.

review_text:
TLDR: a somewhat shallow pve-centered autobattler with pvp at the end of a run. Great visuals, catchy music, sassy dialogue during events, which were a highlight of the game; decent variety of game modes and constant balance updates. Lacking in some qol and, if you go for 100% achievements, it overstays its welcome. Still would recommend DBS: it’s not groundbreaking, but well made.  Developers definitely care about the game.
What strikes right away is a very strong visual side of the game: the pixel art and animation quality is really high, with attention to small things – looks absolutely fantastic. The music is cool and catchy.
Most of playtime is pve with a boss at the end. It’s hard to fail a run, so, even though, most of the time is spent on building your team in pve, it’s all for the 2 mins or so of pvp at the end. The run usually takes, I’d say, about 40 to 60 minutes. Then you are paired against other players who have beaten the boss and, depending on the result of, usually 5-6 battles, you take a certain position in the rankings. It’s asynchronous: you don’t need to play at the same time. During subsequent runs, if you improve on your pvp part, your standings increase. Every 4 weeks or so there is a new season and generally, if you did all right, you move up the rank and repeat the cycle.
Your basic unit is a puny human whom you upgrade with items, which promote it to a certain class. Each class has 5 item tiers. By collecting several items with different tiers of a single class, you gain that class’ special ability. The variety comes from mutations, which you pick up as rewards: these come in form of passive bonuses, can give new abilities and synergies. During a normal run you easily acquire several dozens of mutations and these affect your build in a major way. In a sense, these are your build, and your team of humans is what actualizes it in game. You also have meta progression which affects only your current run.
Combat itself involves unit positioning: it matters (especially noticeable with smaller underpowered team) but the arrangement in the final build can be lenient as long as you put everyone where they generally should be. This was my first autobattler aside from small amount of hs: battlegrounds, so could be wrong on this one. 
Events are the highlight of the game. There are a lot of them: most occur at the beginning of a level and involve choosing options in dialogue that lead to different results. The writing and humor are great – enjoyed this part of the game very much. There are a dozen or so additional, level events which involve gameplay. These usually offer currency or an evolution, which is thematically connected to what an event was about. What I didn’t know for quite some time is that you can choose which level events you encounter: at levels 1,5 and 9  there is a lever in the wall. By pressing it you cycle through icons, each corresponding to a particular event. This way you can choose an event which is relevant to your build and not rely on rng. 
There are several game modes present: the standard 12-level run, but there is also a shorter, 7-level version: takes less time, but levels are more packed with stuff, so in the end it all more or less evens out. There are no food modes too. Food is a cost which you pay every time you move through a maze, 1 per unit, so balancing your upkeep with how big is your party becomes important. For achievement hunters: play with food as soon as you can: certain events proc only in food runs, otherwise you won’t be able to collect all mutations. There are pve only modes too, so technically you can ignore pvp part of the game, but imo that is the most fun aspect. Balancing is also made around pvp. There is also a mode, which closely resembles tft and autochess gameplay: you fight against other players every 3 encounters. The teams are smaller and much less powerful, so the dynamics is quite different from standard runs. I played just a few runs so don’t have too much to say about that.
Its fun exploring and discovering what works, which combinations are synergetic. Your best performing build during a season is what other players will fight against when they finish the run. This also allows you to prepare for certain players, whom you know you’ll eventually fight. Building counter strategies was the most fulfilling experience during my time with the game. I didn’t get to high rank, mostly because you are gated from doing it too fast (not a skill issue, trust me;) You can only move one rank per season at max.
Note about achievements: the bottleneck is killing wheelmen. These are rare and it’s easy to have 4 or 5 runs without seeing one. There is a trick which can cut your grind time substantially, of which I learned too late. Always pick and carry a button which restarts current floor, preferably two. Once you get a wheelman, using an item will allow you to kill another one (or more. I think I had just one run with 3, rarely 2). With even better luck you can go infinite: kill the boss before encountering a wheeler. If the boss happens to drop a restart item, pick it; go kill the wheeler and reset. You’ll spawn after the boss and will be able to pick a button again. Highly suggest taking advantage of this trick if you get it: the wheelers are THAT rare. 
Now for the criticism:
1)Despite many moving parts, there is not that much variety. It doesn’t take long to try all the classes and combos. Depending on the season, some builds are way stronger, which makes an amount of viable options even smaller. The strategy part of the game is not very deep. Not necessarily a negative, but I would like more depth.
2)I learned after 30+ hours that you can move with wasd. The first thing I do in any game I start is go to options, check those, and next – to controls. The game has a section with controls and shortcuts, but no wasd there, so I didn’t even consider trying that. Devs, PLEASE, inform me as a player of ALL hotkeys available in game.
3)There is no comprehensive in-game wiki. It shows all item tiers for respective classes but that’s all. So I can’t check the stats of units, I don’t know what class abilities do. Nowhere in game there is exact info on those. Sure, the game is rather casual, but it’s not that hard to include stats on all units and abilities. 
4)Your opponents’ builds in king of the hill (pvp part) are not saved anywhere. I don’t need infinite storage, but at least 5-10 of latest oppos’ builds should be saved, so I could check their mutations, meta and unit positioning. This can be solved by printscreening and then alt-tabing constantly while in-game and scrolling through couple dozen similarly looking screenshots. Not convenient at all.
5)Animations are great and I watch those for several runs, but then I want to skip through everything. There is an option to speed through events which very welcome and you can increase game speed; however it’s still WAY too slow. I’d say it’s marginally faster than what I would consider the base speed of the game should be. I’d prefer maybe x2 of current max speed. I would even use skip combat option, like in HoMM. Runs take too much unnecessary time. 
6)Some mutations are locked behind achievements, so I never used or encountered the wheeler one in game, because after the grind was over, I didn’t want to play anymore. Not enough variety or depth. The fix is simple: increase wheeler spawn rate or even make one guarantee to appear in any run.
Ultimately I would recommend the game. It has issues but the vibes are nice. I doubt many players will sink more than several dozen hours, but the time spent was fun. The writing, memes and references are great. Plus the game gets constant balance updates - developers definitely care. Good job!

review_text:
Pathologic 2 is a challenging game, but the difficulty is done in such a way that it adds to the experience rather than detracting from it.

The resource scarcity forces tough decisions, items you need to survive are also needed to save NPCs from the plague. Combat is high-risk, and dying comes with penalties that persist across saves. Every choice can cost vital resources, which are often better spent elsewhere.

Time is probably the most valuable resource. You won’t be able to do everything or save everyone. You have to prioritize which objectives to complete, often at the expense of others. Do you take the shortcut through plague-stricken districts at great risk to yourself, or take the long way around and spare your immunity boosters?

The game is bizarre, harsh, and utterly compelling. "Fun" isn't quite the word I’d use to describe it, the game seems to work against you at every turn, but overcoming its challenges is deeply satisfying, and it makes for a really memorable playthrough.

TLDR: Balanced, but grindy rougelike FPS with amazing leveldesign and atmopshere. It's good!

[b]Leveldesign![/b] I used to work as a leveldesigner. It takes a lot to get me giddy about leveldesign. Witchfire is amaaaazing in that respect. Easily the best part of the game. They crafted environments that are so full of detail, little stories, believable and grim.. from all the brickwork in the castle levels, to the decaying chappels, the narrow alleyways of medieval cities and sewers.. it all feels and looks absolutely amazing. And yet.. it also play great. Buy the game for the leveldesign alone!

 [b]Sounddesign[/b] Great. Nothing that stood out.. but that's a hallmark of great sounddesign. They nailed it! It's atmospheric, subtle, dark.. perfect.

 [b]Gameplay[/b] Okay so the gunplay is really good. Hitboxes seem a bit wonky sometimes. But nothing that would even be noticable to your average player. Every weapon feels balanced and is fun to play. The gameplay loop itself is fun.. however it feels very grindy. I'm at Gnosis V now and there are certain areas i just can't beat. So i'll have to run the same map 50 times to get the Witchfire to level up my survivability. Eh.. not the kind of gameplay i like. I get that they're creating a lot of replayability like that. But i'd rather have more story and a bit less grind. But then again.. the game is what it is and to complain about a banana not tasting like pineapple is silly when you bought yourself a banana.

review_text:
Short Version: Weird and annoying mechanics make the game a confusing on the best things to do during a level, like exploring and taking your time, or playing quickly using your crazy movement abilities. Levels are very samey and difficult to navigate due to being monotonous. Starting a new run after death is annoying due to two cutscenes and a separate little map you must go through before returning to the hub. It's strange over-all.

Long version: The health system is much better. You don't have to kill enemies right next to you or be forced to use the medkit equipment: you can gain health by using bandage equipment, picking up healthkits around the level, or pick up enemy health bits they drop. You can also find secrets and, for some reason randomly sometimes, get an overshield that makes you quite a bit tankier.

It still takes forever to get the points to buy items, use machines, etc. Keys, which function differently than how they did in the previous milestone, makethis annoying, as they are now a new currency of sorts. You get keys (rarely) from enemies and interactables or guaranteed from hanging red lights. They are used to open "bunkers," little sealed off areas with weapon upgrade benches, places to buy items/weapons, and multiple interactables, depending on your luck. The best way to get anything is to find a bunker, but for that you need a key, and the fastest way is to explore the level, which is quite risky if you do so too fast.

As you explore the level, it triggers enemy pods to spawn. Enemies no longer constantly trickle in around you like the previous milestone, they only seem to spawn for a little bit after a pod activates. If you got through the level and activate all the pods to explore and find keys quickly, you become swarmed by enemies and die quite quickly, too. If you take it slow and try to kill every enemy to get points/try for keys, that increases the enemy threat level quickly, making more enemies spawn per pod and lets more difficult enemy types spawn.
If you manage to activate all nearby pods and defeat them, you are left with an empty section of the level and are forced to progress to get anything of note by finding more pods. If you found a bunker but don't have a key, but get one later, you have to backtrack through a now empty part of the level with no enemies to fight. If you activated the last pod in a level, the only way to fight more enemies is to trigger the door-unlocking event...

The most annoying part is that, to unlock the door to beat a level, you are forced to kill a set amount of enemies, an annoying element from the previous milestone that carried over. This forces you to raise the enemy level, making the door-unlocking fight even more swamped with enemies and making it possible for new enemy types to spawn as you kill the amount needed. Unlike teleporter events from Risk of Rain, which are usually quite fast and end upon killing a boss rather than a massive swarm of enemies, these can last quite a bit if you've had rotten luck and were unable to get any weapons or equipment during the level. Unlike Risk of Rain where enemies get harder as time progresses in the run and constantly spawn near you and trickle in, in this it seems to be a bizarre system where you're punished in terms of difficulty for going fast and also punished if you are meticulous and go slow. Each enemy gives a measly amount of points, and as the level increases those points become much more dangerous to get for the same amount per enemy.

There are new enemy types and all enemies have been redesigned. In most cases, their inspiration is obvious, which leads to enemies like Imps standing out noticeably from the rest, where most are inspired by the Covenant from Halo. Enemies can now teleport short distance and climb around, making them annoyingly mobile and relentless, capable of stalking you for a good while and fire pot-shots at you from extreme distances if they can't get to you due to water or pits. At least they all use projectiles. Weapons have had a complete visual replacement. Where before they had their inspirations, like the Heavy Rifle being the Covenant Carbine (except ballistic), most newer designs are more generic. Weapons are more "modern" and feature tac-rails and the like rather than being simplistic and more imaginative. A lot also appear completely dark rather than being colorful with tron-style glowing parts, which seems odd to me.

The levels are still aimless blobs of various parts that lack significant landmarks besides the rare open clearing or orange bunker doors. It is very difficult to get your bearings in a level otherwise, as everything tends to be a monotonous black with occasional highlights besides the wall-run green/white billboard-things.

If you die during a run, you have to watch a prolonged dieing cutscene, end up in a permanent upgrade shrine area, use the shrine, even if you can't buy anything, have a loading screen, and then end back in the hub map after another cutscene. You can't skip either cutscene (as far as I know), so you have to go through all these steps before you can start another run every single time. I'm confused as to why you enter the small shrine map between the cutscenes when the hub also has a shrine that offers the same permanent upgrades to buy.

I really don't get the purpose of how the mechanics work and function together. Similar to ADACA, there are a whole bunch of ideas crammed into one package that makes the whole thing a bit muddled. 
Should I play fast like the movement wants me to, or slow so I can get points to actually get things? 
Should I be backtracking so much for bunkers or just move on to the next level with no real gain? 
Is it better to kill enemy pods for maximum points or leave stragglers so you don't raise the enemy level too quickly?
I am just left confused on what the best and intended way to play actually is, and the game doesn't offer help in that regard.

review_text:
Eastside Hockey Manager, developed by Sports Interactive and available on Steam, is a deep and comprehensive simulation game that puts players in full control of managing a professional ice hockey team. For fans of the sport who relish the behind-the-scenes decision-making—from roster building and scouting to financial management and tactical planning—this title offers an unmatched level of depth. Though it lacks the glossy presentation and mass-market appeal of mainstream sports titles, it more than makes up for it with its authenticity and meticulous attention to detail. It’s a spiritual sibling to Football Manager, built around the same philosophy of realism and strategic control.

At its core, Eastside Hockey Manager allows players to take charge of nearly any professional or junior team from a wide range of leagues around the world, including the NHL, AHL, SHL, Liiga, KHL, and countless others. The breadth of leagues and player databases is staggering, and Sports Interactive has clearly made a concerted effort to reflect the real-world structures and dynamics of global hockey. Whether you're managing a perennial NHL contender or a small-market European team, the game adapts to your environment, with different rules, financial constraints, and player development paths. This global authenticity provides significant replay value, allowing players to test their managerial skills in vastly different hockey cultures.

Gameplay is structured around daily team management tasks. You’ll be handling contract negotiations, training schedules, scouting reports, player morale, and even media interactions. The game features an in-depth scouting system that mimics real-world evaluation techniques, including tracking player potential, mental attributes, and developmental ceilings over time. Drafting young prospects and nurturing them into first-line stars years down the line is one of the most rewarding aspects of the game. It requires patience, long-term vision, and strategic roster balancing, especially under salary cap constraints or when dealing with injuries to key players. The level of micromanagement can be overwhelming for newcomers, but for experienced sim players, it's a dream come true.

The tactical aspect of Eastside Hockey Manager is equally complex. You're not just setting lines—you’re building chemistry, creating power play and penalty kill strategies, deciding on forechecking intensity, and adapting your style to your roster’s strengths. Matches can be simulated quickly or watched play-by-play, with commentary that reflects real-time decisions and player performances. While the in-game visuals are limited to 2D representations and text-based feedback, they provide enough context to understand what’s working and what’s failing. The tactical feedback loop is robust, with detailed statistics, form trends, and opposition analysis allowing you to refine your approach game by game.

Visually, the game is utilitarian. The interface is dense and packed with data, with hundreds of screens dedicated to stats, reports, and rosters. While it can feel dated and intimidating at first glance, the design favors function over flair. Once you're familiar with the layout, navigation becomes second nature, and the sheer amount of available information becomes one of the game’s greatest strengths. However, this no-frills presentation may deter casual players or those expecting a more dynamic graphical interface. Still, for the hardcore hockey strategist, the spreadsheets and data tables are part of the appeal.

One of the standout aspects of Eastside Hockey Manager is its community and modding support. The game’s built-in database is already extensive, but player-made updates, real-world rosters, and even custom leagues add tremendous value. The user-driven updates help keep the game relevant long after official patches slow down. Community forums are active, offering advice, guides, and tools that help new players overcome the steep learning curve. Whether you're adding junior leagues, tweaking league rules, or importing historical data, the modding flexibility opens up near-limitless possibilities for long-term play.

That said, Eastside Hockey Manager is not without shortcomings. Its learning curve is steep, and the game does little hand-holding for newcomers. Tutorials are limited, and much of your early experience will involve trial and error. The lack of dynamic media narratives, visual flair, or player personalities—features that titles like Football Manager have increasingly embraced—can make some seasons feel clinical or detached. Additionally, the game occasionally suffers from user interface lag or minor bugs, especially when managing large databases or simulating multiple leagues.

Despite these limitations, Eastside Hockey Manager remains the definitive experience for players who want total control over a hockey franchise. Its unmatched realism, strategic complexity, and deep customization tools offer a uniquely satisfying simulation experience. It demands time, attention, and a love for the minutiae of the sport, but rewards that investment with a gameplay loop that feels endlessly rich. For hockey fans looking for a cerebral, spreadsheet-driven experience rather than arcade thrills or quick wins, Eastside Hockey Manager is not just a game—it’s a long-term project that captures the soul of managing a team in one of the world’s most dynamic sports.

Rating: 8/10

review_text:
[h1]Non-flexibility at killing gets annoying after a while[/h1]

I like the animation. And the sounds are good too.
The game does have a good suspense - horror atmosphere.

The story is simple. You're the son of the devil and you've to kill everyone in the mansion.
You do that by wandering in the mansion, picking up stuff into your inventory and then using it and your powers (which you get after killing a certain number of people) to [i]figure out the correct way[/i] to kill the person.

Which is difficult since the person can be killed in a particular way only and you have to guess that exact way. I didn't find the hints that helpful.
Once, I had to break a lawn-mower and I spent more than an hour [spoiler]trying to hide at different places to use Telekinesis to break it and each time I would get caught. Finally I gave up and learned from a guide that I had to place a fricking stone (that I had picked up a long while back) in the specified position so that the mower run's over it and breaks![/spoiler]
Basically, there is no flexibility in the way you kill people and it's difficult to guess the [i]correct way[/i] and that can make it a bit annoying at times.

Also, the mansion is huge! Going around from one place to another takes time and feels annoying and you may have to interact with a lot of items to find those that you can put in inventory.

Running the gamut, EHM takes what's good about Be A GM mode in EA's NHL series and turns it up a level. Despite the minimalistic animations of the game, which essentially consist of watching 10 dots with small sticks running around the ice,  the clear meat of the game is within the management aspect of the game, hence the title.

From assigning individual scouts to scour specific countries, leagues, teams or even individual players, to keeping up to date and managing contracts on an annual basis. You will need to continuously conduct scouting missions in order to have information on upcoming prospects, if not, come the annual draft you will find yourself staring at barebone details regarding individual players. When it comes to contracts, be sure to re-sign and add free agents or claim players from waivers as needed, you'll regret it down the line if you forget to re negotiate with one of your star players. 

Players in EHM do not have a single 'overall' skill number and instead have over 25 different skills ranging from things like Slapshots, Flair, or Stamina. As well, the coaching staff, including physiotherapists are also ranked with a number of different skills. 

This is a great hockey management simulation, at a very reasonable price. However I almost wish I never discovered EHM, because now I have no life.

10/10

I definitely recommend this game, even if games like these aren't typically what you would think of playing, and definitely if it's on sale, I believe the story makes it absolutely worth experiencing.

Samorost 2 is pretty cool. People will go on and on about it, out-snobbing each other with cries of BURRR THIS IS A FLASH GAME IT SHOULD HAVE BEEN ON NEWGROUNDS, REAL GAMES FOR HARDCORE GAMERS ONLY PLEASE!!!!, but ignore them. They're dumb.

I love the way Amanita Design makes their games - a lot of love clearly went into the worldbuilding. You're a little man in his PJs exploring floating mushrooms that have been uprooted from the ground and left in space! Your spaceship is made out of a discarded can of weenies! There's a sewage tank and the water stains look like a pastoral farmscape! So many little beautiful details that are worth the price of admission alone.

I'm not so much a fan of the puzzle-solving. Most of the puzzles are fine and are nice little breaks from the art, but sometimes they are a bit of a pain when trying to decipher context clues in a small Flash window. (FYI, this game was released ten years ago and it holds up well, though it's hard to see things sometimes.) Sometimes, there's areas that you need to click on that weren't clickable before and the game doesn't bother to tell you whether or not they're activated. It's not a perfect system, but it's fine.

Samorost 2 is uneven but overall fine. If you want something with more difficulty, check out their games Machinarium and Botanicula. There will be a sequel for this one coming out very soon, too.

review_text:
To The Moon, developed using RPG Maker, may not boast cutting edge graphics or elaborate gameplay mechanics, but it delivers something far more enduring: a deeply emotional narrative interwoven with philosophical depth and introspective storytelling.

The game follows two doctors, Neil Watts and Eva Rosalene, who work for a company that grants dying patients their last wish by altering their memories. Their latest client, an elderly man named John, wishes to go to the moon but doesn't know why. The story unfolds as Neil and Eva dive into his memories, moving backwards through his life to uncover the origin of his mysterious desire.

What makes this narrative structure so captivating is its meta layer: we, as players, are essentially watching two characters experience a man's life as if viewing a film. Their commentary serves as both comic relief and philosophical reflection, drawing us deeper into the story. It feels almost like watching your favorite Twitch streamer or YouTuber play through a game except here, the game is someone's life, and the stakes are heartbreakingly real. (But imagine watching your favorite Youtuber or Twitch Streamer playing the game and controlling Neil and Eva who are watching Johns Memories through the Memory Machine. So many layers)

The emotional impact is heightened by the game's masterful duality between romance and realism which is a reccuring theme in the game. At the heart of the narrative is the complex relationship between John and his wife River. These two characters embody the game's central philosophical theme:

John, the dreamer, represents romanticism. His longing to "go to the moon" is not just a literal wish, but a symbol of his search for purpose and transcendence. He's driven by emotion, nostalgia, and the yearning to rewrite a life filled with missed connections and unanswered questions.

River, by contrast, is the anchor of realism. Her actions often seem puzzling or emotionally distant, yet they're grounded in quiet intention and a deep, unspoken understanding of life's limitations. She clings to truth, even when it's painful. Her struggle with her autism spectrum disorder is portrayed with subtlety and respect. River doesn't seek to reshape the past or escape into fantasy; instead, she holds fiercely to moments of sincerity and authenticity.

Their relationship is where the emotional weight of the game truly lies. John wants to change the past so that he can find a sense of fulfillment, but River quietly accepts the imperfect present. This conflict becomes a lens through which the game explores profound philosophical questions: Is it better to remember a comforting lie or a painful truth? Can a rewritten memory give life meaning or does meaning come from how we face reality?

Despite its many strengths, To The Moon is not without flaws. The story, while moving, can at times feel overly sentimental or emotionally manipulative, leaning heavily on tragic tropes to evoke a response. Some plot points especially involving River's condition and John's childhood could have been explored with greater depth and nuance. Additionally, the setting, though charming in its pixel art simplicity, sometimes feels too static or sparse, which can make the world feel a bit underdeveloped compared to the emotional weight it carries. Some of the situations between Eva and Neil can be a little cringeworthy, but at least they break up the serious tone from time to time.

And of course there are also the logical questions that naturally wonder whether it wouldn't somehow be illegal to access the memories of others due to data protection laws or human rights and why a company would specialize in this and conduct research without thoroughly protecting itself from the law and consequences. Yes, there's certainly something to that, but this is a romanticized story and not everything has to make sense. Deal with it, you realist.

That said, these shortcomings are relatively minor when weighed against the game's overall achievement. To The Moon may be humble in presentation, but it reaches emotional heights few big budget titles dare to attempt. It's not just a story about a man who wants to go to the moon, it's a meditation on love, memory, regret, and the quiet power of a life lived.

Over the weekend I started playing Kingdom come deliverance 2 on PC and I cam to realize this game basically pulled off what most of AAA games publishers already long forgot.

They created a fully realized world, super detailed with actually interesting quests and dialogue that on the same level as Witcher 3 side quests. Even small side quests could become like a 2 hours detour and they are actually interesting. Your choices in the game actually means something and could effect the world around you and how things developed and determine the end results of a quest. Cyberpunk 2077 tried that and based all of their PR on that notation but in reality they were not even close to what KDC2 pulled off here . Even how you look and what you wear and in what condition could effect how NPC will talk to you. This is something that has been long forgotten in modern video games where the only things that matter is graphics and cosmetics.

The combat is really refined now and works so much better than when the first game came out. The NPC reactions to hits and battles are also really impressive like when you pull off master strike or perry or an interesting combo they actually react to that.

on the technical side the PC ports works very well, no stuttering at all consistent frame rate and frame time while the world and the game looks very realistic. I am playing on i9 14900kf and RTX4080 16gb and able to get locked 60 fps in 4k on ultra. it's honestly so rare this days to get a good working PC port.
If you have a good gaming PC, you should very much check out this game, it's really a fantastic game.

I have been playing 12 hours in one sitting yesterday I don't think I had this much fun in an open world game since RDR2 or Witcher 3 and in a day where all of the AAA games are focused only on graphics and cinematics this is a very rare game.

This is my game of the year!

I'd recommend the first in the series if you want a more full and enjoyable experience that's still free.

review_text:
I like and also don't like this game. It's hard to explain, so I'll be simple about it.

You attack really slowly, so you have to plan your attacks in advance. Only problem with this is that you encounter new enemies pretty fast and their attack patterns are so fast that you can't react right away. Some have multi-hit attacks. For instance, I encountered some slime girls, and they were easy enough to figure out, but then I found a blue one and immediately expected something different, but wasn't expecting it to be a close range activated attack that hit SIX TIMES while I was in the air and could do nothing about it. At that point I decided that playing this game wasn't worth the effort, there are other, better games that do similar things, so I'll just play those. But that's not all the issues I saw.

Second most egregious issue I found was that checkpoints and save points don't heal you - at all. You collect plenty of health resources and all from killing monsters and exploration, but... The items aren't very good. It's not forgiving at all. Even Dark Souls' campfires healed you, so what's the deal?

Third strike for me was the fact that most traps aren't obvious at all. I could see where the spikes come up from the ground all over the place except one, and when I hit it, I almost threw up from how bad that design is.

Ways this way could be better? Make those checkpoints HEAL you. Have mana replenish itself slowly automatically. What's the point of having fireballs if I can't use them on flying enemies when I need to? The enemies attack faster than you do, rhythmically. Either increase our attack speed, or reduce theirs. Heavy weapons suck and have arguably 0 use case, since they're insanely slow to use for all the power they've got, resulting in them being lesser picks.

The only thing I liked about this game really was the artwork and atmosphere. Should have gone with Ender Lillies or something.

review_text:
A good game with great graphics, decent story, but becomes repetitive after some time. 

The graphics were something that made me want to buy this game alone. I had not heard of any reviews from people or had done any research for this game, but when I saw the graphics… I was amazed enough to buy it at that moment. 

The gameplay and all seem to replicate that of the Dead Space franchise. Headshots can count, but if the enemies don’t have limbs, they will die. And the gravity arm? This was what I wanted from Dead Space… I love the upgradability of the weapons too, seems rather nice but ofc, the first weapon that they give you is basically enough to last the entire game. 

The story was alright, follows the same story as with every other game… damsel in distress, someone important dying, antagonist suddenly coming back to life, oh and what’s that? The antagonist also becomes stronger? But still, I was still hooked on it even if other may find it basic. I think after playing games for a while, you kinda start to see a pattern with game, since… that’s the recipe of a game that works best.

It’s quite a melee-based game overall… apart from the big boss areas but the game will try and keep you stocked up on ammo and healing equipment as needed, that or you just keep throwing random stuff at the boss, but the boss battles will take much longer. 

There really isn’t anything new that stands out from this game. Was a fun experience and definitely worth trying, just don’t expect to be wowed if you were expecting to find something new. 

I also wish there wasn’t so much crawling through vents in the game… such a slow and bland process. Don’t get me wrong, I get why… the ship is infected or broken or damaged in such a way that, of course, every single door or hallway will not be accessible, but still… might’ve been better if the MC would be able to crouch instead or if you could fight in the vents to make it more difficult or tense. Since for now, if you get into a vent, you would know you’re safe. 

Overall, it was still a fun game.

review_text: This game recently popped back up for me and made me remember everything that happened with it so I figured I would share what happened. My situation is not unique though as I'm sure many other players dropped the game for the same reason. I started playing the original PSO2 about 6 months before NG came out. Every few weeks I would drop back into the game and grind really hard for some AMAZING F2P content. PSO2 was genuinely one of my favorite MMOs I've ever played and I was starting to get really sunk in and learning all the deeper things in the game. NG comes out and it just completely kills the game for me. Not only were you forced to download the new game, you were forced to play it for about an hour to get access back to the original PSO2. Logging in, wanting to play PSO2, only to be met with a different game that I was forced to play to get access to my account. I instantly uninstalled the game. PSO2NG also didn't run the best on my system so it was such a bad experience just to get back to PSO2. Seeing some of the new trailers that are out new, it looks like there is some cool stuff, but the reviews speak volumes and I will never forget what I was forced to go through.

review_text:
10/10 Sekiro if it was good /hj

If you like Edo period Japan, this is the game for you. If you've never played a stealth game before like me, you don't have to worry, Shadow Tactics does a great job introducing its mechanics and you'll never be overwhelmed. The characters are also very well written, the interactions between Hayato, Yuki, and Mugen are really sweet and you'll come to love all of the characters.

The stealth is excellent, in each mission you have access to a unique combination of the five main characters with complementary abilities. Often, you'll get stuck on an area trying to figure out what the right approach is, and then suddenly the solution will come to you. It's so satisfying to get that aha! eureka moment and watch the crew slice through an area.

I originally got this game on Epic a few years back when it was available for free, but picked it up on Steam when it was on the sale for $4, which happens very often. This game is great value, if it's on sale, buy it. It's sad to hear that mimimi are closing their doors but I wish the devs the best in their future endeavors and thank them for this wonderful game

review_text:
I actually really liked this game until just now. 

I really enjoyed experimenting with how to conquer as fast as possible one region with balanced economy. 
But then when I was about to win and destroy last corner covered with corruption. I sent 4 builders to build a Stone Wall so I could attack with long distance Ballista tower however they instead of building the wall attacked one of the last 2 Graveyards and one after other hit the Graveyard and with each hit there came small army of enemies = 4 hits = +/-25 monsters (Out of it was like 8 Fire Elementals and 5 Skeletons) = Which destroyed my entire defense with blink of an eye :/ 
Over 14 hours put into this region for what? Not being able to set priorities to Workers what to do when I give them specific work? Why do I select Workers as "Builder", "Farmer" when they still do what they want? 
There should be possibility to choose if I want Worker to fight or not - Not that they decide themselves (Some run away from threat, some march towards it). 

Until this moment I would give positive feedback, but if you choose in any scenario to build something close to an enemy structure, Builders just go attack that structure instead of building a building with highest set priority.

Also there is no way to "Cancel" dismantling an already build wall or wall with resources already on place (Or any structure). Only way how to destroy/dismantle something is that you take all the resources with your "God power", like... Why? Are my Workers that stupid that they don't know how to use a hammer and smash things to pieces? 

One last thing which is quite bothering is that if you select rock or tree to harvest, there is no way to cancel it after. So after you select harvest something, it will be harvested sooner or later. So if you decide to be more strategic in the future in the game, that you decide that "Rock" or "Tree" could be like a piece of wall, you can't because you never know when your Workers will decide to harvest it since you can't cancel that harvest... Eh, great...Also if you select too many trees to be harvested they randomly go harvest those trees all over the map instead of most closest place to the structure they are building... *facepalm*

I DON'T RECOMMEND THIS GAME:
 - If there will be priorities what Workers should prioritize (If fight or do their selected work first) and 
- "Cancel" button when you choose to dismantle things and 
- "Removal button" for already selected harvested areas.
After this I would recommend this game.

Let me start with this.
Despite what SEGA wants you to believe New Genesis is not PSO2. They could have easily called it Phantasy Star Online 3, it is a completely different game that shares the same launcher with the original PSO2. 
I think because they chose to call it "Phantasy Star Online 2: New Genesis" it created a stigma that the game has yet to live down. The head developer claimed it was to allow the players to keep using their purchases "Glamour mostly". 
They share the same launcher there was no need to keep the name Phantasy Star Online 2 attached to NGS. it isn't like other games haven't continued stories in the same universe but had different names and separate game play.
Here is how I rate this
Phantasy Star Online 2 8.5/10
New Genesis 6/10 and that is me being generous
What does NGS have over PSO2 Classic. Superior controls and better graphics. the UI feels like a huge step backwards though. What NGS doesn't have is a very good story unlike PSO2 Classic which has a pretty good story. 
I would recommend it to players knowing this. The devs have all but abandoned PSO2 for NGS Occasionally they have good stuff going on in PSO2 but some of it is really hard to do solo. NGS is mostly a solo game honestly with a few things that are less desirable and way too difficult. Some things are set up solo that absolutely should not be while other things that would be easy to solo with good gear are set up as 8 or more player instances.....
Again, NGS is good but it's no PSO2.
This review is my personal opinion and does not reflect that of the community at hand.

Don't be scared off by the "Early Access".   Iknow the tag has been abused by many devs in recent memory, but this is not really a new franchise.

EHM is a game series that has been around since 2004 with EHM: Franchise Edition, and in spirit since 2001 when the original freeware EHM was released.  After EHM:FE, SI Games released EHM 2005 and then EHM 2007.  The fan community has kept 2007 alive and updated since then.  So this is not a brand-new, from scratch game.  This is a game built on an already successful core from EHM 2007.  Riz and the SI guys are not new at this, and SI is the company behind the super-popular, long-running Football Manager series.  EHM:EA marks essentially the 4th release in the EHM series after a hiatus of many years,

There is not a more-detailed, in-depth hockey management simulation game available on the market, period.  As with any sports management sim there is a learning curve.  But once you get it, you'll be willingly sinking a whole lot of time into it.

Don't touch this game.

The issue isn't the game itself; which is great. The issue is a complete lack of customer support when you engage through STEAM.

To use their "customer support" link, you must have an account through the game developer itself. To have that accound, you must create it on their website. When you do so, you can link it to STEAM; but that means the existing account becomes UNlinked. It appears that they can no longer find your STEAM account and provide you with logon information.

If you go directly to their website and chat, as soon as they find out that you created your account through STEAM, they apologize that there is nothing they can do for you.

I have concerns about products I have purchased with real money that I should have access to, as per the text ("unlocked for all characters on the account") which I don't have. The game provider will give me all the support I want or need -- after I abandon my current account (of which I have invested literally hundreds of dollars AND hours) and start fresh; thus losing every bit of my investment.

These issues sincerely need to be addressed and fixed before anyone even considers spending one dollar on this game. You may not get what you paid for, and there is nothing that anyone can or will do about it if you don't.

Until these issues are fixed, steer clear.

Pso ngs weapons suck, endgame sucks, gameplay is fun but it's all pointless because Sega doesn't know how to make an endgame enemy without one hit kills. Weapons all have 0.1% battle power increase and are otherwise useless. Classes don't matter as they're all forced to play the same (close range and must parry regardless off class). No weapons are unique with special abilities anymore (heaven punisher from Pso1 had a chance to rain beams of light from the sky to attack the enemy on hit).

All new weapons are ugly ad, potentially intentional due to weapon skins. Pso seems to have gone away from photon blades entirely.

Purple enemies / triggers / etc are completely pointless as they drop nothing worthwhile, and even if they did the drop rates are so abysmally bad that most people probably wouldn't care. Fixas are so rare that I haven't seen a single one during this entire seasonal event.

Elemental weapons are weaker than non elementals. Elemental effects don't do DOT such as burn or poison.

I want to love ngs since I've been playing since GameCube but in all honesty the only reason I stick around is for my old psu buddies who came back for ngs. But in reality we're all incredibly disappointed.

Story lacks depth and character development. The story and characters feel shallow and one-dimensional, with little motivation or backstory provided for the main protagonists.

Dialogue can feel stilted and unnatural.

Pacing of the story, the plot moves too quickly, and that important events happen without proper buildup or explanation.

In addition, awkward translations and inconsistencies in dialogue and characterizations.

As they delve deeper into the mystery, they discover that the planet is being consumed by a dark force known as the Void.

Act 1: The player starts on the surface of the planet Coral, where they explore the abandoned ruins of a once-thriving civilization. The ruins are haunted by strange creatures that seem to have been mutated by the Void. As they venture deeper into the ruins, they find clues that lead them to a laboratory where the scientists were conducting experiments on the Void. The laboratory is now overrun by mutated creatures, and the player must fight their way through to find the data logs left by the scientists.

Act 2: The data logs reveal that the Void is a powerful energy source that was discovered on Coral. The scientists were studying it, hoping to harness its power for the benefit of their civilization. However, they soon discovered that the Void was uncontrollable and dangerous. It began to spread across the planet, consuming everything in its path. The scientists tried to contain it, but it was too late. The Void had already spread too far.

Act 3: As the player continues their investigation, they discover that the only way to stop the Void is to destroy the source of its power. The source is a massive machine hidden deep beneath the surface of the planet. The player must fight their way through hordes of mutated creatures and overcome deadly traps to reach the machine.

Conclusion: As the player destroys the machine, the Void begins to recede, and the planet Coral starts to heal. However, the player soon discovers that they have been trapped on the planet. The machine's destruction has created a rift in space-time, and the player is now lost in the void between dimensions. The game ends with the player stranded and alone, drifting through an endless void, haunted by the memories of the creatures they fought and the planet they failed to save.

Although I really like this game and Star Trek in general, the problems I have with it are the same I have for any other Perfect World game I've played. Like Neverwinter. I was a HUGE Neverwinter Nights fan and was insanely excited to play the MMO...and it is actually a brilliant game.

Cryptic are brilliant devs and make a mean game but I believe it's PWE screwing it all up.

Firstly they're all pay to win...don't care what you say...they're pay to win. Sure you can play the game 24/7 and grind your life away and you won't have to pay but come one be serious. Throw €500 at one of their games and you'll be top of the score board in no time.
Secondly the games and full of bugs. They may or may not fix the bugs but normally they just leave them till the next expansion comes out and they just leave the bugs in the past.
Thirdly they suffer from connection problems. I'm not sure how to explain this one properly as I don't know anything about how game servers work but at least once a day your connection will keep timing out. You'll lose the connection and won't be able to log back in for ages. You'll contact support and they'll blame your ISP so you'll contact your ISP but they'll quickly point out that none of the other programs on your computer are having internet problems. Just today I decided to give STO another shot and I can't even get the STO launcher to download. First it will take like 15 minutes to download 50Mb then it will tell you that the connection timed out and it cannot connect with the server. I've tried this several times today over the span of around 10 hours. So here I am writing a review. I've had enough and I'm never playing any PWE game again.

This does make me sad because like I said before I really do think STO and Neverwinter are fantastic games and I love the worlds they are set in. I just can't deal with this crap anymore.

I know this has been more about PWE than Star Trek Online but I think the main problem wit STO is that it's owned by PWE. PWE just need to get lost and trade on the stock exchange or speculate on sub prime market bull crap and get the heck out of the gaming industry because they've ruined at least two games I love and would love to play. I would pay a lot of money to play STO and Neverwinter is they were done properly.

Boom that's it.

review_text:
This game is very cool. The music slaps supremely, the character design is crazy, the graffiti is awesome. But overall, I don't recommend it myself. The storyline is pretty bare bones, and the actual pacing of the dialogue (or rather the spaces between dialogue) realllly emphasizes how stilted it is. On top of that, the gameplay itself is really shallow. As a huge fan of the old Tony Hawk games and SSX Tricky, I was disappointed that the only actions in this game are: graffiti, jump, air dash, grind, manual, wallride, trick 1, trick 2, and trick 3. The main way to get a good score is to lean into corners. I shit you not, an excellent combo consists of grinding, pushing the stick left or right a couple times, and spamming the Y button. Lastly, the weird combat sections with police are even more formulaic - sometimes you jump into someone, and then you spam B to punch them all a billion times. 
So between the story and mechanics, I unfortunately didn't find it very compelling. It feels like the world's coolest demo that never got developed and polished into a real game.

review_text:
Witchfire is a game that I think has a lot of fun mechanics...in small, SMALL doses.

The developer says they believe it's "Fairly priced" but it's more like a demo in it's current state. $40 is a lot to ask for what is essentially a handful of stages with no variance. It bills itself as an extraction roguelike. It has little to no features of either.

Weapons are pre-set, and upgradable, and the overall core mechanics are fine, but the roguelike elements rear their heads at the very start of the run and pretty much never again. The upgrades are limited in quantity and the effects they provide tend to be very similar or unimpressive.

One thing I WILL praise the game for is it's graphics, sound design, and atmosphere. But that only lasts so long for a game based on doing the same thing over and over. A vista may be beautiful, a cavern haunting...but only the first handful of times you see it. After that, it becomes just another PNG. Just another hole.  And once you've seen the handful of events on a stage, it's done. There's not enough content to draw me back. The leveling system is soulsborne to it's core, and that is both a blessing and a curse. Each level feels like a slog, each run, a promise of miniscule progress.

The best I can say is that you should get it....on sale. $30, maybe. $20, absolutely. Because as a one-time experience, Witchfire can be a lot of fun. As a Roguelike? As an "Extraction shooter"? It's "OK". That's it. Just "OK."

I love sports games but dislike roguelites, so I hesitated picking this one up for a while, but I'm glad I finally gave it a chance.

This game has creativity and new ideas that you rarely see in today's vanilla sports games. The hockey gameplay is good enough, though it has some faults. It doesn't feel as smooth or responsive as the retro hockey games it's inspired by, and some of the puck and goalkeeper physics feel janky.

This led to me losing a lot of games where I was dominating my opponent on the ice but lost the game due to a cheap goal. With all the roguelite power-ups, luck feels more important than skill, which can lead to some frustration. I found the Easy difficulty to be too easy, while Standard felt cheap.

The early access version of the game is also quite short and low on game modes. That said, if you go into it with the mindset this is an indie sports game with some new ideas, I feel like it's worth the relatively low price of admission. Whether it eventually evolves to something greater remains to be seen, but I'm glad there are people still making sports games with original ideas.

Would recommend to anyone who loves a challenge and enjoys games such as Rimworld, tower defense games, etc.

review_text:
[h1] ST:E - A Flawed Gem In Need Of Polish [/h1]

[h2] This will be a slightly longer review. What is there to be said about ST:E that hasn't already been covered by the various, mixed reviews? I've put over 800 hours into this game (as of the time of this review) and have to say I still have mixed feelings, though I lean more towards a positive outlook, considering I am still playing the game fairly regularly. I can also say, without a doubt, that playing ST:E with a Discord group (the Joint Space Force) has made the experience immensely more enjoyable.

I will break down the things that I love about this game, as well as the things that I, well, [i] put up with.[/i][/h2]


[h3] [b] What I love: [/b] [/h3] 
[*] The core gameplay - The gameplay loop, game modes, classes, weapons, etc.
The game's core gameplay, set within a universe I love, has managed to keep me coming back for more. The weapons are fun to experiment with, the game modes allow you to change things up depending on what you feel like doing, the classes are unique enough that you can get a pretty decent amount of depth from them, and the perks and utilities make it possible to tailor your classes to your playstyle without feeling exploitable or cheap. The mutator system helps to keep things feeling fresh, so much so that playing without them can often feel too easy or boring by comparison. The challenge of dealing with ambushes or random hordes while trying to gather resources during ARC can be challenging and fun, forcing you to adapt from both a micro and macro level, lest you run out of tickets and fail the mission.

[*] 16-Player PvE
Having so many players working together (well, usually) can be ridiculously fun. It leaves many opportunities to make friends or meet cool/memorable players. I was lucky enough to find a Discord group known as the Joint Space Force rather early on in my ST:E career and this really boosted the amount of enjoyment I got out of this game. I have made [i] many [/i] friends from [i] many [/i] backgrounds that have only served to make the game [i] that [/i] much more enjoyable to play. Having people you can joke and screw around with really adds to the experience of getting ran through and shooting Bugs.

[*] The Arachnid Threat
The Bugs of ST:E are really cool; I can't help but feel like the design and behavior of the Bugs are just about spot-on. There are complaints to be made about the little details, such as how Warriors and Drones may get stuck on geometry or clip partially into the ground, but that's to be expected from time to time. Admittedly, it probably happens too often to really defend, but there is a lot of potential here.

The Tigers and big and imposing, leaving your with a strange mix of contempt and respect, almost like a respectable rival that you trade blows with. Sometimes you win, but sometimes you lose. The Grenadier commands a comical, but deadly threat, They're big and blue, leaving a distinct impression that sticks out among the earthy colors of the Bugs and can lead to some hilarious (and frustrating) situations when you're blown halfway across the map . Gunners  have a distinct glow and rotund shape that will become the bane of your existence if you aren't able to adapt and improve. They often act like a positioning skill-check for new or ignorant players and command a unique presence on the battlefield.The addition of Bombadiers has been both a frustrating and entertaining experience because of their small size and incredible jump. I've had some great times both watching and being the target of Bombadier ambushes that lead to joining Fleet in orbit.

Last, but not least, the Warrior Bug. The iconic design and ferocity of the Warriors walk a fine line between being too tanky and too squishy. Almost every game can make the Warriors feel like a unique threat, based on your current objectives, class, weapons, etc. A worthy adversary (most of the time) that are the bread-and-butter of the Bug army. They feel good to shoot, generally speaking, and provide a interesting, ever-changing experience while on the battlefield. I hope you learn to love their 1-shot charge attack on Hard difficulty, otherwise you are really going to hate these guys. (Ha)

[h3] [b] What I loathe: [/b] [/h3]
[*] The various bugs (lowercase 'B')
I have played a lot of different iterations of this game over the past year, including: An engine swap, various buffs and nerfs, class revamps, weapon and perk releases, class tweaks, mechanic revamps, etc. Every update has been accompanied by their own new, or even altered, bugs. The worst have consistently been related to the performance of the game. From crashes and frame drops to servers closing and intense rubberbanding, we've experienced it all. If I had to pick a runner-up for worst bugs, it would have to be the comms. For months we've had to deal with issues of voice chat completely breaking and getting [b] 0 [/b] voice comms, mics constantly on, some players not being heard by others, and push-to-talk becoming a toggle (leading to 'hot mic-ing'), and rendering cooperation almost impossible outside of using text chat, something that is difficult in a PvE game with hundreds of enemies and fast-paced action. Other gripes include equipment causing crashes, being unable to respawn, deployables breaking Bug AI, Bugs spawning in walls and geometry, attachments not working/loading, getting stuck in 3rd person, being unable to use any inputs, being unable to climb/mantle, stuttering while jumping, etc. .etc. .etc. .No, seriously. The list just goes on and on. . .

[*] Development
OWI has made an awesome game, from an awesome IP, with awesome features. BUT. Much of the content has felt half-baked on arrival. With the 1.0 launch we're been unable to get much use from the new Company system due to the exclusion of what could be deemed as standard QOL features, such as invites for friends or a search bar for finding a specific Company. The Carnage system has been really cool, but I'm sure I can vouch for many of the other Early Access players when I say we'd much rather have the game in a stable, smooth state before adding [i] new [/i] content to the mix. Many of the major issues with the game have taken far too long to be ironed-out while we're trying to play the game we've come to enjoy with our friends. It's only been made worse by consistent crashes. It really kills the desire to play the game when your game crashes, making you lose out on all of the experience you've earned, only to find out the Devs would rather roll out their new Bug corpse system or switch to a new game engine.

[*] Rushed launch
Those of us that have been playing ST:E in early access have been holding out hope to see the game become the best it can be. We've hoped and prayed that the 1.0 launch would be the saving grace for the dwindling numbers of players that have left due to the instability and bugginess we've been experiencing for months, but deep down, many of us knew the game would not be ready by the announced release date. The combination of low player count mixed with a shoddy launch could very well kill the game's reputation and, if the mixed reviews are anything to go off of, it seems our fears have been confirmed. We want the game to succeed, but we knew the game just wasn't ready for 1.0 launch, especially to the console market

[h3] [b] In Summary [/b] [/h3]
ST:E has (had?) a lot of potential. A combination of various issues has plagued this game since day 1 and growth has been slow, but there is a lot to love here if you are a nerd who loves the Starship Troopers franchise or if you can laugh and have fun with your friends in a fun, yet flawed game. The gameplay is cool, the Bugs are awesome, and the large team make for a fun experience if you can manage to play with some friends. There are many issues that need to be addressed here and, so far, we don't have a definite answer for whether or not ST:E will be here to stay.

review_text:
Although breathing fresh air into a regular hockey game by implementing various roguelike elements, the gameplay isn’t groundbreaking. But that isn’t a bad thing. It’s easy to pick up. Manages to be both fun and frustrating like most sports games and can easily be picked up to have a quick game or two. Tape to Tape can be proud of it’s innovations and its core gameplay. I had endless amounts of fun trying to get further and further in my runs across the three acts. Finding the challenge fun rather than off putting like some games end up being. It’s difficult to get the levels of challenge and fun right, it is a hard thing to balance. However, Tape to Tape pulls this off tremendously and I can’t wait to see how it continues to improve throughout Early Access.

Overall Rating: 9 – Outstanding!
