review_text:
[h2] The Callisto Protocol: A Beautifully Flawed Horror Experience [/h2]

The Callisto Protocol isn't a bad game, but it’s only a good game if you’re willing to overlook several significant shortcomings. It shines in its opening hours, with impressive graphics, lighting, and facial animations. The game’s atmosphere is particularly strong, offering something that Dead Space fans would likely appreciate—if only it maintained this quality throughout. Unfortunately, it falls into repetition soon after, and much of the initial potential feels wasted.

One of the game's biggest weaknesses is its combat design. The shooting mechanics are basic, paling in comparison to a game like Dead Space. However, it’s the melee system that baffled me the most. Every encounter boils down to the same rhythm of "dodge, dodge, shoot." What’s strange is that the dodge system isn’t active like you’d expect in other third-person games. Instead, it’s reactive—hold a directional key (A or D on PC) to auto-dodge incoming attacks, switching directions if a second or third attack comes. This system removes any sense of urgency or danger from combat.

In most survival horror games, keeping enemies at a distance is crucial, and the tension of being grabbed adds to the fear. But in The Callisto Protocol, you want enemies close, because dodging and melee attacks are too easy and repetitive. It saps the game of the dread you’d expect from a true horror title. A stamina-based dodge system might have injected more challenge, though it would have borrowed heavily from other games.

The game’s design also becomes repetitive. You’ll find yourself cutting identical cables, crouching through vents, and squeezing through walls again and again. As strong as the game’s opening is, the repetition that follows drags it down.

That said, I didn’t encounter many of the performance issues that plagued the game at launch. On my mid-range system, it ran smoothly, with DLSS (even modded) helping me maintain 80–100 FPS most of the time. There were rare dips into the 60s, but these were isolated moments. However, ray tracing is still a mess. Not only does it kill performance, but upscaling doesn’t seem to help, and hardware utilization drops drastically when ray tracing is enabled, underscoring poor optimization.

Would I recommend The Callisto Protocol? It depends. If you can get it at a discount—say around €20—it’s worth it. The base game at that price offers decent value, and adding the "Final Transmission" DLC for about €15 adds an extra two hours of content. But at €60 or the €77 deluxe edition price, it’s overpriced for what is ultimately a very atmospheric but mediocre game.

If you’ve never played Dead Space, I’d recommend the Dead Space remake without hesitation. But if you’ve already experienced Dead Space and want something new, The Callisto Protocol does provide a fresh narrative—just don’t expect it to rival Dead Space in terms of gameplay. Ultimately, The Callisto Protocol excels in atmosphere but falls short in gameplay and variety. The game could have benefitted from another year in development to flesh out enemy variety and mechanics.

I've been trying to give this game the best possible chance to impress me and I, frankly, can't give it a positive rating for a few things that really should be minor but aren't. That said, I *really* like the way this game works, most of the time. It takes most of the annoyances I had with similar games and throws them out.

That said, the minor things tend to add up. I often find I have issues with the placements of enemy spotters and rival bounty hunters. There's this one map where a sniper spotter, for the enemy, is placed waaaaaay out of bounds on a ship with a bunch of shipping crates. I was looking around for him for several minutes because I, quite reasonably, assumed that the spotter would be on the actual world map I was playing on, and not in the background where things usually don't even have collision detection. There are a few other placements that seem goofy as hell, where they're on rooves that have no reasonable way for anyone to get to.

And then there's the sentries. Later stages have them in spades and there's just no good way to deal with them. With the rifle I use, it takes eight shots to shut just one down. EMP grenades and ammo restocks aren't plentiful enough to account for all the sentries you deal with later on, and the range on those grenades is so ridiculously small you can only ever knock out one sentry at a time. Even if you do that, good luck doing so without blowing your cover, the blast radius is so small you have to be very accurate with your throw. I often find it more worth my time to just try and run past them.

And then there's the issue others have mentioned, where if you even slightly bork one shot, and don't immediately kill that person as soon as the next shot is ready, every enemy knows your location instantly. You can be prone in an area where the game recognizes you as fully hidden and you'll still be exposed. Meanwhile I can be shot by an enemy sniper and the recognition as to which direction I got shot from is so vague it's unhelpful beyond telling me which cardinal direction to look in.

And then there's the bounties. If you're not ready to tackle them, make SURE you don't enter the areas for them, because if you try to leave, the game will act like you died and reload you at the last checkpoint in the bounty area. You cannot leave until you kill the target.

But for positives, I like that you can use silenced secondary weapons and sidearms. I like that there are infinite marks you can use. I like the story explanation for unrealistic abilities (healing, surviving falls, aim assistance with wind/distance etc.) in an otherwise hyper-realistic game. I love the environments, with how beautiful and realistic they are. I like how the game gives you multiple ways to approach enemy strongholds so that you're not forced into a singular way to deal with them (great for replay value). I (mostly) like the way the AI works regarding their alert system. So much of the game is just on point that it's a pity the downsides bring it down.


This game is actually really fun. I really liked the way it works and will probably continue playing it, but it has significant gameplay issues that should be minor but aren't. I'm really mixed on this one and would give a neutral rating, or 6/10, for informational purposes if I had the option, but it's just a binary choice and I have to pick one. It has everything it needs to be a stellar game... if they just fix the above issues.

review_text:
Just to start with, this game is indeed an excellent RPG. You can tell the creators loved what they are doing, they put immense amount of effort into the environment and referencing history. You can immense yourself in the world of the Holy Roman Empire.
But if you are looking for a fun game where you want your decisions weighted, and you seek a sense of accomplishment for your epic deeds, this game is not for you.

So for those who played KCD1, after overcoming overwhelming odds, you finally gain recognition with the Lords, and they start sending you on more important missions and even include you in meetings. Then, in the ending they send you on a mission with Hans Capon to deliver a message to Trotsky. So throughout KCD1, you had this theme of hardship and survival, revenge and growth, you go from a Blacksmith's son to eventually being a right hand man that's even [spoiler] involved in a siege of a castle. [/spoiler]

Then in KCD2, all these is thrown away. Well, it has to be, you argue, because it's a new game and there has to be some sort of reset. Alright. Then, the game proceeds to drill the fact that you are indeed a helpless peasant and a joke to the world for a huge chunk of the game. You actually lose agency repeatedly in ridiculous ways. [spoiler] Basically, Henry gets played. He is scripted to lose whichever side he is on. He's always locked up for stupid reasons for the first part of the game. It's nearly like playing prison simulator. [/spoiler] I guess they want the theme that Henry is resilient and doesn't need his reputation to succeed, but personally I think it's too much to the point of misery.

At every point, I questioned: well, this is about as bad as it gets, it's bound to get better right? Honestly it doesn't. To continue I'd have to write a huge chunk of spoilers, so for now i'll summarize: a lot of story feels like induced stupidity just to move the plot along. They force events and narratives to create "moral dilemma" just for the sake of it and it doesn't flow naturally. Nearly all your effort and work comes to naught, they erase all your accomplishments in the next plot. And when it is all over, you deserve to be the hero of Bohemia, [spoiler] half the nobles owe you their lives [/spoiler] yet you have Hanush assigning you a menial task and if you argue through dialogue option, he tells you to "do as you are told". I'll try to support my points with some spoilers below later.

Summary: All in all I had a pretty miserable time playing this, there's no positive moments in the plot, you are constantly forced to face defeat and it feels your achievements are never properly acknowledged unlike in KCD1. I would say the feeling is comparable to working without wages in real life. I never had this excitement to explore the world and level up my character like in KCD1. Game mechanics felt worse than in KCD1 too.

Major spoilers ahead:

Forced moral dilemma:

[spoiler] Istvan Toth - Brilliantly written villain from KCD1 and stands out in a sea of more "generic" villains. Istvan Toth is actually a charismatic schemer and scumbag and you can tell he loves it. There's this sense of childish glee in his voice and actions. He's sadistic but in a pragmatic manner where he doesn't enjoy torture for the sake of it, only if it moves him towards his goal. What happened here is they tried to inject a moral dilemma, they suddenly showcase Istvan Toth's caring side, making him look regretful and worried all the time, and even acting like he knew his time was up and was waiting for Henry. Now, this could be a side of him, but the scenes felt forced into the player's face at the last moment to push a "you want your revenge, but is your target truly evil and deserving" kind of message which cheapens Henry's revenge. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Samuel - You are sent with him on a mission, everybody's lives and possibly the fate of Bohemia hinges on its success. You find out that he endangered the entire mission by pursuing a personal vendetta and he is serious hurt. You can choose to save him, but if you do, the resource everyone is fighting to protect is lost. If you leave him, you save the resource but Samuel dies. This doesn't sound so bad until you actually play it, the game makes a massive deal of this decision, if you do the logical thing and save the silver Henry starts whinging about Samuel's death and everyone consoles him, and the endgame becomes a mourning instead of a celebration. Meanwhile, dozens died heroically defending the castle, while I barely know Samuel and he died due to his own doing. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Markvart - Basically at death's door Markvart started blabbering about how you are the same as him, he is a just a normal man with a loving family. This was enough to trick me at first until I realize the bullshit he was sprouting, he basically set Cumans to rape and kill innocent villagers while Henry is thrown into circumstances where it was live or die (well in my case, I can't speak for your playstyle..). Alright this is actually a pretty powerful scene, but I'm just quite surprised to see some people convinced by his words and think he is a honorable man. [/spoiler]

Issues with relationships

[spoiler] Radzig and Hanush - So in KCD1, you eventually build up a reputation with them, they constantly remind you to not risk your life. Here, you went through basically hell to get out with Capon safe, only to finally meet them. I thought this was finally the turning point of the game, but Hanush treats you like you screwed up and whatever you went through was a inconvenience, then instantly, you are sent on a mission to spy on freaking King Sigismund himself, and when Henry protests, Hanush basically says "Good grief, figure it out, do I have to teach you everything?". What happened to advising caution and caring about Henry? Then, they sort of just disappeared on their own mission. I mean after all Henry and Capon went through, it doesn't seem in-character for them to just leave without any further instructions. Hanush was even more concerned about a damned wedding when all this is over. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Hans Capon - Basically he had 0 character development. His main issue remains, he think having noble blood triumphs all, you are just "one of the good ones" and a half noble, so he treats you better. But remember KCD1? He treats you all better for saving his life but that all breaks now the moment he finds himself in a pickle. He doesn't become smarter despite facing death either. [/spoiler]

Complete lack of recognition:

[spoiler] Think about it, freaking King Sigismund himself acknowledged you, giving you more praise than any of your allies in game. Hell you even get to go to Sigismund's camp and a commander called you his best soldier a day in. Meanwhile, you sort of just followed Zizka as commander without fuss, when by deeds alone, you should be co-commander with him. Hell, you should be the Hero of Bohemia. I know people will say "its realism, people acted like that back then", but man, Henry go around fighting 20 soldiers single-handedly and succeeds in impossible missions, hes the most powerful man in the Empire. There's no way he's treated with this level of disrespect. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Forced helplessness. For eg at Raborsche, somehow at a gathering of so many nobles, nobody thought to place lookouts, nobles were instantly attacked and kidnapped. You steal Silver, and you are betrayed and force to take refuge in a castle. Then you get word that Sigismund is retreating, and it would be too costly to feint a retreat. While celebrating, it turned out it was a feint and you come under siege again. Then, you can end up losing the silver base on the choice you make. [/spoiler]

Forced defeats:
Cutscenes force you to lose. [spoiler] Significant one is you losing to Erik, that was pure bullshit. He's just distraction at best, and the game forces him to defeat you. [/spoiler]

review_text:
What is a game if not a mirror of life? Yakuza 5 Remastered is not simply an upgraded title—it is a sprawling, ambitious reflection of human struggle and perseverance, painted across the diverse landscapes of Japan. It is operatic in scale and yet deeply intimate. Few games have dared to go this far, and even fewer have succeeded in making every step feel meaningful.

Five protagonists. Five cities. Five personal odysseys. This is no ordinary sequel. It is a meditation on identity and purpose. Each character walks a path riddled with ghosts of the past and dreams deferred. Haruka, especially, stands out. To make a pop idol's journey as emotionally resonant as a former hitman's path to redemption? That’s bold. That’s new. That’s art.

As a person who believes that gameplay should echo the philosophy of the narrative, I was impressed by how Yakuza 5 Remastered handles tone and variety. The shift between combat, racing, dancing, and managing an idol career could be jarring in the hands of less confident developers. But Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio pulls it off with finesse. These transitions don’t feel like detours—they’re vital arteries of the game’s emotional and thematic structure.

What I admire most is the meticulous worldbuilding. Each city—Fukuoka, Sapporo, Osaka, Nagoya, and Tokyo—feels like its own character. The snow crunching under Saejima’s boots in Hokkaido. The neon pulse of Sotenbori. The modest shops tucked away in Nagoya's alleys. These are more than backdrops; they are living, breathing environments that root the drama in reality.

Technically, the remastered version sharpens the experience without losing its soul. The enhanced visuals honor the original while respecting modern standards. Frame rate improvements smoothen the pacing, but it’s the storytelling—always the storytelling—that elevates Yakuza 5 Remastered to something greater than nostalgia.

This isn’t just a game about yakuza. It’s a game about dreams. About people trying to hold onto something—honor, family, truth—in a world constantly trying to tear them apart. It is, in many ways, a game I wish I had made.

No numerical score can capture the layered beauty of this title. Like a good film or novel, it lingers in the mind long after the credits roll.

In Yakuza 5 Remastered, the fight is never just physical. It is always—always—about the heart.

9/10

review_text:
I wish there was a neutral option for this. So far, the story and most quests are a lot of fun, and it is a very immersive enviroment. Most quests let you make choices that matter in the end. 

However, combat is not fun. I am still early but so far I have lost even the tutorial battles and struggle with the training person that is recommended - because of the equally unhelpful way this game sets checkpoints. Unless you brew a potion to save or walk all the way to a bed (most of which you have to unlock first so very limited early on) if you die - which happens really fast - you go back potentially 1 hour in terms of progress and have to do everything again. If you only have like 1-2 hours to play per day it can lead to 0 progress in a session pretty fast, and it discouraged me personally from even wanting to get into any fights, so there is also no way for me to practice and get better. 

What I really hated was that at one point I was off on a quest to find a lost cart, and because I accidentally got food poisoning (bc the game did explain that mechanic AFTER the fact) I had to abandon the quest NPCs and go get healed, or revert to a save I made like 5 hours back. I assumed the quest would restart, but instead the NPCs eventually returned, told me what they found and were even mad at me. The game softlocked me out of the main quest. 

All in all I would say I'm enjoying it as long as I can avoid fighting, but it is easy to get frustrated if you accidentally die and have to redo all the shit since your last save. There is such a thing as too much realism, and I wish there were some options for more casual players to get more enjoyment out of this. Due to the tutorial alone being several hours long, I sadly didn't have the option of a refund upon finding out that the combat is simply not for me. Will see if I can Skyrim-Stealth-Archer my way through.

It's a good, really well made game with a ton of thought and attention to detail, with the charismatic writing that one would expect from this studio. But the core game loop is rather tedious with too much of a good auto-battler being stripped away. Slow death spirals are very common and there's a serious lack of satisfaction from going through a run.
 
Even the typical roguelite element of unlocking more things when dieing. Isn't interesting since you cannot view what it is you've unlocked outside of a static image.

I've also read through their patch history and they seem to prioritize balance for their incredibly niche multiplayer mode. Which has managed to strip away a lot of the diversity and interest that the singleplayer mode used to have.

review_text:
After about 6 hours, I've seen most of what the game currently has to offer. Which isn't much. The next 6 hours were exactly the same with no change in gameplay at all.

What's here is badly balanced, requiring immense amounts of grinding.

The game can be mildly enjoyable when listening to a podcast or something otherwise engaging. It is not engaging in and of itself.

[h1]Identity Crisis[/h1]

The game has a big identity crisis. I'd recommend skipping the Early Access period until the developers balance what's here or decide what type of game they want to make.

Is it a movement shooter like [i]Doom[/i]? Kind of, but no. Not with limited stamina and a useless melee. So why do dozens of enemies spawn out of nowhere?

Is it a Souls-like? Kind of, but no. You're not able to play slowly and deliberately with enemies spawning in behind you. So why do enemies kill you in 3-4 hits?

Is it a monster hunting game? No, but kind of. Bosses will run away/disappear/teleport after taking minimal damage like this is [i]Monster Hunter[/i]. With limited stamina, chasing after retreating bosses just adds tedium. And then more enemies will spawn in behind and around you.

[h1]Difficulty & Combat[/h1]

The "difficulty" in this game this:
- you die in 3 hits
- enemies die in 10-50 hits
- you'll fight 4-15 enemies at a time
- 4-12 enemies will spawn in behind/around you
- at range, your weapons do almost no damage
- at range, enemy weapons still do full damage

I think I ran into about 7 enemy types and killed each hundreds of times. Hopefully, more will be added in the future.

[h1]Progression[/h1]

Gaining levels is very slow, especially after the first few hours. You'll need to dip into and out of the two starting regions numerous times in order to gain enough experience to level up, just so you can take on the more challenging areas. Very repetitive.

Upgrading weapons is very slow. What is a "first mysterium activity" and how do I do it 25 times? I've done it for some weapons without knowing what it is, and 0 times for other weapons. Why not just tell me what this required activity is?

Clearing danger areas is very slow. There's often one enemy that you can't find, that isn't really aggressive, that is the only one left to clear the area. Sometimes, I'm convinced the game is just bugged and the last enemy never spawned in. Very unrewarding.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Not worth $35-$40 USD right now. Maybe when the full game is released. Currently, $20 is probably a fair price for what is offered.

The art style is excellent.

Somehow, the devs were able to make a game in 2024 that has high graphical fidelity without crippling performance issues.

As is, this is just not a fun experience right now.

[h1]Similar but Better[/h1]

review_text:
(at the time of this review, the game is currently in the past and present early access version. will update when the full game releases)

This game is INCREDIBLY fun. solid game play loop, fun movement, beautiful areas, and some really sick animations (especially for the guns). however, there are still some pretty big flaws that need to be addressed for this game to really stand out.

1. There is little to no build variety to runs. blessings matter very little when 1 babe'd gun can carry you to threat 50+ easily. and the blessings don't feel super unique. more health, more resources, explosion on kill if the enemy is burning. there are very few synergies between them that make them feel boring. 

a random idea i had was keeping the blessings at the end of the level (Similar to Gunfire Reborn's end of stage chalice) and giving the bunkers something like relics or artifacts (EX: something like slay the spire's relics or Enter the Gungon's passives where they give a buff that is active at all times) giving each their own sort of purpose. something like a shoulder missile launcher attachment that gives a chance to fire a homing rocket when an enemy is hit with non elemental weapons or sliding leaves behind flammable oil that can be ignited to make a wall of fire (effectively an AOE DoT). they all dont have to be super unique, some can just be damage or reload buffs, but more ways to scale yourself in a run can really add to the replayability.

2. The curses are REALLY COOL. the curses are done incredibly well with some EXTREMELY fun combos with weapons and even between themselves. some standout ones being: 2 skulls that home onto people you shoot, re rolling your guns every threat level (complete chaos LMAO), launching ice spikes that can hurt you by freezing already frozen enemies, enemies who die spawn as a phantom that explode into frost when killed but will revive if not killed quickly. 

3. bunkers feel empty and keys drop far too often. the bunkers are probably the most "unfinished" feeling part of the game with one bunker layout just straight up having a message saying "tee hee sorry not done yet" (which is really funny honestly). something i would love to see is more straightforward bunker types, stuff like the arsenal bunker and the cargo tunnel bunker with ways to tell what a bunker is by just looking at it (EX: blessing bunkers have vines overtaking the door, arsenal bunker having a heavily armored door, cargo tunnel bunker looking worn down and abandoned from the outside with rust covering the door and a crooked light above it, alpha cash bunkers having a shiny golden door) so players can make choices that can impact their run.

4. the clothing system in general. incredibly restrictive and most being not very impactful to your build. there are very few options in the pool as well. HOWEVER, i would love to see a system similar to BPM's where you have 4 slots (1 head, 1 glove, 1 chest, 1 boots) allowing for combos, but still being restrictive enough for there to be an important choice with what you take and leave.

5. the hub. its empty and has very little to do other than leave. something to make the harbor feel more lively is maybe something like how Hades handles its hub. i know that this game is gonna be pretty heavy with story in 1.0, though maybe sometimes seven, eight or nine could drop by the harbor from time to time and have a bit of dialog. dialog between six and the mother when you spend jade vines to level up. maybe the mother could give you some encouragement when you start a run (similar to Hades where Hades just insults you) small bits of world building do wonders for keeping people interested in the world. though, i dont really know where the story is going (i read the wiki for a bit) so maybe this wouldn't fit thematically

at the end of the day, i would love to see more replayability and unique synergies with items. most of this has been me just spit balling ideas (take them with a grain of salt(i am NOT a game dev)) that i think would add to runs. nothing is meant to insult, its just some criticism of some of the systems. i am very excited to see where the game is going to go from here, it has a LOT of potential to be amazing.

review_text:
In the briefest possible sentiment, my feelings for Lucius are mixed. With clear thematic inspiration from the Omen, Lucius offers a fresh foray into horror by giving you control over the demonically-influenced child, Lucius. You're directed to kill the staff of your parents' estate, and it isn't your lot to question why. Lucifer himself appears in a dissapointingly trite manner: an obliquely evil man in a suit, grinning maniacally. Preferable to depictions of a man in a red leotard and a trident, he still fails to convey a palpable sense of dreadful terror or villainy. 
 Blessed (or cursed?) with unholy powers, some light puzzle solving is required to kill the servants in seemingly-accidental and  gorey fashion. The staff aren't exactly likeable, so there's no sense you're doing any real harm to innocents. One could even argue that the devil is being quite helpful by terminating unsavoury workers. Lucius never does any of the murdering directly; rather, he manipulates the environment into creatively lethal traps. These traps are clever, and the ensuing death scenes are appropriately violent.
  Dissapoinment stems from three areas: the cheesiness, the impotent morality, and the wasted oppurtunity. The most obvious failure lies in the seemingly deliberate nature of the game's campy vibe. The narration provided by the investigating officer would fit perfectly into a b-movie horror romp. No one's reactions to the freak-accident murders carry any sense of gravity. Lucifer himself is better suited for a cartoon villain than a manipulative murderer. The tone isn't ominous, oppressive, or morally horrifying- all qualities it *should* be. Think about it: you play as a child who is being directly influenced by Satan to kill innocent people in unspeakable ways as part of a grander purpose known only to the devil himself. This subversion of moral principle- that children are innocent- should lead the player into feeling they're proceeding into the blasphemous; which ties into my second point.
  Feeling is subjective, but if the game is trying to make you feel as if you're really controlling a murderous child, it fails. Instead, you feel as if you're zipping around and doing Myst-lite style puzzles to knowck off a few annoying charicatures. There' sno sense of innocence lost, since Lucius is devoid of any character, and the game isn't scary. The buildup to the kills is monotonous, with gathering items and some stealth-lite gameplay. You don't feel that there are real-world consequences to the deaths, as neither your parents nor the other staff are seriously disturbed or upset. There's no repurcussions, no mourning, and no shocking cruelty about it. Contrast this with one of my favorite morally torturous moments in gaming from the Amnesia DLC *minor spoiler*: You are forced to kill an NPC that's strapped down to a table to progress. His pleas for help inspire guilt, and you feel horror at what you choose to do. There are similar moments in SOMA.
  One should feel that, as Lucius, they're doing something abominable. A child killing innocent people is something inherently abhorrent, and yet Lucius fails to provide that.
 Ultimately, Lucius is an example of wasted potential. Evil protagonists, when done right, make the player feel guilt vicariously, and from that guilt a sense of dread develops. Or an angle where there's sadistic pleasure would have also been welcome, as you take a sick joy from doing what you're told. Lucius should be praised for seeking to do something not already hashed and rehashed a million times. It avoids tropes like the Insane Asylum, Hospital, or Zombies. It does not, however, avoid being totally unfrightening or monotonous. 
  I want to like Lucius, and I'm not strongly negative towards the game. I don't, however, recommend it to anyone save the truly dedicated fans of indie horror. Lucius isn't a bad game, only sadly mediocre.
                   Overall: 4/10 (Only the very curious will gain any pleasure or satisfaction)
                   Art Direction/Graphics: 6/10 (Passable, and the environments are well done, if uninspired)
                   Sound Design: 5/10 (A decent soundtrack, but repetitive)
                   Voice Acting: 4.5/10 (While not abysmal, the dialogue is too cheesy to take any of what is said very seriously)
                   Replayability: 2/10 (I can't imagine what you'd go back for)
                   Longevity: 2/10 (Too cyclical. ONce you've played 30 minutes, you know what you're in for)

trite manner an obliquely evil man in a suit , grinning maniacally . preferable to depictions of a man in a red leotard and a trident , he still fails to convey a palpable sense of dreadful terror or villainy . blessed ( or cursed ? ) with unholy powers , some light puzzle solving is required to kill the servants in seemingly-accidental and gorey fashion . the staff aren ' t exactly likeable , so there ' s no sense you ' re doing any real harm to innocents . one could even argue that the devil is being quite helpful by terminating unsavoury workers . lucius never does any of the murdering directly rather , he manipulates the environment into creatively lethal traps . these traps are clever , and the ensuing death scenes are appropriately violent . dissapoinment stems from three areas the cheesiness , the impotent morality , and the wasted oppurtunity . the most obvious failure lies in the seemingly deliberate nature of the game ' s campy vibe . the narration provided by the investigating officer would fit perfectly into a b-movie horror romp . no one ' s reactions to the freak-accident murders carry any sense of gravity . lucifer himself is better suited for a cartoon villain than a manipulative murderer . the tone isn ' t ominous , oppressive , or morally horrifying- all qualities it *should* be . think about it you play as a child who is being directly influenced by satan to kill innocent people in unspeakable ways as part of a grander purpose known only to the devil himself . this subversion of moral principle- that children are innocent- should lead the player into feeling they ' re proceeding into the blasphemous which ties into my second point . feeling is subjective , but if the game is trying to make you feel as if you ' re really controlling a murderous child , it fails . instead , you feel as if you ' re zipping around and doing myst-lite style puzzles to knowck off a few annoying charicatures . there ' sno sense of innocence lost , since lucius is devoid of any character , and the game isn ' t scary . the buildup to the kills is monotonous , with gathering items and some stealth-lite gameplay . you don ' t feel that there are real-world consequences to the deaths , as neither your parents nor the other staff are seriously disturbed or upset . there ' s no repurcussions , no mourning , and no shocking cruelty about it . contrast this with one of my favorite morally torturous moments in gaming from the amnesia dlc *minor spoiler* you are forced to kill an npc that ' s strapped down to a table to progress . his pleas for help inspire guilt , and you feel horror at what you choose to do . there are similar moments in soma . one should feel that , as lucius , they ' re doing something abominable . a child killing innocent people is something inherently abhorrent , and yet lucius fails to provide that . ultimately , lucius is an example of wasted potential . evil protagonists , when done right , make the player feel guilt vicariously , and from that guilt a sense of dread develops . or an angle where there ' s sadistic pleasure would have also been welcome , as you take a sick joy from doing what you ' re told . lucius should be praised for seeking to do something not already hashed and rehashed a million times . it avoids tropes like the insane asylum , hospital , or zombies . it does not , however , avoid being totally unfrightening or monotonous . i want to like lucius , and i ' m not strongly negative towards the game . i don ' t , however , recommend it to anyone save the truly dedicated fans of indie horror . lucius isn ' t a bad game , only sadly mediocre . overall 4/10 ( only the very curious will gain any pleasure or satisfaction ) art direction/graphics 6/10 ( passable , and the environments are well done , if uninspired ) sound design 5/10 ( a decent soundtrack , but repetitive ) voice acting 4 . 5/10 ( while not abysmal , the dialogue is too cheesy to take any of what is said very seriously ) replayability 2/10 ( i can ' t imagine what you ' d go back for ) longevity 2/10 ( too cyclical . once you ' ve played 30 minutes , you know what you ' re in for )

Overall i'd recommend this one if you can stomach the dated look to the game.

I've been eagerly awaiting Scorn ever since it first debuted on Steam Greenlight, but now that I played and finished it, I'm just sad and disappointed. Gorgeously disturbing art and atmosphere can only take a game so far when everything else about it is a janky underdeveloped mess.
Years before release, Scorn's developers have been showing off the game's nifty combat system and importance of moral choices on the progression - all of that is gone now. The released game is a clunky linear puzzle game, where you can expect to play such bangers as:

* A convoluted sliding tile puzzle.
* Guide-a-light-through-a-maze puzzle.
* Align asynchronous rotating disks puzzle.
* And the all time classic - light up all the nodes puzzle!

The fact Scorn wraps such trite exercises into its gorgeous Geiger/Beksiński art style feels utterly insulting.
But then "combat" is introduced three chapters in, and it gets so much worse! Your fragile, lumbering, meat-man with slow, imprecise short range attack on a 10 second cool down is suddenly pitted against aggressive fast-projectile-lobbing damage-sponges. And so, you die, and die and die and die some more, each time sitting through a painfully slow death animation and a lengthy load time, then get respawned at the last checkpoint that may often be 15-20 minutes ago, forcing you to redo puzzles, or re-watch long unskippable cutscene animations. Health and ammo recharge stations don't regenerate, so if you used one up, then got mauled or missed a few shots shortly after, you might as well restart the chapter and lose hours of progress, as Scorn has no qualms about soft-locking progression and generally wasting player's time.

I am not mentioning the game's story because there isn't one. You just move from one gorgeously grotesque setpiece to another without any real connection, until your meat-man is murdered in a convoluted, completely undeserved way, and the credits roll.

Don't bother playing Scorn - it's clunky and boring, with a borderline broken checkpoint system, and no respect for player's time. If, like me, you were allured by the art of HR Geiger and Zdzisław Beksiński - watching a LongPlay on youtube will be a much better experience. Don't waste your money, especially at the current asking price of $40! Holy crap it's not even close to worth it!

In the current state, I can't recommend it, to a friend for example, over another game.

MXGP Pro: Tokyo Drift is not worth your £40.

Gameplay

Yes it's more challenging than previous iterations with pro physics enabled, but 90% of this percieved difficulty seems to come from constantly trying not to slide out the back end. Whips are schocking. Worst yet in any iteration of the game. They look horrible and unless you land perfectly straight, which is awkward and clunky, will basically ping you off sideways.

Graphics

The same as GP3 from what I can tell. Some pop in in menus while stuff is loading. No complaints.

Audio

Bikes Good enough, seem a bit samey but haven't yet ridden all the bikes to compare. Hitting 2" puddles for some bizarre reason is the loudest sound effect in the game, far louder than your bike or the crowd. No matter how tiny or short they are you get a loud splash.. easily patched but annoying.

I've yet to play multiplayer. The compound is fun for 10 minutes.

No Matterley Basin which was disappointing!

Don't buy it unless they do some serious patching.

review_text:
I would say that ultimately I wouldn't recommend the game. It's just too frustrating.
On a more accurate note, I'd honestly put it as an iffy, neither yes nor no.
It's a walking simulator with an unbelievably awesome aesthetic, though I think the last level was a little bit much to be honest.
That part it does wonderfully.
The issue is that it seems confused over what genre it is.
Is it a Walking Simulator? Or is it Survival Horror?
It doesn't bloody know and that's the biggest problem.
It shouldn't have combat if it's not going to design the levels around those enemies and more importantly the resources for dealing with them. Game's really stingy on health, which by the way I'm going to go ahead and say that the game shouldn't rely on you button mashing or going into the settings to figure out what button heals you, really stingy on ammo.
And by god you'll need that ammo.
The combat system is just a flaming hot mess that detracts from the core premise of the game.
Next issue is the save system.
Or rather the lack of one.
You can't save. It relies on a series of soft checkpoints and hard checkpoints. Hard CP's are the ones you can manually reload to, like say if you encounter a game ending glitch where a bull bugs out and blocks the tunnel, and these are only available near as I can tell for the beginning of the 'act.' The game is divided up into 5 acts.
Yeah. 5 saves. Or so it seemed to me.
Now if you die, as will happen a lot because some of those situations were absolute garbage fires of level design, you'll go back to a soft save which can sometimes be quite a waaaaays back. Like I'm talking this is a game mostly dominated by walking and puzzles and death can result in you having to do all of it all over again.
You can't manually use these which is just a horrible addition with the combat system or ya know glitches.
The game can be improved by removing or redesigning the combat system and adding a proper save system (that tells you when it's a checkpoint, you could put this on the damn biogun for immersion if ya wanted).
SPOILER PART:

Now the ending... yeah. It's extremely anticlimatic and disappointing. Nuff said. The game's focus on a complete and utter lack of any form of narration or guidance honestly harms the concept as a whole and renders a lot of what you're doing completely random and unconnected. I've seen reviews of people critiquing a lack of narrative, and like I get that, but that's not really the issue. The narrative of a walking simulator is delivered primarily by the aesthetic and the setting and importantly what you're doing in that setting. And if you don't know what you're doing... well, that harms the narrative.

review_text:
Sorry to say, but this game is inferior to [i]Arkham Asylum[/i] in my opinion, adding unnecessary complexity to an already-established design. There's not much positive I can say here, honestly.

The major element of [i]Arkham Asylum[/i] that I enjoyed was the confined metroidvania layout of its map, giving a tighter focus on the cast of characters (which was nice for me, as a newcomer to the DC Universe). Sure, [i]Arkham City[/i]'s evolution to a less claustrophobic, more linear and open layout is impressive for its generation, paving the way for future games like Insomniac's [i]Spider-Man[/i], it's still primitive in its design, lacking choices existing in games prior to it, notably fast travel.
And don't even get me started on this combat. I'm in full agreement that [i]Arkham Asylum[/i]'s brawling did feel a bit barebones. However, in building upon these systems through more moves and weapons, it not only adds complexity to controls and systems as a whole, but it often feels broken when trying to land hits. There would be several occasions where I would try to pull a knockout move on an enemy, only for it to be canceling out because the animation didn't finish before I get hit by an attack I couldn't even counter, leading me to question whether or not I was going to have to just mash buttons for 5 minutes straight. In certain moments, it's frustrating (especially when the final boss is way easier than the encounters prior).

I found the narrative to be weaker this time around too, putting partial blame on its more open nature. It's much more simple, seemingly focusing on Batman and Joker's own mortalities than a major threat itself, culminating into one of the most anti-climactic endings I've ever experienced in a video game story. Doctor Hugo Strange is a character I was very much intrigued by, given his mysterious and menacing nature. But by the time I reached the final act, learning about his true motive and still not fully understanding what the hell "Protocol 10" even is, it felt all for nothing. What's even more crazy is that, having played the latest version of this game, I didn't realize until afterwards that these Catwoman interludes are just DLC and not part of the original game, which makes it even more disappointing that it wasn't a launch choice to begin with, given the added nature to her relationship with Batman during the narrative.

[i]Batman: Arkham City[/i] overextends itself as a sequel to what came before it, sacrificing a tight narrative and design with something more technically impressive than anything during the generation. It's not a bad game and it has some moments of stealth and action that shine through, but it's definitely one that I'll probably never understand its full praise for, other than maybe how abrupt its final act is. If you want me to invest in this world and cast of characters, don't make the world so vast and fluffed... or let me at least land a hit without wanting to throw my controller down.

review_text:
A true escape from reality, into a dark, fleshly pit of despair.

As someone who doesn't enjoy puzzle games, and gets irritated quite easily by overly complicated scenarios, I enjoyed this one! This was a fun ride into madness and beauty.

Scorn is genius; H. R. Giger would be proud xD

Be warned! This is important to know before going in. This game requires a different mindset. Scorn is a slow burn, quiet, immersive, and puts you into a meditative state. Go in knowing full well the hardest puzzle awaits at the beginning of the game. Don't let the starting puzzle discourage you at the beginning. The puzzles get easier as you go on. Look at the first puzzle as inoculation. Now you're ready to enjoy the journey.

It took the developers 8 years to make Scorn. Wrap your mind around that level of dedication. I commend the artists who worked on this game, and well deserved for such a visceral adventure. Best puzzle game I've ever played.

Do not miss out on this game; trust me on this... nothing will prepare you for what you're about to experience.

9/10

review_text:
This game is pretty fun but makes numerous terrible design choices that doesn't bode well for its longevity. I really want to say this is a game that I'd TRULY recommend but it's honestly not. I can say that the base PSO2 is a superior game but I can't even properly gear up when playing it. It's much easier to gear up in the inferior PSO2:NGS.

Pros: 
- Combat is pretty fun and responsive.
- The character creator is extremely deep and liberal with what you can do.
- Graphics aren't "amazing" but they're okay

Cons:
- The story is kind of simplistic and stupid compared to PSO and Base PSO2. No substance and kind of boring. You don't really get to know the characters at all.
- The game has a dying community. After each update, less and less people log on to check out what changes are made.
- Enemy types are redundant. Reskins over reskins over reskins.. The combat isn't getting more interesting because the enemies you fight aren't doing anything different. This I feel is the game's biggest flaw. If I fight a slightly different variation of the same monster 6-7 times, it's not fun. I want NEW enemies to fight.
- I don't mind ascetic microtransactions but it kind of bothers me that they're all locked behind a gacha system. I'd rather just buy them straight out than spend money on a bunch of things I want for the slight chance of getting something I want.
- The game recently added an instant level up and story skip option in the game. This just goes to show how little confidence the devs have in the meat of their content. review_text:
While this game is certainly not bad, it's not exactly good either. But since most reviews are positive anyway, I might aswell tell you why it just didn't work for me.

-The story
In it's core I thought the overall concept was actually pretty original. You pay as two scientist who travel back through a dying man's memories in order to grant him his last wish artificially: taking him to the moon (roll credits). Though during the story, your original objective is often questioned, as you begin to understand that this wish is not what would make your patient truly happy.
So, it's really not the story that set me off, it's rather...
-The dialogue
You'd think that in a story that's supposed to make you sad and teary, you wouldn't need a character for comic relief. But damnit, the second main character suplied you with a steady ammount of jokes in all the wrong places. I just couldn't take the game serious anymore. At the first half of the story, whenever there was an emotional moment, that same guy, messed it up over an over again. And by the time the game was starting to get deep, it was just too late for me. 
You see, the sad moments of the game largely depend on how you attached you grow to the characters over time. And maybe it's just me, but I hated both of them.
-Gameplay
Well, interesting gameplay is virtually nonexistent. But that's really not an issue in a story driven game. As I mentioned before, it has a great outline, but it just feels so unrefined at some places that it just wasn't enjoyable for me.
-The length
You'll probably finish the game in 3-4 hours. And while I don't want to badmouth the content, you may think that it's been a short ride if you don't even have all the trading cards by the time you are done.

All in all, I'd say it's okay if you can pick it up during a sale. But I really don't think it's worth the full price if you take a look at what it offers. Just about 4 hours of gameplay which aren't even amazing. But I assume that most people have a far better time, given that they don't dislike the main characters as much as I do.

I really thought I would love this game.
And I did at the start, and on earlier difficulties

But once you progress and go through the difficulties, game gets unbearable to play. 
It's just a spamfest of tanky or EXTREMELY TANKY enemies. Combined with extreme damage dropoff, it becomes suffering. 
enemies just spam you so you can't close the gap to increase your damage, but they can delete your healthbar unrelated of the distance. 

It's filled with artificial and fake difficulty with no thought behind it. No careful enemy placement, no thought behind the attack patterns. The game gets the difficulty from your weapon damage dropoff and from the sheer health and number of enemies that get thrown at you mindlessly and that's it

It doesn't feel satisfying to fin fights. It doesn't feel rewarding. Except earlier on, when you're learning the game and discovering new things.
On later difficulties, it feels more like "oh tank god this is over..." when you win a fight with no further emotion. It feels like suffering.
And if you increase the difficulty, you can't lower it. So the only solution is deleting the save file and making a new one

And, also, the game is quite grindy. Usually I wouldn't mind it, I love grinding in games, but this is suffering. So even if you decide to make a new save file, you'll have to get through the grind again

I really can't recommend this game. It's fun in the beginning, but later it turns into pure suffering. I don't see it worth playing if that's the direction it's going in.
especially for full price of 40 euros. If you want to get it, maybe wait until it's on sale for 10-15. You could get a few hours of enjoyment out of it for that amount.

I don't remember the last time I was this disappointed in a game

review_text:
Shadow Tactics is an RTS puzzle game that is a mixed bag of some enjoyment but a huge amount of frustration and terrible design.

You get 5 characters throughout the game and they essentially all work the same with the exception of the sniper.  They all have a close range blade attack, a special move only they can do, a different distraction/luring technique, a limited use flintlock, and a 1 time use medkit.  The sniper has limited ammo in his long range rifle as his main attack and a limited number of grenades as his special move.  Early on you only get a couple characters per mission but later on you'll get access to 4 or 5.  Unfortunately the balance isn't very good.  The 2 female characters make the male characters pretty much useless as Yuki's trap/whistle combo can take care of pretty much every regular enemy and once Aiko gets a disguise you'll run around with her killing every lone unit or distracting someone so someone else can kill the person he was watching.  The only time you'll need the male characters is to take out an enemy samurai.

So to get to the frustrations and terrible design.  The entire game is a giant grindy save scum.  You will be quick saving after pretty much every enemy you kill, every time you move to a new position, every time you get ready to set up a new kill, every time you hide a body somewhere, etc.  Then you'll constantly be quick loading as something goes wrong, whether you get screwed over by the god awful camera, whether your character does something completely random you didn't want them to do, you get spotted by some enemy 2 miles away, spotted by some guy who looks like he's looking in a completely different direction, or spotted by some dude who just happened to walk into view range as you started killing.  Anytime you're spotted you're going to press F8 since being spotted alarms enemies.  They swarm the area for a minute+ before they go back to their normal spots.  It's always quicker to quick load.  Fortunately the game quick saves and loads quickly.  I want to be entirely clear here.  I am not exaggerating in any way, shape or form.  On average, you will be quick saving or quick loading at least every 30 seconds.

The cursor and character actions are a gigantic problem.  The cursor will often completely miss what you're trying to do.  Did you tell your character to walk up and stab that guy?  Well instead the game interprets it as you having told your character to walk right in front of that enemy and stand there.  F8.  I don't even want to talk about dragging bodies because this p!ssed me off all game long.  Tell character to drag a body over to a bush and drop it.  Come back to that character later and they're standing in the bush still holding onto the body.  Especially frustrating is when the ninja or samurai do this as they don't duck when holding a body.  So enemies will walk by and spot them standing upright in a bush with a dead body in their hands..... F8.  God forbid you try to get your character to drag a dead body to a door right after killing that enemy.  50% of the time they'll grab the body, then immediately drop it and start walking or running to the door for no reason.  “No you f.cker, that's not what I f.cking told you to do”  F8.  The number of times my characters did completely random things for no reason is too high to count.

The camera might be the absolute worst part of the game though.  Anything blocked by the camera is essentially unreachable for your characters.  On a narrow pathway with walls around it?  Gotta swing the camera so it's centered on the pathway so you can get your character to go down that path.  Want to go around that corner up ahead?  Well you can't just click around the corner, you've got to re-angle the camera so you can see down that pathway.  Want to get into that door around the next corner, gotta re-angle the camera.

The game has a severe problem dealing with ground/building levels.  If the camera is not exactly positioned correctly, character prompts like jumping, dropping down, throwing bodies off something become impossible to do.  For instance, it looks like there's a secret path you can jump to over there.  Well, the camera is off by 10 degrees, so the prompt for jumping doesn't appear for your character.  So you assume that secret passage isn't in play.  Then 10 minutes later at a slightly different camera angle you happen to pass by that area again and now the jump prompt appears.  Gee, would've been great if that would've shown up 10 minutes ago, would've saved me a lot of trouble.  Especially awful is being on rooftops as you must constantly swing the camera to move around.  One mission has you assassinating some enemy and there's a 3 level building nearby him. The game has a massive heart attack trying to interpret your actions up there.  You will constantly walk places you don't want to walk, jump down when you don't want to jump down, hookshot when you don't want to hookshot, etc.  Especially fun is that the prompt for the hookshot spots are always visible so you'll want to walk somewhere and keep getting the hookshot prompt because where you want to walk happens to have a hookshot prompt in the background somewhere.

The game has some inconsistencies with its noise mechanic.  To give a simple example of this, one of your characters has a technique allowing them to whistle.  Guards and villagers in range will be lured by this.  Sometimes enemies who are clearly highlighted blue indicating they'll hear this noise somehow won't hear it and continue along their way.  Other times enemies who are clearly not highlighted and outside of the range will hear the sound and come investigate.

Another problem with the game is that the vast majority of levels play out almost exactly the same due to the lack of enough puzzle elements.  There are only 4 enemies in the game.  Villagers who won't attack but will run away or report your position.  Guards who can be killed by everyone and be lured/distracted.  StrawHats who can be killed by everyone but won't leave their positions by lures and who will only briefly look at a distraction.  Samurai who work like StrawHats but can only be killed by your Samurai or by shooting them and then running up and stabbing them.  Samurai can also see through Aiko's disguise.  You'll have seen pretty much everything by level 6 but there're 13 levels total.  There's just not enough puzzle here to remain interesting and the vast majority of the puzzle is the same exact thing.  Picking off lone enemies or figuring out which enemy you can lure out and kill in a spot where someone else can't see them dying.

Shadow Tactics has some good ideas but the execution is amateurish.  There simply isn't enough new content/puzzle elements to warrant the number of levels in the game.  The camera, cursor, and random actions your characters take will provide no end of frustrations and swearing.  The game simply isn't polished enough to provide a worthwhile experience.

Objective score:  Nothing special to write home about, anything its praised for is kind of what should have been the min standard over a decade ago, im sorry these are min standards that should have been the norm 10 years ago if gamers were NOT bankrolling AAA slop, so such slop or lazy efforts wont get such praise from me, nor anything slightly above it.

This game is objectively lazy, dev tools, software, hardware and game engine tech has been streamlined so much in recent years even indie makes better graphics and complete games with 1 man armies and pocket change now, yet we are still praising min wage standards.

so at most this game gets a passing mark as it achieves that min benchmark, but nothing else.

Personal score  i will be honest... i got bored, combat is a bit jank it feels like someone did a remaster to a old 2003 game on 2010 hardware. Since the main story was a bit meh... and actual choices you get in many points are actually pretty linear (i reloaded saves at many points to check, basically did f all, only some of the words changed) basically if you go of the expected path, the world starts to feel as deep as a puddle and as wide as a floor mat, the devs kind of expect you to get distracted on the main mission and side missions, but if you go completely of rails it becomes pretty obvious there aint much else to do and the world is pretty broken and repetitive, all the kind of short cuts you would expect to see on a game from 2 decades ago that needs to cram it onto the cartridge or disk, so they cut corners... meanwhile 2025 and they are still acting like hardware and the internet hasnt improved and instead of cramming in more game play, they tend to just cram in more un-optimized textures and assets instead.

Though i hear the game has mod support, long as its well supported and the games flexible, then this could easily turn out to be another skyrim or cyberpunk when modded, but... i guess i will let things cook for a year or 2 and check back then.

review_text:
This game may be 17 years old, but it’s still a blast to play. The gameplay is smooth and enjoyable, with modes like Survivors vs. Zombies and Survival keeping things fresh. The ability for players to jump in and control bots adds a fun, dynamic twist, and the custom mod support breathes new life into it. Surprisingly, the cutscenes are visually stunning even by today’s standards, adding extra immersion to the experience.
That said, it’s not without its quirks. The terrain can be confusing, and the game lacks clear direction, which can make navigation frustrating. There’s also little distinction between difficulty settings, and the final campaign feels near impossible to finish with bot teammates. The base content is limited compared to modern games, but mods help fill the gap.
The player base may have faded over the years (expired), but this game still delivers plenty of fun for those willing to give it a try. If you enjoy nostalgic gems or are open to experimenting with mods, this one’s worth your time!
👍 Pros: Fun gameplay, amazing cutscenes, great modes, custom mod support, and a charming old-school feel.
👎 Cons: Confusing terrain, lacks direction, tough final mission, and limited base content.
⭐ Rating: B-Balanced.

review_text:
it starts out alright, but when it starts trying to challenge you with the puzzles, most of the frustration isn't from actually trying to work around the physics to build a connection but 90% of the time will be that the game wanted to trick you with the order of building. For example there will be a big gap of fire and you have matchstick goo and regular goo. You'll have to both build a bridge to cross the gap while keeping the matchsticks from being lit, but what you may not initially notice is that the fireproof goo needs to go on top in order to maintain a connection after you have to purposefully light the matches. If you don't notice this then you will have to start the entire level over again. This is opposed to some of the better puzzles where a spinning spike block needs to be built around with your goo in order reach the top.

Whenever the game tries to get more complicated it just gets more frustrating from annoyance rather than there actually being a puzzle. I think the only time I ever really had an "aha moment" was when I had to figure out how to lower a bomb to a specific level in order to destroy 2 walls that you then need to cross using the hanging thread. That's an incredible puzzle. It's just that most of the puzzles after the first world or 2 are going to be more of the former example than the latter. When I reached the digital realm I just decided to call it quits. It became about flinging the goo instead of actually building and so it just became click drag click drag and then they decided to expand upon this by having "corruption" that will make some of the goo red instead of green which will be important for the 3 layers of what you need to approach. Hope you didn't waste half an hour of your time flinging THESE green orbs when you needed THESE orbs to be RED orbs so your GREEN orbs can go over HERE but some of the orbs need to go HERE first and you might THINK you need to reset, you can't be sure since you don't know exactly how many of each orb you'll need to use or if they all need to be red at all since we won't let you survey the area unless you fling and stick some of the goo everywhere just to make sure you have a bad time.

Couple these frustrations with the actual game and then realize that the game both doesn't have an options menu to turn down the volume forcing you to either lower the entire volume for your pc or stick with the shitty soundtrack blaring over everything else on your system, and ALSO HAS THESE SETTINGS IN THE FILES that also are carefully laid out and explained thoroughly how to change these settings that you won't find unless you google how. Like holy shit, you put all this effort into laying out a file for people to find in order to let them change these specific settings and you couldn't just, like jesus christ if you needed 5 extra months just to make a menu system take the 5 months over whatever the fuck this is.
What makes that even worse is that the file doesn't even fucking WORK anymore, if it did at all in the first place. Setting the sound value to 0 doesn't do shit, setting it to 5 doesn't do shit and setting it to 0.5 doesn't do shit. 

My god, and if you thought that maybe the story carries any of this over the top, it really doesn't. This game can't fucking figure out if it wants to be the most frutiger metro ass motherfucking "stick it to the man" story about how "like if you think about it dude, like we're all just like cogs in the machine and like dude really like WE'RE the products in society like if you think about it." OR if it wants to constantly playfully poke at how the game is here just for the sake of being a game with constant signposts that'll say things along the lines of "oh don't worry in like level 4 the mechanics are going to be more interesting whatever that means but I'm sure you understand - the sign painter" or something meant to be poking fun at the game itself being a game. You can't have it both ways, if you wanted to have a message about society, as fucking on the point and shoved down your throat as it is then stick to that, if you wanted to have a video game ass game that's made just for the sake of providing the players some fun puzzles then you should lean into that and do literally whatever you want with the setting design and gameplay, even if the way the game itself is right now probably wasn't restricted at all by the premise it has currently, which should speak volumes to just how toothless and on the fucking nose most of the story is. They'll just jump between murky goo swamp to beauty pageant to fireworks from the top of a tower to idk the internet and stonehenge and it'll still all have the bottom line of "like dude society like kills our spirit if we like live inside their machine you gotta like get out of the system because like it's bad cause like they'll kill you and stuff for money or something?" You know this because they'll constantly remind you how the story exists so you don't need to worry about misunderstanding, forgetting or even not caring about it. You'll be constantly reminded regardless!

Look the first few hours should be an alright time for anyone, and to be genuine the game isn't bad enough with all of this to probably keep me from maybe finishing it if I have nothing to do for a big chunk of time and need something kindof simple and easy to pull out. It's just so full of annoyances and problems that I don't think I'd even recommend paying 5$ for it, maybe 1-3$ but I feel like so much of the game actively fights against you to play it, and when I'm this critical about the story as well, it's just not something that I can recommend from the position of my personal experience with the game.

review_text:
Pros: As usual with these developers, the voice acting is top of the line. High quality actors with great dialogue.
As with the previous game, the story is split up into multiple parts with different characters. Three of them return from the last game and one is new.
If you were tired of Kamurocho then rejoice because you will visit numerous new areas in this one.
Also as per usual with these devs, the game is perfectly optimized. Everything is on max settings on a 1440p ultrawide with smooth gameplay and no frame dips.
I rarely ever see bugs in these games either and never a single crash in any Yakuza title to date.
I like the new combat features and I don't dread the fights like I used to in some of the earlier titles (well the first 3 characters are fun to fight with, I didn't care for the last guy).

Cons: There are so many minigames. The earlier games had them too but this is even worse because they aren't optional. You'll find yourself street racing, taxi driving, making ramen noodles, driving a snowmobile and hunting animals in a blizzard, doing rhythm/dance minigames and playing baseball. It was horrible. I just want to beat bad guys up and watch a story unfold, geez.
The first part of the game had a ridiculously long and drawn out intro which really wasn't all that interesting.
The second part was worse as most of it was spent in prison just running around looking for the right person to talk to. Then the hunting stuff made no sense and was highly unenjoyable...even fighting a bear at one point which is absurd.
The third part was even WORSE than that. You spend half of that part of the game training to be a pop idol and not even fighting at all. You do dance battles instead...that's not a joke. At least half of this part you get to play as Akiyama, probably my favorite character but that's another con right there, my fave character gets the least screen time.
The fourth part was somehow EVEN WORSE THAN THAT. You have to play baseball and run around a horribly designed town full of cones and things that will hang you up and experience one of the most boring stories ever. It really doesn't feel like it even fits, it was like they just shoved it into the game as filler. I almost gave up at this point but I pushed through because I wanted to see how it ended.
The finale is usually one chapter but in this one it is 5 chapters and they are quite cheesy. There is so much to this story that doesn't make sense. I don't want to spoil anything so I won't go into details. Suffice to say, they usually knock the stories out of the park (pun not intended) but in this game, they absolutely dropped the ball (that pun was though).

This is the first time I have to go negative with a Yakuza review, it just isn't good from beginning to end. And unlike the 3rd game which was not fun but at least had a cool story, this one has basically nothing going for it. If everything I said above sounds as bad as it does, then avoid this one and watch a video summary/review or read a synopsis. However, if you like the Yakuza minigames and substories then this might be just another great title to you.

review_text:
5/10     Plays like and should be a $39.99 game.

Full breakdown

This game has so many great ideas that it refuses to explore more than on a surface level. It's not terrible just so very mediocre and by the numbers. You walk around reading a stack of notes and audio logs left behind by people while also gathering resources. You do one or two smaller enemy encounters to whittle down those resources you just collected. You visit a safe room right before a bigger fight so you can use currency and points to upgrade your equipment. Unfortunately the weapon upgrades don't have branching paths or any interesting bonuses to them, it's the "number goes up" type of a deal.

The game draws heavy inspiration from action focused survival horror games like Dead Space and Resident Evil 4. It however doesn't include fun or useful quality of life features like quickturning or a map. There is no separate inventory for quest items. There were multiple times where I had to backtrack to a safe room to store some items or simply waste some bullets so I could pick up the next mcguffin required to proceed. Inventory is very limited and needs to be upgraded with points for more space.
You only have one gun that transforms between different types so why is it that all the different forms take up one more inventory slot? This resulted in me not experimenting with the different variations simply because there wasn't enough space to carry them around.

You can charge your weapons up for more damage but this causes the crosshair to start shaking around violently while the enemy is barreling towards you. This adds a nice risk&reward mechanic that forces you to risk getting hit by the enemy. Character movement is deliberately slow and slightly clunky. Enemies are rather slow so it balances out decently enough.

Enemies aren't very interesting. It's the very trope biomass that deforms people into hideous monstrosities. This type of body horror loses all scare factor when used too much. Almost every area is just goopy flesh walls so it trivializes the horrid nature of the sickness that wiped out the world.

Game includes minor environmental puzzles where you have to route electricity by shooting spikes into a wall. I wish you could charge up these spikes so you could use them to stun enemies during combat or to create electrical traps during fights. The spikes are used on puzzles only and nothing else.
You can also rewind time at certain points of the game. Usually this means uncollapsing a structure so you can walk forward. It also allows you to rewind exploded barrels so you can reuse them during combat. This makes some enemy encounters trivially easy.
There is also gravity defying platforming similar to Dead Space remake but those are at very set points and usually just a way to get the player across longer distances. The gravity shenanigans aren't used in any interesting way, simply to get player across floating platforms in a boring void. Towards the end of the game there is a glimpse of what could have been when you get to fight upside down against some enemies.

The enemies themselves can merge with dead bodies becoming more powerful but this was rarely an issue. It did put nice pressure on the player during some of the early fights in the game when guns aren't as powerful and ammo is scarce. Later on this whole thing is trivialized by your powerful guns and the abundance of explosive canisters in nearly every big arena you fight in. You can also reuse the explosive canisters by rewinding time to reconstruct them.

WHOEVER WAS IN CHARGE OF APPROVING THE FOLLOWING ENEMY DESIGNS NEEDS TO BE PUT IN THE NAUGHTY CORNER! It is as if they tried to take the worst types of enemies from other games. Exploding acid blisters that are hidden behind corners or on walls. They can be shot to pop them or triggered by going near them for a second and running away. They spew acid on the floor forcing you to wait for a moment before proceeding. There are also tiny crawling explosive acid enemies that crawl towards you, explode if you get too close and jump at you exploding at contact. Worst ones are the wall enemies that quickly grab you forcing you to complete a quick time event to break free. Very often they are placed in very cheap spots or trigger when you pick up resources from a certain spot. Did they not listen to any of the playtesters since I can't fathom anyone enjoying these miserable time wasting traps.

The game has a poor balance between resource gathering and combat. There is too much snooping around for ammo and not enough situations to use said ammo. Whenever the game showed me a hallucination of a massive enemy horde I was ecstatic "FINALLY A BIG FIGHT!" only to make all the enemies vanish.

Boss fights early on are alright and those types become standard enemies later as is typical. Closer to the end of the game there are two boss fights almost back to back and both are such annoying ordeals to slog through. Acid spitting one liner repeating flesh totem with wall blisters that need to be popped and a teleporting bastard that has nearly unavoidable attacks. The final boss has two cutscenes right before you encounter him and thankfully you can skip those.

The performance of the game was all over the place. Lots of moments where it was stuttering and dropping FPS. I haven't tried the game on the Steam Deck yet but I'm very sceptical about them getting it Verified when it runs this poorly on a gaming PC on medium graphics (with DLSS on ultra performance setting).

I would recommend picking this up from a 50-75% sale if you're really thirsty for some third person shooting. Just don't expect to do that much shooting.

EDIT: Nope, nope. I've played about half of it now and I CANNOT recommend it. If you really want to play Hakuouki, try Aksys' versions on 3DS, PSP or PS3.

I've never left a negative review of an otome game like this, and I didn't think I'd advise against Hakuouki in my entire life, but here goes.

They censored Kimigiku's status as an oiran -- a courtesan -- to a "geigi", or geisha. The translation has been changed in certain spots and is much poorer, with a typo right in the first few minutes of the game.

Chizuru seems dumbed down, screaming things in all-caps, and even more timid than before. This is partially to blame because the game has been lengthened. In some cases the extra scenes are welcome, in others it feels like pointless padding to make the game longer. But the more she talks, she gets more indecisive and it gets boring.

They added plenty of scenes that made it drag and drag unnecessarily. But, then, bafflingly, they cut and altered certain scenes. Scenes such as when Nagakura and Harada are speaking of the coming war -- changing this in favor of Chizuru doing silent expo-speak.

The new music is awful, and is way too modern in certain places. The battle music is a form of techno, for god's sake. It's 1864!

I think it's part of a plan to "youth up" the game. The achievements for this game are impossibly annoying -- memes and slang like "New guy, who dis?" and "Still a better love story than". That and the techno REALLY make me think that they're trying to sell this to a younger crowd.

But Hakuouki has always been timeless, and if someone is too immature that they can't play a game without sharp, techno battle music and have the characters using more slang -- Harada says "like" as in, like, the way I just used it -- then they shouldn't be playing Hakuouki in the first place.

And the new characters are boring, droll and take up too much time. I kept skipping through their parts.

The only GOOD thing is that there are more scenes with the original characters -- the five main Shinsengumi and Kazama -- and you can now romance the other 3 Shinsengumi characters: Sanan, Yamazaki and Nagakura.


One more thing? Kyoto Winds + Edo Blossoms are one whole game if you purchase the 3DS, PSP or PS3 version. So you're not shelling out tons of money for what is supposed to be one entire game.

____

What is there, really, to say about Hakuouki? Other than, if you're an otome fan, this is an essential game. The artwork is beyond amazing, the story is richer than the best chocolate, and the routes are so emotionally involving that you'll feel sucked into it all. You'll laugh, you'll sob, characters will die, they'll leave their "brothers" behind as life goes on... It's quite moving.

I've loved Hakuouki for a decade now, since high school, when the anime came out and I streamed the fansub. Then when it came out, I had the Limited Deluxe Edition for the PSP. I'm just glad I'm able to continue playing this beautiful and romantic game long after my little portable console died.

If you love anything otome that Idea Factory has put out, or if you love otome games period, and somehow haven't played Hakuouki yet, do so. It's like a rite of passage.

It's worth it at any price.

Just Cause 4 can be a great buy if you find it on sale! However, it didn't quite capture the essence of a typical Just Cause game, which is known for its over-the-top destruction. It felt more like an experimental entry in the series. I really missed the overly ridiculous weapons from Just Cause 3, like the gravity gun and the lightning gun, and even the copy of Berrillium wingsuit that they offered was, let's just say the original mech wingsuite is the OG!

While the biom and world design are among the best in open world genre, the game overall felt a bit half-baked. Even the story in the original Just Cause was more engaging than this Espinosa crap...

The only thing they did good was graphics, but it's a shame they didn’t include a photo mode, an odd omission that feels like a missed opportunity.

Overall it's a enjoyable but somewhat lackluster experience.
