review_text:
If you first played Desperados and then this game there is chance you will get very frustrated now and then because of all kinds of small missing functionality in Shadow Tactics which was made a couple of years before Desperados. Argh!

Some of the annoying things are:
- not being able to click the enemy view cone, even if the enemy is highlighted, but the camera is not pointed into his direction. Therefore when an enemy is going into the direction of one of my characters i first have to move the camera around before i can find out if it will one of my characters and if so it is already dead because i was frustrating with the camera.
- not being able to jump into the water from a pier and instead running away from the pier, but being able to jump into the water when i first do a step aside.
- not being able to jump from a roof, but being able if i turn the camera a bit more. This breaks many attack moves because of needing to handle the camera like a little child that has to be told everything.
- when climbable objects are being highlighted and the camera is at the opposite site of a large mountain and you click on the mountain then it assumes you want to climb the object on the other side of the mountain. So it starts running along all kind of enemy partrols unless you cancel it fast enough by executing another move.
- in a later mission: gather in a boat, but take someone hostage. The hostage is like half a screen to the right, but the boat cannot go to that pier. Instead you have to take the hostage through the crowded enemy base and then to the enemy pier and then onto the boat. Isn't the principle of a boat that it can move through water?
- the strategic mode (shadow mode) does not pause the game, so planning multiple actions does almost never occur. The only thing i use it for is for distraction purpose (e.g. throwing a rock). Because if i want multiple actions like throwing a rock, wait 1 second, throw a knife, and then attack, that is not possible with the shadow mode. Also when 3 or 4 enemy guards are coming my way and i have 4 characters available then i cannot manage to have them respond all four. Simply because the shadow mode does not pause the game, like in Desperados. - Level scaling that is not calculated based on total xp (it is based off 'xp till level up', which means earning any xp before breakthrough is xp waste)
- Fishing has too much trash and requires two buttons to reel.

review_text:
10/10 Masterpiece!

This game is fantastic. It's a better version of Yakuza 4. This time we play five characters (Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama and Shinada; Tanimura is no longer playable). 

I think the story is really great. In my opinion, it has the same level of hype and emotion as Yakuza 0. 

The graphics and soundtracks are also fantastic. 
It's also cool that we can play in five different locations in this game, whereas in the previous games there are only one or two locations available to explore.

But my highlight is the gameplay. The combat system is almost the same as Yakuza 0 and I got along well (much better than Yakuza 3 and 4). You can also automatically assign the points you earn when you level up. 
But that's not all. I think it's cool that the characters have different jobs: Kiryu as a cab driver (almost had a GTA vesion to Yakuza/Like a Dragon T_T), Saejima (then as the game progresses) as a hunter, Haruka as an idol pop star, Akiyama as a laid back loanshark (like in Yakuza 4), and Shinada as a journalist who used to be a baseball player. 

[spoiler]The game ends with a cliffhanger, and the story continues with Yakuza 6. Boy, am I glad I only discovered the game series last year. I'd be impatient if I had to wait a few years to see the game's sequel.[/spoiler] 

Overall:
Anyway, I'm grateful that you guys released the series on PC, Sega.
It might almost be my favorite Yakuza/Like a Dragon game. But I'll come to that conclusion once I've played through every game in the series.
I look forward to playing more of your older games. ^^

Everything is really rigid and with little to no clues, you'll find yourself running around aimlessly looking for things to interact with.

The only enjoyable part is watching the ridiculous ways people die but you'd be better off watching a YouTube video showing all the deaths than going through the actual game.

review_text:
What would happen if Titanfall and Tron had a steamy night of passion while listening to darksynth and vaporwave? This, probably. Although a more mixed option would be more appropriate for this game, I'd still rather recommend it, as it's an amazing concept that is fun as is and has amazing potential to be a lot more in future. TLDR: gud gem, get it.

The good:
-The movement: to say that it's Titanfall inspired would be an understatement (this applies to the whole game and is in no way a bad thing). There's some sprinklings of Ghostrunner, Doom Eternal and Superhot too. You have a wide variety of options and the movement is super smooth, fast and satisfying. Running around in this game never gets old.
-The guns: there's a lot of them, all of which feel amazing, are superbly precise and are made even better by some outstanding sound design and reload animations. Like seriously, I've seen AAA games do far worse in this department.
-The loadouts: this system gives players a lot of choice on how to start each run and provide a wide variety of playstyles.
-The soundtrack: look at some screenshots. What do you think the game sounds like? Yes, exactly. And it's awesome.

The bad:
-Level design: while not bad, it's not as good as it can be in my opinion. There's more fun things that can be done, especially with all the wacky movement options available
-Enemies: they're alright, but the problem lies in that you are soooooo much faster than all of them. Like, in this game you literally play like a speedrunner most of the time and this leads to you simply blasting past the enemies and running circles around them. They simply can't keep up and that kinda cripples the game and stops it from utilizing its full potential.
-Visibility: related to the previous, because of the visual style chosen (while I do like it a lot) visibility can be an issue. From far enough away, enemies just become this blob of light that's barely distinguishable, some enemies are hard to tell apart at first glance and attacks can blend into stuff too. I would suggest that things should be colour coded, similar to Mirror's Edge or Superhot. For example all enemies are coloured red, all wallrunnable surfaces are green, all edges are blue, the escape door is orange (obviously) and so on. This would make things easier to see. Some more minor gripes are that the pure black surfaces are kind of hard to see. You can't tell where there is a slope or whether you can climb onto or wallrun on something when looking from certain angles. Perhaps more lines to designate this should be present. Also, the fish-eye effect from the FOV is a bit too extreme when you widen it to decent levels. If possible, this should be toned down.
-Bugs: it's an early access indie project, so I can forgive this, the issues aren't too severe either. Andrew also tracks these and does his best to fix them in a timely manner. But they still warrant a mention in a thorough review like this.
-Lack of content: this is the biggest one, easily. For now, all you can do is pass through the few levels available or fight in endless modes in the same arenas. Also a lot of features are not implemented yet. Now, I know this is an early access indie game and I have nothing bad to say about Andrew, he's done an amazing job so far. But there's a lot of stuff still missing and the game is sometimes a hard sell with an IOU sitting in place of so much of the content, merely promising what the game could be but isn't yet. I can only wish Andrew all the best in making this vision a reality

Conclusion:
GTTOD is a weird one. I still recommend it, as it's exceptionally fun and cool. Beware though, there's a lot of missing content and you may face some minor issues. Adjust your expectations accordingly. For what it is, this game is still really fun and exciting and worth a try. While we all wait and pray for Titanfall 3, this game offers some epic single player on demand fun. I also sincerely hope that before that, Andrew can flesh out his project and turn the obvious potential that this game has into a rich and complete experience.

I know that I played the game only a few min on the PC, but I played hundreds of hours on the mobile version. Many people were complaining that Battle Nation is a typical 'Facebook game' bougth to steam, but I need to disagree. Battle Nation was designed for mobile Phones and Tablets, what you can clearly see when playing the game. It is a game where you play for 20 min and then stop playing until all your task are finished. But if you want, you can stick up to a few hours without a break into the game without getting bored. But i also need to go over a few bad things. While there is no requirement to ever pay money, there are advantages for paying player. You can buy yourself nanopods to speed up thing, but anyone that does this is an idiot. The only real use for nanos are the fact that you can buy yourself some special units that are a little bit better that their normal counterpart. But  thanks to the level system, F2P player can have units that easy match there Premiun units counterpart. The most expensive units in the game cost maximum 4 dollar, but when you get one of them you can see them as a long time investment. Every month there is a so called Boss Strike event in the game that usually introduces a premium limited time unit that can only be purchased with nanopods for a certain time ( about 5 days). These units are very powerful and are always designed to help players with the Boss Strike if there are lacking the units to compete in it. For every enemy that you kill in this wave styled event, you get Boss Strike points, which when enough collected will give you exclusive plane units that are in the current state not being able to purchase. You can even get in every Boss Strike free Nanopods worth about 8-10 dollars. I hope that I was able to convince a few people to try the game out.

Overpromised, underdelivered, abandoned.

BONELAB is a game that owes its entire monetary success to an initial wave of unearned hype. Let me make this clear: I LOVED Boneworks. It's one of the best VR titles available - even now, years after its release. But this game, despite all the bold claims of having "full modding support!" and being "like Boneworks but bigger and better!", BONELAB is nothing but a hollow shell with a pretty painted exterior - a glorified tech demo for a promising concept that will never see the light of day. 

Never before have I felt so scammed by a developer I had come to trust. Stress Level Zero, you should be ashamed. And to anyone reading this review who is considering buying BONELAB, do yourself a favour and just go play Boneworks instead. There's nothing worthwhile for you here.

I did not start playing this series on Pathologic 1, and I'm not the type to shy away from a difficult game at all. But this game left a sour taste in my mouth, the cryptic and uninteresting dialogue, gratuitous and unnecessary female nudity and bulging nipples, and strange fever dream scenes that just pointlessly plopped down executor and giant bull assets. Very strange game design direction overall.

I can still run around the town, up and down side to side, while dying of starvation and lack of sleep. How on earth am I still able to do these things while starving and tired? How was this an oversight in a survival game? I ended up being as reckless as possible with hunger and sleep so that I could get a couple more objectives done. And for what? Just so the game can get harder as I died from hunger and illness attempting to complete an objective. 

On a positive note, the sound design for ambient sounds was phenomenal, kept me on edge and pushed my face in the dirt and dragged me along with how eerie and oppressive it was. 

I really regret buying this game and giving it a long and honest try, because now I cannot refund it.

review_text:
If we don't get a Just Cause 5 Imma riot. Cause this game has some issues and most people don't seem to like the progression but I don't think it makes any sense to kill a franchise because they tried a really cool idea but it wasn't liked by most. 

The whole army and front lines system is super cool. It's mostly the quantity of the challenges that don't give you anything and you can't easily tell that I have an issue with, within the new system. Everything besides the progression is either as good as or just a straight upgrade from Just Cause 3. 

The new grappling system is super fun and with lots of ways to customise it leaves a lot of options for the player to have fun with. The new AR lens is a nice addition for a couple of reasons. 1. It lets some of the things the player can see make sense within the story(like the rings to fly through or objectives markers).The Nitro and stuff I don't have an issue with but I do think could be improved by just giving it to all vehicles that have no other use for the Left and Right mouse buttons but I would say only when you call them in a supply drop cause it's a bit weird to have a crappy car have Nitro and jump on it if it's one an civilian owns.

Imma list some of the things that annoyed me about the game.
-I don't like the grapple being finicky with regards to whether or not it's just going to pull you in or let you tether something but that was in JC3 as well so nothing new.

-Not to do with the core game but the hoverboard cable riding mechanic is clunky and annoying to use IMO
-I would LOVE to be able to use my mouse to fly a plane instead of WASD.
-Not being able to call in multiple things at once
-Weapons not being supply dropped with max ammo.
-A couple of the missions didn't use the AR lens to mark where you need to go as to let you figure it out but with how free the movement of Just Cause is you can end up completely missing whatever the game things you will see to help guide you. The Main one is the "Follow the lights to find the generators" or something like that. I tried following the lights but I could only find 1 path the lights went and just grappled around the place to try and find them without utilising the intended method which I try to do to get an idea of what the game wants to happen in games to not miss something. But all of that is pretty petty and not a massive issue but it's a pretty accurate example of what most of the issues with the game are. Just small QoL things or questionable execution on some ideas on a very small scale. 

I can't remember why I didn't play this game on launch other than performance and I just lost interest because something more interesting came up and drew my attention until I forgot about JC4, IDK. 
This game is a good sequel. It might not be better than JC3 but it does almost everything the game before does but it expands and builds upon it. And it may have made some bad choices. And it's not ever going to be as good as JC3 is because most of us grew up between then and now.

The setup for JC5 is super good and makes me want it so badly. I really hope we are going to get it.


Lastly I wanna add I like all the DLC but the Demon one. That one is not very fun and doesn't give you very much, just a crossbow.

review_text:
So id have to call this game a mixed bag, the humor and art i love, and the game play loop isnt exactly bad but it becomes stale after a while, i could recommend this game but theres things i would wanna see looked over first not that im saying some things i dont like are the entire point but here we go.

1.Class stacking/level cap: i dont hate the whole "have x different types of unit for a buff" as an idea, but in the late game it takes a goofy turn with levels being capped at 5 so the lower teir tank you have had for longer will always be worse then a higher tier one, but you cant get rid of them because you lose the class buff and you become stuck with it, some classes have less of this problem like cultists because you can have any amount and you get more benefit but most classes seem to hit a point where spamming higher tier units and ignoring the class buff works out best for raw power.

2. Healers: The main form of healing needs a light twist, this is a small gripe but the healers should really be focused on healing the most damaged party members rather then the closet damaged ones, helpful buffs ended up hurting a team because healers starting pumping backliners who took a small amount of damage ruining the point of having them.

3. Paid Mutations: if the currency is shared between shop/food/mutations thats not necessarily a problem, but i cant help but feel that the purchased mutations might be better as something placed in a shop, a lot of people complain about RNG here but i noticed after a while you start to pick out which mutations are the best to buy and every run starts to blend together a bit in doing so, its not a huge deal but it takes away some of the excitement of finding what your looking for.

4.unique quests: Ive played through some of the level quests different characters will give you and i like the idea although you may want to generalize the bonus they give a bit more, tokens are nice if you dont like that particular buff but it feels a bit lame in my opinion when compared to getting something the team can use.

5. Classes themselves: the classes are very neat and i like the style for a lot of them, and this is more of a suggestion then a gripe, but multiclassing characters who have hit level 5 as a sort of second job kinda thing might make things more interesting as well as help push away some of the meta feel about which groups are worth taking and if tiers or buffs are more useful.

Overall i had fun with the game when i first played it, came back after a few months to see how it looked after a bunch of updates and while it isnt bad i cant say id be itching to tell someone to play it, its funny, it looks good, but it lacks replay-ability outside of trying to complete challenges. If mixed were an options for recommend id put it there.

review_text:
1. Remember when you destroyed bases and villages to liberate them? That’s gone now.  

2. Make racing a paid DLC.  

3. Replace all missions with escorting broken AI that has awful pathfinding.  

4. To liberate areas now, all you do is escort broken AI, click "liberate" on the map, and that’s it. No more rewards for destroying bases. If you blow up a base in Just Cause 4, you get literally nothing for it.  

5. The game menu is far more complicated and cluttered with unnecessary junk.  

6. Not sure why the developers keep changing Rico’s appearance. He's had three different skin tones across the games. With a new voice actor, he doesn’t sound like himself either. It’s like the devs still can’t decide what Rico should look like. it's like we're playing a cheap ripoff of Just Cause  

7. Graphics are somehow worse than Just Cause 2 and 3. The water is a huge downgrade.  

8. Destruction is better than Just Cause 3, but you get absolutely nothing for doing it.  

9. Not sure why developers feel the need to inject monsters or aliens into DLCs that make zero sense.  

10. Outpost liberation is now locked behind DLC and only available on cargo ships. Worse, every cargo ship is an exact copy-paste with no variation.  

11. The main villain, aka your dad, who seems to be the dictator in this game, only appears three times throughout the story and you never get to fight him.  

12. The Wind Gun is amazing and super fun to use, but since destruction is pointless, what’s the point?  

13. Enemy AI is absolutely abysmal. Remember in Just Cause 3 when enemies hit hard and forced you to keep moving? Now, they just stand there and shoot. On top of that, they tank more bullets than they did in Just Cause 3.  

14. Every single mission in the game consists of hacking consoles, defending AI hacking consoles, or defending some tower. That’s literally it.  

15. Explosives have been removed. No more blowing bridges sky-high like in Just Cause 3 with explosive charges.  

16. You can no longer barrel roll with the jetpack or pull off cool movement techniques.  

17. Weather effects are completely wasted. The tornadoes and lightning storms were hyped as game-changing, but they barely impact gameplay in any meaningful way. They feel more like a gimmick than an actual feature. or to better illustrate my point look at Battlefield 2042.

18. The grapple hook has been nerfed. While the new tethers and boosters are fun, movement feels clunkier and lacks the fluidity of Just Cause 3.  

19. No chaos system. Blowing up bases in previous games contributed to overall chaos progression. Here, destruction does absolutely nothing.  

20. Weapons feel weak and unsatisfying. Many guns lack impact, making combat feel dull compared to previous games.  

21. The wingsuit feels worse. It doesn't feel as smooth or fun as in Just Cause 3, making traversal less enjoyable.  

22. Side content is dull and repetitive. There’s barely anything worthwhile to do outside of the main missions, and the few side activities that exist feel copy-pasted.  

23. Vehicles handle terribly. Cars and bikes feel stiff and unnatural, making driving more of a chore than a thrill.  

24. No real incentive to explore. The map is huge, but it feels empty with no real rewards for going off the beaten path.  

25. The game feels unfinished. From bad AI to missing features, it seems like the devs rushed this out the door without polishing it.  

26. The story is the weakest in the franchise so far, which is usually forgivable since players come for the gameplay. However, when the core appeal of causing chaos is stripped away and the fun factor is missing, the game becomes pointless.

27. The game looks much more dull and toned down compared to the more beautiful and vibrant 3 which still holds up today if you swapped 3 and 4 around you can see how much of a downgrade this is.

28. Music is worse than 3, 3s music was absolutely amazing

29. things don't stay destroyed and respawn

30. Rico's Iconic Duel weld pistols were removed and in general you can no longer duel weld any weapons      

Overall, I have no idea why this game is even called Just Cause when the entire point of causing chaos has been removed. Somehow, it even gives Ubisoft a run for its money. I get that developers sometimes cut corners, but this isn’t just cutting corners. They've stripped almost everything from the game, leaving behind a dull, broken experience filled with escorting incompetent AI and tedious console hacking minigames in a series known for blowing things up.  

After this i'm genuinely concerned for the future of Just Cause mainly with the fact that a 5th instalment has been confirmed and I hope they really take the criticism seriously

review_text:
Pretty good at what it's trying to do, but definitely not for everyone.

The game sets itself apart from most platformers with a veneer of player hostility in most of its design elements--weapons attack slowly, many weapons are single use, your dodge roll is clumsy, enemies deal brutal damage with quick attacks, HP and MP aren't refilled for free anywhere, etc.

However, it's kind of a smokescreen. Healing items are showered on you as you go, the AI is braindead, and many of the items are gamebreaking (including items that grant infinite free healing/MP refills, negate all traps/bad terrain, and infinite use ranged weapons).

Fortunately, none of that stops it from FEELING like you're triumphing over stacked odds and an unfair game. It's just hostile enough to feel good finding and using the stuff that's broken. You will have to proceed slowly and use your brain, but it's not actually that difficult except a few spots.

Other stuff: Visuals are quite good with great monster design and great animations. Enemy design+variety is pretty good. Boss design is hit-or-miss. Despite looking like a metroidvania basically none of the stuff you gain are used for exploration or movement.

Here, you have to obtain the metaknowledge of exactly what to do in the game to have a chance your second time through, which could mean like 15-20 hours wasted, and then the exact same amount of hours spent retracing your exact steps up to a point.

“Would you kindly enjoy one of the best games ever while questioning your morality and fear of the ocean?”

Pros:

Rapture is a beautifully dystopian underwater city filled with wonder, terror, and way too much leaking.

Splicers have better cardio than you and never stop screaming nonsense.

Relatable Humor:

Verdict:

If you love immersive worlds, philosophical debates, and wielding superpowers while frantically scavenging for health kits, BioShock is a masterpiece. Just be ready for plot twists that hit harder than a Big Daddy’s drill.

Final Score: 10/10. Would get ambushed in a creepy hallway again.

review_text:
The aesthetics are brilliant. The new player experience as of Webgrave, is seamless. I was incredibly surprised to hear that the new playable map, as well as the tutorial area, were very recent additions - it all flows extremely well.

The gameplay is basically like the open world locations of Destiny 2, but with a lot of those Events, to use destiny terminology. Now, this sounds boring. But why isn't it?

Because the gunplay is as good as in Destiny, and more importantly, the game emphasizes secret hunting (both for progression, and for unlocking trinkets for your rosary), and has pretty captivating ARPG and rougelike-like elements, so you always have new weapons, demonic weapons, spells, heavy spells, rings, etc to grind towards.

And yes, you grind through the same few levels.But whenever your character levels up, all enemy encounters are drastically changed. Even without levelling up, each time you re-enter a map, it is randomly re-filled with secrets, loot, enemies, and even new things to experience, all paced really well. You might feel like exploring off into some interesting corner of the map, only to find another bead for your rosary. Nice collectible hunting. (Did i mention that the rosary is apparently also a recent addition? I can hardly believe it, as it fits so well.)

Each map has an excellent boss-fight at it's end (apart from the first map, though i suspect there might be a boss in an area that i'm unable to explore yet - as the game gives you reasons to return to older maps once you reach certain levels of Gnosis.)

The combat is pretty great, and it can actually get incredibly difficult. This is the first shooter game in a long time where my deaths have felt genuienly avoidable, and yet i died either way. Ya gotta keep track of the enemies circling around you, ya gotta dodge, ya gotta jump, ya gotta duck behind cover to avoid ranged fire, ya gotta learn the enemies' attack patterns so you don't get flattened while trying to shotgun them in the face (Really, it's almost as if this is *gasp* the Dark Souls of first person shooters?)... so yeah. Relatively simple gameplay, but well done. And excellent aesthetics. I always appreciate some semi-victorian semi-medieval witchcraft-themed games. And this one even has some architecture to rival Bioshock Infinite's, though with a slightly more muted colour palette. But *man* is that castle location awesome!

review_text:
If you love devlogs and being behind the scenes of a game while it's in development, then GTTOD will be your bread and butter. As a game alone in its current state, it's hard to recommend. Off-Brand

Diving a bit deeper, I originally saw this being played by a YouTuber, the footage looked good, their commentary and recommendation was good, and I thought... movement shooter with some roguelite elements? I can get behind that! So I haphazardly bought the game on a whim, I mean, it's pretty cheap and when it's on sale it's really cheap. Even for an Early Access game.

But it's still really rough around the edges. I think most people, if they're not informed will buy it now and be disappointed (and I think that might be why the Steam rating is at 89% at the time of writing). I look at GTTOD, and think of it more as a promise, that one day, I'll go back through my Steam Library, find this game at its full 1.0(+) release, and have a blast. For players like me, it feels more like I've thrown down money as a pledge, and I'm happy to do so in order to support the project & the dev/s. I love the style, love the concept, hope it all gets realized. This is the main reason why I might recommend it.

Some players might be really into the idea of following this games progress along, and will be happy to know that the main developer is super active in their discord, and takes community feedback very seriously. Some people love seeing behind the curtain of a games development and having opportunities to possibly shape the direction of a game. If that's you, I think you'll love joining this game on its journey and being an active part of that community.

But I don't think the majority of people coming to this game will be in either of those mindsets and I believe for them it might be better to wait for this game to develop a bit more. Some of the games mechanics aren't flushed out entirely. The gunplay feels good enough, but gets stale after awhile, because the game just hasn't developed to that point yet. There is no real goal at the moment besides leveling up your character for marginal starting differences. The view bobbing and overall camera shaking is crazy... You can look through the reviews to find more of these kinds of complaints. GTTOD has potential around every corner, and promise at every horizon... it just might take a while in the oven to get there and it's important to realize that.

I think with all that information you can make an informed purchase. Don't buy into the exceptionally well done marketing or the words of YouTubers... and remember that you're not really buying a game right now... but rather the proof of your belief that the devs can put in the work to make and release a great game someday (with the added bonus of an ever changing alpha version of this game on the side).

I find the controls clunky and unresponsive. The story is nonsensical in its presentation while at the same time predictable as it works thru every genre cliche. It isn’t helped that I’m certain the game is mostly machine translated and voiced by AI. The characters are also uninteresting genre typical stereotypes. All in all, it doesn’t excite me but rather leaves me bewildered. 

Some of the mini games are very poorly explained and the map is cluttered with things to discover like an open world game from UbiSoft. On top of that the game world is littered with notes from other players that mostly want to troll you, take away the joy of discovery or solving a puzzle yourself. 

Not to mention the game probably has every monetization scheme in existence in it, including unreasonable pricing. It also comes with a ton of sub-systems and UIs that make it overall just overloaded and confusing. 

The game is an unfocused mess filled with AI slop.

Rooftops & Alleys: The Parkour Game’s ethos is perfectly described by its own subtitle. This is quite simply, “The Parkour Game.” For decades, we’ve had many big-budget open-world titles implementing freerunning into their exploration, like Assassin’s Creed or Dying Light. Parkour in these games feels satisfying, but the controls are simplified as it’s just another tool in games with very broad focuses. When you get a game more holistically focused on parkour, such as Mirror’s Edge, it’s usually an extremely fast-paced experience that wraps up after a few hours.

Rooftops & Alleys breaks these trends by focusing on an elaborate freerunning system whilst also providing total player freedom. Whether you want swift, efficient movement or ridiculously elaborate displays of style, Rooftops & Alleys has you covered.

But how much can an excellent parkour system carry a full game? Well, if it’s fun enough, I’d say it absolutely can, but Rooftops & Alleys stumbles just often enough to make enjoying the game a constant battle. Despite an excellent core, issues across its movement systems and empty levels always seemed to limit its potential. How much these issues will bother you will come down to personal experience. When Rooftops & Alleys is at its best, it’s an amazing experience. Unfortunately, it’s rarely at its best.

about 30 minutes in and so far it's just a bunch of unskippable cutscenes. not even good cutscenes. these cutscenes are awful and there's 10 seconds between each line of dialogue and there's nothing you can do. the developers have zero respect for your time. also you can't just leave it running and come back later because you have to periodically press A to get past one of the dialogue lines.

there is a tutorial mixed in between all these terrible cutscenes but it showcases some pretty bad gameplay. basically just a walking sim with some combat. the combat is... laughable. spam button and eventually the enemy will die or magically disappear. it's so bad.

the tutorials are borderline insufferable. the game does not feature complex gameplay. most things are automated. do we really need these forced tutorials to learn how to hold W? actually you don't even need to hold W a lot of the time. for example, once you start grinding on a rail, you can just walk away and the character will continue going until the rail ends. even if the rail goes straight up in the air or around corners. why do we need all these boring tutorials for that? just put us in the game

there are predetermined places to place graffiti and the game auto chooses which graffiti goes up. there's a mini game for placing the graffiti that involves moving your cursor around, but you cannot fail. so you can just swing your cursor around in a circle until it's done. you don't have to get it right because you're not allowed to fail. lol.

the tricks get old fast. there's 3 tricks and they do the same thing every time. there's no way to change the tricks or gameplay in any way. you will need to chain the different tricks together for speed. thats about as deep as the game gets. again, it's worth comparing to Hover which had a number of different characters with upgrades that you could customize for different builds to suit your playstyle.

as for the post-tutorial world. it's bland and flat. there doesn't seem to be much in the way of verticality unlike Hover which had tons of verticality  from the get-go. theres also... more forced cutscenes. in fact, all this game does is make me want to play Hover again.

this game feels like more of a demo for some kind of open world adventure game where you get around by skating, but there's nothing in the world that's worth exploring or finding. just graffiti spots. it's a boring, repetitive, shallow game.

the game also does not mute in background or even have an option. that alone earns it a negative review.

skip it. play something with actual gameplay.

review_text:
EDIT (Final thoughts after completing the game):

After finishing Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2: doing every task, side quest, and side activity - I have some mixed but definitive conclusions. The game starts off incredibly strong. The writing is tight, the world feels wide open, and the level of detail is frankly astonishing. It gives you the illusion of limitless freedom, and for a while, it really feels like you're inside a living, breathing medieval world.

But somewhere around the Kuttenberg main quests, the seams start to show. Voice acting quality dips noticeably—some characters sound like they were recorded on a webcam mic by budget Fiverr freelancers. The quests begin to drag, and worst of all, they include hidden, progress-breaking decisions that aren’t communicated clearly. By that point, I stopped feeling immersed and started playing out of “FOMO,” afraid to turn in quests or even talk to NPCs without saving first or Alt-Tabbing to a quest guide or reddit post. (Thank god for the save-anywhere mod.)

The ending was... a disaster. Cringe-inducing. A good writer knows when to stop, and this one didn’t. The whole "bad/good ending" premise is misleading. There’s no impactful branching conclusion like The Witcher or even Metal Gear Solid: Twin Snakes. Just a strange dream dialogue and a flat, forgettable finale that left me thinking: That’s it? That’s what I spent dozens of hours building up to?

All in all, I can’t recommend this game to most people. especially not if you’re looking for a coherent, satisfying narrative. That said, there are moments where this game truly shines: scenes with von Aulitz, Adder, and several side quests are genuinely unforgettable. But those moments don’t reflect the bulk of my 215 hours.

The save system is another major flaw. I get what the developers were going for, but restricting saves, or forcing players to save constantly - ultimately pulls you out of the role-playing experience and reminds you you're just "playing a game." There has to be a better way to support immersion without punishing the player, even if I don’t have the perfect solution myself.

OLD REVIEW (early impressions):

Probably amazing if you’re not over 30 and busy with real life. The lack of manual saves (until you mod it) is a dealbreaker when paired with game-breaking bugs. Even after installing the save mod, the AI keeps screwing me over and making me lose progress. Wait for a patch. Or three.

review_text:
As a fan of star trek it's easy to look at this game and get the occasional shot of nostalgia. From universe accurate weapons, factions, lore, persons of interest, voice acting, sounds, and  music, the game is a nostalgia trip for anyone who has or is exploring the Star Trek Universe.

The good:
 Mechanically, there are two different combat systems:  Sace, and Ground.  Space combat, under most circumstance, is why people play this game.  Space combat, despite mostly being automatic with some offensive/defensive/HOT cooldowns needing to be pressed to to inject some player agency into the combat, is good, and really drives home the game concept, and drama of the setting. There are a number of ships, including famous ships from the series 5 and a half decades long lore, and several small factions you can join, though eventually those smaller factions need to choose to join one of the two larger factions.  Attacks happen in space on a 360 degree ring around your ship, and some weapons have firing arcs, which in turn require you to aim, pivot, and allow you to smartly dodge, or even counter enemies should you maneuver away quickly enough, use appropriate skills, or fly strategically.  Space combat is intuitive under most circumstances, and in a number of situations, the space missions can be varied and interesting, like flying a shuttle through a significantly larger ship to scan and find it's weakness.  That said, most of the missions are generic affairs of "go to system, scan thing 1, fight off 1-2 ships, scan thing 2, fight off 3 ships, scan thing 3 fight off big bad ship while big bad proselytizes at you, and eventually angrily shakes their fist at you while their ship explodes in a generic explody gif, or, if they're romulan, gets resized, and eventually consumed by a rapidly expanding singularity, which eventually explodes in a ring of green generic explody gif.

The Character customization, despite much of it being locked away behind a paywall, and a decade old, is good.  There are several races available each with their own traits (you can even make your own race), and multiple ways which you can customize your Character's outfit, ship, even your Away team/bridge crews outfits, faces, hair styles, even in some cases, their race (if you have an "Alien" bridge officer).



The Meh:
The ground combat, under almost all circumstances, is very bland.  You can choose between a tab targeting style of meh ground combat, or by pressing B, go into a meh and clunky version of third person mouse driven shooter-like combat with powers.  You could be easily deceived that hiding behind cover will protect you.  It will not, and you will primarily be engaging in ground combat via the same combat system utilized in Conan Unchained:  A normal attack that hits one guy, a secondary attack that either hits one guy really hard/stuns/knocks them down or aoe flavor of secondary, While a third attack that in the case of STO, is a melee attack, if you're using ranged weapons.  In the case of melee weapons, it's just Conan Unchained, Left attack, right attack forward swing, in varied flavors based on the weapon in hand.  Much like in space, you have access to powers, heals, grenades, summon more allies, resuscitate fallen away team members, dodge roll, kneel, sprint and aim.  To add to this, your away team NPC allies, have a degree of agency and will randomly throw out their own abilities (grenades, heals, turrets, etc.). 

STO ground combat tries very hard to be something it is not capable of due to old coding, and is mostly okay, just easily forgettable- which is a shame since you will be spending what feels like half of your time kneeling in corridors, and zapping baddies with phasers/disruptors.


The Bad:
From a sub-client launcher, to the antediluvian graphics engine, wonky at best animations, and awkward interface, the game quickly, despite layers and layers of caked on makeup, shows its age.  Character heads are often made of singular polygons, and do not have facial animations.  Character models in cutscenes will emote like NPCs from Fable 1 at you, flailing head, or limbs relentlessly until you finally decide to end their suffering and skip the cutscene, OR will stand there awkwardly seeming to lean forward  as their massive low fidelity forehead takes up 70% of the screen so close that you can count the individual pixels that make up their forehead wrinkles.  Game glitches, like severe rubber-banding, memory leaks, graphical glitches, geometry errors, pathing errors for NPCs/enemies and companions,  seams in maps that players and NPCs alike can fall through, old in game videos, that display these errors, sound/music being poorly balanced, and egregious bad hud design.  I understand that the HUD needs to fit the star trek aesthetic, but it can do so, without being so ugly.

The REALLY BAD:
As you'd assume, there are Three major points of contention with this game:  The Cash Shop, The Publisher, and The Developer.

We'll start with the big one:
The Publisher, is Arc Games.  A publisher that is so universally hated, vilified and  that they had to change their name from Perfect World Entertainment, to Arc Games. Perfect World Entertainment (PWE) has notoriously published, and slowly destroyed such games as Champions Online, Neverwinter, Torchlight, and now Magic The Gathering, through predatory cash shop practices that proceed to whale-bait their clients into spending money.  Several features of the cash shop in STO include, $10-30 purchases of clothing and bridge/duty crew,  $30 purchases of ships, $200 purchases of ship bundles, or fast track content clear tokens costing nearly $100.

Cryptic Studios:
You may know of this company.  A company that has released games that could genuinely be good mmorpgs, Champions Online, Magic The Gathering, Star Trek Online, and Neverwinter.  Both  Star Trek Online, and Neverwinter once had a feature called"The Foundry," that allowed players to create their own in game content such as missions that could span several planets, space combat, political intrigue, and ground combat missions.  This feature was Sunset in 2019 for several reasons.  The most obvious reason was that a player could create a mission that would allow other players to level up rapidly while avoiding the monotony of the in game grind.  So, some players were making missions that could be played on repeat, where you could gun down several ships in a row and level up to cap within a few hours, if that is what you wanted to do, BUT, you still needed to play through the main campaign to unlock new areas and gear.  Alongside Cryptic Studios other games, STO feels like it's always in a state of life support mode, where new content will either be promised and never show up, or come out in such a way that you need to use the cash shop to advance through it in any meaningful way.

The Conclusion (I have no doubt that many people who read this will skip straight here):

I understand that some people, will really love Star Trek Online.  STO is an interesting game with fun lore about Exploring space, seeking out new life and new civilizations and blasting them into an inevitable nuclear winter until they submit to your rule as their federation overlords... or klingon overlords... I'm not judging.  The game has some real fun moments, and some exciting story points (especially the romulan campaign), but beware the publisher.  Arc Games aka "Perfect World Entertainment" is such a predatory company that it makes EA look like an angel.

I truly wish I could refund this game, a 6 hour play time is rarely worth $40, and this is not one of those times. I never really followed the development, and bought the game because of the interesting world it attempts to build rather than the gun play, so the FPS part of the game is not a letdown for me. I actually rather enjoyed the FPS aspect, even though it only lasted about 30 collective minutes.
My issue with the game is the setting and your actions lead you to believe there's this grand story you can unfold and you can find out what happened in the past, only for it to actually just be a large metaphor which honestly isn't even that thought-provoking. I feel as if none of what you explore, encounter, and alter matters because instead of being explainable and contributing to world building, it just exists to further the metaphor that the devs want to illustrate. It's a shame, because the world is beautiful (and grotesque) and has so many stories to tell, but you get the story where your effort explains nothing and effectively means nothing, and neither does your $40, all because the game is designed to "send a message", or something.

review_text:
(Mild Spoilers) This game is terrible. Not only are the controls clunky, the characters obnoxious, and the gameplay tedious at times, but it's also grossly ableist. It's made very clear that River is autistic, but the game never even uses the word "autism" and makes it seem like it's a bad word. They keep referring to it as "her condition" and going on and on about how hard it is for her husband, John, to tolerate her. Mind you, these two are supposed to be in love. He explicitly refuses to learn about her "condition" when given the opportunity, and also makes it clear that he only started going out with her because she was "weird" and "unique" and he didn't want to be "boring" so he uses her to make himself appear more interesting.

I found out after playing that the creator has donated to Autism Speaks in the past. It seems he has since learned about the criticisms against Autism Speaks and no longer supports them. I think it's great that he acknowledged his mistake in supporting them, but he still has a lot to learn about autism. It's clear that he did not reach out to the autistic community during the development of this game.

It's very problematic, and honestly even if it wasn't, it's still a terrible story. It tries to be funny, then romantic, then heartbreaking, then creepy, round and round again, failing at each. By the end of the game, I hated all but a few side characters and River. I felt little more than annoyance during my playthrough. The ending was so unsatisfying, and there were a few loose threads that are never acknowledged (perhaps in a sequel but I'm not sticking around to find out).

I did enjoy the soundtrack and the visuals, and I liked the idea of going through someone's memories in reverse order. The main premise sounded really interesting and could have been done very well. I typically love games that involve facing the reality of death and questions of morality. This one, however, was a miss. I would not recommend this game to anyone.

review_text:
PSO2 is an iconic game, and one of the most successful anime action RPGs of all time, I want to call it an MMO but it really isn't - story content is solo and most of the multiplayer content can be done solo also. A few endgame urgent quests will be near impossible to do alone, and at this point of the game, you probably will never do them anyway as PSO2 is practically neglected to death in favor of their PSO "2.5" New Genesis.
New Genesis brings a lot of new things to the table: Improved graphics, a semi open world, better character customization, and more modern gameplay (that means casualized, but stylized and more responsive)
However, it has crushed the expectations of most of the original PSO2 fans almost entirely and I will explain why:
New Genesis has completely fumbled the legacy it was given from PSO2. As the name "New Genesis" suggests, the developers decided it would be a smooth move to ride the fame of PSO2 with a game that practically has nothing to do with it anymore - your player character might be the same character as the one in PSO2, but they haven't confirmed anything yet, and I won't go spoiling anything here.
Another thing they botched was was the combat customization and skilltrees, but I will admit that they have done some leaps towards a better direction over the years of it's lifetime.
That said, the core gameplay itself has barely evolved at all since launch, as you are still mostly just playing rhythm games with enemies, spamming and abusing invulnerability from parry/counterattacks.
Anyway, I'm not too good at deconstructing it, so I'll get simple.

The good:
+ One of the best character customization options in MMORPG genre (though this does not apply to the character creator much, and I still don't want to call it an MMO)
+ Smooth gameplay (Dumbed down, far easier than PSO2, but it's still a lot more responsive and free)
+ A pretty open world (though it's sparsely used for anything after initial exploration)
+ A great home building system "creative space", one of the best I've seen in an MMO

The bad:
- Neglected PSO2 to the point where it's all but dead
- NGS combat is not very customizable and most classes play too similarly to each other, lacking proper identity (the skill trees will give you almost everything, making a unique playstyle is nearly impossible - even after they added things like "MARS" and a couple of skill variations, the latter in particular is extremely unnoticeable compared to PSO2 where skill customization could make the ability and class function almost entirely differently)
- Bad story (they tried to fix it later, though I haven't gone back to see if anything's improved)
- Boring endgame and the leveling process is fast (After you've done all the story content, and whatever good urgent quests there are, you'll be left doing nothing but pointless grind and the drop rates are horrible)
- EXTREMELY UNFRIENDLY TOWARDS F2P PLAYERS (You cannot even sell things without premium membership subscription or rare 3 day shop passes)
- ingame trading was removed in NGS (They probably did it solely to fish more microtransaction purchases)
- Ingame marketplace is completely crap (The prices are insane, the item search is too specific and a lot of toxic players are playing stock market and monopoly with it, making buying cosmetics or earning money very hard unless you're a whale who basically trades real money in to In-Game money)
- a cesspool of degenerate players (but you're free to decide if that's a flaw or not yourself)
- almost unused openworld (it isn't very rewarding to do anything outside of urgent quests or dailies)

It IS a fun game, but the fun is drained rapidly - there is hardly any reason to dump hundreds of hours in to this game, which most people are doing anyway.
The actual endgame content isn't the gameplay at all, is pretty much just customizing your character(s), what I mean is that everyone is just standing in the lobby "cities" flexing their latest whale cosmetics such as expensive and distasteful bikinis.
A lot of people tend to make freaky unnatural anatomies on their characters, among other monstrous creations. (Some people have a good sense of humor or some great looks, but the majority doesn't :D)

IF you want to play this game, I very much discourage it - it is designed to make you want to pay money.
You can play F2P, but it is never ending inventory management and lack of money/storage space.
Now, if you still want to play it despite all of the complaints, feel free, but I strongly advise you not to support SEGA on this one, and don't get attached, they will either pull the plug suddenly, or take YEARS before the game is in a state where people want to actually come back to it, so it's not worth investing in to. If I was a new player, I'd just play the story and leave it at that..

I can't recommend the game right now
PSO2 (before they ruined it) 8/10
PSO2 (after they abandoned it) 5/10
NGS (at launch) 6/10
NGS (now) 7/10 
(but only if you get to actually have fun with the best, most polished part of game, that is character customization and buying cosmetics. Maybe the creative space too, otherwise it's hardly worth it)

Got the game for free with my GPU purchase back when, the RX 6800 XT.

The game went through abnormal performance issues at launch with ray tracing issues on AMD and even without then having massive stutters in menu. 

 I gave the game time to cook, some 2 years later, and performance is good. 
If you want to enable raytracing you need to enable temporal anti-ailising for it to become available. AMD & Nvidia. 
 With RX 6800XT on 1440p and FSR 2 and 3700x CPU (and 48GB RAM), I was able to run max RT settings without noticeable performance issues.

Regarding the actual game play and story, it is decent. Despite being created by former Dead Space devs, the game's atmosphere isn't that anxiety inducing / scary. The story is decent and I believe you need the DLC to conclude it, but the base game is good on its own. Combat is easy and for most part you never feel in danger / scared. 

It is only on the end game boss fight (main / base game) that you really get challenged. I still have yet to play the Final Transmission DLC that continues the story, so things might change in that.

Overall, game is decent and better priced now than at launch. If you are interested but wary, get it on sale. I got the season pass recently at roughly $2 for additional content.

So, decent game and easy enough combat with decent story. Worth it for good 20 - 25+ hours play time (excluding DLC).

review_text:
Scorn has an incredible art style, good animations, and well-crafted level design. Visually, it’s a masterpiece. But beyond that, it falls short.

The game is very short—I finished it in just 6 hours, even taking my time exploring and admiring the world. There’s also no reason to replay it, as there are no choices, secrets to find, or alternative game modes. There’s no story context either: you don’t know who you are, what you’re doing, or why. The lack of guidance, combined with unexplained controls, made finding my way especially frustrating. The environment is alien, filled with buttons and interactive objects, but the game never makes it clear where to go or what to do next, leaving you to wander aimlessly and hope you're in the right place.

Combat is clunky and unrewarding. Ammo and health are scarce, and there’s no stealth option, making fights more of a hassle than fun. I ended up avoiding enemies altogether, either by waiting for them to despawn or simply running past.

At 40 Euros, I can't recommend it. For under 15 Euros in a sale, maybe—if you love the art and atmosphere.

review_text:
1. This game isn't good. Sorry you had to hear it from me.

2. W/ that out of the way, the music to this is stellar, absolutely on par w/ the very best game soundtracks of all time. No kidding. Go to Freebird Games's Bandcamp page. Buy the album, skip the game. Win/win. 

3. Even the presentation beyond the music is fine. It's done in an old school pixel art style, which is pretty cute even if it doesn't feel all that fresh these days. But even how these simple graphics are done reveals the kind of lack of attention to detail that makes this game a chore to play ultimately. It is  640x480 natively and there is no way to change that. It upscales just fine and I don't mind 4:3 w/ bars on the side of a modern monitor but on top of that, for the majority of gameplay, there is typically a black bar both on the top and the bottom of the window as well. The end result is only about a quarter of the available real estate on a normal screen is being used at any given time and since sprites are already pretty small, things are needlessly hard to see. Lots of games get an old-school feel in 16:9 so I just don't see the reason for this design decision. It is not a dealbreaker on its own but it is just the kind of thing [i]To The Moon[/i] gets wrong over and over.

4. The controls here are pretty bad too. There is controller support but mouse and keyboard works better, which doesn't really fit w/ the bit-era aesthetic. I can live w/ that but the controls are weird and wonky anyway. I constantly found the mouse pointer getting sort of stuck on a previously clicked object and would report the same bit of dialogue no matter where else I pointed at the screen.

5. One of the small challenges presented (intentionally) by the game designer was essentially a pixel-hunt so number 4 gets really annoying. 

6. The other small challenge is these tile flipping puzzles for the first half of the game which are either really simple or can be solved in a matter of minutes by trial-and-error. 

7. All of the above technical limitation could be forgiven in such a story driven game, which leads us to the real kicker. The story here is really, laughably bad judged by the standards of any medium but video games. Again, sorry you had to hear it from me. 

8. The premise is a pretty solid sci-fi trope along the lines of "We Can Remember It For You Wholesale" or [i]The Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind[/i]. There are two technicians who have the ability to somehow actively enter into a person's memories and change them for fun and profit. In this case, this astounding technology is used to improve education and fuel scientific development into even more amazing technologies... Wait, no, it's used to make dying people feel better for the last few moments of their lives by manipulating them into thinking they did things they didn't do. Hooray for science!

9. Predictably, our two technicians run into some pretty unusual things when exploring this dying patient's head-space. Unfortunately, the presumably reliable details of this poor fellow's past are odd enough that it makes it difficult to suspend disbelief--and this is after you've swallowed the idea that people can act as video game characters in another person's brain box. It is hard to explain w/o spoilers but, in my opinion, a hefty majority of the backstory presented would occur only if every actor in it were insane.

10.  There is one joke in this that is actually funny.

11. Even w/ everything wrong w/ it, the story would not be so bad were it not told in such a painfully slow manner. The pixel hunt sections I mentioned in 5 can span multiple screens and really fill up a lot of time. I think this story could easily have been a short story that might take an hour to read and the game is going to take most people 3-6 hours to finish. The game play really adds no challenge and the story is completely on rails so your choices don't add anything to it. I just can't help but feel a game was a really bad choice of medium in this case. It might have made a great comic book. 

12. Right at the end, [i]To the Moon[/i] almost redeems itself w/ an ending that would seem to drive home a valuable life lesson but then takes a hard turn into a swamp of sticky-sweet sentiment and happily gets mired there. I guess if you liked the plot up to that point, this is what you'd want.

13. So here we have it: great music, problematic design choices, poor controls, unbelievable story, unfunny humor.  One could be forgiven if they thought this whole game wasn't just a brilliant soundtrack subjected to death by a thousand cuts but it is somehow not a total disaster. I have spent a lot of time thinking about it since completing it which is something I can't say about a lot of games I actually like. Unfortunately, I am mostly thinking about how no plot points jibe w/ how normal people actually act in real life.

review_text:
If you consider yourself a fan of the first person shooter genre, buy this game. Period. Most innovative, cohesive vision of a single player FPS in the last decade.

Incredible presentation. Sound design is flawless. Movement and controls are slick, intuitive and reactive. Level design is tremendous and ingenious. Seriously, the level design deserves a second mention of praise. Right down to the bones, they are soaked with atmosphere and tone, and every single one presents uniquely while conjuring its own vibe and feel. Progression is fun and rewarding and never feels like a slog. The arsenal is devilishly satisfying with some excellent gun play, mechanics and perks. Replayability also punches well above normal because of the looter shooter RPG aspect. I'm 50 hours in and haven't beaten the game yet. 

I've been playing shooters since Wolfenstein. It's hard to impress and innovate on one of the oldest computer game genres. Let me say with complete honesty, Witchfire impresses me. This game is quality, better than any "qUaDruPLe A" title you can buy right now.

review_text:
TL;DR - I don't recommend this game at this price for the average gamer. For a big SAO fan, it does have it's merits - but at the end of the day it's [i]just[/i] a "good SAO game", but overall: it's a pretty mediocre game. At best it's realistically worth ~30 USD. Wait for a sale unless you're really into SAO imo.

Okay first off I need to rant about how dogshit the PC port to this game is, because the performance/gameplay issues are my biggest personal complaints. Here's some of the vErY FuN "features" you'll experience playing this game on PC / with Mouse and Keyboard:

[list]
    [*]Your mouse sensitivity will randomly decide whether it wants to actually use the settings you set or not. This makes playing gun characters incredibly inconsistent because your sensitivity will never feel the same between different maps / runs.
    [*]Your camera sensitivity will be tied to your FPS, so certain maps will fling your sensitivity to the moon when entering a new room unless you set your FPS to be locked at 60.
    [*]Skill direction will be decided on your character's position instead of your mouse/camera's direction. So if your character is facing to the left, and you try to aim your mouse forward to use a skill in that direction: the skill will just go to the left. You need to move in a direction before using 90% of skills. There are a handful of skills that can be aimed with the mouse, but if you're playing on mouse and keyboard it'd feel more natural for all skills to be aimed with the mouse.
    [*]Targeting is awful, and "aim assist" is actually just a janky aim debuff on mouse/keyboard. To consistently hit the things you actually want to hit, you need to turn off automatic targeting and constantly untarget/retarget mobs while ONCE AGAIN needing to "aim" your targets with character movement instead of mouse/camera direction.
    [*]Flying characters feel janky as hell due to the combo of bad targeting and in-air movement also feeling clunky. It's not very easy to move your character up/down in the ways that you want to try and target a weak spot on a boss, for instance.
[/list]

This might seem like a kinda nitpicky list of issues, but consider that these are all fundamental parts of combat. At the end of the day this is a grind game, so combat is going to be 90% of what you do. If that combat is janky and buggy as hell for people who feel more comfortable on mouse and keyboard, then obviously the relatively small issues are going to feel fucking horrible when you've been dealing with them for the 90-100 hours it takes to unlock the highest level of content. Which speaking of: the grind.

The grind in this game is kinda awful. Like I said, it takes roughly 90-100 hours of dedicated grind to get to level 90 (with a max of lvl 100, so add another ~10hrs), which is the required level for taking on EX Raids. These are limited timed raids that only last for a few days whenever the dev team decides to run them, and they're only live for 3 hour intervals every few hours. You can't respawn in these raids, and many mechanics one-shot you, so it's basically a challenge mode with the only reward being a random CHANCE at a recoloured cosmetic. It's kinda neat, kinda disappointing (slogan for the game).

So what do you do for those 90-100 hours of mindless grind? Well, for the first 85-90 hours you spam the same 1-2 highest level co-op quest maps you have access to (there's a total of 6 maps in the game, but only 1-2 are relevant for your leveling at any given moment) until you hit level 85. After that, you spam Tier 3 raid bosses which rotate between 5 different raid bosses daily. There's 2 other raids you have access to earlier in the game, but they're not very worth doing for pure leveling. The bosses range from pretty neat, to kinda eh. If you've played actual MMOs, they're all pretty simple tbh. 

At the start of the game, you have access to 21 different characters, and leveling characters to 30 will unlock their passive to be used for other characters (only 2 equipable on a chara at a time). This incentives you to play different characters while leveling to try and get good passive for your mains. And honestly, that's probably a good thing. The characters and their kits are probably the most fun part of this game. Most characters play very differently from each other, and many of them have very fluid kits (once you cope with the dogshit targeting and being forced to aim your skills with movement, of course). Honestly the only thing that helped me push to keep grinding this game which was how fun and different the characters can feel to play, and seeing the interactions between different heroes/villains from across the SAO series.

oh and the story is... fine? again, neat for SAO fans - nobody else will probably care. you have to play through like ~2-4 hours of it (while spamming) to unlock all the characters for multiplayer content. going back while not spamming/skipping cutscenes leads to much longer playtime ofc. not much to say on it, just kinda fine.

so.. yeah. secondary tl;dr - game is meh and grindy with a shallow pool of maps/bosses, characters are fairly diverse with some fun kits, lots of neat character interactions for SAO fans, there's a lot of AFKers and they're all cringe, Eiji / Yuuki / Heathcliff are the most fun characters, and there's plenty of better grind games to play tbh but this one is decent-ish and SAO themed :3 ok bye

review_text:
I thoroughly enjoyed most of what this game had to offer. I guess you could call it a slasher game, where you are the villain / monster.
The story is a bit ridiculous, the voice acting is so bad its good and the characters aren't exactly well written. But is genuinely a captivating story despite its many flaws. And i could not wait for what came next.

Its a bit clunky. But not to such an extent that it ruins the experience. The graphics are bad, at least to modern standards but it runs almost flawlessly because of this.

When i said i enjoyed most of what this game had to offer i meant it. The main story and the secrets were fun, and the kills are satisfying if not comically macabre.
However, the extra game mode is nonsensically bad and the completion was basically not worth it.

You see, in actually this game took me 11 hours to complete. However, there are two achievements that are just as cursed as the mansion the game takes place in. And that's the 20 and 40 hour achievements. They are nonsense! Legit!
So i played this game through and through in many ways and did a lot of shenanigans to get these two achievements. It did not ruin the experience but they make the 100% process of this game unnecessarily long. Compared to how much it actually takes.

Other than that, it was worth it. And except for the two arbitrary achievements towards the end. (That they removed in the demake) it was a fun game.

And its especially worth it if you don't plan on going for 100%, i guess if you're not insufferable like me you could just leave it on when you're at work or something.

8/10

6/10 if you are going for 100%

review_text:
Understand something: This game is hard. It's frustratingly hard. It's not bad. But it is strictly for fans of the genre. It is absolutely not for people interested in trying something new. If you are easily frustrated, and not already a fan of real time stealth (think Commandos and Desperados for examples), this is not the game for you. Don't waste your time and money like I did. Try the demo.

Why is this a negative recommendation if I've already said it's not a bad game? Because I cannot know if you are already a fan of the real-time stealth genre, and this game is quite literally not for anyone else, except perhaps a masochist. Look, some people like running headlong into a wall over and over again. Some people like the challenge of being absolutely frustrated constantly until they "git gud," beat one tiny obstacle, and then have to start the whole process over again at the next one. If that's you, great. Have fun. It's not me. This game isn't made for me. It's probably not made for you, either. Hence the negative recommendation.

I'm not trying to insult the people this game was made for - you have your tastes, and this game was designed for them. Have fun. I'm trying to provide a small public service. I'd have appreciated a warning that this game is a massive exercise in frustration for anyone but the subset of people who have already mastered real-time stealth puzzle-solving and who like save-die-repeat trial and error gameplay. I should have tried the demo. I didn't. That's on me.

TLDR: It's a good game in a genre for very specific people, and literally no one else. Try the demo to find out if you're one of them. If you're not, save your money.

review_text:
You know those MMOs that get bought by other companies that milk them for every cent they can before shutting down the servers once all the players have been driven off? Undoing quality of life changes, making gacha the main content between "major" updates, "major" updates that are feeling more rushed and unfinished every time (they sped-run their own story in the latest update), doing the most half-assed job possible on everything from collabs to repeatable challenges? That's what happened to PSO2, except Sega never sold it. They did it themselves.

At this point I'm only here because of character customization and cross-platform play with friends. And character customization is getting worse all the time. All the outfits look like they're designed by the same guy, they're all variations on the same few themes, the best outfits are still from the base game. And there's zero quality assurance process. They slap them on a rail-thin character model and call it good, because they don't work on any other variation of the character model, textures glitch out or things balloon up like there's antigravity built in. I should mention the disappointing collabs, with a handful of items packed in with dozens of rerun items just to make you spend more money. And in the latest collab you couldn't even change the outfit color or turn off accessories, two of the main selling points of NGS's alleged customization upgrades. It's pathetic what this game has become.

review_text:
To the Moon is an emotional, narrative-driven game that really shines through its story and dialogue. I especially enjoyed the witty exchanges between Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts—they added a nice dose of humour to the heartfelt plot. The atmosphere also fits the story perfectly, enhancing the emotional impact.

However, the controls were a major downside for me. Most of the game is controlled with the mouse, and I found the movement clunky and awkward. It often pulled me out of the experience, which was disappointing given how immersive the story is. There’s also a horse-riding segment that uses arrow keys, but it’s surprisingly frustrating—the horse randomly stops, making what should be a fun moment feel more like a chore.

Overall, To the Moon is definitely worth playing if you’re in it for the story. I’d give it a 7/10—it could’ve been higher if not for the poor controls that chipped away at the experience.

Just a heads-up: you’ll need a save file near the end of the game to replay the final section. So make sure to manually save before finishing the game—or you’ll have to reload from wherever your last save was.

review_text:
I finished all of the Lucius games recently.

If you want an interesting story about the son of devil, than play this or the demake version (or both), than Lucius 3.
If you want to be a child serial killer, play Lucius 2.
If you want both, no luck for you.

All of the games have bugs, except Demake, but all of them are something you can use to it.
If you have the patience for that, you will have an unique experience.


About games:

 - Lucius: It is a 3D "point and click"-like game wich focuses on storytelling, gore and wandering around and in the manor. It uses slowmos very badly, even ruined the tense of the last chapter for me. Try to talk to everybody in every chapter for more infos and hints.

 - Lucius demake: First demake I ever played. Much easier to find items. The last chapter is teasing and besides that I like it much better than the original. Also it has the best OST from all of them.

 - Lucius 2: It is now a challenging game, where you have many ways to harvest souls. It is very well made that way (besides bugs of course). In exchange, it has the worst storytelling and character development, but in Lucius 3 they reflected to it very well.

 - Lucius 3: The 3D "point and click"-like gameplay returns with open world and again it´s rather focuses on gore and storytelling. Back to the roots, but better.
 Even it is not a finished game as intended, it´s story is phenomenal. My jaw dropped in front the genuie of the writer(s?).
 It is my favourite from all, because after those mixed stuff the other games gave me, I have finally seen the true Lucius I ever wanted to see.

If I can say that, the first Lucius game is like a movie, the second and demake is like a game and the third is a series that didn´t finished, but closed properly (as possible).

The strongest part of all games are Lucius itself and his strange character development. He never talks (khm...), he just kill poeple, but the small things, like the way he does the murders or how he reacts to certain situations build his style, but you never really know what he really feels or think. That´s his true power, beside being a kid.
In Lucius 3 he is very strong, but he still use that power to outsmart others like in the first game, while in Lucius 2 he is rather aggressive and the gameplay is about that too.


Focus on Lucius itself,
Don´t care about bugs, get used to them,
Have patience to find what you need
And you will have a very great experience you will never forget.

review_text:
Batman: Arkham City is a really underwhelming game. It honestly doesn’t succeed in any facet. Its gameplay is unengaging. Its story is abysmal. Its characters are uncompelling. It is needlessly padded out with tons of filler. It’s dragged down by a host of issues. The game does not deserve “Overwhelmingly positive” reviews. I can only imagine it received such widespread adulation because it is a Batman game and it certainly is a Batman game, but is it good? No. Is it terrible? No. It’s middling at best.

The combat is unsatisfying. It can be fun here and there, but there just isn’t any depth. It doesn’t feel earned. I didn’t come away from it feeling like Batman. I felt like I was just playing a very violent rhythm game. On top of that, it’s weird in practice, too. Sometimes Batman will leap across two screens to attack a bad guy, then he’ll fumble an attack on a bad guy right next to him. There’s no rhyme or logic to it. And you’ll be pissed off when it happens because you then lose your combo for no good reason.

The game is utterly filled with content, but that doesn’t mean it is good content. It is Filler City. It is seriously padded out with a lot of meaningless content that is either trifling at best or just atrocious at worst. It suffers all the pitfalls of a Ubisoft-style open-world and is no more compelling for it. The side activities are shoddily implemented and feel tacked on as a way to expose the player to more of Batman’s rogues gallery. Unfortunately, it just doesn’t work for creating a fun or interesting experience. Why would I care to see more of these characters when the experience is the same for every one of them? They aren’t interesting to see. They are window dressing. I feel like 75-85% of the game could have easily been cut. And the resources dedicated to more meaningful, interesting content. 


The story is just abysmal. Batman himself is completely uninteresting here and the central dilemma plaguing him and the world at large is equally uncompelling. He has zero personality beyond delivering gruff lines to everyone around him while all the characters you interact with are homicidal maniacs that would be better off dead. The villains are particularly heinous here and it beggars belief that Batman lets them live after the crap they pull off repeatedly in the game. Even the villains that aren’t wholly evil act idiotic here, too, and it drags the story down even further.

There are two massive drivers of events in the game and one is completely shrouded in mystery til the very end, so you have zero reason to care about it. And the other is much more immediate, but due to the flat performances and needlessly tacked on filler, it doesn’t feel urgent at all. It is barely a blip in your mind. And you feel there are no stakes whatsoever to what you are doing.

I know Batman is a gruff character with a somber demeanor, but he’s more than that. We have seen him across a large variety of media. And he can be so much more. And be more dynamic and interesting. He’s complex with a lot of issues that extend well beyond the surface. And we just don’t see any of that here. It’s just the most surface-level interpretation of Batman being Batman and that’s that. 

I came away from this game feeling like I may have enjoyed parts of it, but it was ultimately just a tedious experience and after playing other games, my opinion has been revised downwards. It just isn’t a good game. It wasn’t even a good game for its time. I’ve played a ton of games from its time period recently and it doesn’t measure up to any of them. I know my opinion is in the minority, but hey, it is what it is.
