review_text:
I consider this game to be an improvement over Hiveswap Act 1, but ultimately it should still appeal to the same people (and most of those people will want to play act 1 first).

As before, it's effectively a visual novel disguised as a point and click adventure. However, despite most of it being literally on-rails this one has more legitimate puzzles and requires you to think a bit. The focus is almost entirely on social interactions with the trolls you meet, rather than "use item X on background object Y", which is a great change from traditional point-and-click fare and really plays to the author's strengths.

And yes, Andrew Hussie is in peak form here. The characters you meet are all fun and quite varied, the scenarios they place you in are creative, and several puzzles have more than one solution you can find. The story is focused on the parts of Homestuck's lore that everyone already found most interesting. The worldbuilding holds up with or without knowledge of the prior work. The comedy and character development is on point. There's plenty of silly secret remarks you can get from using every item on every person or talking to people at different points in the story, but since you're actually TALKING to people it doesn't hurt the pacing much this time. And the change in format renders it 100% immune to the pacing problems that Homestuck itself suffered from.

That being said, the brief portion at the start of the game where there AREN'T a lot of characters around suffers from the same slow pacing as Act 1. Maybe even worse since not much is happening.

Don't worry about difficulty. Most puzzles can eventually be solved by just talking to everyone about everything, and the one section with deeper puzzles (the trial) has a hint button that starts vague but will hand you the answer if you hit it enough times. There's no other skill-based minigames (one got removed and if it gets readded it'll probably be skippable) so anyone should be able to beat this game.

The game is longer than Act 1. Took me about 13 hours to complete (with moderate reloading to explore other options), compared to 8 on the first game. For replay value, there's a lot of hidden achievements based on the multiple ways of solving certain puzzles, on preserving certain items for the whole run, etc. In fact you'd need several full playthroughs to get all acheivements since some are mutually exclusive. But since you can't fast forward dialog I have a hard time imagining myself doing more than just a second playthrough (not counting reloads just before a part I want to retry).

Some people on the forums complained about bugs and softlocks, but I didn't see a single one in my play experience.

Overall, anyone who liked Homestuck, or even liked parts of Homestuck, will probably love this game. And Act 2 is better than Act 1. But I'd still suggest playing Act 1 before Act 2.

As an SAO fan, I was lucky to get to try the game early in the Closed Beta Test, and from that I immediately knew that I wanted this game badly. Fast forward to now, I would say that this game did not disappoint me, despite its quirks. The character rigging is weird during cutscenes, blocking and dodging can be hard due to the delay and stuff, the map doesn't show the edge of the map makes exploration a tad bit more annoying, the way you start at level 1 on every coop game can get tiring, etc. It's definitely nowhere near perfect, but in a way, that's the charm of SAO games. It basically hits all the marks I expect from an SAO game.

With that being said, this game is definitely not for everyone. If you're one of the people who tells people to buy Grandblue Fantasy Relink instead, you're kinda missing the point of this game. We play and like it because it's SAO, and to me, this is one of the better games in this IP. It kinda has the vibes of Fatal Bullet, but with SAO elements and uncapped fps. If you're not into SAO or you only just knew about SAO, I wouldn't really recommend this game especially at these prices, and you're probably be better off buying that other game or play earlier SAO games to familiarize yourself with SAO games as I personally think this isn't the best game to start the journey. I might be biased, but that's kinda the whole point with games based off of IPs.

review_text:
I really have tried to like this game - it has so much style, great influences and the soundtrack is fantastic, but ultimately I do not have fun playing it.

I'm a huge Jet Set Radio fan, so this was on my radar for a long time. It doesn't take much to see the influence and all of the ways the studio have tried to recreate that magic. It has all of the things it should have, and especially the art team have gone nuts on this game.

But I just do not find the gameplay fun. It is quickly repetitive, mechanics that aren't enjoyable on pretty lacking level design. The objectives are rarely fun, the direction confusing and it just becomes... quite frustrating to play.

Nothing is more frustrating than the police system, which seemingly only exists to make the game less fun. Do you want to be grappled and slowed constantly? How about a mandatory combat segment with some of the most laughable combat mechanics? I do not understand why it was added other than to emulate the (pretty great) police system in JSR.

Jet Set Radio was a lot of style, but at its core it was an enjoyable game. I do not think Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is, as much as it pains me to admit.

For someone who got to play this game for the first time in 2021, I don't recommend putting 35 hours into it (I finished it).

I had higher expectations from a game that sold 38 million copies and was considered one of the best games ever.
Start of the game is very attractive and atmospheric, then slowly you get to feel the repetitive gameplay style for a good while until you reach Fort Frolic and get to accomplish better designed goals and assassinate important characters.. only then playing it becomes fun.

Combat is my main issue, you get to collect and upgrade weapons and special abilities .. also you will do research on things to gain experience. But you can't measure the effect or see where your upgrade progress is because game doesn't provide meters or upgrade trees for them.
Also you don't really see the effect of upgrading weapons until you use the proper ammo for the enemy. It's funny that it boils down to use Wrench and Shock ability as the best weapon despite Rocket Launchers and what not.
Switching between weapons and ammo types is frustrating especially when you are under pressure like when facing Big Daddies. Map wasn't that great.

If you want to play a might and magic style game then get Arx Fatalis, Dishonoured, or Dark Messiah.

I enjoyed graphics, sceneries, and the underwater concept a lot. But was not enough for me to recommend the game!.

I have Bioshock 2, will watch couple short videos then decide if I want to play it as well.

review_text:
Waited for years as a huge fan of the Dead Space series. Left hugely dissapointed.
--------------
The good:

> UI. Minimal. Clean. Sharp. No map. Really immersive. All UI is inside the world in 3D and exceptionally well implemented.
> Cinematic and nice looking. Eye catching.
> Graphics.
Yes. That's all

The bad:

> Story. I forgot it even existed. This is a scinematic game yet the story is boring. "go there for the sake of going somewhere". Noone cares. Nothing after nothing happens with explosions everywhere. Only first 30 min were good.
> The first 3 bosses you fight is the SAME EXACT boss. There are 4 boss enounters total. I could not believe. And it's a poorly designed one too.
> The combat system is a gladiator 1v1 lock-system. And for a horror game, it's attrocious from every single aspect. Prime example of how not to design a combat system. You cannot be afraid of what can't lurk behind you. Only jump scares.
> Broken input. Sprinting rarely works. It literally has a mind of it's own.
> Blocking is useless and sets you on a massive dissadvantage. Introduced mechanic and forgotten.
> Moving left thumb horrizontally is your dodge. WHY? Navigating during combat was already hard.
> Enemies wait to attack you when fighting multiple. You can fight one monster for 2 whole minutes while 3 more dance around you. They will never engage.
> A lot of stuttering with shader compiles on a 7950X3D/RTX 4090 system. Even with the added precompile phase, it's really noticable.
> Stealth system is so poor it shouldnt exist. Yet it's forced for hours 'round mid-game.
> No DLSS. Ray Tracing is poorly implemented but it's fine. Couldn't care less with graphics, they are amazing as is.

About hardcore difficulty:
> It is unbalanced with no skill requirement due to the extreme RNG elements. All enemies can do an undodgable instant grabs which make you lose 30+% HP. If you roll bad and they do 4 in a row, you lose automatically. You can't heal mid-fight. And you have to fight 8 enemies in a row per engagement. What are the chances you get grabbed 4 times within 15 minutes of combat? You can get hit 0 times and still lose because you can't dodge grabs .
> Broken economy and bad upgrade system. Getting hit once sets you back 120G in heals where defeating an enemy gives you 5G. On average an upgrade costs ~900 and they give nothing. Why are they even there. Decor?
> You can't run or escape fights. Damn camera lock. If I don't want to fight in hardcore difficulty where health and ammo is this scarse and 80% HP is often 1 hit from death, DON'T FORCE LOCK ME?


I have about 20 more reasons for giving a bad review but no point writing them.
I didn't refund because I do want to support the devs. Hope the next game is better.

3/10 purely for the graphics.

review_text:
Like Kingdom Come: Deliverance, the sequel suffers from the same issues as the first game. Wonky and unreliable lock-on, a bad stealth system, bugs and above all the saving system. 

I want to have fun when playing games instead of running around the map looking for herbs just to be able to brew Saving Schnapps to save the game when I want to. Being able to have fun should be above realism at all times and having to put in work to be able to save the game whenever you like is not the way to go.

I will give credit where it is due. They did a great job with the cast of characters, such as Zizka, Godwin, Dry Devil, Adder and so on. The cutscenes were great and they were weaved well into missions.

The game itself is surprisingly well optimized and I never experienced any lag and remained at a smooth 144 FPS at high settings throughout my entire playthrough.

The world looks very nice, the loading screen artwork is amazing and the locations are memorable, such as Trosky castle and Kuttenberg.

Towards the end of my playthrough I encountered a bug that made my character invincible and I could not find a solution for the issue and it did not go away until the very last bit of the story at the siege of Sochdol. Understandably this made combat unbelieveably easy and I didn't even have to abuse Masterstrike. I was even able to slaughter everyone at Von Aulitz's camp outside Sochdol. Obviously this made everything boring as nothing could harm me.

Honestly, the story could of been better but damn, these developers do know how to cook up the worst saving system and lock-on system ever.

review_text:
This game made me space out for a while.

I travelled back in space and time, back to my grandma's house, on her living room's wooden chair, eating an icicle one hot summer day. The windows were open, the fan was on, the icicle was melting and she was in the kitchen washing the dishes with the radio on, while I was sitting in front of her small CRT playing videogames. Grandpa fell asleep on his rocking chair, he did it while watching me play. My mom was at work, and my sister playing with her dolls right next to me. Back then I didn't know that I was living the best moment of my life. I hope the nostalgia effect hits you hard as much as it did with me.

I miss my grands, and I've found a way to sit back with them for a while.

review_text:
[b]tl;dr: the gorgeous art direction and sound design are ultimately undermined and held back by super bland puzzles, frustrating interactions/combat with enemies, and infrequent checkpoint saves.[/b]

i followed the development of scorn since its initial announcement where it was unclear what type of game it was going to be. it was clearly going to be heavily giger (and beksinski) influenced in its visuals, and that was enough to pull a lot of people into the hype. sadly, it feels like the early trailers being largely/completely devoid of gameplay wasn't coincidental and was just representative of what had been developed for the game to that point. it really feels like all the art concepts, materials, models, shaders, pre-fab level parts, etc were created first, and then gameplay was kind of tacked on in the last year or two, which makes it not particularly fun to play!

before going into specifics, i want to clarify that i am not predisposed to dislike a game like scorn, nor did i go into it with unrealistic expectations. i like horror games, i like walking sims, i like puzzle games, i like fps games, i like games that are not direct in their storytelling, i like games that can make you feel miserable (ie: pathologic 2). i really just don't think these things feel like a cohesive final product in scorn though. 

[u]visuals:[/u] visually i don't think i have to say much beyond the game is stunning and so much thought seems to have gone into every element of the visuals, from obvious things like textures, models,and animations, to deliberate sight lines from different parts of the maps. you could easily set your computer to screenshot scorn every 5 minutes as you play and have 90% awesome pieces of art.

[u]sound:[/u] i think the sound was also quite good an contributes immensely to the atmosphere as a whole. it was understated and largely ambient sounds and environmental noises. everything sounded suitable gross, or mysterious, or vacant. i only really noticed music coming in once, and thought the track was nice, but me "not noticing" a soundtrack isn't a sign of a bad soundtrack at all since i absolutely adore the trent reznor/nine inch nails soundtrack for quake as well.

[u]story:[/u] there's no traditional story in scorn, and i don't recall any dialogue or text through my playthrough (outside of text in the menu/ui). there is still environmental storytelling and some in-game cutscenes that highlight things occurring and changing throughout the playthrough. i thought seeing how things developed with the player character was interesting, and i thought any non-enemy characters that showed up alive were able to communicate emotion in a way that resonated with me.

[u]puzzles:[/u] so the puzzles... with few exceptions i really felt like the puzzles throughout did not seem realistically integrated into the environment and were super simple to work out. there wasn't anything really unique or novel with the types of puzzles either, they reminded me of the ads i get on free duolingo for puzzle game apps. i know puzzles in other games are mostly the same handful of puzzle types over and over again, but doing a puzzle in any other random game rarely pulls me out and shatters my immersion like it did for me in scorn where the puzzles interrupted the pacing and felt hard to justify their inclusion in a space that otherwise felt cohesive (largely due to the strong art and sound direction).

[u]combat:[/u] i saw reviews on steam and elsewhere online around the game's launch complaining about the combat, and i figured people just didn't have the same tolerance for jank/kinda cruddy fps combat that i have, but nope, i was wrong, the combat is abysmal and possibly the worst fps combat i can think of in recent memory. ultimately, combat fails because aiming and reloading take absurdly long, ammo capacity is low, and enemy placement often has them body block you in corridors or gang up on in you a space that is very difficult to avoid physical or splash damage from them. it doesn't translate into a survivor horror kind of stress and item management, it just becomes a slog of a cover shooter. i am not trying to turn scorn into doom eternal or anything, but i kept feeling like if i was in the player character's position i would have abandoned the weapon(s) after about 2 enemies and just fought from there on with my bare hands. i feel like i could do more damage more quickly with uppercutting some monstrosity than i could with the weapons in game.

i will post one spoiler here (spoiler tagged) that touches on my most frustrating experience with the [u]combat[/u] and [u]save system:[/u] [spoiler] there is a (tedious) boss battle towards the end of the game, and after defeating it i gained the "grenade launcher" equivalent weapon. i didn't know how it worked or what it was at first, so i shot a few shots, damaged myself, and then realized i used all my ammo. i figured i'd load from checkpoint and get my health back and all that ammo, but the checkpoint took me back before the boss! i guess there are either 2 bosses back to back or one enemy-type boss twice depending on how you look at it, and i tried to reload between the fights without knowing there was a second. maybe player error, but i don't know any other game that doesn't save after a boss fight if you're given full control of your character again without a boss present. i died over a dozen times in those boss fights cuz i was stuck with a save at low health and no health resources, and i had to keep watching the same cutscenes each time without an option to skip. [/spoiler]

i am often drawn to games with strong visual presentations regardless of genre, and that can be enough reason to warrant a purchase from me. scorn's grotesque visual splendor was my main interest in playing the game, but the visuals alone were not enough to carry me through the trials and frustrations of its gameplay and have an overall positive reflection on it. i think an extraordinarily patient person may enjoy this game for its gameplay, but i think most people who recommend it are doing so for its incredible setting and atmosphere. i think i would have greatly preferred a version of scorn that focused on only one type of gameplay vs. the one we got that ended up flirting with multiple genres but only developed them on an incredibly basic surface level.

review_text:
I have never felt contempt for a game since F3AR. If The Callisto Protocol was intended to be a spiritual successor to Dead Space, it failed in every way.

The gameplay boils down to: Jacob has to open a door, so you press E to open it... and it plays an animation of Jacob preparing to pry the door open, prompting you to press E again to have Jacob open the door. Or Jacob opens a door by playing an unskippable animation of Jacob opening a power box and cutting a cable. And let's not forget the innumerable amount of times Jacob has to crawl through a vent, shimmy through a tight corridor to reach another vent and/or climb up.
These things can happen in sequence. Sometimes in that order exactly. Back to back even.

Oh and sometimes you get to fight enemies. Very poorly.
The combat is: hold left or right, hold right or left, attack enemy. Rinse and repeat. Such interesting and engaging gameplay.
Then they introduce tentacles and enemy mutation, and it FUCKING sucks. NOTHING QUITE LIKE EVERY SINGLE ENEMY DOING IT IMMEDIATELY AFTER INTRODUCING IT.

Then the game deleted my save 6 hours in. Forcing me to go through it all over again.

I cannot in good conscience recommend this game for anything less than the price of free. If anything they should pay you to play the game. Though even THAT is a stretch.

Edit 8/24/24:
It deleted my save again. Fuck this game.

review_text:
Visuals are cool, gunplay itself is pretty solid and the thematic of the game is real cool, but it's just not fun.
You can't shoot enemies further than 20 meters away without doing fuck-all damage wise, your melee and spell cooldowns are way too fucking long for how little they do, you can't dash mid-air, despite stamina already limiting your mobility anyways so I don't see why that limitation has to be there, the "roguelite" element of each run on the same map being "different" is laughable, the upgrades you get after clearing each enemy camp are boring and don't change your gameplay in meaningful ways, which is important cause the game expects you to clear the same set static maps over and over with the only variety being enemy camp setup and upgrade choices, especially early game where you have no other weapons or spells than you started with. Just an hour in and I was already getting bored, the game has very little depth despite trying to seem more complex than it is, with loads of different stat numbers for both your character and weapons.
There are so many other roguelite shooters than this, that aren't in early access(despite already being EA on EGS for over a year) and don't cost 40 US DOLLARS. This is a measly offering for that amount of money, buy a different game.

review_text:
Must-play for SAO enjoyers. It's gorgeous, fun, authentic and the music feels straight out of a 2000s eastern MMO game (good). The character interactions are endearing and often funny, cute, wise or emotional. The way characters smile after delivering a line of dialogue is adorable, and the lipsync tech they used is very enjoyable to look at.

The combat is satisfying for several reasons, but I think the one I'd like to bring up is the iconic red slices that appear as your blade slashes an enemy, accurately displaying where your attack landed. Combine that with weak points on monsters and it makes for a combat system that feels very deliberate and cool.

Every character feels unique to play as because of their different abilities. Not just attacks, but movement as well. There is some skill overlap of course, so as you play the game and increase your familiarity with the mechanics, you'll get better with every character. So don't hesitate to try them all. Loot is fun to collect and I love that there's alternate outfits and accessories to find in each level.

Overall the game has a very pleasant atmosphere that sucks you in and makes you want to keep existing in its world. A rare sight indeed these days. Of course, you should watch at least a couple seasons of SAO before playing this, as it is a game for the fans.

Speaking of, this game is so good it got me to watch Ordinal Scale and start Alicization as well. I basically wake up every day and put on my metaphorical NerveGear to watch SAO, before fulldiving into this game and experiencing more SAO. Then I go to bed and dream about SAO. This game really makes you FEEL like Kazuto Kirigaya.

Overall, I was left feeling disappointed and would not recommend it to others.

review_text:
If you ever wanted Dead Space but with less tension, easier combat, and way more time crawling through vents, here you go.

The game looks and sounds incredible with truly top-tier visuals and audio, and also with varied, spectacular environments. Sadly, the moment you start actually playing, the cracks show fast.

The story? Bland and predictable. Scares? Mostly cheap jump scares. Tension? Almost nonexistent, because combat rewards sprinting straight at enemies and smacking them. Enemies (mostly) politely attack one at a time , dodging is laughably easy, and stealth is a joke: the "blind" monsters are apparently deaf too, letting you stroll up and one-shot them.

The GRP gauntlet is absurdly overpowered - it recharges, it's easy to use, and it can clear most fights without effort. Use it regularly and you'll basically never run out of ammo. New weapons? Just different-shaped guns for the same handful of enemies.

Expect lots of narrow corridors and ventilation shafts where nothing happens, plus a gameplay loop that barely changes from start to finish.

Lastly, performance swings from very smooth to massive stuttering without warning, and there's even a save bug that can wreck your progress (yes, you can fix it externally - I had to).

It's not terrible, but in the end it's a shallow, forgettable game hiding under a gorgeous coat of paint. Fun enough to keep you going, but nothing that will stick. If Steam had a "Mixed" rating, that's where this belongs - but since it doesn't, I lean negative.

[*] Pathfinding of your characters is sometimes very questionable
[*] Partially way more tedious than a tough puzzle - either due to very tight timing windows and hence some repetition or because you almost have to lure the enemies into their death one by one
[*] Story is kinda garbage
[/list]

review_text:
For a dev group of 2, the game shines! I'm always on the look out for a. Farming/Homesteading sims and b. Unique art style

Echoes of the Plum Grove covers both of those bases and then some. There are some aspects of the game that weren't advertised and I was very pleasantly surprised of! No spoilers of course. ;) I also very much like the idea that it takes place in the colonial era and you're just trying to get by.

There are some QoL aspects that I would like to see implemented in future updates (the devs are planning more updates) that would make this game sparkle:

- inventory sorting and chest sorting: as of writing this, there is no way to auto sort your inventory and chests. If you put away an item that already has a stack in a chest, it will not automatically stack. Instead it will occupy an empty space in the chest.

- sprint ability: while you will unlock the means to move faster rather early on in the game, it's a temporary consumable and the ingredients are hard to come by early on. Not to mention the means to craft it is on the other side of town. While there is fast traveling, it still consumes day time, which already passes rather quickly anyways.

- crafting at shops: until you get a random quest with the recipe or unlock with leveling up, you cannot create artisan goods or smelt. While there is a perfectly good forge available in town, you cannot use it, leaving you to pay a rather large sum of money (and time since NPCs stock may only have 1 or 2 available for the day) for nails and bars until you can craft one yourself. The forge, along with other artisan machines that are in town, could be available to use if the shop is open, if the player pays a small fee, or if their friendship is high enough with one of the shop owners. 

While I have other nit picky thoughts, they're just nit picky and don't affect the quality of the game in its entirety. The devs are clearly hard workers, their love for this project is very apparent, so I don't want my complaints to be detrimental  to anybody purchasing it. It's cute, fun, cozy, whimsical. Please do it give it a try! It's worth the $20.

review_text:
+ The economy in this game is well-developed and intricate. You have multiple ways to obtain resources, and you will have to find balance between money, reputation, and time. You will also have to think about what is better for you in the long term, but if you invest too much, you will be faced with setbacks and sometimes even death. 
+ It employs something that could be called nonlinear storytelling. You will be looking at a branching and interlinking mind map with multiple agendas for progressing. Sometimes small ideas could lead to huge discoveries, and you will have to decide which have importance and which are just dead ends and filler.
+ The map is really pretty and well laid out. No district place feels the same while still making navigating challenging. It does not lack detail, and you can experience so much by just walking around.
+ Stepee wives boobs.

- The art and music are really bland. It tries too hard to be dark/indigenous and have an eggy aesthetic. I think that the main point of the game is the balancing of different aspects of reality, so even though this one-dimensional representation of the world works from the point of view of a main character, it does not capture the complexity of the whole town.
- I really don't understand why every npc hates you so much. Is that just to feed more to the already depressive atmosphere? It mostly doesn't make sense in the story and serves just to humiliate the player. Then there are moments when everything treats you as the only savior and God of the universe. review_text:
Beautifully made, but clumsy and needs more editing.

I waited a while before picking this up in the hopes that some of the negative reviews were overblown. On the technical side at least, it runs great and looks incredible (on a 4080 & 12600k). All of the audio cues are a frame or two late, but that's WWISE's fault, not the game's.

The voice acting is good and the facial capture is impressive - art direction is well executed if generic. 

I only played about an hour before returning it, but I can tell this isn't for me. The combat is interesting, and feels good - and I have no doubt that it will evolve decently enough over the course of the game to be rewarding, but it was clear that the game suffered from a lack of editing and clear direction.

The way the mechanics are introduced and painfully explained to players is a pretty clear indication that playtesting showed that 'hey folks aren't getting this and we can't design a better solution, just explain it with a popup'. 

Similarly, in that first hour I saw a lot of systems bump up against each other in locomotion and combat. A lot of decent ideas, but without adequate editing. 

Narratively there are some pretty wild hand-wavy justifications for mechanics or narrative methods that are just laughable. Maybe it gets better the more you play (again I only played an hour) but there are some real groaners in the opening of the game that took me out of it.

It's a beautifully crafted game, but really shows a lack of direction. If anyone was asking 'but is this good? could we do this better?' in the design reviews, it doesn't show - which is too bad because I am a big fan of the genre.

review_text:
A mixed bag of a horror game. 

Created by Glen Schofield, the creator of Dead Space and developed by his new studio, Striking Distance, The Callisto Protocol was meant to be the spiritual successor to Dead Space, ushering in a brand new Triple-A horror IP in a era where survival horror is rarely seen in the Triple-A space. Unfortunately, we got Dead Space at home and after a disastrous PC launch and the fallout of both negative critic and player reviews, we are left with a horror title that could've been so much more but unfortunately ended up as a mediocre dud.

Pros:

Visuals are great across the board, the game runs on Unreal Engine 4 and there's been a incredible amount of care of bringing this world to life as everything from the cold, overwhelming darkness of Black Iron Prison, the game setting to the frozen wasteland of the prison's outside areas help to create a genuinely tense and horrifying atmosphere and with the right settings on PC, the game can look stunning at times. 

The all-star cast on display here is also great like Josh Duhamel who plays the game's main protagonist, Jacob Lee or Sam Witwer who plays one of the main antagonists in the story. Even the smaller roles still shine here, all delivering some good performances with the script that they're given here. 

Unfortunately, this is where the positives end. 

Cons: 

The gameplay of The Callisto Protocol is extremely dull and boring as hell as the game's central focus on melee combat with very little deviation of the formula itself makes every fight feel samey and not scary or tense in the slightest. Here's how most combat encounters go, you walk up to an enemy with your baton out, whack them with it, then they block it or dodge it then you have to evade their attacks using the A or D keys, it does not matter which direction it is, just hold these keys and then return back to whacking them until they fall over dead. Rinse and Repeat for 8 hours straight until the credits roll. Some fights may force you to use a gun every once in a while but the same strategy still remains of dodge attacks and then shoot them some more till they fall over dead. There's one part of the game where they reuse the same mini-boss four times in a single section and it's so BORING. Deadass, who thought that was a good idea? Due to this, combat gets extremely boring as the game rarely tries to spice things up or give you something more interesting to do like puzzles for example. There is a upgrade system but it only helps to make the combat even more dull with the benefit of making combat encounters go by faster. 

The story is everything you expect from a modern horror sc-fi game and with very little punches pulled and every twist you  can see coming from a mile away. While the acting is good, the characters here are bland with very little going on in their respective stories with everyone pretty much spelling out their motivations and with very little nuance or mystery behind their decisions. It's bad when I can relate to Issac Clarke, a silent protagonist from the 1st Dead Space more than a professionally voiced main character throughout the game's 8 hour playtime. It makes for a story that at it's best feels like everything you've seen before in much better games and movies and at it's worst, it's something that leaves you bored and wanting everything to end as fast as possible. 

The horror is extremely lacking here which is damning for any horror title. It's like forgetting your job description while you're still at work. Everything scary here feels like everything you've seen before and done better like the story. For example, Dead Space did space zombies better with the Necromorphs than the Callisto Protocol's Biophages. While the atmosphere here is great, the game's focus on lazy jumpscares, heavy focus on gore, and the extremely boring combat brings that atmosphere crashing down with not much else to replace it with. Nothing here feels distinct and that's my biggest problem with the entire game. It's this heavy feeling of "been there, "done that" that made me feel bored rather than tense and excited to see what the game had in store and that feeling sucks.

Verdict:
The Callisto Protocol was a big disappointment especially coming from someone who was excited for this game and wanted a developer to take up Dead Space's mantle again and give us something new in the sc-fi horror space. Instead we got Dead Space at home with a developer desperately trying to recapture that same spark that Dead Space had but with none of the quality that came with it. I really hope that someone else takes up the dead space mantle and gives something completely unique rather than a big, boring slog of a game to go through while failing to take notes from it's original source. 

5/10. P.S, Wait for a deep sale or buy Dead Space Remake if you're looking for a good sc-fi survival game.

review_text:
First of all I have to say that the game has a dedicated fanbase that can honestly piss off. Noone likes  you. Also spoilers
 Visuals: Without going on extreme detail, that is unneeded, pathologic 2 is a visually good game with amazing visual direction. The town feels alive and the style is unique and well implemented. 
 Audio: Very good audio mixing with extremely stylistic and unique soundtrack. The game has many distinct sound cues that really help with the overall experience.Again I do not want to go to great detail on visuals and audio, because I want to focus to the gameplay experience. Speaking of...
  Gameplay: First of all whatever I say will be about the intended difficulty that the developers want you to play. It is a mess. Many hardcore fans, which you can recognize by looking for the biggest assholes in reddit posts and game forums, try so hard to cope with the difficulty being a good thing and that it is immersive and fun. I am sorry, it isn't. The game has you try to balance four bars: health, hunger, thirst, and immunity. In a quick summary, health is good when it is up but you never need more than half for anything really, thirst is a joke that is reducing stamina if it builds too high, but it never does cause water is plentiful and when it isn't, water bottles are. Infection is complete BS that the game forces on you, even though you are careful and have enough immunity not to catch it. The game basically goes: oh you are careful enough to not get infected, but fuck you smartass you are going to get infected anyway so that you have to balance 4 bars instead of 3. Everything till now is good tho. Not many complaints overall. Then there is hunger, and what a cruel joke it is. Basically the immersive game experience is running around in town looking for trash to trade and breaking into houses for food, because food is expensive and the hunger bar is rising too quickly too often. The basic idea is, in order to explain what a braindead pathologic 2 enjoyer wakes up at 4am to write to a forum, le town is suffering, you are in le town, you are suffering. Gotta say, the logic is there. The town is indeed in a bad state and the fact that you have to survive in it like the people themselves immerses you in your environment. Problem is, needing to eat 3 whole fucking fish per day is not immersive. I am sorry, but needing to run around because every 2 hours your hungry boy for a character has to eat a whole steak to be satisfied is not immersive. And that drives you to actions that are not immersive as a consequence. For example: you are a doctor who tries to save a town, instead of just finding a cure for the people in general and giving the folks the middle finger shows that you care for your kin. Having to go around robbing 4 houses per day or killing people, you are trying to save, just because your character has to eat a 5th meal while the town is having a famine is not immersive for me. I understand you can't save everyone, you can't  do every quest and you have to prioritize in order to survive yourself. I get it, but the implementation of the idea is bad. It is not immersive to waste 6 hours every day to do rob houses, kill people and trade with children just because you have to eat too much. Infection is manageable without even clothes. The game has clothes shops to help with infection and you never need them really. A whole mechanic is not needed cause of poor balancing, and yet the hunger is overshadowing the whole game. Prices rising makes sense, there is a famine but I do not think doing what you have to do to get food is immersive. I would not mind having to eat less and having debuffs for being malnourished or something similar. The idea is good but the system is bad.
Another bad mechanic is ironically death. It is such a cool idea to have a death system that is basically actors replacing the previous one and that the journey becomes harder with each death. Problem is, again a good idea and a bad implementation of it. You basically die and go to the theater to speak with the impresario or whatever to talk to him and take the role of the main protagonist. You then get a debuff and fuck off to your previous save. This it the problem. As said before, your main problem is hunger and maybe infection if you are not careful. So when you die you will most likely have high infection, or high hunger. SO IT SENDS YOU TO YOUR PREVIOUS SAVE, WHERE YOU HAVE HIGH INFECTION OR HUNGER AND DIE AGAIN IN A MINUTE AND THE DEATH LOOP CONTINUES BABY. How is this a good a game mechanic. I get it le game le hard but this is just bad. Here is a better mechanic for death so people do not say I just complain without providing some alternatives: You die, go to shadow realm and talk to the theater director and then you get dropped off outside the theater, which makes sense lorewise since you are litteraly exiting the theater after you die, and the game lowers your bars by a little. The debuf is punishment enough for gameplay reasons, you do not have to drop me in a bad save spot 2 game hours back, that I can not play without dying again, and in my attempt to do so, I die another 5 times and get applied 5 more debuffs, just for me to have to load a save 6 game hours back in hopes of doing better and not go to a deathloop again. I am sorry but this is bad. Again drop me outside the theater, which is a central location, lower my hunger a bit and give me a chance to play the game.
There are other problems imo, like every night has at least 56 bandits just roaming around every street, so all you hear is "get over here", "eh cyka","Get ove.  get over hr eh cyka eh cyk get over cyka". Ah yes.. immersion. Also you can decide to give medicine or immunity pills to people you want to save and still have them die, because the chance of living is pathetic, but this is not universally bad, I just don't like it. But I think the death system and the hunger system are bad in general.
 Conclusion: I can not give a thumbs up and recommend a game, that I do not want to play. The game is unique enough that you should try it perhaps, but know that unless you are that guy that wakes up at 2 am and writes a blog on how pain and suffering are helping him succeed in life and that the only weakness is the human will, you will most likely not enjoy the experience. Idk maybe that's the point of it, not to enjoy what you are experiencing, but then do not be surprised when people do not buy the game. I do not regret having played the game, I just wished it had some more sophisticated mechanics to convey the state of the environment you are playing in, instead of le hunger bad.

review_text:
There needs to be more simple, generic, just games like this. It's an open level base infiltration game with outposts sprinkled in across the map, their layout is fine, fun to sneak through. As for sniping, it feels like the sequel to this sacrificed the areas you can actually infiltrate to enable the meme over 1000m shots, which is fine for a flash game or a separate type of small side content, but I'd rather have actual levels like here than shooting galleries. If sniping from around 300m doesn't satisfy your sniper fantasy, just zoom out and pretend your range finder shows you 10km, Jesus. 

The AI is fine if you ghost, but if you try to go panther, as in eliminate enemies quietly but hard, leave the bodies etc. then it kinda falls apart. They have very short "suspicious state", and if one enemy gets alerted, suddenly the whole area is, instantly, and they know where you are. Would be much better if, for example, after finding the body, the AI first alarm the nearest squad members, run a search, and then call it in by radio and alert the base. It's gamey, but it's a game, it would give the player a chance to react and correct his mistake instead of loading a badly placed checkpoint.

I really like that this game knows exactly what it is, no patronizing, no deep message, no forced gaming tropes like open world, the devs clearly learned from SGW3 and found the type of game they are comfortable with making. Thematically enemy installations are just soldier camps and post-soviet bases but there is a suprising amount of soul here. Each level has some nice vistas and clearly takes place in a different region, with different weather and time of day that suits the area best. First level is cool, mountains at night, a slight blizzard and northern lights in the sky.

Should be way longer though, same as the sequel. Devs claim it has replayability like Hitman, but that's BS, after running a map once you've seen every path you can take, no reason to replay, first time is nice though.

review_text:
Shadow Tactics is a stealth game where the player completes assassination missions with five characters that each have different skills. The gameplay is quite repetitive and the controls seem to have been designed to actively hinder the player. For example, it's not possible to queue up actions other than moving so it's very difficult to use multiple characters efficiently. On top of that, the characters often just ignore queued movement commands and sometimes the game even registers mouse clicks at a wrong location.

Bad controls make it very difficult to execute any complex and interesting tactics. Therefore, most missions boil down to just picking out one enemy at a time while distracting the others. Often there are no other options than to wait for an enemy to move out of the way, which is the most boring game mechanic imaginable.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is a phenomenal sequel that significantly improves upon the excellent foundation of the first game. If you loved the original, this is an even better experience.

It is highly recommended to play the first installment, Kingdom Come: Deliverance, beforehand to fully appreciate the story and characters.

The world is incredibly dynamic and alive, offering a sense of reality rarely seen in RPGs. The visuals are beautiful, making the new areas a pleasure to explore.

The game offers a huge degree of freedom, supported by a genuinely interesting main story and high-quality, non-repetitive quests.

The combat system is deeply rewarding and satisfying. It’s tactical, requiring you to think strategically, especially when fighting multiple skilled enemies. You truly feel like you are fighting for your life.

Dialogue is well-written, meaningful, and often very funny, adding great character to the world and its inhabitants.

This is a must-play for anyone who enjoys immersive, historical RPGs.

The bigger issue is the advantage some may get when buying said DLC, because the devs can't and never will properly balance their game.

This isn't a new issue as are all the things I mentioned above. Even in 5 years the game will still be unbalanced, buggy and have a monetization of a Free to Play game. There is no reason to buy this game or spent any amount of money on it. Frankly the people that run DBD don't deserve the Support. Buy something else or support some Indie Dev on his passion project.

Let me start by saying this is my own opinion and I only have a few hours in the game so far but already a few things are starting to annoy me. And I will come back to edit as i play.

Feel free to comment and ask any questions about the game if you're thinking about buying, i'll try my best to reply.

Negatives
-Getting pushed off track, not even able to hold your own line because you just get side swiped and crash from an AI touching you in a corner, Holding 1st place then get punted off the side of the track. It's like racing against rocks for fucks sakes man! C'mon...
-After all the hype this game has with "Free The Whip" which is complete garbage by the way... The whips are atrocious, god awful, Unless you land very nearly perfectly straight you'll be off the side of the track or fighting for your life trying to bring the bike back after landing, now think about scrubbing a jump into a corner? Yeah... No that doesn't work at all (for me anyway) 
-Ruts seem like a graphical feature only, they're there but you don't feel like you get anything from them unlike MXGP3/MESX.
-Pro Physics? Haha..ha..ha. Literally just normal physics with front/back braking instead of combined and a tiny bit more impact on landing not to mention pro physics put you at a huge disadvantage when going for hot laps or leaderboard times.
-Random parts of the track on corners most of the time don't feel like they rut, when leaning full into a corner sometimes I hit what feels like a huge bump, and it bounces you up a bit and slows you down a lot.

Now...After that here are some ok/good points.
-The riding physics in general feel pretty good, Cornering really has a "Valentino Rossi - The Game" Flat Track feeling to it (If anyone has played that you'll know what i mean) The back end wants to spin out alot of the time which I kinda like.

-Graphics. Well i mean Milestone have always been decent with graphics.

Take from that what you want. Everyone has their own opinion. But for me I really hope there's patches soon for these issues.

 Dont buy it full priced as is, wait for sale or buy from 3rd party website (much cheaper)
After playing for 6 hours i don't think i'm going to play much more, i'd rather play MXGP3.

review_text:
Welp, I loved those games back when they came out. The story was great, and the gameplay was great too!
I didn't understand why critics seemed to give it all around 5/10 grades, and I know many other people loved it too!

Replaying the whole thing plus the new episode now, I can say that...I actually get why the press didn't like the game much.

Many aspects of this game have not aged really well. The gameplay is incredibly repetitive, the dungeon/field areas are very limited, side-quests are few and boring, the combat system is good, but subpar, and there's many mechanics that seem designed to waste your time (like not being able to just choose a city to log-in to, or login in to the game, see a cutscene, go back to desktop, to then log in again for another cutscene).

With all that said, I don't think the games are bad. I replayed through all three, and I had a good time with it, but I definetly needed a breather now and again. There's just something about the battle system that's kind of addicting, and the story is still as great as it ever was (with a few cheesy moments here and there I didn't remember, but hey, all around pretty good).

Vol. 4 is also a pretty good (if short, though I didn't mind it after around 70 hours on the other games) extra send-off to these characters and their stories, the new animated cutscenes are a blast and the whole soundtrack is still spectacular.

The combat is indeed nerfed and the entire experience feels too easy, but then again, with the whole grindy feel this pseudo-dungeon crawler RPG has, I actually didn't mind it much, because I would've quickly lost my patience otherwise (Forest of Pain tested my patience back then and I didn't complete it, only now being able to).

As for the port, it's a bit shoddy. It gets the job done, but you still need Special-K's mod to fix some stuff, and the draw distance is pretty pathetic. Not to mention I feel they could've polished a bit more, but it's no dealbreaker.

If you're an old fan, it's a chance to relive the games and a get a bit of an extra on the side. If you're new and like JRPGs, you're probably gonna enjoy it well enough too...just come in prepared to deal with a quite a bit of archaic design.

If you ask whether or not you should play this game? Yes. The graphic are good, fun gameplay, everything's fine. The only downside IMO is the NGS story is not yet finish, and development of it are quite slow... But this is a 2 in 1 game. Why i said it's 2 in 1 because, you can download the classic PSO2 as DLC for free. The classic PSO2 still fun to play, story is awesome too, though there's not much player left in it, but you can still make a party with NPC no problem.
Don't bother to invest your time in exchanging for endgame powerful weapons/armor, it's not needed for story mission, only for the extra challenges. Play for the story, if nothing else.
Play for fun, it's worth spending time on, and it's free to play too. I'll say you'll have like hundreds of hour playtime before you're bored and try to get endgame gear for endgame challenges. Also i heard Ship 2 are quite active, more players. I'm in Ship 4, not many players in it. But the missions are all 4 shipwide matching, instead of previous only the same ship matching. You'll get what i mean when  you get on board.
Player customization are awesome, and oh, this definitely not a P2W game. The subscription do have benefit, but not in P2W way of benefit. No SSR gear, no SSR perks that leans to the benefit of combat. Most of it are cosmetics, which helps in your avatar customization. 
If you have some Stargems (SG), you may want to hold on to them for the season gold pass, which only cost 100 SG. It gives more items per tier you unlocked. Like mobile games having extra items to get by purchasing battle pass? Then you unlock them as you progress the game? Yeah, that kind, but this is purchased using in-game currency. Or purchasing material storage, extra storage 1. Those are where the SG really worth spending in.
You can earn SG in classis PSO2 too, so there's another reason to play classic PSO2. Also there's casino in classic PSO2. Earn some casino coins, exchange for SG. Or complete story mission challenges, get SG for reward (and secret camo too if im not mistaken). Those extra challenges i mention earlier also have SG to exchange.

Lastly, as of now, this date i posted this review, NGS have powerful gear reward for achieving certain level, so yeah, you don't need to grind for material as hard as your senpai (old PSO2 players) anymore. Me myself also using these weapons, can play in 90% of content and extra challenges. You may want to craft specific gear for some specific challenges, if you're up for it, but not mandatory to do so. Just something to kill your time with. Also friendly warning, do not annoy people by auto spamming messages in public. Ask the senpai, they know what it is. If they're kind, they'll just simply turn it off. If they're not kind, you might get reported for spam, or blocked, and now you'll wonder why nobody answering you.

Although the game has several problems for me, including no idea how far along you are in the game to decided stopping/continuing based on time available, I was enjoying the slow reveal of the story.

Unfortunately, the story went from being the selling point to a betrayal. If the story had been weak from the beginning, fine. But after starting strong and continually getting better, this game has become one of maybe 5 entertainment items (mainly movies that I hate and hate passionately.

To have good set up, rising tension, and then totally and completely fail on the climax and denoument makes me wish I'd stopped playing after it took so long to find the path to the house the first time. I regret every single moment spent with this game. In no way can I comprehend how the writers/developers went from an obvious-at-the-last-minute perfect ending to the utter and complete failure they used instead.

If the story had ended with the obvious, perfect ending, the graphics that leave direction unclear (clearly defined paths leading nowhere and stairs barely different fro walls), a horse scene that has people offering saved files immediately post horses since it's so hard/buggy to get past, and repetitive "banter" between the two doctors that is not nearly as cute as it thinks it is, those would all be minor annoyances.

Whatever is beyond regretting every minute of time spent on this game is how I feel. Like they should arrange for extra time off work or something? 

Negative rating, avoid all cost. Obviously I am in the minority, but I truly hate this game.

review_text:
[h1]A simple story game with a good scenario, childish dialogues and great atmosphere[/h1]

[b]What this game is:[/b] A game based on an emotional story, an interesting scenario and some good ideas.   [b]The childish dialogues unfortunately are the low points of this game. [/b]  I would give a 5/10 for this game, not much more.  The music though is its strong point IMHO.  

[b]How does it work?:[/b] The game has two main protagonists, the two scientists that work for a corporation dealing in last wishes.  Their work is to try fulfill the wish of a dying person by going back into its past memories.  That way you discover interesting things about the soon to be deceased character.   The game makes you move not only around the basic setup of the game's world, but also into the present and past of the dying character.  

[b]How does it perform?:[/b]This is a game that will provide between 4 to 8 hours of gameplay, it has very good ambient music, a relatively easy interface, and a very linear story.  It has some very very basic puzzles when you are trying to combine the "mementos", a few basic "games" (not sure it could even be named that) at some place in the last half of the game. 

[b]The good points:[/b] a nice ambiance, very good music, very basic puzzles, an easy interface.  Takes limited space on your HD (less than 200 MBs).  You get one Achievement (which may need a partial replay to get if you are not aware of a couple little things that might interfere).  You also get Steam Trading Cards.  

[b]The bad points:[/b] The game has been made with RPGMaker: some people do not like the look and feel of it, the basic interface and limited interactions.  Do not forget to manually save in order to keep your progress.  The only Achievement you can get may not unlock on the first try for two reasons: (i) one is that you were not playing originally in English, in which case resetting the language to English (in "Properties") and replaying the last part in that language will you help you get it, (ii) the second possibility is that you have to go to the "Properties" section in your Steam game overlay and switch to "Achievements" in the Beta section.  That should do the trick, after playing through from a late save in the game, you should get it.  Having to replay the ending was not something I expected to have to do and was not fun.  

[b]My take on this:[/b] a relaxing game that has a nice storyline that may prove emotional for some people.  It has a very nice music that helps build a good atmosphere into the game.  Were it not for the childish dilogues that really ennoyed me more than anyhting else in this game  [b](you have the impression the two scientists are nothing more than teens playing at doing their job) [/b] I could have recommended that game with more freedom.  Kids and teens might find it more palatable than I did.  As it is, I would recommend it when at a serious discount, I do not believe that it merits more.  I get the emotional side of things, the good story, the great music in this game, but the rest is for me not worth it.  Again, the strong point in this game is the music and the way it is used to enhance the atmosphere.  The music is worth buying if you are interested in it.

review_text:
This is a tricky one. As a Jet Set Radio Future obsessive, and later, Jet Set Radio, (the two left-field rollerblading, spraying, future-grinding games that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a direct homage to), I put off playing this for a bit. The possibility of disappointment was too great! But turns out this is a super fun game that kept me plugged in, and not just because of mis-placed nostalgia. That said, it has a high bar to live up to, and I don't think it quite clears it.

The start of this game is a goddamn slog. The game *does* have fun characters, but they sure aren't around at the start. The starting areas are drab and the cut-scenes are SLOW. The music hadn't grown on me at this stage, and I was pretty mad that they didn't just get 2 Mello (absolutely jammin' JSR-style music producer) to do the whole soundtrack. And skateboards? This is a goofy game, and having "cool" skateboards and bikes (with no futuristic add-ons) is jarring. For the first couple of hours I was having a pretty grumpy - but not terrible - time. I was sure that it was going to be nostalgia that pulled me through.

Then, not too far in, the game opened up, I'm unlocking tags, new areas, and hooking together combos like nobody's business. There are improvements in this game! The tag system is great. The flip-phone map and camera system is GENIUS. The cut-scenes are still boring, but you get to meet a claustrophobic masochist, who is always in tight spaces having a terribly good time. The police enemies are annoying (on brand for JSR). The main thing is that the flow is gooooood. I maintain that some of the level design is very poor, with some unlockables requiring specific backtracking or annoying hidden access points, but if you find yourself going for the unlockables and achievements that require combos, you will be in for a treat as you start to flow through the large levels. The soundtrack grew on me, and I have the soundtrack LP on order...

Overall, an incredible achievement. The team put this together with a lot of love, and without a big budget. Nailing the look, getting the soundtrack together, the tags, the amount of characters... an absolute lifetime achievement. It's not perfect, but I'll be damned if I would give this a thumbs down - if only because I want Bomb Rush Cyberfunk Future so badly! Get this, and get the Jet Set Radio remaster, and fall in love with a absolutely unique vibe.

review_text:
Undoubtedly horrifically beautiful throughout, with the full-on Geiger-style alien biotech being juxtaposed against the rotting decay caused by the infection that's taken hold, there's some suitably brutal scenes peppered throughout your dystopian journey, and some better-than-the-norm puzzles to be solved as part of it. Despite being fairly linear, don't expect this game to hold your hand at any point - you're pretty much alone on this ship, and nothing's there that wants to guide or assist you.

The one weakness is the combat system - most encounters are highly repetitive given the lack of diversity in terms of enemy type, and it felt that they'd have been better served by being rarer and perhaps done without weapons (without wanting to give much away regarding the story, manually ripping some of these things apart in some way, and struggling to do so, would have felt more apt), then there's a battle towards the end which felt both unnecessary and frustrating, simply for the sake of being so. Rather than a sense of achievement, it was much more one of relief that it was finally out of the way, and I could continue with the story. On the plus side, accuracy counts, as this isn't a game to throw ammo boxes out there in every corner.

Scorn's stuck with me since playing, which is something I can't write about many games - the atmosphere is undeniably brilliant, and discovering the alien world plus fragments of the history *is* the experience - so on this basis i have to recommend it pretty wholeheartedly. Given the issues with combat, I still have to qualify this as being a highly unbalanced experience - removing the combat and leaving this as a 'walking-sim' with puzzles might have been a better option in retrospect - but overall it's left the right kind of impression on me, which is very much a good thing. Give me a unique, relatively short experience like this over something mundane that's typically also dragged out anytime.

review_text:
DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME! yes, it have OVER A THOUSAND HOURS recorded, and i will continue to play it. but this was a MASSIVE mistake on my part. i regret coming to the "global" version of pso2 nearly every day that i play. but I've now invested too much time and money in this version to switch back to the Japanese game. 

you don't need to read this review. just know that the Japanese version is free, easily accessible, has way more content and is cheaper if you decide to put money into it. AVOID THIS VERSION!!! 

the game itself is... fine, but where it falls apart is the people running this version. tech support alone is bad enough that i'd never recommend this game. if you have any problems with purchasing in game items, or experiencing some sort of bug, you're 100% on your own. the support staff have a totally hands-off policy. they won't compensate you for mistaken purchases, or if you lose something you purchased. even if you can definitively prove that it was an in-game glitch or error that caused it. and this is absolutely a game where something like this is bound to happen to you at some point. 

you're literally better off playing the Japanese version of the game, and using google translate if you encounter an error in game through their support. its a nightmare. 

on top of that, this version of the game is missing a ton of content. everything from clothes, to weapons, to emotes and even story cut-scenes. 

basic items that are available for in-game currency in japan, are only available for cash in this version. and not re-salable on the player market. 

on top of this, in game currency is about 10% more expensive in this version than in the original. so every single thing in game is going to cost more if you decide to play this version. 

another element to consider, is how lazy and downright awful the translation is. honestly, its one of the worst I've encountered on an official product. simple things like characters with themed names, like "tea" and "coffee" have been translated directly without thought to "tia" and "cofy." there is even a main character in pso2 named lisa, laughably translated to "risa" its... quite embarrassing. 

even worse, is basic spelling and grammatical errors through the bulk of the original games' story. and even names, titles, events and places having their names change mid-story. If i hadn't played the original version of this game, i doubt I'd even know what the story was about in this version. 

and it gets even WORSE. the translation is incredibly inconsistent. to a level that affects gameplay and item management. on more than one occasion, a character in game will request an item, and the item actually has a differently translated name than the item requested. its a joke. 

here is an example. the primary nation you'll be fighting for in the episode 5 story, is a kingdom called Cuentia. but if you want to wear some of the outfits worn by the characters in this story, half the time the item will be named "Cuentian" and half the time it will be called "Cuentica" 

there are dozens of clothing outfits where one item is translated a couple letters off, so you'll be unable to find them in the player shop, unless you use an external website and copy/paste the name. since searching for specific items, REQUIRES you to spell the name correctly. to the letter. 

and, the worst of all, in my opinion anyways. is how many things are simply not translated. 100% of the weapons and items in game have NO description. there is no flavor text. they'll simply have a generic "this is a clothing item" description in the info box, which in the Japanese version would be filled with lore details. so you are missing out on a MASSIVE amount of world building by playing this version. its inexcusable. 

one other thing, which I'd just like to mention, is that the character creator in this version is... censored? I'm not sure if this was intentional, or a glitch. but you can't make your character shorter than 152cm. for... no reason i can think of. in the Japanese version, you can make your character as small as 140cm? this doesn't really matter, but its... weird?? 

anyways, a TL;DR to summarize. this entire version of the game seems to be developed by a group of incredibly lazy, incredibly greedy devs who don't care about the playerbase, and simply want to make a quick buck. please don't put your money into this game. go play the Japanese one instead.

Once more I wish a "mixed" option existed for reviews, oh well.

The ambience of the game grabbed me immediately, good graphics, good performances, immersive audio.
The world building, the creatures, everything was gripping and tense, the combat was sluggish and death came quickly, reinforcing the oppressive environment and the dire situation our character found himself in.

It took me 2 sittings and about 8 hours total to get through it, 

That being said...

I will not complain about the ending and keep this review spoiler free.
After completing the game, I briefly started a new game to collect the hidden achievement, pondered for a moment: "Is that all?" and uninstalled the game.

In the game industry, if you do not release a game, you have nothing. There is no consolation prize for never-released games, I know this reality on a personal level.

It is pretty clear at this point that the game had to be aggressively cut down for release as evidenced by the lack of tier 6 locks (despite the visuals indicating there are 6 security levels) and the myriad of evidence from the art book, teasers, and mentions (on the steam store as of today) about non-linear, open world adventure, that the game was supposed to be "so much more" than what it is.

There is no real way of knowing how much was axed in the end, or even why.

As a result, I cannot recommend that you get this game, it might be worth playing if Giger & body horror is your jam, but otherwise? Wait for a sale.

review_text:
I would not recommend this game, even at sale price.

There must be something wrong with me as this game has rave reviews and it falls in the category of the exact type of game I like. I loved RimWorld, I'm a huge fan of population simulators like Tropico and Anno so this isn't my first rodeo.

This game, quite simply, doesn't work. It's not that it has a high learning curve, again, I've played Rimworld. It's just that it doesn't work well, at all.

You can assign workers to a building and they, just, won't do anything. Ever. For days. The "produce until no storage is available" function does not work. You cannot possibly convince me otherwise, it's just broken. So I'm guessing all the people who enjoy this game manually set values or tell it to disregard storage. Having an in game feature that seems incredibly important just, not work, is not really my idea of good game development.

The game encourages you to build building quickly, based on the in-game hints, they expect you to have a bow tower before the first night fall. This requires a bowyer, a lumber shack, a lumber mill, a crystal gathering station, etc. etc. It's not reasonable. You will be spreading your 11 man population so like 1 person is at each station.

This brings me to my next point, Population. This game doesn't like it, they don't want you to have any. You're going to be sitting on your hands waiting for something to happen because you simply don't have the personnel to accomplish anything. This became such an absolute roadblock I had to look it up online and the suggestions recommended un-tasking everyone in your village so they could socialize with one another and mate.

That has got to be the laziest and stupidest game design I have ever heard of.

I am just amiss at how this game has amazing ratings. Maybe if you slog through the broken and tedious beginning, getting attacked every night and spending half of your time rebuilding your structures because there is no feasible way to establish a defense early on, maybe then it starts to get interesting.

I don't have the patience for such a lazy approach when there are much better options out there. If you're looking for a unique, complex and procedurally generated survival game, save yourself the headache and buy Rimworld. Even Dawn of Man was a more enjoyable experience than this, and that one is fairly shallow.

review_text:
Pathologic 2 is a reimagining of the horror-survival game Pathologic. The point of Pathologic (2) is not to feed your ego. Really, it perhaps can only be accurately described as starving you, your ego, and your empathy. Because the point of Pathologic 2 is different from other games, even within the survival genre. It wishes to challenge you, the player, to engage with a game that is so outside of the realm of anything you have experienced that it is as foreign as the setting itself.

If you have no experience with survival games in any fashion, this will be a wild ride unlike any game you have ever played- and likely will ever play after.

Once you've booted up Pathologic 2 you may see a funny little button placed within the settings, a 'difficulty' bar. This is automatically set to 'Intended difficulty'  and requires flipping off before you can see a detailed breakdown of all of the literal torture devices the game has crafted for you. Because this isn't just a game about surviving a thirst and exhaustion bar, only to eventually and inevitably become the king of the wilderness; this is a game where there are only bad options and you will never, and I do mean never, be a morally upright hero. 

You are literally playing a doctor turned ripper. A 'menkhu' that cuts and cuts. No matter what you do, you become a murderer through and through.

Without spoiling the incredible story in any other way because it has to be experienced yourself, this game is worth playing for the narrative alone. Your main motivation against such seemingly impossible odds as a plague in a town secluded from all other civilizations needs to be excellent, and the developers know it. I have been playing this game since day 1 on global, these hours do not reflect my time on my xbox which in total ive spent over 8,000 hrs on this cursed game. I went out and bought a new Xbox Series S just for this game since my potato laptop could no longer run NGS when it switched over from base. 

The Pros: Great character customization, the combat is fun, housing system has a ton of options, the collabs are pretty cool, and I must say the new cell shading option is neat. 

The Cons: This game has no vision, no future to look forward to. Developers have already said things take FOREVER to create and they have no plans on adding new classes, new areas/planets, or new PA's (skills)! This means we are stuck stagnant for the next couple of years if not longer with noting new other than fighting re-skinned enemies in the same 4 generic, lifeless areas (forest, sand, snow, fire). We have gone back to the beginner area 3 times now to level up! Its just a maddening cycle. NGS has killed PSO. Sad. I had to quit the game several months ago, I would fall asleep in combat zones. People fight you over how to play because their way is the only way. NGS does not care about type 1 (male) characters, there has not been a new hairstyle in the AC scratch in I swear a damn year but type 2 (female) gets 3-4 new hairstyles every scratch. So unless you want to play as a waifu you are pretty much screwed. I could go on forever, how the player market is forever cursed due to SEGA not stopping PC cheaters tanking the market, how F2P players get one "3 day pass" to sell stuff on the market once a month. Not enough ways to earn money, and the other ways are so so boring you just skip it. They tried new modes like canon ball rumble but the levels are just grid training levels so it just looks so boring. The FOMO (fear of missing out) is strong in this game. They hook you in with daily login bonuses, and even exclusive items making you feel like you HAVE to play every damn day. The game pass or whatever it's called here is so lame, filled with pointless stuff, only a few new accessories that are still meh, and they recolor the same damn outfits over and over again and put them in the pass. Good luck trying to find a room of players to grind in a combat zone because everyone has to hoard into one room, all of em just sitting around the lobby doing pervy things all day! 

Conclusion: NGS has turned into a Sims/Minecraft game, if you do not mind waiting years for meaningful updates and want to play as a waifu then this might be the game for you. Its like IMVU but with some very light combat mixed in. If you are a new player you will get some fun out of the game at first, the more time you sink in the more you realize how empty this game is. I will forever miss base PSO2! The memories, the zany levels, the cool af characters, all washed away by the stain of NGS!

Bonelab feels like a step back compared to its predecessor Boneworks. While it introduces new mechanics like body morphing, the overall experience feels underwhelming and unfocused.
   The campaign is bland and lacks the engaging narrative of Boneworks. Instead of telling a compelling story, it mainly serves as a showcase for the body morphing mechanic. While fun at first, the novelty wears off quickly due to shallow implementation and limited meaningful use. This oversight makes the campaign feel more like a tech demo than a fully realized game.
   Core mechanics like climbing, reloading, object interaction, and jumping feel noticeably janky and inconsistent. Despite spending hundreds of hours in VR, I found myself experiencing motion sickness during certain sequences, a surprising issue given my experience with similar games.
   If you’re into modding, Bonelab might offer some appeal, akin to Garry’s Mod. As a standalone experience, the game feels below the visionary standard set by its predecessor.
