review_text:
Long rant. I had fun playing this game, most of the time. It's flashy, the sniping is fun, but the game hardly ever gives you an incentive to do so. As others have mentioned, most objectives are things you have to interact with, so why use a sniper and risk alerting everyone when I can sneak in undetected? I have to be in there anyways. In fact, the most fun I had in this game was NOT sniping, it was sneaking with a close range weapon.

This game has the bones of a game from 2012. Some examples:
- Enemies will immediately shoot if they see you, no surprise animation or window. If you try to rush around a corner to take someone by surprise, the enemy will most of the time immediately shoot, alerting everyone. This happened once while falling towards an enemy to do a death-from-above, in the time it took me to fall on top of him, he had turned around, seen me, and drew his weapon.
- There are no [i] meaningful [/i] stealth detection mechanics, just what level of crouched are you, and are you "concealed" in some foliage. One of the best moments I experienced in this game was being prone in some foliage with two enemies stopping to have a conversation almost right on top of me. Only to be immediately spotted a few seconds later by an enemy almost 70 meters away. Splinter Cell had dynamic light based sneaking figured out in 2002. Snake Eater had an in depth concealment system in 2004.
- It plays very much like Far Cry 3. Most of my gameplay loop was throwing a rock to distract an enemy, sneaking behind him, watching the kill animation, and hiding the body. Enemies don't care if patrols go missing, they don't react if their friend goes to check something out around a corner and doesn't come back. Enemy outposts don't communicate with each other if one comes under attack. It's very dry, and I constantly found it hard to believe that I was playing a stealth game that came out 4 years after MGSV, and 7 years after Dishonored and Far Cry 3.

What ultimately turned me off from this game was the glitches. Over my few hours I experienced:
- Multiple instances of getting stuck on an object and entering a free fall where I'm unable to move or shoot, causing me to reload
- Multiple instances of Autosave working inconsistently, especially on hidden paths. Autosaves only seemed to trigger on the main paths, so approaching an objective from a hidden path was often met with a 15-20 minute reload if you failed.
- Two instances of me being in stealth, and an entire outpost becoming alerted for seemingly no reason and immediately converging on my position. Maybe they saw one of my placed gadgets OUTSIDE of the base, but this then caused 25+ enemies to know my exact location.
- Multiple instances of reloading a save putting me not at all where it was supposed to. One instance reloaded me along a path I had been on 10 minutes prior, in the middle of the enemy camp. Another instance loaded me into somewhere on the map I hadn't been at all yet.
- Foliage being wildly inconsistent at concealing you. Standing still, my concealment icon would sometimes flash repeatedly when trying to hide in a bush, like it couldn't decide if I was concealed or not.
- More than one occasion of enemies spotting me through solid objects.
- Two occasions of the map menu ceasing to work, requiring a full game restart.
- I'm not sure if this is a bug or a feature, but occasionally, after dying to an enemy and reloading the checkpoint, that enemy would be missing from their spot, gone entirely. 

TL;DR: I had fun, there are some good moments in here. But it feels like a game which came out a decade before it did. It doesn't do anything new, and is lacking features from games released 20 years ago. It doesn't do anything interesting, besides the fun sniping mechanics, which it's constantly discouraging you from doing. Even after paying $3 for it on sale, when asked if I would recommend this game, the answer is no.

review_text:
Really want to like this game but I just can't.

I feel like they really nailed the controls, gravity, and the graphical style of the "Jet Set Radio" games, but they really dropped the ball in some key areas.

The art style (like the character designs) doesn't live up to its inspiration, the soundtrack, while far from bad is a hodgepodge of different artists with sometimes radically different styles, the open maps in the vain of, but dissimilar to the likes of "Jet Set Radio Future" feel empty. 

Honestly, the whole game feels rather confused. Despite being a score boosting game, the trick system is woefully shallow and is essentially impossible to fail at. The maps are open, but the game's linear platforming segments feel the best to play. 

The graffiti and authoritarian police force in "Jet Set Radio" was a statement on freedom of expression. "Graffiti is art" (but vandalism is a crime, etc.). Nothing in this game's vapid, overly serious plot has anything to do with that message. It feels more like an homage. Or a formality. Or rather the game's going, "Hey, we're trying to be 'Jet Set Radio', do you get it?" 
(Although, I do like the graffiti system from a gameplay standpoint.)

It sucks because the core controls are everything I wanted while playing "Jet Set Radio", but even with an active modding scene, barebones platforming isn't going to keep your attention long past the end credits.


As an aside, you could say comparing this and JSR isn't entirely fair. You know, the game doesn't have to be exactly like JSR to be fun or good, but first of all, when the game is assuming JSR's identity it only makes sense to compare the two, and second, the game is doing its own unique spins on that identity badly as well.

Terrible from my point of view. I'm not saying you're all bad people, but the ones I've ran into are.

It was really hard to ask anyone inside of the game for help. Most players are already in their own circle so they outright ignore you or make fun of you.

Alliances only inviting you so you can help with tasks before removing you at a later point in time.

Players telling you how they want you to play the game. Then getting annoyed when you tell them no. And sometimes they'll even have their friends chip in to harass you.

Players gear checking you even when doing the simplest things like farming in low level Combat Sectors. Players leeching and AFK'ing in things like Combat Sectors.

Populated blocks and ERP. A lot of passionate people out there.

• P2W or Convenience •

Simple Quality of Life things locked behind a paywall. Or you can spend your months grinding out gems to pay for these Simple Quality of Life things. It gets harder to obtain SG the later you are in game.

Scratch Tickets with the overpowered augments.

• Gear Progression •

It honestly feels like gearing up is pointless.

Catch-Up events because you can never get away from the complaints of sweaty players. Free equipment with almost Best in Slot augments for everyone. This is Sega's easiest fix to reliably get newer players to do casual content and possibly upcoming content.

review_text:
Cronos: The New Dawn is one of those rare games that grab you from the very first minutes. I played it twice and a half just to see every ending, and each run remained just as gripping. The world is dark, oppressive, and beautifully designed - at times genuinely terrifying, yet always fascinating. It’s easy to draw parallels with the Dead Space remake, but the game confidently carves out its own identity.

The phylactery system, limited to three active at a time, adds a nice layer of strategy, even if it could have been explored in greater depth. I loved how the trapped souls occasionally whisper to you, sometimes at the worst possible moment, delivering perfect jump scares. The notes scattered throughout are worth reading for once, adding substance to a narrative filled with twists.

If there’s one drawback, it’s the final boss, a real bullet sponge that slightly dulls the finale’s impact. Still, Cronos: The New Dawn stands as a gripping, underappreciated experience that deserved far more recognition, sadly overshadowed by Hollow Knight: Silksong releasing on the same day. A dark, haunting, and memorable journey that easily earns a place in my top 5 of the year.

review_text: Hiveswap Act 2 is an amazing continuation of Hiveswap, featuring much more content and interesting material compared to Act 1. The majority of this game involves talking with the many Trolls of Alternia, learning their culture, making friends, and completing tasks to progress the story. A major improvement over the first game is the branching options for completing tasks, resulting in different outcomes and scenarios that will continue into the next Act. Your inventory from the previous game’s save can also impact this. The cast of trolls to interact with is greatly varied and personably, with lots of fun dialogue and different personalities. For fans of Homestuck, this is a great source for additional lore, while being an approachable introduction to Alternian society to newcomers to the series. The visual and animation quality seems slightly worse compared to Act 1, but still very charming and presentable. The music is well composed and very catchy, although lacking in variety due to an overarching leitmotif for most of the game. This is one of the few places the first Act outshines the game. Backtracking becomes annoying for multiple playthroughs and the lack of keyboard controls can lead to sore hands, but these are the only major problems with the game. Tailing points based on several attributes (Story: 10/10, Gameplay: 8/10, Controls: 7/10, Content: 7/10, Presentation: 9/10, Music: 9/10, Performance: 8/10, 58/70 total), this game scores an 83/100. For anyone who played Act 1 or enjoys Homestuck, this is a must play.

review_text:
I first got wind of this game from a YouTuber way back when, and revisited this game recently to see how it held up all these years later.

I wanted to enjoy this game. I thought the concept had plenty of room to get creative and unique, but the game always felt like it was one step behind from actually taking that daring leap into something more sinister. The concept of having to plot the demise of the other characters is fun, and the deaths themselves are unique per each character, but there was always this lacking element that just made it short of something special.
The ending was very lackluster, and it felt very rushed and left me feeling like there was no ultimate payoff for the time I invested into this game. Not to mention, along the way I encountered a lot of graphical bugs and errors that made me have to reboot the game entirely to reset the mission I was doing.
The biggest thing I think this game has going for it is its soundtrack. Each tune has a sinister, very unnatural beat that sets the tone for the game. I only wish the plot and the game itself matched this.

If you want to give it a shot, it's a pretty straightforward, and short game. But it's definitely nothing special and not a title you'll remember or think about once you're done.

MXGP Pro: Tokyo Drift is not worth your £40.

Gameplay

Yes it's more challenging than previous iterations with pro physics enabled, but 90% of this percieved difficulty seems to come from constantly trying not to slide out the back end. I can see what they are trying to do but it's too far. You can no longer case jumps and just keep riding like nothing happened but again it's completely unbalanced. Theres basically an arbitrary number that once exceeded you will crash upon impact. Theres never a scenario where you almost crash and manage to recover.. its either you keep on riding or you collapse off your bike instantly.  

AI seems unchanged, they still take more or less the same line and only seem more difficult since the game is now harder for the player. I'm playing on medium for now and usually play realistic.

Very little interaction with ruts, they seem mostly shallow and inconsequential. 

Whips are schocking. Worst yet in any iteration of the game. They look horrible and unless you land perfectly straight, which is awkward and clunky, will basically ping you off sideways.

Graphics

The same as GP3 from what I can tell. Some pop in in menus while stuff is loading. No complaints.

Audio

Bikes Good enough, seem a bit samey but haven't yet ridden all the bikes to compare. Hitting 2" puddles for some bizarre reason is the loudest sound effect in the game, far louder than your bike or the crowd. No matter how tiny or short they are you get a loud splash.. easily patched but annoying.

I've yet to play multiplayer. The compound is fun for 10 minutes.

No Matterley Basin which was disappointing!

Don't buy it unless they do some serious patching.

review_text:
I was a big fan of the old Starship Troopers game, so I was pretty excited about this one. It can be a blast if you pick the right class, have teammates with actual brains and a decent server connection and don't face any of the many below mentioned most common bugs, but that's a lot of "ifs". It's still a long way from being well playable. There are a lot of bugs that ruin the experience (no pun intended, and not talking about the ones actually attacking you).Some of the most common ones include:

- No dropship icon visible on the HUD or on the map. Go for extraction, but where to is your guess.
- Weapon positioning on the HUD being off after switching weapons. Sometimes you just see the grip and the underside of the shaft (usually you can fix this one by aiming down sights)
- Engineer turrets cannot be mounted. You can build them, but when you "use" them, nothing happens.
- Q / Ability / Cooldown not being shown. This happens pretty much every single match. Sometimes you can "fix" it by dying and respawning, but it's really annoying when you're playing something with high cooldowns like engineer and you can't see them.
- Sometimes you get hitmakers for hits but no actual points when the bug in question dies.
- Teammates not being shown in your squad list.In the lower left corner of your HUD, your teammates should be shown. But even with a full squad (4 players), you'll rarely see three other names there.
- Server issues are also common. The ping is usually pretty good, with a delay of about 1 second between "using" something and actually using it. This is already much better than your usual Overwatch experience, but there's still room for improvement. 
The building mode could be easily improved by changing the view a bit (otherwise it's really difficult to place big structures like bunkers, while small structures like wall-mounted turrets need millimeter-fine adjustments in order to be built).
- Currently, the demolisher class seems to be the worst trash ever programmed in video game history. A main weapon & a skill which deal exactly 0 damage and mobility is comparable to a pregnant whale. The only fun thing about this class is the suicide explosion, which deals about 5 damage.This class needs a complete rework or simply deletion.
- Sometimes, you cannot sprint anymore. Usually you can fix this by respawning, but not if you're playing demolisher and got the suicide explosion equipped. In  this case, you can't respawn anymore.
- Sometimes when you join a match not at the start of the mission, you are instantly killed and cannot respawn. You can still switch repsawn locations, but actually respawning is not possible.

I know the game is barely out of early access, but there is still lots and lots to do. Considering all those bugs which really ruin the game at the moment, it's definitely not worth spending 50 euros.

Roughly 2/5ths through the game I would start getting game-overs left and right. Inn the myriad fetchquests you need to do on the train-car, I spotted several times where an item wasn't put into Joey's/Xefros' sylladex, and was simply passed through via initiating dialogue. While this could be forgiven if it was consistent, the game starts using the sylladex again later.
The horrid icing on the crummy cake was the final strife and ending cutscene. I absolutely could NOT have beaten the drone flawlessly unless I abused the hint system constantly, which, again, is not an enjoyable experience. Unless you the player are an Alternian bio-engineer, even if you killed the drone without fail,you will probably get a game-over thinking it's safe to divert the tracks, only to get a game-over without ANY cutscene or dialogue telling you WHY you got it.
If you're a diehard Homestuck/Hiveswap fan, pick this up on sale and use a guide- otherwise, if you still want to see the story, wait for your favorite Let's Player or Walkthrough channel to post.

Fun little metroidvania! Recommended for fans of the genre who want something with some bite, or for those who like cute anime girls.

Takes a little bit to get the hang of the rhythm of combat, but once you do it's pretty smooth and not too terribly difficult, while still having some challenge. Has a good focus on resource management that a lot of metroidvanias lack. There's a ton of build variety, it's very fun to play around with different gameplay styles and it's fairly easy to swap between them at will. 

The pacing of the game does lack at times though - the ability to swap equipment in the middle of combat is both a good and bad thing. It provides lots of flexibility, but also slows things down as there's no reason NOT to constantly swap equipment in the middle of combat as the situation changes, which really slows the otherwise fast-paced combat down. If you don't like fiddling through menus, I'd maybe give this one a pass.

review_text:
Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a vibrant, high-energy love letter to the cult classic Jet Set Radio, yet it manages to carve out its own identity with a dazzling world, infectious soundtrack, and tight traversal mechanics. Developed by Team Reptile, this indie title thrives on style, attitude, and momentum, placing you in a futuristic cityscape where graffiti crews battle for turf while dodging militarized police and uncovering layers of mystery hidden in the neon-drenched streets. From the moment you dive in, the game bombards you with color, rhythm, and motion, inviting you into a kinetic playground that rewards creativity and precision in equal measure.

The story follows Red, a cybernetically enhanced graffiti artist seeking answers about his missing past while aiming to dominate the city’s graffiti scene. The narrative is intentionally pulpy and stylized, drawing from anime and hip-hop culture, mixing humor with moments of introspection. While the story isn’t overly deep or dramatic, it offers just enough structure to keep the action moving and lends some emotional weight to the crew dynamics and rivalries that unfold. Characters are over-the-top, cool in that ‘early 2000s rebellious youth’ kind of way, and they fit perfectly into the game’s larger-than-life tone.

Gameplay revolves around traversing the city with a mix of inline skating, BMX biking, and parkour, chaining tricks together while tagging designated graffiti spots across sprawling urban environments. The core loop is instantly satisfying: you gain points and speed by executing tricks, wall-riding, grinding, and flipping, all while maneuvering through a level design that encourages exploration and experimentation. The controls are responsive and smooth once you get the hang of them, and there’s a rhythm to chaining movements that gives the game a natural flow. It’s not just about flash—it’s about learning the terrain and moving through it like a skilled performer, turning the city into your canvas.

Each area in the game is packed with secrets, rival crews, and challenges, and the open-ended design encourages players to revisit zones with new abilities or tactics. Unlike traditional linear platformers, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk wants you to explore, improve, and master each corner of its map. Finding the best lines to maximize your trick combos or reach hard-to-tag areas gives the game a feeling of progression beyond simply unlocking new levels. Boss battles, rival crew face-offs, and hidden collectibles add layers of depth, keeping things fresh even after many hours of play.

Of course, a game like this lives or dies by its soundtrack, and Bomb Rush Cyberfunk absolutely delivers. The music is a diverse mix of funk, hip-hop, electronica, and experimental beats from both well-known artists like Hideki Naganuma (of Jet Set Radio fame) and a roster of indie musicians. Tracks blend perfectly with the visuals and gameplay, often matching the pace and tone of your movements as you cruise through back alleys, rooftops, and neon-lit railways. The sound design, from trick sounds to ambient city noise, complements the soundtrack without overwhelming it, and there’s a sense that every corner of the game world is alive with rhythm.

Visually, the game is a stunner. It uses cel-shading and bold color palettes to create a world that’s both futuristic and nostalgic, reminiscent of the Dreamcast era but brought into the modern age. Character designs are stylish and expressive, and each city zone has its own identity—ranging from sleek downtown areas to gritty industrial zones. The art direction embraces exaggeration, from the over-the-top animations to the stylized graffiti tags that explode with personality when painted. It’s a joy to simply exist in this world, let alone blaze through it doing tricks.

On the downside, there are a few moments where the camera can be finicky, especially in tight interior areas or while navigating vertical sections. There’s also a learning curve for those unfamiliar with trick-based movement systems—timing, momentum, and positioning are essential, and some players may struggle early on. Additionally, the combat system, though functional, feels underdeveloped compared to the rest of the game, with most encounters being little more than minor interruptions in your flow. These issues don’t seriously detract from the overall experience but are worth noting.

Ultimately, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk succeeds because it knows exactly what it wants to be: a celebration of movement, music, and rebellion. It taps into the spirit of a subculture often ignored by mainstream games, creating a world that feels both nostalgic and forward-thinking. For fans of Jet Set Radio, it’s a spiritual successor that finally fills the void left behind. For newcomers, it’s a wildly creative and exhilarating ride through a world where self-expression and style are your greatest weapons. It’s not just about tagging walls—it’s about leaving your mark on a world that dares you to keep moving.

Rating: 10/10

review_text:
Scorn

A visually interesting world with puzzles and combat thrown into the mix all while you take in the scenery of this alien world. 

The story of Scorn may be vague or may appear difficult to understand so I am going to assume most is up for debate aside from a few more concrete details. If you feel confused or lost you are most likely not alone. There is no dialogue or text at all.

Combat is point and shoot. Puzzles are not too difficult or too easy but there are many. I would say the main gameplay revolves around solving puzzles and the visual experience.

I would not recommend Scorn to somebody looking to play a combat-focused game, or looking for an easy to understand lore/story. This is also not a Horror experience. Although what is presented in this game may be viewed as a form of horror, a scary game with more traditional horror elements is not present. It does not play or feel like a horror/survival horror game. That said I don't think they intended for it to be.

The length of the game should average about 7 hours if you go at a normal pace and do not get caught up too much on a puzzle or combat area. Of course, this can be cut down depending on your play style. 

I came into this game blind and unfortunately left feeling unfulfilled. I don't want to say it was a bad game, but It's definitely ok to pass this one up.

review_text:
I loved SGW3, I know it was buggy, but I can live with getting stuck in a rock once in a while or on an elevator in the missile silo in exchange for the amazing open world go-anywhere-you-please-ability. If I wanted to get in my truck and spend 10 minutes driving to the top of a mountain across the valley from the target in order to take a long shot, I could. With this game the "open world-ness" is just an illusion, you are just funneled through the playing field with fences, mine fields, un-climbable rocks and cliffs on either side everywhere you go. If you do happen to find a spot to try to slip away, it immediately gives you a warning message that you have left the area and you have like two seconds to return or you just die.... The AI sucks, half the time the baddies just stand there and let you shoot them all, other times, you will be completely alone, nobody in sight, but then a camera spots you and thirty dudes are instantly on top of you. The other snipers rarely ever fire at you, they spot you from thirty miles away, but then just lay there... violently shaking for some reason.  In the whole game, 99% of the shots were at 200 yards or less. Most of the time the Desert Eagle pistol was the most effective way to clear a scene... The 12 gauges are useless unless you are three feet apart. Again, I loved SGW3, the only thing about this that was better was the ability to blow baddies arms, legs and heads off. I turned the "bullet cam" off right away because even though the footage was cool, it was like you were holding your breath the whole time and when you return to the scope view, you're out of breath and the baddies have all ran away.  I hated it compared to SGW3. 
Dear CI, please make more maps for SGW3, fix the getting-stuck-in-the-terrain bug and add the dismemberment stuff. 
 Thank you.

review_text:
This would actually be a solid 5/10 or maybe even 6/10 game if the execution was decent, but the game is overall of poor quality.
I will not include the story in my rating as I think it's irrelevant and almost non-existent in this title.

there's a couple of things that I like in this game, and it's the pretty decent equipment variety and side objectives/challenges, especially bounties, some of which have unique scenarios that keep things fresh. but that's all that's going for the game.

My biggest problem with this game is how clunky everything you do feels. Jumping, climbing, placing gadgets, throwing knives, ADS-ing etc. all feels off, and all of it has that very awkward split second where you feel like you can move on but the animation is not done yet. I think the biggest offender here are the throwing knives, which take 7 business days to allow another input in.
Another huge problem the game has is the AI and its hivemind like behaviour, where ALL of the enemies in the area suddenly know my location. What's weird is there are aspects that indicate some work has been done to make a proper AI for a stealth game, like a delayed alert state spread or enemies investigating bodies alone before alerting others, but it feels like the system was rushed and/or cut short.
The balance of weapons and mods is also atrocious, there's no reason not to slap a suppressor and a special mag on your heavy sniper rifle. Mobility is a cool stat, but it's not enough to deter people from using heavy SRs.

Overall, the game has a lot of problems that cripple it on every step of the way, souring the whole experience which could've been a not so bad casual shooter to boot up from time to time.
I'm guessing the game was on a strict schedule or just rushed in general because it feels like it desperately needs another month or two of development at the very least.

review_text:
My affinity for the movie and book brought me here, with hope that there would finally be proper realization of the IP. Upon purchase, that affinity was crushed by disappointment. It is surprising that this game is considered fully released and not early access.

ST:E presents you with moments of fun fights, but is hindered by glitches. RUBBERBANDING. When the screen is full, enemies are there, then back over there, then pause, and actually still way back there. WTF and that’s if they’re not walking in place. It is also easy in late game to get stuck or lost in a pile of bodies, and/or broken base pieces. The base is sometimes enemy restrictive and other times an enemy clip-fest. Furthermore, you can climb the base wall until later when the glitches/lag make you fall. 

To add insult to injury are the cosmetics for sale with incessant popup reminders. This is disheartening considering all of the existing issues and initial price point. Even I, a Starship Trooper fan with an admittedly low bar, think Offworld should fix the game first, then ask for more money.

This game is a Free to Play title, overlaid with a marketable IP, priced to hoodwink the consumer, and chased with a couple extra nut shots masked as "Supporter DLC.”

This is not worth its base, nor sale price, but maybe around $5 and only if these issues are fixed. 

Thankfully I found Helldivers 2 and you should too.

If you want stealth gameplay without too much focus on story, by all means get this game as it will give you all the stealth action you'd expect on a budget game. However, if you play for the story like I did, expect to be a little disappointed as the story doesn't flow very well and there are so many ways the dialogue could be improved to keep you in the loop. But I can't help but feel disappointed with the fact that the story could've been written better and there aren't really any shocker moments in it. That's why I'd buy this game for the gameplay and even then, if it's on sale.

What do I like about this game? I like the stealth element of it. I like having an area filled with different kinds of enemies like standard soldiers, snipers, armoured enemies, CCTV cameras and sentry turrets. It definitely feels good once you've spotted all enemies and strategically take them all out one by one whilst they are all oblivious that their friends are getting hardscoped quietly. However, the lack of a proper save system means after you've completed an objective without taking everybody out, one mistake that'll alert everybody in the area would mean you've wasted a whole hour on your strategy and you'd have to start again. And that gets very repetitive. All in all, decent game but the story doesn't really make up for the gameplay.

Best looking SAO game to date, with good models and some of the best animation work the game series has ever had with a lot of real time cut-scenes

Customizing your favorite character out of this roster of 21 with costumes and accessories. 

Depth in a very simple weapon and item craft, as you search for skills to make your build different from other players

With this game's Story Mode being based off the events of the anime and not the previous SAO games, you can jump on in and learn what these characters are about, as they try to stop an app gone haywire, merging all the VR worlds together. Kirito teams up with friends and foes from the many arcs to solve this problem

Online Crossplay! You can play with your friends on other systems

Price. I'm not gonna sugarcoat it, this should of be at least a 40 dollar game if not free to play. It's got live service model all over it, with battle passes and real money costumes to buy. No english dub. Yeah I know that's just me, but damn give Bryce Papenbrook his money!

So yeah, fun game, cost a bit too much, wait for a sale unless you a big Agil fan and wanna see him Klein and Silica be important for once lol

review_text: This game is very cool. I've heard a few people call it a love letter to Dead Space, and that definitely seems to be the case here. The only thing keeping me from loving the game is that it's kinda just...harder than I want it to be. I've beaten a lot of really difficult games in my time, and while this isn't TOO difficult, it is difficult enough for me that I almost don't wanna play it to be honest. Like if I got just a bit more ammo, or if a single round didn't cost all the currency I found in the last 10 minutes of exploring, it would feel a little more reasonable. It also doesn't really help that the enemies "combine" with corpses and become wildly more dangerous. Initially I would try and focus the one that was going for a corpse, but that became impossible in situations where there were too many enemies. Well the game has a mechanic to help remove the bodies with a torch so they can't do the combining. Problem is, there's often so many enemies, that by the time I get the ones chasing me off, one or 2 of them have gotten their meal, and are ready to fist fight my ass while I have 3 bullets.  Idk if I really think they should change the game or anything, but it feels like I did a fair bit of exploration and still am not getting nearly enough resources to deal with the crazy amount of enemies that come at me. Yes, even if I run away from a lot of them. Hopefully, I either get good or something gets nerfed, because I would really like to finish the game. I was genuinely having a great time with it until the difficulty felt like it hard spiked out of nowhere,

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

The music is fantastic. The environment and feel is amazing. The weird/creepy/dark style is great.

I suppose I could also just let a center game character die. I already am fine with the "you can't save everybody" shtick. I've made choices to that end when others were in danger. This doesn't feel like a choice.

review_text:
So after 19 hours I'm ready to draw a conclusion - also because the game really annoys me with some game mechanics. In this review there might be some Spoilers so beware. Conclusion at the bottom.

[b] Graphics: [/b]
First of all - the game is all in all nice to look at, because it is based on the CryEngine. You have several graphics options etc. There is also a FoV slider - which is not always guaranteed nowadays.

[b] Story: [/b]
It's about a fictitious republic in Russia, more precisely the Republic of Siberia. After an uprising and a fight for independence, this republic is now autonomous, albeit by force of arms.
One is assigned as a sniper to kill important members of the said republic and to reveal their researches / secrets.

[b] Gameplay: [/b]
Let's get to the point that will last the longest.
This is a sniper game - you kill 90% of all targets or enemies with your sniper rifle, you have to take into account the distance and the wind speed (the game gives you help even on the highest difficulty level). This help is provided by a mask that you receive from your client at the beginning of the game. This mask has some useful functions, like detecting enemies, mines, weak points of vehicles and as already mentioned it helps with sniping. Also as mentioned before there are different levels of difficulty - in this case three of them. You are able to purchase different Snipers, Pistols and Assault Rifles. All of your guns can be customized aswell with Silencers, muzzle brakes, differenz Scopes, Ammuniton and of course Camouflages.

Let's get to the points that are annoying. It can happen that at some points in the game you fall through the map and have to reload it. There are times where your character or NPCs are having trouble walking some paths and sliding down some slobs is not really fun. At some terrain points it seems to me as if our "professional sniper" is the greatest amateur there is, he can't even climb a bigger rock without problems and move around there, no you have to keep on jumping like a fool to get one little jump further up. Most of the time when it comes to this point you will be seen or almost seen by opponents which is of course annoying.
The AI in this game is a bit split in two, in some moments the AI is not able to think at all - the next moment the AI is as smart as a supercomputer. You can snipe away enemies one by one without anyone noticing, but if you miss twice, EVERY enemy in the area knows where you are AUTOMATICALLY via TELEPATHY. If you can still kill the enemy fast enough, nothing happens, but if you wait about 2 seconds too long, you have to reload the checkpoint. Of course the enemies can also spot you trough objects and terrian, also the kilometer wide shooting with assault rifles (and hitting) is included. In some moments it is really easier to just kill all the enemies in the area (no matter if someone has been alerted), because as soon as you go to another area nobody knows what happened in the other area. Even if you work with mines, hand grenades and C4 or shoot your way out with an assault rifle, in my eyes a bit strange.
In every mission there are main tasks that have to be done and also "Challanges" these are completely optional. Unfortunately some of them do not fit into a sniper game at all. For example - kill enemies with hand grenades or mines, blind enemies with flash bangs etc. I find it a little bit incomprehensible what such tasks are doing there, I am there as a sniper to (actually) only kill my target and not to start the third world war.
The missions usually last between 25 minutes (if you already know where to go) and about 1 hour+ if you want to be extremely stealthy or your just not getting lucky. For the missions – you have 5 Missions and a Trainings Mission.

[b] Conclusion: [/b]
I think the game is not bad, but unfortunately there are so many little things that are simply not solved well (e.g. telepathic communication between the enemies).
I can recommend this game if you just want to have some action and don't mind taking out all the enemies instead of sneaking through.  On the other hand, if you want to play the missions the way they are supposed to be played, it becomes very difficult to recommend it..

[b] gameplay [/b] let ' s get to the point that will last the longest . this is a sniper game - you kill 90% of all targets or enemies with your sniper rifle , you have to take into account the distance and the wind speed ( the game gives you help even on the highest difficulty level ) . this help is provided by a mask that you receive from your client at the beginning of the game . this mask has some useful functions , like detecting enemies , mines , weak points of vehicles and as already mentioned it helps with sniping . also as mentioned before there are different levels of difficulty - in this case three of them . you are able to purchase different snipers , pistols and assault rifles . all of your guns can be customized aswell with silencers , muzzle brakes , differenz scopes , ammuniton and of course camouflages . let ' s get to the points that are annoying . it can happen that at some points in the game you fall through the map and have to reload it . there are times where your character or npcs are having trouble walking some paths and sliding down some slobs is not really fun . at some terrain points it seems to me as if our professional sniper is the greatest amateur there is , he can ' t even climb a bigger rock without problems and move around there , no you have to keep on jumping like a fool to get one little jump further up . most of the time when it comes to this point you will be seen or almost seen by opponents which is of course annoying . the ai in this game is a bit split in two , in some moments the ai is not able to think at all - kill enemies with hand grenades or mines , blind enemies with flash bangs etc . i find it a little bit incomprehensible what such tasks are doing there , i am there as a sniper to ( actually ) only kill my target and not to start the third world war . the missions usually last between 25 minutes ( if you already know where to go ) and about 1 hour+ if you want to be extremely stealthy or your just not getting lucky . for the missions – you have 5 missions and a trainings mission . review_text:
TLDR *Gorgeous looking game. Clunky and unrewarding gunplay that feels like it's incomplete. Interesting world with great atmosphere and mysteries, but told in a slow monotonous manner that eats away at your patience. Not really "scary". Fairly linear design, puzzles are mostly absent. A couple gameplay gimmicks that don't add much to the overall experience. Not Dead Space whatsoever but the aesthetic will remind you of it. Step down from Silent Hill 2 Remake. Cats*



Tried to like it and I was enjoying it to an extent for the first 10 hours but the gunplay overstays it's welcome very quickly and the game becomes a slog.

I guess the game is "difficult" but I wouldn't call it a selling point like it is for souls likes and other similar games in the survival horror genre. A lot of the larger encounters can lead to trial and error to progress. For me the difficulty comes from having to dig deep within yourself to muster up the effort required to actively engage with the games combat to overcome the challenging encounters the developers place in front of you.

 If you enjoy the gunplay and are fully engaged, I would say the game is fairly easy. The combat really revolves around understanding what attacks the enemies will perform based on their startup animation, and taking the necessary maneuvers to evade them. Then you start shooting them during an opening with whatever gun you choose, and repeat. There are other systems that allow you to stun multiple enemies and control the chaos, but the basic gunplay is dodge, shoot, repeat. This game feels like it wants you to find out how to cheese every encounter, which doesn't take long.

Now this might sound fun, but you aren't really given many tools to interact with this loop. Unlike the developers previous game, Silent Hill 2, there is no dodge mechanic with I-frames, and the melee is reserved for desperate situations when your ammo runs dry. When you aim your gun, your movement is severely limited, which reminded me of Resident Evil 5 where you could not move at all while aiming (that game is amazing though). Ammo can be sparse, similar to other survival horrors. Your movement is pretty clunky as it is, so when you engage enemies within the gameplay loop I described above, it turns into this weird strategy of running around in circles for evasive maneuvers in between openings where you can punish the enemies.

As much as I disliked the combat in Silent Hill 2, I feel that Cronos really needed another movement tool like a dedicated evade button to make the combat make some sense. It really feels like there's a mechanic or two that's missing from making the combat feel natural and fluid. Going back to the difficulty aspect, because I found this combat loop to quickly become repetive and boring, my patience ran out and I think that's where the "difficulty" comes in. Because the combat is relatively unforgiving, if you are reckless and impatient, you will have a difficult time getting through large encounters. 

I was expecting puzzles, but I would argue they are largely absent from this game. Most "puzzles" just require you to continue along the mostly linear level designs, find some item that acts as a key, loop back to the local hub of the area you're in, and unlock a doorway that continues progression. There is a gameplay mechanic where you can manipulate the environment by interacting with magical sci fi spheres to open up new pathways or help with combat, but aside from the couple that are lazily hidden behind something, they are right in your face and come off as more of a gimmick than anything. Rarely do these result in you finding optional content, most of it is required to progress. Later in the game you get the ability to jump around in what can be described as a zero g environment similar to the 2008 Dead Space gravity boot mechanic, but this too is largely linear in level deisgn, requiring you to move around your camera to find the one platform you're able to jump to.

What kept me going in this game was the interesting world building and mysterious plot. I won't spoil anything, but everything, from the state of the world to who your character is and how they fit in the world was very interesting to me. I thought this would be enough to will myself through the slog of a gameplay loop, but the pacing and dialogue were so slow and plodding that eventually the whole game turned into a complete chore. 

Major characters in the game, including yourself, talk in a slow monotonous robotic tone. I understand that there may be reasons for this in the lore, but after a while I found myself completely tuning out all the cutscenes because of h o w   s l o w   t h e   c h a r a c t e r s   s p o k e. I found myself staring at the armors and details of the characters, studying the background of the scenes, and before I knew it the cutscenes were over and I had learned nothing. Maybe for others this is not an issue, but I could not care less about the cutscenes.

But even with all those issues, is the game actually scary? I would say not really. It's more of a mysterious and atmospheric game than a full on horror experience. Even moreso that SH2. And this aspect I think is done very well. The only times I felt myself engrossed in this game were when my curiosity was fully piqued. I would walk down the corridors taking in the details, big and small, that painted a picture of what happened in this world. Then I'd encounter combat and quickly lose interest.

A lot of comparisons to Dead Space have been made. This is purely an aesthetic similarity; the gameplay is nothing like it. The combat is much more in line with Silent Hill 2 remake for obvious reasons, though I think it might be a step down (I hated SH2 combat). 

All this is disappointing because the game looks amazing, the trailers got me excited even after I found SH2 remake to not be my cup of tea. But when I really got into the meat of the game I just found I had to convince myself to not quit and play literally anything else from my Steam library. Even though I mentioned this game is nothing like Dead Space, it really did make me want to play that game instead. 

I'm aware a lot of people have performance issues with this game, same as SH2. I will say the games runs very well for me, without the constant stuttering that I experienced in SH2, but I do have a relatively beefy rig.

Overall, I think this is a definite step down from SH2 remake. Somehow the combat has gotten worse. The level design became almost completely linear. Puzzles have disappeared aside from a handful that you could argue aren't even puzzles. The game seems to be built on the premise of difficult and strategic gunplay, but difficult games only work when the gameplay loop itself is rewarding. But hey, there's cats you get to pet and collect.

I hope one day I can gather the patience to complete the game, I really do want to uncover the mysteries the world presents. But right now, I just can't run around in any more circles and listen to anymore slow dialogue.

review_text:
I have mixed feelings about this game, so my final rating is mixed.

Scorn is an atmospheric horror with an incredible setting, heavily inspired by a type of horror that frightens more through its alien nature than through the presence of classic horror tropes. The setting is clearly influenced by Giger’s artwork, and many structures in the game are reminiscent of the Alien saga. What hits like a punch in the gut in Scorn is the overwhelming sense of disorientation the player experiences, but unfortunately, that’s also its biggest flaw.

Scorn is essentially a walking simulator. The few puzzles it has are simple and pose no real challenge, not even in the endgame. On top of that, its short length (about 8 hours on average, 16 in my case since I explored at a slow pace) prevents the player from truly immersing themselves in a setting that would have deserved far more depth. In my opinion, it’s a wasted opportunity but I still recommend it for the outstanding graphical work that went into it.

Dope as hell overall and really fun with satisfying combat and a surprising amount of variety especially for early access.
This has HUGE potential to me.

A few suggestions that I'd give to the devs,
* The atmosphere is solid, keep that same theme going
* The environments so far have been pretty varied which is good
* The challenge level for regular encounters is pretty good and the way leveling up works could use improvement (but it's already planned it seems)
* Whoever is coming up with these guns, keep it up, the guns are friggin cool. My only suggestion would be to add more that feel like they really pack a "punch" like the stake gun

Some suggestions to stop doing/work on,
* Please, I urge you, stop creating scenarios where the player takes high amounts of damage for no telegraphed or logical reason. If I'm taking damage the game should somehow be communicating why, I need to actually understand what mistake I have made. I have ran into multiple scenarios in boss fights, or vaults especially, where this is a huge problem. Mystery in why you are failing isn't difficulty, it's frustration. For example the vault with the green statues - okay, I get I'm not supposed to look at them or I take sanity damage, but it's crazy inconsistent and you still take it anyway even if you look away because I guess you're still near it or something (?) so it doesn't really make sense.
* It's partially the cause of the above con on it's own, but the visual effects while cool need to be toned down a bit on higher difficulties and when more enemies are involved. There are occasions where there are so many visual effects happening on you, and you can manage to basically get one hit for no discernible reason in a flurry of attacks triggered by one minor mistake that you made because you literally couldn't see anything through the massive onslaught of sudden visual noise, and that's just not fun.
* There are or is some enemy or attack that seems to darken your screen I believe, honestly I find the visual impairment of that super annoying. I don't think being randomly and momentarily blinded in the middle of combat is a good mechanic. It gets frustrating when you suddenly start combining something like that with enemies that freeze you and block your dash at the same time. Suddenly not being able to see or move, not super great.
* This might be a bit controversial, but stamina loss on hit is a mechanic I would like to see removed. The challenge it adds isn't the good kind of challenging, it robs the opportunity to use skilled play to recover from mistakes too often, and conflicts poorly with other mechanics like freeze effects. It just doesn't add difficulty in a good way and you hate it more and more the more you play. At a minimum, increase the cooldown period (ex don't make every single hit do it) so it feels less frustrating while still actually doing something.

Edit for thoughts after the "Brewing Update"
Good
* The new guns are really good, someone legit cooked here
* The additional incense options adds a little bit more depth and is a good addition
* Stability was really good on release, I only saw one crash issue myself and it was fixed by verifying game files

Not as good
* It's not actually directly related to the update, but one thing that I would definitely like to see changed in the next one or few. The fact that calamities can stack up and actually trigger in the middle of boss fights is completely silly, just flat out remove that. The bosses are already challenging and tanky enough as it is, and it doesn't add anything really.
* Bosses are meh, I mean not bad and they are cool, they feel too "spongy" though, especially with the insanely quick gun damage dropoff. It isn't terrible, but I never feel the urge to want to fight them more than once because it feels so long and repetitive to wear them down. I would reduce the health a good bit, communicate the attacks more clearly to the player (as in how they should avoid them properly), and then bump up the damage slightly. Would probably make it a lot more interesting to fight.

Update: Post Webgrave update release, 0.7.2

So, I finally caved and dropped being able to recommend this game. Which kind of sucks because it's not inherently bad. As I had already alluded to it's still very cool, there are so many good ideas here, but seeing update after update where fundamental broken systems continue to not be improved wore me down. The devs seem completely deadset on ensuring that the game needs to be as frustrating as possible to play to create "challenge" and seem to never know when to say enough is enough when stacking together systems that don't mix. For a long time (aside from a core set of rabid insufferable fans who seem to think their beautiful perfect game can do no wrong) a lot of very valid suggestions to fix even some of the issues have been given by the community.

None of them would cause the game to lose its core identity, they would only make it more enjoyable to actually play.

So with that, I'm throwing in the towel. If you like this, then good on you, have fun.

review_text:
I'm not recommending it simply because I didn't enjoy it overall and won't be interested in further chapters. It was an interesting idea & the devs did some nice work - I just think it's lacking the gameplay and enjoyment factor. It might be worth a buck or two, but I certainly wouldn't pay the $10 asking price for it (I got it in a bundle with many other games)

Pros:
* Pleasant story
* Nice visuals
* Nice music
* Short game (<4 hours)

Cons:
* Juvenile humour (more annoying than humorous)
* Tedious gameplay (slow walking, mostly wandering around just to find the next orb/memory just so you can get on with the story)
* The minigames are repetitive and suck
* No plot choices

I really wish I could move faster than a snails pace (or not have to walk at all and just click things immediately) and that there was actually something to do that made any difference (story choices). As it was I just felt like I was in a walking-simulator, slowly going through the paces to unlock the fixed story. 

It was hard to be emotionally involved with the story when I was just wishing it would end already - I was glad when it finally did!

review_text:
- Played KCD2 before KCD1, so no nostalgia or bias shaped my view.  
- Gameplay is excellent—smithing, animations, and medieval simulation are top-tier.  
- Combat is smoother but less realistic—too many perks, less tension and consequence.  
- Story feels weak—mostly about securing an alliance, with little emotional payoff.  
- Final twist (losing silver to save Samuel) felt forced and illogical.  
- Samuel’s character wasn’t developed enough to justify the sacrifice.  
- No real growth or moral weight—unlike KCD1, which was rich in meaning.  
- Overall: brilliant systems, but the narrative feels like a polished DLC, not a true sequel.

name: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II

review_text:
A moderately fun campaign that seems to have been scaled back compared to Boneworks to be able to run on a quest natively, the levels contain smaller set pieces overall and don't give off the same liminal vibe that Boneworks does. Aside from that, the game plays more like a 2h campaign followed by a collection of tech demos that show off cool-ish mechanics that the devs added to this title that weren't in Boneworks. Would be fine if it was like 20 bucks, but at a 40€ price tag I expected a LOT more. It's more expensive than it's predecessor while having LESS content ffs.

The gunplay is slightly improved but also feels lacking in certain areas (HK slapping is extremely inconsistent for some reason, you cannot slap the bolt release in the M4, etc). There is also a distinct lack of different hand poses when holding the gun (lack of a C clamp position, for example) and mag poses (Not having the choice to grab either from the bottom or from the side). Aiming with bigger weapons can be tricky since SLZ insists that guns must collide with your avatar's body, meaning that you have to put the virtual stock of your virtual gun against your janky physics-based virtual body, which more often than not makes the gun tilt to the sides due to goofy collisions. 
You can press grab by the magwell to pull out the current mag on your pistol (which makes no sense since you already have an eject mag button), the issue is that you'll end up pulling your mag out when trying to 2-hand your pistol from the bottom (where you would usually place your palm irl). Shotguns only fire slugs for some god forsaken reason which would be fine if we had the option to load buckshot, but no, only slugs here. Kinda defeats the point of using a shotty in most scenarios since a good rifle headshot tends to kill most things from long range. At the end of the day it's still one of the most satisfying aspects of the game nonetheless, but I expected more improvements when compared to their previous title.

Melee combat is, simply put, abysmal. It seems that the recent patch made it even worse which I find impressive since SLZ never really nailed melee combat. Your character almost always holds the weapon like a complete lobotomite (I can't count the amount of times I unholstered a hammer just to be holding it sideways) which you have to correct manually. Swinging the weapon is another, even sadder story; Your avatar cannot swing a sword normally, period. I don't even know how to explain what he does with the sword, but I sure as hell wouldn't call it a swing. Slashing as a whole simply doesn't exist, you bump your blade against the enemy and sometimes a "damage spot" appears on them like you just hit them with a blunt weapon, stabbing feels good enough though.

The avatar system is interesting but it's clearly meant as a modders ressource more than a proprer game feature, by the time you have all the 6 avatars the game is almost over. The amount of avatars available could also be better (variations of the avatars would be cool, why only have 1 strong, 1 light etc?)

Enemy variety is a real issue to me, you'll see a huge amount of recycled enemies from Boneworks, and not enough interesting new additions. One gripe that I have is that all the human enemies only fistfight you, even the guards in the street puncher level dont attempt to grab an object to hit you with. The only enemy that can shoot you at all in this game (not counting the turret since it's more of an object rather than an enemy) is the omni projector, which is literally just a rolling tripod with a gun that isn't satisfying to shoot. Skeletons are basically nullbodies with a new coat of paint, villagers are all bald for some reason and behave like a ford with altered voicelines, etc. There really isn't anything new here which is a shame.

The story is kinda vague and seems to be there just to set up their next mainline game, but that's alright since the story of Boneworks never really made much sense to me in the first place.

Climbing is still pure jank.

The holsters are still janky.

Hand to hand combat is weird, as blocking doesn't really do much as you still take damage, and since the new patch you can only really use jabs against most enemies since hooks dont seem to be registering as attacks.

I will aknowledge that this game was build more as a modders ressource, a VR Gmod of sorts, rather than a proper mainline game, but the near abandonment this game suffered from by SLZ killed any momentum the game could have had, the modding community is basically dead, you have some weapon packs, NPC reskins and some low quality maps made by children but that's it. I expected to be able to make up for the lack of content in the main game with mods but no, there really isn't anything to do after the game is done. Unless you want to collect every item in the game.

And yeah, item collection is back from Boneworks, albeit with improvements (you dont have to carry the capsules to the end of the level anymore). My problem with this system is that they put EVERY MOTHER-FUCKING PROP IN THE GAME in those capsules, meaning that 95% of the stuff you find is boring. I opened a secret room after backtracking from the office area with a developer keycard, only to find FUCKING [b] TRASH BAG B [/b] inside. Yes, a variant of a trash bag inside a secret room. I just installed a full save after that because there's no way I'm running through the whole game again to get a variant of a park bench.

The soundtrack is an absolute banger though, just like in Boneworks. The karting section for example, which is painfully short and boring on it's own, is made 10x better by the pseudo-eurobeat that plays when you start racing (against no one lmao). Basically, they cooked with the soundtrack, no complaints here.

Stress Level Zero, for the love of god, give this game some love, add some content, interact with your community and try to revitalize interest in this game. Buying the game right now feels like stepping on a sinking ship that never really left the harbour in the first place. There's no real post story content, and there doesn't seem to be anything approaching on the horizon either.

TL:DR Interesting game, way too many reused assets without enough new additions to balance it out, not enough improvements, short story, not enough content overall, great soundtrack, and not worth 40€.

Get it on a sale at best, but curb your expectations (and pray that older mods get updated soon if you're hoping to get more than 6h of playtime).

EDIT: Also noticed some pretty blatant AI Art on the Rooftops level for the anime ads, very weird to add those considering the fact that other billboards seem to be human made. At any rate the point is that they look very "off" (some characters are missing fingers, etc). I don't know why SLZ decided to cheap out those, that kills the Bladerunner vibe of the level IMO.

I randomly picked To the Moon up while it was on sale, figuring I’d try something new. I honestly didn’t know what to expect, but I’m so glad I gave it a chance and stuck with it. What started as simple curiosity turned into one of the most moving gaming experiences I’ve had in a long time.

The story is absolutely beautiful. The way it slowly unfolds kept me hooked the entire time. I found myself relating to little pieces here and there, and that made the emotional weight hit even harder. Overall, I ended up tearing up more than once and absolutely bawling by the end lol.

What makes it so special is how human it feels. It’s not flashy and it’s not over complicated. I also loved feeling the roller coaster of emotions throughout. 

Absolutely a 10/10 experience for me.

review_text:
Lucius is a dark and intriguing horror-adventure game that plunges players into the unsettling world of a young boy with sinister powers and an ominous destiny. Developed by Shiver Games, the game offers a unique twist on the horror genre by placing players in the role of Lucius, a six-year-old child who is, in fact, the son of the devil. This premise sets the stage for a narrative that blends supernatural elements with a disturbing exploration of innocence corrupted, making it a standout title for those who enjoy psychological horror with a strong narrative focus.

The gameplay centers around exploration, puzzle-solving, and stealth as you carry out a series of diabolical tasks within the confines of a sprawling mansion. Lucius’s abilities allow players to manipulate the environment, possess objects, and craft deadly traps, which must be used strategically to eliminate the unsuspecting inhabitants without raising suspicion. The game cleverly encourages creativity, giving you multiple ways to approach each target and experiment with different methods of causing mayhem. This freedom enhances replayability and adds layers of depth to the overall experience, challenging players to think like a sinister child orchestrating chaos from the shadows.

One of the most compelling aspects of Lucius is its atmospheric setting and narrative tone. The game uses its eerie mansion environment to great effect, creating a sense of creeping dread that permeates every corridor and room. The sound design is subtle but effective, with unsettling ambient noises, distant whispers, and haunting music that heighten the tension and contribute to an immersive horror experience. The storyline unfolds through cutscenes and interactions with various characters, slowly revealing the dark family secrets and the boy’s connection to the supernatural forces that drive him. While the pacing can sometimes feel uneven, the narrative remains engaging, especially for players interested in a story-driven horror adventure.

Graphically, Lucius presents a fairly dated but serviceable visual style that suits its eerie atmosphere. The mansion is richly detailed, with a variety of interactive objects that players can use to their advantage. Character models and animations might not be cutting-edge by today’s standards, but they effectively convey the unsettling mood of the game’s world. The design choices emphasize mood and storytelling over flashy graphics, which works in the game’s favor, especially for those who prioritize atmosphere in horror games.

review_text:
Game is fine. But it is a letdown in many ways.

Difficulty: Easy. very easy. Controls are lenient. You can easily miss jumps and go wrong ways and still hold combos. Died a couple times to weird game situations (not bugs).
The music is good. Not great like the Jet Set Radio games. But they would get stuck in my head and they were nice. The Hideki Naganuma are actually the only ones I don't care for. The music is more tame in multiple ways, less punk, more mainstream. Less exciting, more chill.
Game has many mechanics added to it that would be great to see in the previous games. No complaints there really. Maybe just that they make one so powerful that there is not much risk/excitement when playing.
Basically all the characters are super lame. The one I can think of is cool in a sensei kind of way, not a punk kind of way.
The levels are entirely forgettable. Every stage is walk around, spray some graffiti, then do some menial tutorials disguised as competing with other crews. The level design in terms of riding around and doing cool lines, felt lame to me. It feels like there are big obvious lines that you take, nothing really on the side.
The story is down to earth in this game relative to the zaniness of the Jet Set Radio games. But the zaniness meshed well with the punk nature of the Jet Set Radio Games. With this game, the combination of down to earth + lame characters + being not punk, doesn't work, and the story feels both flat and faux.
The "genre" now has skateboards and BMX which is cool, but it exposes one of the most egregious sins of this game: there are not many tricks. Even worse, characters do not have unique tricks! This may sound unimportant, but in Jet Set Radio Future, spamming the trick buttons looked nice and felt nice. In this game, the tricks are kind of cool, but there are only the few tricks that you are stuck with, and get old quickly. One used to be able to play a different character to change things up. Not so here.
The only thing that differentiates characters is which annoying voice you choose to hear. No stats, and as told above, the tricks don't change.

If this game added more tricks, tricks per character, and added a fun post-game, this game would be good enough for me to recommend. But it feels like a lame story that gave me no emotion and left me with no post game to play with.
If one didn't play the Jet Set Radio games, this game will be amusing, but nothing special nor impactful. But it is a moist version of the Jet Set Radio games, and feels incomplete/rushed out. You should play Jet Set Radio Future instead. Jet Set Radio is cool, but it is pretty old and janky.

NGS is a stillborn game with predatory monetization schemes and infinite content draught. NGS is an online ERP simulator for all kinds of weebs and creeps. 

Every update only reuses the exact same but slightly reskinned enemies, leading to incredibly repetative quests with close to zero variety and ingenuity to them, and adds more fashion as well as P2W gacha banners for whales to sink their money into. There is zero point to do anything aside from just amassing more and more cosmetics to mess with the only part of the game that's actually good, and that is your character visual customization. The only actual "content" is community drama, which is hilarious to look at, seeing how the game has 0 competitive PVP content aside from just chasing records for completing alliance tasks or speedrunning races/quests. 

Yes, there is a market where a F2P player can buy most of the stuff they might want, but you have to BUY premium subscription to sell stuff on it, while F2P players very rarely get a consumable bare 3 days passes. Any fashion you get from very few F2P gacha banners can't be sold on it, only whatever rare drops you might get from grinding the game for weeks and months. Which leads to whales monopolizing the market and setting prices unreachable for F2P players no matter how hard they will grind. Any good fashion pieces or meta gear will always cost you weeks and months of restless grind. 

And considering how this game is clearly made to be a soulless cashgrab, of course on top of that you have slothful greedy devs that don't care about their own community and can take months, if not years to fix old bugs or add QoL tweaks that players have been asking for since NGS initial release. 

[strike]I still come back to this game from time to time because I have a few friends here I can hang out with, but if you look what to sink you time into, just go and download an incremental idle game or some sort of clicker, it'll be a much more interesting and rewarding experience than whatever you might get from this game.[/strike]

All of my friends and me were basically forced to quit the game even despite the bits of enjoyment we had with it in the past.

Sega doesn't care in the slightest about global and PC audience, only catering to their small JP community. It even feels as if they're deliberately trying to kill the game, which might not be too far from the truth as rumors say that they're betting all of their budget on some "secret super project" that will, of course, inevitably flop.

As much as I'd like to recommend this game, it really irks me how the whole selling point of the game was the idea that you can mod anything in, then it was released with an incomplete SDK, which as far as I can tell has had no updates in the span of 6 months. 
(Though this is true, I've researched and seen that their goal is to completely rebuild the features from the ground up in order to make the SDK more usable for modders and game developers. So be excited about that!)

Two patches were made in the first month of the game releasing, and then radio silence since then. I just hope this doesn't end up like boneworks where the base game was completely abandoned after the hover junkers update (fair enough as there had been plenty of updates beforehand).
If there is info I'm missing, please update the community where they'll see it and don't expect people to go scrounging through random discord chats or reddit comments aimlessly searching for clues.

There's obvious issues in this game that still have not been fixed, such as the hands completely having a mind of their own under certain circumstances. Climbing needs a lot of work, either you'll be vaulted over a 15 foot long surface, or sent flying backwards 60% of the time. The story (if you can even call it that) was very underwhelming, you get sent through a bunch of trials to unlock an avatar changing system, just for the game to end as you reach your full potential, leaving you to ask yourself what to do next. This is only amplified by the fact that you need to go through the mini-games in order to unlock the story, so most players have seen most of what the vanilla game has to offer by the time it is done.

I was a huge fan of boneworks, so to have to struggle this much to enjoy this game has been a real disappointment, and I truly hope all of these issues are addressed sooner rather than later.

review_text:
This is a very fun Left 4 Dead-inspired multiplayer VR shooter that I recommend playing, though it is *not* a must-play experience. The game does offer a PVP mode, though I have not played it in my 10.6 hours with the game.

At $40, it's arguable how much value you are getting compared to other experiences, as the game has content/progression issues that detract from replayability. I can see many players putting 30+ hours into this game, and I can see others being done with it after just 5 hours.

--------------------------------------------------

[b]PROS:[/b]

-4 Player co-op VR shooter

-Weapon customization is great!

-Weapons feel good, Landing headshots is fun

-Does offer exciting gameplay in bursts

-After getting accustomed to the game mechanics, I would say it has good controls (confusing to learn though)

-You have 2 holster slots to store weapons, but you can essentially carry 4 weapons in total, as weapons and items in your hands are retained. (I carry a rifle, SMG, and akimbo pistols into each run)

-Enemy spawns have *some* variety; Bosses always appear in same areas, but hordes are somewhat variable.

-Lots of control / movement settings available (though the game doesn't explain what some of them really do)

-Manual reloading (realistic) or auto-reloading options available to players

-Game has a Multiplayer HUB area and Party system (party invites, friend invites, etc...), though it is far from perfect as I detail in the CONS section

-Has PVP mode

------------------------------------------------

[b]CONS:[/b]

-Game is short and lacking for content. 5 levels; 4 difficulty settings; 6 weapons; 2 items (pipe bomb + healing syringe); 3 types of elite enemies; 1 Boss enemy. If you make a point to run through all 5 missions before replaying any, you will see 90% of what this game has to offer in your first 2-3 hours.

-Game's Party / Lobby system is under-baked. If returning to the HUB area, it always disbands your party. Lack of player communication options (as outlined below this) compound the issues with this strange party system.

-Lack of voice/text chat in HUB areas. Technically voice chat exists, but if you aren't in the same HUB instance with your Party (which you can't do anything about), you can't hear each other until you enter the match. Accepting a Party invite does not load players into the same HUB Lobby. Too many times I have queued Quick Play matchmaking, got placed into a full Party, and sat waiting 5+ minutes for the seemingly-AFK host to start the match, with no way to communicate with them. I've started Reporting AFK hosts, as at least the game offers this option and 3 out of 4 Quick Play parties I join result in this issue.

-The shotgun is powerful but really suffers from VR-reloading woes if using manual reloading. It's really easy to do in the firing range, but under pressure, reloading the shotgun really isn't an option if you are trying to prevent taking damage.

-Game completely neglects to inform the player of so many mechanics. Weapon storage in the firing range. How to swap items between hands. How to even bring up the Settings menu. Informing the player that having an item in your off-hand doesn't prevent you from manually reloading (aka you don't need to drop a pistol when dual-wielding to complete a manual reload). NPC gives you a wrist-mounted rocket launcher, but doesn't tell you what it is or how to actually use it.

-Allies controlled by AI constantly strafe in front of your shots

-Big progression issues; after beating all 5 levels, the only progression that exists is collecting weapon parts. Compared to the time it takes to complete all 5 missions (1-2 hours), you will experience many hurdles trying to grind for weapon parts that have any value, as outlined below.

[b][u]ISSUES WITH FLOPPY DISKS / UNLOCKING WEAPON PARTS:[/u][/b]

1. Unlocking new weapon parts is achieved by finding hidden floppy disks in missions (color-coded to indicate rarity) and inserting them into machines in the mission's 2 available Safe Rooms, rewarding the entire party with an unlock at the end of the mission. If a floppy is found in the last 3rd of a mission, only the player carrying the floppy disk is rewarded as the final Safe Room has nowhere to insert the disk. Imagine the party is rewarded with 2 of the lowest quality floppy's, and 1 player finds a high-level floppy near the end and only they get to profit from it.

2. Duplicate parts can be acquired. The closer you get to finishing your favorite weapon, the greater the chances of getting duplicates.

3. Since the parts you get are totally RNG, you may get 10 parts for a pistol you don't use before you get any parts for the weapons you actually use.
