review_text:
Dead by Daylight - a name-based breakdown

[b]Dead[/b]
You play in one of two teams (yes, a solo team is still a team), either trying to do the dead to someone or avoiding becoming the dead.
As the killer, it is your job to find people, run in circles of varying radii while dodging pallets thrown at you for at least 10 minutes, attack survivors with often questionable hit registration, and scramble to find a hook in proximity. Rinse and repeat thrice per survivor.
You also get a large cast of characters with increasingly broken and more abundant abilities and perks (scaling with in-game and IRL money cost, of course).
As a survivor, your job is one of: Holding Mouse Button 1 for an eternity and occasionally tapping space, running in circles of varying radii while dodging the killer, dropping pallets and jumping through windows, and enjoying the scenery while [i]hanging around[/i].

[b]by[/b]
By choosing to play this of your own free will, you prove that you are masochistic.
As the killer, the survivors always find some random junk scattered by a tornado to hide behind, and as a survivor, the killer is always slightly* faster than you.
If you are planning to play a killer with projectile or ranged attacks, dont't. Hitboxes in this game have been proven to protrude into the 7th dimension, especially those that don't look that way.
Conversely, survivors have been known to have been hit by attacks through solid objects.
Really shows how our understanding of physics breaks down beyond the third spatial dimension.
Also remember to pray to RNGsus before running through shrubbery, as it might be of the 'solid' genus despite sharing the phenotype of their 'transparent' siblings.
It's also funny how there are never any windows or pallets while you are being chased. Well, back to admiring the level geometry.

The performance is also abysmal. Lowering the graphics settings barely makes a difference, as the game is consistently gobbling up 80-100% of my CPU even while not much or even nothing is happening (e.g. game lobby, transition screens).
Depending on the map, it turns into a PowerPoint presentation as soon as at least one other player is on screen for no discernable reason.
On a positive note, I no longer have to change settings every time I boot up the game, so a big round of applause.

[b]Daylight[/b]
This game is anti-fun regardless of which team you play on, regardless of you win or lose. Good games where neither team is completely steamrolled are few and far between.
It seems like you are placed in the timeout box after dominating too many matches in a row and are free to return after serving your sentence. If that's your thing, good for you, but that ain't it, chief.

Specifically for 2V8 (the only theoretically redeemable mode**) the killer queues are a joke. You usually wait 30+ minutes for a match, and too often just so that the survivors can complete the 'DBD All 8 Generators' 100% glitchless speedrun in 2m 57s.
How is this possible when there is a 5-digit player count at all times? The introduction of 'Survive While You Wait' has done precisely nothing and the priority queue got ditched after one iteration of this game mode for reasons I don't care enough to look up.
At least you may partake in fun activities such as: Holding Mouse Button 1 (but more often because no one else is doing it), getting nothing done while being permanently cornered by 2 killers, and getting ignored by up to 7 players while in a cage collecting hook states (what do you mean that's not the objective???).

I'm being held here against my will by a so called 'friend' who's only into these kinds of games. Please help.

* Top speeds of Mach 3 have been registered.
** Objective fact.

review_text:
This game felt too thin, with too little substance stretched over a very short playtime that does not justify its asking price. It harbours and hogs gameplay mechanics to prolong an experience as intriguing and captivating as observing concept art. Far too little and too late is an accurate description of Scorn, as it extends what little gameplay there is in a game that can be finished in four hours to obscure how barren it is. Speaking of barren, Scorn's Story.

Scorn dumps you in its world clueless with no hints, no markers, no objectives, designed for blind playthroughs, if you will. I initially liked that until I learned this method extends to the game's story. Far from what I would describe as environmental storytelling, Scorn instead walks the path of no showing and no telling. With not a single piece of dialogue, the game does not establish characters, plot or narrative, not even through other means. When I discovered a moral choice in the game, I was amused at how poorly implemented it was. This moral choice only serves to make the game feel unfinished. It's a single moral choice. One of its kind, of little impact and importance. It further establishes the feeling of what could've been, of lost potential, of snuffed excitement.

Visually, Scorn is striking and sombre, yet appealing and unique. It is, undoubtedly, the game's most substantial positive element. The puzzles often blur the lines between puzzles and basic problem-solving. The combat is tedious and monotonous. Once a second enemy enters, the player will take damage no matter what because wielding a thruster tool against projectile-launching enemies in confined spaces is stupid. I felt like the player and enemy characters were designed for different games. It was definitely bothersome fighting far-ranged enemies with a limited close-ranged weapon capable of two strikes at a time, and it added to the dull nature of the combat. I discovered that enemies mostly chase the player for a very short distance before stopping and even exiting the area; from then on, I simply went along with my business and did not engage in combat unless absolutely necessary. The other much more powerful weapon is only used for one section before being rendered useless; hell, the combat, in its entirety, is in two sections, and I'm using both "combat" and "section" very lightly.

The Cream does not recommend Scorn at its full price; get it on Game Pass instead if you want to play a concept art exhibition with a few "puzzles", frustrating combat, and soft locking. Oh God, the soft locking!

review_text:
Dammit, it was starting so good... I really liked it more than Dead Space (both original and remake). Where Dead Space seemed to build the atmosphere mainly by turning off lights and jump-scaring you with monsters, this one seemed to be doing much more than that.

Firstly, it was using proper cinematics when required to show intense situations, to let you feel "the strain" of it all. The way camera was moving, the way the frame was "dirtied" (this does not necessarily mean actual dirt, it means that a frame is not "perfect" and that can help with immersion). It felt like they are really putting you into the game, at last to an extent.

Secondly, there were just those little things here and there, like little unnecessary movements made by characters, they made it feel just a little bit more "natural". And it was also little details in the environment, too. In Deas Space I always wanted to run, and could not, because I needed flashlight, which works only if you aim. Callisto is much brighter, but I never wanted to run here, because it just felt wrong. Something was telling me, that I need to be cautious, and move slowly, even though logic told me that this is a safe area, and everything is scripted either way.

There was also combat. Yes, it turned out to be somewhat repetitive pretty quickly, but the way you were introduced to it, and the way it felt... Like "heavy", "difficult", "important". You know, like, with fighting scenes in movies: sometimes they have this weight, that you feel even though you are not participating.

My point is, I wanted to play the game further. Yes, the second prisoner (Elias, if I remember correctly) seemed a bit forced as a guide, perhaps, since he is a prisoner, he probably should be that knowledgeable if he is in his cell most of the time. But there is enough doubt regarding him, that maybe there will be an explanation. I really wanted to know what will be next, was really excited...
Until on the 2nd evening I could not load my saves. Half of them. Apparently, in some obscure cases the save files become 200+ megabytes instead of 200+ kilobytes, and that makes them unloadable: the main menu just hangs, at some point changes into black screen, but nothing loads anyway.

But, ok, I cleaned those up, lost maybe 10 minutes of playtime, not that big of a deal. I mean until within next 1 minutes from that save I need to go through a door, but instead of loading the room, I get a black screen. And this bug is (or at least was) present on PS4/PS5 even. And there is no solution for it: for some people restarting the game from the very beginning worked, but for some - nothing worked at all. I've tried multiple things on PC to no avail, and I am not that invested to replay almost 2 hours to find out if that door will open for me or not.

So trying for a refund. Luckily, in total I got just a little bit over 2 hours, and since there is evidence of bugs, there is a chance that I will get my money back.

review_text:
This game is too scared to challenge the player.

Keeping your combo is as simple as spamming mouse buttons while rail grinding and holding a manual until you find the next rail/wall. You can say "well the fun is in making your own stylish combos", but since you have so few tricks to work with, that style of play feels pretty underwhelming. The game also doesn't incentivize mixing up your tricks beside giving you multipliers for hitting sharp turns and wall rides. And with boost resetting, it is practically impossible to drop a combo no matter how sloppy your pathing is. The whole system just feels kind of shallow. I think it really could have benefited from some kind of letter grade system similar to Devil May Cry.

The crew battles are a joke, like, just rail grind/manual spamming will completely dumpster any crew. The combat is clunky and confusing. I've never felt like I was even close to dying in any of the police encounters. I mean, why is tagging literally impossible to fail? At least in JSR, you had limited paint and messing up your tags would waste some. 

I love the music and art direction, clearly a lot of love was put into this game. The dream sequences especially are super cool imo. But the system mechanics just feel half baked. Overall, it's not that engaging.

The second part in [i]Samorost[/i] trilogy. This time a little bit longer than the first game, but still fairly short. The graphics are yet again very peculiar, it's a combination of real photographs and hand-drawn images – the world has thanks to it a mysterious and surreal atmosphere. The music is very charming. There are no voices, only various sound effects which are pretty funny.

The story is simple. The little gnome is taking a nap and at that moment mischievous aliens steal fruits from his orchard… and also abduct his dog! As he won't abandon his friend in need, he bravely follows the aliens to their home planet! On his journey, he needs to be rather resourceful and use every wit to get both of them safely home.

Puzzles are pretty straightforward although some can be a little bit obscure to realize (also the final puzzle with seals can be sadly somewhat tedious). There is no penalty if you do something wrongly, so if you don't know what to do next just try clicking on everything on the screen!

All in all it's a very pleasant game and I can only recommend it. :3

review_text: I'm sad to say all the positive reviews didn't pan out for me.  I am a follower of the inteactive fiction game style even when the gameplay is limited.  The idea behind To The Moon is compelling.  You travel back through a dying man's memories.  What it came down to for me is that the story bored me.  While a teenager might be convinced by the anime style and juvenile acting, I just wasn't convinced by the characters or intersted in them in any way.  The main two protagonists that you control in Japanese bobble head Nintendo RPG style are supposed to be adult doctors, but they both talk and act like they are aroud 14.  The girl is of course the more mature with the boy being the steriotypical bumbling overconfident wise guy, typical of most cartoons nowadays.  Unlike many of the reviews there was no point in this game where I felt like I wanted to cry (yes I have been emotionally touched by certain movies and games on rare occasion).  I felt like it was a story about dying written by someone with possibly limited experience with the subject or at least not much ability to convey it.  All I got was scattered moments of cute and shallow sentimentality,  I was far more emotionally engaged and blown away by Kentuckey Route Zero, The 39 Steps, and The Dream Machine, among others, which were much more artfully presented with better plot, atmosphere and characters.  I would also give mention to Hotel Dusk and it's sequel for the Nintendo DS, with very accurate portrayal of the 70s and 80s with terrific character development and art style.  The Shivah and The Samaritan Paradox also impressed me though the difficulty of the puzzles and pixel hunting can be frustrating at times.  One more suggestion; if you want something of Nintendo / Pokemon style with a lot of nostagia and real well developed child characters that may emotionally move you, I'd suggest Attack of The Friday Monsters on the Nintendo DS Store, though it is short.

review_text:
I received the game as part of a new GPU purchase (RX 6700XT).

As mentioned by everyone else, the graphics and audio are sensational. It's just a shame that the rest of the game isn't up to the same standard. 

The game is basically a single corridor, narrative driven walking movie. It simply does not require much effort or thought to play. The combat is sorely lacking, it really is just dodge left, right, attack and repeat. The boss battles are the exact same as any other combat situation making them pointless. There really isn't any point to changing the difficulty due to nature of the game mechanics. The stealth sections are tedious and do not require any tactics. 

The game ran 'mostly' fine for me (R7 5700X + RX 6700XT) using FSR2 at 3K resolution, netted approx 45+ fps at ultra with Ray Tracing on medium. The game does still hitch from time to time for loading, noticeable on a few select doors. The audio did cut out from time to time and I had one complete crash to desktop. 

Saying that, I enjoyed the atmosphere, the story was okay and kept me playing, the few enemy types to face are interesting (but are not new to the genre). It is something I'm happy to have played, it's something I won't be playing again however. 

Saying that this game was a Dead Space successor really hurt it. It would have been better off being an 'Until Dawn' style interactive movie and then it would have been so much better and negated the poorly implemented game mechanics it has. This would have been more interesting with a branching storyline and multiple endings.

I am infected, starving, constantly being attacked by the plague or thugs. 

I'm contantly trying to fulfill one of my most basic needs just to find out that another one is dropping dangerously. It's like I try to grab something that's in front of me, yet it still slips away from me. 

I feel weak, tired, hopeless and am never satisfied. It feels like no matter what I do, I'm always going to lose. It feels like I'm delaying the inevitable. Every second carries death and life. Every decision matters. 

Every day I tell myself: "it surely can't get any worse than this". 
And every day I stand corrected. 

Keeping myself alive is such a struggle it feels like adding any more challenges to my miserable life would be pure cruelty. 

And oh, there are challenges. There are people. There is an entire town that I have grown to like and care about. And I want to save them all, even though I'm constantly being reminded that this can't and won't be possible. Yet I keep pushing through. I save myself to save the others. Death is inevitable. It's everywhere.

I know I can't save everyone. Yet, somehow, I want to try.

On the POSITIVE side: The graphics are beautiful.  The landscapes are well done and the people actually are life-like and act and speak life-like.  That's really neat and so many games could take a lesson from this.  Ease-of-use things like fast travel are very good and actually helpful.  The map is sorta helpful (though using it is not logical or intuitive, and apparently you can't put your own markers on it so you frequently lose stuff).

On the NEGATIVE SIDE: I literally cannot figure out why it has such high ratings unless they just paid people off to rate it high.  

I had to restart it completely three times before I figured out it was going to kill you several times no matter what you did because you can't see where you are going or what you are doing and it puts you in the stocks and labels you a scoundrel no matter what you try to do.  Seriously, developers ?  Who thought that would be a good idea?

Its terrible! It is a morass of broken quests, bugged tasks, UI quirks and and controls so complicated they are miserable to try and learn.  Trying to use weapons (swords, maces, etc) is ridiculously difficult.  Trying to swing a sword is like a hippopotamus trying to do a toe stand with a ballet pirouette - ridiculous ! Most of the time key presses for weapon action are simply ignored.  Press mouse1 to try and swing the sword and maybe it swings, maybe it doesn't.  Press Mouse2 for block and maybe it blocks, maybe it doesn't.   Most of time you just stand there with your mouth hanging open as people hit you and kill you because you can't use the weapons.  

Little banners and markers on the map frequently to not show like they are supposed to (a bug many have complained about but is NOT fixed still) so you can't tell where in the H you are supposed to go.  

If you finally figure out how to find a bed to sleep, you can't sleep all night -- it will only let you sleep a few hours.  Then you have to just sit and wait for morning or use the Time wheel to just wait and do nothing (that is if you can get the time wheel to work -- its bugged and sometimes just won't turn and you have to restart the game to get it to work).  

Most times when something meaningful happens you lose all your equipment and materials you suddenly have no clothes and no money and that causes people to shun you and yell at you and if you are not careful you'll get arrested and blah blah blah.  I could go on and on but there's no reason -- you get the idea.  And no one is going to listen to the issues anyway.

I may play this some more just to see if they fix the quagmire of bugs, but I seriously doubt I'll ever finish it and I certainly don't recommend it.  What a piece of crap!  DO NOT WASTE YOUR MONEY!!

Stunning visuals (especially for 2007) with a unique theme that combines 1950s culture with 19th century fascination with underwater exploration using contemporary industrial technology (a la 10000 Leagues under the Sea). The world is immersive, and the dark, grimy, aquatic and industrial atmosphere add to the claustrophobic effects that you truly have no idea what crazed maniac is around the corner. The enemy design and dialogue fit the story and horror themes very well.

Regarding the story and level design, the first half was excellent, with Fort Frolic being the peak of how engaging the game could be for the 2 hours you run around this abandoned entertainment district. The 2nd half lost the momentum and magic, with no bosses or enthralling plot points (after the plot twist), and it felt like running around the map.

I played on Normal difficulty and found it too difficult in the middle of the game, where you constantly run out of ammo and eve, and the shotgun Big Daddy can kill you in 2 shots. The 2nd half got gradually easier and easier, where by the end, I barely ever ran out of eve, health, or ammo, no new enemies were introduced, and I had overpowered weapons, plasmids, and upgraded slots.

There's also the stupid pipe puzzle in the game. It's fun the first few times, until you realize you'd have to repeat it every few minutes if you want those small discounts, which I realized isn't even necessary since I kept reaching the money cap. It was so repetitive and frustrating, especially when half the time, the puzzles were literally impossible. Once you get to the 2nd half of the game, you should have more than enough upgraded slots to remove most of the overload and alarm tiles to very easily knock them out of the way.

review_text:
After building a few of everything and exploring what i believe to be every avenue of the game in under 6 hours i found myself very confused by the games popularity. It is the most basic management game I've seen that does virtually nothing to set itself apart from others like it. The two main differences are golems and corruption. You get three flavors of golems, move along. Corruption is tainted land you can do painfully little about because unless you build up the ENTIRE map it doesn't stop spawning things. With those out of the way here's a list of things the game does worse than its' competition.

Your villagers are worse than the stereotypical medieval bumpkin they emulate. They will build a wall to block a chokepoint off, procede to WALK THROUGH the wall they just built, then stand on that side of the wall until they starve to death because pathfinding must not work outside of my build zone. Is the AI meant to do this?

Speaking of the build zone, it is the absolute most infuriating thing in the game. You know how certain games require you to build power lines to connect your buildings? Instead of needing to construct additional pylons because machines need power you have to build a fire every 10 squares. This is a medieval survival game therefore your citizens don't feel safe making a building without being able to feel the warmth of a fire. I say feel the warmth because for whatever reason if you build anything next to a fire it completely blocks off the build zone. Have fun daisy chaining a dozen fires down to the next bottleneck in the terrain, it'l take two days in game to dismantle everything if you didn't put a small fire in the middle of your defensive wall. It feels so gimmicky like it was just thrown there because it seemed like a clever mechanic.

Did you know each of your citizens have an intelligence score? Wow, maybe it's like Rimworld and the smart guys get to be wizards or something! No. They don't. There aren't any non laborer jobs besides being a guard. It's even easier to get them the best armor in the game because you need 3 buildings to do so which are all available from the start. Your citizens are doing the same tasks as the 10+ people next to them for the rest of the game with the only difference being leveling up.

Your free upkeep defensive options are the guards and your basic towers. In order to survive after your first blood moon you need golems and magic towers both of which cost fairy dust. This means the only thing you need to concentrate on after the early game is fairy dust. Que 3 sets of gatherers, refiners, golem makers and watch them slap everyone into your late game. There is no other way to do this, it is a rigid system that requires fairy dust. Even your best guards will die and because you gain people equivilant to a person per day you cannot hope to keep up with the hordes of enemies with any casualty rate. This is not a complaint that you need to do certain things in order to win. This is a complaint that no matter where you set up your village and no matter what the terrain is like and no matter how many times you play it will be the same exact thing over and over. No different units. No different towers. No different maze walls. After your first blood moon its pump fairy dust into metal golems and ballista towers until your bored. There is a clear optimized build that cannot be changed and that means your replayability extends to your second village when you know the controls.

Oh wait theres that god mode element right? Shooting fireballs and bringing back people from the dead? Don't do it. The only thing I used my benevolent powers for was growing crops and spawning holy golems during the blood moon. But in all honesty this feature can be safely and completely ingnored in a successful game. Especially once you realize you can't break the stupid corrupted graveyards with a meteor because.... I don't know. Maybe the corrupted land forms some kind of shield generator into space. In which case I should build on it because my village gets plastered with earthquakes and flaming meteors twice a season while the enemies remain unscathed! It would make sense that as god i smite the enemies of my people right? Or maybe protect them from some calamity like an earthquake? Can i part the river or something? Nope you can use 2 flaming rocks on your own village to help defend against the 20 enemies raiding them. No thanks, I'll stick to making carrots grow, I don't think i'll make much of a difference anyway.

This review is already frightening in length, though much of it could have been overlooked had i not seen the game was released 4 years ago. What in the actual hell is in this game that requires 4 years? Braid took a year to make then the rest of the time was spent on artwork. If anyone reading this has attended a college class or short seminar for game development then you know the first thing they tell you is how hard it is to make it in the industry. The second is that if you want any hope of making a living off your game you have to make it something unique and put some of your own blood into its' creation. There is potential here, but given the time that has already gone into development and how much the game still looks like a horizontal slice I cannot recommend it.

review_text:
Its hard to start a review of Turbo Golf Racing without instantly comparing it to Rocket League. Its obvious that the art style, environmental design, vehicles, cosmetics, and general 'hit the ball with vehicles that have advanced aerial controls' gameplay is trying [i]so[/i] hard to capture that same audience. However, I think there is enough deviation from the 'Rocket League formula' that makes this game stand out well on its own.

Basically, you vs others are racing to get your golf ball in the hole as quick as possible. There are a good amount of variation in the tracks, with high elevation changes and multiple routes to go through. There are also power-ups that can be used to benefit you or hurt your opponents, whether you equip them or pick them up on track. The game is also refined enough that its much more worth it's price vs other early access games. It does still need more work, with its sound design and music being its current weakest point.

So, if you are just looking for a game similar to Rocket League, you aren't going to find it here as this is car golf, not car soccer. However, if you ever wished that Rocket League had a racing mode, this game is for you. I'm hoping this game sees a resurgence once its out of early access, because its just [i]that[/i] fun.

After hours of battling the Pathfinder, I can say it’s the worst-designed final boss ever. 

The game sets you up for tactical combat, but phase 4 flips everything: relentless teleports, the guy spawning behind you, and broken hitboxes make melee feel useless. 

It’s a dodge-focused fight with no decent dodge mechanic—a dark pattern that feels like a cheap trick. 

I beat phases 1-3 and Eliza, so don’t tell me it’s a “skill issue.” 

No i-frames, overwhelming teleport, and heavy RNG reliance break the flow with an absurd difficulty spike. I wanted to uninstall. Such a shame, because the rest of the game was quite solid, but not being able to “finalize it” ruins the experience.

Why on earth is this so childish?  I don't mean the graphics, either... cute graphics work in games.  But that's usually where the kid stuff stops.  But not in this game... it's so adolescent, it's not enjoyable.  

The vast majority of gamers who play games like this are adults.  If you look at games that this is clearly inspired by like Gungeon, those games had cute elements to them but they weren't made for children.

From the story, to the dialogue, to the characters themselves it's like sitting down as a full grown adult by yourself to watch old episodes of blues clues.  It's ridiculous, and I can't imagine how people enjoy that.  It's literally like watching a mediocre children's cartoon, and having to sit through all the characters talking and telling their children's humor jokes.

I get sitting with your kids to watch that stuff, but I cannot imagine why any adult would want to sit on their own time through a game like this that is so clearly out of touch with the age of its primary audience.

The achievement "Good Morning, Time Traveler" is awarded for completing the very first story mission.  5.8% of players have this achievement.  I guess I stuck around for the juvenile stuff longer than 94.2% of people did.

The gameplay is fine, it's actually decent enough if I'm honest.  That can't rescue the game from what it forces you to sit through and listen to, though.   If you can stomach the horrible 7 year old humor, characters, and conversations you may enjoy the game.  I cannot.

review_text:
Beautiful, brutal, and criminally underrated – The Callisto Protocol is a true sci-fi horror gem.

The Callisto Protocol is one of the most underrated games in recent years. Visually, it’s absolutely stunning – the level of detail, lighting, and character models are top-tier. The atmosphere is dense, dark, and oppressive, exactly what you’d want from a sci-fi horror experience.

If you enjoyed Dead Space, you’ll feel right at home here. The sense of isolation, constant tension, and the game’s brilliant sound design all add to the immersion.

The only downside is that it’s relatively challenging – without assists, combat can be unforgiving, but that difficulty makes survival in Black Iron Prison all the more intense and rewarding.

Overall, a highly underrated title that truly deserves a second look – especially for fans of sci-fi horror games in general.

review_text:
"Just because a game is difficult, doesn't mean it's FUN." 

If you know what group I am talking about who like to deflect other games issues when you say that you get the clown emoji's. Not every game is dark souls and yes. I have played EVERY souls game and beaten Elden ring and it's DLC pre-patch. Don't bullsh*t a bullsh*tter.

I will include bulletpoints at the bottom for those with short attention spans.

I have edited this review a couple of times trying to explain how the game has various issues with enemy attack hitboxes or gamefeel where your weapons don't actually get to do more damage they just get things like "Aim at 3 enemies to lock onto them and your bullets will bounce between them for 50% damage and proc a lighting bolt between them every 7 bounces."

The progression doesn't actually make YOU do more damage scaling up. Like you don't slowly get bigger and bigger numbers and there very much is a plateau where you have a damage cap which you have to try and circumvent to mediate enemy spawn clutter in the third (Currently final) map which causes most people once they hit Gnosis 3 to have horrible ammunition and suitability issues.

Gnosis is akin to "Bonfire Asceitic" from DS2. If you know...You know. Enemies get more prevalent and the higher HP and more irritating enemies spawn more frequently. As the dev says "Their HP remains the same no matter the Gnosis." which is true except for Elite enemies which spawn more at higher Gnosis. 


1. You can get more health, potions/estus, stamina to dodge but your guns themselves don't ever get more damage they just get gimmicky "Hold aim and fire at final moment for bonus damage" or "Lock onto 3 enemies and have bullets bounce at 50% damage with an arc of lightning between them every 7 bounces." but the weapons themselves will from start to finish not actually grow in their flat damage.

2. Ammo is a major issue at higher difficulties/Gnosis on the current final map. 

Explanation: 
The enemies are more clustered and the ammo boxes you find spread around said cluster poorly. Meaning if you had a particularly difficult situation where in your attempt to be mobile and avoid getting swarmed you ended up backing into another group, and another group, and ended up with a "Horde issue" and can very easily run out of ammo before you make it to an actual ammo box. There are purchasable consumable ammo pouches but those are limited you can hold per run and don't fully fill your ammo.

3. You become reliant on gimmick combos of weapons and spells later on. While this seems like a continuation of #1 this one is about "Fun" so understand that that joyful feeling of "I HAVE FINISHED FARMING AND I AM HERE TO CLEAR" you can get with RPG's is completely absent. This can limit your enjoyment pretty severely.

4. Stamina for sprinting and dodge are tied but you lose stamina from being hit, using a certain sniper rifle, and dodging repeatedly VERY QUICKLY. This makes you move slower, easier to get chain-hit, and unable to dodge until you have enough stamina to fill one dodge. This making the situation scale far worse against you depending on being swarmed.

5. Enemy melee hitboxes are wack and have about 6 more feet to hit than they should. Their bullets and spells are on point but melee is awful.

6. Snipers are useless. There is a chargable basic rfifle that can out-damage snipers and has near 2.5 times the ammo when you max it. There is also a sniper which to use causes your stamina to drain aka your dodge which is a terrible idea when to aim you usually want to be still for a moment which can already be impossible if swarmed. All in all from difficulty finding windows to scope in to their terrible ammo pool and mediocre gimmicks for upgrades they get binned pretty quickly.

7. Spells don't feel good. They do not have damage themselves and you can't go around being a wizard with a gun as secondary if you now what I mean. The spells work as stuns or debuffs or even a sort of "Totem" radiating damage if you follow it's mechanic but you don't ever just throw a big ass fireball and kill a group of enemies or call down a thunderstorm to cover an area. They feel truly secondary to guns and if you were wanting that spells OR guns then this game is very much not for you.

8. Game poorly explains it's own mechanics (Beyond weapons/trinkets/spells) and a lot is in text when to the gameplay junky can get skipped in thinking they will look at it later...Which if you skip because you just want more gameplay can end up with you upgrading Gnosis too early and making the game far less fun for you by upping it's difficulty (More spawns, less ammo, difficulty unique enemies and elites) before you finish upgrading weapons, spells, and trinkets before tackling them.

9. Upgrades/Boons for clearling a skull AKA a cluster of enemies feel insignificant outside of 3 which are reload speed, firing speed for not automatic fire, and what amounts to a "Glass cannon" perk.

10. The "GTA STARS" mechanic built into the game which can occur while fighting for your life can easily overwhelm you in the third map requiring you to use an item to reduce it which defeats the point of it really being there once you have it and makes it incredibly frustrating to deal with..Tiresome specifically, and should you forget and not have a way out means that the run can be essentially over as you can be low on ammo, health, or potions and have no way out to deal with what that event spawns and attacks you with.

11. Ultimately there isn't much here. For a roguelike the growth is limited and again with damage growth essentially capped you can never overtake the game and "Bully the bullies" like you can with roguelikes in general. You end up seeing the same enemies after a while and with the same 2 weapons, 2 spells, and 2 trinkets you end up growing bored.

12. Early access is not an excuse for dull or frustrating gameplay. Community currently is trying to jingle that in front of you like a pair of keys to a toddler to distract your from an otherwise dull game when you finish upgrading gear.

It's 3 maps for nearly 40$ and about 14 guns 8 trinkets, 8 small spells and 7 big spells. I am 28 hours in and I have hit the point where my frustration and boredom have met and I just do not want to continue and the grind to upgrade your gear can be asinine. "Kill 125 enemies with this gun" to upgrade becomes tedious very early when a map before upgrading Gnosis has like 25 enemies on the first map and like 45 on the second. (You need gnosis 2 to get to the third map)

It is not worth your time as of current.

I played this game much later in its life span, so I missed its “glory days.” What I experienced was a game very much of its time, with all the hallmarks, and frustrations, of games from that era. The pacing didn’t match how I personally like to play; the story didn’t develop in a way that kept me engaged at my pace, and the world, full of collectables and exploration, sometimes felt tedious. Inventory limits meant I could carry 500 spoons but struggle with more practical items, which highlighted the game’s focus on immersion and depth rather than streamlined action.

Looking back, my frustration came less from the game failing and more from my own expectations. This isn’t a twitch shooter; it’s a deep RPG emphasizing exploration, and by design, it rewards patience and curiosity. While it may not have aligned with my play style, it’s undeniably a well-crafted game. My reaction is more about the conflict between my current perspective and how I imagine I would have enjoyed it at the time, rather than an indictment of the game itself. In short: it’s good, just not for me.

review_text:
I wanted to recommend this game; I really did. 

A lot can be said about Scorn. It's visuals are stunning, the art direction is uniquely horrifying, the puzzles were simple yet compelling, and it's atmosphere is one of a kind. I have never played a game quite like it. I felt that the inventory system was immersive, and it seemed like the game knew exactly what it wanted to accomplish. It didn't overstay it's welcome (literally).

Now, reading that above, I could understand why you - the reader - may be mildly confused to why I don't recommend this game. I'll be honest; Scorn is an okay game, but it still left so much to be desired.

I feel for the people who have followed this project since it's conception. I didn't learn about Scorn until late 2021, so I didn't wait in anticipation for 8 long years for its release. Although I enjoyed this game, I felt like the game doesn't deserve a $40 price tag. Even at the 10% off price that I bought it, I still felt like I was a bit scammed out of $35. I can't believe that the deluxe version is $50! Yes, the art direction of the game was fantastic, but the level design was quite poor in multiple areas. There were a few times were I found myself getting turned around in the linear labyrinth that is Scorn. Just because you make the area look good doesn't mean you throw level design out the window. On top of that, the combat was lackluster, the "boss fight" (if you want to call it that) at the end of the game was slightly frustrating, and the overall fun factor of the game was relatively low.

Sure, make a cool art horror experience, but maybe if it's gonna be 5 - 6 hours long make it about $15 - $20 cheaper? 

TL;DR - Get Scorn on a Summer/Winter Steam Sale; otherwise it's not worth it and overall disappointing for the price.

review_text:
First off, I love a lot of aspects of this game, but I struggle to see myself finishing a year due to some issues I have with it. Those issue ended up piling up enough that I just wasn't having fun with the game. It kind of just became a chore.

- Firstly, The death mechanic. Literally every day until the middle of my first summer was filled with either a holiday, a funeral or one of the two weddings that I saw. After the second week, most of the characters I had talked to were already dead, lol. This kind of crushed any desire to get to know anyone else going forward, knowing that they just die almost immediately. I made it almost to Fall, and that trend seems to just keep going with maybe a week or two between waves of death. Maybe I'm just unlucky?

- Second, Your characters movement speed is just insanely slow and a lot of the areas are designed to make you need to walk a long way through mostly empty paths (The mine, limbo, etc). I genuinely don't understand this design decision, as it just makes me want to do less in the game. Should i go to the mine? Nah, I really don't want to spend 3 minutes IRL walking one way just to get 2 iron. Should I go to limbo? But those stairs...

- Third, There is no automated watering mechanic. We have mermaids and witches and ghosts, but no irrigation? wtf? 

- Fourth, Can't see NPCs on map. This became an issue due to having so many NPCs dying that I couldn't keep up with who lived where. You can go into the village menu and scroll through all of the villagers, but with everyone being swapped out every few weeks, it is hard to keep up with who is who.

- Fifth, Family members/NPCs are not smart enough to just go get medicine when they are sick. You end up kind of having to babysit them.

- Sixth, NPCs being unreachable for long periods of time. There were multiple times where I took a mission for an NPC, only to have them either gone in the woods, or unreachable in the lighthouse until the mission timed out. Quests for NPCs who are not reachable should at least be put on pause while they are gone.

- Lastly, Friends and marriage. I don't understand how it is possible to do some of the limbo quests like making 20 friends without entirely disabling several of the game mechanics. Virtually my entire village has died twice over. How am I supposed to make friends with someone when they only live for like a month?

Towards the end of my playtime, I ended up adding unlimited speed potions for myself (Only using them for myself, not to make money) and this made the game so much more enjoyable. I wish that they would add a few quality of life things to the game, or just to options. 

Overall, I don't dislike this game, but several of the issues I mentioned just ended up making it kind of unfun for me.

review_text:
2/10

After playing for hours to finish both parts, what was I rewarded with? An awful, awful ending of an awfully outdrawn, tragic and depressing story. I mean, who came up with the idea of making an otome-game set in the paradigm shift between the Shoguns and Samurai and the rapid implementation of modern Western-warfare? War is depressing enough; war between an underwhelmingly small force armed with sticks and swords and an overwhelmingly large army armed with the time's most advanced and modern weaponry - that's just cruel and brutal. So if that's what they were going for, they did a really good job at making you feel inferior, constantly, and hopeless. Yes, the devs made an otome game into a horrific take on micro skirmishes, which are undoubtedly the most brutal occurances in war, and they made your character - and the guy you like - a part of it.

Going into the game, I expected there to be charming Samurai and perhaps a touch of the occult, seeing as some of the screenshots of part 2 depicts vampire-esque behavior. I expected there to be a lot of characters and a compelling story for each of them with plenty of ups and downs - with at least one happy ending for each of them. I didn't demand more, just one good ending to satisfy my vicarious, "guilty pleasure"-urge. However, for the guy I chose, there wasn't, and all throughout the playthrough, people died left to right, both major and minor characters. Sometimes, they just were killed, while sometimes, they commited "honorable suicide". Every time, there was nothing but a passing mention of it, with no impact on the "chosen" storyline or your character.

Also, the female MC. She was awful. Awful! Personality like your frugal grandma's sixty-year-old dishrag and with as much activity in her brain as a goldfish with an extra chromosome or two. She was unbearably frustrating, like a young cousin you're tasked to take care of during a family gathering just because she's a young and cute and adorable. I seriously wanted to grab her and shake her to see if at least coins would fall out of her ears. Alas, I couldn't, but if this crap was in VR, you know I'd grab a baseball bat and smack myself until I, too, became as vapid and insipid as her, if only to escape her painfully suffocating wallflower personality. Fortunately and unfortunately, she didn't have very much to say, but practically just stood there, watching the men, being "supportive" and "down-to-earth" and "lovable" at times. *shudder*

The "bachelors" are the best thing about the game, as should be. The voice actors are top-notch, and some of them really carry the overall performance, eliciting emotion within me. But they're not nearly given enough screen time, and the choices you have to pick to win their favor is incredibly--no, ridiculously vague. I'm serious, the choices you must make to increase your relationship with a certain guy are so random and bland: a good example is when you have to choose between either seeking out the men, fleeing on your own or staying where you are. Now, do any of these choices say anything at all about the man they're connected to? No! This game must be either savescummed or played with a walkthrough - there is no intuitiveness or clever game design where you can sort of figure out what guy would prefer a certain choice. I'd recommend looking up a guide and having it right next to you, or else it will take you more than double the time to finish the game, and most likely, you will have ended up on the completely wrong dude's path. 

What with 12 guys to choose from, there are just way too many characters. Side characters and antagonists that just appear for a single or a few scenes - only to disappear and never be heard from or mentioned again. I get that the devs want you to replay the game through its many endings and character paths on where you can meet and learn more about these random people, but the romance is just not good enough for that dedication to be warranted. And though the devs managed to build quite a cast and a sort of emotional resonance with some of the guys in which their personalities really showed, they throw all of it away in plot turns from hell and abrupt character death. It's like GoT before the scriptwriters decided fanservice was more important than a compelling and unique story.

Although the writing is rather average in both a good and bad way, there were a few times when I laughed or reacted in a "nice one" or "ahaaa!" way. Though, that might have just been because my brain was putrefying under the duress of roleplaying our female MC's astronomical IQ level. You won't find any gems here, and the translation quality varies at times. Knowing a bit of Japanese myself, there are discrepancies at times. None too damaging, except for one that practically ruined the "sweet tender confession moment" at the end of the storyline since he already had told this empy coconut-head of an MC that he loved her. There's also this weird dissonance between the time that passes in these transition slides and what the MC narrates. It won't be game-breaking, but it will be frustrating and break immersion.

And now, the story. The guy I chose was the gorgeous, hard-shelled and relenteless leader of the merry band of wannabe-samurai. I just can't resist guys like that, and I don't think any female really can (though I will say, he got uncomfortably verbally abusive at times). The story was alright during the first game: there was mystery, intrigue, several factions that plotted against each other, all against this historical backdrop - with a hint of the occult. Not only was the story in the second part incredibly boring, drawn-out and uninteractive, I didn't at all feel connected to the guy until the very last day - to only have that happiness (or at least satisfaction, because trust me, I wasn't at all happy when the two characters got together after excrutiating hours of conversations about war and politics with names you forget as soon as they mention them) ripped away. You also feel just like an observer most of the time, with no proactiveness of your own, and your character barely reacts when they finally find their missing father, whom they have been searching for for years.

This is a visual novel, yes, and technically an otome with surprisingly much blood and swearing. However, if you're looking for that rush in your system when the two main characters interact, and the gradual climax of a relationship, you're looking at the wrong game. I bought both games for 6 euro, so it wasn't that damaging, especially since the voice acting, again, is nothing short of incredible. And there's this fun silly atmosphere with an accompaning banter that you can expect from this tight-knitted group of samurai/childhood friends, which you can bask in at rare occasions. So if you've got the money and time, and this thing is on at least 85% sale, sure, go for it. Enjoy. But do not expect to indulge.

Play Cinderella Phenomenon or Amnesia: Memories instead. The first one is free and the second one is half the price of this first part. And though Amnesia: Memories is nowhere as complex in terms of worldbuilding as this game, it excels at romance and chemistry between you (the player), the MC and the male interest - which is what otome games should do.

------------
Update:

After finishing some more playthroughs, I'm bumping up the score to 6/10. When I wrote the review originally, I was just so freshly heartbroken and furious that I spent so much time and emotional investment into what ended up being the worst relationship progression and ending of them all. I've still not played through all the bachelors, but I will give credit where credit is due. Saito, Iba, Sakamoto and Kazama are great - my two favorites being Iba and Sakamoto. Save these for last.

I would still not recommend for you to buy this game unless it's on ~85% sale, something that should occur during Steam winter/summer/Black Friday sales.

most likely , you will have ended up on the completely wrong dude ' s path . what with 12 guys to choose from , there are just way too many characters . side characters and antagonists that just appear for a single or a few scenes - only to disappear and never be heard from or mentioned again . i get that the devs want you to replay the game through its many endings and character paths on where you can meet and learn more about these random people , but the romance is just not good enough for that dedication to be warranted . and though the devs managed to build quite a cast and a sort of emotional resonance with some of the guys in which their personalities really showed , they throw all of it away in plot turns from hell and abrupt character death . it ' s like got before the scriptwriters decided fanservice was more important than a compelling and unique story . although the writing is rather average in both a good and bad way , there were a few times when i laughed or reacted in a nice one or ahaaa ! way . though , that might have just been because my brain was putrefying under the duress of roleplaying our female mc ' s astronomical iq level . you won ' t find any gems here , and the translation quality varies at times . knowing a bit of japanese myself , there are discrepancies at times . none too damaging , except for one that practically ruined the sweet tender confession moment at the end of the storyline since he already had told this empy coconut-head of an mc that he loved her . there ' s also this weird dissonance between the time that passes in these transition slides and what the mc narrates . it won ' t be game-breaking , but it will be frustrating and break immersion . and now , the story . the guy i chose was the gorgeous , hard-shelled and relenteless leader of the merry band of wannabe-samurai . i just can ' t resist guys like that , and i don ' t think any female really can ( though i will say , he got uncomfortably verbally abusive at times ) . the story was alright during the first game there was mystery , intrigue , several factions that plotted against each other , all against this historical backdrop - with a hint of the occult . not only was the story in the second part incredibly boring , drawn-out and uninteractive , i didn ' t at all feel connected to the guy until the very last day - to only have that happiness ( or at least satisfaction , because trust me , i wasn ' t at all happy when the two characters got together after excrutiating hours of conversations about war and politics with names you forget as soon as they mention them ) ripped away . you also feel just like an observer most of the time , with no proactiveness of your own , and your character barely reacts when they finally find their missing father , whom they have been searching for for years . this is a visual novel , yes , and technically an otome with surprisingly much blood and swearing . however , if you ' re looking for that rush in your system when the two main characters interact , and the gradual climax of a relationship , you ' re looking at the wrong game . i bought both games for 6 euro , so it wasn ' t that damaging , especially since the voice acting , again , is nothing short of incredible . and there ' s this fun silly atmosphere with an accompaning banter that you can expect from this tight-knitted group of samurai/childhood friends , which you can bask in at rare occasions . so if you ' ve got the money and time , and this thing is on at least 85% sale , sure , go for it . enjoy . but do not expect to indulge . play cinderella phenomenon or amnesia memories instead . the first one is free and the second one is half the price of this first part . and though amnesia memories is nowhere as complex in terms of worldbuilding as this game , it excels at romance and chemistry between you ( the player ) , the mc and the male interest - which is what otome games should do . ------------ update after finishing some more playthroughs , i ' m bumping up the score to 6/10 . when i wrote the review originally , i was just so freshly heartbroken and furious that i spent so much time and emotional investment into what ended up being the worst relationship progression and ending of them all . i ' ve still not played through all the bachelors , but i will give credit where credit is due . saito , iba , sakamoto and kazama are great - my two favorites being iba and sakamoto . save these for last . i would still not recommend for you to buy this game unless it ' s on ~85% sale , something that should occur during steam winter/summer/black friday sales .

[h1]tl;dr[/h1]
I really wanted to like this game.

[h1]PROS[/h1]
+ GREAT concept (akin to the Omen)
+ Well-crafted map layout

[h1]CONS[/h1]
- This game WILL crash on you. 
- Limited storyline that starts strong and then disappears
- Poor voice acting and sound design
- Linear, point-and-click puzzle game masquerading as a 3rd-person adventure game
- No variability in mission-completion pathways (there is only one way to complete each mission)
- Unstable and buggy AI interaction that breaks immersion completely
- Limited mission-guidance results in aimless walking around and clicking on everything around until the path becomes obvious
- Limited to no player agency -- point and click your way to the next goofy cut-scene.

I cannot recommend this game. Once the novelty wears off, this game quickly becomes [u]not fun[/u].  I played through the first six missions and decided that my time was worth more to me than to spend any more of it on a game which I kept hoping would be better.

review_text:
Worst of the series. The writers did not have a consistent story they wanted to tell and took too long to say it. The central theme is "dreams" and people chasing them, but they could not tie them together in the 11th hour without throwing in nonsensical twists.

All in all, if you are a fan of this series, you're probably going to play it on your way through the series, but just mainline it. The payoff is not worth the toil. Spoilers below:

[spoiler]
Kiryu's Part:
His part was fine. The setup is okay for the central plot. Daigo is missing (again) and Kiryu is in the middle of an Omi-Tojo problem. Unfolds pretty good. Watase is rad.

Saejima's Part:
They didn't know what they were doing with him. Same plotline we got in 4. Saejima is forced to go to prison again and have prison shenanigans... again. Dream sequence, snowmobiles, and a giant bear fight lead to a hunting minigame that can be ignored. Baba is rad.

Haruka's Part:
Park gaslights and projects her dream onto Haruka in a trauma-dump for 15 minutes before getting killed offscreen. The man responsible (Ogita the dance instructor) proceeds to come back to the scene of the crime to find the mcguffin letter only to throw the idol company's secretary off the roof in the same fashion with no serious damage done to him. While it is understood that Yakuza doesn't know how firearms work, it can now be stated that Yakuza doesn't understand how falling from the roof of a five-story building works. Also if the big-bad Kurosawa was acting as a cop, why wouldn't he use the opportunity of a closed crime scene to search Dynachair for the letter?

Akiyama's Part:
If Akiyama isn't on screen for more than a minute, all the other characters should ask each other "where's Akiyama?"

Shinada's Part:
Baseball man realizes that baseball is a dirty sport run by crime people fifteen years later. His loanshark boyfriend is cool and he punches Daigo in the face. He's alright, but his relevance to the central plot seems weak.

Finale:
I tend to go through as much of the content as I can, but when I dump a dozen hours into Haruka's part, grinding her abilities to be the best idol I can be only to see her banned to cutscene dimension in the finale is unacceptable. Aizawa being the big bad is stupid. Kurosawa has no thought out plan. Daigo sucks. Finale boss is a damage sponge that regens his health. Haruka once again ends a Yakuza game with a dying Kiryu in her arms. Yume yume yume. Dream dream dream. [/spoiler]

review_text:
Feels more like John Carpenter's Escape From New York than most superhero movies or traditional comicbook plots. If you've seen most superhero games or films you know that's probably for the best, but the plot itself is still pretty dumb. Batman has zero charisma, so why he even has lines I don't know. He sounds like a moron.

There's one important caveat I need to mention since nobody ever criticizes this game's combat, and judging from the forums, blindly defend this game no matter what. Spamming the counter attack button can wipe out a crowd of seven guys without suffering any damage to yourself. You don't even have to face them to counter, rendering the first few hours a complete joke. 

The worst part of the game is that the melee combat system also has an annoying auto-targeting system which means you aren't guaranteed to hit the person you're aiming at. There are moments you will be confused as you fly across the screen to hit someone you didn't see, sapping all the joy or sense of accomplishment out of the game. Of all the games that copied this fighting system, THEY ALL DID IT BETTER. Button prompts in the middle of fight just gets old after a couple hours. To simply hit a guy on the ground you need a special combo move, just to clutter combat up even further. Later you'll have to remember about twenty individual buttons/combinations just to progress. 

The combat in this game is garbage but the controls are just as bad, a bad port from consoles. Because sprint, climb, and roll are all one key, you'll often do random moves you weren't intending or be twirling around a wall when you want to climb over it, kind of like in Assassin's Creed. The controls and gadget selector are all clunky and overly complicated, requiring you to hold down multiple buttons just to do one simple task. Why? 

The game has decent stealth, but the platforming is drudgery and boss fights can be pretty laborious bs. I've tried playing this three times to see if I was missing something, and each time I hate it more as I see more of its flaws.

review_text:
Lucius could have been a great game. It could have been gruesome horror  fun but man... It's an absolute mess of a game.

- Story is as cookie cutter as they come. They pretty much picked up everything from the "Omen" series there's nothing new or interesting done here.
- Linear to a fault
- Controls that feel stiff and unresponsive
- I was constantly struggling to grasp what I'm supposed to do almost at all times.
- The powers are as cliche as they come: Mind control, Telekinesis, Pyrokinesis and there is a WHOLE SLOT in your powers list dedicated to what ultimately adds up to a simple Use button. Yes you have to choose USE first and then you can use stuff or open doors. When is this game from? 1986?!
- Gameplay Does NOTHING to differ itself from better, more revolutionary games in the genre (e.g. Messiah). To be frank, it's quite a miracle the game runs at all.
- It's janky and ugly but plus side is that the manor itself is a cool place to hang out in for a while
- Boring in every conceivable way
- Not even in the "so bad it's funny" gamut of titles out there (e.g. Goat Simulator). It's just a plain bad game that feels super dated and the gameplay is boring and too linear to have any real fun with.

Props to the music composer though some nice tunes in the menus and during gameplay. Voice acting is also kind of OK for a "B-horror" (or more like D-horror) game like this.

review_text:
The best way that I can describe this game is instant regret. This game's developers appear to be from the community of another game called The Isle. Some of their devs were apparently admins on an old isle server called Rogue Realism. I suspect it is because of these people and the biased opinions that they formed from the other game that makes this game such trash. In my opinion the game is extremely unpolished, clunky, chock full of bugs, and heavily in favor of the carnivore faction. It makes the same mistakes of Isle Legacy where a$$riding is the favoured mode of combat. 

The combat is cartoonishly bad and the animations are janky and unrealistic. The balance is so bad that a single male lion can stun lock an animal like a rhino with slappy paws and shred through an adult elephant like its skin is made of paper. The devs have an unrealistic view of carnivores and seem to think that a single male lion should be able to stack up 10 pile high bodies of elephants. Realistically, the only animal capable of doing that irl are humans with guns. If we take a look at realistic hunting rates, which the devs try to use to claim to back up their bias, the lion has a relatively low success rate when compared with other carnivores as referenced here: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/hunting-success-rates-how-predators-compare/

The game seems to be a shallow attempt at making playable african animals with minimal effort all for the sake of profit, while being a time sink with no true goal outside of that fact. Save yourself some time and money and treat yourself to something nice instead. This is probably one of the worst purchase's I've ever made and I regret everything. How they managed to take what seemed like such a cool concept and then botch it this badly is beyond me. In conclusion, I'd recommend not touching this game or its seemingly biased shady devs with a 10 foot pole.

review_text:
[i]Unique.

Adjective: being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else.
Particularly remarkable, special, or unusual.
Belonging or connected to one particular person, group, or place.

.....

"Belonging or connected".....

Connections.... Lines.... 

"Emshen"... He who sees the Lines... Draws the Lines... Makes connections.[/i]

.

When I started Pathologic 2, I thought I was playing the role of the character Artemy Burakh, and I took for granted the notion that this was a "role-playing game", and could affect a certain level of control over the world I was inhabiting by means of the choices I made--choices that were, as a surgeon, very literally matters of life and death... But eventually, I learned that even a doctor administering treatment to the sick (though he may very well determine whether his patient lives or dies) is still subject to the [i]Lines.
 
.

A line is a path, a direction, a singular course. From past to future, from here to there...

A line connects all points having a specified common property

A line is the precise demarcation of a boundary, a notional limit, a way of thinking...[/i]

.

He performs surgery by the very act of cutting [i]Lines[/i] into a body: Should he perform his Lines well, he will be known to the Steppe folk as [i]Emshen[/i]--"Knower of Lines"--or he can (both literally and figuratively) [i]butcher them[/i]. The Steppe folk have a word for this too: [i]Yargachin[/i]. It designates Artemy by his profession as a surgeon, but the word also means "butcher", as in, someone who simply cuts up the meat of a living being. And so the the distinction is made between cutting haphazardly into meat and performing surgery.
 
[i]A Line is drawn.[/i]

It's not an accident that the word chosen to refer the player's path (i.e. the [i]Line[/i] one follows through the unfolding of events)--is the very same word used to refer to an actor's dialogue within a theatrical production.

It turns out that Pathologic 2 is indeed a role-playing game, but only in the same way that an actor in a stage production also [i]plays a role[/i]: He has no real say in the unfolding of the events of the play, nor even in his own part therein, but he is nonetheless given the opportunity to embody the character and give expression to his part.

[i]Try not to butcher your Lines, Yargachin...[/i]

This, ultimately, is the lesson of Pathologic 2. In fact, this is the explicitly-stated philosophical underpinning of the entire game. The developers even tell you this directly through the fourth wall, via the character of Mark Immortell, the stage director. He literally tells you these things to your face--repeatedly, in fact, every time you die--but it wasn't until I had already sunk several dozen hours into the game before I fully considered the scope of what his words meant: that no matter what I did or what I said, the outcome would always be the same; that although I could not [i]overcome[/i] death, or [i]transcend[/i] it, I could [i]achieve mastery over it.[/i] The difference between performing surgery and cutting haphazardly into meat. 

[i].

He who follows the Lines needs not know of their existence; his path is still preordained.

The play remains the same. The role of an actor remains the same.
 
All he can do... is know the Lines.[/i]

.

Initially, I was disappointed with the lack of agency I had while playing, particularly when it came to dialogue interactions. I would save, enter into dialogue with a character, and come out of the interaction feeling like the choices I had made and the things I had said had produced a tangible outcome in the world. But when I would reload my file, re-enter the same conversation, and choose different dialogue options, I would [i]produce the exact same outcome[/i]. It bothered me that what we said to each other ultimately had no effect on what we did. It felt like what would otherwise be a source of agency, or even a system to be gamed in order to produce a desired outcome, was actually completely ineffectual.

Upon reflection, I'm not sure this is such a bad thing... Much of the game seems poised to instill a sense of futility; why should the dialogue sequences be any different? After all, the people who inhabit the world of Pathologic lie to you and mislead you and distract you with all kinds of wild goose chases and false promises.... So why should I believe that anything I could say could really make a difference here? Maybe this is the developer's commentary on the emptiness of words and the primacy of action; a slap in the face of players who believed that they could simply achieve their goals by assembling the right combination of utterances, the fools (like me) who tried to phrasemonger themselves into a happy ending...

It is through painstaking realizations such as this that Pathologic forces everyone it comes into contact with to re-evaluate their preconceived notions of what it means to play a video game.

[i]What even is a game?[/i]
 
At its most fundamental level, a game is just a closed system of variables with which players can interact in order to achieve a win state. Pathologic 2 fulfills this description, of course, but it is [i]so[/i] much more than that. On the surface, the system of variables that Pathologic employs are primarily immersive sim-style survival mechanics: Your character needs to eat, sleep, and take medicine when sick. This system is absolutely "gamed", but it is also simultaneously working on a deeper level: Pathologic uses these game elements as vehicles to force the player into simulating extreme, even apocalyptic survival situations. The moral weight of these situations are treated with an incredible level of acuity: Questions of the soul, morality, violence, trauma, desperation, perseverance, authority, truth... these are the real preoccupations of Pathologic 2.

I know what you're thinking: A walking simulator that's more concerned with getting the player to philosophize than to actually play a game sounds heavy-handed and pretentious as hell.
 
[i]But it isn't.[/i]
 
The game isn't pretentious, or pompous, or blowing hot air. Not even a little bit. In fact, much the opposite. It is frequently tongue-in-cheek, and well aware of its own absurdity. It asks only that the player make decisions and then deal with the consequences... or, worse yet, to reckon with the fact that the decisions they made had absolutely no effect whatsoever on the outcome.

I'm finalizing this review on the 10th of July, 2024--a full year after having last played Pathologic 2. And yet, I continue to think about this game. I'm writing this right now because, even 12 months later, I [i]can't help[/i] but think about it. It is completely unlike anything else within the gaming world, whether digital or tabletop, and has left an indelible mark upon me. Pathologic 2 is a work of art. It elevates video gaming as a form. 

It is completely unequaled in the world of video games for a work to be so high-minded and philosophically ambitious; to directly inform the player of its lofty goals through the fourth wall, and then achieve said goals in spectacular fashion.
 
Pathologic 2 is totally distinct among its peers.

A singular experience.

[i]Unique.[/i]

review_text:
I will keep it simple, because the game severely needs to revise some of its content, but there's no point in going into detail when the problems are very easy to solve.

- First, make proper accesibiltiy options. Some of us don't have 20/20 vision. I can't see shit, especially when there are opaque poison clouds, camera shaking and even the environment itself obstructing my view. Half of the time I get attacked, I don't even know how or where it comes from even when it's in front of me. Just put an aura around enemies that highlight them and make the damage compass work frontward too and that's it, easy as that.

- Second, add projectile fall-off damage for enemies too. Some of the maps in the game are so open, you can get caught by dozens of enemies that can do full damage from so far away (unlike you, since you have limited range), you can't possibly manage them all, and with how skittish stamina is, continously dashing or running away may not be a solution.

- Third, the previous one brings me to my next point. Once, while immersed in one of those absurd large-scale fights, I was ultimately killed by a Creeper from a 200m away because it summoned a red sun I couldn't destroy... because it was behind a leafless tree that constantly blocked my shots because it had an invisible wall between its branches. FIX. YOUR. HITBOXES.

- Four, better documentation. Put an in-game wiki that fills up with more information about each enemy/event/challenge/mechanic the more we encounter them. That would solve 90% of all the problems regarding intentional or unintentional obfuscation of information. I'm tired of having to look everything up because there's not even an attempt at explaining a single bit of what to do.

I'm really mad because the core gameplay loop is great, and so are the aesthetics, ambience, music, sound design and so on. But there are just so many odd game design choices that break the experience.

review_text: Really good. Glad to see the dev really branch out this time and probably reach a larger audience with options for casual and hardcore players alike. I think I own all of the games this guy has made unless there was something before WTTG. But this is the first one I'm actually playing for more than five minutes before deciding I'd rather not poop my pants and just go watch a YouTuber play instead. You are still very much in danger, but (without spoiling the mechanics I believe I have down so far) each death seems fair and explainable, which in turn makes you feel like you are learning how to combat your enemies instead of just getting frustrated. (Except for the one time I got sniped in the bedroom even though there was absolutely no angle to make such a shot, I think I know why, but I'm still going to keep this mechanic spoiler free). The main goal of the game, which others have already pointed out is like Observation Duty, is also much more interesting and fun to me then looking for hidden keys on websites in my opinion. Overall I think it's great, I'm glad to see this dev is still making games, I thought the final game from Reflect was going to be Rides with Strangers, so either I was mistaken, or he has decided to continue on developing. I sincerely hope that future games after this also continue the same trend of appealing to all horror players instead of the hardest of the hardcore. Scrutinized showed a step in that direction, and Dead Signal has brought it where it needed to be in order to be accessible to all. Great work Adam, people love your style, myself included, and the world that you have built with everything interconnecting. I think the key, which you must already be well aware of, is that this world feels grounded in reality. There's no ghosts, or wizards, or impossible experiments gone wrong. Each game feels like it could potentially happen to a person who was just in the worst place at the worst time, while being involved with the wrong things. The only thing all these characters lack is the common sense to call the police, but hey, if that was the case there would be no game.

A 2025 REVIEW 

I didn't play this on launch but I have heard it was rough - unsurprising knowing the brass at Krafton and the state of the industry as a whole. 

However, I bought this on sale, because I was craving more Dead Space - and that is more or less what I got. Didn't pay much attention to marketing or post-launch press, just bought it because it was cheap. And I had a pretty good time, and would like to share this positive sentiment for others to see. 

It's not a full on clone of Dead Space, but it keeps the most important parts of DS alive - the vibes, and weighty combat. I'm not a massive fan of the melee focus, but its serviceable enough. TCP even seems to forget that it's meant to be a melee game with the way that guns are provided, ammo supplied, and the enemy composition encourages gun use. If you're not hot on the melee, guns are viable permanently after the 5h mark - which is roughly half of the campaign. you can play the way you want for more than half of the game which I appreciated. 

The presentation and worldbuilding are absolutely stellar, it's a crying shame this game flopped and left the public sour, because a sequel could and would correct many of the issues that elevate this from a 6/7 out of 10 to an 8/9. 

I do like the more cinematic approach to survival horror/SH-like games, it feels intimate and appropriate for the story attempting to be told. Unfortunately it does mean QTEs, but they're not as egregious in TCP as they were in other AAA games from 2010-2015. 

Overall, since the Dead Space 1 reboot exists, this is definitely a second rate product in comparison. But I believe it is good, and I couldn't recommend it enough at the price I paid for it - if you see this game at the price of $30 or less it's worth every penny. I hope the more recent critical praise around the internet grants this game "cult classic" status and they get Glen & Co back to make TCP2. I'll probably buy the expansion when it goes on sale, will update this review after I play that. But I expect more good things.

review_text:
Good with some caveats.

To be clear, I love that this game was made. I enjoy tactical games and am fascinated by Japanese culture and history. Clearly the developers enjoyed designing the levels and characters of the game and overall the production and attention to detail is admirable. I initially thought this was going to be a game I come back to over and over again but after a few levels it was clear this wasn't going to be the case.

Pros: Level designs are all different, mostly interesting and populated with various guards and enemies. Some tactical planning and quick thinking/execution is required to excel at the game. Production is well done. Story is serviceable and fits the characters and setting, if not surprising or deep.

Cons: It feels more like a puzzle game than a tactical game. If you've played the hitman mobile games you'll know what I'm talking about. You have some freedom but the options to distract and sneak by are limited. Memorizing/anticipating guard movements is key, which is not inherently bad, but it gets monotonous, because that is what you'll be doing the entire time. Distract guards, sneak by, kill: Repeat. Coordinating attacks with different characters does feel rewarding and there is some decent tension created in a well timed combo. However, the controls are just awkward enough for you to be stressed out about them just as much as the samurai you know are about to turn a corner.

Verdict: Overall I liked the game and would recommend it.... but only at a discount. I like the setting and the blending of genres. It really isn't as much of a tactical game as I would have liked, though the elements are there. The guard vision puzzles are the meat of the game and lost some of their luster about half-way through. But there is enough variety with your characters to make solving the puzzles fun and satisfying.
