The developers then decided to spice it up by adding combat... giving you weapons that have sluggish fire rates and take a handful of shots to take down a single enemy. The pacing of this game is way too slow and the maps themselves are confusing and have no guide what so ever so that game is literally a combination of choosing random hallways to walk down and hoping you don't run into any enemies just because you don't want to have to deal with the combat.

Edit: looked it up and apparently you actually aren't even supposed to engage the enemies. The game is designed where the enemies are tough to kill so you just leave them alone and they will literally just leave and walk away. So I take back the part about the devs adding combat to spice up the already super boring game

review_text:
Are you a casual player who likes to beat singleplayer games with overwhelming power?

Are you a PvP-focused player who likes to theorycraft builds while precisely managing economy and randomized upgrades?

If yes to either, there's something here for you. Do be aware that the PvE portion of the game is quite easy to beat on most settings, but that's also not the point. Its easy if you maximize your current power, but there's incentives in place to handle the PvE as lightly as possible while you bank resources for a huge power spike late in the run. Because if you do, you'll be more competitive in the post-run asynchronous PvP.

Also, be aware there is a non-trivial unlock system that may put you at a disadvantage for awhile (~20 runs?), and a PvP bracket system that prevents newer players from being exposed to the top/active players until they do well in a few seasons worth of newer opponents. Realistically, this is good for most players, but if you're the hardcore competitive type, this means waiting potentially months before facing harsh competition.

The class system is well thought out, giving players a variety of roles to pick from, whether it’s the heavy gunner mowing down waves of arachnids or the engineer fortifying positions with turret placements and walls. The sense of camaraderie with your squad is real as you build defenses, call out warnings, and fight together to survive the waves of bugs.

review_text:
*Some JC3 to JC4 comparison talk
Get it on sale. Otherwise, no.

Pros

-If you mess around with the settings, you can get some rather beautiful landscapes. The draw distance for foliage and such is not great, no better than JC3 I guess, but this doesn't really kill the pretty views. It's a different lighting compared to JC3, not as much glow and maybe more shadows but certainly beautiful in their own rights. The lighting change between regions can be off putting but it's quick so eh.

-Some abilities from JC3 are just standard in this one (no more having to do challenges to unlock abilities). 

-The map is massive (the rivers are small). It's a large map with a lot of verticality and areas with updrafts near cliffs (not a lot though).

-The tethers easily make this game. 3 different tether load-outs each able to customized (activate via tap/hold/automatic), 3 different tether types (balloons, tether, and boosters). Each have mods and can be used in clever ways, balloons to make cover from aerial attacks or to just fly away those threats, the boosters can just launch people away BUT they can overclock to be used kind of like in JC3, and the tethers....well, they can do a power yank otherwise the same. I've had a blast realizing I can attach boosters in the right spots on the mech to fly around with it with perfect control, mild control with a flying limo.

-The freedom of movement. I have been enjoying this game mainly for this fact. I got the DLC, get when on sale, and even without the jet boost and the hoverboard it's still crazy fun. The tether to pull yourself around in the wingsuit is as satisfying as ever.


Mixed:

Challenges Gone:
-Challenges are pretty much gone. Replaced with "pass through x going x kph", "pass through x in x", "wingsuit through 3 rings in x time", and maybe something else as dull. They're easier to do which is nice and do enough of a type and you can unlock tether mods or wingsuit mods. I think some other stuff but nothing I can remember right now. -If you get the DLC to have the jet wingsuit f you will be sad to know that you cannot take off from land or sea and the minigun is gone replaced with missiles instead. -Airbraking looks and handles awful, if you stall too long you just cancel out of the wingsuit. It just felt more sensible in JC3

-The game is jank. I had to reverify my files, a common need, because my DLC didn't appear in the black market drops. Thankfully, only had to do this once.

-No pistols. Stuck with 2 weapons. Resupply!

-The map is massive, but it's still barren. The devs get how to do landscapes, but cities they just cannot seem to understand that they need more. Solis is 80% barren and 100% black hand everywhere. -No distance is reflected when setting a waypoint or tracking an objective. Just kills the scale.

-No running.

-The "cutscenes" are just awful. I've messed around with my settings but I just cannot fix the sharp light, lip sync issues, and character faces looking awful. They don't look bad in game, even though the cutscenes are in-game (maybe that's why?). They are just poorly optimized

I'll try to do it and Rico just doesn't shoot the end of the tether so I have to press the button again and it just cancels the tether out. Sometimes I'll try and I'll reel myself into certain death. It's just as if the game cannot handle wanting to shoot 10 tethers in succession.

There's no sense of accomplishment from destroying bases as things will just repopulate (kind of like when you beat JC3 and you can select to do that but you don't get to choose). 

-So little to blow up, no grenades or c4 to even do it with. They're just gone, enemies have grenades but you don't. The lack of this forces one of your weapons to always be an rpg or another reliable explosive. Or using tether mods for balloons and boosters to handle them. While you never need to blow up anything big anymore (sad) I'd think you'd still want some explosives to help with that tank or helicopter making you hate life.

-The water near or inside Solis looks so awful. Waterfalls look anti-climatic, calm river just goes into a gushing waterfall, they all do this. The mixed to this is the water outside is really nice. So I am not sure how much of this was deliberate but couldn't be realized how they wanted perhaps.

-Wanted Forever. If you get on alert, honestly, just call a pilot and fast travel to the same spot, it cancels the alert lazily... Can't really escape by air because the helis go the speed of jets and the jets are already shooting at you, go on the ground? They will hunt you down hard. I will go into the mountains and just as they call off the the search there's always a heli just a moment away from actually spotting me. It makes doing some things just a pain.

And they all have grenades and decent aim and blend into the environment because the devs didn't give them a highlight or outline silhouette to help you distinguish them beyond their muzzle flash or all the red and green dots aimed at you. It gets worse when you have to stand in a small area to complete an objective and the enemies just keep coming and building up

-Resupply is tedious beyond all reason. Do you need to resupply your 2 guns and get a vehicle to bail out? Easy, call in 3 separate pilots and wait for 3 drops one by one to do so :) 

Rebel Drops / Pilots: (Kind of sucks)
-Rebel drop and fast travel beacons have been reworked into Pilots. Pilots can call down ONE thing or fast travel you to a location. Afterwards it's a several minute cooldown to use them again. You can have a good amount of pilots, so no more having to get more beacons, yay. BUT pilots can only call down one item at a time AND pilots wait for each pilot to drop off their supply one by one. I haven't timed it but, opening comms link, going to resupply, opening their options, selecting the option, selecting to call it in, selecting where I want to call it in, waiting 7 or so seconds to fall (+ however longer until it is settled on the ground), then grabbing it. Only to wait 7 or more seconds again to get my next resupply drop or my getaway vehicle. You can sit in the comms and this does speed the timer for the resupply and pilot but...why not make it that fast always?

I honestly didn't expect much buying it when it had 80% sale tag. 
My favorite Otome being Nightshade, I thought- ok, I'll give this one a try. (After many many failed attempts at finding good otome fitting my taste.)

Overall, i think this game really pushed the story far, which made the gameplay experience very engaging. 
As a VN/Otome lover and a narrative illustrator myself, I look for tightly knitted plots with as few holes as possible and illustrations that are easy on eyes, without too much tryhard sprinkles (Im not a big fan of beautifying excessively)
As for me, who prefers watercolor-y, soft aesthetics, in terms of art-- this game was easy to fall in love with.
Story-wise, I was mostly busy reading the terminology and explanation of the world's political conflict and why they are important-- yet even trying to understand the world was interesting enough for me to spend hours and hours learning about it.

There are things that made me sort of "eh...." about the game BUT are still very well resolved were:

1. Character art being a bit too similar to each other (mostly fit, tall, charismatic feature of hunsbados... BUT i don't think that bothered me too much since they ARE all samurais, fit to wield swords) 
2. Kind of difficult to understand/grasp the world (being unfamiliar to Japanese history doesnt help with the historic fiction that dives very deep into political conflict as its core plot. ALTHOUGH they did a great job with the encyclopedia and terminology explanation throughout.)

3. Too big of a time gap between each chapters/major events (this had me sort of lost in thoughts of "what happened to that problem" "Did it really take this long for that to be resolved?" "WHAT HAPPENED TO SEARCHING FOR YOUR FATHER" a lot. But I do see why the devs had to do it this way, since they are trying to match the story with the historic events)

4. Romance is more like..... "ok, I choose you. Now go do your own thing. Duty calls!" which is admirable (realistically speaking) but frustrating (doki doki girl in me is screaming "I WANNA SEE MY CHOSEN HUSBANDO MORE OFTEN") at the same time 

5. A bit of a forced plot: I say this, and I do have to remind those who are reading this review that I'VE ONLY PLAYED THROUGH Hachiro Iba route ONLY. I'm not sure if this applies to other husbando routes, but as much as I love Hachiro, his plot seemed a bit forced, kind of out of nowhere ending. (idk how to do the spoiler thing, so I just wont say it LOL) Sen Character is a bit outta nowhere, Kaoru character wasn't explained at all, Takeshi or whatever that sexy beast's name is, he was kinda WHAT! wait, WHAT!!!! HOW DID YOU... WAIT DAD??? sorta moment for me. (kinda spoilery but don't worry, not too much.)

6. LET ME WEAR PRETTY KIMONOS PLEASE PLEASE. throughout the whole game all i was thinking was like, ok, let me... let me turn back to a girl..... yeah? no? i guess no.... sadface LET ME BE WHAT I AM!!!! (let me fight!!! i wanna be like you, Kiku!!)

But I do have to say, that all these things I just listed are very minor things that caught my eyes, and is sort of resolved. Its not like they are major flaws that will bother majority of otome lovers, it might be just me. 

anyways, BIG RECOMMEND! :)
Interesting world, interesting concept, very soft and pretty illustrations, GREAT VOICE ACTING. 

(also HACHIRO I LOVE YOU)

review_text:
I am sure if anyone reads this they might be confused why I don't recommend this game despite playing it over 100 hours.

I like this game, but I think everyone who would also like this game probably likes it for the same reason I do. I was a big fan of the original series, which are MUCH better games in comparison. G.U. allows for more of the same gameplay, but absolutely does not stand on its own.

Graphics: The game looks pretty great, they did a good job on the remaster. No complaints.

Sound: Some terrific music, sound effects, and the Japanese voice acting at least isn't bad. The Grunty sounds are awful though.

Story: Alright, so here is where it starts to fall apart. The story is entertaining enough, I find myself wanting to see what happens next, but there are so many parts that just doesn't make sense. It is mostly in how the characters act, I understand that role playing is a thing but they act like they aren't in an online game and at the same time, act like they are. There are so many lines that conflict with each other with regards to what is going on in the story. Characters will say something like "This is just a game." and then 3 minutes later they are completely serious. The writing for the main character is atrocious. He's annoying, rude to everyone, and just an overall child. There are times when you think he's gonna stop being mean and then he just says something else. I could do without the awkward online dating storyline too.

Gameplay: Okay so the core combat is just as good as the original game. There's some other stuff added that seems to mostly improve the game...except the bike. The Bike is the absolute worst thing I have ever driven in a game. Luckily, it really isn't required unless you want to complete Ryu Books and it gets slightly better in game 2 since you can mod it, but its still not fun.  The absolute biggest problem with the combat is the game is just too easy. You can ignore ALL the mechanics of the game if you want, in group and solo battles. It is almost impossible to die, I've only had a character come close once and that's just because I wasn't paying attention. There's also a severe lack of actual boss fights unless you play on going out of your way to do side areas, but there's two problems with that. 1.) Doing more than the main story questions will get you overleveled quick, making the game even easier. 2.) Even then, they are barely bosses and more like  regular enemies with more health.

Overall, don't bother with this game if you never played the original 4 games. Its just not good enough without that nostalgia.

This is Early Access Review. I will come back once 1.0 releases.

Whilst I like the game, the gameplay, gun shooting, animations are super smooth, the lore and visuals are great as well. However, the over all game loop exhausts quite early and becomes very samey. I am not sure what the solution is - but you will hit that wall that is same thing over and over rather fast. 

My guess it it needs bit more fleshed out carrot on a stick to make me go back to same map over and over (map layout doesn't change every time you load in). The novelty of the gameplay wears off after hitting 8-10h mark. I am aware that there are plenty of things to 'unlock' still - but as it stands I feel the game needs just bit more fine tuning and content for in between stages when you're working towards next goal. Only thing that seems to change is the enemy difficulty as you progress, everything else remains the same and is rather easy and simple.

So in short, this is a great game, but needs a bit more agency why you should continue playing after novelty period wears off. 

I'll check it out again after 1.0

review_text:
This game is honestly a mess and a nightmare to play.

Same missions over and over (destroy the generators, flip the switch, hack the terminal, raise the transmitter, and then the dreaded defend said transmitter). Rinse, repeat ad infinitum.

Horrible UI and controls in general.

Driving makes you go mad, and with the amount of driving in this game, good luck. The camera angle sucks, and no way to change it. While driving you will get stuck on every little piece of debris on the road and will constantly spin out of control, and crash.

Terrible missions that are borderline impossible. Defend X mission objective - good luck without some of the DLC with overpowered weapons and vehicles. Waves of enemy tanks spawning from nowhere that will blow your defense object to hell before you even know where the missile came from.

HORRID performance. The game will stutter at times, will go from 160 fps to 20, will microstutter, and some of the "fixes" are hilarious. One common fix is to unplug your ethernet cable to fix stuttering. Even blocking all online components of this game doesn't fix the stuttering / lag, but does help a tad.

The frontlines part of the game aren't bad, just badly implemented. Just Cause 2 and 3 had it down where you just blow ♥♥♥♥ up, in this one, it doesn't matter. You don't "create Chaos" like in the previous installments, instead you fly into a base, flip some breakers, kill endless waves of enemies, die from a single sniper/rocket shot from nowhere, reload the save, and try again.

I love Just Cause for it's mindless braindead fun, but this game is just braindead unfun. Play Just Cause 2 or even 3 (which has it's own issues). This game looks great, when it's running at full performance with no hiccups, which never happens.

If you want this game, buy the complete edition for like $3, and you'll get a weekend of half-fun, half insufferable pain.

review_text:
Glorified Humiliation Ritual.

In a nut shell, this game treats Henry & Hans Capon as if they are some sort of entitled colonizer. It honestly seems like the story writer (who did a largely great job on the 1st title) started to hate himself somewhere post KCD1 and pre-KCD2, and projects it onto the protagonists as a consequence. 

What's that? You spent hundreds of hours on building your Henry in KCD1 and were expecting your skills & gear to transfer over, considering that KCD2 picks up right where KCD1 left off? 

TOO BAD. Even though the time between releases was not very long, the 1st giant mistake by War Horse was not simply allowing you to continue on from your last KCD1 save - the way several other franchises have done with their sequels.

Of course, they HAD to make you start from scratch - because if they didn't, how could they force you to humiliate Henry for the first 10 hours of game play? 

Did you think at the end of KCD1 you'd actually deliver that message the way a competent company of knights would? 

No, sorry, the game opens by demonstrating how Hans Capon & Henry are just soooo dumb that they camps next to a road that the company is warned is crawling with bandits. 

Then they go for a nice swim ensuring that the company will be literally caught with their pants down when the bandits inevitably raid your camp and still the scroll that has the message.... such wow writing. 

So you have no gear, no skills, no anything. Hans gets literal poo dumped on him... when trying to convince the castle of who he & Henry are emissaries for (since the message & your armor was stolen you have no proof). 

Which was a cheap laugh I guess... but the amount of actual feces in this game has me worried about the creative team. Like it comes up so often it's strange.

You're forced to talk to an African NPC (who is supposed to be likable) that talks about how filthy white Europeans are and how he's had intimate relations with the European lord's wives... what the actual hell?

You are given an option to romance Hans Capon. Yes, that's right. Henry is bisexual now.... in early Medieval Europe.... 

When you sleep with a woman in game, she's sure to tell you how terrible of a lay you are....

The fantasy that KCDI delivered of becoming someone you can be proud of in a historically accurate Medieval Europe is completely absent in this game. It seems more worried about shaming/cucking white people and forcing you to endure constant humiliation from the narrative, that you are not able to navigate around whatsoever. 

It honestly seems like someone was paid to just pervert the narrative of this game entirely.

Even the combat seems to have taken a step backwards. AI is worse, and there are less options for attacks. Even technologically/visually the progression isn't anything noticeable. I was hoping for greater battles with more people (the only thing that really broke the immersion at time in KCD1), but the technical limitations still seem identical to the 1st title that was released years ago. 

Kingdom Cuck II. Thanks for making me waste my money on this. No fucking idea what changed on the creative side between both games here.

review_text:
I would recommend scorn as a very disturbing and atmospheric experience but as a game it has quite a few shortcomings that might turn off a lot of players. The puzzle and exploration aspects were very good but if you treat the game as a shooter it would be an unforgiving and frustrating way to play it. There is a disparity here with what the game excels at and what it mishandles almost to the point where I wonder if there should be combat at all. I have found through my playthrough that it's possible to ignore a large majority of threats if you hang back and let them pass to wherever they are trying to go. That does remedy what I think is the biggest problem with the game, and maybe even helps flesh out the world with creatures that become part of the level design instead of things to shoot at.

The game is at its best when you are exploring the world and solving puzzles to progress, which is what most of the game is anyway especially in the first half. There isn't a plot exactly, you wake up as a nameless being making their way through the locations in the game. Everything is vague, there never seemed to be a story to follow. It made the game feel like a walking simulator through a disgusting yet gorgeous Giger-esque world. I can describe it as an industrious complex that has fallen to ruin. The machines are bio-mechanical and everything that is left alive appears to be in some kind of agony. You scoop creatures from egg-like pods, killing them for their body parts. Tools you get are screwed into your flesh, blood coming from the wounds you now have. Even the weapons are some flesh and metal thing you rip apart and reconfigure to the few weapons you have. I found I enjoyed the game just by watching how horrible the world is and how you interact with it, trying to work out what all of the machines you discover are really for.

review_text:
[h1]Good stuff. Play on hardest.[/h1]

This is a really good game, and I would also countenance that it has some elements that remind me of playing games in the 'good old days' if you play it on the hardest setting!

[h2]Meat[/h2]
It's very obvious once you start playing that this is based on the Far Cry/Ubisoft dunia (?) engine, and that's a good thing, as it's one of the only ones that allows decent M+K (after some fiddling) and controller to coexist. 

Also good is that it's basically Far Cry bases stringed together with a few loose bits of tiny open world. This is good because you might have noticed that the thing lacking there are any forced 'on rails' elements of gameplay to further the story.

[h2]Two Veg[/h2]
That's because there really isn't much of one (which is fine) because you are a sniper, and you're doing killz, innit.

There's a number of glitches, which because you might need to jump out of some rock you've become Excalibur within, might cause you to be noticed ... this is frustrating ... but I can't remember ever wanting to smash everything and rage quit as a result.

[h2]Pudding[/h2]
So finally on to that hardest setting/ye olde gaming thing. Yes, basically, I'm not a competent gamer, but playing this on hard is really satisfying, because there are none of the previously mentioned forced/on-rails sections with cheap 'gets' for the AI. There's *always* a few ways to get anything done here.

So why is this 'ye olde'? Because I treat raising the alarm (meaning that the enemy has both spotted you, and raised said alarm) as death. So with that comes either a last checkpoint quick reset, or starting the mission fresh. This is ingrained in me from years of FC play, and in old gaming terms ... well, it's like falling down a hole in Mario, or crashing into the trench wall in an Atari Star Wars arcade run. You restart, and you get a TINY bit better (sometimes worse), and play some more.

[h2]A Pair Of Teef[/h2]
So, sure, there's little story, and sometimes you might find yourself talking to the lady in the lake ... but it's engrossing stuff, and you'll find yourself spending hours camped watching patterns, trying to separate two guards that are clearly 'together', or just drinking in the scenery.

Stick it on hardest and enjoy.

xx

review_text:
An impressive feat in quality and genre mixing!

At the time of this review the game is in early access and has had the Webgrave update released for just over 1 month. Review is subject to change depending on content added. 

The Story is very reminiscent of something like the Witcher while taking the approach of doing things in Fromsoft fashion with item descriptions and environment to tell the player the story which is a narrative style i do enjoy. There aren't really characters in this game except for notes but the game does a great job at focusing on the main goal rather than wasting time with exposition that would drag the experience down. 

The Settings are so well crafted and feel very lived in. I really like how each map that you can explore has many secrets that reward the player for exploration and dedication to leveling up and getting better at the game. Each zone within a map feels like a mini arena that offers a lot for players to explore and navigate during combat. It's very clear that the devs had a clear goal in mind and wanted to put out the best content that they possibly could. 

Visually, its gorgeous. Performance was solid for the most part with the newest map having some frame drops, but with this being early access and with the amount of updates and care that the devs give, this is only a minor hickup that will soon be fixed. Apart from that I didn't run into any bugs or glitches throughout my playtime. The Art Direction has this mix of both realism mixed in with a gothic aesthetic which i just love in games and definitely was one of the main selling points for me. It definitely feels very gritty which for a game like this is just the perfect vibe for the overall experience. 

Sound and Audio are on point with the soundtrack being really tense and mystical, keeping with the vibe of the experience and giving the player the right information depending on interaction. The Audio design is just so good as every weapon you wield feels like they pack a punch and even shooting enemies such as some of the armoured ones sounds great with the bullets hitting off metal. Its just a treat to hear and is great feedback. 

In terms of Gameplay, it somehow manages to take some of the best elements of different games and puts them into one experience without loosing focus. The movement and combat feels like its ripped straight out of Destiny which makes me feel right at home. The rogue-like elements are pretty cool, but its clear to see that this game focuses more on other aspects other than this. I'm not saying that its bad, but you shouldn't come into this thinking that this is a pure rogue-like. I think the extraction shooter elements are really well implemented and the game does a great job at making the player feel like they can loose all of their earnings in 1 run. Enemies are actually smart and will try to flank and use different abilities against you making difficulty interesting rather than making them bullet sponges. The guns, spells, items are all well varied and offer so much customisation when it comes to gameplay, even with the upgrades offering new playstyles which is just a breath of fresh air in the greater scheme of things. Finally, the boss fights definitely feel like they take inspiration to souls games and just feel great to go against. 

Overall, Witchfire prides itself on quality over quantity and I can't wait for what the devs have next in store for this game. Can't wait for it to be in 1.0!

But, all of the characters were lively and fun and it had beautiful backgrounds and art. It feels like a fleshed out world and I would recommend it to my non-Homestuck friends.

Where's the video of a famous streamer holding this game in their hands looking regally into the selfie stick proclaiming their love for this? I started to spit apple seeds I was so limed. But this game came and now I'm swallowing it.

Annie ways... this is actually a good game, ACTUALLY a g0od game. ACTUALLY A GOOD GAME ACTUALLY. Actually, it's a fun game. Is it good? I don't know what kind of personality quiz that reviewers use to rate a game good or not, I think people forgotten about 'reviewers' a long time ago because putting faith into a single person who definitely does not have your best interest in theirs, is foundation for a short and fleeting relationship that lasted one or two videos. The idea of flying cars is a joke now, it's a joke because we all know what the future holds... our hope is all but diminished. However, there is still this game... a perfect rendition of the fate of man kind. We are all useless until we are holding a device or tool in our hands, because without we are just fodder for the taking. We are all underneath a cyber over lord, dictating every move we will ever take... death is the only free will. 

This is the end of our culture... a face protruding from a computer screen is above us all, watching, grimacing, demanding more from us of our time. Despot's Game.

review_text:
This JRPG 4-pack is an incredible journey; very few games can take this many hours of my life without garnering a sense of resentment, but this was special.  I can't say that I was left wanting more, but it didn't wear out its welcome, either.  Keep in mind that as big a fan of the genre as I was back in the Fourth and Fifth Generation (I didn't play much else back then), I've really fallen out of love with the genre, so there may very well be better ones out there that I just never picked up.  I also probably didn't play this the way that I was supposed to, so keep that in mind, but that also means that I had the freedom to even do that in the first place.  With most of my biases out of the way, let's get started.

The gameplay was pretty refreshing, and I don't know why more games of the era aren't like this.  Devil May Cry came around and revolutionized 3D Action, but it took other genres a while to try their hand at this type of combat system.  Like my beloved Rogue Galaxy, these games have a similar, but watered-down type of combat; you run around and slash at things in real-time, and the mechanics, while not all that deep, are pretty solid.  You've got your standard combo, your charge attack, and your over-the-top specials, and while that's mostly it, you can get enemies into a special state where your special moves do more damage and give everyone a bonus in experience.  Doing all that, you also fill a bar that lets you go into berserker mode.  There are tons of options, and your main character's warrior class is a jack of all trades, so you'll have access to several different weapon types over the course of the 4 games.  Your companions are controlled by AI, and you have a few basic guidelines to give them, which isn't a whole lot of control, but they mostly act intelligently.

The basic structure of the game allows you to dial in an address out of hundreds or thousands of possible combinations; dial it in to a level appropriate to your party, and go on an adventure!  There isn't a lot of variety - most of the areas are pretty cookie cutter - but all of the outside areas have different times of day, and what's there is designed beautifully.  Even though a lot of the areas look the same, I found myself getting really absorbed into the scenery, though mostly outside; the dungeons are neat, but not as pretty, and they're a lot longer.  Each area gives you a rank once you finish, but thankfully, how quickly you cleared it is not a factor; you can just take your time and do a good job.  Most equipment can be customized with extra goodies that give you benefits such as status ailments, elemental damage, and HP drain.  You don't really have to worry about grinding, either, because your levels skyrocket with little provocation; if you're looking for a challenge, keep on walking.  That said, there is so much to do: the game keeps track of which items you've possessed, which monsters you've battled, etc., and the more you do, the more your guild grows, which gives you extra benefits.  With that and all of the different quests available, there's plenty to do, and honestly, I found it fun just going on adventures to random areas, maybe even more than the story missions.

The actual story... well, it grew on me.  At first, I hated all of the characters (except the one who established early on that she's just OVER IT), but by the end of the third game, I found myself even getting attached to random NPCs that wandered around town.  I became genuinely happy for my extremely stereotypical shounen protagonist when people showed a genuine interest in his wellbeing.  Even some of the more annoying characters grew on me by the end, and with a cast this big, and an attitude as cynical as mine, that's no small task.  The actual plot has a lot of weird things happening, and not having played the other games or watched any of the anime, I was pretty lost at times, but almost everything comes together in the end.  If nothing else, it's a thematic departure from the usual settings of a game like this.

The environments, as I've said are beautiful, and the more unique elements of the game generally look pretty cool.  Most characters have some form of tribal tattoo on them, and they all look pretty neat.  In typical anime fashion, the main character's outfits get progressively more ridiculous, as do the weapons, but once I started to lean into that, I began to enjoy myself.  The monsters look very unique, especially the avatars, and even though some of them are a bit outlandish, they are very creatively designed.  Special attacks, spells, etc. are all appropriately flashy, and usually not too hilariously over-the-top.

The audio is pretty good; nothing really blew me away, but there's a lot to like here.  I didn't notice too much of the music, but the fields have appropriately serene music by day, and somewhat unsettling music at sunset.  A really nice touch is that at night or in the rain, there is no music, and you can just enjoy the atmosphere.  Most of the voice acting is good and not only fits the characters, but also frames them in a way that makes them work, not to mention that Liam O'Brien plays one of them, and that man is a national treasure.  You have a couple of duds now and again - one character sounds like a little girl making fun of how little boys talk [b]all the time[/b] - but they aren't too common.

If you're looking for something that's going to let you just pick up and go on an adventure at a whim, this might be up your alley.  I'm not a big anime fan, and despite that, I found myself really getting really into it.  I can't recommend it just for the extra fourth game that's never been released before; it introduces a few cool new things, but it's shorter than 5 hours, and in terms of plot, it doesn't add much.  That said, if you're looking to play these again, or are a newcomer (like I was), it's a pretty good value, and is pretty fun once you finally get into it.  See you in The World.

Initially, I was going to give this game a 6/10. While combat is a bit simplistic, since you can beat most enemies by mashing the attack button, you can also take more strategic approaches by using the multitude of gadgets available to you. review_text:
People, that are not me, seem to absolutely love this game without really caring about it's glaring issues at all. These issues are things that severely impacted my enjoyment of the game as a whole, and the resulting review of the whole experience is therefore negative.
If you are planning on buying this game, beware that you're buying it for the story, not the gameplay. 

[b]Pros:[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]The story.[/b] If you're anyone other than me, you'll probably love the story! 
    [*][b]The artstyle[/b] of this game is somewhat pleasing to the eye, and pixelart is one of my favourites. It might seem a bit too flat and boxy at times, but the game looks quite good as a whole. 
    [*][b]The music[/b] is quite beautiful and fitting, as the classical piano tunes fit right in with the relaxed atmosphere of the game. The same tune does however get played on multiple occasions throughout the story, so you'll hear it many times.
[/olist]

[b]Cons:[/b]
[olist]
   [*][b]The resolution[/b], or lack of thereof. The game runs in a tiny window that makes it basically impossible to play the game, or in stretched out and blurry fullscreen which looks horrible. The "fix" to this issue is is to use the Windows magnifying glass, a part of the operating system, to zoom in on the tiny game window. That is great design right there. 
   [*][b]The Puzzles[/b] are seemingly impossible to fail, and it becomes very repetitive to complete the same puzzle time and time again, simply to progress. The only real change from puzzle to puzzle is the image that you complete, the rest is all the same. 
   [*][b]The gameplay[/b] is lacking at best, it's very monotonous, and more or less acts as filler content between segments of storytelling. The controls are not very responsive and it all just feels wrong, an example is when you have to use both the wasd and arrow keys in a very counterintuitive way [spoiler]to navigate and shoot your way through the school full of zombies[/spoiler].
   [*][b]The story[/b] of this game apparently causes players to cry. In fact, it is sooo good that it makes up for the rest of the shortcomings of the game. According to others at least. The story didn't have any emotional impact on me though, and it was surprisingly uninteresting considering I'd heard such good things about it. It was in fact boring enough for me, that I played a large part of the game at three times the original speed simply to get through the most boring parts quicker. 
[/olist]

As you might be able to tell, I've focused mainly on the things I found to be bad about the game, and that is because so many good things have already been said in basically every other review. Go read those instead to get more positive picture.

review_text:
This is a game that knows what it wants to be and accomplishes it well. It so easy to look at this game and say "Oh this is just some rocket league clone" But i can promise you its not. So many aspects are adjusted from rocket league such as ball weight, power, purpose, speed, and flying that it truly feels like its own unique game. The gameplay elements are all stellar, and the game only gets more fun as you get better at it. The "Cores" (powerups you equip before you start a match) are fun and quirky, they don't completely change anything about the game that would indicate any particular one of them is better than the others.

The gameplay itself is simple. drive a ball to the flag before anyone else. if a guy is in front of you shoot a rocket at him it'll make him do a lil flip spin like if he got tagged by a red shell in mario kart. you have a couple tools at your disposal to help control where your ball is going, between the cores, tilting, and angles you come to realize pretty quick this game isn't necessarily about speed, its about precision. The speed helps dont get me wrong but hitting it to the right place matters so much more than hitting it faster. 

Honestly, I've got another 14 paragraphs of praise for this game. I'll save you the reading. TLDR, buy it, 100% worth the money.

review_text:
I've only just scratched the surface of what this game has to offer, but I can give it a thumbs up reccomendation without hesitation or doubt already.

What an experience!

Comparing it to Left 4 Dead or Back 4 Blood are not comparisons without merit, but being VR, the immersion is brought to a whole new level.
And the VR aspect is done extraordinarily well, and in a fashion that will suit just about every VR user!

For example, when it comes to motion, you can use teleport movement ala Half Life Alyx, or you can use regular movement via the toggles. Both have their drawbacks and positives, both suit different players.

The firearm handling is fantastic for a game like this, and again, is designed to suit all players.
You can use your off hand to steady a weapon, even one handed weapons such as pistols, or duel wield pistols, or use consumables ect.
Weapons have weight, recoil is noticeable and reloading has been handled perfectly. There are two settings, manual and easy.
Easy is where, to reload you just bring bring your firearm to the ammo on your rig and bam, magically reload your weapon - in the same vein as a lot of wave shooters.
Or you can manually reload your firearm - eject the magazine, push in a new one, rack the slide ect. As a bonus for taking the harder route and extra steps of manual, you gain a 35% damage increase to balance it out against easy reloading, which is just fantastic and opens the game to everyone.
Again, with weapon storage, you can choose to have holsters like in Saints and Sinners, or you can go for a traditional gaming weapon select wheel.

TLDR: The devs have really taken the time to make After the Fall as approachable as possible for every type of VR gamer, whether they come from Pavlov, Half-Life, Saints and Sinners or obscure wave defence games.
Firearms are fun to use, they have weight, oomph, recoil and can be operated realistically or not.

Graphics are pretty nice! If it was a PC title, not so much, but in VR they look fantastic and are very atmospheric. 

There are a large number of unlocks, a hub area, you can play solo with bots or group up with friends or strangers to tackle different difficulties or even game modes.

I don't (yet) have the playtime to declare this a must play title for VR gamers, but I'm close to doing so.

when this game was announced, i was super hyped. by that stage every instalment from the just cause series got better and better, and i was hoping that 4 would follow that trend but it seemed that for every minor improvement they added, they would remove a feature from 3 that made it awesome. on its own merit the game itself can be fun, but compared to 3 its not that great. i do want to give it some due respect. the graphics are good, the word and weather are interesting to look at, the enemy ai is smarter and there's a lot more variety to them, the physics are visually and technically impressive, and the guns feel a lot better to use.
now let me give you 20 reasons why this game is a pile of peepee.
1. the world may be more varied with a lot of attention to detail then 3's but it feels very bland and empty, 3 did have this issue but not as much as 4 and navigating through it can be a slug
2. the new weather systems add nothing to gameplay other then "oh cool a tornado"
3. the story has a much more serious tone then 3 but in turn it makes it come off as corny and slow
4. just cause 3 starts with a sick montage, just cause 4 starts with a mindless exposition dump
5. they removed c4
6. the bad guy is a cliche rich man, just cause 3's villain was a cold, ruthless and yet lazy dictator
7. the secondary fire makes each gun feel uniqe but it kinda feels like an after thought as i would always forget about it.
8. you cant blow up bridges
9. they removed c4
10. the plot structure is go here, meet new person, do things for them. build a tool to stop weather thing, done. and that happens 4 times
11. you cant liberate towns
12. the atheistic went into a more si-fi rout which is more of a personal preference thing but i like the idea of a one man army going up against an actual army rather then teched up soldiers
13. the characters are far less likeable then in three
14. the plot starts with a strong sense of finale and personal connections but ends up devolving into 'this happened once, remember just cause 1? and this is the next game"
15. the army of chaos feels more like a sales point. its there to give chaos points an actually reason for existing but it removes the liberation of bases and instead gives incentives taking over land. this adds nothing to gameplay or mission structure. what if they added big battles that you can fight, win or loose in, what if you could train your army to be better and have them help liberate towns. in the end it feels more in the way then anything as you have to use them to move forward in the story
16. they removed c4
17. the ui is a mess
18. the different grapple options are kinda cool but mostly forgettable as its easiest to probably just stick with the retracting one. its mainly there to send goats and cows flying through the air
19. probably the main problem, they changed the way you liberate bases, instead of blowing everything up, you insted have to do a mission that range from escorting someone, breaking prisoners out, hacking something, ect, kinda like in just cause 2 this is so incredibly stupid. in 3 it gave you so much freedom in the ways you can blow things up and that was essentially the main gameplay. in 4 they hold you arm back and forces you to do stuff you don't want to do, when what you actually want to do (explosions) just sits there teasing you.
20. why oh god did they remove the c4
in the end i wonder why i got this rather then just playing just cause 3

review_text:
Negatives: It has a few glitches here and there that can drive you crazy. I kept having one with my horse going into the woods and it just stuttering in place. My biggest complaints would be that at the start of the game, it takes quite awhile before you can actually do anything. It made me get bored and consider having a refund just based on that. My biggest issue is that the combat system can be really frustrating. Specifically, when you have a couple enemies fighting you when you're solo. You basically just get killed, and it's difficult to escape once the fight starts. Your stamina bar always seems to be empty, and enemies will chase you for a long, long time. The money system is annoying until you get a feel for how to make some quick and easy money consistently, so that's only temporary annoyance.

Positives: Beautiful game to run around in with incredible voice acting. The freedom to do whatever you want, to a point, during the story is awesome and accounts for many different actions. The attention to detail with people calling you smelly or asking why you're covered in blood is a great touch. It reminded me a lot of a really good Fallout or Elder Scrolls game with how the choices shape the game and just the entertaining places some of the quests go, but the close combat fighting being not nearly as good as those games. I've had no issue with the long range combat, hunting, or unarmed fights you get into. 

Overall: I'd absolutely recommend if you like story driven action/adventure games. You'll have all the things you're used to, like sneaking around, stealing, and general mayhem you can cause, You can be a total jerk or decent person if you want and your reputation will reflect that. The story itself is very deep with plenty of twist and turns as a result of your actions from main, side, or optional quests. Great game despite whatever negative things I can come up with. I'd say a solid 8 out of 10.

review_text:
I'm going to try to keep the review as spoiler-free as I possibly can, because it's a game that the less you know about it, the better, but tldr; I would say IMSCARED is the best horror game I've played, but it's more like an incredibly unique experience that no other horror game I've seen has done, and is the FIRST horror game I would recommend to anyone interested in horror, outside of even just horror games as a whole. 

Most, if not all games I play that I thoroughly loved and enjoyed, tend to stick in the back of my mind for a week or two, and that's probably how it is for most people on here, too. And although I didn't spend many hours playing IMSCARED, as I do with most other games I love that live in my head rent-free for weeks, the limited time I had for it felt a lot longer than the number steam says I have in the game! 

Despite its age (2016 is the remaster afaik) the pixel style/art hasn't aged bad (In fact I LOVE it! Popular pixel horror is rare nowadays), moreso it retains the uniqueness of the game/experience. The sound design is simple too, making it complementary to the world. The most unique part is of course, the "external" experience outside of the game; the folders being created, the text pages leading you through the puzzles, on your computer etc. People seem to give a lot of credit to [horror] games that interact with the user/play outside of the games window, such as breaking the 4th wall, reading your pc info, saying the name of the owner of the pc you are playing the steam game in, Doki Doki Literature club is probably the biggest one that comes to mind. And don't get me wrong, I think that's a creepy and cool feature that they should use from time to time! But as far as I know, this game was one of the first to try this intrusive feature that some don't give credit for, and furthermore, making it the core idea of the whole game; a creepy, stalking entity that's like a sentient computer virus that wants to befriend and play with you.

[spoiler]The finale/end of the game was SO freaky, I won't go into details but I haven't felt my hair raise from a game in many years. review_text:
This game is like [b]Rocket League meets golfing.[/b] The concept is much more fun in comparison to its competitor, IMO. However, the game isn't without its flaws. I put 8 hours into this game so here are some of my thoughts.

[b]Pros:[/b]

➤ As I already mentioned, the concept is pretty unique, fun and addictive
➤ The mechanics are easy to learn but hard to master, also they are somewhat more complex than in Rocket League, making the game all that much more interesting
➤ Varied vehicle customazation
➤ A lot of active and passive skills you can equip
➤ Great amount of maps
➤ Active updates
➤ Free battle pass
➤ Decent achievements worth grinding for
➤ In-game mission which keep you coming back

[b]Neither:[/b]

➤ The playerbase is small, you tend to play with the same people over and over again, most of the matches therefore are filled with half bots but the queue times are short, meaning you don't need to wait usually more than a minute
➤ In the first hour you kinda get to know everything about this game but you can always improve when it comes down to your skills (for some it gets repetitive real quick)

[b]Cons:[/b]

➤ There are a very few game modes you can choose from (solo = time trial, more players/bots = casual + ranked)
➤ Uncertain future, due to the small playerbase, I can see the game dying in the near future. Most likely, I see the game going free-to-play (the fact, the game was already bundled just makes my theory all that more plausible)
➤ No voice chat (it doesn't matter since there are no teammodes, still it would be a nice thing to have and let those, who don't want it, simply mute it in the settings)

[b]To sum it up,[/b] it's worth giving this game a try. After all, the game is still in early access. I had the chance of trying a demo during Steam's next fest and it was, hands down, one of the best games I tried. Maybe wait for a bit. 

I have my [b]doubts[/b] about the future of this game as I said above and even though the game seems to be getting updated regularly, it's mostly new maps and cosmetics, there doesn't seem to have been any new gamemodes or any groundbreaking updates since the game was released to the public.

There's a reason this came out at $30 because they knew they couldn't charge $60 for pure dog shit like this.

In my opinion, this is the worst mainline Yakuza game. Y4 had its problems, too, but I think this one is overall worse. Y5 has better fighting gameplay than Y4, sure, but:
- the story is on par with the bad quality of Y4, which is an "amazing" "feat". 
- it has too many characters trying to share the spotlight; 4 was already crazy, and here we have 5
- the characters are all just miserable in a way that just consistently brings the whole atmosphere down and is just exhausting to even watch

review_text:
[h3] TLDR: Try it if you really think you want to, but you are not missing out on anything if you don't. [/h3]

This game relies [b]HEAVILY[/b] on jumpscares. Every single attempt at making the player feel fear is through some kind of cheap jumpscare attempt. 
I am not someone that plays horror or survival horror games, I do not enjoy them and I do not enjoy feeling fear or terror. I avoid them like a plague.

Thankfully (and also unfortunately), this game does not do any of that.

There is nothing frightening or "scary" about this game. There is no terror. 
Every jumpscare is extremely predictable, so they rarely work, if ever. 
Later on in the game it becomes "roll your eyes" laughable even.

I think one big reason why this game also struggles to make the player feel any kind of fear, is that the player is WAY too powerful. Yes, you can run out of ammo, and ammo isn't always abundant, but the melee combat system, while innovative, is also so simplistic that it rarely matters. 

The player is also always aware where enemies will come from or when a fight will take place, as there are environmental objects like conveniently placed spike walls, explosives, grates on the floor, or air vents that always signal this. 

Upgrading your weapons is a chore as credits (in game currency) are difficult to come by. You are guaranteed to not upgrade all weapons or items on your first playthrough. 

Visually the game looks great, but suffers from some performance issues at times. 

Audio and sound design are good. 

Voice acting is good.

Combat is okay. I enjoyed it for the most part, despite how divisive of a topic it is, but it can quickly become repetitive. 

Story is nothing to write home about either. There was great potential in terms of the futuristic setting and politics involving bioweapons and the future of humankind in space, but the game never really dives deeper into it beyond a surface level presentation. 

Everything that happens in the story is also very cliche and predictable. 

Character development of our main protagonist, Jacob, is also pretty mediocre. 

That's a lot of negatives, so why would I still recommend this game? 

It's not a [i] bad [/i] game. It's just okay or "meh". That, and Steam does not allow a "maybe" or "indifferent" vote.  Also, i'm quite convinced this game took an even more major hit in reputation and negativity by trying to "piggy back" or build hype off of the Dead Space name (and ultimately failing to meet those expectations). 

I however, have not played dead space, so I am able to remain completely neutral in that regard.

review_text:
I have to agree with the other negative reviews here - While I like the general concept of the game, the difficulty and binary nature of winning or losing combats doesn't feel great. The lack of any real comeback mechanic can leave you effectively dead but forced to play through another four or five combats to finally die against the floor boss that you could never have beaten. One of the bigger issues here I think is the lack of meaningful boosts to your units outside of the mutations - something like armour or other individualised boosts you could put on key units to boost their survivability, or perhaps a mechanic to smush several units into one superunit (would be pretty on brand). 

The general balancing of the different classes also feels way off - healers seem to become pretty useless as the game goes on but practically essential early, and cultists/eggheads feel very bad and awkward to use - while mages and tricksters feel very overtuned at the start and scale very well into the later floors. Some of the enemies have a tendency to just decimate your frontlines and, if not outright end your run there cripple you in the aforementioned 'already dead but forced to keep playing' way - cerberus has ended three of my runs so far by effectively oneshotting my entire set of frontline units. 

Food is a mechanic that just feels like it has no place in the game.  You aren't rewarded for having plenty of food - just punished for not having enough, It's a resource that has the sole purpose of eating into your tokens 
 and I'd honestly rather just receive less tokens and not have to hassle with it. In a practical sense it places a cap on the number of units you can field at a given time, which doesn't feel too great as after a certain point MORE MEATSHIELDS is the only real strategy to get stronger.

The design ethos of the game seems a bit confused, in that it simultaneously tries to treat your units as expendable 'puny humans', while also making them quite hard to replace in a practical sense and providing you with various mutations (e.g 25% chance to revive) that only really make sense if you're fielding very large numbers of these units, which food heavily limits.

review_text:
AEM is basically a repository for Haiku games that are (mostly) of the adventure/puzzle genre. The stories and characters are interesting, the games themselves are fun, colorful and enjoyable.

The in-game purchase mechanic where in order to get more keys you need to pay with real money initially I admit, that it kind of annoyed me. You have max 2 keys and you need a key to unlock a chapter of a game (each game usually has 8 chapters) in order to play it and then it needs 3 hours to regenerate. However, paying isn't absolutely necessary, since you can just wait for them to regenerate. And honestly I don't mind. In fact I grew to like it since it felt like it made the game last longer. The fact that new games are added frequently keeps the whole thing relevant and interesting not knowing what story you're going to come across next.

Overall, it's not a bad way to pass the time and you might get to play some fairly interesting stories.

review_text:
I may be the minority here with this take, but I genuinely didn't enjoy the game as much as I hoped. 

It's such an unoriginal, uninspiring gameplay design. This game takes the ideas of Dead Space & RE4 and makes them horrendous.

It's the same copypaste survival-action formula from every modern RE title ever.
The only difference being how terribly implemented it is.

Significantly worse inventory system.
Awful balancing.
Limited "upgrade" system.
Boring and overused enemies.
Clunky movement & combat.
An overused trope of body morphing.. done terribly.

The inventory system racks my brain. I cannot fathom why you'd want such a frustrating system in your game.
Imagine needing to collect a progression item and having no room for it. Why not have a quest-item inventory like every other game in this genre does? I'm sure people are just jumping for joy having to use up their spare meds / ammo in order to free up ONE slot to move on with the game. I feel bad for those that have to back track through everything just to clear 1-2 slots for quest-progression items. Speaking of, why is it that the main weapon of the game is a singular pistol that can change forms, but takes up a slot for each form? You're just making the already-terrible inventory system worse by default with this decision. 

I can't tell if this is a chronic skill-issue on my part, or the RNG is absolutely horrendous. Anytime I break open a yellow-tape box (yes, those stupid things are littered in this game too), I get.. absolutely nothing! That's right, nothing! Break open 3-4 crates and receive completely nothing in return. No ammo, no meds, nothing. When I DO on the off-chance actually get SOMETHING from the crates, it's just energy.. and the smallest amount possible at that (energy is this game's "currency" for the shop). Due to the poor distribution of supplies, I find myself being LUCKY to have 10 bullets to use at any given time. If you're not using the charge shot ability on the pistol at all times, you're literally wasting ammo. 

Upgrading your suit & weapons is as bare bones as it can get. Nothing gives you a special skill, ability, or perk. It is quite simply "number go up" and that's it. Wanna upgrade the duration of burning enemies? Spend a core to make it burn from 1 second, to 1.33 seconds! Wow!!

The enemies are so overused & limited it hurts. I dunno why they do the Dead Space method of "Black skin = strong." Somehow a darker version of the same enemy just has more health. Not only that, but why the worst kinda of enemies? Why slugging pus-balls? Why Spitters? Why wall-attached enemies that just trigger QTE events constantly? These aren't fun, they're annoying. Couple this with the jank movement and you've got boring, clunky combat. I can't lie, I had more fun running up to them & slugging a mean right hook and stomping them than actually trying to shoot. I wish melee was actually usable because the animations are clean. I assumed it was supposed to be a replacement for the utter drought of ammunition, but a loading tip says "Don't rely on your fists, only a last resort." TL;DR melee does absolutely no damage, and no.. you can't upgrade your melee strength / force whatsoever. Which begs the question; why even add the ability to melee, knowing it does nothing and you can't upgrade it? Especially considering the vast majority of enemies spit acid puddles everywhere forbidding you from getting within 20 feet of them. 

All in all, I expected better. It takes existing ideas from other popular titles and.. that's it. It doesn't expand upon any of them, nor does it explore anything deeper than face value. It genuinely just doesn't feel original, new, or fun.


Summarized:
As someone who lives for the horror genre, this doesn't do it justice for me. I wasn't scared a single time, I never felt engrossed in the atmosphere, and to top it all off--I just couldn't care. The game gives you no reason to give an inkling of thought or consideration towards anyone or anything--leading you to have no interest in seeing the results. Final verdict? It's... mediocre. Average. Mid. Generic. "Okay." It's a game, that's really all I can say. Not great, not terrible. Get it on sale.

review_text:
Pathologic 2 feels more like an art piece than a video game, and that’s a good thing. Never before have I been so immersed in a world as I was here. The characters, the city, the atmosphere, the sound—all of it makes you feel as though you’re truly in this eerie place of mystery and danger. The creators clearly had a vision in mind for how the world was supposed to be. There were no constraints, no one telling them what to do—total creative freedom.

Because so few games achieve this so well, I felt compelled to leave my review here. Sure, the game has its flaws, but they never get in the way of completing it. In fact, they have the opposite effect—the clunkiness feels intentional, not like a result of the developers’ lack of skill. The world feels alive, and I deeply appreciate the incredible writing and worldbuilding.

It’s something so different from all the generic fantasy and sci-fi games out there. This game is a rollercoaster of emotions, whether it’s the in-game characters you fear for or the labor of love poured into it by the developers. Pathologic 2 is not just a true indie marvel but also an inspiration for other developers.

I thought with it coming back and how you can support the Patreon to get access to the beta, they would add or at least change some QOL issues, but so far it's the same. It's still the old wait 8-24 hours for progress and then level up just to get quests that take forever to complete because they are just sit and wait for resources. 

	The game is still weirdly laggy or just delayed in combat. I can click on a unit, and it just never registers, or it's really delayed, and dragging a mortar attack can just not work. The quests can give you some strong fights, but most of the time they are quick, and I bet if you spend months getting to the late game, it's more interesting, but I'll be dead by then. So far the grinding to level up my troops is super boring. The cost for promoting units is insane too; for instance, the recon vehicle that they give you costs 2800 iron just to promote it once. If you spend money, then it's easy because the paid versions are just far better because, like every cash-grab mobile game, it's pay-to-win.

I really liked this game, don't get me wrong, but I thought with how long they were working on the game, they were going to really do some changes like some online play or at least make it feel more fluid, but it's still a single-player game. and still feels clunky. I can see why people would like to play the game as it was from all those years ago. I just think there are just new games out now that, although they may not be exactly the same, have a more fulfilling feel and are worth your time.

review_text:
Wonderful aesthetic, great build flow and scaling up of tasks and tension, especially for the first few towns when you don't have the proper view of where exactly all of your support structures and whatnot can go.
Villager AI is sometimes incredibly stupid, and what constitutes a dangerous environment or an undesirable time to actually do some work for once is either really inconsistent or really vague. If lumberjacks won't clear trees near a fire elemental, repairmen shouldn't repair the slightly damaged fire pit next to him. And if the bowyer is swimming in silk, I expect full cylinders firing on quiver production, instead of the French-style "we'll get to it when we feel like it" mentality that most refined and manufacturing villagers tend to hold. Very tempting to soak one or two of those slackers in Cullis Gate goo to set an example...
The big reason I write this review is to help spread the word of the great middle ground that most reviewers seem to either miss or ignore. Yes, the game starts as a town builder and transitions into a steadily tougher tower defense game. But each town map can be completely cleared of corruption, turning the tower defense into a once in a Blood Moon insurance policy, and turning that town into a economic powerhouse for all surrounding maps. 
To explain: World map is broken up into lots of strategic maps. Each scenario has a single spawn point for the enemy, that grows over time. But your buildings prevent the spread of the corruption. And one building, fire pits, both have great anti-corruption properties and are totally ignored by enemies. To boot, if any building is built near corruption, over time, it will force the tainted land to return to its former self, preventing enemy spawns. Repeat this cycle until all the corrupted land is removed, and it will never return on that scenario. Ever.
Fire pits remove corrupted land, but enemy buildings also have to go. Thankfully, the game also has automated golems to help your towers defend. But these golems consider ANY build space your town, including around fire pits. Build a pit near an enemy structure, and your golems will swarm on the attack and obliterate it, keeping your fragile villagers safe.

Hopefully this long winded guide-within-a-review helps both old and new players understand that the objective of the game is pacification, not resistance, and the game is a really great hybrid of a lot of genres. Use the advantage of infinite golems and glory to your nascent empires!

review_text:
Lost Ruins is not a bad game, but it struggles with conflicting design choices that prevent it from being a great experience.

The game begins as a challenging, horror-inspired experience. Traps can kill you in two hits, healing items are scarce, and monsters are tough unless you manage a sneak attack. This tense, survival-horror atmosphere holds until around the second boss. At that point, the game shifts dramatically, offering an abundance of powerful tools and weapons, transitioning into a more action-oriented style.

Both styles—horror and action—can be enjoyable on their own. However, the abrupt transition between them weakens the overall experience. By the third boss, the challenge diminishes significantly. The final bosses can be beaten by simply turning invisible and attacking a few times, stripping away any remaining sense of difficulty and horror.

This shift is unfortunate because the game's early survival-horror design shows real promise, similar to what games like Fear and Hunger achieve. However, the developers' desire to give players as many tools as possible undermines the initial tension and challenge.

On the positive side, the animation style is very well done, with clever little details in every character's movement. Whether or not this style appeals to you is subjective, but the trailer gives a clear idea of what to expect. The small amount of story is enjoyable, and the characters have just enough personality to be engaging during their brief appearances. While not groundbreaking, it feels like genuine effort was put into the narrative and characters.

On the downside, some of the music was genuinely headache-inducing, and my controller would randomly vibrate for no apparent reason after starting the game, which was frustrating.

Overall, Lost Ruins feels like someone's first serious attempt at creating a complex video game—a project they likely learned a lot from. Thankfully, the game's short length (about eight hours) means its bigger issues don't completely overshadow the fun.

If you like the visual style and aren't too concerned about having a true survival-horror experience, there's still plenty to enjoy in Lost Ruins.

While the game has really nice visuals, there is a lot about the game that generally just irks me. 

1. This game is heavy on AI. I can tell that at least some NPCs use AI voicing, and it sounds horrible. 
2. This game has a really bad issue with translation/localization. There are parts of the game in Mandarin/Cantonese, without any way of translating it. Some text things have a built-in translation function, but not all... so some aspects of the game you just kind of have to guess.
3. The first day I played, everything loaded/rendered in very well. Every day after, my character T-poses while running and falling. I walk into an area and it takes a minute or two for assets to render in. I click "F" to interact with something and it takes like 5 seconds for the interaction to start.
4. The game does a really poor job of explaining aspects of the game. After nearly a week, there's still so much of the game, including combat mechanics, that are/were never alluded to at any point, especially in the "tutorial" in the beginning, so I guess you're expected to find out things on your own? This also speaks to how convoluted this game is combat-wise. Sometimes less is more. 
Overall, it feels like the developers did the bare minimum to create the game and overutilized AI. At the very least, the game is free, or I'd probably want to get my money back. Honestly, if this game is a representation of using AI in video games moving forward, the future is B L E A K.

review_text:
I am...having this game on edge between a positive or negative recommendation. There are definitely things that I liked, yet around equally as much that I disliked.

Liked:
- The graphical features of the game itself. I am not talking about the content they were used for, be it the design choice for the looks of the map or the way they wanted enemies to look like. Graphics were looking nice and I cannot complain about any unpolished "that stuff glitchin'!" looks. Especially when you can view fragments from the "outside" of your usual area, the view with its lightning is looking quite fancy.
- The simple gameplay choices. For that I'm considering about the survival itself, low need of ammo management, HP management, how to approach enemies, how to get around in your current area and the rarely appearing, easy puzzles as a change.

Disliked:
- "Running in circles" being the main gameplay mechanic. I don't mind basic objectives being "do xy to access area yz" but if action xy expects me to get back to the same spot, we're not even talking about an area here, 3 to 4 times to get to progress...it certainly gives off a monotonous feeling. While this may only be true for ~half the chapters, it definitely left a mark when thinking about the game.
- The price-playtime ratio. Now...I know everyone plays at their own pace and I may not be the fella taking a look at every pixel of the environment, atleast in this case, yet I think that I spent a fair amount analyzing the environment to figure out what to do in a decent time and still got through this game too quickly. This is probably the tipping point towards the negative recommendation from my POV. 

Warning:
- This game does not treat the use of gore lightly. Its presence is available for atleast 98% of your game time in every aspect, map design, characters, enemies and probably every action you find.

TL;DR:
- Simple, enjoyable playstyle, graphics itself looking good. 
- Danger of repetitious feeling, too pricy (tipping point).
- Care for extreme use of gore if topic sensitive.

The puzzles are either overly obvious or ridiculously indirect with very few being in that sweet spot. There have been many times when I go "Would have never done that because it make more sense to just [XYZ] skipping having to do [ABC]." 
It's also ridiculous how translucent the hint points are out side of the tutorial because It feels like they're 5% opacity in comparison leading you to just click everywhere to see if you missed any. Of course there are guides for the hint points but I'd rather just pull up a guide for the puzzle itself since the hints scale in cost and aren't guaranteed to aid you [maxed out the hints and had to brute force my way through the puzzle at one point because it repeated everything I already knew].

review_text:
Tape to Tape provides exactly what we need on PC - A fun hockey game.

While it doesn't have the franchises and true-to-the-sport nature that EA NHL games have, it makes up for it in fun and replayability. You can play through the campaign countless times - picking different skills, choosing different superstars, and selecting different paths along your journey. I spent nearly 40 hours playing this game to get 100% of the achievements completed and IT'S STILL IN EARLY ACCESS. I look forward to seeing what a "Finished product" will look like. 

I give the devs a lot of credit for this game. They are incredibly active in their Discord, they listen to player feedback and implement changes accordingly, and they host amazing Twitch streams where they are transparent with their roadmaps.

The humor of the game is perfect if you're a fan of hockey, the gameplay feels perfectly arcade-y, the characters all have their own unique greatness to them that makes them easy to love, and for a world based on a silly hockey game, the storyline is fantastic.

If I had to nitpick, my list of complaints would be pretty small. The CPU AI can be a little weird at times causing players to get in your way more than help you and there lacks exciting functionality like online multiplayer and team customization that would be fantastic to have.

All things considered, this was easily worth every penny I spent on it. I can't wait to see it ran at AGDQ2024!

--------UPDATED REVIEW--------

Since my review, Tape to Tape has received significant free QoL updates and amazing content that builds on the already 10/10 game. The AI has gotten much better and will continue to improve with additional updates coming soon and team customization has been added, far exceeding my initial expectations.

The roadmap for future updates look amazing and every time a new update goes live, I find myself jumping back in for a run or three.

Still looking forward to the final product and the new bosses.

yes... BUT - there's a lot of BUTS with this game (spelled B-U-G-S). See list below.

The good - it's fun with friends. If you like shooting waves of zombies it's entertaining. There's not that much to the game other than slogging through various maps killing zombies. Sometimes I'm not even sure why I like the game. 

The bad / annoying stuff - BUGS. There are LOADS of bugs. Some of them are extremely irritating. Even after the recent update the devs did not fix almost any of the common bugs that have plagued this game. They seemed more interested in nerfing the over-powered weapons. The OP weapons were fun to use, but they did render 95% of the other weapons useless. Now the game seems too hard - it might be difficult to know what weapon configurations are good and how to use them. There are tons of weapon mods, but hard to know how they compare. Running out of ammo is a new problem - an annoying one.  

List of bugs:
- Horde mode - zombies get stuck where you can't find them and the game can't be completed. This is game breaking. I hope they fixed it. It would be easy to have a wave reset or something. 
- Can't talk to players (voice) in your party if they are in a different lobby. There's no text chat
- If someone is in a party, there's no way to contact them (like, if you want to ask if they want to party up with you, or when they'll be done their current round, or anything). You can "nudge" them but that's it.  
- The game hangs / doesn't start if a member of your party leaves as you are loading in, or even if you try to continue to a second map after the first when one player has left. You are forced to restart, and when you do you lose your party members and can't find them again because they're in different lobbies most likely. 
- If the party leader disconnects or leaves, the entire game stops and the remaining three players are forced out without being able to finish the round. 
- New bug - can't seem to pick up partially full ammo mags when dropped 
- Very difficult to know exactly what the chipsets do and how to compare their relative performance (add something to measure in the shooting range perhaps)
- Warheads don't always explode when thrown, and disappear
- Matchmaking - a complete disaster. Hard to say everything wrong with it. Best to bring your own friends. Very hard to get a full party of people who are looking to play the same level and difficulty as you.
