review_text:
I wanted to love this game so much.

And at first, I did. My first few hours in the game were pretty nice, but certain issues became apparent with more playtime. The love and work the Devs put in are clear to see, and I'm sure lots of people will have a great time with this. But for me many of the features that set Plum Grove apart also harm it in the end.

The generational gameplay loop, the fact that NPCs can marry, die, etc. It made you think the town and world would feel alive, but that's what killed it in my opinion. The NPC interaction is so shallow and lifeless, so meaningless ultimately. As an old timer of the farm/life sim genre, I know you rarely get novel-level character development, but this was so much less than even what Harvest Moon had on the SNES. 

The NPC weddings that come and go throughout the seasons feel like nothing more than a game of random ''pair the spares'' since no one really has any relationships with each other. No rival events, no dialogue hinting at who they might be interested in. It all feels so pointless, that not even the deaths shake you that much, most of them you never really even know by name anyway.

Even your own marriage is a dull affair. Again no relationship events, no special dialogue, nothing. All the NPCs are basically just randomly generated sims meant to keep the wheelwork of the generations going. In essence, in order to have a game where infinite generations were possible it made none of them matter. 

I could add that the economy is sort of broken besides. As crops are almost so worthless I nearly stopped growing them apart from a few to eat. But I realize that could get sorted out with tweaking and such.

Overall, I love the art and I respect the dedication of the Devs, but please consider what you want out of the game before you buy.

People are complaining about trash. They are not exagerating. I bought this game before that feature was implemented and I might have given it a more positive review them. Let me describe how bad the issue is:

As soon as you chop down a tree and it drops wood, a timer starts. If it is not picked up and stored by then it will turn into wood waste. Bad, but still kinda salvagable because you can process it into material at a loss. Your fault after all, get more haulers. However, this is not where the cycle of trash ends. To process the wood waste into useful wood, you have to bring to a processor and have the trashmen process it into something useful. This takes a while and the wood waste continues to rot while stored on a trashpile or inside the processor. I REPEAT, THE WOOD WASTE CONTINUES TO ROT WHILE STORED PROPERLY. After it rots, it will turn into trash move from the wood waste stockpile to the trash stockpile inside the same building, but after a while the trash stockpile will get overfilled and the trash will be ejected outside the building. This causes issues because slimes will spawn and attack your people if it's not cleaned. This slows down the economy even further and causes more trash to accumulate. As far as I've seen the final stage of trash doesn't rot away into nothing but must be stored permanantly, effectively turning the game a WALL-E simulator. This happens not just with wood, but food, STONE, METAL, CRYSTALS and CRAFTED ITEMS as well. You can open a chest and thousands of gold worth of equipment will rot into trash before it can all be stored.

This is probably the worst issue I've had but there are a lot more.

I really wanted to like it, but honestly, rarely have I had such a feeling of [i]wasted[/i] time while playing a video game.

review_text:
I tried so hard to enjoy this. I played it months ago, got bored, and dropped it for a while. But the reviews were so positive that I gave it another chance and committed to finishing it, but it still left me feeling disappointed. I do love the style of the game. The 2D look is super cute, but that's as far as my praise goes.
The world just has no life. The townsfolk have no personality and add nothing to the story, and I really didn't care about any of them. They only existed to complete quests. That's it. It was also incredibly confusing and annoying that everyone would sell things, and you would only be allowed to buy a finite number. For example, if you want to have a nicely organized farm, you might make crop fields 5x4 so you'd need 20 seeds for each crop. Well too bad because the farmer is only selling 14 seeds, so you have to go around to everyone in town looking for 6 more seeds and wasting your whole day away. And don't even get me started on if you're looking for a particular person, say the blacksmith to fix your pickaxe. If he's not at his forge, good luck, you'll never find him because the map will only show you either your family or people whose quest you've finished.
I was also very disappointed in the whole "you can die from disease!" thing. I never vaccinated my character or took any sort of medicine and didn't get sick ONCE. I was hoping for some typhoid or small pox or something! I never even saw any of the townsfolk get sick! Every single one died of old age. I was so desperate for my character to die in the end so I could get the achievement that I ended up just letting her starve rather than wait for her to die of old age.
Like I said, I really REALLY wanted to like this game, but if you want a life sim game with LIFE, this just wasn't it.

review_text:
Should you buy this? Maybe

If you love guarding missions, or missions that force you to stay in one place while NPCs "hack" systems while enemies pop in out of nowhere and attack you from all sides then buy this game. If you hated JC2 or JC3's more free flowing game play and wished that missions were absolutely required to take over an enemy facility then you will love this game. If you love needlessly complex systems that make game play frustrating while trying to deal with a chaotic game then you will love this game. If you love how enemy units would spawn in out of nowhere to attack you then you will love this game.
If the above sounds great, then buy the game now and ignore what I say below.

The good things from this game. I loved feeling like there was an actual revolution going on. Having revolutionaries join in the fight was nice. It really felt like you were fighting a battle to free people. The past games felt like a solo war with the occasional battle with incompetent NPCs that I largely ignored. As cool as this is, it just becomes background noise after a while.

I like that there are weapons with so many different neat features. The gun that turns into a shielded turret and the guns with various explosive weapons. They are kind of fun. But I also miss having separate grenades and various explosive weapons.

The really big, annoying thing is the missions. I loved the free flowing nature of the previous games. I could approach capturing the map however I pleased. Now I have to perform missions to capture virtually every part of the map. I hated having to complete missions in JC2&3, but I did them when I had to. Missions are a major part of JC4.
You have to protect someone or something while waves of enemies swarm you or travel around activating things. There is some variations, but they are not terribly fun.

I miss having the supply drop available. Along with many of the things from JC3. The mechs and jet suite were fun. Yes, you can get them as overpriced DLC, but I won't. It is not a fun enough game to warrant buying it, at least at full price.

Long story short, am I happy with the game? I know that I am not enjoying it as much as JC2 or JC3. I have played 6 hours, and I am honestly getting tired of it already. It has some innovative and interesting things added to it. I wish that they would mix the good from the earlier games with the good from this one for future games. We will see if they do.

If you are going to buy it, buy it on sale. I don't recommend buying it at full price. If you love the series, then try it. If you are looking to get into it then buy JC2 or JC3, they are more fun.

review_text:
A fun little Metroidvania with only a handful of very minor stumbling blocks.

As the biggest pro, the spire artwork and animation is consistently amazing. Light sources reflect dynamically on the characters which gives the scenes an incredible feeling of depth. Attack animations have a good amount of heft to them, though slower two-handed animations look a bit floaty instead of giving a feeling of 'gravity' to the swing arc. For enemies, all attacks are well telegraphed and simple to read.

Combat has an odd mix of slightly floaty weapons with punishingly strict committal, though enemies are forced just as much to watch their attack whiff as you jab them in the back with a dagger, which makes the combat 'fair' for both parties, at least as long as you manage to keep it to a 1v1. Fighting multiple enemies at once is more often than not suicidal and sometimes you best choice is to run away or leave and reenter the room, resetting all still living enemies while dead ones remain temporarily disposed of (moving through enough rooms will revive all enemies in passed rooms). Weapons can feel somewhat floaty because one-handed and two-handed weapons are swung in an arc, but that arc has a steady speed throughout the entire animation, which can make especially slow attack swings feel very weak and weightless. Since being able to modify the swing speed through equipment is an option, I'm not sure if there is an elegant solution to that however.

I think the biggest roadblock a lot of people will face getting used to combat isn't its grounded attacks, but the fact that attacking mid-jump will completely void all horizontal momentum, meaning that if you attack while jumping forward you will just drop straight down instead. This paired with how the game likes to place ranged enemies across precarious jumps makes platforming a lot more dangerous than one would expect from a very platforming-focused metroidvania.

The typical solution to that of course represent magic and the disposable single-use wands that litter the environment. Magic is tied to MP which does not naturally regenerate, meaning you have to rely on consumables to refresh your MP or use equipment with provides you with some level of MP recovery. Wands are a reasonably abundant resource, but they are still limited in use, so they're best reserved for situations where melee would be too dangerous to commit to or open a handful of doors that require magic to activate their respective levers.

For the minor stumbling blocks I brought up in the beginning, while combat is pretty fun once you get the hang of it, the game has somewhat of an over-reliance on status effects and DoTs. Pretty much any attack won't just deal flat damage, but also give you increasingly long stacks of bleed, burn or poison, freeze you in place, invert your controls, and so forth. On Veteran difficulty these can also stack repeatedly on additional hits, frequently providing you with DoT effects that exceed even your maximum possible HP. Most ofthese effects can be countered and even temporarily negated with consumables, but in the heat of combat it can feel rather frustrating to have defeated a a single enemy but losing several items just to counter the DoT and replenish the health you've lost just as the result of burning.

Traps and trickery are our best allies in this game, learning which enemies are too dangerous to take head-on and how to bypass and/or defeat them without even allowing them to fight back are typically your best choices.

review_text:
Kingdom Come: Deliverance II - A Departure from Its Roots
This isn’t Kingdom Come: Deliverance II; it feels like Embracer Group-funded fanfiction that betrays the spirit of the original. At most 6/10.
What Went Wrong?

Historical Accuracy? Vanished.
Gameplay Improvements? Barely noticeable.
Story? A disjointed mess.
RPG Elements? Reduced to a cinematic adventure game.

Gameplay: Stagnation with a Side of Simplification
The gameplay is a near-carbon copy of KCD1, but dumbed down for broader appeal. Combat feels marginally smoother, with ranged mechanics seeing slight tweaks, but it’s nowhere near a leap forward. It’s safe, uninspired, and lacks the depth to elevate the experience.

Story & RPG: A Narrative Trainwreck
The story unravels like a feverish nightmare, devoid of coherence or purpose. You begin with a simple task (deliver a letter and negotiate), but the game railroads you into a relentless series of disasters. Your choices, the heart of any RPG, are meaningless. Obvious pitfalls loom, yet Henry stumbles into them like a hapless fool, stripped of agency.
The narrative subjects Henry to a grueling 100-hour humiliation ritual: beaten, imprisoned, degraded, and lectured by caricatures. The capable agent of KCD1 is reduced to a bumbling observer, disconnected from the world and his own story. The plot feels like a betrayal when played after the first game, with events that clash jarringly and fail to build on established lore. By the end, Henry’s quest for revenge fizzles out for the most contrived reasons, leaving him aimless, hollow, and devoid of growth. He’s a shell of a protagonist with no desires beyond shallow “romance” options, no arc, and no future.

History: Sacrificed for Modern Sensibilities
The soul of Kingdom Come, its commitment to historical immersion, has been gutted. Real events are warped with fictional liberties, anachronistic elements like a synagogue appearing centuries early, and modern buzzwords that shatter the setting’s authenticity. Historical figures are misrepresented, and the game leans into heavy-handed, unquestionable narratives that feel like propaganda. Henry, and by extension the player, is forced to nod along, unable to challenge or engage with these jarring inclusions.

Final Verdict
Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is a disappointment, trading the gritty, grounded charm of its predecessor for modern slop. It’s a game that forgets its roots, alienates its fans, and leaves Henry—and the player—lost in a hollow, directionless experience. But just as the bible tells us: to a starving man every bitter thing is sweet; Gamers are starving.

I sadly wouldn't recommend Scon to the average player as its gameplay just doesn't feel fun to engage with but if you're looking for a beautiful world to look through and admire then Scorn might be for you.

To put it simply, Scorn is fundamentally a piece of artwork that has a game slapped onto it. Scorn involves elements of combat that feel out of place and unnecessary with enemies feeling like more of an inconvenience whether you engage with them or not. There are plenty of puzzles that usually feel fine and aren't too challenging to complete but feel used incorrectly as they tend to push you through a linear world when I feel they could have been used to feel like  they are opening up this strange world to you. HOWEVER Scorn is truly one of the best visual experiences I've had in a game as its clear inspiration from H.R Giger creates a disturbing and foreign world that ingolfs you in its atmosphere that unsettles you with the fear of the unknown in an alien world. There is little narrative or lore which I personally feel works in its favor as it feeds into this feeling of fear of a world that you don't understand. It's a world that clearly has a story to tell but wants you as a player to create your own understanding of the world that makes sense to you. Scorn is an extremely flawed masterpiece that tries to be something that it isn't and shouldn't be but still manages to be one of the most beautiful games i've ever played.

review_text:
[h2]Full Game Review[/h2]
This is a hard game for me to review. Objectively, Arkham City is a good game. However, I was very disappointed by this game. Maybe it is a product of its time, or maybe my expectations were too high after playing Arkham Asylum, but Arkham City felt like a disappointing sequel. It does not innovate itself enough to warrant existing as a sequel, both narrative and gameplay wise.

[h3]Narrative[/h3]
The pacing of the story was awful and all over the place. They jammed so many villains in the main story, and this left no room for Titan-stuff/Protocol 10 to breath. You were constantly chasing various macguffin for the first half of the game that did nothing to advance the story. Then out of nowhere, the game presents you with a twist regarding Protocol 10. In addition, the twist was so bad that it could have only came from a mustache-twirling villain. To be fair, Arkham Asylum also had a "chase macguffin from villain to villain plot", but that worked as an origin story. If the second entry of your trilogy had no meaningful character nor plot progression, then you are doing something wrong.

It's not all bad though. The second twist regarding Titan-stuff was quite good as it made sense logically/narritively + was foreshadowed. And the boss fight against Mr Freeze's boss fight was was executed (even though it does not make sense narritively for them to fight in the first place, but I digress).

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The gameplay felt repetitive due to poor level and quest design. Various locations would get reused throughout the main story mission, which meant navigating through the same corridors multiple times in a single playthrough. And you cannot excuse the game but calling it a metroidvania! Blocking access to parts of the game due to plot-specific reasons should not make it a metroidvania! Walking around in the same crammped cooridors as Batman is the anti-thesis of fun! I would take a thought out, but linear game like Arkham Asylum over something like Arkham City any day. At Asylum had the decency to give previous locations a redesign if they had to be revisited.

Gliding through the city is fun, but gets tedious after a while. There is a huge circular restriction zone right in the middle of the city which cannot be glided through. This forces you to always travel in an arc around the circle, making the city essentially feel like a straight line. And the main quest would often take you go from one end to another which added to the tedium.

On the plus side, Arkham City does include a new gadget that was incorporated in both traversal and combat in an interesting way.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
I was initially going to give this game a thumbsup, but then I played Arkham Knight. Now Arkham Knight is not perfect. However, it addressed all issues I had with Arkham City game which makes Arkham City game is easily skippable. And life is too short to play skippable games.

review_text:
I played this game for the first time a long time ago, and I fucking loved it. I can't say exactly when, but it was when the game was just an arena shooter with a Grab-A-Gun at the beginning of each arena. I played it for hours and hours in one sitting, I was addicted to it for like a month straight
I used to run JUST explosives, grenades, shotgun secondary fire, that pistol that shoot C4's I forgot the name of...

Now, I actually bought it and it's not bad, it just changed. Not for the better, nor for the worse, it's just different.
Basically, the game is just the combat of Titanfall 2 with the core gameplay loop of Risk of Rain 2. It used to be haha fun arena shooter, shoot guy in head guy dies neuron activation, but now it's just Risk of Rain.

Now that would've been fine by me. Sure the core gameplay loop was not what I liked, but the gameplay itself is fun right? Well yes but actually no. Don't get me wrong the gameplay is fantastic still, the movement is fluid and fast and the shooting itself felt punchy and satisfying, but it's just so buggy and inconsistent.
Wanna boost yourself using an explosive? depending on how the game is feeling that day, you might get launched 2 inches or to the stratosphere.
Wanna use the C4 at all? you just fucking can't because it keeps clipping through the ground.
Just fell through the map after accidentally clipping into it while trying to wall run? don't worry, you'll keep respawning off the map so you can keep falling forever
The game is just buggy as hell, the amount of times I dropped a x64 combo because of random stuff like this happening is extremely frustrating

A couple of more points: the objective is never explained to the player, the starting area is pointless, the alternate fire modes for some of the weapons barely change anything at all, melee range feels weird, accidental clipping happens all the fucking time, and there are areas that exist just for future updates (which makes no sense)

TL;DR for the DEV: please bring back the grenade launching shotgun, fix the bugs (obviously), take out the areas that just exist for future updates (like the dungeons), bring back the box arena as an alternate gamemode (please?), and make movement more consistent and exploitable. Then I'll buy the game instantly

TL;DR: the game used to be simple and polished, now it's inconsistent, pointless, and FILLED with more bugs

FINAL VERDICT: 4/10

Wouldn't even recommend it if it's on sale, wish I can refund it.

review_text:
Not here to try and convince anybody that TGR isn't worth their time.. doubt with a Steam population as low as it has, barely anyone will even see this. Still, I left couple lengthier feedback posts on TGR discord for the devs past season, and wanted to see if Season 2 brings any welcome changes - not seeing any, so I'll lay down the truth here as well.

This should not have been an online requirement live service game. I think the devs thought this would be some big hit to take on bigger giants in the market, and instead it just dwindles in its very low playerbase, making the online part of the game (one that earns all the fancy cosmetics) a real chore - long and ridiculously unfair matchmaking (whilst not even filling up most spots in a match) ; brutally grindy season track (exponential curve, so first 10 levels is like one last) ; and a lot of cores and every single cosmetic tied to online progression only, so if you want to have fun by yourself trying to do better on some tracks solo (whilst looking fly), then be willing to invest a bunch of time into playing with others just to get bombarded by missles every 5 seconds, trying to finish some dumb daily missions like a good little sucker. 

Can't just have a fun game, no no no - got to have that seasonal track and daily logins, to keep the player retention like every other BS live service game, right?!

First season took me approx 50 hours to finish, and I had a winrate of over 50% over 327 matches (games should fill up with 8 players, but most of the matches it was me vs 1-5 other players, making 6-8 player lobbies very rare, and I did try both NA/EU servers at all kinds of different times.. after a few weeks into the season the waiting time (matchmaking > loading players/levels > flyby cam > potg) takes up as much time as actually going through the 3 maps in one match, so by that conclusion a single season will waste tens of hours of your time, just by mindlessly waiting around.

As mentioned, the player count is kind of low (not screaming the game is dying.. but expect some queue times go upwards of 2-5 minutes further into the season). Steamdb shows around ~20 people playing (it was around 60-100 when the first season launched), so most of the players come from this game being a freebie on Game Pass, so if that contract ever ends (which they usually eventually do), expect the player count to totally plummet. To make things worse, there are 6-7 regions to play in (good for latency, but terrible for a very low population in online games, forcing segregation).

Also this game is centered around online-only, so if TGR crew doesn't have a end-of-life plan for this game, it can just shut down over the next year or so with the usual "oh well we tried, but we're so glad to have people come along on this journey (but this aint profitable for us anymore so we're shutting down)" type of bs as usual. I hope I'm very wrong about this, but TGR does not have any client-saves, nor can this be played in offline mode, even if you're just interested in solo-ing some tracks for better times or to have simple casual fun. And to top it all off, this will be another one of those infinitely in Early Access type of games, to justify whatever is wrong with it - and all the diehard fans can always make excuses "oh well its still beta" or "oh, this is planned to be implemented sometime / soon / who knows" like any of it matters if the game is already in full motion with selling itself and pumping out seasons.

To touch on cosmetics, this game goes hard on exclusivity, so hey.. if you didn't play in Beta / Season 1 / Season X, then feel ready to see others with stuff you'll never own, because clearly you're not worthy to be with the cool crowd. As far as other games doing seasonal track better, Minecraft Dungeons has a way to let people progress whatever season pass they choose for those rewards, but I guess 'fear of missing out' is better to keep people active from season to season. 

Also the store, for no good reason at all, rotates out items daily (and some smaller stuff every 6 hours).. So, why does that matter? Again, purely for suckering people into logging in daily, so if you're after an item to come back into rotation that you weren't able to afford (or missed out) when it was last in, be ready to log in daily for 2-3 months with your fingers crossed (quite literally that was the time for something I wanted in Season 1 to come back) - all of the cosmetics governed by 'you playing vs others' (something that this game doesn't even feel to mention on its store page).. if you buy the game, you get no cosmetics apart from one base car. More stuff added in these little rotations also mean less likelyhood of you ever seeing them again.

Still no cosmetic presets either, and there's already a decent amount of items in the game that this should have been long implemented (should've simply done one loadout for each car body), but its not like anybody plays this game for the cosmetics anyway, right? RIGHT?!

There are a bunch of other smaller issues as well, but I doubt the devs decided to consider my feedback on their discord (which is actually nicely done for this game), and I doubt they will consider anything mentioned here either. I don't hate the game, but I do despise the GaaS model they decided to tie this game onto and then sink it. It plays fine and was fun at first, but personally I'd suggest investing your time into Rocket League instead, if hitting balls with cars is your thing - as terrible and toxic as that game can be, at least you can still get better at it after playing over 10 hours, and it will probably be around in the coming years - something I can't see TGR have a future for (and I do hope I'm wrong).

Sadly, if/once I'll be back to complete S2, I won't care for player competition in it, and will just have to idle-macro my PC for those cosmetic rewards for 3-4 days straight, whilst I play some other game that is fun and values my time. 

Everything I mentioned here, can be fixed, even if not entirely, then surely for much better, hence the negative review until they do.

review_text:
Quick Description:
-Despot's Game is a dungeon crawling autobattler w/ charm and intrigue for days.  This game is the perfect mix of challenge, mystery, full on weirdness, and a good shake of tactics.  The learning curve is quite steep, but this is one of the very best autobattlers out there.  There is a ton of content already, less than a year into early access, and I am really excited to see what gets added by the 1.0 release.

What's Good:
-I love how strategic this game is.  You will need to decide which room to enter in the dungeon, how to position your units, which upgrades to purchase, when to buy new types of units, and when to buy more food to keep your army at full strength.  This is exactly what I was hoping for from an autobattler.  When you are successful, it is b/c you have made good decisions, which makes this game feel really tactical.  
-I am a huge fan of the visual style!  The pixel art is detailed, really cool visually, and I love all of the different types of army units, monsters, and terrifying bosses.  I love the blend between robots and monsters, and it works really well here.  
-The skill ceiling is extremely high in this game.  This game will kick your ass until you start to adapt.  When I play this game, it kind of feels like if Enter the Gungeon were an autobattler and had really bizarre robot monsters.  I have played for almost 7 hrs, and I still have so much more to learn on my way to having a victorious run.
-There is a good amount of build variety during runs.  The devs keep adding more content which is great, but as of now, there is still a ton of unique and really cool synergies.  Putting together the perfect army that is balanced is such a great feeling.  I love being able to steamroll a group of baddies in the dungeon when my army starts to become powerful.

Could Use Some Changes:
-Hopefully, by the 1.0 release, the devs will add a more detailed tutorial.  This is fairly complex game.  I didn't even realize for the first few hrs that I could manually upgrade my units in a skill tree.  This is something that should be covered in a tutorial.  
-I would also like to see more variety in enemy types, alternative bosses, and dungeon variety.  The more variety you have, the better.  It's challenging for the devs, b/c everything must be balanced, but it would help make runs more unique and keep players coming back for more.  It would be great if there were alternative dungeons that you could visit or potentially alternative paths that you can select from, just a thought.
-As I mentioned earlier, every roguelight in early access needs more items, more synergies, and more meta progression.  This game is no exception.  It seems to be lacking quite a bit in meta progression, so that's an area I'm hoping they focus on in the future.  I'm really excited to see how this game shapes up over the next 6-12 months.

Consensus:
-Solid Game (Tier 3 and makes up 35% of my reviews).  This looks like the quintessential autobattler, but really shines in artistic direction, really unique army balance, and really high fun factor.  I wasn't the biggest fan of this genre before this game, but I'm now a believer.  I'm really excited to explore this genre more and see how this gem turns out once it reaches it's 1.0 release.

review_text:
Nah. 

Walking simulator with some tedious survival mechanics slapped on. Highly overrated. There's an interesting story hidden somewhere under a lot of symbolism, cryptic dialogue and some fourth wall shenanigans. 

The presentation of the game is very bare bones, there's very little interaction between the PC and the world or between the NPCs and the world, which makes it feel very artificial and bland. This puts a lot of strain on the dialogue and gameplay to carry the story and it just doesn't work. The gameplay is virtually non existant aside from walking around from highlighted NPC to highlighted NPC and bartering with people for resources needed for the survival mechanics. And I could forgive all that and play it for the story only, if the dialogue wasn't so intentionally witholding of information. It's all very weirdly written, like the people involved forgot how to describe mundane events using concise language. I get that it's supposed to create an aura of mystery, but it just doesn't do it for me.

And now for the trigger that made me stop playing and uninstall: while looting an important quest item from a container, I accidentally right clicked. This usually quick-loots the item and puts it into your inventory. However my inventory was full, because for some reason the game devs thought it's a good idea to have a very limited inventory in a game built around scavenging barter items and supplies for the numerous needs that your PC has. Failing to fit into my inventory, the item was taken out of the container and dropped on the floor, which normally wouldn't be a problem, because you can pick it up. However, before I was able to make room in my inventory and pick the thing up, the time advanced to midnight, where everything you dropped on the floor during the day gets magically destroyed. Which wouldn't be that much of a problem, because you can just reload the game and replay the last few minutes of game, right? Of course you could, if the game devs didn't severely restrict your ability to save by forcing you to physically travel to certain spots in town in order to save. And if I had actually remembered to do that less than 30 minutes ago. 

Nah.

EDIT: After ~44 hours in the game, 3 playthroughs and 100% completion I can safely summarise:

The bad - game has incoherently presented story, mediocre graphics, misrepresented setting, only two unique bosses. 

The good - solid gameplay loop, great level design (functionality wise), stable performance with minor issues (yeah, it is a plus nowadays).

It does not have same impact or quality as original Dead Space, why is it even compared to that game? The matching aspects are quite superfluous. The game costs too much, it is not an AAA product and UE5 is not giving the experience any favours. 

If you wanna get it - get it at a bigger discount, 30 euro is max you should pay for it. I do not think it will sell that well now considering how people taunt it as "hard/punishing" with "heavy story". I was hoping Bloober would get it right after success of SH2. It is absolutely a passable game. Especially if you are a hardcore survival horror fan, as it is a linear action horror shooter. The resources are slightly scarce only initially as you buy them, you can craft them, find them and get some in drops, too. My stash was overflowing at around 60% into the progression.

The combat statement made at first - I do retract, it is too easy when you quickly figure out the mechanics (I died around 5 times in the first playthrough on normal, on none on the bosses except the last one, where I died 2-3 times. 2nd playthrough on NG+ HARD I completed with 6 heals used and 0 deaths...). I do think someone sweaty mighty enjoy New game on Hard with absolutely bare start, but it might be legitimately unfair considering types of some random spawns and bullet spongy upgrade to the enemies.

I am not gonna mention a lot of aspects I found lacking as that has 0 benefit to anyone (there are too many things I naturally noticed). If your expectation bar is low and you need something to play, and have a lot of patience for seeing any story development after completing at least 70% of the game - godspeed!


Initial quick review (2.5h in):
This game is incredibly hyped and touted as a new Dead Space. So I will be quite critical about everything I saw in these few hours of gameplay (I plan to finish and update the review if it changes my perspective).

review_text:
Title: A Glitchy Grindfest That Deserves Better

Review:
.hack//G.U. Last Recode is four games bundled together—Rebirth, Reminisce, Redemption, and Reconnection. On paper, that makes the $50 price tag seem fair. But honestly, this remaster feels more like a relic that aged poorly than a celebration of the series.

First off, the technical issues are brutal:

No cloud saves (thanks, Bandai, for removing them for some ungodly reason).

Frequent crashes, often during scene transitions or critical story areas.

Huge risk of losing hours of progress, or even your entire save.

Buggy freezes that feel more like bad coding than the “rogue A.I.” storyline.

Gameplay-wise, it’s monotony wrapped in nostalgia. The combat is basically a stripped-down Tales system—okay at first, but quickly stale. Nearly everything funnels you into endless copy-paste dungeons. Need info? Dungeon. Want a boss fight? Dungeon. Trying to progress story dialogue? Yep, dungeon first. Grinding isn’t optional—it’s the backbone of the design.

Story & Characters:
The premise is cool—stopping player killers in an MMO-gone-wrong has superhero vibes. But the pacing kills it. Vol. 1 in particular drags with back-to-back tutorials and a tournament arc where every single match is robbed from you by cutscenes. Characters aren’t bad, but generic; they feel like archetypes you’ve seen in 5+ other JRPGs. The “coma from playing a game” storyline works if you squint and accept “because magic.” Otherwise, it’s pretty juvenile.

There are some good moments—the avatar fights are exciting, Atoli’s crush on Haseo has its cute beats, and the overarching narrative has potential. But the grind, pacing issues, and technical problems bury it.

Personal Take:
I stepped away multiple times out of sheer boredom—ended up playing 7 Days to Die, Pokémon ROM hacks, Hot Wheels & Lego rides with my kid, and Diablo IV with strangers instead. That says it all. As of 8/19/25, I officially retired this game and deleted it from my backlog.

Verdict:

As a movie? Solid 6/10—watch the cutscenes on YouTube or revisit the anime.

As a game? 4/10 at best. Tedious, buggy, and outdated.

If you want to experience .hack//G.U., you’re honestly better off emulating the original PS2 versions on PCSX2 than wasting time on this watered-down remaster. This deserves a true remake, not this lazy port.

Would I recommend it?
❌ No. Not even on sale. I wasted $20, don’t repeat my mistake.

review_text:
I like the OST, visuals, and the story. But this might be one of those times where a game just doesn't click with me. I don't like the gameplay very much. 


-Movement and trick system
Something I would say is probably the most important part of a game like this, I felt underwhelmed by the movement and trick system. It's well-polished, but it's way too easy to get a high score in this game. You can grind on a rail, lean into a corner for a point boost, and perform different tricks on the rails effectively just mindlessly spamming 3 buttons with no coherency. If you are on the ground you just need to hold a button to keep the combo going while you look for another rail to repeat the same action on. It gets way too easy after you've practiced for a couple of hours and it made the game feel like a chore to complete. The game punishes you for using the boost function as it doesn't work with your combo. Why is this the case if performing tricks gives you more boost? 
tl;dr getting points is way too easy and I got bored. 

-Cops
They are so easy to avoid, and with the cutscenes that happen every time you get a higher wanted level it just becomes an annoyance. The combat in this game functions with the points system, which is neat. Unfortunately combat is even more braindead than the trick system. You can spray-paint cops, why not make different spray-paint affect them differently? Why not add more variety to enemy types? Why do the boss fights all feel so generic and same-ey? 

I'll try and finish this game at some point. There is a lot to like, but for me personally I just wanted more from it and the game failed to deliver on it. If anyone has any suggestions for mods I may try it again at some point.

review_text:
The game mechanics are pretty decent for a Left 4 Dead style VR shooter, and the optimization is pretty decent. The shooting feels nice and aiming is purposefully a little sluggish to help you stabilize shots (it's hard to explain, but it's almost like trying to aim underwater a little bit. It isn't tedious and actually helps against the jitter often seen in these VR shooters. This is a big positive). It's also one of the few games where when I throw an item, it actually goes where I intended it to go, another common issue in VR games. Returning from launch, a couple of things have changed since launch. a handful of guns were added, the grind eased up a little bit (it's still an extremely grindy and luck-dependant game, just not as much anymore), manual reloading has been improved but is still finicky and forces you to often crash your VERY expensive controllers together every so often, and horde mode was added along with one new mission and mutations to old missions that change daily.

There are still many issues, however. The AI bots are still completely worthless, won't pick up items, can't aim, and will actively protect zombies by constantly blocking your shots. Remember to mute NPC voices in your setting to protect your sanity against the AI constantly complaining their face is blocking your bullets. Because of this, you'll be subject to the games community, which is a hit or miss. There are some people who will help you along the way you'll have a great time, but most of the time people will hotmic shitty music, be on the phone, complain, pester, whine, scream, bicker, refuse to communicate, run off on their own to die, try to command your every action, and/or will not speak English. This isn't much of a fault of the game developers but god damn does it ruin the experience. Gun stats and upgrades are often extremely vague and true values hidden in patch notes, which isn't very helpful when you're trying to modify your guns to suit your needs and it's extremely frustrating when the game refuses to give you upgrades for your favorite gun, while you've managed to unlock everything for a gun you never want to use. The content in the game also gets old very quickly, and the devs seem to have a very slow pace adding new ones.

Overall, this game, even after all of the updates in the last couple of months, is STILL not even close to being worth 40 bucks. If you're someone who's fortunate enough to have 3 other friends who often play VR games and are also willing to play this game, I can see this game being an absolute blast. Unfortunately, if you're like me who's only got one friend like that, and have to choose between the horrible AI or horrible people, this game is a hard pass.

TL;DR: this game is art (and in a good way). Wether you like art-made-videogame or not, it's sure to give you a ride. Period.

For those waiting on a slasher survival horror, go play another game. But for those craving for art made videogame, give this one a try. Although it's kinda short (3 to 6 hours mean time, but I played a bit more), it's sure to give you a thrilling ride. In every corner, road, tunnel or just about everywhere you will find yourself asking: "wtf happened here and why?"

It was a really good job on the developers. I appreciate a lot the Cronenberg, Giger, Beksiński and Freud influences. No wonder why it took so long for the devs to get this game done: the worldbuilding is just flawless. And yeah, you're gonna have a bit of puzzles and combat but that's not where this game shines, and in a way, it feels like those aspects are complementary to discovering a world long gone and long long lost. 

8/10, would've wanted it to be a bit longer. Looking forward to see it they ever make a second game of this.

-Leveling: Early game leveling is rewarding and you will feel the satisfying effects of it from zero up to about lvl 200. After that the effects are less noticeable.

-Difficulty: Once again, the Devs did a great job at giving the player control over the options of difficulty. -Maps: Each map is very different from each other and have their own excellent detailed ambience. 

-Bosses: Each boss is unique and fits really well into the map they're apart of. Each one is more fun to fight, then they are a "horrible challenge to dread". But I've no idea what giant tentacled horror awaits in the Labyrinth and technically they're all mini-bosses and the coming witch is ultimate boss.

10/10 Highly recommend

review_text:
We Were Here Expeditions: The Friendship is a two person co-op puzzle game where you must work with a friend to escape an abandoned amusement park. There are three different puzzle rooms that must be solved via communication with your partner. 

Overall, I found this title to be the best of the entire series, which is somewhat amusing given it was free for a weekend and of the titles listed for a price, it's the cheapest. It is relatively short (comparable to the first title in the series, which is/has been always free to play). Whereas other titles in this series feature much less clear puzzles, each puzzle in this game was more obvious. Now, you might think that takes away some of the fun, but I found it didn't. Instead, it allows you to focus on solving the puzzle as opposed to trying to figure out what the puzzle even is to begin with. 

One playthrough took ~2 hours and a second playthrough for achievements (getting the max score for each puzzle) took another ~2 hours (mostly due to some RNG in the second puzzle). If a co-op puzzle game sounds like something you'd enjoy, I'd recommend this game. That said, I definitely recommend playing the original as it is free and will give you a good sense of the type of gameplay you'll be getting into.

review_text:
Christ, what a mess. This game is a lot. Both sides of the coin, killer and survivor will always tell you that the other side is handheld by the developer, the other side is too easy, it's too broken, blah, blah blah. Let me ask you, then. Which side are new players AFRAID to play? Is it the half of the game where they are hunted down like prey, slaughtered while they run and complete objectives? Or is it the one doing the slaughtering, the one holding those lives in the palm of their hands? It's killer. It's always been killer. Because killer has always been the centerpiece of any match of DBD, killer NEEDS to feel good. Killer needs to feel powerful. Killer needs to feel... fun. And recently, it feels like BHVR has been trying their hardest to prevent that from being possible.

 I try my best to leave survivors alone when they get unhooked, unless there's a damn good reason to do otherwise. I've never slugged someone out in my life. And yet, I'm being punished by the devs for the actions of bad actors by having survivors be granted 30 seconds of fucking god mode on unhook. Wicked and Resurgence are going to allow survivors to go down, get hooked in basement, self unhook in front of my face at FULL HEALTH, get hit, run away for 29 seconds, get hit again because they still have endurance, and then make a break for it. The pallet density is still off the charts. And what do killers get for these survivor buffs? One tier of bloodlust. .2 meters per second of movement speed. Most killer's base movement speed is 4.6 meters per second. That is a microscopic increase. And not only is the increase microscopic, it is very fragile. If I'm playing a mid-tier killer, one that is supposed to benefit from this move speed increase instead of making the top tiers stronger, what do you suppose the first thing I'll want to do after hooking a survivor is? Looking for another survivor. How does The Knight do that? Well, it's easy! I'll just send out my guard, check this generator, and... my movement speed bonus is gone. All because I tried to play the game.  How does The Doctor do that? Let me just charge up my static blast, and... the movement speed is gone. Any teleport killer? Gone. Any information? Bye-bye. Stealth? Nope. This is the kind of ass-backwards design that BHVR comes up with to keep the playing field "fair". It's nonsense. 

Let it be known. I'm no fool. BHVR is no stranger to swinging the pendulum the other way. I remember Call of Brine Eruption. I was there for original Hex: Ruin (which was only so universal because survivors were given more tools than killers had at the time, but I digress). Killer has been miserable for survivors to play against too. But that's the problem. This is a fucking video game. Why should we be miserable? Why should we sink another 500 hours and 2000 auric cells into this game when we could do literally anything else? Learn a skill. Read a book. BHVR doesn't respect your time. Please respect your own.

review_text:
I'm on the fence about this one.

And I'm really, REALLY easily pleased, so me being on the fence means that for most people, it's a bad choice.

Contracts has some amazing things in it, like the bullet cam, and the sniper scope. The windage metres, the modifiers for distance that go up and down, etc, they all make the scope intuitive and so great for sniping. It's such a refreshing change from (even previous entries in this series as well as other sniping games) holding your breath and having a diamond show up showing you exactly where to aim. It's a beautiful innovative bridge between the worlds of just telling where the player where to aim, and giving them the tools to figure it out on their own. So instead of sitting down and trying to figure out where the bullet is going to land, you can instead focus on picking off targets and the order of killing, figuring out how to clear a base, etc. It's nice.

It's just a shame that almost everything else in the game is so very poorly executed.

Case in point. There are about six 'secondary weapons', and none of them can equip a suppressor. This game beats you over the head with stealth, and punishes you harshly for being discovered, and your assault rifles can't even equip suppressors.

They even have a SLOT for 'barrel' attachments. Just none of them actually have any attachments there. Like so much of this game, it feels [i]incomplete[/i]. It feels like a demo of a larger game, with all of the cool shit locked off. Except it never unlocks. You're just stuck with this.

The world is technically 'open'. But it's open like a Hitman game. Lots of small, interconnecting areas with very few ingress points. Objectives are 'randomized' in the most ephemeral of ways. A computer you need to hack might be in a different room, for instance.

The interface is... confusing. Confusing as fuck. And the maps are really rather small. Some parts are complex, but there really is just no reason to explore them. You can't find hidden resources for extra money, or hidden upgrades for your guns. Everything you have and can get is based around [i]money[/i], and the only way to get money is by completing objectives, looting bodies, or completing challenges. So any complexity in the map is immediately lost to the wind since there's no cool shit to find and gather while you're moving through the rooms.

The game page implies that there's this ever-changing world of contracts you can take. But there's not. Go and play a mission in Ghost Warrior 3, except move one of the secondary objectives to a room 15 metres away and that's about all the 'randomizing' you'll find in this. And even though you can tackle each 'objective' on a given map any way you want, it somehow stills feels incredibly linear. Your objectives for each map never change. They're static. And they'll force you to visit each main area of the map. There are some small side passages you can do 'for the funsies' but all you get out of it is looting 5 more bodies worth of money or whatever.

Your assault rifle (woefully unsuppressed for no good goddamn reason) is also inaccurate is fuck. You'll miss about 85% of shots beyond 50 metres away. Oh, and your 'contract killer for hire' in all the missions I've done so far, at least, has been killing 'morally repugnant' individuals. So even that bit from the main page was a lie. You might as well just be a peacekeeper or a vigilante, the whole 'mercenary' thing only seems to be shoehorned in to explain why you get money for capping the evil bad guys, and (very badly) explains why you have a cool high-tech sniping mask.

So in short, some decent ideas let down by horrific execution.

If they took this 'contracts' concept and made it actually randomized, used the maps from Ghost Warrior 4, scattered a wealth of collectables and unlockable gadgets and attachments and paintjobs and whatnot around the maps (maybe even having some of them locked behind difficult static contracts in between the random ones) and got rid of this juvenile 'I want to be a contract assassin BUT I WANNA BE THE GOOD GUY TOO' bullshit, then I would be EXCITED for that game. I'd suffer through the wonky controls to play it. And I would love it.

But that is not what this game is.

The best way I can describe the mechanics of this game is that 'it feels like a well-made Arma 3 mod'.

review_text:
It breaks my heart to say this, but I can't recommend the game, even from a Free to play angle. 
There was a time where this was THE game I played, it was more then just "My mmo of choice," but the game I spent most of my time playing. Over time though the game has shifted more and more away from a content rich MMO to a more and more grossly priced packages and more predatory gotcha mechanics. 
A clear example is when they took items that used to be free rewards for completing a mission, like unique skins or items, and packed them up into small bundles for real money on the cash shop. 
Sadly it's only gone down hill from there.
Futher more, it's not just the monitization that has gotten worse, but the in game story and features as well. At one time I would have said that STO was worth playing though if you were a Star Trek fan and wanted to experience something other fans had created. While those stories are still in place, including an amazing tribute to DS9, most of the story since that arc have felt like "new trek" that has been shoehorned into the game, complete with newTrek's hallmarks of poor writing, plot-holes, unexplained sudden changes in character and nonsensical outcomes. In once instance, for an entire season a character behaved as a literal war criminal and by the end of their next arc was being held up as a hero for no reason reflected in the script, it literally just happened "because." This is one of many plot points that appear to exist just to inject newTrek content into the game, In one case a long running game figurehead was replaced by a one off Discovery character, who was literally, I shit you not, a zombie woman brought back from the dead using literal magic. This trend is likely to continue as the director behind STO these days has flat said they will continue to chase the shows that are currently on the air rather then let STO make it's own stories.

If this wasn't bad enough, the staff at STO have seemed to stoke a sort of para-social relationship with fans. Case in point, there was a situation not long ago where a week long event was announced that was lauded by the head of social media as "the biggest event in STO history." After a weeks long ARG it was revealed that the "biggest event" was that a handful of ships from STO would be in the background of an episode of Picard. Some people were disappointed and upset, they had been hoping for news relating to the game, an update or a change, a new expansion or perhaps, finally the ability to change our character's gender. I know that I was excited at the idea of an expansion, since every other major MMO was getting a big fun new expansion. Most of us were disappointed.

People who expressed any disappointment were shouted down and the community leader encouraged it by saying that people were being selfish and trying to do a mental 2-step to try and justify the hype.
Since then there as been some quality brought back to the campaign arcs but now they are far more shallow then previously, mostly just a few scant story missions released in clusters about 6 months apart. Before a new story arc would have been a new Reputation line with new gear, a new PvE battle area for all players, 2 new que missions and a line of new ships in the cash-shop rather then in loot boxes exclusively. 

This is the disappointment of  a fan who played at the beta for the game years ago, saw the game make an incredible comeback, release some amazing content and then fall from grace. I hope it can make a comeback again, but the game is getting older every year and some parts are continuing to fall further into disrepair.

review_text:
Great game, real fun. I have a few things, but let it be known I've only played on PC, so I'm only speaking for that control scheme:

1: Camera should be more maneuverable mid-air.

I understand the camera influencing movement, but movement influencing the camera, while it looks smoother, is really painful for precise lines. This is mostly in reference to wall ejecting/wallrunning, where it feels like I have little to no control while executing them quickly in a row.

2: Trick sensitivity needs to be increased.

Its happened too many times now when I go to launch off a short wall or a stack of pallets that my character does a 360 gainer out of nowhere even though I don't even move my mouse at all. I do like the whole "button hold + directional input" formula for tricks, but the sensitivity definitely needs to be increased. I see happening to other people in multiplayer as well, so I'm sure I'm not alone on this. Just increasing it in general or a trick sensitivity slider for it in the settings would be great.

3: Movement and responses need to be snappier.

When I turn around, it's like I'm rotating around a fixed point even if the only inputs I'm making are forwards and backwards. This makes it really hard to reposition my character while it's standing on a ledge or beam because half the time that small rotation will just make you fall off. A suggestion I have is that if you're sprinting and suddenly start hold S, the character should skid to a stop and then start running in the opposite direction. The skid distance should be determined on your speed and if you're walking, it's just a quick turn. One that doesn't rotate you anyway.

I think its a really good idea, executed almost perfectly. Good emphasis on flow, amazing looking tricks, while also having a clear respect for technical movement. The game isn't all just backflips and roof gaps, there's actual meaningful movement and the maps encourage you to look for places to use it. Even with all these complaints I still really enjoy the gameplay. It's met my expectations visually and mechanically, with these three things being the only real exceptions. 

If you're looking for a good parkour game to play while we all wait for STORROR PARKOUR PRO, I'd say try this one out.

This is an entirely biased opinion from a kickstarter founder and a Relic Hunters fan since their first game in the franchise. 

These devs are just amazing. Not only are they transparent, they actually care about the players to the point where they make cosmetics a non-premium players only. 

It will be free to play on release but they actually don't prey on players like every other fucking f2p game out there and that's why I trust these devs. 

The gameplay is very well thought and fun, the characters and the story are interesting and with their own missions to know them better and all of it really just feels like being a kid again.

To us grownups we can feel a bit of cringe here and there due to the game being made for all ages and therefore the script being family friendly, but please. Just look at the trailers, get a feel of the game, if you enjoyed them, you will enjoy the story presented in the game. In any case, the game will be free to play after early access is over so feel free to check it out later but I personally have been waiting for this game to come out since 2017, holding off from exploring everything in the alpha and beta so I could properly savour it along everyone on the early access.

I wanted to pour all my feelings in this review rather than talk a lot about the game because I want people to know this is a game worth caring for. I'm no expert in the genre so I cannot nerd about mechanics, game design and stats like I usually do, but once again, this is definitely a game you should care about if you're into this kind of games.

EDIT: Due to Unity pricing thingy, I don't know if the game can survive being a free to play so it might not be f2p. If that's the case, I'm perfectly fine with it.

I could have gone well, but you have to decide for one thing here. The way it is currently built, it's barely any fun to draw swords.

The support for steam link and in home streaming is still broken since the release.

review_text:
Playing this since 2015 - started on JP base game... and since then some aspects which making me sick didn't changed at all.

First con is a graphics. It became better since then but still simplified pastgen one with ugly poligonized player models.

Second con is an annoying, stressfull and not relaxing combat system with neverending incoming attacks and tight defence timings (Slayer class step-dodge I-frame window for example is only 0.34 seconds), And it became even worse with recent updates because new bosses got overlapped attacks with uncertain hitboxes and timings.

Next con is also about combat system - a targeting marker which sticking to different spots on an enemy... yet you can play in fully targetless mode but without hitting it you'll never get good results. And this targeting maker's behaviour is just awful because it tend to jump between these spots like a crazy.

Another con of this game is a damn camera which didn't changed at all since from a very beginning. It have only 5 zoom levels and can't be put away from a character enough for a comfortable MMO gameplay experience (like World of Warcraft released about same time for example).
Moreover during combat it's feeling free to zoom in and out whenever IT wishes to and not a player...

Also there's a thing called Lock-on camera which is also awful: player can lock a target marker at a certain spot on an enemy and a camera getting attached to it... I mentioned zoom levels aready did I? So you can have a better hit rate on a boss's weak spot in cost of fully losing an ability to observe a situation on a battle area which is also annoying.

Another major con of this game is a retarded drop system which overflowing you with garbage items but have ridiculously low drop rates (like 0.000002%) for best and most expencive ones. Also grinding for various kinds of seasonals points, currencies, tickets and resources is also annoying.

Also a con in this game is an unstable market which always tend to be ruined easily - all expencive resources and weapons can become a garbage in instant after each next update.

Not a big con but still can be annoying - awkward chat system where you need to switch a Private message (Whisper) recepient and channels too so not rare cases when you sedning a PM to wrong person or writing in a wrong chat... It can be especially annoying when you're writing a private things there.

And for a last con - this game is very hard to understand most functions and not friendly at all for new players. Many times I witnessed how new players were throwing various questions in chat related to Tasks which should introduce in-game functions to them.

For a last the very few pros of this game:

1st one is a newly added Creation Space so players can build whichever thay want there.

2nd and main one - is an unique character customisation system.
PSO2 is an ONLY MMO which have it in this way: you may alter you characters looks in any moment on a fly using various outfis, hairstyles, acessories e.t.c
This is an only reason I'm still playing this damn game despite it having so many cons in every each aspect >_<

review_text: No game, upon its completion, has made me feel as disappointed and as enraged as To The Moon. What was supposed to be an emotional journey through an old man's memories to fulfill his final wish turned out to be a horribly offensive and inconsistent story that isn't subtle about its hatred. There isn't much gameplay, but I didn't mind that as the focus of the game is supposed to be on the story. The tone is all over the place. It aims to be a heartbreaking game, but the constant unfunny commentary from the two main characters (one of whom makes blatantly sexist remarks to his partner throughout the game) ruins any tension the game would otherwise build. I don't think any real autistic person was involved in the making of this game. I really wanted to like To The Moon, and the glowing recommendations and reviews I saw made me think that I would, but its disgusting sexism and autistic rep make me hate this one. I won't be recommending it to anyone, and I will be trying to remove it from my memory.

grenadier is peak enemy design rofl

gnosis as a progression system is so fucking braindead. you can tell there's absolutely 0 effort and/or thought put into it. and stop pretending 'but you can just grind to be strong too' is an excuse for this poorly designed enemy scaling. you are effectively discouraged from using a new, non-upgraded weapon because they just don't pack that punch at all. Imagine a fucking auto shotgun taking 5 shots (in a 10-bullet mag) at point blank range just to kill a random lowest-tier ranged mob. running out of imagination? fortunately you don't need to imagine anymore because that's already in the game and it's called gnosis fucking 2.


More detail at the bottom because these are not as important:

95% of in-run blessing (arcanums? i'm super good with these names) also adds close to nothing, rendering the remaining 5% must-picks. 

In the former category you get: less flinch when damaged, but costs stamina; +chance to drop healing potion (in reality this is 99.9% negligible); +damage when low hp, +1 healing potion carry capacity, +chance for missed shots to not consume ammo, +defense when casting/switching/reloading, and the majority of elemental blessings (unless you have a elemental-focused weapon like midas' burn)  They are either extremely situational or has negligible effect or has very low uptime, you pretty much don't feel their existence.

In the latter category you get the must-picks. these are: +stamina regen. +max HP. +weapon dmg when aiming. reload 20%(?) of the mag when dashing. +stun effect for bullets. Mmmm. balancing at its best.

The gunplay in this is good, like genuinely great, reminds me of good old times when destiny 2 wasnt trash (ancient times, i know). HOWEVER, the repetition between each runs makes the grind infinitely worse. there are only 3 maps in the game yet, and one of them isn't ideal for grinding because it's too hard to reasonably grind on. So that leaves the same two maps to be played on again and again. You get exactly the same set of ~10 enemy types each time, excluding special events. And fun fact, that gets boring quick. different guns with different niche does play out nicely, but the fact that you need to unlock the upgrades(mysteria) to get the cool effects going is really dumb. So the problem becomes that, even if you have the skill (I prolly dont, but lol) it's still the same grind before a weapon reaches its full potential. and thats.. not cool, frankly speaking.

On top of that, skill points (ascension) in this game has absolutely no effect other than a flat boost to your stats, which even is not that much of an improvement at all. 1 point vitality confers +4 max HP? yeah, count me in...

review_text:
This is an absolutely amazing game so far. I am only in summer of year one, but I can't remember the last time I enjoyed a farming sim this much. There is a longer questline in the game that feels like the main goal, but it has very little impact from a storytelling point of view, especially since I have too few resources to tackle it atm. This is more than made up by the cast of villagers though. It's like your own soap opera. Came to town, got set up, suddenly everyone got married within 1 week, left with like 3 single people in the entire village, first one rejects me, contemplated going lesbian, nevermind people died, married a widower, had to befriend my nemesis for that, found a homeless child that lives with me now, have aspirations to get my daughter into the mayors family so I can commit tax evasion. Bridgerton could never. 

The artstyle is also very cute and the entire atmosphere makes it really feel like I am in the 1700s. You rely on the other villagers and their professions to trade a lot of materials, and once a week there is market day with a whole tradeship coming into port. Livestock can (allegedly) be bred and also butchered for meat, which I have not gotten to but am looking forward to. 

There are also a lot of settings to customize your experience, like toggling aging, sickness, food and tool decay or the fishing minigame which is just good QoL. There are of course a few known bugs, but the devs are amazing with their responses and working on fixes already. 

The only negative things I can say about this game is that SO FAR, there is no way to auto-sort your inventory, and some of the item pricing feels a bit unbalanced, as does the cooking when a meal gives you less food or coin than the seperate ingredients would have given. I would also like for new learned recipes to have the name pop up along with a picture of the item, as I have goldfish brain and could not match some of them to anything on my crafting list. But if that is the extent of my complaints, I think it is safe to recommend this game wholeheartedly.

Overall, I love the game and recommend it to anyone who loves all genres of gaming!

UPDATED REVIEW:
I want my money back.

2021:
Yeah this is all still accurate. Give me back my fucking money.

Pros:
Realistic Weaponry: The weapons are really well modeled and are based on real-world weapons
Realistic Bullet Physics: You have to compensate for both bullet drop, wind and even lead your shots on a moving target.
Satisfying "Killcams": They very much took a page out of Sniper Elite, giving you a sick slow-mo cinematic camera on your bullet flying directly towards your target's cranium or nutsack (No X-Ray).

Cons:

Don't come here expecting the most accurate experience. Sure, there's correct wind and gravity compensation, buut what training do these soldiers go through? Unless your character uses tracer bullets, I have no idea how these soldiers are able to see and perfectly shoot a camo mercenary from 300 meters away. Sure you can say "tHeY hAvE bInOcUlArS", but your merc (who, I must say, is a total fucking wuss since you can die instantly from falling higher than like 10 or 15 feet) has access to the most advanced technology available including "Advanced Camo".

They say this game is in "Sandbox Worlds", but there's [b]COUNTLESS[/b] invisible walls that restrict you from getting incredible vantage points that could put the odds in your favor immensely. Not to mention, if the ledge you're trying to grab doesn't have a piece of paracord next to it, it's impossible to climb unless you're able to jump high enough.

Each and every level is against you. No matter what, you are guaranteed to get detected once. Out of the 4/5 worlds that I've played in, I've been detected each and every time. 

There's these "Side Contracts" you can do, and you faiil them automatically if you leave the contract area. This wouldn't be an issue [b]if they ever showed you what the contract area is[/b]. There's no blue line, no border area, not even an outline on the map.

Half of the upgrades for your character don't even work or change anything, just placebo effects. The Camo upgrades do nothing at all, still detected within 1.5 seconds of a camera or person seeing me, even in bushes. "Drone Towers" are like Jammers, but for your drones, and are on nearly [b]every map[/b], they're indestructible as well so Drones are pretty much pointless. The "Wraith" upgrade is supposed to make your character silent when walking or running, but enemies still hear you as if you didn't have the upgrade, the devs just remove the walk/running noises. Not to mention, the "chain attack" upgrade only works when the guards are quite literally shoulder-to-shoulder, if they're ~4 feet away from you then good luck. This wouldn't be too bad if they couldn't [b]still kill you while in the chain attack cutscenes[/b].

Nearly every challenge is nigh impossible.

There is supposed to be "creativity" and "open-endedness" to your approaches, but this is just as creativity-stifling as Fallout 76. There [i]is no creativity[/i]. Your options are:
1. Shoot, get spotted by binoculars, sneak around to another side/distract with a drone (if there's no tower, which there probably is), rinse and repeat until the whole complex is empty.
2. Guns blazing, die because of a heavy being nigh-indestructible without AP/heavy bullets, restart, snipe the heavy you died to last time, and continue.
3. Metal Gear Solid.

There are glaring issues that the devs could easily fix, but no. They want you to suffer.
3/10. Give me my f---ing money back.

review_text:
[h1]Please note that this game is the first part of a two-part story. It's also a remake.[/h1]

In Hakuoki, you get to play as Chizuru, a girl who is looking for her father in Kyoto. She ends up staying with the members of the Shinsengumi, a feared police force that existed during the Bakumatsu period in Japan.

The choices you make in the game will lead you towards a path where you end up with one of the 12 available bachelors.

One important thing to keep in mind is that the game ends halfway through the story. Up to that point, there's also not much romance, but more of a buildup of the relationships and events that happen during the story. Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms is the second part of the story and includes much more romance. I'd recommend playing a route in Kyoto Winds and then switching over to Edo Blossoms to continue the story since you can pick the route you want from the start in the second part.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

The gameplay is like any visual-based novel, you read through the story and you get to make some choices every now and then. All the lines except the narrative and main character are voiced by good actors/actresses and the background music is also beautiful. There are some characters that may sound a bit louder than the others though (like Shinpachi) so keep that in mind.

It's really easy to immerse yourself, partly because of the stunning visuals but also because the story is quite long and complex. Most of the events and characters in the game are historically correct and you can learn a lot of Japanese history this way. However, some parts are fairly linear and play out the same in a lot of the routes and it takes some time to really branch out into the unique parts for a specific character.

All characters have their own story and they are not copy-pastes of each other. You may dislike a route or two but I personally find most of them enjoyable. I will not dwell too much about the characters though because this topic can be very subjective.

The only bugs and errors I found were some minor spelling errors and the lips of the characters being out of synch when speaking. I also had to use my gamepad to change the resolution and to play it in fullscreen.

[h1]My final conclusion[/h1]

Hakuoki is personally one of my favorite visual novels, mostly because of the historical setting (Bakumatsu period) and because I love stories with samurai warriors. It's among one of the first few otome games that were localized in the west, and it's a quite good introduction to the genre for those who are new to otome. I played the 3DS version which was shorter and had less content, so the extra material in this game made me quite happy. Hakuoki can feel like a drag sometimes though because the common route is quite long and there are so many bachelors to choose from. The amount of bachelors can also be considered a positive, since you're bound to find at least a handful that you really like. As for the MC, Chizuru is not the most enjoyable MC because she feels too meek but considering the historical setting and her young age, she is at least realistic as a character. Nevertheless, I feel that the story, visuals and voice acting make up for the small downsides. I enjoyed this game a lot and I feel that it should be played by anyone already interested in otome as well as people who just discovered the genre.

review_text:
With this kind of game you really have to take a gamble based on reviews and in this case, the reviews really let me down.  I'd really like my 4 hours back.

The controls are terrible but that's kind of to be expected for an independent release like this.  Still, there are levels where movement is painfully slow, it's easy to get caught on odd items in the background, and it takes more effort to do what you want to do than it should.

All of this could be forgiven, however, if the story made up for it.  It did not.  I had to wait an hour for the hook, then got dragged along a poorly paced and poorly told story that concluded with an ending which was unneccessarily empty and disappointing.

There are several great examples of indie games that focus on story, but this is not one of them.  Save yourself a lot of wasted time and play something else.
