review_text:
I should've known how strange and surreal this game was gonna be based on [strike]attempting to play[/strike] playing The Void so many years ago (maybe the single other most stressful video game I've ever played lmao)

This game is a miserable and draining experience and somehow also one of the best games I’ve ever played, and that’s with me not even playing at the intended difficulty (I’d quite probably keel over from the stress of it all and die irl if I had)

So Pathologic 2 is a remake/reimagining of the original Pathologic from 2005. The original allowed you to play 3 different characters to experience the game 3 different ways. Pathologic 2 however focuses only on the Haruspex character, a surgeon (emshen) named Artemy Burakh who has returned to his small isolated village at his father's behest only to find his father murdered and himself the prime suspect on Day 1. Queue the townspeople instantly hating you and beating the shit out of you on sight for 2 straight days as you attempt to get it all straightened out and find your father's murderer.

[b]AND THEN BAM. A PLAGUE.[/b]

Now you, the hated son-returned-home, are the man the town is (nearly) solely relying on to find a way to cure this ailment before everybody dies, as, for lore reasons, Artemy is the only man allowed to autopsy bodies. But you also gotta sprinkle in being the town's therapist, detective, chemist, marathon runner, Kin defender, father <3, and murderer or saint depending on your playstyle (look, Artemy’s going through a lot okay).

Now you have 12 days to figure it all out and keep your loved ones from dying.

And when the game says you can’t save everyone, it really really means it. From the start the game is punishing and as the days progress it only gets harder and harder. The fighting is quite wonky in this game, and your resources are very limited. Also everyone is fighting in the streets? Very dramatic stuff. Some of your most beloved characters are most definitely going to die, some quests each day are going to go unfinished, and sometimes the game might piss you off, but it’s worth pushing through despite it all. Many of the characters are quite lovable despite how strange they all act, and you’re gonna wanna keep them safe. Also the kids were my favorites despite the fact that they all talk like omnipotent beings lol. 

Now, the worldbuilding for this game is pretty insane. I thought it was gonna take place in some backwoods Russian town but instead we’re gifted a richly imaginative world with a lot of depth and lore. And despite said town being a microcosm of a larger world that we don’t see at all, we still somehow learn all about the different customs and rituals and beliefs of the Town and Steppe. It was all so rich and detailed and unique as hell (comparable to Disco Elysium imo).
Also, despite it’s longer length, it feels like the type of game that is begging to be played again. The next time I do I’ll play it at intended difficulty (and suffer). 

Anyway, it’s a very thought provoking and original piece of art, and even though there was only one playable character this time around, it didn’t feel like anything was missing. I’m so excited for the sequel and am excited to play as the loml, the pretentious Daniil (and then hopefully Changeling next).

At the end of the day I at least saved my kids and that's what mattered.
Time for me to go play the Quarantine demo now!

[/b] now you , the hated son-returned-home , are the man the town is ( nearly ) solely relying on to find a way to cure this ailment before everybody dies , as , for lore reasons , artemy is the only man allowed to autopsy bodies . but you also gotta sprinkle in being the town ' s therapist , detective , chemist , marathon runner , kin defender , father <3 , and murderer or saint depending on your playstyle ( look , artemy’s going through a lot okay ) . now you have 12 days to figure it all out and keep your loved ones from dying . and when the game says you can’t save everyone , it really really means it . from the start the game is punishing and as the days progress it only gets harder and harder . the fighting is quite wonky in this game , and your resources are very limited . also everyone is fighting in the streets ? very dramatic stuff . some of your most beloved characters are most definitely going to die , some quests each day are going to go unfinished , and sometimes the game might piss you off , but it’s worth pushing through despite it all . many of the characters are quite lovable despite how strange they all act , and you’re gonna wanna keep them safe . also the kids were my favorites despite the fact that they all talk like omnipotent beings lol . now , the worldbuilding for this game is pretty insane . i thought it was gonna take place in some backwoods russian town but instead we’re gifted a richly imaginative world with a lot of depth and lore . and despite said town being a microcosm of a larger world that we don’t see at all , we still somehow learn all about the different customs and rituals and beliefs of the town and steppe . it was all so rich and detailed and unique as hell ( comparable to disco elysium imo ) . also , despite it’s longer length , it feels like the type of game that is begging to be played again . the next time i do i’ll play it at intended difficulty ( and suffer ) . anyway , it’s a very thought provoking and original piece of art , and even though there was only one playable character this time around , it didn’t feel like anything was missing . i’m so excited for the sequel and am excited to play as the loml , the pretentious daniil ( and then hopefully changeling next ) . at the end of the day i at least saved my kids and that ' s what mattered . time for me to go play the quarantine demo now !

review_text:
.hack//G.U.
I have so much to say about it... but I won't, because else it would take just as much time as cutscenes in this game do.
TL;DR: 6.5/10 game. I really want to recommend it, but I cannot do so, as it didn't age well. The snail's pacing of the gameplay, the pointless grind (due to the speed of XP gain), and every scene drawn out just a little bit longer than it should be all take away from the experience. Worth buying during the sales.

Let's start with the good things. The atmosphere is amazing. It ACTUALLY feels like you're immersed in the world of The World (haha... sorry, i'll see myself out)
Even though the console takes forever to load, I genuinely enjoyed launching the game and exiting it to read some emails in the system. I mean, come on, it's been what, 13 years and you still alttab to read some msgs outside of the game, there IS some truth in that.
OST is, well, hard to remember, but it's ok enough to pass. General sound design is decent, but definitely not remarkable in any way. Still, plays to the games' strengths, adding to the immersion quite well.
Writing is, well, not stellar, but gotta pay my respects to the fact that the franchise itself is like the granddaddy of a significant part of current media. Love it or hate it, forgot how the stupid meme goes, G.U. somehow makes you feel that stupid nostalgy even if you've never played it before, because it FEELS like a classic RPG experience. I was looking exactly for that and oh boy did it deliver. Keeping myself awake through the trainwreck of a story about a bunch of idiots unable to properly communicate was way over me though.

Somewhat of a middle ground are... The characters. DEAR LORD, how annoying almost everyone is, ESPECIALLY mc Haseo himself. I think it's the first time ever I've hated the protagonist so much. Fairly sure the writers had a competition of who's going to make the edgiest and asshole-est character possible, and I can say for sure they did deliver. I do know the full story of a game, I know all about his reasoning even though I never finished the trilogy, but even so controlling the most uninterested in video games angry online gamer ever felt like driving a car without brakes on a downhill road - the guy is so much of a jerk you can't relate to him even if you try.
Credit where credit's due: deuteragonists and other side characters you actually interact with fit all the tropes but still manage to feel like real people you would meet in an online game, each with their own personality, motivation and yadda-yadda... Buuuut even though they have some depth to them, it's still more like 2.5D with no real third dimension to them. For example, the twins are a good concept that was kinda poorly executed.

The worst part: gameplay. As I said in the beginning, every single scene is drawn out. Awkward pauses, repeated delivery of the same information, constant need to log out and log back in just because of some mail... Then there are the party members you don't actually need, relationship system (which, while well implemented outside of combat, still urges you to just hit those finishing strikes every single time just to max it out. like, come on, show me a single person who'll start loving me due to the fact i managed to pummel a virtual teapot), sidequests that require talking to every single character in the game (gotta be honest, i do that in JRPGs anyway, like talking to every single NPC i meet in Kiseki or Tales, but that's because they usually ARE interesting to talk to, not just "DID YOU KNOW THAT ENEMY CAN HAVE A WEAKNESS". damn, talking to people in FF is more interesting than those walking cardboard cutouts). 
The alchemy system is really not deep at all. The equipment all feels the same. The skills are... well, bland. Trading with other characters is great, but pretty much useless. Randomly generated dungeons are BOOOORING. Not like grindy boring, more like text-based games feel like they are filled with action next to those stupid corridors and square rooms populated with groups of three to five mobs.
How exactly do the players manage to play the game without gaining any levels at all? How does one walk around the world populated with enemies four levels above them and never get into a fight with any of them? What do they actually online if they don't participate in anything the game has to offer? G.U. doesn't appear to be written outside of the necessary world building and story canvas it needs to deliver the plot to the player.
It wasn't really a good RPG even for the time it was released. Damn, 2006 had Oblivion, Grandia, Suikoden, Kingdom Hearts 2, and so much more...

And yet even due to all the shortcomings, due to the fact the game feels outdated in 2017, it still is genuinely a good experience.
Buy it during the sales if you've never played it.
Buy it for full price if you played it some years ago and consider refreshing it in your mind.
Feel the nostalgy. Embrace The World.

review_text:
TLDR: Avoid, especially at current full price it is simply not worth it. 

Huge disappointment and very lackluster content for a allegid £30 game.

My only positives are:

The gunplay feels really good. It’s satisfying to use the weapons and land shots. 

The basic enemy engagements are fun, they are both slow and fast so that you have the chance to enjoy honing your aim and can take some time to enjoy it over the frantic clip empty parts.

I only paid £24, but even that is over what I think this disguised as a AAA early access tile is worth.

Really poor default VR controls. It’s extremely clunky to begin with until you edit them. Yes it’s comfigerable but I shouldn’t need to configure 20 options right out the gate to get it towards what most other games have perfected as a standard.

The missions are too short & there are only 5. Given how simple these “missions” seem, I’m shocked there isn't more.

Safe rooms don’t feel like safe rooms and the dumb arcade machines become unsuable if one of your party hits the door button for the next stage. 

They are clinging to this arcade game style options menu that is cumbersome to use repeatedly and causes more issues than it solves.

The lobby system is appalling. How this passed UX / QA is an absolute mystery to me. In a nutshell,if you, the lobby leader, decide to move away from the arcade machine that allows you to select a mission you have no idea when your party is full and ready to start. Meaning you have multiple lobbeys that you have no control over picking and keep getting put back into the same inactive party / lobby. Stupid.

This game got so ingrained in my head I kept worrying the in-game time was still running even tho I'm not playing it

I wish more people experience the game but I also very well know why people wouldn't like it. Its a very memorable game. It's beautifully miserable. It's incomparable. I sometimes still dream about it

review_text:
As of the Webgrave update, I can no longer recommend this game. The stat system was significantly nerfed such that, at my same level of 455 prior to the update, I now have 45% less health, 60% less stamina and earn 2.5x less witchfire. You also carry two less healing elixirs for a total of three instead of the previous five. Moreover, each elixir heals you for significantly less while enemies still hit you for the same amount of damage. You can remedy part of this with their new rosary system in which you equip rosary beads, however the stat based ones are weak, you can only equip a few at a time, and they are scattered throughout each map or perhaps earned in other ways.

I feel it is important to continue the discussion around difficulty in gaming and the accessibility challenges it presents. I'm no stranger to difficult games - I've completed Dark Souls, Dark Souls 3, Bloodborne, Sekiro, and Elden Ring to name a few. But I feel these games established a standard of difficulty that can exclude certain players. Witchfire is a difficult and demanding game. But I had found a way round this by leveling up my character, pushing him higher and higher so I could enjoy the game. Even my playstyle changed - I was a long ranged, passive player at early levels, using sniper rifles and freeze spells to slow my enemies. I evolved to blasting my way into enemy camps and taking the challenge head on. But I could do so with the strength I had earned from the levels I earned. 

To make matters worse, the Gnosis difficulty curve system the game incorporates is essential to fully level up to even make it to the end of the game. If I'm struggling at Gnosis level 3 in the current form after the update, then in conjunction with your stat changes I no longer stand a chance on completing the game.

One of the most iconic, if not the most iconic, FPS games is Doom and, too this day, continues to have difficulty levels allowing everyone to access it at a pace that is comfortable to them. The developers of Witchfire have said that they changed their stat system because higher level players were essentially "playing with cheats." I find this statement bizarre. If I'm having fun, what does it matter? The prior stat system allowed everyone to play as they wanted - you could level up as much or as little as you wanted. There was even a video posted by the developers of a very talented player who completed an incredible challenge. Players will always find ways to challenge themselves within the limitations of the game.

I'm more sad and disappointed I have to let this game go. I was following it for years prior to its release. I bought it day one on Epic and bought it again when it came to Steam. I was having so much fun. It breaks my heart to change to a negative review. But this is a warning to casual and even mid-core players who may not enjoy the steep difficulty adjustments with minimal payoff from the new stat system.

Original Review:
I was walking around Irongate Castle in awe of the visuals, the small details, and the atmosphere. The music, audio, sound design - it's all on point. The roguelite aspect and the gameplay loop is absolutely perfect - the player isn't Doomguy with infinite stamina or access to countless healing items, but with limitations to his character which are entirely fitting in this grimdark world. That said, player movement is smooth, responsive, and in close partnership with each weapon - it is a delight to play. Everything is stitched together in such an outstanding way and is always authentic to the world around it.

The developers are also 100% engaged to feedback and have such an honest way about communicating that it is such a breath of fresh air. That said, they are also committed to their vision of this game and they've maintained such an excellent balance with player feedback.

This game is a labour of love. And it shows. I wish them nothing but the best venturing forward from Epic EA to Steam EA.

review_text:
After 4-5 hours and completing several missions, Shadow Tactics feels more like a rigid puzzle game than the creative stealth experience I was hoping for. Coming from games like Hitman and Dishonored where you have multiple approaches and can experiment with different solutions, this felt surprisingly limiting.

Every guard is watched by others, creating tedious chains where you must clear entire sections just to eliminate one target. Despite large maps, there's typically only one viable path forward.


The game is well-crafted and polished, but it becomes monotonous quickly. Each area feels like solving the same puzzle: figure out the correct elimination sequence, execute it perfectly, repeat. If you enjoy pure logic puzzles with a stealth theme, you might love this. If you're looking for the emergent gameplay and creative problem-solving of games like Hitman, you'll likely find it frustrating.

A daunting game start to finish. Although I bought all three games in the franchise, I can't say that the sequel made as big of an impression to me as the first game.

In this franchise, you are the devil's son, and like the devil's son you will act, wrecking havoc and creating despair within the manor in which you reside. The kills feel like they have weight to them; people will react, fear will rise, and unlike the sequel (haven't gotten around to Lucius 3, so can't comment on that one yet) your actions will have consequences. The story is fitting for a game of this caliber, nothing too extreme.

The music is chilling, but never too in-your-face. I've read somewhere that the game's graphics designer produced some of my personal favourite tracks for no extra cost (e.g. Devil's Fairground) because the team was running short on budget, but needed more music, which I find really really cool and creative of them. 

The animations and controls are Lucius' weaker points. This game attempts to touch on taboo topics in cold and unforgiving ways, but oftentimes fails to visualise it properly because of the weird lighting, choppy animations, or outright goofy bugs happening quite often during gameplay. But even still, I wouldn't say that those are reasons not to try the game if you're interested.

Overall the first game definitely has a story to tell, and is certainly worth trying out. The atmosphere can reel the player in right from the start, I found myself binging this game up until late at night to figure out what the next step is gonna be, or how the story and characters will unfold next.

I wish the sequel carried this energy or expanded on it. Amazing work to the team!

review_text:
"Look around you. This horrible bunch of psychopaths are all begging to join up with me, but unfortunately for them, I only take the best. And today, best means whoever can kill you. Come on out lads. It's initiation time."

[i]Batman: Arkham City[/i] is an action-adventure game developed by Rocksteady Studios and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment.

[b]Story[/b]
I suggest playing through Arkham Asylum first, as events from that game are used as a setup to setting of this one.

Arkham City takes place 18 months after Arkham Asylum events. Taking credit for stopping Joker's siege, director Sharp becomes a Mayor of Gotham City. Declaring Asylum no longer suitable, he creates immense prison enclosure known as Arkham City inside Gotham's slums, taken care of by mysterious Hugo Strange while monitored by private military firm TYGER Security. Our protagonist, Bruce Wayne, opposes that idea and ends up in a titular prison himself. Here as Batman he wants to find out more about mysterious Protocol 10 and real intentions behind the prison.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
If you played Arkham Asylum, you already know what to expect as City builds up upon gameplay from previous game, providing third person open world venture where you will investigate, explore, stealth and brawl through the prison as our favourite Caped Crusader, searching for truth (and few faces to soak your fists in).
First thing you will experience is the main dish of the game- combat. Punch, kick, smack thugs before they smack you to avoid a dreadful fate of watching villians laugh in your face as you lose and reload a checkpoint. Counter or dodge incoming attacks, chain up combinations to gain speed and power, utilize plenty of gadgets to surprise your opponents. Game provides improved version of the "Freeflow" combat system, meaning you can now perform more moves, such as option to counter multiple attacks at once or being able to chain combinations for long enough to unleash deadly special attacks. Enemies can be armed with different armor and weapons, forcing you to adjust your moves accordingly.

Sometimes you get a chance to resolve encounters silently. Similar scenario as with first game, utilize vantage points, environment, detective vision and your gadgets to eliminate enemies without them noticing you. Watch as fear strikes their minds and heartpulse keeps rising with each performed takedown on their buddies, but just like in combat, thugs are a bit more Bat-proof this time so they come with more firearms, jammers and extra tools that will make your life harder, as tides can quickly shift back and forth. Know when to strike and when to wait for opportunity, or just create your own!

Arkham City opens up the area, providing way more space to explore. Glide, grapple and sprint around looking for collectibles that expand the narrative and lore, side activities, or just seek out local thugs waiting for a fight! (Or to be knocked out silently by a sneaky Bat.) Fans favourite Riddler returns with his trophies and riddles, while other villians make an appearance in side quests spread all over the prison, unlockable as you progress through the story. Same applies to gadgets, so you might have to wait a bit to obtain a tool or two before you can enter certain buildings or collect specific trophies. No pressure, you can always return to every area you visited.

Combat and exploration grant you experience points, earn enough to level Batman up and unlock new skills, moves, or improve gadgets.

[b]Playtime, other modes[/b]
It took me roughly 13 hours to complete everything in Arkham City. After beating the story you unlock New Game Plus where you can utilize everything you have unlocked with increased overall difficulty to balance it out. Additionally there is "Riddler's Revenge" mode, where you tackle on different challenge maps and campaigns for medals! Fair to say you can spend a bit more time in City than you might think at first glance, if interested. Especially as this version comes with extra DLC, Catwoman content, and extra characters in RR mode.

[b]Impressions[/b]
Out of the gate I will go out with a very bold claim- Arkham City is probably the best sequel I ever had a pleasure to play. A textbook definition of how they should be made. It's not a revolution, but an evolution. If you played Asylum you feel right at home almost instantly as game keeps same great controls and fantastic core gameplay allowing you to quickly get into action, increasing and opening up the location where game takes place, addition of side quests and expanded lore make it feel like an entirely new experience. Already great combat is now reaching superb levels, it's smooth, it's intuitive, with very tight controls and top notch precision when it comes to inputs as if game knows which thug you want to hit before you even do. Some annoying moments from Asylum where Batman in the middle of combination would decide to punch ghosts are gone, combined with new moves and gadgets it practically makes you beg for as many enemies on screen as possible to go wild.

But game knows when to slow down, when to give you a stealth section to showcase pretty solid enemy AI, allowing you to fully lean into Batman's strategic side with various gadgets, careful planning and utilization of environment to his advantage. Quite frankly it's a shame that because game is no longer as linear as first title, plus complete change of area where game takes place so it's almost impossible to just give you a stealth section in the middle of the city, it doesn't actually have that many of those section. But when you get them, it's an absolute treat to play.

Asylum no doubt had it's own unique atmosphere, but City is no slouch in that department either. Prison filled with crime in the middle of gang wars, with secrets on top of secrets, the mash of destroyed slums with iconic locations, freedom you get to explore it and encounter many more and lesser known villians across short yet satisfying side quests, it hits right. Fortunately game never feels too long, it doesn't drag on, even if you decide to dive into the madness that is collecting those forsaken trophies.
Fantastic audiovisual side, strong art direction, top of the game performance from voice actors and animators, game even today looks fairly impressive. Forgot to even mention expanded extra side mode of the game in which you can spend plenty hours, if running around Arkham City gets boring for you.

If there something...mixed, I can say about this game, it would probably be about the story. In my book the main villian in this one was a bit..disappointing? Especially as he was pretty much a "main face" when it came to promoting the game. I expected a better conclusion of certain arcs and felt like it could have focus on just one story, instead of jumping around and trying to have two main storylines branching out and at least for me, that never really worked. So yeah, story is enjoyable but I would like it to go into a different direction.

Nonetheless, Arkham City is simply superb. Easy recommendation. Combat feels great, explorating feels enjoyable, still holds up visually and it's a treat for fans of DC/Batman.

[b]Final words and conclusion[/b]
Said it before, gonna say it again, GOTY Edition comes with everything released so you get all the fun stuff- alternative costumes, post-main game DLC and extra characters- in one pack!

Batman: Arkham City improves pretty much everything from first game while still focusing on core strenghts- fantastic combat, great audiovisuals and intriguing exploration. Buy it, play it, enjoy it.

review_text:
To preface, this game is easily one of the better free MMO's out there. It has an interesting dichotomy of ground based combat, and the real glean of the ship acquisition and gearing. The story is decent enough, though the co-op content (resource intensive fleet/guild system) are the main aspects of the game. I'd consider the first 20-200 hours to be reasonably fair, and the recruitment events offer amazing acceleration to endgame content. With it, in a few months you can be on your way to a T6 ship. 

Obviously, a free to play game comes with expensive caveats. A great deal of customization is paid for, and (arguably) many pay to win ships are also locked behing ZEN. You can spend a decent enough on this game and get what you want, and ZEN and most of the cash shop items go on sale on occasion, so I consider this to be an okay method, all things considered.

I really want to like this game. I really want to keep playing this game. But having experienced a 16 day outage during the recent Summer event, causing me to miss out on the T6 ship, completely buzzkilled this game for me. Having gotten 18/20 progress, having farmed the entire gear set, and gotten a 1000 favor floater all from scratch, to be hampered at the finish like was the absolute peak of frustration. I was strung along the whole time, then told with patronizing platitudes that they would not give me even the slightest recompense. With months of rubber-banding (Australia, I know), the game is close to unplayable and I have to call it quits. 

I'm sure the vast majority have few qualms with the game, and I expect I'm just a 1/2500 edge case, and I understand the devs probably have bigger problems than free-to-play nobodies, but this was my experience of the game and I hope it doesn't happen to others.

Life long and prosper lads

review_text: I loved the first game and am very experienced in its world. The sequel is similar to the first in that it’s not an RPG but a linear story with sandbox maps as areas to explore freely. The gameplay is fun, combat can be challenging, and I enjoy the survival mechanics of hunting and exploring the immersive world. I ran into numerous bugs and crashes. I watched many reviews praise this game for being polished, but I ran into issue after issue. Realism is still front and center,  but the sequel is more streamlined to reach a broader audience. If you played the first game, then you’ll enjoy this one as much as I did. My biggest gripe is that the storytelling in the sequel dragged down the overall experience for me. There’s not much in the way of action and consequence, but you're presented with the illusion of it. As the player, I figured things out before the game would allow characters to know such information, which would hinder any chance of me making any choices outside of what the writers wanted me to do. That's when I realized I was just along for the ride and had to accept everything for what it was. I stopped asking questions and went back into consume-product mode. The game is plagued by millennial writing and humor, making it difficult to take anything seriously. Act 2 crushed the momentum that Act 1 had going for it. Some jokes might appear funny, but I'm looking for a more mature theme in my realistic medieval game. A lot of the cutscenes felt like I was watching a bad movie filled with cliches and tropes. I was taken out of the experience many times due to the “Uh oh, whoops!” and “That just happened” type of humor. The only parts of the story I enjoyed were fulfilling Henry’s revenge quest, but the rest was a humiliation ritual for our boy. Characters, such as Musa, speak down to Henry. Even with a high scholarly skill, I could not retort to his blatant hypocrisy or lies. Then, the game has you solve a murder to clear Musa as a suspect. You’re forced to help him. Otherwise, you receive a game over screen. Another illusion of choice. It’s as if the writers were lecturing me with this character and others for no good reason. I didn't mind carrying sacks and being an errand boy, but now they’re just insulting our intelligence. The game is very loosely historically accurate. You can tell the writers had their own story to tell in history with their interpretation of what happened. I don't believe in buzzwords nor do I care about sides, but I see how people claim this game has woke elements. I saw the controversy regarding the creative director, and those elements bleed into the game. I rushed the story because, at a certain point, I gave up on the game when it gave up on me. I only stuck around to see Henry’s resolution across the finish line. I'm waiting for Hardcore mode to release because the decent enough gameplay pushes me through the rest of this game.

review_text:
This is a MIXED review. I'm very torn on Scorn, but after considering the pros and cons, I'm more leaning towards giving it a thumbs down now. Do I recommend Scorn at its current price point? No, not really. Do I still think it was a worthwhile journey, and a game you should see? Yes.

Scorn is a one-of-a-kind game, I'll repeat what everybody else said before me and start with a simple fact - the game is absolutely breathtaking visually, and the sound design and atmosphere compliments the graphics in every way possible too. But problem is, that's kinda where I must stop with the positives, because aside of the great artstyle, visuals and sound, Scorn can't really offer much else. 

What I kinda disagree with a lot of other people is the puzzles. I don't think they were bad, actually to me they were the most enjoyable part of the game, what I didn't like was the weird scaling of puzzle difficulty, cuz to me the first hour of the game was by far the hardest and most confusing, even tho I don't believe it was supposed to be. The first puzzle and the first big area were the hardest the game ever was during it's (mind you short) runtime. After the first level it becomes a lot more linear and clear on what you're supposed to do, the puzzles remained fun throughout though I think. So while the difficulty scaling was kinda in reverse, the individual puzzles were fun, not too hard, not too easy.

For me, the game peaked around it's penultimate chapter, I feel like Scorn would've benefitted alot if it extended it's full-geared parts by at least one more level. I felt like it was the most fun when I had all the weapons, scattered and limited resources all around, plenty of creatures to fight and some little problem-solving. Unfortunately, the game doesn't stay in that state for too long, you finish the most dangerous penultimate level, and then it kinda dies out completely. And while the last level is also quite interesting, gameplay-wise it offered some of the most frustrating mechanics which I won't get into, find out for yourselves.

And while we talk about the mechanics, let's touch on the combat. I don't think the combat was as terrible as some claim. It has the typical survival-horror charm. Resources are VERY limited, character movement is very slow and unresponsive, and so is the aiming. The weapons (except the melee one) feel satisfying to use, and I liked the designs. Though my main gripe with the combat was how linear were the scenarios you fight in. Once you've figured how to defeat each enemy type, it was the same everytime you've encountered them, with very little room variety. There's also almost zero opportunity to flee if you think your ammo is low, one of the enemy types in particular is almost impossible to out-maneuver in a tight room cuz your character is so slow. So ultimately I think that's what bothered me the most with the combat, very little creativity to the encounters, and the movement being a tad bit too slow.

The story is also something I didn't quite enjoy. Since there's zero dialogue, zero notes, zero protagonist inner-monologue, zero ANYTHING really, then everything you come up with is a theory, which makes the story ultimately none-existent, as everything comes down to your imagination. So anyone who's claiming there IS a story, is wrong, it's all a theory based on what you see. I think Scorn would've benefitted from at least a little bit of context, at least a flavor text at the beginning or end would help greatly, to at least give some kinda clue on what's happening. Cuz yes, there is environmental storytelling going on, but without anything to go off from, you can't really say anything is set in stone, hence it may aswell be all a dream...

So that's my take on Scorn for now, in the end I give a rare thumbs down on Steam, but I liked my time with it, and I was happy I could support the devs, cuz there's serious potential here for a next, bigger game to come out. They have a talent for artstyle and world design, so now just construct a serious game around it, and we might be cooking here.

For now, only buy it on sale, or if you really wanna experience the world for yourself.

review_text:
Ssometimes simplicity is what we need when it comes to our game mechanics. Though, we should not misinterpret simple for easy in all senses. After going through several suggested Metroidvania list I found this title would keep popping up as a must play in the genre. I saw that it was a short title so figured, to give it a try and see what all the fuss was with it. 

The game has an intriguing narrative if not honestly predictable from the start. It also plants may seeds of doubt in the player. Why I am doing this? Are they really bad? If you go through and collect the notes in the world and read the dialogue of the bosses and NPCs you encounter you will see that not everyone is who they are portrayed as. 

The gameplay is simple in you, have a weapon and some items and a couple of magic abilities. You rotate through and use them for environmental puzzle solving and combat. However for a Metroidvania the combat can be challenging at the recommended difficulty. Even the lowest of enemies can kill you in a few hits. You constantly will be going to your menu to find the item that will counter a condition you have so you don't die if poison or bleeding because you are losing a point per second and you only have 10 health and 20 points of bleeding. This simple but complex system feels like it can easily take you out of the game since you are constantly scrolling through menus in the middle of a fight. 

The game also seems to mess with you as you go, at least on Steam. After I beat the first boss, the achievement popped up "defeat every boss" but when I checked it wasn't completed yet. So instead it seems to be counting as you go to keep you guessing how close to the end you are. After finishing I can see that there multiple endings and new ways to experience the game. I probably won't play again since ai typically do not go for the other endings in these titles, but it's a nice touch as a single run can go about 5-7 hours depending how long boss fights take you. 

Overall it was a fun game, with some twist that made the game play feel rewarding. Oh and it has cute (though sometimes creepy) anime girls if that matters to you.

review_text:
Reviewing this game is difficult.
The game is trying really hard to mimic the iconic game mechanics of its superior counter part (Dead Space) while also trying to introduce new elements that I believe slow and sour the experience.

[b] Things I loved about the game [/b]

- Graphics are quite insane in this title
- Ambiance and atmosphere are definitely on par with the OG Deadspace
- Using a prison and abandoned mine colony as the setting is brilliant, and the contrast between each place does make it feel very unique. 
- Sound design did a meticulous job and its ear candy.
- While the story is predictable and very similar to other Sci-Fi stories, it servers it purpose.
- Monster design is cool as well, while not a 1 to 1 copy of this brother, it definitely keeps those body horror elements.
- Tension is good for the most part.
- There are so many great death animation for our main character and the game embraces the gory elements in them.
- The game is fairly polished as of the date of this review, I did not encounter any bugs or crashed. An unexpected surprise
- I felt immersed in the universe for the most part, partially due to the lack of HUD and details.

[b] Things that I disliked: [/b]

- Having to crawl through small or cramped spaces in video games usually server the purpose to move to the next section in order to not have a loading screen. However, in this game it slows down the pace significantly for no reason and there is A LOT of that in the game. You will be crawling or squishing your way through so many corridors, tunnels and air ducts and it creates FAKE tension, you can do anything besides crawl, therefore you know you can not get attacked in the air-vents. There was only 1 instance where it was successful at creating tension and a scare for me.
- The combat / melee system is not as bad as people make it out to be but is not good either. Instead of using strategy you just have to use rhythm, which immediately kills off almost all the tension from encounters. 
- Switching off weapons is odd, they tried to reinvent the wheel here but instead made it unnecessarily complicated to do.
- Healing is VERY slow as well, which is a single shot, it should not be. Its a way they decided to artificially increase difficulty.
- Reusing bosses several times is always been frown upon, unless they become a re-acuring enemy later down the line, this is not the case. They re use the same boss 3 times and honestly it makes the game less exciting.

[b] Things that I HATE: [/b]
- Performance is not good and honestly unless you have a beefy card I would say stay away from the game, even with a 4080 I had top use Lossless scaling since the game does not have any frame generation and the upscaling method does not have DLSS.
- Manual / Auto saving is so bad in this game, even if you save before a specific part, the game will respawn you all the way back to a different checkpoint forcing you to sell your items and perform the upgrades again.
- Changing game graphical settings is a pain, you can not do it in game and you have to back out to the menu to test the settings and change them.

Overall, I do recommend the game for enthusiast of horror and ambiance. However, for the amount of content I Highly suggest to GRAB IT ON SALE. the story is about 8 hours long which is on the short side and some replayabilty features are locked behind a paywall which is an L in my book.

review_text:
Completely disagree with other opinions regarding this as a masterpiece, or even one of the strongest entries in the Yakuza series.  This is one of the most [i]different[/i] in the Yakuza series, which doesn't necessarily translate to good.  

The problem is, the game is trying to do too much, and be too much at the same time.  This contributes to a lack of focus, poor storytelling, and pacing. 

There are multiple characters to play as this time, and each character has a story, alongside their 'regular activity' simulator.  Kiryu has his story in the first chapter, and along with it, you also drive a taxi.  A lot.  Saejima goes hunting.  But the worst... the worst is Haruka.  There's an entire seemingly interminable chapter dedicated to her.  It's a cliched, trope-filled 'story' as she chases a dream to become an idol because reasons. Instead of fighting, there are dancing minigames in which we have to match button presses as they appear on screen, while she performs passionless robotic movements with dull lifeless eyes gazing out in innocent wonder at the world.   I lost all interest in the game at this point and only continued as I had heard that Yakuza 6 was a direct continuation of this story.

Speaking of which, the stories of each character is supposed to be interwoven, but they decided to go with a cliffhanger at the end of each character's chapter, which results in a rushed, dissonant final chapter.  It doesn't help either that the plot is very convoluted with a lot of references to other people and their machinations, and I am not convinced the writers themselves know what is going on. Several times, they had to rely on expositions and even then it took a long time to get through it.  

The fighting itself, which is the main attraction of these games, is decent in its combos and heat moves.  Each character has their own best moves and combos, but due to the massive gaps in playing between them, I found I was forgetting a lot of what made them strong.  Despite that, I found that the boss fights weren't very action packed or satisfactory, they were just OK and most were quite simple, and over very quickly.

An interesting mechanic that's unlocked this time is the second health bar, filled only by food but not restorable through medicine.  It makes for a nice advantage before you're about to head into a big fight.  

The towns are, as usual, nice to explore; there's a decent amount of detail and places to shop and eat.  But, due to the multiple locations, eventually the exploration became a wearisome task.  


I do hope Yakuza 6 isn't more of this.

review_text:
This game has fun music and art, and it wasn't made by The Odd Gentleman -- always a plus -- but it needs some major fixes.

Major:
*  The train is frustrating to walk up and down in: there needs to be a jump-to-room map.
*  The trial goes on FAR too long: it needs to be possible to get the "bad" ending early so you can carry on with the game.
*  You can trade away the pogs early and later a character wants your pogs and says "Sorry, play the game better next time".  Given the (fixable!) problems this game has it was a  mistake to try to be cute like this and it comes across as stuck-up and pompous.

Medium:
*  The "art" fetch quests are in series: you need to hand out all at once so you can work on them all at once.
*  The bee minigame never triggered for me, the Lusus just spat on us immediately.
*  Xefros can use his psychic powers to unlock the farm door but not the teal lockers.  I'd already tried to get him to do that, but even unlocking the farm door doesn't trigger until you try to walk into the forest.

review_text:
NA PSO2 is such a sad sad story, and what makes it really depressing is how high the highs were before NGS dropped. I played on JP years and years ago, but stopped due to the fanmade partial translation and the idea that surely it would be going global in the near future. Fast forward nearly a decade later and it finally does drop, during a global pandemic no less when I had infinite time to play with no commitments.

That was an incredible time - playing the game with an insane amount of players, Urgent Quests popping of at any difficulty level, hanging out in the casino with alliance between grinds and the best part was we knew the next chapter was coming. NGS was on the horizon and NA would be able to explore the content at the same time as the rest of the world. What a gratifying end to such a long wait.

Playing NGS at launch was an enormous disappointment. There was virtually no content, every classes play patterns were the same, the story was non-existent, and every character had a weird uncanny valley plastic feeling to them. The PSO experience had been sanded down to the point where there was effectively nothing left but a character creator/phashion for these very odd looking new character models. Even now, any new game time I put into this game is base PSO2, jumping into NGS just still feels the same from launch. There might be new content, housing, and various new zones to explore but fundamentally the well has already been poisoned. The bones just aren't good, the systems aren't engaging and never were. I managed to hold out around a week in NGS at launch but just went back to PSO2 when it was clear the new offering wasn't fun. I've come back to NGS periodically over the years only to be disappointed over and over again.

Unfortunately base PSO2 doesn't hit like it used to either after nearly four years of NGS splitting the community.  That coupled with the obviously dire state of Sega's future plans has caused the playerbase of base PSO2 to hemorrhage.  I'm on ship 2 and even during peak NA hours I'm lucky to see more then a handful of players in the gate lobby. Of that handful some seem to be permanently AFK, and others are juiced up horny on main characters that I don't really want to interact with to begin with. Today I took a break playing solo after adding a Free party member and upon them loading in they literally had a gigantic dick and balls just hanging free in the wind for the world to see. It's impossible for me to recommend or talk about this game to any of my friends or family because A) it's a sinking ship and B) the first thing they are going to see on logging in is going to be someone's character with thighs wide as a mighty oak and baps large enough to effect the trajectory of celestial bodies.

PSO2 has been left to rot on the vine and NGS was DOA. It's just really sad to see happen to a game that captured my imagination and enthusiasm for almost ten years even while I couldn't play it. If you're a new player reading this, don't waste your time with this game and certainly don't waste your money. Maybe Sega will be able to turn it around somehow but I doubt it. I think the lights will be on for as long as predatory gatcha monetization is legal, and the second it can't prey on its remaining die-hard true believers will be when the servers go down for good.

I felt like this game had those types of things but that they weren't balanced well enough to feel like a change of pace. For example, you get the jumping thing and then you spend a very long time using it for some reason in the next section. It was feeling very much like "okay I get it now, thanks!" I think it's very cool that this was set in Poland but I actually felt like the settings were super boring and same-y... basically Silent Hill's otherworld but the whole time. It got very boring. The non-fleshy areas would've been more interesting if I could see them but the flashlight blows. GET A NEW ONE, TRAVELER.

review_text:
CP... nah, I'm not using that acronym. I got Callisto in a bundle, went in expecting to gag on a diarrhoea-laced slop... but suddenly liked the taste. I wish I could recommend in good conscience a battered game I so enjoyed, but it still feels a tinge aborted. It came out deformed. Wheezing, gurgling, choking like its very world I waded. And it hasn't bloomed since. I've seen nasty loot bugs, graphical glitches, and unearned framedrops. What's sadder, the game flings a greasy sales pitch in your face even before the main menu pops up. There, Downloadable Content is the top option, which betrays a greedy mindset. The "content": bonus death animations, skins, an ending! This is ASS. To boot, everything transpires in the PUBG universe... eh? Why not FNAF? That's one too many compromises. It could be done more elegantly without inciting a PR disaster, guys. Instead, you played yourselves by alienating the audience. Regardless, bracing for impact, I kept an open mind because the setting is my jam. And I found many things to admire.

After all, this is violent sci-fi featuring an adequate horror score reminiscent of Alien, fleshy visuals, and impactful smackdowns. You play as Jacob, a generic merc man delivering some sort of cargo to a prison planet. You're boarded by terrorists, crash, and get arrested on the spot. Mutants attack, so prison break it is! I love me a saucy prison setting. This one is bulky, gritty, with an almost vulgar amount of gore splattered around. The normally disruptive claustrophobic FOV suits the theme. I'd call Callisto an eraserhead child of The Suffering and the new God of War, bearing a touch of The Evil Within in its monster designs. A high praise coming from me. But everyone expected Dead Space, which it isn't, only having flimsy parallels like your dead co-pilot acting as a guilt-tripping ghost wife for a minute. Jacob soon meets a friendly inmate who guides him, then Kimiko from The Boys. All of them are well-acted yet forgettable, including the main villain, the preachiest one I've ever seen! He operates solely on platitudes in the vein of "humanity must overcome its weakness and embrace evolution". Said evolution is giving everyone cerebral palsy and bloated alcoholic mugs. If you say so, fruitcake.

[h3]Face/Off[/h3]
Welp, the main course is combat. The first fight is done clumsily. I expired twice and had to beat up the 3 tutorial fodder losers again because of the autosave placement. Seldom it forces you to shop for goods again if you die, which can be a hassle. However, it made me learn faster and helped to retain the tension throughout. Besides, I don't remember going for more than 10 minutes without a save. Useful for a crab like me who blocks punches with his face. On the bright side, I got to enjoy the bloodbath of painful fatalities. I wish there were more of th... ah, right, paywalled. Either way, I won't deprive the devs of their grotesque achievement. Callisto celebrates its violence and I'm down with it. Yet, I'm not down with a puny stomp. It doesn't gib right and you can't even mangle EVERY body you come across! The rest fits the bill. It's a forgiving system. As long as you hold the stick down, you block. But why? Hold it left or right and dodge no matter the timing. No need to read the telegraphs, except when an enemy does a combo - swap direction for each consecutive hit. You can perform perfect dodges for a bigger window, but it's optional.

Combat is fun to master thanks to its brutality. It's satisfying to smash someone's skull to pieces in a dilapidated bathroom, covering the walls in teeth and tissues. His face gone, limbs torn off, then you shatter his rib cage. Hell yeah! Enemies do the same to you. There's a learning curve to that simple system and it flows nicely when you get the hang of it. Except most enemies can take way too much beating, turning bigger fights into a slog. During those, you aren't allowed to make more than a few mistakes either. Serves me right for playing on Hardcore. But I'm glad Callisto made me bleed like a virgin for my victories. Oddly, fighting several foes wasn't as bad as I imagined despite the finicky lock-on. The ones you don't fight currently are less aggressive, which is the oldest trick in the book. I've heard this wasn't so from the start. Overall, the game is punchy to the bone and I enjoyed the encounter design, for the most part. Although, there's a power creep problem because enemies get stronger alongside you, partially negating it. If only I could upgrade on curve.

[h3]Survival Hobo[/h3]
There's a progression system in place, which allows you to enhance your baton by turning a block into a riposte or adding a heavy attack. Not to mention the guns. Those look badass and don't interrupt the flow by being weaved into your melee combos, staggering and dismembering opponents. Slick! There isn't enough ammo to go guns only, but you can utilise a telekinetic glove to launch stuff, bring a guy to his knees, or plant him on spikes. Almost free of charge. Great, for Callisto is both bugged and beyond stingy on Hardcore. I welcome the resource scarcity, albeit, here it goes from survival horror to survival hobo. You call 1-7 credits loot? The cheapest stuff costs 200!  Half the time, all the loot in a room DESPAWNED upon loading a save! As a result, I got to tier 2 upgrades just for my baton in the endgame. That evil bug was the offence that turned that thumb upside down. Yet, while having a bug-stifled progression and few weapons to choose from isn't a riot, I liked the combat system. Could it carry the whole game, tho? Not if it was any longer. Because in survival horror exploration is the adhesive holding the loop together.

Here, it's lacking. It's a robust grossout-themed beat 'em up, alas, that's all it is. Callisto was fashioned in broad strokes, short on nuance in anything that isn't innards being ripped apart. Ishimura it ain't. Linear non-interactive environments feature minimal backtracking and many pointless dead ends. Expect unsightly darkness and slow crawls through tight spaces, juggling them fuses, and partaking in inoffensive stealth. I sure welcomed free quick kills. In the meantime, you find valuables, gun schematics, and, again, pitiful crumbs of scrip. If you're lucky. And sometimes you get rewarded for your trouble with chip damage from slugs or heads-in-the-box springing out of nowhere! Lovely. At least every other enemy drops a bit of instant health, for you can't hold too many health items. Or any items. I accept limited inventory space as a staple. I don't accept the game's habit of locking doors behind you, blocking off the loot you left for later. Loaded a previous autosave to sweep up, hotshot? The loot has despawned. A nightmare for us greedy guts.

[h3]Dead End[/h3]
And what are these goofy QTEs? Why does Jacob just stand there while I mash the button? Only then, when I finish mashing, he does something like prying the door open. Doesn't feel tactile, defeating the purpose. I ended up setting those on autocomplete. Probably missed out on a few cool deaths. All that said, I adore Callisto despite being critical of its terrible mercantilism and lousy exploration. It ticked a few boxes. I dig the setting, the brutality, and I enjoyed the difficulty. Hell, the lack of loot sure made for a tense hobo challenge! But I don't expect the same attitude from others. It upsets me, yet how can I ask of you to invest in a game that can do you so dirty? And still it's an endorsement for the brave who crave its things macabre. At its ripped-out heart, it's pure 80s horror pulp. If only they didn't mess up the marketing! No technical or mechanical flaw could cripple Callisto as hard. Better ratings may have paid for repairs. As it is, the game has merits, but it's a forsaken dead end. If you consider a visit, do it at a bargain price.

review_text:
Were some of the tricks in Bomb Rush Cyberfunk physically possible? Perhaps not. But were they rad as hell? You can bet the head on your shoulders!

Mechanics: 9/10* (Not including combat, which was a 3/10)
Narrative: 6/10
Art: 7.5/10
Audio: 9/10

I loved the movement and tricking systems, for the entirety of my ~20 hours, including after the story to snag all the achievements, I found myself taking long parkour routes just so I could spend more time doing tricks and watching the sweet animations. Everything was really fluid and it felt [i]good[/i] to string together huge combos for points. I simply [b]loved[/b] how the phone + camera works. Seeing the character's head glued to the screen if you're trying to check the map while moving was entertaining. I even tried playing phone games while high-speed tricking. [spoiler]It didn't go well. Remember to never text and parkour.[/spoiler] 

The story was alright, a few twists and turns to keep things interesting, but nothing to knock your socks off. I will say that I liked the feeling of the individual characters, they kept a strong sense of personality throughout the story.

The combat I would say was the game's weakest point. It was a button spam fest with some small variations on the later enemies. I was really left wanting when some of the bigger boys showed up to be killed faster than a group of the most basic ones. However, I will say that I don't care too much since it was weak in the direction of being easy. I really just wanted to spend more time doing tricks, and that's what I got.

The soundtrack was pretty sweet all throughout. It really solidified the skater vibe throughout and I felt myself doing tricks and planning my route to the tempo of whatever was playing. The art was also stylised in a consistent way, I would've liked to see a bit more variation with some of the NPCs beyond the main cast, but the character design was solid for them. Loved some of the graffiti designs.

Overall, [b]7.5/10[/b]. Great fun game, give it a shot if you're looking for something funky fresh.

Now with the non-relative review done, I would like to give a special mention since I grew up with Jet Set Radio Future being one of my favourite games. This really hit the nail on the head for a spiritual successor. You could feel the influence with the camera work, some sound effects, and the general idea of the game. However, I think Bomb Rush Cyberfunk still held its own, it was clearly in its lane while paying tribute to an old classic.

Thanks for the devs for letting me relive a bit of the Jet Set days, good work on this one!

review_text:
It pains me that I can't recommend this, because I was an absolute shill for Boneworks. Ironically, Bonelab's own predecessor feels so much more like a game than it. The game that was kind of tossed around as a tech demo originally now feels so much less like one than its damn successor.Everything feels like such a downgrade, with gun handling and general physics feeling super jank in comparison to Boneworks, which had its own myriad of issues. It feels like Bonelab amplified these issues. 

But bleeding-edge VR tech jank aside, the actual content is utterly disappointing. The campaign itself can be completed in just a few hours, with more than half of the levels feeling like a showcase for the character-swap (Bodylog) mechanic, which kills replay value because it's so narrowly and linearly designed for specific characters in certain sections. Only in the last few levels does the game open up a little and let you go ham with all of the options that this mechanic has to offer. And then it ends, in such an anticlimactic way. 

It makes you ask for more, and the game's answer? Modding. I genuinely hope I eat my words, but at the time of writing, the modding scene is incredibly lackluster, with the official SDK not receiving an update in a fair while. Basic levels and avatar skins are at your disposal without dipping your toes into fan-authored tools instead. It's still awesome that the fanbase is devoted enough to do this, but it's frustrating that the modding tools for a game that heavily holds itself up with modding potential are so lightweight and barebones at the moment.

The price tag is a killer too. 40 bucks, really? Something like $20-25 (maybe 30??) and we have a deal no problem), but Bonelab charges almost double the price of its predecessor and doesn't offer something more enticing and more content-rich. Yes, the game was advertised primarily as a sandbox rather than a story-heavy experience. But 40 dollars is not a fair deal when the sandbox elements don't really bring much replay value to it. In fact, the more I replay Bonelab, the more I feel frustrated and just miserable at the state of the game. It feels so incomplete, and this isn't even tagged as early access!

I dunno, man. It feels hollow right now, empty and bare. Maybe there was a lot more planned for it? It's like the game was chopped in half, and who knows where the other half is. Maybe after some content updates things will be different? I hope so, but the patches so far that have added content to some of the levels feel sloppy and rushed (thanks for the hardly-avoidable hitscan helicopter on Sprint Bridge ya nerds) like duct-tape solutions, so I dunno at this point. Fingers crossed, right?

I recommend Boneworks instead if you want a longer experience for half the price. For now, personally, Bonelab feels like a minigame-esque experience in a VR industry presently drowning in bite-sized cheap-feeling experiences. YMMV, of course. If anything, wait for a sale and nab this then.

EDIT: Patches have done utterly nothing. Game's less buggy, I guess, but it's still hardly a game. Mods are still just stuck as player skins and that's it. No amount of John Halo skins can redeem this.

review_text:
Nicely fills the void left from 2000s era wacky sports games. Easy pickup for folks who enjoyed the old Midway games like NHL Hitz, NFL Blitz, NBA Street, etc.

In current state of game's early access, the campaign is a series of 5v5 hockey games where you play against a variety of wacky teams. Successful runs on normal take maybe 1-1.5 hours, with individual games going as short as 30 seconds but usually less than 5 minutes.

As of this writing I got ~20 hours out of it and feel satisfied with the available experience, and am excited to see what comes as EA progresses.


----------------------------
Unsolicited feedback time:

I said the game is 5v5, but most of the time it feels like 1v10; me vs the 5 opponents, my 4 teammates, and the controls of the game itself. At first, this was EXTREMELY frustrating, but then I kind of came to enjoy figuring out how to play around my teammates refusing to position themselves in ways that make sense. Remember playing hockey/soccer as a kid and how everyone just clumps up around the puck/ball? Yep. Frustrating because the most effective way to score is one-timers (20 hours in and I'm really not sure if it's possible to score with pure slapshots), but teammates will rarely position themselves to take advantage. Also the 10th opponent, the controls, frequently enjoys passing to teammates who have no business being a valid target for the pass. Sometimes I'll be putting up goals one after another effortlessly, and sometimes I feel like the game is purposefully pumping the opponent goalie with OVR so I can never possibly score. I know the programming the logic for each player and the various physics isn't easy at all so I'm willing to forgive the current system quite a bit and I'd wager this is where most dev time goes, still gonna throw my voice out there.

The RPG elements are frankly criminal. Having to spend rubber on Angus getting better might make sense from perspective of 'people get better at things over time', but this is a video game where things get absurd quick and then magically return to status quo. It feels like I'm intended to have artificially worse experiences early on for the sake of inflating gameplay time. The game is fun, you don't need to do that. Remove this, give Angus static stats that can be improved/changed during a run.

Speaking of, the hockey blacksmith is a very funny hook right from the menu, but is wasted on a lame metaprogression shop. Why is he not appearing during the run? Forget the Rest areas on the map, that should be hockey blacksmith forging better gear to increase stats/equipment. Meta shop should be saved for more interesting meta elements, see the mirror in Hades
as an example. The power to reverse a goal once would make sense as a meta option, similar to Death's Defiance. Just spitballing, current system is joysucking. 

The map in general could be made more interesting. As is, I don't know why anyone would willingly go to rests/events over games for talents when given the choice. Some events are actually curses, and some are good but have obvious options. With the bonus to OVR during a period, why would anyone not take +50 OVR in the first perior? Thanks to the mercy mechanic it's the only option that makes sense. Then for the bad events, you can skip but you still lost a talent by not choosing the correct option in the first place. Would really benefit from copying Slay the Spire's homework a bit more: a 3 pronged map at all times, not being forced into the current pattern of talent, rest, full game, talent, full game, boss. Let me choose between elite games for talents/artifacts, playing it safe if things aren't looking hot, or training/blacksmithing. Let me recruit and swap in new players and switch gear around after the fact. There's already a gear system, and a blacksmith! Lean more into sportsy-ness and let me modify my team a bit more.

I get the game is a delicate balance between keeping it grounded enough to still be an accessible sports game, and full on video gamey roguelike wackiness. Personally, I would enjoy leaning muuuuch further into roguelike wackiness. Longer runs, weirder powers, weirder and more varied opponents. Wouldn't even mind if runs were significantly longer. Putting it out there.

All that said, I got 20 hours of enjoyment current state and eagerly await more so all these criticisms are from a place of really liking the game and hoping it achieves greatness and gets more attention.

review_text:
Bonelab is a wildly ambitious VR title that pushes the boundaries of physics-based interaction in virtual reality. Developed by Stress Level Zero, it acts as a spiritual successor to Boneworks, expanding on its ideas with a mix of experimental levels, sandbox gameplay, and modding potential. Rather than focusing on a traditional narrative experience, Bonelab is more of a platform—a physics playground that encourages players to discover and shape the world around them.

The campaign, while present, feels more like a guided introduction to the game’s systems than a self-contained story. Each level presents a different theme, showcasing climbing mechanics, driving, puzzle-solving, and combat across various stylized environments. There's a surreal, almost dreamlike flow to the progression. The body-swapping mechanic, which lets you change your avatar's physical traits on the fly, adds a unique twist that’s tightly integrated into gameplay. However, the campaign can feel fragmented or unfocused, as its primary purpose is clearly to prepare players for the open-ended experiences that follow.

Where Bonelab truly shines is in its sandbox and community-driven content. The game offers a powerful physics engine that supports a massive range of interactions, from wielding medieval weapons to flinging enemies across rooms with makeshift contraptions. It thrives on emergent gameplay—moments that aren’t scripted but born from the systems interacting with each other in unpredictable ways. The inclusion of mod support from day one means the game evolves constantly, with the player community contributing everything from new levels and characters to completely custom game modes.

The VR implementation is solid but not without its challenges. Movement is fully physics-based, which makes for immersive, grounded gameplay but can also lead to awkward climbing or locomotion quirks. There’s a steep comfort curve; newcomers to VR may find some of the motion nausea-inducing, especially during high-speed sections or more chaotic environments. Still, for experienced VR users, the tradeoff is worth it—few games offer this level of tactile control and player expression.

Combat and traversal feel more refined than in Boneworks, but they’re still rough around the edges in places. Melee fights have a satisfying physicality, and gunplay is responsive and detailed, but some mechanics—like enemy AI and environmental interactions—can feel inconsistent. Fortunately, the game’s modular design and constant stream of user-generated content help smooth over these issues, providing fresh challenges and tools long after the campaign ends.

Bonelab is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be: an experimental, mod-friendly physics simulation wrapped in a VR framework. It’s not trying to compete with tightly scripted action games or deep RPGs. Instead, it hands the keys over to the player, saying, “Here’s a box of tools. Go break stuff.” While not for everyone—particularly those who crave structure or are sensitive to VR motion—it’s an outstanding example of what sandbox VR can look like when it fully commits to player agency. For fans of Boneworks, modders, and VR tinkerers, Bonelab is a chaotic, fascinating, and ever-evolving experience.

Rating: 8/10

review_text:
I learned a lot during this game, first and foremost that I am, apparently, an unfeeling clutz because the story did absolutely nothing for me. I found the main protagonists annoying, the humor was juvenile and did not fit the theme of the story, and frankly, the story itself was also at best ok-ish. And the gameplay and mechanics are simply atrocious. 

It's a complete mystery to me why this game has an overwhelmingly positive rating. 

[h2]Story and characters[/h2]

As the blurp says, you play as two doctors who go backwards through a dying man's memories to artifically fulfill his last wish. That sounds great, but in practice it means that you visit scenes from this man's life that were significant to him but, in-game, you are just an observer, it is all very surface-level. You do not interact with the man or the other characters (with very few exceptions), you can't really investigate anything, you are just dropped into the scene, read a few lines of dialogue (no voice-over), and that's it. 

At one point, you manipulate his memories, and then skip through his life events again, this time in the right direction, to see how this manipulation affected his "life", and if you managed to "fulfill" his last wish. But, and there lies the main problem for me, it does not actually affect anything. It manipulates a dying man into misremembering his whole life (on his request). What you see didn't and does not happen, and could not have happened in reality. 

It is a bit sad if you think about it, but you do not get to know any of the characters well enough to get emotionally invested, at least in my opinion.

The memory scenes are presented through the eyes of the two doctors, who are the real protagonists, and I found them pretty much insufferable. They were clearly intended as comic relief, and they are constantly squabbling in a mean-spirited and at times childish way. I think there's supposed to be a romantic undertone but the inane dialogue completely ruins it. 

[h2]Gameplay and the rest[/h2]

The actual gameplay consists for the most part of you dropping into a scene, trying to find the very few points that you can interact with, and collect five "memento" points and a core memory. If you have found everything, you can leave the scene and have to solve a mini-puzzle. It is always the same type of puzzle, and it is neither difficult nor fun. 

There is no indication which parts of the scenery are walkable and which aren't, and there is no logic behind the mementos, so you are randomly clicking everywhere to either move somewhere else or find one of the mementos. 

This is even worse in the few "action" sequences, in which you can run around with the arrow keys. There is no excuse for having such buggy and clunky controls even in a game from 2011. 

[h2]To sum it up[/h2]

Currently, the game is tagged as "emotional". In my case, that emotion is annoyance.

I do not recommend this game.

review_text:
I don't know if I'm angry or disappointed. Maybe both. Most bad stuff you heard about this game is true. So much, that I can't comprehend that this was made by same folks that made Dead Space. But again, people who made Left 4 Dead made Back 4 Blood... and Evolve, so there's that. Callisto Protocol is a pale, miserable copy of Dead Space.

[b][u]PROS:[/u][/b][i]
+ game looks incredible
+ they fixed most technical problems game had on launch
+ it's not the worst game ever[/i]

[b][u]CONS:[/u][/b][i]
- actual ending is locked behind a DLC paywall. They did the same thing with Dead Space 3, so i'm "glad" they're copying the worst parts of that franchise
- game is just miserable to play. Melee is slow and without any depth at all, shooting is somewhat usable, GRIP was developed as an afterthought
- enemy design is bad and not scary. They all look like bunch of mangled ballsacks and the variety in enemies is pretty slim. Just visually uninteresting and very generic looking
- story is pretty much Dead Space-like, only worse in every aspect
- gameplay is very repetitive. There is like, one type of boss that you fight couple of times and there is also the "main" antagonist, who is absent 99% of the game. Every room is empty, there is no point in exploring everything when everything is barren except some ammo here and rarely an audio log there. And the game is big but a lot of that space is non-interactable empty decorations
- you wouldn't believe how many times the main character falls from something or through something or the bridge breaks, building collapses and he falls on the bottom and has to fight to go up. It's just silly and it breaks game tempo and immersion completely after 5th time it happens
- crafting is... well usable but very basic, uninspired, looks kinda cool but after some time you just want it to go faster but no, you have to have an animation. And resources needed for crafting are very scarce, so much so, that I don't think you can upgrade everything through first gameplay. I didn't and don't plan to in New Game+[/i]

---

I'm sure this will be the best game ever for someone, but I don't think most people should play it. Even in 2024, most things they fixed are performance problems that made the game almost unplayable on PC during launch. But the core gameplay and content is just not there and they can't fix that. Also, for me, locking actual ending behind a paywall in a form of a DLC is unforgivable. 

Some boss fights tend to be pretty nerve racking because of the ammo scarcity in that right moment. Weapon swap is also often nightmarish, reloading is somewhat slow and using healing stuff is even slower. I have no idea how GRIP battery works, sometimes I have to use it manually, sometimes it's auto applied. To make it even worse, health bar is small and GRIP indicator is even smaller so can't see sssshieeet

Story wise, it's dull, not bad, just very cliche filled sci-fi fare. And everything looking the same, despite the size of the game areas, doesn't help but to create pretty generic dull atmosphere as well. 

Playing this game is just not fun or satisfying and looking at the people who made this and how good the game looks, it's incomprehensible how is this not way, way better? Every part of the game needed something more, some X factor, love and care it didn't get. Callisto Protocol is playable in 2024, I just think you would not enjoy it much.. if any of it.

What I write for this review is the experience I had with the game, everybody will experience things differently. This is my honest review if you don't like it well tough. Also no game is safe from a review whether its early access or full release now onto the review.

So After The Fall is another vr game made by Vertigo Games, their other popular game Arizona Sunshine zombie game was really fun. That set the bar for their vr game to like that & better but with After The Fall it kinda fall flat. For $39.99 you expect to get good quality graphics, decent optimization & good content. Here you get well only one of those which is the graphics but its not far from the Oculus version, almost nearly the same. Optimization is bad, the game keeps phasing in & out during game play quit a lot & the content is well lacking. Four or five maps, 6 weapons, 3 mini bosses & 1 super boss but its just a re-skin of one of the mini bosses just scaled bigger.

The deluxe edition for same price as launch version ($9.99 upgrade) you get access to an additional farming run, an additional pvp arena, additional game mode, additional weapon & exclusive character skin. After downloading the deluxe edition I saw no difference in content from the launch version & deluxe version. Same maps, weapons  & character skin. I don't know why you have a deluxe edition for content that is that same as launch version.

I feel that this was made for Oculus in-mind more & they imported it over to steam without really testing it. Here are issues I found in both steam & Oculus
1. Magazines will randomly drop out of my hand
2. Ammo pouch can't be moved in different area
3. Training doesn't give you full training
4. Settings doesn't let you full customize to your liking  at start up, have to manually go & do it
5. Manual reloading with off hand is jank, doesn't fully track reloading

These may seem small stuff but to some this is important to their gameplay experience. So with that After The Fall gets 4/10 making it under average. Maybe with more updates, more content & better optimization this game could be a better & not so cold to play. I would not recommend buying After The Fall but instead recommend buying Vertigo Games zombie game Arizona Sunshine.

That's the pony review for After The Fall
