review_text:
If you're looking at this game while its on a deep discount, it's actually a recommend. I'm giving a not recommended based on the retail price. 

The story for the main game is alright, though rather short and honestly nothing ground breaking. If you're not going to play the game 5 or 6 times on NG+ for all the achievements I imagine you'll get 10-14 hours out of the base game. The DLC adds another mission but without spoiling anything I could do without that part of the story. 

If you do replay the game multiple times I don't really see much of a point outside of the achievements, honestly. As long as you loot all the enemies in your initial play through you'll almost have everything upgraded. The final upgrades are just an extra weapon ability that causes the weapon to use more ammo, for example. There are other modes added in DLC as well so I guess if you like that kind of thing maybe you'll get more out of it.

The combat is rather strange... to dodge you need to hold down a or d (or the joystick if using a controller) when the enemy goes to attack. It's somewhat fun for a little while but when there are multiple enemies it can get rather annoying. There isn't a perfect timing for dodge, you just have to be holding the key when the enemy swings. If you tap the key you can get a perfect dodge that kinda slows time for a sec but the time slow is only during the animation and outside of an achievement for doing it 5x in a row I don't see an advantage to perfect dodging. The combat rotation that seemed to work best for me was dodge the enemy, melee so that you stun them and get the little targeting circle, then fire at them to finish them off. 

Also, there is a lot of crawling through vents and squeezing through small spaces. I feel like 2 hours of the total play through was spent either in a vent or squeezing between pipes. 

It's not all bad though.. especially if you're paying less than $10 for it. It was somewhat enjoyable or I wouldn't have finished it but looking at the achievement for completing the game on any difficulty only 40% of people have actually completed it. If it's on sale and you like these types of games it's worth trying out.

review_text:
Maybe this game is good, maybe it's bad, I'll likely never know. I've never seen a game so mired in awful design and obtuse controls. The UI is so horrendous that my entire hour of playing this, at time of writing, was spent in sheer unbelievable confusion of just trying to get the most basic of gameplay to function. Again, the core of this game 'could' be very fun and it 'could' be very well developed. The experience I forced myself through however, was one that I can't possibly recommend to anyone without massive overhauls to the UI and UX Design.

The UI is so massively overloaded with blurry, hyper-pixilated images with the smallest possible font and buttons that I think might actually be measured in tens of pixels. It was borderline impossible to figure out what was interactable and what was just information, not that I could read any of it without my computer's magnifying glass function.

Just getting the basics of getting a lumber yard built (ie the first building you're given) was a harder task to comprehend than the entirety of Rimworld (a vastly superior game). Trying to figure out how many resources I had took multiple menus. It's ultimately just this microscopic pile of pixels at the top of the screen, but not knowing that, the image for your storage space always looks like it has resources. So for about 20 minutes I was hitting every key trying to figure out why they weren't taking the resources I could SEE WERE THERE to build. Only to find out those didn't exist. 

Next up, I finally just took the 10 min to HAND PICK the wood myself and drop it in because I couldn't get anyone to harvest anything. Of the literally multiple dozens of menus, there was not a single option for "harvest the thing". I defaulted back to over a decade ago with Black and White / Warcraft, that this game apes off of, and thought "Oh, obviously I need to pick them up and put them on the resource." which you CAN DO. Doesn't do anything. It took me pressing literally every key on my keyboard to find out that there were two buttons not included in the trainwreck of a UI THAT WERE VITAL TO THE GAMES CORE FUNCTION. You need to select INDIVIDUALLY which tree/stone tiles you want harvested. They won't do a single thing if that's not selected. An option, that again, was not presented, on screen or any menu.

review_text:
There are some fundamental flaws with the core gameplay loop that bring it down from a game with potential to a game that frustrates.  I'll list below the major issues I have and hopefully the devs can take the feedback such that I come back one day.  I love a lot of what is here but some serious yet easy to fix flaws hold it back.  

-In a fast paced game, having the gauge for the powers be these tiny circles in the bottom left makes it nigh impossible for me to use my powers that come off cooldown midfight because I can't squint at the bottom left of my screen while also dashing around trying to kill things in the center of my screen.  Powers/cooldowns should have indicators and visual flashes/indicators that pop up when an ability is fully charged.  ALSO GETTING ANIMATION LOCKED TO PUNISH THE PLAYER FOR HITTING THE POWER WHEN IT IS ON CD IS INCREDIBLY ENRAGING AND IS RESPONSIBLE FOR MOST OF MY DEATHS 8 hours in.  

-Weapon balance feels very inconsistent.  Elites need to die fast, and some guns have dps that is incomprehensibly lower than others such that I cant understand why they are even an option.  Also If it takes 50% of my ammo to take down an elite with one gun and 5% with another that says a lot especially since resource management is so important.  

-Game takes too long to "get to the good part". I can tell that the early game is somewhat slowed down to bring the player in, but when Im spending 90% of my time walking between fights rather than fighting for the first few hours that is going to kill player interest real fast. I only played more bc I was told it gets better.  Part of this is caused by nothing indicating to me that I needed to unlock the blocked off hallway to make the game actually fun...that should be a quest or something. I kept upgrading my character level and couldnt afford to open the hallway but I didnt know the hallway was important.

Just a passionate gamer who wants to see this game do better.

Samorost 2 is the sequel for Samorost 1 (now also available on Steam) and a short and cute point & click adventure game. You play as a little white gnome embarking on a space trip to free your dog, which has been kidnapped by aliens.

I found the game quite entertaining and somehow relaxing thanks to simple gameplay and the soothing soundtrack. The artstyle is absolutely cute and pleasant, not to mention the smooth and well executed animation. It's a flash game ; regrettably, you can't take screenshots and the menu is visible the whole game at the bottom of the screen. The puzzles aren't always obvious because you don't know for sure what you have to do. It remains amusing all the same.

Edit: You can now take screenshots of the game and they added several achievements.

I'd suggest to buy Samorost 2 on sales because the game is about 1 hour long only. I recommend this game, obviously, because even if it was a short adventure, it was a wonderful one. If you enjoyed it, know that [url=store.steampowered.com/app/421120/Samorost_3/]Samorost 3[/url] is available on the Steam Store as well.

review_text:
TLDR; I do not recommend it, but only barely. Game is slow and rewards a methodical play-style, and I'm hesitant to continue because of how the devs prioritize gun-play over spells, in addition to boring rogue-like boons that don't affect game-play much throughout each expedition. Each run feels almost the same. 

A pretty decent rogue-like extraction shooter combo, it has a lot of gun-play inspired aspects from Destiny (that is a good thing) like weapon frames. They do, however, also use a lot of "rogue-like" boons similar to destiny (that is a bad thing).

A lot of boons you earn throughout a play-through are pretty mild, and don't affect game-play all that much (including a whole whopping 1% extra drop rate for healing elixirs, wow), which makes each run feel nearly identical. Similarly, there is an emphasis on gun-play compared with the spells we earn and use, which I'm not a huge fan of. 

The spells feel pretty weak, and seem to be secondary to guns (even though ammo is also sparse), as they have pretty large cooldowns and very low damage. None of the heavy spells I've gotten so far are very satisfying or useful, especially for how long they take to recharge, and very few light spells are very useful either. Mostly they seem to be used for staggering enemies, or afflicting them with an elemental affix, which isn't bad in and of itself, but if that's their main purpose, their CDs should definitely be reduced imo. If their damage is so low, I don't understand why their cooldown isn't lower either. I'm sure it has to do with the balance they want with how fast-paced the game feels, since it definitely feels like a conscious decision, I just don't think it's a very good one.

Speaking of pace, the game is pretty slow. I saw someone else mention how it's a very dad-game, if that makes sense, and I can understand that view. It's not a bad thing, but man oh man I wish the game was faster. Even just a little, but more than a little would be better. I really really wish stamina consumption was not a thing out of combat, and everything generally feels very slow/sluggish once you get used to the dance of things. I'm not going to speak on the balance of weapons, but some certainly feel stronger than others. 

Ammo consumption is directly linked to how good at the stun mechanics you are, which is a great idea in concept, but feels kind of bad when you realize you're going to be doing 1/2 damage and losing ammo unless you're constantly abusing the stun mechanics, even when it doesn't feel necessary.

I'm not sure how often the devs update the game, although it's been one or two months since last I played and everything has been the same since then, and it's difficult to want to continue just because of how unbalanced the game feels with guns vs. spells. Maybe the later game is different, I don't know, but 7 hrs in and it isn't looking like it, even after unlocking the other inventory slots.

Falling off a cliff into void/depths also immediately ends your run, which generally I wouldn't mind, if it was my own fault. However usually, the circumstances are questionable. More often am I pushed horizontally by a projectile coming at me from a perpendicular angle than running off of my own volition. Projectiles *pulling* me forward and thus into an abyss is also an issue I have, especially when they look identical to all other projectiles and just behave differently for some reason. Or at least I assume they look identical, maybe they don't, but I've never noticed a difference.- look, I don't mind losing player autonomy, especially when it's purposeful, however when it happens for some willy-nilly, not-so-easily-identifiable reason, over and over again, it really knocks the wind out of your sails. Especially when that reason ends a long winded run unceremoniously. I'm not saying to remove the mechanic, but at least give only a specific enemy enemy the ability, or maybe give the projectile a very obvious look about it compared to the other projectiles. Something that allows players to know when there's a different threat to be aware of. Readability in games is a legitimate issue and one that isn't always obvious. When a unit that you've been fighting begins behaving differently when only in certain locations, maybe just make it a different enemy instead.

Sorry, I got lost in the sauce. It's a decent game, although there's a lot I'm left wanting for. Maybe once it's out of EA it'll be better, but it's difficult to recommend atm.

review_text:
This game is so close to being fantastic, but I'm afraid the dev's vision of "survive until you die" stands in the way of what the game COULD be. Let me explain.

You start with a great little city builder! Yes, we can quibble about the oddities of farming/water resource management, etc., but it is tremendously satisfying to watch as your village grows and comes alive! Then, the monsters attack. Mostly at night. You transition to a tower defense game, constructing towers and golems to fight the enemy, weaving a maze of walls for the enemy to traverse, holding strong as your villagers cower and attempt to reinforce every defense while balancing seasonal survival needs. This is all very cool... until it's not. 

You WANT to send out a force to counter-attack the enemy base camps. The game isn't designed for that. You WANT to eradicate the threat from every sector of the World Map one by one. But again, that’s not what this game is about. The best you can do is... survive. For awhile. And then die. Yes, you can play on more peaceful settings, but you miss out on the tension which, early on, is really very good. But this game makes me long for more, like the days when I played the Majesty games where you could assemble a bunch of heroes, select a threat, and have them go trounce the enemy (or get trounced if not up to the task). If you play your cards right in Majesty, you can actually win! Here, in Rise to Ruins, you grow until your villagers are defeated, with goals like "Survive 21 days!" as your only incentive to keep going. But why keep going if the end is inevitable and the enemy is guaranteed victory every time?

All defense and no offense creates an artificial limit on what this game COULD be. The potential is there, but ultimately it's a bust for me. Sigh. Back on the shelf of my Steam Library, hoping someday a developer in inspired by the many great elements from this and builds something with a more expansive vision - one with a path to overcome the threat and Rise FROM the Ruins to fight back!

review_text: I don't have enough good things to say about this game. I got it on a whim while it was on sale but it's 100% worth buying at full price (if that's in your budget). Challenging enough to keep me engaged, but not so difficult that I wanted to quit. And you can make it more difficult for yourself if you want, by playing on Difficult mode or trying to achieve some of the (very hard imho) optional objectives. The story is emotionally engaging, and the characters feel real (to the point that I got annoyed with some of them like I would real people lol). Each character has strengths and weaknesses, which influence how you can use them on each level. Every action has a consequence - if I set a trap *here* it will affect *this* set of guards, but how will the nearby civilians react? The art style is really attractive, the voice acting is top notch, and the soundtrack is phenomenal - the combination really transports you to the game's world. I played through the original game twice, the second time incorporating the Aiko's Choice expansion (which takes place in the middle of the original game), and I might dabble in a third playthrough one of these days, once my game backlog is a little better. If you like the challenge of strategizing an entire mission and overcoming all obstacles in your path, this game is for you!

review_text:
This game is getting a lot of consistent work and polish, and I appreciate it, but it still falls into a major category of frustrating that I can't seem to get over, and that is that villagers, that backbone of your economy are complete idiots.

Builder is the default worker position, where the job assignment for the villager is "go get whatever is needed to build the building that is on the top of the builder priority list." It's not extremely efficient role but it's very versatile and useful, especially at the beginning of the game. However, if you have built too many buildings, they just... stop functioning; they get stupid and stand around like brain-damaged penguins. in the meantime, your town gets overrun.

If I decide to add 30 building plans to my town, let me do that. Don't have the game punish me for ambitiously planning ahead of what my town is going to look like. The builders don't need to drop everything, they can just finish what they were doing and move onto the next thing when they are done.

"That's not how the game is played!"

That's how I'm playing the game. If it doesn't let me play that way, I'm gonna stop playing, and this review will stay red.

Edit: Years in, achievements have been added, and villagers are still brain-damaged penguins. I spend more time dragging single resources to buildings and dropping monsters into sacrifice pits than I do playing an actual game. It's not compelling gameplay. This is a simulator desperately in search of a game. It's sad too, because if the villagers weren't phenomenally stupid, this wouldn't feel like such a slog.

Edit 2: Alright, I finally gave in and bought Rimworld. HOLY hell. Talk about exactly what I was looking for.

I know that the purpose of this game is to be god and let your humans do the work, the problem is that your direct action in the game consists of dragging items to objects, one at a time. It's TEDIOUS AF. The gameplay on this BEGS for increased direct engagement. Rimworld admittedly, isn't perfect in this capacity, but the ability to draft your pawns and make them do ALMOST exactly what you want at any give time sets itself apart from this game. I'm sorry, but this discrepancy has been the difference between fun and not fun. Rimworld is tedious, but it's fun, RoR is tedious, and it's not fun.

What will fundamentally change this game for the better is a spell that automatically supply a building with materials. You click on the unfinished building's resource with the spell, and the tool simply grabs the closest resources required to finish the project and drags it to the building, spending mana based on distance of said resources. At the very least, allowing the grab spell to pick up stacks of material would probably suffice. In the long run, a holy golem might be more efficient, but when give the choices between efficiency and engagement, watch players choose the engagement every time. Right now, the spells are badly implemented, an entire array of options that have next to little practical utility, all drawing from a single resource that you use to tediously drag and drop materials.

No, I don't think I'll ever upvote this game, not unless spells are seriously re-imagined and empowered in a way that reflect gameplay agency for the player.

This is basically a more boring Warframe with more story/textboxes, more singleplayer-forced segments, and a lacking playerbase that's mostly just in endgame and nowhere else.

You're clearly meant to have other people at your gear level in the normal levels, but nobody's present, not even bots, and when players are there via helper queue, they're endgaming nukers with high gear levels who are gonna speednuke forth leaving nothing for you to shoot or do (optionally pressuring you because you're not keeping up with them)... Just like Warframe. Even the mission variety is basically Warframe's but slightly altered.

If you try to do it alone, you'll quickly notice how annoying getting swarmed is and how empty the levels really are, and, because there's 6 different damage types that are good in different ways against different things, you're seemingly expected to swap between Nature, Magnetic, and one of the other normal types against Health, but here's the catch: You only have two weapon slots and certain weapon types don't spawn with certain elements, so you have to make do with weapons you absolutely loathe in order to get through in the time you're meant to.

Oh, and of course, if you're a solo player, you NEED to build whichever character you're playing as as a dodging tank, otherwise the swarms will quickly decimate you... and that leads to grinding and farming to get dodge gear with affixes that complement your tank/dodge build. It likely gets a lot worse later, but it's already exacerbated when you play a character other than 7 who needs a different armor type and can't just use what another character has, oh no no, you're meant to grind like this is a phone-mmo, which it basically is. Grind not only for the gear, but also the enhancement mats, several times over because the game tells you you can just transfer the item level, but you can't do it to higher-rarity items, so you have to keep grinding with your green until you can finally upgrade your blue-or-above to a usable state.

review_text:
Great game. Fantastic gunplay. I thought I wouldn’t be able to play it because of the insanely high difficulty. And yeah, at first, it really was tough. But then I started getting into it. And after that, I just couldn’t tear myself away. I love literally everything: the environment design, the enemies, the weapons, the music, and that thick, grim atmosphere. This is the Painkiller 2 we wanted.

At the start, I thought I was really missing those sweaty brawls with dozens of enemies on screen, but that didn’t last long — once I got into the more serious locations, I ended up in fights where for a couple of minutes you literally forget to breathe, locked in a bloody dance of destruction, tearing through everything alive.

If you understand how the game works, you’ll have a blast. But if you try to play it like a regular shooter, without using literally everything the game gives you, you’re in for a rough time. I often caught myself thinking that most shooters I’ve played let you ignore most of their mechanics — just shoot and you’re fine. But here, using your entire arsenal is absolutely essential. Without it, you’re in for a quick and stupid death.

And once you find your favorite weapon, upgrade it, and put together a build that feels just right for you — that’s when the real flow starts, especially on the highest levels of Gnosis.

Highly recommended for anyone looking for a deep and dynamic shooter.

But if you're intrigued enough to read reviews, it may just be for you. Everything I'm about to say applies to the game's intended and hardest difficulty, which I recommend you play on.
 Here's why this game is genius: the goal of most games is to be fun and satisfying for the player. All their systems are tailored to achieve that. The goal of this game is to produce a state of stress, anxiety, and desperation in the player -*but also a sense of hope, a sense that you can win.* All its systems are finely tuned to enable you to stay on top of the various things dragging you down (hunger, lack of time, exhaustion) - but only by the skin of your teeth. As you come to understand it more, you realize that the game, despite going to great lengths to seem unfair, is in fact very fair - it always gives you access to the things you need to survive and win, as long as you pay attention and plan carefully. But your life in the game is never easy, you always have tough choices to make, and relief is only ever temporary. This combination is what makes it so engaging - not to speak about the story, world and characters, which are all wonderfully weird and vivid. 
Only about 7% of players have the achievement for beating the game on its intended difficulty. Clearly, these design principles don't click for everybody. But if or when they do, this game becomes the most mesmerizing and compelling game out there.

In short it is every bit as good as 2007 and in some ways better. The AI seems far less likely to accept garbage deals such as dealing a large quantity of mediocre players for a 1st round draft pick which is great. There have been a few bugs but overall they have been fixed quickly in my eyes. 

Your players get suspended often and for longer amounts if they fight too much. I both like and dislike this. I used to employ psychos strictly to go after the other teams top players but this tactic is hamstrung by the suspensions. I don't really mind that much. 

Overall if you have enjoyed previous Eastside games in the past you owe it to yourself to check this out. One of the few games I can sink hours into on end and not notice the time fly by.

review_text:
TL:DR Base was/is way better.
NGS can be fun with friends for a while, it's a lot of wasted potential. A hollow shell of what it could've been, sink your time in pointless stats and numbers and maybe some good looking phashion.

NGS is dog water. You have West SEGA to blame for that (and let me also blame Microsoft too, totally personal).

Transition from Base to NGS was poorly done, the game was released in a very primitive state, and their priorities are Paid gacha Phashion, crappy vTubers collabs and seasonal farming events with constant reuse of assets.

Version 2, the next big step for the game was just Creative Spaces. Why would SEGA care to put out good content when we can have the community recreate a Sonic stage! 

Story is lame and you can clearly see the lack of passion and budget.

Races no longer matter because with "Body Type A/B" you can make whatever character you want. It doesn't matter that Dewmans are the only ones with Tattoos, Horns and Heterochromia, higher damage output and less defense. It doesn't matter that Newmans are best suited for Photons but fare worse with actual weapons. It doesn't matter, there's no real point, just get rid of it all and make it just cosmetics. Forget whatever lore we had.

The gameplay is probably the best part of the game, with the most potential... but it ends there. It's flashy, it's satisfactory and has some variety... for a while, but every single end-game point was just grinding for your preferred rare weapon, to have it become obsolete by a new set of weapons that will be even harder to get. Rinse and repeat.
It lacks all the depth and variety Base PSO2 had. The enemies are all the same with just a few differences between regions.

The Open World was cool and novel at first, but then it became old very quickly, and it's now just a hindrance, a chore. It's empty, there's no lore, no enviromental story telling, there are no real traces of civilization, of work, of humanity. Just mobs and enemies. ARKS means nothing, you are alone, no one is working out there, no one is fighting out there, you as a player are alone.

There aren't "Quests", NPCs lack identity and personality, tasks are lackluster and the whole game feels very disconnected from the whole Phantasy Star universe and atmosphere.

The best you can do is play a bit with friends and AFK/socialize in Cities/Settlements. Outside of that you get bored and tired pretty easily.

The BGM is pretty nice though.

The environment in the game is pretty cool ... at first. It's incredible how dull it gets after the first couple of hours. Everything looks the same. It's sometimes hard to find the things you need to interact with since they look like everything else.

Then there's the combat Combat in this game is absolutely atrocious. Every time an enemy comes on screen, I'm filled with absolute dread. It's not a fear of the creature, but instead a fear of the game mechanics (or lack thereof). It's just so cumbersome and tedious to fight in this game. I can't remember another game where I hated the combat this much.

Unfortunately I ended up playing for a bit too long, otherwise this would have been the second game I'd have ever refunded on Steam. Since I missed the chance for a refund, I decided to stick it out. This time, I took a friend along for the rest of the ride. He didn't believe some of the negative things I said about the game, so I let him try it for himself. I had him start from the beginning and about an hour in de was as baffled as I was as to how they could have screwed this up so bad.

We decided to play through the rest of the game, to see how it ends. We both wish we hadn't bothered. Not only is the game EXTREMELY tedious, but the ending is just horrible. Maybe I'd be willing to look past the ending had the game actually been fun to play, but it wasn't which makes the ending an absolute middle finger from the developers.

I absolutely can't recommend this game. Not at full price and not even on sale. There are much better ways to spend 3 - 4 hours.

review_text:
This is my favorite game in the series tied with Arkham Origins.

It feels like everything that was great about the first game was improved on and refined to perfection, and some of the rougher bits were rounded out.

The world is much bigger than the first game, and it's absolutely full of great missions, including both side missions AND main story missions. It feels like this game has just the right scale for an open world. Big enough to not get boring, but small enough to not feel daunting or overwhelming. Because of this, the game feels alive, and like you can find a completely unique interaction anywhere.

The character writing is at some of its best in the whole franchise. Some of the weird characterization bits from the previous game have been whittled down by a LOT! The stakes are much bigger than the previous game, and the characters, although they're still recognizable to their comic and animated counterparts, feel much more realistic and believable than the last game.

This game has some of the best art direction I've ever seen from this series. With notes of Tim Burton's influence, the architecture of the city feels exactly like how I'd picture my ideal version of Gotham City. I absolutely love the graphics in this game. The character designs are also FANTASTIC.

The story and gameplay is much more dynamic than the last game. The combat flows fantastically, and there's a learning curve that makes it really fun to keep on coming back to. You switch between playing as multiple characters throughout the game, which keeps things fresh.

Overall, I would say that this game is ABSOLUTELY worth playing and has nearly zero flaws whatsoever.

review_text:
I tried hard to love this game...and I did! But I can't recommend it, not without some major caveats.

First things first: the look and feel of the game, its environment, lighting, and sound design, are 11/10. Ebb absolutely killed it and I'm happy they took as long as they did to do so. Fans of Giger, Beksinski, and Cronenberg will be drawn to this game for obvious reasons. In Scorn, your feeble, tormented character wanders around a cold, disgusting, biomechanical superstructure, a monumental and unwelcoming presence which wholly envelops you, making you feel like a speck of dust: small, forgotten, hopeless, and insignificant. Sickening machines of unknown purpose stand ominously next to piles of gore. The croaks and gurgles of ungodly creatures echo through the skeletal halls. Everything you see and interact with is hideous and captivating, in the best way. I'm not only impressed, but inspired by the wickedly immersive and thoughtful aesthetic experience of this game. It's something to aim for. Other studios and projects will struggle to carry tone and artistic vision the way Ebb did with Scorn.

The level design is also phenomenal. Orderly, geometric floor plans are broken by tasteful asymmetry, dilapidation, and corrupted organic growth. Each chapter has its own architectural styles and motifs that gave them a unique flavor as you progress, a reward in itself. Verticality is a huge aspect of the layouts, twisting and folding back on themselves, which succeeded multiple times in making me feel like I had wandered far away only for me to notice that I was above or next to an area I recognized. This is also a huge part of the aesthetic experience, as you'll be shouldering around the tight throat of a hallway one moment, then come out to a stunning, decaying vista the next. There were probably a dozen moments in this game where the view in front of me was so stunning, my jaw fell open and I had to just stop in place and take it in. Even backtracking was rewarding in that the paths in reverse had details of their own.

But wait, how much backtracking? A good amount, and that leads into the first downside...

Initially, the gameplay is not unlike a point-and-click adventure, in that you walk around, find items, and use those items somewhere else. Immediately in the first act, though, after wandering around and inspecting all the interactable things on the level, I was confused. Eventually I worked out that I needed to [spoiler] solve the (now infamous) sliding pod puzzle [/spoiler]. Not only was it too subtle that this was even a puzzle at all, I found the "cues" for what you had to do to solve it kind of unintuitive, already a concerning sign for a puzzle game, made even more concerning by Scorn's minimalist approach. I play a lot of logic and puzzle games, so I enjoy a tricky or "hardcore" challenge like this, but it gives me pause in broadly recommending Scorn. It demands patience in a way that will turn many people off in its first hour (and I've seen many reviews to this effect). To be fair, the puzzles from that point on felt more intuitive. But considering it's the first major roadblock you face, I think the devs could have better eased the player into it, guiding them a bit better. Be prepared to backtrack and search around while you determine if you missed something earlier. And, unfortunately, be prepared to encounter things while you backtrack and search.

So yes, let's talk about the gunplay, this game's weakest point by far. Scorn is not a shooter. I remember early on when it was announced, there was more of a focus on the gunplay, but Ebb seems to have de-prioritized that element, and I'm glad they did. But I wish they went even further. The combat in Scorn is unnecessary and feels stapled on - for example, most enemies you can and should avoid altogether, or fire one shot at then run past them rather than try to kill them. It's like Ebb either didn't want to let people down by removing it, or throw away the weapon art assets and design decisions they'd already worked on, or both. I feel like the combat could be removed from the game and it wouldn't have had less of an impact on me; in fact, its inclusion is distracting and too tastes too "game-y" compared with all the wonder of its environment. I've seen other reviewers hope for something like the "safe mode" in SOMA, which optionally turns off enemy encounters altogether, and I agree. The best compromise I can imagine is for enemies to still be around, maybe [spoiler] still block your path sometimes in the case of the big "charger" guys in the later acts [/spoiler], just not aggro or attack you. Then they're more like an interactable part of the environment and you can consider the impulse to kill them or not.

Other people seem to have crashes and graphical issues and stuff, but I haven't experienced much of that. Assuming they'll patch that out, I haven't factored that into my recommendation.

[b]Overall I would recommend buying Scorn on sale if you are interested in a challenging aesthetic experience over compelling gameplay, willing to play it with patience, and willing to forgive its shortcomings.[/b] The current price point of $40 given its length (appx. 5 to 8 hours) is a bit steep. However I will say that if you're speedrunning this game, you're totally missing the point. Play it slowly. And it /does/ have replay value, but not if you're only motivated by Steam achievements, lol. I will definitely be playing this game again.

Some grab-bag improvements that could be made:
- As many reviews mention, checkpoints should be more frequent, especially right after completing a puzzle. There is no reason to make players repeat these sections if they die.
- Only show controls which display on the pause menu that are currently available and relevant. I was stuck on a part where I thought I couldn't switch weapons, because there's a control simply labeled "Switch", and it didn't do anything. Turns out this "Switch" control is only available during the last 5 minutes of the game - so why is it shown on this screen the entire time? I think it would make more sense to only show that control during the small section where it matters. Similar idea with the weapon and item controls as they're unlocked.
- Would be nice to holster my weapon when I'm just walking around. Better for screenshots and immersion :)

Criticism aside, kudos to Ebb for an incredible art game and I can't wait to see what they do next!

review_text:
Genuinely one of the greatest games to come out this year. I have had countless fun and runs with different builds, varying up in playstyles. I wasn't a huge fan of the first game back in 2015, when I was introduced to the series. It looked really in depth, and it had a lot of nuances that games don't have anymore. 

The first game, albeit very clunky, lack of polish, and experience breaking bugs (like getting stuck in a 360 spin while being hit) are very infuriating. What kept me though was the drive of story, and the protagonists passion to check off a bucket list throughout the game. He wants to avenge his parents, get the sword back from Istvan Toth, and make his Lord [Lord Radzig Kobyla] proud by fulfilling his duties and upholding his promises that he will get the sword back. By simple determination to get this sword, his story - and all of the countless events through his travels begin. From random vagrants on the road, to a riddle master, even saving a peasant or two from an ambush - you're never left without some kind of action.

This game is riddled with side quests, hunts, camps, and random encounters on the road to bring you countless memories of enjoyment. It was a truly beautiful creation, and I'm happy to see it come to a close at such high graces. I admire the developers attention to detail, and making it fun to play around and experience different aspects of the game - keeping a high immersion rate and really enveloping it's player base. 

I genuinely thank you for such a beautiful duo of games, Warhorse Studios. Even if I don't like the first one as much, it was very enjoyable from a story side perspective. You're a studio that people should learn from, on how to make a proper RPG. 

Thank you for your journey and experience through the life of Henry, and I hope you have wonderful endeavors with your next project.

Much love<333333

None of the character relationships feel organic anymore, they just feel like Henry is a Mary Sue, with everyone liking him and helping him as the story demands.

Another example: By watching my farmers I realized many were idle. Turns out farms don't take a lot of routine maintenance and I was able to unassign a ton of my farmers (now I have about 0.75 farmers per farm, depending on efficiency bonuses)

Towers are the same way. Position, type, wall design. There's a lot more going on than just "make a maze for baddies." The village's entire economy has to be considered.

Overall 10/10 for being utterly fascinating to play.

Update: it appears i do not need to wait for all the dlc to release as this game is pretty dead due to mismanagement(what a shocker for sao games right?)

TL;DR: a game that once had potential, mismanaged and starved to death, do not buy as you will not find matches. buy one of the others such as Fatal Bullet or Hollow Realization

This game had alot of potential aside from the jank combat system and rather stiff movements, it was at release what we wanted for a while though the roguelite element probably not.

Instead of releasing more content they released serial codes thinking that's what players wanted and implemented a system that requires a certain amount of players to start a match instead of just filling with bots(the bots are bad.. you'd be better off just playing solo if it let you unironically, another shocker).

Original review beyond this point.

Edit: I will be redoing this review once all the dlc drops to judge the final product, as it stands currently fatal bullet is still better but my statement below still stands, this is "probably" the best one if they handle it properly
TL:DR: If a fan of grinding, buy now
If grinding can become tedious for you, wait for sale or skip, this game is 100% grind

This is probably the best sao game we got so far, but it is not without its flaws or issues as a long term sao game player you may already know most of them as the formula is similar.

I'll begin with the good points
-The battle pass is free and gives you tickets to buy outfits in the shop instead of spending more money(I am unsure if ones in the future will be paid, considering sao game track record, I wouldn't put it past them especially considering how dimps handled the fatal bullet dlc)
-The gameplay loop isn't to repetitive or tiring to do, the structure allows it to be entertaining similarly to base pso2 or psu
-Each character plays in a different way be it a minor alteration or larger alteration, if your bored of one you can swap to another and have a mostly different experience
-(potentially good/grey area)The gear is ran off of an affix system, for gear hunters this allows you to hunt for the best gear possible, these affixes will impact your gameplay noticeably or minorly depending on affix build

Neutral: this game is like a roguelite from mission to mission in multiplayer, only your gear carries over

With the good out of the way, there isn't very many actual bad points I can personally make note of so most will seem minor
-The story makes absolutely no sense, if you are familiar with sao you are probably used to this as it is a stable basically(I personally don't mind this considering it is a multiplayer pve game, I would just rather the story make sense or be enjoyable considering it's somewhat forced on you)
-The gear drop rate for legendary items is quite low, for gear hunters like myself finding the best affix combo can be annoying especially with low drop rates and when something does drop it has a potential to have entirely useless affixes(similar to how anthem was at launch, for those not familiar with it an example would be a light element weapon dropping with water damage increase or such)
-This game has a habit of dropping inputs if you use a controller so you may often find yourself just standing there for a moment when you try to combo or use abilities

Overall, despite the issues I would recommend to give it a try depending if you need a game to waste time on, if you have played phantasy star(not new genesis) or previous sao games, you will likely enjoy the gameplay loop provided. There is also a hidden game in the artbook/soundtrack called "Kirito The Hero"

review_text:
Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is everything you want in a Jet Radio spiritual successor: dripping with style, an interesting world, smooth controls, and an eargasmic soundtrack. Yes, everything you'd want... except a satisfying gameplay loop.

The problem isn't that that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is not an arcadey, race the clock, high-scoring graffiti-em-up; it'd be fine if it kept the stylish trappings of its inspiration but went a different way with the core mechanics and challenge. It feels like the game left out the game entirely.

Most charitably, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk's core game is a 3D Platformer Collectathon, but instead of collecting Power Moons or Jiggies the game is figuring out how to reach the tagging spots scattered throughout the level, as well as the occasional music track, costume, or graffiti style. It also throws in the occasional "trick combo scoring" challenge and boss fight to mix it up, but neither of those are particularly interesting, for reasons I'll explain. It's all just a bit... boring.

Tricks and Combos and Scoring: This is the closest the game gets to a clever mechanic - you rack up combo multiplier by stringing elements together (specifically: wall runs, ramps, and sharp corners), with each unique element only counting once. If you're not on an element, you have a limited time to manual to a new one or the combo ends, encouraging you to scout the stage for a line that combos as much new stuff as possible. 

Unfortunately, the game faceplants this mechanic in two ways. First, it quickly teaches a mechanic that lets you manual infinitely, eliminating the challenge of finding a tight line through the stage. Second, there's no downside to repeating an element, just no new multiplier. In almost every challenge, it's enough to hit a 10x-20x multiplier from rail corners and then just grind a single loop forever while mashing buttons so you don't risk losing combo. It would have been much stronger if the game focused on stringing as many elements (including graffitti spots, which are hardly rewarded!) in a combo without repeat, as the stages are clearly designed for lines like that!

Combat: Boost into things and kick them. If it's a machine, kick it and graffiti it. There's a fun mechanic where you can tag a cop the moment you deal the killing blow to it, but the window is very small and there's no reward for doing it. If the game forced you to tag police to defeat them it would have been unique and interesting, but here it's just a silly nod.

Besides, outside of the four or so (very short) boss fights, the police element is pointless. In the Jet Radio games, the police presence got worse as the stage wore on, and they could interrupt your tags, requiring you to frantically put enough distance between you and them to get your tag in before they could catch you, then book it under the gun of the clock. In Bomb Rush Cyberfunk, there's no stage timer and no risk of cops interrupting your work, making them just kind of annoying when they spawn. And the mechanic is rendered entirely pointless by the fact that you can clear all police presence by touching a bathroom, so the mechanic might as well not have been included at all during free stage exploration.

Characters: In the Jet Radio games, different characters had different stats like health and graffiti combo length that affected scoring and strategy. In Bomb Rush Cyberfunk, they all... look different. It feels like a mechanic introduced just because the Jet Radio games had them, and not because it adds anything.

In conclusion, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is an homage to everything you remember about the Jet Radio games, minus the _game_. While I did enjoy my time with it just for the style alone, I honestly can't recommend it to anyone - there's not enough interesting gameplay here to attract anyone not familiar with its inspiration, and for fans of the inspiration the game feels like a shell of what it's inspired by. If I could give it a thumbs-middle, I might, but not at $40.

review_text:
There is only one reason why I cannot recommend this game...at least for now.

And that's because of the ridiculous amount of buggy stuff going on in this game. The story is amazing, and the side quests are great, but all too often I find myself with a broken immersion when:

- I cannot really hunt well because animals move randomly af, and I mean backwards, sideways and sometimes they even fly off.

- I can't really commit crimes because NPCs are omniscient and will always blame you even if no one saw you, and if you try to stop them by killing all witnesses, they will still find out, and while chasing them they can literally teleport and go trough walls and fences.

- Mounted combat is completely broken and definitely not recommended. Despite having some perks available on the perk tree, the only viable way of fighting on a horse is from a distance and running away pretty much all the time because NPCs can run extremely fast without getting tired, even in full armor, all too often they might be even faster than your horse and then teleport to you, hit the horse and then dismount you, and charging them basically doesn't work at all.

- The DLC of the simthy is great, but every weapon that you forge literally looks the exact same. You only get to craft 3 types of things: short sword, long sword and an axe, and they all look the exact same. Even the axis that you're supposed to craft in the story quest is literally a short sword. They didn't even bother making a different mesh, not even for the main DLC quest, which feels incredibly bad, to be honest.

- And the most annoying bug of them all, happening all too often (I've already counted it 32 times in my playthrough, and that's when I started counting), is when suddenly my inventory gets bugged and I find myself in the middle of a fight, unable to change my weapon or drink any potions, even though I have them already equipped. The only way to fix this is to exit the game and re-launch it, because reloading a saved game will not fix the issue, and that means that all too often you will probably lose all your progress because of this random bug, and be unable to fight at all.

- Another mention I'd like to add is that melee combat happens on rails. You can only dodge attacks if the green shield pops up, and for some reason many times this will not happen, and enemies will hit you as if their weapons were heat seeking missiles, even if you're well outside of their range (they will literally teleport to you), which is incredibly annoying, and makes the dodging gameplay extremely unrewarding and overall, really buggy. In fact, many times you'll find yourself in a fight where you cannot win with skill, because the only way to block your enemy's attacks is by having invested enough money on your skill tree abilities with that weapon, or by training until you get a high enough level. You cannot win otherwise because your enemies will have essentially infinite stamina, strength and their attacks go towards you on rails. In the end, the best choice is a bow with poisonous arrows, which by the way is incredibly broken as well. You can down an entire army with just that.


So yeah, many people will think I'm being unfair because the game has a genuinely good story, but the game is so heavily scripted that it comes with a lot of stuff that will break the immersion, and that also makes the gameplay incredibly restrictive and linear. I'm not saying that the game is bad, all I'm saying is that it still needs a lot of work in order to feel like a polished, properly finished game, that's all.

And by the way, I'd gladly pay extra as long as this work gets properly done, after all, I've bought almost all the DLCs with the intention of supporting the developers, and trying the new content because I love the KCD series. But I really can't properly recommend this game until it's polished and released in a much better state.

Cronos: The New Dawn is a solid survival horror game that hits many of the right notes for fans of tension, monsters, atmosphere, and a little narrative depth. If you like the “classic” feel of horror-third-person games, you’ll find much to enjoy here.

That said, if you’re hoping for genre-reinventing mechanics or a story that shatters expectations, this may not fully deliver. It has ambition and stands out in its world, but it also plays it safe in places.

review_text:
Yakuza 5 expands on the multi-protagonist approach of its predecessor, this time featuring five playable characters: Kiryu, Saejima, Akiyama, Haruka, and Shinada. Each character has their own storyline, which eventually ties into the bigger picture. 

Story:

The narrative takes some questionable turns. Kiryu leaving the orphanage felt out of character, even if it was "necessary," and his stint as a taxi driver didn’t really suit him. Saejima’s story starts off with another prison sequence (which felt like a rehash of Yakuza 4), but his survival story in the mountains was fantastic—I wish they had focused more on that instead.

Haruka’s storyline, which introduces her as a playable character, was a fresh idea but could have been done better. Akiyama, unfortunately, felt like an afterthought. Shinada, on the other hand, had the strongest arc, with an interesting baseball backstory that connected well with Dojima.

The finale had a few twists—Kurosawa being the Omi chairman instead of a detective was decent, and Aizawa being his son. But overall, the villains felt underwhelming, and the story didn't live up to its full potential. Especially compared to say Yakuza 2 and 3.

Gameplay:
Combat remains largely unchanged from Yakuza 4. Each character has their own strengths—Kiryu and Saejima are the powerhouses, Akiyama is fast, and Shinada relies on weapons. Regular enemies are easy, even on Legend difficulty, but the coliseum is another story.

The coliseum fights are tedious, with enemies blocking almost everything, having multiple health bars, and  reducing your heat action damage. Instead of being challenging, they’re just drawn-out and grindy. Some characters, like Kiryu and Saejima, can exploit certain moves to win, while Shinada struggles because he isn’t built for these fights and you can't even use weapons with him. The rewards aren’t worth the effort unless you're aiming for 100% completion. 

Side Content:
The side jobs were some of the best parts of the game. Kiryu’s taxi missions were surprisingly fun, and Saejima’s hunting segments were excellent, they should have focused his story more on that. Haruka’s idol career was interesting (even if repetitive) and something new for the series. Akiyama, unfortunately, had no job-related activities, while Shinada’s baseball minigames fit his character well. 

Minigames are the usual mix of returning and new activities. The worst one remains fishing—river fishing is okay, but sea fishing is pure frustration, thanks to the constant fishing of steel barrels. Casino and card games are trivialized by cheat items, while SEGA games are only challenging until you figure out their exploits. On the bright side, the UFO catcher was the easiest in the series—finally, no frustration there.

Bugs:
I encountered a few technical issues. The game occasionally froze when getting a weapon revelation, which made me stop doing them altogether (not that they were worthwhile). Another annoyance was the prize ticket system—despite having a “good day” status, I kept getting pocket tissues, forcing me to reload 12 times just to get a pearl. The gacha mechanics in this game were frustrating, and I hope they removed them in later entries. The game is supposed to be fun not a chore.

Conclusion
Despite its flaws, Yakuza 5 is still a great game, as my 150+ hours prove. However, it could have been better with a tighter story, improved combat balancing, and fewer grindy elements. If you're a Yakuza fan, it's worth playing, but be prepared for some frustrating moments along the way.

Rating: 7.5/10

review_text:
It's very cryptic. There's no actual tutorial. As many have said here, villagers keep dying from starvation, and you, the player are left to wonder what's even happening. I've now sunk almost a 100 hours into the game and I still don't understand the food mechanics completely.

Here's a more in depth example of maybe the biggest downfall of the game:

There is a *complete lack of proper notifications* and the visuals are hard to understand.

There's no notification, for example, for when an enemy is within your village, attacking your villagers, or even destroying your buildings. Then you suddenly get notified that 5 villagers died almost in an instant, and your screen shakes as a few buildings collapse, due to them having been taking damage from an enemy mob for the last minute or so, which you didn't know was happening. You can't for example distinguish the screen shake effect of a meteor hit, which are very common, and a building collapsing. Ok, well now you at least know the enemy is within your village, right? Good thing you have a grab tool and banish spell that you can use to move unwanted enemies elsewhere, right? Well, that would be the case, if you could distinguish what's even happening on your screen. There's like 40 villagers and 30 animals running in every direction with exclamation points or question marks above their heads. Then there's the massive amount of clutter caused by the destroyed buildings, then there's the magic effects, with pixelated fire and purple fizzing, and finally there are the enemies in your base, who either blend in with the panicking villagers, or they hiding behind villager sprites who are attacking the enemies, or then they might hide within the buildings they are attacking. All you would have to do is cast spells at or grab these enemies and your problem would be solved. You might have already fixed what was causing the enemies getting inside your village. Too bad it's nearly impossible to get rid of the enemies inside the village, as you will be completely unable to distinguish anything from this mess. Try to grab that pesky skeleton or zombie child? Nah, here's a random animal or a piece of trash for you. Managed to grab a fire elemental that killed +5 villagers? Well, plenty more will die and buildings will collapse, as you can't distinguish which villagers or buildings the elemental set on fire.

For some reason I'm still a little drawn to this game, I really would have wanted to enjoy it. The idea is great, I think, but the execution has a lot of room for improvement. It's just far too messy, cryptic, and in general, it's not a game that's pleasant to look at. All in all, it just feels tedious to play. I do not recommend buying it, unless it's on sale and less than 5 euros. If you do buy it, get ready to be very frustrated.

A mighty samurai warrior still has a quiet side.  ---- All of the elements of a Japanese action game are here: ninja, samurai, and martial arts. But you do it in a stealth setting. Even if you've never tied a stealth game before, I recommend you try it. I had never played one like this, and was pleasantly surprised.

It's a cool concept well done but the player base is there. 9/10 you'll wait several minutes for a match with 1 real person plus bots, but you never get a run of matches. Whoever is actually playing this is only staying around for 1 match apparently, because it's several minutes more for another match. And the matches are only about 2 minutes long, so you are spending way more time waiting than playing.

I hate to say it, but this needed to be FTP, because it will die with no players.

There are things they could have done to mitigate this. Let me play through the solo challenges whilst I'm waiting, instead of making me leave the queue to do this. Make a live lobby where I can just drive around and practice. Put me into a match with all bots if the waiting time is more than 30 seconds.

Ultimately, I don't understand who this is marketed to. Somebody with an attention span of less than 2 minutes, because that is how long the matches are, but who also has patience to wait around doing nothing for several minutes in between. Who is that person? And this is why I'm giving it a thumbs down. I would have liked to be positive to encourage more players but it's just fundamentally pointless.

The game would have been 1000% better if it was just offline against the bots for fun instead of a FTP-like experience with but an upfront cost. As such this does not belong in my library.

I want to recommend this game, especially given the AAA price range, but I simply can't.

Close to no content
Flailed around with AI for 2 hrs seemingly getting brutally slaughtered on the lowest difficulty.
Played 5/6 missions on veteran with my bro and 2 rando's once over 3 hrs, pretty much completing most of the game in a single session as it always had the same 4 enemy types with 6 guns, a healing item and a pipe bomb.

Matchmaking is good!
All members of the community we've run into were communicative and friendly. Automated matchmaking worked heavenly without any dropouts. Inviting people in the hub was more troublesome and not recommended. You also likely don't get to be in the same hub as your friend so invite over social tab by their id.

Customization is there, but luster
Me and my friend got different drops (barrel and gun) and neither could really tell a difference. In fact, my buddy dropped the new assault rifle to go back to the pistol due to the considerable ammo constraints.

The same Boss you fight on each level is a dumb bulletsponge
My buddy basically did the same trick running around in circles for what feels like forever shooting a glowy bit until it finally goes down. The terrain somewhat changes but once you see the circle and 2 replenishing ammo crates you know what time it is, even if it's your "first time on this map".

Conclusion: not recommended
The shooting and gun handling is ok (Although you have close to no recoil) and the visuals/audio are solid.
I also think what little of a story there is, it's alright. You can tell the team has improved a lot on for instance animations since Arizona Sunshine.
Unfortunately we're 2021 and Pavlov Zombie mod handled many of the above pointsbetter at a quarter of the price. LOOK ELSEWHERE!

review_text:
Scorn : By Triple F

"Scorn," developed by Ebb Software, is a unique and unsettling horror game that immerses players in a world heavily inspired by the biomechanical art of H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński. Released in 2022, "Scorn" offers a distinct first-person experience that focuses on exploration, environmental puzzles, and atmosphere rather than traditional combat or jump scares. Set in a surreal, alien landscape filled with organic machinery and grotesque, otherworldly structures, the game pushes players into a strange and deeply disturbing universe without guidance, dialogue, or explicit storytelling. This silent descent into horror is as much an exploration of its aesthetic as it is a journey through a twisted world, and "Scorn" stands out for its dedication to creating an immersive, almost meditative experience of body horror and existential dread.

The visual design of "Scorn" is undoubtedly its strongest element, meticulously crafted to evoke an atmosphere of dread and unease. The environments are a blend of organic and mechanical, with structures that feel alive, pulsating, and decayed. The walls, corridors, and machinery appear to be constructed from bones, flesh, and strange tissues, giving the game an unsettlingly tactile feel. Each area of the game is rich in detail, with careful attention to textures and lighting that cast a haunting, monochromatic glow. This design work allows players to feel as though they’re exploring a decayed corpse on a massive scale, creating a visceral, immersive world that is both beautiful and revolting. It’s a visually striking experience, where every corner feels carefully constructed to invoke discomfort and fascination in equal measure.

Exploration and environmental storytelling are the core of "Scorn’s" gameplay, as players must rely on observation to navigate the labyrinthine world and uncover its secrets. Without dialogue or a clear narrative, the game communicates its story through the environment, forcing players to piece together clues about the world’s history and purpose on their own. There are no maps or quest markers, and the minimal UI leaves players feeling vulnerable and isolated, amplifying the horror of each step deeper into this biomechanical nightmare. This design choice serves to make exploration feel intentional and personal, as players must move forward based on their instincts and memory alone. However, the lack of direct storytelling or guidance may frustrate those seeking a more linear narrative, as "Scorn" leans heavily on abstraction and ambiguity to create its impact.

The puzzle design in "Scorn" is varied, often requiring players to manipulate alien machinery, connect circuits, or navigate complex structures to progress. These puzzles are an integral part of the game’s experience, blending seamlessly with the environment and often requiring players to interact with disturbingly organic controls and mechanisms. While some puzzles are straightforward, others require careful observation and experimentation, reinforcing the game's philosophy of exploration and discovery. The tactile nature of each interaction makes the puzzles feel more unsettling, as players handle machinery that resembles living organs, adding a layer of horror to each task. However, some puzzles lack clarity, and the absence of tutorials can make certain sections feel obtuse, potentially slowing down the pace for players unaccustomed to the game’s cryptic style.

Combat in "Scorn" is minimal and unsettling, more akin to survival horror than action. Players occasionally encounter hostile creatures that resemble malformed beings or twisted anatomical constructs, and the few weapons available feel as organic as the world itself, often resembling skeletal or fleshy tools. Ammunition is scarce, and combat is clunky by design, with slow, deliberate attacks that make every encounter feel threatening. Rather than empowering players, these mechanics reinforce a sense of vulnerability, making it clear that fighting isn’t the focus of the game; survival is. For some, the combat may feel frustrating or unsatisfying due to its deliberate sluggishness, but it effectively amplifies the horror by encouraging players to avoid fights when possible, heightening the tension of each encounter.

The sound design in "Scorn" is hauntingly atmospheric, composed of subtle mechanical hums, organic squelches, and ambient noises that fill the game’s environments with an eerie sense of life. The absence of traditional music allows players to focus on every small sound, from the clicking of strange machinery to the unsettling groans and sloshes of the alien landscape itself. This minimalist approach to audio intensifies the sense of isolation, as players are left alone with the unsettling noises of the world around them. The soundscape builds tension effectively, giving players no reprieve from the dread that permeates every environment, enhancing the immersive horror experience that defines "Scorn."

Narrative interpretation is open-ended, leaving players to piece together the meaning of "Scorn’s" world and its biomechanical horrors through visual cues and environmental details. The game doesn’t provide explicit answers, and players are left to draw their own conclusions about the nature of the world, its inhabitants, and their own purpose within it. Some may interpret the story as an exploration of life, death, and rebirth, while others may see it as a grim commentary on the merging of flesh and machine. This ambiguity makes "Scorn" feel almost like a piece of interactive art, where meaning is subjective and rooted in the player’s individual experience. However, those seeking a more straightforward plot may find this aspect lacking, as the game remains cryptic from start to finish.

In summary, "Scorn" is a unique horror experience that prioritizes atmosphere, design, and environmental storytelling over traditional gameplay mechanics and narrative structure. It’s a game that invites players to explore a beautifully grotesque world at their own pace, immersing them in an aesthetic of surreal body horror that is both captivating and horrifying. While the lack of guidance and minimal combat may deter players who prefer clear objectives or a more action-driven experience, "Scorn" stands as an ambitious and immersive work that challenges conventions of horror gaming. For those willing to embrace its slower, more abstract approach, "Scorn" offers an unforgettable journey into a world that feels disturbingly alive and a dark, visceral descent into a biomechanical nightmare.

review_text:
[h3]Would you kindly stop scrolling and read this review[/h3]

Bioshock was groundbreaking in the way it introduced many gamers to an obscure art style and a niché political philosophy; namely art deco and objectivism. Both of these are weaved into the games DNA and helped to create its iconic look, deeply immersive and memorable world, and its well written story and characters.

The opening few minutes are also iconic and almost perfect in the way they introduce the player to these two concepts, as well as to one of the game's antagonists, Andrew Ryan. It is mostly on the rails and involves lots of delightful visual storytelling as well as a recorded speech from Ryan. As the haunting music sores your 'ride' culminates in a sudden reveal of Bioshock's underwater city, Rapture, a place founded by Ryan in the hopes it would become an objectivist utopia.

"[I]I am Andrew Ryan, and I'm here to ask you a question. Is a man not entitled to the sweat of his brow? 'No!' says the man in Washington, 'It belongs to the poor.' 'No!' says the man in the Vatican, 'It belongs to God.' 'No!' says the man in Moscow, 'It belongs to everyone.' I rejected those answers; instead, I chose something different. I chose the impossible. I chose... Rapture[/I]"

On arriving in the city it quickly becomes clear that Rapture is far from a utopia and that something has gone very, very wrong. 

Now I'm no political expert, but it's obvious from Andrew Ryan's opening monologue that this is a world built on objectivism. As I understand it, objectivism, a philosophy cooked up by Ayn Rand, is a form of right wing, hyper libertarianism, married to extreme capitalism. If selfish greed were a political philosophy, it would be objectivism. The needs of the few outweigh the needs of the many, as a mirror universe version of Spock might say.

Bioshock isn't a celebration of Rand's politics though; as you explore Rapture you'll quickly realise through the narrative that this is a critique of Ayn Rand's political philosophy. It turns out that in an underwater city where everyone is working for themselves, nothing useful or necessary gets done and there's no-one to do the menial, less 'creative and fulfilling' jobs; those jobs that are vital to maintaining and running a vast underwater city. There is also no money to pay the people who are needed to do those jobs, and no supervision.

The citizens of Rapture also discovered a substance called Adam. When refined into a Plasmid, Adam rewrites a person's genetic material, giving them superhuman abilities. One of the downsides of plasmids use is their addictive qualities and they can also cause mental and physical degradation when over used. The second 'person' you see in Rapture is a victim of Adam abuse and has lost their mind, becoming a murder happy Splicer. You see them through a small window, gutting the first person you see. So Plasmid use isn't healthy; luckily as the player you will inject yourself with many many plasmids!

In a democratic society, regulation, ethical considerations and/or law enforcement of some kind could have led to better safeguards and more thorough testing of Adam. But in Rapture that would be hampering creative genius.

Then some sort of conflict began on new years eve 1958, between factions loyal to Ryan and those loyal to somebody named Atlas. With plasmids added to the mix things clearly didn't go so well, and this becomes apparent soon after you 'land'. Things are fucked, to put it mildly.

You piece a lot of this together within the first hour or so through the visuals alone. Rapture's beautiful, clean, simple, symmetrical 1920's art deco face is cracking. The imposing bronze sculptures are tarnished and some are toppled; the gold plaques are grimy, and the green marble and ceramic tiles are pitted, shattered and broken. There are leaks everywhere too; maintenance having been largely abandoned. The city is flooding and large parts of it are without power. Machinery is malfunctioning and there are there are bodies all over the place. Many of the dead are in evening wear that is age worn and tattered. Some are wearing masks, like they died during a masked ball. The Splicers are similarly attired but those without masks are horrifyingly deformed. Mutated.

The atmosphere is unsettling and meloncholic, and sometimes, when the lights are flickering, casting strange shadows and the faint, nonsensical noises of one of Rapture's mad citizens are getting ever louder, and closer, the game is outright frightening.

This would be a decent way to tell a story but there are also audiologs made by the citizens before things went to shit, and NPCs that aren't currently trying to kill you. When taken together this is world building at its finest. Later on you'll start learning about the player character and their connection to Rapture, the two philosophies of Ryan and Atlas and the ultimate fate of the city. This is the game's story and it's wonderfully paced and told, and  incredibly immersive.

I'd be remiss if I didn't talk about the gameplay, but it's only important as a part of the whole, nothing about the FPS mechanics is outstanding. None of the guns are particularly memorable but they sound meaty enough and can be upgraded, as well as fitted out with different ammo types. You can also hack cameras and sentry bots to help you in combat, and these skills, along with heath and energy can be levelled up. You need the energy to use plasmids. There are a large number of plasmids, some of which you find and others you have to buy. They too can be levelled up and range from basic magical attacks like incinerate, winter blast and electrobolt, which are pretty self explanatory, to more tactical ones such as telekinesis, a decoy and one that charms enemies to fight for you. 

Enemy variety is a rather limited, there are only a few different types of Splicer, but each benefits from a slightly different approach to takedown, and there are generally plasmids that are better at countering certain Splicers. Encounters can be hectic if there are multiple Splicer types and then there are the big baddies. Not Splicers themselves, these armoured giants stomp around Rapture often in the footsteps of small girls. These little sisters are Adam gatherers* and you need Adam to buy plasmids, but before you can deal with the little sisters you have to get rid of daddy. Now you can just leave these pairings be when you encounter them, and as long as you don't get too close to the child the big daddy won't attack. It's always worth it though, and these fights can be some of the best, and worst when they're messy, in the game, requiring lots of ammo and plasmid use. 

This is where the game's morality system comes into play, you can 'harvest' the little sisters for a large amount of Adam, killing them, or release them from their drugged servitude, saving them for little material gain. It's one of those shit good/evil binary choices that video games do, that are never really choices because the good option is obviously the one to go, especially if it effects the ending. You're not even really punished for choosing the good option because after you've saved enough little sisters they'll drop off presents stuffed with Adam. It's definitely one of the most poorly thought out aspects of BioShock, along with the hacking mini game. Nothings perfect though. 

I've wasted enough of your time. Bioshock is a fantastic game worthy of its iconic status; it's beautiful, dark, deep,, smart, engrossing and unforgettable. Get it.

Now. [b]Would you kindly[/b] give me all your points.

*They get it from the dead
