review_text:
This game has so many great ideas that it refuses to explore more than on a surface level. It's not terrible just so very mediocre and by the numbers. You walk around reading a stack of notes and audio logs left behind by people while also gathering resources. You do one or two smaller enemy encounters to whittle down those resources you just collected. You visit a safe room right before a bigger fight so you can use currency and points to upgrade your equipment. Unfortunately the weapon upgrades don't have branching paths or any interesting bonuses to them, it's the "number goes up" type of a deal.

The game draws heavy inspiration from action focused survival horror games like Dead Space and Resident Evil 4. It however doesn't include fun or useful quality of life features like quickturning or a map. There is no separate inventory for quest items. There were multiple times where I had to backtrack to a safe room to store some items or simply waste some bullets so I could pick up the next mcguffin required to proceed. Inventory is very limited and needs to be upgraded with points for more space. 
You only have one gun that transforms between different types so why is it that all the different forms take up one more inventory slot? This resulted in me not experimenting with the different variations simply because there wasn't enough space to carry them around. 

You can charge your weapons up for more damage but this causes the crosshair to start shaking around violently while the enemy is barreling towards you. This adds a nice risk&reward mechanic that forces you to risk getting hit by the enemy. Character movement is deliberately slow and slightly clunky. Enemies are rather slow so it balances out decently enough.

Enemies aren't very interesting. It's the very trope biomass that deforms people into hideous monstrosities. This type of body horror loses all scare factor when used too much. Almost every area is just goopy flesh walls so it trivializes the horrid nature of the sickness that wiped out the world.

Game includes minor environmental puzzles where you have to route electricity by shooting spikes into a wall. I wish you could charge up these spikes so you could use them to stun enemies during combat or to create electrical traps during fights. The spikes are used on puzzles only and nothing else.
You can also rewind time at certain points of the game. Usually this means uncollapsing a structure so you can walk forward. It also allows you to rewind exploded barrels so you can reuse them during combat. This makes some enemy encounters trivially easy.
There is also gravity defying platforming similar to Dead Space remake but those are at very set points and usually just a way to get the player across longer distances. The gravity shenanigans aren't used in any interesting way, simply to get player across floating platforms in a boring void. Towards the end of the game there is a glimpse of what could have been when you get to fight upside down against some enemies. 

The enemies themselves can merge with dead bodies becoming more powerful but this was rarely an issue. It did put nice pressure on the player during some of the early fights in the game when guns aren't as powerful and ammo is scarce. Later on this whole thing is trivialized by your powerful guns and the abundance of explosive canisters in nearly every big arena you fight in. You can also reuse the explosive canisters by rewinding time to reconstruct them. 

WHOEVER WAS IN CHARGE OF APPROVING THE FOLLOWING ENEMY DESIGNS NEEDS TO BE PUT IN THE NAUGHTY CORNER! It is as if they tried to take the worst types of enemies from other games. Exploding acid blisters that are hidden behind corners or on walls. They can be shot to pop them or triggered by going near them for a second and running away. They spew acid on the floor forcing you to wait for a moment before proceeding. There are also tiny crawling explosive acid enemies that crawl towards you, explode if you get too close and jump at you exploding at contact. Worst ones are the wall enemies that quickly grab you forcing you to complete a quick time event to break free. Very often they are placed in very cheap spots or trigger when you pick up resources from a certain spot. Did they not listen to any of the playtesters since I can't fathom anyone enjoying these miserable time wasting traps.

The game has a poor balance between resource gathering and combat. There is too much snooping around for ammo and not enough situations to use said ammo. Whenever the game showed me a hallucination of a massive enemy horde I was ecstatic "FINALLY A BIG FIGHT!" only to make all the enemies vanish. 

Boss fights early on are alright and those types become standard enemies later as is typical. Closer to the end of the game there are two boss fights almost back to back and both are such annoying ordeals to slog through. Acid spitting one liner repeating flesh totem with wall blisters that need to be popped and a teleporting bastard that has nearly unavoidable attacks. The final boss has two cutscenes right before you encounter him and thankfully you can skip those. 

The performance of the game was all over the place. Lots of moments where it was stuttering and dropping FPS. I haven't tried the game on the Steam Deck yet but I'm very sceptical about them getting it Verified when it runs this poorly on a gaming PC on medium graphics (with DLSS on ultra performance setting).

I would recommend picking this up from a 50-75% sale if you're really thirsty for some third person shooting. Just don't expect to do that much shooting.

review_text:
You probably already know if you want EHM or not. If you aren't a hockey fan, and if you don't like pretty deep simulation-based games, there's nothing for you here.
However, if you like those two things, EHM isn't perfect, but it is the best option in the genre. Sports Interactive know what they're doing, and EHM is no different, although it is a little barebones. It's a shame that, for what is ostensibly a new game, there's no modern features such as achievements. Thankfully it does have Workshop support, and it's here we see EHM's trump card.
EHM's modding community is what, for me, pushes the game from standard sports-sim to something engrossing. Real-world rosters and clubs, as well as facepacks, allow for something more realistic - and thus, fun. For me, trying to turn my beloved Calgary Flames from perennial bottom-feeders into an actual force is far more enjoyable than doing it with a fantasy club, with fake players. Without these mods, EHM is pretty sparse.
On its own, EHM is a tough sell. Even with it's fantastic mod support, it caters to a pretty small niche. If that niche includes you, though, you'll be treated to a game that demands time and patience, but yields great reward.

review_text:
The sweeping comparisons to Dead Space, however favorable, still do this game a massive disservice. This truly feels like a new breed of horror and a natural evolution of the genre, one that not only borrows liberally from Dead Space's punchy, visceral combat and a similar central gimmick, but also weaves in key elements from most of the genre's greats, be it Silent Hill's eeriness, RE 1's resource and inventory management, RE 4's genius linearity, RE 7's crafting system, and even Returnal's moody atmospherics. The game is a technical marvel to boot, with a soundstage that demands headphone use, evocative art direction, and generally great performance for a UE5 game, provided you turn off ray tracing. Admittedly, the story can be weirdly both too cryptic and overwhelming, and the final boss is a lesson in tedium, but none of these nitpicks can detract from the fact that we're dealing with a mandatory 2025 gaming experience that we'll have to take into serious consideration when discussing essential horror picks.

Such is our calling.

review_text:
I believe Lucius is best described as a puzzle adventure game, perhaps also a reverse-horror. I personally enjoyed the game but I don't believe I can recommend it to the average player. I have a lot to say so you're in for a long read, you've been warned.

You play the role of Lucius, a little boy with demonic power tasked with slaughtering various members of the prestigious Wagner household one by one. You will make use of a few paranormal powers and usable items to covertly assassinate your victims and sacrifice their souls to your real father, the devil himself.

I'll be blunt: the game has weak mechanics, a rather bland story and incredibly stale voice acting.

In regards to gameplay mechanics, the core of Lucius is problem-solving and item-finding. Each chapter of the game tasks you with the murder of a specific individual, which needs to look like a freak accident or a suicide. To do this, gameplay consists of figuring out what item you need to use, finding said item, and using said item in the right place/context. That's pretty much it. You also will be unlocking a number of paranormal skills that will let you use items in a certain way, though I feel the skill system is rather barebones and underutilized. The game will drop you a few hints as to what item you need and where you can find it, which will have you do some exploration. These elements don't do enough to prop up the gameplay loop which feels like playing a point-and-click adventure. If your 3D game is as mechanically engaging as a point-and click adventure, I dont quite see the point of making it 3D to begin with? I think this is underscored by the fact that the Lucius Demake was better received than the sequels. Ladies and gents, I am a gameplay-first kind of guy, but I can forgive weak mechanics if I am at least engaged by the story, which... speak of the devil.
The story of Lucius is essentially an abridged, campy version of the Omen movie, played from the perspective of the devil child. Obviously names are changed and story beats are different, but the premise is the same. The cutscenes in this game are actually very neatly done, especially for an indie game.Now here's the thing: I'm a slut for supernatural horror so I was always gonna like Lucius, but I will admit its story is not very original or engrossing, and none of the characters are very compelling (most serve only as cannon fodder). Even the Devil himself is portrayed as little more than a cartoon villain. The narrative, while dark on paper, doesn't carry the weight of the Omen film. The execution cutscenes, while gruesome, display more of a cinematic, flashy feel. The frequent use of slow-mo highlights the theatricality of gore. They are clearly designed as a reward for the gawking player, rather than something to be sincerely disturbed by. I'm not big on campy horror, so I never found the game truly scary or disturbing (though I will admit that playing tons of horror games has desensitized me over the years).

All of this is fine, btw. Just don't come into the game expecting a serious tone.
 
In the end, while I enjoyed the game for what it is (playing as the kid from the Omen movie and killing every idiot in front of me), I don't believe I can recommend it to the average player because I didn't find either the gameplay or the story very engaging. If you still want to play the power fantasy of being a demon child then sure, give it a go, but temper your expectations and enjoy the ride for what it is.

i think this is underscored by the fact that the lucius demake was better received than the sequels . ladies and gents , i am a gameplay-first kind of guy , but i can forgive weak mechanics if i am at least engaged by the story , which . . . speak of the devil . the story of lucius is essentially an abridged , campy version of the omen movie , played from the perspective of the devil child . obviously names are changed and story beats are different , but the premise is the same . the cutscenes in this game are actually very neatly done , especially for an indie game . now here ' s the thing i ' m a slut for supernatural horror so i was always gonna like lucius , but i will admit its story is not very original or engrossing , and none of the characters are very compelling ( most serve only as cannon fodder ) . even the devil himself is portrayed as little more than a cartoon villain . the narrative , while dark on paper , doesn ' t carry the weight of the omen film . the execution cutscenes , while gruesome , display more of a cinematic , flashy feel . the frequent use of slow-mo highlights the theatricality of gore . they are clearly designed as a reward for the gawking player , rather than something to be sincerely disturbed by . i ' m not big on campy horror , so i never found the game truly scary or disturbing ( though i will admit that playing tons of horror games has desensitized me over the years ) . all of this is fine , btw . just don ' t come into the game expecting a serious tone . in the end , while i enjoyed the game for what it is ( playing as the kid from the omen movie and killing every idiot in front of me ) , i don ' t believe i can recommend it to the average player because i didn ' t find either the gameplay or the story very engaging . if you still want to play the power fantasy of being a demon child then sure , give it a go , but temper your expectations and enjoy the ride for what it is .

review_text:
After playing through this game and really giving it a chance I've come to the conclusion that it fails as a horror/story game but has moderate success in being a action shooter.

The game is beautiful, the visuals are really awesome and is 10/10. Animations are great the atmosphere is stunning.
But it also lacks in being immersive. For example, the game wants you to use the environment to kill your enemies but instead of using immersive objects one would find in a prison it just places random spikes against a wall or blades that spin and is a complete safety hazard to anyone within 40 meters. The amount of yellow spikes screaming "hey throw enemies against me" is absurd. Like come one, why would anyone place deadly spikes in a marketplace bathroom or a bedroom?

The combat also is absurd for being a horror game. Literally all you have to do against enemies is hold A then switch to D, that's it. You dodge every single attack and there is no intense fighting for your life moment. If there are multiple enemies they all wait for their turn, they all don't attack at once. Boss battles are the easiest boss battles i have had in a game, they can't even damage you.

The game fails in being scary. Enemies are as explained earlier not even a challenge, you never feel in danger. The game also never uses tactics that Dead Space used (Same creator that made Dead Space made this game) the tactics I'm referring to being attacked when you don't expect it. Going back to the area you just passed through? Get jumped by a enemy (Sometimes) or even being attacked when standing in the shop. You never feel safe in Dead Space. But this game just goes easy on you, if you back-track you never encounter enemies, NEVER. It's those small things that add up, this game has none of that.

The story feels very weak, generic "unknown virus" that infects a planet. Could've worked but this game just feels to similar to Dead Space for me to not feel like it is.

For being a 60$ game it just absolutely fails. I have no idea how someone who was the creator of Dead Space could make this. I'm sad the studio basically is dead now but i feel like Glen tried and failed and now has to suffer the consequences of his actions.

review_text:
I really want to like this game, but it has too many bizarre shortcomings to work for me. The clever art style, the overall "goal" and the hybrid RTS/city builder/tower defense should combine to be a ton of fun. However, this game is probably best described as a frustration simulator; a steep difficulty curve, a relentless enemy AI, and your greatest obstacle- arguably the worst pathing/friendly AI ever coded join forces to waste your time. Your best winning strategies means nothing, as your builders will disregard your build orders, obvious pathing routes, and will even starve to death rather than survive even when food is readily available. Priorities you the player set are flatly ignored. Builders wander into enemy territory to be slaughtered without reason at least once every scenario, losing more than 2 or so is debilitating to your economy, and you're quickly overrun. Your towers and defense systems target priority is laughable, and there is no means for the player to directly control any of this to fill the gulf in logic between what is happening and what the AI thinks it should be doing. I would compare it to another game, but I genuinely can't think of any game in any of the genres Rise to Ruins taps into that relies so heavily on micromanagement that then leaves it entirely to an AI that is, at it's very best, incompetent. Credit where it's due, Rise To Ruins is a beautiful looking game, and it's clear the developer(s) put a lot of heart into the final product- I don't feel this game is "broken" for lack of effort on their part. 

Granted you're the sort who doesn't mind having to restart your scenario every 2 hours or so because your villagers all decided to wander into harms way for no apparent reason (as there's only one save slot per map per difficulty, so no quicksaving!) then this game may just be your cup of tea. If you (like me) prefer a strategy game where you are actually in "control" and not just shouting suggestions at a dimwitted AI, then Rise to Ruins is best skipped over.

review_text:
This is the 2nd "overwhelmingly positive" game that I've said is not as good as the ratings indicate (the other being the UFO series reboot).

Honestly, this game as an actual game just isn't that good. It doesn't make sense. The missions are laborious until you learn to exploit the mechanisms. The AI is ridiculous. "Oh there's like 50 dead bodies here, let's look around for 30s then give up and go back to our positions like nothing ever happened." It doesn't make sense. Then there's the sneaking mechanism. Until you realise you can actually walk like 5m in front of guys looking straight at you and they have no idea you are there, then you might try all kinds of things. Once you realise you literally walk straight in front of people then the game gets a lot easier. Once you realise you can execute people with loud killing moves (slashes, screams, gurgles, slumps) right next to a guy looking the other way and he'll never know... it just makes no sense the way the gameplay is designed.

Once you work out those gameplay mechanics then the game itself no longer makes sense. It's nonsense to be "sneaking" out in the open right in front of a guard and not having him notice you from 5m or more away. It's nonsense that guards give up the search and forget about all the dead bodies (why bother even hiding them, to be honest). Etc.

Just like with the UFO games, the production values are top notch. The voice acting is great. The graphics are great. The game runs great. Just like the UFO games that is where all the effort was spent, because games that are great looking and run well tend to get rave reviews. In the end I got more out of watching the missions on YouTube and skipping working around the bone headed mechanics, getting the "cinematics" without the frustration/stupidity. I say cinematics, that's the other bit the game lets the player down. It's all in game stuff and some of the dialog goes on and on and on. The writing isn't very good, it is full of filler. But it sounds and looks good, right? So everybody loves it.

Masterful Stealth and Strategic Prowess Unveiled: A Review of "Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun"

Rating: ★★★★★

"Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun" is a remarkable masterpiece of stealth and strategy, delivering an enthralling experience that will captivate fans of the genre. Developed by Mimimi Games, this tactical stealth game showcases a meticulously crafted world and an intricate gameplay system that will challenge even the most cunning of players.

One of the game's greatest strengths lies in its compelling storyline set in feudal Japan. The narrative unfolds with a tale of intrigue, espionage, and political upheaval, offering a rich backdrop for the thrilling missions that lie ahead. As players assume control of a team of skilled assassins, each with their unique abilities and personalities, they are immersed in a world of danger, deception, and relentless pursuit of their objectives.

The gameplay mechanics in "Shadow Tactics" are nothing short of exceptional. The isometric perspective provides a strategic vantage point, allowing players to meticulously plan their every move. Each character brings their own specialized skills to the table, and successfully navigating the intricate level design requires careful coordination and timing. Whether it's using Hayato's quick sword strikes, Aiko's ability to disguise herself as a geisha, or Yuki's swift and silent assassinations, the variety of playstyles and approaches keeps the gameplay fresh and engaging throughout.

The levels themselves are masterfully designed, with multiple paths, hidden alcoves, and intricate enemy patrol patterns. The attention to detail is remarkable, encouraging players to experiment, discover new strategies, and unleash their creativity in overcoming obstacles. The feeling of satisfaction that comes from executing a flawlessly orchestrated plan, bypassing guards undetected, and silently eliminating key targets is truly exhilarating.

The visuals in "Shadow Tactics" are stunning, with beautifully rendered environments that showcase the beauty and brutality of feudal Japan. The attention to detail is evident in every aspect, from the lush landscapes to the authentic architecture and atmospheric lighting. Combined with a captivating musical score that heightens the tension and adds depth to the overall experience, the game truly immerses players in its world.

It's worth noting that "Shadow Tactics" offers a substantial challenge. Some missions may require numerous attempts and careful observation to uncover the best approach. However, the feeling of accomplishment that comes from successfully executing a plan that seemed impossible at first is immensely rewarding.

In conclusion, "Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun" is a standout title that excels in its stealth mechanics, strategic depth, and immersive world. With its gripping storyline, meticulously designed levels, and diverse cast of characters, it sets a new standard for tactical stealth games. Whether you're a fan of the genre or simply seeking an exceptional gaming experience, "Shadow Tactics" is a must-play title that will keep you enthralled from start to finish.

review_text:
As much as I enjoyed Hiveswap: Act 1, I can't recommend Act 2. It continues the story begun in Act 1, and about 80% of it is just fine; Joey and Xephros continue their journey across Alternia, trying to find a way to get Joey back home. It's the remaining 20% that spoil it, though.

First, there's the trial scene. It involves ten or so people I whose names I couldn't keep straight, but none of whom were sympathetic. Add to that the extremely low stakes (someone stole someone's book and tore some pages out of it), and I really couldn't bring myself to give a crap about the situation. None of it concerned Joey or Xephros in any way, either; this was just something that needed to be done to get to the next bit. But even with a walkthrough, it went on for-bloody-ever.

The chapters at the end got rather weak as well: there's a problem in a lot of point-and-click puzzles where you get stuck and wind up combining every object in your inventory with every other object, in hopes of finding the magic combination that the game designer had in mind. Hiveswap isn't big on inventory puzzles, but it had something similar: with few or no clues on how to proceed, I wound up having to talk to every person in every location, to see if they were the one with the information our heroes needed.

In short, there's nothing fundamentally wrong with this game, just some lack of editing. But that's bad enough to spoil the overall experience for me.

review_text: I really enjoy this game. Taking it slow and replaying maps just to get the satisfaction of ridiculous shot and trying to get as many enemies as possible without tripping an alarm is pretty damn fun. Its not really about story or lore but there are many different ways to go about each map. The enemy ai are fun, not too smart, but not too dumb either. On the hardest mode, it is an actual challenge and there's tons of optional tasks, hidden stuff, etc. to keep you going for a while. Super long shots without assistance are very rewarding and the animations are still fun. This version (ghost warrior contracts 1) is much better than the newer version in my opinion. I have both Contracts 1 and Contracts 2 and I really didn't think the newer one was very good. The maps and extra shot distance added wasnt enough to beat the map design and stuff to do in Contracts 1. I choose to play Contracts 1 whenever I am in the mood to just slowly snipe the crap out of ai and play through a map I have already beaten. There's a ton of detail in the world and enough ai conversation when they don't see you to be entertaining and somewhat immersive. The weather effects are pretty sweet and the maps are huge. With everything turned to Ultra on my Super Ultra Wide Monitor, the immersion is there for sure. The abilities are not realistic but they are fun and awesome to have / use. The whole point is just to be fun, to empower the player, and to be a bad ass sniper with many advantages over the enemies. They will still kill you though if played on the hardest mode and like I said, playing through the maps and taking your time to kill everyone without raising alarms is an actual challenge that is quite rewarding. This beats the crap out of that boring recycled Sniper Elite IMHO.. Totally worth a buy if you're into awesome but unrealistic sniping games. There really aren't many out there so this one as of right now is my favorite in this sub genre of FPS.. The stealth / hiding system is funny to if you piss on enemy ai and then hide in bushes while picking them off. Kinda reminds me of the good old days playing splinter cell and wrecking enemies from the shadows. Love it. Its really a fun game and it can be played in both a laid back style or in a serious challenge way. That's probably my favorite thing about this game.

The narrative, to rescue your stolen dog, is formulaic at the beginning but the 2nd half of the game, the struggle to return home, leads the story away from the classic archetypes into it's own moments of brilliance. 
The best thing about Samorost 2 is that it also doesn't have ridiculous puzzles, as with so many flash or adventure "point n click" games. Samorost makes sense, which was refreshingly original.

It isn't long which is the biggest flaw, but a game that wants you to keep playing, is always easy to recommend.

I really, really wanted to enjoy this game. It just felt like it wasn't actually ready to be released.

Interacting with the characters was very flat and didn't offer much to keep me interested in learning about them. They each have three traits, but that didn't really seem to affect anything about their contributions to the game. 

It was also extremely difficult to survive. There was not much available to forage and the hunger bar goes down quickly. Food also decays after a certain time period in your inventory. I'm a cozy gamer and the stress of having to worry about dying/my game ending led me to turn off both of these functions. But it was either all or nothing and then there wasn't any challenge at all. 

I really just wanted to request a refund and move on without having to leave a "bad" review, but because I played over 2 hours, my request was rejected. The main issues I had with the game aren't things that would be obvious with only 2 hours  of game play. Now I'm stuck with the game, so hopefully these are issues that are fixed in the future. 

Positives: the music is beautiful, I loved the sound effects of the NPCs, the emotes are fun.

review_text:
The time gating is as annoying as it gets and the main complaint I have about the game.  At first it wasn't that bad, a day or two.  However, once you start hitting 50+ that gate goes to 9+ days.  Absolutely horrible design decision.  While I can understand the need to slow content clears by speed runners, putting a time gate in what is essentially a single player RPG is flat out ridiculous!  As if that wasn't bad enough, you also get a weekly cap on how much you can earn for coin, jade fish, and other currency.  But wait, there's even more gated content!  10-man raids - only one a week.  New story?  Wait another week.

The scenery is beautiful, the story in engaging, combat needs a little work but is pretty solid.  Each area has had a great amount of thought put into it, that much is evident.  

With all the different martial arts, compendium entries, trials, lost lore, etc you'll spend a great amount of time just trying to complete a single area of a given region.  Unlocking everything will definitely fall into the 150+ hour mark unless you look everything up with little to no exploration on your own.

With the game being playable in solo, co-op, and online modes you have the freedom to play how you like.

Overall, a decent experience so far with much more to explore.  As a free-to-play game, you can't really complain too much.  However at the current pace of the game, the constant time gating, and the one character limitation I don't see many players continuing to play WWM after finishing the main story arc.  

The cosmetics available without buying anything in their shop, which is absurdly overpriced, more than suffice to get the job done.  Be smart and don't sink a single dime into this game until you reach level cap and have an actual desire to continue playing.  Games like this work off of impulse purchases and with random chance boxes for the gambling addicts trying to get that super rare cosmetic with the 0.00001% chance to get it.

review_text:
This is a really fun game for an arcade VR shooter, and I have had a good amount of fun with it, which is why I'm sad to give it a negative review. Why? The biggest reason is that not very many people play this game. It does have crossplay with PlayStation, but even with that, it can be difficult or even impossible to find a game to play. According to Steam charts, this game has a hard time getting 70 people to play, and I can't imagine it's any different on PlayStation.

Another crippling factor is that even when you do find a squad of players, there is a very good chance that someone will lose connection while the match is starting or have atrocious lag. On higher difficulties (since that is all anyone ever plays), this is a death sentence, and you might as well leave and try to get a full squad. The loss of that one player and their firepower is enough to tip the scales against you, even if the rest of you are armed to the teeth with the best equipment in the game.

I also want to touch on progression, as this game's progression is very grindy. Since people only play on the hardest difficulties and you are just starting out, you will be next to, if not entirely, useless until you unlock the things you need to be useful. Even with the time I have put into the game, I am not at the point where I am useful to my max-level teammates. The only silver lining to this is that sometimes veteran players will take pity on you and give you one of their max-upgraded guns, but don't go into the game expecting this. It's only happened once to me, and for them to rebuild it for themselves is a significant resource investment and something they might not want to do for a random player.

I also don't think any of these issues are going to be fixed since Vertigo Games is going to be making "Metro Awakening." It's safe to assume that all the devs who worked on this game have moved to this new project, which is very disappointing as I had hoped this game would have a longer lifespan.

review_text:
I really want to recommend this game as a hockey fan, but I just can't in its current state. It certainly has its moments, and it [i] almost [/i] has that addictive quality that great roguelikes have, but it has some absolute glaring issues that make it incredibly frustrating to play beyond Act 1. 

[b] Issue #1: The AI [/b] 
The teammate AI is a mixed bag. In some ways it works well; it's clear that effort was taken to ensure that it plays well in the offensive zone, with the AI-controlled players reliably getting in position to receive cross-seam passes. The issues with the AI become more obvious when you don't have the puck. The AI seems to have no concept of "last man back", and will charge straight towards the puck carrier in the neutral zone. This frequently gives your opponent scoring chances, and I'd wager at least half of the goals I allowed were scored at least in part due to this. 
The other annoying issue is how bad the AI is at moving to get the puck. The bots aren't very good at predicting where the puck is going, often completely missing what should be an easy rebound to bang home. This is compounded by how awkward it is to pick up bouncing pucks. 

[b] Issue #2: The Opponents [/b] 
The early opponents are just basic teams with simple themes. As the run progresses, the opponents get more varied and interesting, but also much worse to play against. In Act 3, teams are spamming their special abilities so much it becomes impossible to play with any strategy or skill; I beat the 'final boss' team by just dumping the puck and trying to win the faceoff. This is boring, but anything else is nearly impossible because otherwise your players are more often than not knocked out. These teams should provide a challenge, but are really just a slog. 

[b] Issue #3: The Progression [/b]
Tape to Tape draws massive inspiration from Slay the Spire, but seems to completely miss what makes that game so addictive. In StS, winning a run with a character unlocks the next level of Ascension for that character, which is essentially a slightly-harder version of the run you just beat. As the player improves, the game offers harder and harder challenges to match them, which makes them want to keep coming back for 'one more run.' In Tape to Tape, you get currency to buy upgrades between runs to make the game easier, which kills the feeling of wanting to come back to do it all over again. 

[b] Issue #4: The Content [/b] 
I can cut the game some slack as an early access indie title, but that doesn't change the fact there's just not enough content for the price right now. You play almost the exact same teams in the exact same order every time. Other roguelikes like StS put players into completely different builds and scenarios every run, but Tape to Tape starts to feels repetitive after just a few hours. There's a decent variety of starting abilities for the player to use, but they're mostly totally useless by Act 3 anyway. 

So yeah. I want to love this game, but it's incredibly frustrating and repetitive in it's current state. Losing runs rarely felt like the consequence of a mistake but instead the result of janky mechanics or pure RNG (I once outshot an opponent 25-to-1 and lost...) I sincerely hope these issues are addressed, because the core of this game could be awesome if it were improved upon further.

review_text:
TL;DR: Just go play Dead Space.

As much as I respect Glen Schofield, I can't say the same about The Callisto Protocol. According to interview I saw, the game was shipped prematurely, and he couldn’t stop it. The lack of polish is evident throughout, and the story feels incomplete. The final cinematic — and especially the last few minutes — suggests that the full story requires a €15 DLC. A cliffhanger ending that you have to pay extra to resolve is just outrageous.

The combat is dull and repetitive: dodge, melee, dodge, melee — rinse and repeat. It quickly becomes tedious, and the dodging mechanic is frustrating. One wrong move, and you’re dead. I lost count of how many times I was one-shot because the system felt unforgiving.

There’s no map. The level design is linear and sometimes pretends to offer exploration. You’ll find side rooms, but there’s always only one way forward. Worse, it’s not clear which path progresses the story and which is just a dead-end detour. In most cases there will be an autosave indicating that you're now progressing the story, but that will not always be the case. Additionally you will have no space to carry the loot you find in those extra rooms. The environment feel repetitive — everything looks the same. I sometimes got lost, unsure what to do or which object to interact with to progress. And with no objective reminders or prompts, I often forgot what I was supposed to be doing after a break from the game.

Autosaves are terrible. Manual saves are pointless because the game always reverts to the autosave. These saves often happen at the worst moments, killing any sense of pacing. They also scream, "Something big is about to happen!" I’d much prefer save stations like in Dead Space.

The balancing of health and ammo is a mess. Sometimes you’re drowning in resources which cannot carry back because the door is locked behind you, other times you have nothing at all. Just your melee weapon. Maximum ammo capacity is limited, and picking up a new weapon adds another ammo type to juggle. Healing items come in two forms, but the slower one is useless because enemies can interrupt you mid-heal. Why even bother carrying it?

The game’s reflective surfaces are misleading. They often shine like item pickups, leading me to chase phantom loot. Breakable windows and environmental hazards like cysts respawn if you revisit areas, which is ridiculous. Simple things like opening a box can be fatal if your health is low.
The flashlight is another head-scratcher. Its light source seems to come from some tiny, invisible dot on the suit, and it doesn’t even glow. And there is no indication from where the inventory is displayed in front of your character. In Dead Space you at least had a screen built-in front of your suit.

Outfits are lackluster, and inventory space tied to them feels restrictive. The one story-mandated upgrade doesn’t compensate for this. Every chapter transition is interrupted by a black loading screen, shattering immersion.
The intro scene is particularly bad — your character immediately adopts a generic "ready to get jumped" pose, even when there’s no danger. Everyone looks perpetually sweaty, like they’ve run a marathon. Holograms randomly pop up without input, which raises questions: Is there a motion sensor activating these things? Were they turning on every time someone walked by when the station was alive?

The kinesis module (or GRP, as the game calls it) has no clear recharge system. It blinks when it’s low but gives no gradual feedback. You’re stuck waiting around when it’s empty, doing absolutely nothing. Similarly, the inventory system is unnecessarily split into two categories for weapons and then gadgets, ammo and health.

The game is riddled with immersion-breaking bugs. One standout was a giant 2D rat silhouette sliding across the environment. Silent kills are anything but silent, yet enemies remain oblivious even when you kill their buddies right next to them. However, stand up from crouching, and they’ll instantly hear you.

All the weapons look and feel the same. Switching between them is confusing, as you can’t tell what you’re holding. Swapping weapons is painfully slow, and the absence of something as simple as number keys for quick selection is baffling.

The music is almost non-existent. Was this supposed to build tension? If so, it failed. The game isn’t scary. Not once did I feel a moment of fear or suspense, and I’m pretty jumpy.

The difficulty settings are unclear. “Maximum Security” sounded like an option for a safe and secure experience. Nope — it’s just prison terminology.

The Callisto Protocol had potential but squandered it with poor mechanics and uninspired design. I don't see my self playing New Game+ mode. Maybe if the DLC is on discount, I'll revisit the game once again, but I hear the DLC is even worse that the main game.

review_text:
I must admit, when I first tried the original "Pathologic," it struck me as a strange indie project, and I quickly abandoned it. Later, after reading enthusiastic reviews, I promised myself I'd revisit it but never found the time. Now I've had the opportunity to play "Pathologic 2," which is presented as a full reimagining of one of the original game's three storylines. Having completed it fully, I'd eagerly dive into the remaining two-thirds if they become available.

It's no big spoiler to reveal that the game unfolds in a remote steppe town gripped by a terrifying pandemic. The disease is unknown, spreads through airborne droplets, ravages the body swiftly, and proves fatal within a day. Although the town supposedly houses tens of thousands of residents, this is visually understated—just one of many gaming conventions. Among the population are dozens of significant characters with whom you interact extensively.

The protagonist must constantly manage hunger, thirst, immunity, exhaustion, and health. The core gameplay revolves around survival amidst extreme resource scarcity, especially time. Time moves inexorably forward, compelling you to make painful decisions since completing everything you wish is physically impossible. The town itself is a maze that changes daily, with barricades and obstacles emerging regularly. Losing precious time by taking a wrong turn is frustrating, often prompting a reload, though saving is restricted to specific locations. The narrative spans eleven in-game days (excluding the twelfth day), and with each passing day, time moves faster! This relentless pace ensures you're never truly at ease. Interestingly, the game allows you to bypass plot tasks entirely—provided you have sufficient food and water, you could theoretically sleep through to the ending. This isn't an oversight but another intentional design choice, reminding players they aren't always the central hero capable of saving everyone.

The game's atmosphere is intensely grim. Your character, a surgeon, must practically apply his skills—saving lives through operations, dissecting bodies to study the disease, or selling organs on the black market to afford basic sustenance. The agonizing infected are visually and audibly disturbing, and townsfolk gradually descend into madness, escalating from knife fights to burning people alive in desperate attempts to halt the epidemic.

Additional immersive elements include crafting items, repairing mechanisms, sewing clothes, sharpening weapons, and brewing medicines. There's also a distinctive mini-game for diagnosing illnesses and prescribing treatments. Though depicted simplistically, these elements add artistic charm.

However, not all mechanics were to my liking. Inventory management is particularly cumbersome. The game features nearly a hundred items, initially seeming like useless junk, yet each can become crucial for repairs or trading. The limited inventory size necessitates meticulous planning and creating stashes near save points to avoid unnecessary losses.

Additionally, the artificial limitations on item durability are frustrating. Clothing logically offers disease protection, but it deteriorates far too rapidly, as does weaponry, breaking after a few uses.

Combat is disappointing as well, particularly enemy AI. Bandits stubbornly continue to attack bare-handed despite being shot at with a shotgun, lacking any instinct for self-preservation.

Story-wise, however, the game is genuinely captivating, blending detective elements with mysticism and surrealism. Merely surviving becomes secondary to understanding unfolding events, unraveling mysteries, and attempting to rescue beloved characters. Yet no one is safe: any narrative character can contract the disease, and medicines are scarce, particularly since the protagonist also requires treatment. The developers deliberately instill a sense of fatalism—for instance, achieving one specific accomplishment necessitates allowing a particularly cherished character to die.

Game rules change daily. Neighborhoods become infected, risking contamination upon any contact; starvation drives locals to violence; barricades arise, water sources vanish, and shops close, replaced by illegal stalls. Prices and even currency fluctuate abruptly, rendering accumulated wealth worthless. Children, the primary source of medicine trades, eventually disappear from the streets. These perpetual changes maintain continuous engagement.

Notably, the death mechanic uniquely complicates gameplay: each protagonist's demise applies various debuffs, making subsequent survival harder. After repeated deaths, the game offers a "deal with the devil" to remove all negative effects—at a significant and irreversible cost, even if you reload a save. My advice: avoid this deal until you've completed the game at least once.

The standout feature remains the narrative itself. Explicit explanations are rare, and nearly every dialogue introduces new mysteries and enigmas. Its atmosphere somewhat evokes "Twin Peaks," rich in metaphors and allusions found in texts, imagery, and environment design. Unfortunately, there’s hardly time for contemplation due to the constant urgency. Occasionally, the protagonist's thoughts manifest as dialogues with shadowy versions of other characters. The developers also daringly break the fourth wall, portraying events alternately as dreams or theatrical performances, casting the player as an actor playing the protagonist.

"Pathologic 2" is undoubtedly not for everyone. It's challenging, tense, and occasionally irritating, yet its profound intrigue and depth firmly hold your attention until the very end.

review_text:
This review does not cover every weakness in this game. SEGA does not know how to utilize their resources to provide meaningful content for one of their most beloved franchises. If you put enough hours into this game, you will see many flaws with New Genesis and it boils down to the fact that the NGS developers do not play their own game. This review won't guide you through all the problems, but I will highlight one in particular.

NGS will always put in the barest minimum effort and expect to profit from it. You deserve better.

Over the course of 2 years and 4 exploration zones, the Halpha continent is basically complete. As of writing this review, NGS is celebrating their 2nd Anniversary with an event that rewards players with goods from a limited time trinket shop in exchange for seasonal points. I will use this example to fortify my next paragraph that summarizes the remainder of the game's "content". If you are new, seasonal point gathering might be a great time to group up with friends and grind out a combat zone or Limited-time quest, earn some points, spend it on the shop. If you have been playing for 2 years you've already seen this event structure 10 times by now. It is monotonous, unimaginative, and most egregiously, recycled. The NGS Team performs a copy-paste of their previous event and hopes you can't spot the difference. Each time this event returns, it is an insult to your time, your effort, and your intelligence. Daddy SEGA knows that customer engagement is important to profits, so giving you an mindless task  every "season" is a perfect example of scamming players of their time (possibly AC) for a product they've been recycling since its introduction. 

You say, "But that is just a transient event. What about the permanent content?" True, a lot can be said about the quantity of "permanent content" presented in the current version of this game. But I ask the question to the veterans: 

"How many VR/Purple cube/Blue cube tile-set instances filled with monsters/bosses would it take for you to realize that the content releases have zero deviation?"

You've fought these monsters/bosses before, now NGS has kindly repackaged them for you to fight them again. And possibly again! Congratulations on a higher score-- or a faster time. Give me a fucking break! How much of this game is speed-running through cube-rooms shaded over with a VR texture that burns your retinas? It takes less than an afternoon for a developer to create (or recycle) a purple/blue cube arena for you to play in. Are you enjoying something new or what SEGA wants you to perceive is new? Do not praise NGS for new or innovative content, because nothing you've experienced is new. You have been doing the same dodge/block/parry combat against recycled monsters/bosses, just in a different backdrop.

PSO2: NGS does not intend to create a fleshed-out game. There is no effort put into creating meaningful activities. Developers are just clocking into work to meet a deadline on their next poorly executed project -- that is probably a VR cube room that spawns a boss; it will ship with almost zero play-testing. Every week some whale pays for AC, so that the NGS developers can keep the lights on at the office and continue scamming you of your time. So if you are still asking "Should I play this game?" The answer is: You deserve better.

review_text:
Game is alright, it tries it's best to be like a Dead Space. Thats a good thing and unfortunately a sad one, i really love Dead Space 1 and 2, but i'm slightly dissapointed that this game didn't tried to have its own identity.
Monsters, atmosphere, UI and other things felt like copied from Dead Space. I know that Glen Schofield created both games but i wish that he tried to create something new with the Callisto Protocol.
But then again i might sound like hypocrite, but i love everything visual about this game. Immediately the game gives you familiar feel, like you are playing Dead Space.

I know i have been yapping about the atmosphere but i freaking LOVE it, maybe it's Glen's worldbuilding that he makes that i adore. Graphics are top notch, there are few hiccups at some places but its alright.

Monsters look great but they act like the monsters from Dead Space (VENTS EVERYWHERE), i wished to have some innovation here because the behaviour of the enemies were 100% the same like in DS games, even enemy types were almost 1 to 1 copies.

Sound was good but i felt like it was used poorly half of the game. (In moments where there is no combat or anything, and you would hear most intense music of your life, like why? Like nothing is happening in the moment and i felt like this for half of the game.)

Story/Dialogue..Story is alright, i like the idea, that you end up in prison and you have to fight your way out, BUT THERE WAS SO MUCH LEFT OUT. I felt like this game wanted to go more psychological way, when Jacob had his visions of Max and stuff. Those moments were gooood but then they happend like only 3 times in the whole game and jumped back to basic story. Voice acting was good, everyone did amazing.

Combat is ehhhh... I did liked the idea that you have to use your melee and get close and personal with the enemies (bash heads). But the dodging man, whaaaaaaaaaat. Dodging felt like an joke. :D Someone here mentioned that the combat felt like bad For Honor experience and it kinda is. Loved the idea with mixed melee and ranged combat, but i think it was executed wrong. Dont even want to talk about stealth in this game...

Boss fights were a joke, because of 2 things.
1) enemy types 
2) bad combat 
Boss fights felt like last minute add on, you guys should had added variety for boss fights. Fighting same looking dudes with same tactics, kinda blow cheeks.

I will stop yapping here, the game overall looks amazing, feels great and plays alright.
If you enjoy Dead Space games then please try this game.

Ladies and gentlemen, finalmente aqui estamos, depois de 3 anos a continuação dessa serie linda finalmente chegou, e OH BOY COMO ESSE JOGO É MARAVILHOSO, Hiveswap act 1 é um dos meus jogos favoritos de todos os tempos e Act 2 não me desapontou de jeito nenhum, na verdade eu até acho esse jogo muito melhor que Act 1!! Hiveswap act 2 conseguiu melhorar e consertar todos os problemas que existia no Act 1 e simplesmente conseguiu criar uma experiencia maravilhosa e incrivel, mas antes que eu va muito longe vamos começar do começo

Hiveswap act 2 segue diretamente depois do primeiro jogo na historia, não vou explicar muito para não dar spoiler mas basicamente segue Joey e Xefros em sua aventura e dessa vez eles precisam se encontrar com um troll para Joey descobrir como escapar do planeta, a historia desse jogo não é tão complicada mas segue bem com o primeiro jogo e tem varios twists e surpresas interessantes voce vai adorar, agora vamos para o primeiro detalhe incrivel de Hiveswap, seus graficos, como hiveswap act 1 os graficos desse jogo são maravilhosos, toda animação é fluida, expressiva e muito bonitinha, e os designs de todos os trolls e personagems são muito boms e carismaticos, eu tenho certeza que voce vai amar cada personagem que conhecer, os artistas de Hiveswap estão simplesmente de parabens com esse jogo lindo

Vamos a outro ponto incrivel desse jogo, o gameplay, Hiveswap é um jogo point and click igual a aqueles classicos como Monkey island etc, um dos problemas do Act 1 era que os puzzles não eram muito boms e as vezes meio confusos, mas isso é totalmente resolvido no Act 2, a gameplay e puzzles nesse ato são muito mas muito melhores que o primeiro ato, tendo puzzles bem criativos e com dificuldade até que grande mas balanceada e legal de resolver, Act 2 não é so um jogo bonito mas tambem um jogo muito divertido, se voce gosta de point and click, vai adorar esse jogo, um outro fator que foi melhorado desde o primeiro jogo é sua duração, Act 1 era um pouco curto demais, agora esse ato completamente resolve isso, na verdade isso é ate uma critica que tenho com o jogo, as vezes algumas partes ou até o jogo em si podem ser meio longas demais, tipo a sequencia de julgamento no meio que pareceu ser a metade do jogo, mas ao mesmo tempo a duração muito mais longa desse jogo é um fato muito bom porque faz parecer ser uma aventura muito mais cheia, Act 2 tem gameplay o suficiente durante sua duração longa para voce adorar cada segundo dela, então talvez tome cuidado que hora for jogar esse jogo para ter certeza que vai ter tempo o suficiente, mas tenha certeza que vai adorar cada segundo

em conclusão, eu quero me casar com esse jogo lol, todos os jogos do Hiveswap são simplesmente experiencias incriveis e Act 2 não sei como mas conseguiu ser um jogo ainda melhor que o primeiro, mesmo levando 3 anos para completar esse jogo, eu acho que valeu muito a pena, incrivel

Graficos: Muito lindos e bem desenhados, maravilhoso
Gameplay: Point and click muito divertido
Soms e Musica: Incrivel
Requisitos: Nada pesado, apenas um jogo 2D simples
Dificuldade: Puzzles um pouco dificeis mas muito boms e divertidos
Historia: Simples mas muito legal e cheia de surpresas

PROS:
Gameplay muito bem feita e divertida
Arte muito linda
Historia muito engajante e legal
Muito mais longo que o primeiro jogo

CONS:
Certas partes um pouco longas demais

highly recommended! I cant wait to see what they add.

I cannot in good will give this game any good review.  I've been playing since 2011 and the game has progressively gotten worse with each year.  Lets start off with why I feel this way.
Zen to Dilithium is broken.  The Devs said awhile back that they had this great idea of fixing it and it did.  For about a week or so and it went back to retarded number again.  They've done this a few time and each and every time it doesn't fix it.  Why?  Because the makers have no concept of how economics works.  I own 2/3 of the ships ingame.  Most of them I refuse to buy is because it's a reskin of another ship.
Lock Boxes, you have a better chance at win the Lottery than getting a ship out of these things.  Go look up your chances.
Reskinning ships and calling them new with a higher price tag.  Sovereign Class from the Mud market is over $100 US just because of on Module.  
Clipping issues with the outfits.  This has always been a big one for me on how poorly they've done with the game over the years that they have yet to fix this.
Some of the outfits are still pixelated.  The swim wear is that is now pushing over 5 years has yet to be updated.  I have uniforms that are the same way.
Uniformity in the outfit would be nice, but its not.  Each event outfit has it's own color, but all of the rest of the outfits you can change the colors at your will.  The makers are so desperate for people to play their game that they have to come up with ways to get you to play an event over and over until you get what you want.  
Wait months for new content and that last for a week or 2.  There is nothing worth while in the game to do because they removed the one that helped with this problem.  The removal of the Foundry was the biggest mistake that STO ever made.
The UI interfaces never function the same way across the board.  Example. The Admiralty mission when you click to complete them never move up on the menu, but every other menu that has this does.
The game makers idea of making content more difficult is add zeros to the heath bars of enemies and strip of bonuses against them.  Mirror Event for example, a Mirror shuttle will have as much health as your ship does.  
Your captain doesn't even make any noises when they get hit or do something.  They have sounds for everything else, but yet the captain and crew are mutes.  There are Free to Play games that sounds for characters for god sake.

If none of the above what I said bothers you, then go for it.  I have standards for games and what I expect out of them.  If you want to just putt putt around space fart around.  Then go for it.  Don't expect game breaking content nor quick fixes when something breaks unless it's store where you can spend money to buy things.
My advice if you want.  Buy ships in packages and not singles.  Sales are around major Holidays, so if your wanting something from the shop.  Wait until then too see if goes on sale which most likely happen.  This game loves giving out free shit all of the time.  Low tier ships and outfits things they like to handout a lot.  Play only one or two captains.  Any more than you don't need unless you want to farm for Zen.

On a side note.  I do know that the people who are working on the game are very good people.  They are doing what they can with what they got, but unless another studio comes along or they get more help.  This game is going to be what it is for a very long time.

review_text:
What started out as a love letter to JSR quickly turned into a disappointment. Trust me, I wanted to love this game, as a fan of the original Jet Set Radio, but the game has so many issues that I can’t in good faith recommend this at all.

Firstly, the stages are too spacious, nothing is happening within them. There aren't many cool landmarks and most of the stages begin to blend together at a certain point. The level design is something the original game did well, but here, it’s just not fun to grind through through them. A certain point you kind of lose interest in exploring at all.

Secondly, there is no energy to this game. Remember how the original Jet Set Radio opens up? With Professor K’s iconic JET SET RADDIOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO blaring into your eardrums. That game commanded your attention from the start and you, the player, knew you were in for a ride. Here, there’s no voice acting. Sure, we get some grunts and a few short words here and there from the many characters, but you can’t help but notice that something is missing from the cutscenes. Everything feels so quiet… so lifeless… despite the game wanting you to be invested its story.

And that finally brings us to the story. I will say right of the bat I didn’t like it. The story started off well but halfway through, I was bored. Could it have helped if the game had a better presentation with voiceovers as well? Maybe. But the writing just isn’t that interesting. I thought it took itself a bit too seriously.

The music is great, possibly the best thing about the game and I’ll leave it at that.

review_text:
What can I say about Carbuncle Protocol?

It’s a game, one they want you to think is of ‘quadruple-A’ quality, so what does that mean, and does it hold up to that claim?

It’s got great sound design, nice graphics, it’ll set your CPU to broil for downloading/installing and shader cache collection on first boot, that guy from every fuckin’ transformers movie except the three most recent ones, and boring gameplay.

There isn’t a real way to summarize that last part effectively. You look at this game, in every review video, and think “wow, it looks so good, no way that is boring to play!”—but it is.
Exploration is composed of walking around and either stabbing in the back, getting jumped by those stupid fucking pod things that can only be avoided if you played the game and remember where they are so you can shoot them ahead of time, cutting the same serial cables on every box, crawling in vents, shimmying through gaps, and occasionally crouching. As a ‘spiritual successor’ to Dead Space, this feels alright, at first, but then you realize there’s no tension.
Despite the sound quality making you think there’s someone around the corner or behind you, 9/10 times you’re alone and don’t need to worry. Enemies are louder than women in spring, so you won’t doubt there’s someone behind you, maybe one will slip past, but you’ll turn the camera and see them just in time. But then there are these screams from the enemy that just grab you, make you turn around—you can ignore those. I’m confident 98/100 are just background sound clips on some kind of shuffle.

The graphics, where do I begin?
They’re ok.
That’s it.
Ol’ Transformer Actor himself is recognizable, but his head activates that part of my brain that makes me remember the uncanny valley. Everyone looks recognizable as humans, but there’s something off. It’s somewhere between Mass Effect Andromeda and Fable. With this absolutely stellar sound design, the visuals are so lackluster in comparison that you are forced to focus on it. You’re not buying this game because it looks good, and if you are, you’re going to be disappointed, especially when you get into—

Combat! Don’t bother shooting. Melee is how you will win, but it’s tedious. Dodge an attack by picking left or right, then tilt your controller in that direction, and start alternating until you’re ready to beat them in the face like they suck.
You will repeat this process from start of game to finish, with the only variety being windows of opportunity, how long you will beat them in the face, or special weaknesses…which are ignorable.
The security bot is the only time you’ll really need a gun. If you need help finding their weak spot schedule a visit with your local lobotomist expert. Enemies fight neatly one at a time which…they’re fucking feral, right? Why are they so Imperialist-era England about it? All they were missing was starting off the battle while standing in a line. You can sever limbs, or shoot them—but this is dead space, so shooting or dismembering the head is worthless, so why have a gun? What about the quick shot system? Honestly, that works well, and all it really does is serve as the gun in Bloodborne; you will use the quick-shot to stagger enemies so you can interrupt their attack and beat them in the face. If you’re not doing this, you’re doing it wrong. So even in combat there’s no tension, no reason for you to feel rushed or intimidated.
What about all those fucking death animations? What ABOUT them?
They shitty, and rarely happen. 90% of the time Transformerdude just falls over dead and I’m wondering when he’ll get up, because he doesn’t look dead when this happens, it looks like a lifealert moment. He’s fallen, and he won’t get up—-oh, wait, he’s dead. That’s awful! I should know when I’m dead immediately, so the moment I actually get a death animation how do you think I react?
I’m disappointed! They’re well made, brutal, but they feel soulless, and without the weight Dead Space 1&2 originally had. You don’t get excited when you see them, you rarely do anyways, so if it’s why you’re buying the game save your money and look up a YouTube video, trust me—please.

And that’s it! Explore through the game, find secret audio logs and shit. It’s not difficult, it’s tedious, and boring. The story never picks up, you’re constantly waiting for things to explode and get real…then it’s over, and they’re asking you to pay for the real ending because it’s hidden behind DLC. With games I’m normally hooked to see how things end, but with this game I’m not. It’s boring and tedious to the point where I don’t even care what the story is, or what will happen.

These quadruple-A games that I’ve seen and played are a sign, and that sign has the same writing on the gates of hell.

-2/5 – this game sucks.

review_text:
I almost wish Steam had a "recommend if on sale for xx%", but since not I had to vote No. This one was frustrating, as there are clear improvements that are overshadowed by confusing downgrades. 
[u]PROS[/u]
- gunplay feels quicker and a little more frantic
- enemies move around more, especially helicopters, feel a bit more aggressive
- visuals are pretty, if oversaturated
- the tether is a little snappier when transitioning to a landing

[u]CONS[/u]
- no more base liberation (this was what I did the most JC3; re-oppress and fast travel to capture bases again, it was the main challenge of the game)
- challenges are basically gone. Instead of a full, beautiful wingsuit course, you have literally have "fly through 3 rings in less than 9 seconds". Instead of a race, you have "pass through this ring over 150 km/h". These are a joke I would expect from a single-person indie game, especially after JC3
- no longer have remote mines
- only two weapons can be equipped at once; no longer have dual-wield pistols/smgs

[u]OTHER[/u]
- control changes, the most subjective part:
 -- the d-pad no longer handles weapons. Left/Right now swap between your three tether loadouts, and Up to trigger effects
 -- weapon swapping is handled by holding Reload, hence only having two weapons now
 -- zoom-in moved from R3 to L2, and now must be held down, fine with me 
- you now have three different tether effects:
 -- Air Lift: attaches a lift balloon
 -- Retractor: auto-retracts once attached to two things
 -- Booster: is booster
 -- You can set 0-3 effects on each loadout
 -- You can set these effects to trigger automatically, or by pressing d-pad up, or holding it. You can also set the intensity/strength or each effect
 -- There are also mods, such as making the balloons fly in a direction instead of hover, or pop when they reach full altitude, or change booster direction, etc

review_text:
So i feel like I'm probably a good candidate for a review as I played PSO Episodes 1+2 plus for both Xbox and GameCube, both offline and online. And I had an absolute blast playing those. I then went on to CARD and somehow even enjoyed that, followed by PSU. I've enjoyed every PSO game I've played because simply put. It's formula.  The gameplay has been historically simple and enjoyable for the most part, the elements associated with the plot and story lines have also made for pleasant and heartwarming experience. 

The reason I say this is because PSO2 and PSO2 NGS I feel are more appealing as games for previously established fans of the genre... PSO 2 took what made PSO and PSU successful and implemented those same mechanics, with an introduction of various new features.. such as a slew of more fashion oriented items, a system where you can upgrade weapons and armor and even other various features such as customizable techniques, photon arts, class leveling and more. That said, as a fan of the old stuff, these are awesome upgrades and implementations and definetely add to the richness and enjoyment level of the game and I haven't even touched upon aspects such as clans and player shops. 

NGS took what made PSO2 successful and followed that same style of formulaic upgrading, except now we got a serious graphical overhaul, an open world and a level of richness never before seen in a PSO game. In fact it's so rich that to new players it can be overwhelming! And there in lies the problem I feel new players will struggle with. 

This game seems like a game that you can just pick up and play on the surface (and it is) but there is a learning curve. In PSO2 and NGS there is more tact necessary during combat, you have to learn how things work in order to properly specialize your character, you need to learn how the armour and item systems work over time in order to properly maximize your fighting potential, as with any RPG. But once you do learn those mechanics (which can be done within 5-10 hours of gameplay easily) you really start to appreciate its charm and creativity. There's a lot of life in it, a lot of passion. You get a sense the developers really did try to make a good, enjoyable game. 

And most of all, the game is free. You can spend money on the premium set (and various other cosmetic items) and doing so really does add an even deeper level of richness into the game regarding the quality of life experience (more rewards for your time, expanded storage, access to player-based economy) but the cool thing is you can access this stuff as a free player as well in limited time usage increments, so you can get a taste for it and see if its worth it to you before electing to spend the $13 for 30 days of premium play. Often times there's also sales as well, I currently am utilizing 30 days of premium play for just $5. 

In reality, its a good game. It's free, its fun. Don't be afraid to join a clan and play the main story too. It really helps smooth things out and prep you to be at a solid level to join other players for endgame. Seasoned RPG veterans could grind through it in easily 10-15 hours. In a world where games are commonly feeling like half-finished cash grabs it does feel as if PSO has more respect for your time and wallet. And the nostalgia factor hits hard as well (in case you couldn't tell) 

All in all, I say to fans of the genre and newcomers alike. Give it a chance! It's a lot of fun!

review_text: The game gives me a vibe similar to Sim Medieval, albeit lacking the farming, yet it maintains a familiar atmosphere. I've been playing this game for a full calendar year in-game and have generally found it to be a laid-back and enjoyable experience. However, the enjoyment tends to wane during winter due to the absence of farming activities, leaving me only my two persimmon trees to attended to. The fall and winter seasons primarily involve preserving and jamming everything, which can become tedious after a while. I do enjoy upgrading structures like the house, and I am eagerly anticipating the addition of a chicken coop. The quests are inconsistent—some are rewarding, while others fall short. I wish the family NPCs had more dynamic behaviours. Typically, they gather idly at the stairs, sometimes engaging in minor activities like cleaning a glass or playing with a toy, but often they are just clump together awkwardly. I'd appreciate more interactive options with the family and additional indoor activities like reading or sitting in chairs. Additionally, the ability to turn on the fireplace/stove in winter would greatly enhance the cozy atmosphere of the home. The cooking segment isn't my favourite; I'd prefer the option to create my own recipes with available ingredients. Despite these issues, the game is endearing, and I adore the artwork. As it's a new game, I'm hopeful for ongoing updates that will continue to improve and expand the experience.

review_text:
Lucius is a horror-puzzle game where you play as Lucius, the Antichrist son of Lucifer, and you are tasked with killing everyone in your mansion. I think this game is comparable to the Hitman games, since in both games you have to kill your target silently and creatively. However, while Hitman offers different opportunities and methods to kill your target, in Lucius you must follow very specific steps, so it feels more like a puzzle game than Hitman does. The whole premise of the game is similar to The Omen, a 1976 film featuring Damien, an Antichrist child.

While Agent 47 has many gears to help kill his targets, Lucius has supernatural powers such as telekinesis, mind control, mind wipe, and pyrokinesis. Most of his powers are used to manipulate objects around him that causes the target's death seem like an accident. Pyrokinesis can be used to fight, but it only happens twice in the whole game. There are also "sidequests" in the form of chores, and doing them will give you rewards that can help you. These are not necessary, but there's an achievement for getting all 3 rewards.

The biggest problem of Lucius for me is the darkness, literally. The game applies some kind of dark monotone filter that makes all colors seem dreary. What's worse is when the missions took place in the evening or night. It's literally too dark to see anything, even after raising the gamma and PC brightness. Optimization is also bad, my PC is quite strong but can only run this game in 1280x720 resolution and Medium graphics. Breaking glass objects also causes lag spikes, but easily solved by walking away from that location. 

However Lucius is a pretty okay-ish horror game, so if you like the Hitman games or The Omen happens to be one of your favorite horror movies, don't hesitate to give this game a try. It's quite short and usually goes on a 90% sale, so it's very cheap. I think it would be cooler if Lucius has multiple ways to kill the targets like Hitman, as it increases the replayability.

review_text:
This is one of those times I really wish Steam had a "mixed" review option. The good stuff is genuinely really good, but a recommendation doesn't feel right considering the problems and the current price ($40, or $20 on sale).

Good stuff: 

+ Visuals/Aesthetic
+ Soundtrack
+ Skateboarding/Biking/Skating - Feels really good, but the negative section below makes this point a little bit moot. 
+ Level design (sans collectibles)

Not so good stuff:

-Difficulty - The game is absurdly easy and you will beat the AI's score by a wide margin every time, which gets boring very quickly.

-Collectibles (incl. graffiti) - To progress in the game, you have to paint graffiti throughout levels. You have to find enough of the predetermined spots to write over to get the attention of that area's crew. Probably a third of my playtime was spent trying to figure out where these damn things are so I could progress to the next boss, rather than actually enjoying the skateboarding/etc aspect of the game. I don't mind if optional collectibles are frustrating to find, but graffiti being the only thing you need to progress kind of sucks.

I really wish progression would've been based on skill instead. Get a certain multiplier, or combo duration, or total score to continue, because the skateboarding/etc aspect of the game is actually very fun but there is no reason to go for high scores unless you're aiming for achievements.

-Police - As you paint graffiti throughout an area, police will arrive and shoot at you. They aren't difficult, but they are very annoying at higher heat levels. You can fight them but the hand-to-hand combat (that exists for some reason) is incredibly boring and slow. If police were removed from the game entirely, it would be an overall improvement.

-Tricks - You can press one of three buttons to do a simple trick. You can combine any of the three with left trigger to do the same trick but get more points. There aren't any interesting combos, there's no real depth, you just press buttons to get points. It's not like points really matter much anyway because you will win every time by just button mashing.

-Health - You are essentially immortal, but you do have a health bar that regens very quickly if you do take damage. Aside from the final boss, the only time I ever actually ran out of health and died was when my character got stuck in place (only happened once, not a recurring bug) and police shot me until I died. This feels like a completely useless mechanic alongside police in general.
