review_text:
While KCD 2 has blacksmithing and better alchemy, KCD 1 had much better world building and a far more immersive world. This game should have been a 10/10 for me as someone who bought KCD 1 Royal Edition TWICE, but I've been holding back my review because of many questionable decisions by the devs. Then I realized the fact that I have to hesitate giving an instant positive review when I am already viewing the game in rose-tinted glasses by the fact that I loved the first game so much means I have to give this game a negative review so they do not do it again.

My List among many others:
- Kuttenberg is fake big and anyone who tried to level up thievery in Kuttenberg would immediately realize that like 90% of the doors can't actually be interacted with. This makes Kuttenberg very confusing and very difficult to get immersed in. In comparison, the first map was well done. Maybe they should have just done one map if they are going to mess up the biggest city in the game. Why would you do that to Kuttenberg knowing most of the players at end game would chill in Kuttenberg?

- For a developer praised for having historically accurate buildings in KCD 1 resulting in many KCD 1 vs real life videos, not including the inside of churches in the game is a very unusual and terrible decision. Meanwhile you have Assassin's Creed Unity being praised for having a highly accurate Notre Dame.

- Badly written modern politics characters and storylines in a historically based game. Key here is badly written. I don't care what you do because I'm not interested in politics as long as it doesn't affect the immersion of the world, but you can't tell me, for example, that Musa was added properly and in good faith. Completely different religion, have to cross the Sahara Desert (the LARGEST hot desert in the world), cross the Mediterranean, then end up, not in Italy or Spain with coasts, but go all the way to a landlocked central European country. If you wanted to have a similar character, countries like Morocco, Tunis, Turkey, or Egypt wouldn't have raised any or as much eyebrows. Especially considering Morocco has the oldest university in the world. It would have been much better writing to have an educated diverse character coming directly from there for example. In addition, the North African region shares a long history with Europe such as the history between Rome and Carthage. You even have Morocco trying to join the European Communities in 1987 which shows that it considers the idea of being part of Europe. On the other hand, in games like Europa Universalis IV, you can't even really interact with Mali without getting colonizing technology as a European country or get to late game and that happens WAYYY AFTER the events of this game. Maybe it has something to do with the LARGEST HOT DESERT in the world being in the way... just a guess. I'm not claiming to be some history expert and I'm not sure I got everything 100% correct but these are just basic perfectly reasonable things and trying to give a reasonable solution is always better than just complaining. Anyone saying it is not just at the very least even a little unimmersive is just blatantly lying. Let's not pretend there aren't a billion other options for something similar and far more historically immersive before getting to Musa. And this is just one example of badly written modern politics instances.

- Something about the way the game is written and how the world was made have currently made me not have more than one playthrough. At this point, I still only have one save file. Meanwhile, in KCD 1, I have multiple save files of both hardcore and normal to the point where I have many routes to towns memorized from playing with hardcore mode such as Rattay to Talmberg, Talmberg to Pribyslavitz, Rattay to Sasau just all chilling in my head without the use of the map. I cannot say the same thing about this game.

In conclusion, I would rather have the world and storyline of the first game and just add the blacksmithing, better alchemy, and new crafting items and options such as having your own forge than the world of the second game with its terrible, unimmersive world. There are no similar games in the market so they are allowed to just mess up. Very few "immesive RPG" games even have a functionally immersive sleep mechanic much less all the other things. review_text:
I would've liked this game more if it doesn't turn into "opening inventory simulator". This game offers you the versatility to use anything towards your enemies, whether they're swords, magic attacks, or environment interactions like setting up oil on fire or freezing enemies inside water. 

The problem with this is, there is no presets for you to make to quickly switch from one to another; you have to open your inventory to switch to the weapon or magic you want to use in that situation, and then switch back to whatever you're using before because it's a playstyle you're comfortable with. Perhaps you see water on the floor and you don't want to be electrocuted or be frozen, so you open your inventory to equip the swimsuit. Or perhaps you encounter enemies that does bleed damage, so you open inventory to consume bleed removal foods or wear armor that negates bleed debuff. Or perhaps you're just low on HP, you open your inventory to consume foods.

All of this makes the pacing very slow, on top of the combat being slow already in the first place. I don't mind if I have to commit to the slow sword swinging animations, but what I don't like is having to constantly pause the game to switch stuff around. Sure, I can just stick to one type of build all the time, but in a game where the game can be very punishing because of the character's low HP, no i-frames upon getting hit, and HP and MP are not replenished unless you consume foods, it's better to try and take advantage of the situation you're in.

After all, this game has a popup at the beginning of the run that says the game wants the player to think to solve problems they encounter. I want to do that, but the constant pausing to switch stuff around due to lack of preset options is ruining the experience. The unfortunate part about this game is, there is a bonus mode that fixes this problem, but you have to beat the game first.

the beginning of this game is excellent. theres a sense of mystery and esotericism to the world. something bad happened and there is a huge mystery. someone or something caused the end of all things. but the further you get and the more you learn the less interesting it all becomes. the things that are interesting are not explained and the things that are boring and poorly written are over-explained. in the end its a pseudo love story that somehow dances around the truly fascinating facets of the world and gives too much exposition for the things your most likely not concerned with. the collective is an after thought the virus while seemingly important is never really expound upon. 

in the end the story slowly devolves into a stereotypical and frustrating experience where initially there are incredibly high stakes involving the extinction of life as we know but for some reason focuses on an anoying female character and another character who seems to be a simp for her.

my problem is that a large majority of time your exploring the nuclear winter that is the future of this fictional world and every now and again you go into the past to "extract" people. with such an interesting writing device as time travel they barely use it and the potential it has for providing interesting and diverse areas. 80% of the game is exploring areas that largely look the same. wasted potential.
the combat is fun but the enemies and their ability to combine into a stronger entity is hardly a threat given how many tools you have to prevent it.

what is the collective?

who built the technology?
what caused the virus?
how did everything get nuked?
what is the phylactery?
what does extraction look like?

i have so many question none of which were answered and instead it focused on a shitty love story about an annoying girl and a simp robot.
just due to the incredibly unsatisfying ending i will not recommend.
there is stuff to like here like the world building the envirnmental detail sound design and hit feedback
but there also a lot to dislike...

review_text:
There Are many things good with the original Bioshock game, but there a few gripes I have with the game. During the main story there are a few glitches and bugs (I was playing the non-remastered edition) but nothing major, mostly just rare occasional crashes, too intense for the physics engine to handle (same with the 2nd game, but more on that over there).
The introduction of the plasmids and weapons were very fluid and intuitive and at the ADAM stations, the prices for ammo, plasmids, and tonics were very balanced the entire course of the game. The Game is also very well put together story-wise, aside from at the ending of the game. In which (at least the good ending, I haven't played the other ending) seems very forced onto the player, you get a happy ever after with all the Little Sisters, and not more of a realistic ending where it works out, but some things don't. 

One good thing in the game are the Plasmids; they are the genetic encoding power-ups you get throughout your journey in Rapture. Some are unlocked through Story progression, meanwhile others are rewards for harvesting ADAM, or even just exploring the different rooms in the game, although most are just bought at the ADAM vending machine. They are pretty balanced, being you as the player needs to be able to use plasmids, as well as using the Weapons in order to fairly get through the game. They need to work together, not seperate power systems throughout the game. for example you can get the frost blast plasmid and then freeze a big daddy stunning him. Then you can shoot him with other weapons while he is frozen, which they balance with the incinerate ability (fire blast). which if you use ice and then fire, it just melts the ice, not being able to have both active on an enemy. Another Good aspect of the game is the Weapons; during my play-through I mostly used the Shotgun, Wrench, and Tommy Gun. Throughout the game you can upgrade your weapons, but only up to 7~ times throughout the game collectively, across all your weapons, so you must choose wisely. Even on easy mode, you will want those upgrades. 

Another positive element about the Original Bioshock is the story. You are the sole survivor (or so you think) of a plane crash and stumble upon a lighthouse, bringing you to the great underwater city of RAPTURE. Here, you find your first plasmid on the surface, and are communicating with someone known as Atlas; in which he asks you to help him with helping out in recovering someone/something he needs from the city. "Would you kindly?". Where it leads to you going around a relatively small portion of rapture, searching, finding out what ADAM is, seeing the remaining residents of the broken city; and most of all Andrew Ryan, the supposed crooked villain of the story. But all is revealed throughout the story, As you collect ADAM and grow stronger. In order to escape you will have to turn into a Big Daddy, in order to both, lure the Little Sisters to help you (in the good ending), and it adds an extra layer of defence, armour, and protection to you for the Final Boss fight. Although this is a good game, there are some plot-holes that arise and are never acknowledged in the subsequent games being Bioshock 2 and Infinite. 

All in all, Bioshock 1 is a pretty solid game, story and game-play-wise, but overall does lack just that extra oomph that is to be desired.

Witchfire need way more content to justify the insane price of admission.

A game that, although good in concept and fun for a while?
Feels bland, empty, and like a demo.

The Early Access period was wonderful, giving a showcase of the bones of a game that needed to be fleshed out and seasoned for it to become more.
Customization felt lacking, the maps were small and limited, and the variety of tricks and ways to explore left plenty to be desired.

It slowly added a new map, a few more customisation options, and then? 

Multiplayer.
A great idea, which made me really keen to see where the game would go.
Although the game hadn't been built on enough for me to recommend it to friends, I did have people in my shared library giving it a go and being keen to see where the team would take it.


Then, full release.
One new map, all customisation locked again, and a progression system that makes you replay the same races, or areas over and over again.
Full release

It feels like this game failed to really develop on the early access release, leaving an extremely barebones final product.
Real shame, as it has no competition and could have easily carved out it's own niche if it had been given more time, and a greater scope. Modding support would be fantastic, but, it isn't really here.

Can't recommend buying it, just not a lot here for the price, coming in at close to $40 in AUS
Will occasionally fire it up on my steam deck as it's perfect for it, but aside from that?
Rooftops and Alleys will be collecting digital dust in my library.

I didn't expect to like this one as much as I did. While it unfortunately suffers from an inverted difficulty curve (where a lack of options and power at the beginning of the game makes the first few hours far more difficult than all that follow, even in repeat playthroughs), once it opens up, it feels empowering to find a new weapon or spell or accessory that suddenly makes some other set of tools viable.
It does feel like some of the systems of the game go underutilized. There's a whole system where liquids like oil, poison, or water can spill on the ground and react with fire or electricity, but aside from certain traps, this whole system doesn't come into play too often. It might be possible to work this to your own advantage if you set up your equipment right.
Altogether, a pleasant surprise. Worth pursuing if it looks like your thing, genre-wise.
A word of warning: [spoiler]a quest given fairly early can be easily failed in the very next room, and several other points throughout. Completing it is actually required in order to get the "good ending".[/spoiler]

review_text:
To the Moon is shockingly bad. It's far from the worst game I've ever played, but this is genuinely some of the least I've enjoyed a game in a good long while.

There are two main culprits you can point the finger at, and their names are Eva Rosalene and Neil Watts. The protagonists, especially Neil, are insufferable. Instead of coming off as the lovable bickering old colleagues they were clearly supposed to be, these two just feel downright cruel and nasty. They can't let any moment pass without a snide comment or forced, dated reference and it completely ruins any immersive moments the game might have had. Their struggles with the ethical implications of what they're doing at the end of the game don't feel believable because I genuinely do not have any reason to believe they actually care about the situation or what they're doing because they've taken nothing seriously so far. 

The story these two are so bent on ruining isn't that great either. For the first half of the game, I was genuinely invested. Johnny's portrayal as a less than perfect man who fetishized River's autism is something weird and special and other and ultimately couldn't understand her and hurt her was compelling. The depiction of their relationship made my skin crawl, which I assumed is how I was supposed to feel. I wanted to see how the game would handle helping a man who loved someone very deeply but never really understood them for they were and his last attempt to make things right.

So when the game got to the big twist, I was bitterly disappointed. Johnny and River's relationship struggles are no longer about the two of them failing to overcome fundamental differences in how neurotypical and neurodivergent people think, River literally remembers something Johnny doesn't because he had a secret dead twin all along and took magic memory loss pills to forget his early childhood. That's boring! It absolves Johnny of responsibility for fetishizing River's otherness and not seeing her as a person! It's a stupid twist! It just left an awful sour taste in my mouth and made the happy ending feel completely unearned. It wasn't a happy ending for River, and the game never acknowledges that. 

There's a few other little things. All the supporting characters feel pointless. I would have loved to know more about Isabelle, but she's only present for a few scenes. Lily and the kids are cute, but they never really do anything. Johnny's doctor gets to join us for the big happy ending, but we never even learn their name. And I know this game got sequels so maybe it gets addressed there, but what was up with the game randomly introducing Neil's opioid addiction and not bringing it up again??

The gameplay too is really only there for the sake of it. The puzzles are fine, but didn't need to be there at all. The music is pretty good though. That and some of the first half of the game are the only things worth saving. This game squandered every interesting idea it had and was annoying and uncomfortable about it the whole way through. Even as a product of its time, I cannot bring myself to like it.

One of those games that consumed me. This game is debatably fun, but when you let yourself fall into the world its extremely enjoyable. You are asked to make extremely difficult decisions, and then asked over and over again. Surviving is to grit your teeth and dig your heels in. You must be more stubborn, more determined than this plague. You will fail, you will die, you will let people down, and then you won't. This game is such a work of art, I'm really really looking forward to the release of Pathologic 3 and anything else Icepick Lodge decides to make.

On a more personal note, I played this game in the literal worst period of time in my life. The game is punishing, filled me with anxiety at times, and caused me no small amount of frustration. But it also let me overcome those moments of game play. I was able to feel in control of negative emotions and master them. It provided me with a catharsis that I think no other game could... except maybe Pathologic Classic (which is on my list!). This isn't a game for everybody, but it's a game I think everyone should at least try.

The world is dark, mysterious, and hauntingly beautiful, and every corner feels alive with secrets waiting to be discovered.

What makes it so life-changing is how deep it goes beyond just being a shooter. The story hits hard, with twists that genuinely shocked me and made me question everything. The moral choices, the way it makes you think about power, control, and human nature, it’s the kind of game that stays in your mind long after you finish. I still remember the feeling of discovering its biggest reveals, and it honestly gave me chills.

This isn’t just one of the best games of its time, it’s one of the best ever made. It showed me how games can tell stories as powerful and thought-provoking as any movie or book. It’s exciting, it’s emotional, and it’s unforgettable. I’ll definitely encourage my kids and grandkids to play it one day, because BioShock isn’t just a game. It’s an experience that deserves to be passed down.

review_text:
The inventory is a pain in the a** to use, and you have to use it a lot. It's great that spells and weapons feel different, and that different enemies are susceptible to certain effects, and you can even cleverly use the environment. But the slow weapon selection takes all joy out of this, and the same goes for consumables and armor pieces. If the items were at least sorted by the effects they cause! 

Why there are two different mechanisms for saving is beyond me. There are [i]computers[/i] which let you save your progress permanently, and you can even manage multiple savegames for some weird reason. But then there are also these [i]statues[/i] that only act as a temporary checkpoint mid game. And they can only be activated once! So if you pass the same checkpoint again, your progress until then will not be saved! So when you die you often find yourself in the position of having to do a lot of busywork like talking to a character or picking up items again and again. It's just a frustrating experience.

There's also no real sense of progression or accomplishment. There is no levelling (which doesn't have to be bad in and of itself, but it is in this case) and most items are utterly boring and don't have any advantage over the stuff you already have. Buying items is also almost completely useless. 

I could go on about graphics, combat, and other silly design choices, but these are the biggest deal breakers for me.

After a really, really far-out, confusing, glitchy and lysergic 1-hour long intro sequence with extremely cringe-worthy and incomprehensible dialogue, and which felt more like a very long dream rather than anything substantial, it seemed that the real game finally began...

review_text:
This is a bad game unfortunate to wear the Star Trek name.

Sure it starts off quite fun with a lot of veneer on the surface as you start to recognise the voiced actors from the various shows. But after getting blown up for the umpteenth time in ship-to-ship combat, I wish I could get my money back!

What's that? It's a free-to-play game, you say?

I know, but I still feel like I've been cheated.

The game is woeful in its tutorial only teaching you the basics whilst expecting you to trawl through menu upon menu to find extra keybinds you didn't know your character could benefit from that WOULD HAVE BEEN NICE TO KNOW AT THE TUTORIAL LEVEL!

I can't stand games like this; they look like they're promising you so much, until you sink some time into them and you quickly realise that an awful lot of boot polish has been applied onto a wooden statue only to be clobbered over the head by said statue.

The space combat is so lacklustre that you find yourself dying over and over again without ever really knowing what you're doing wrong. You just get spanked (and not in a good way!). Hints would be welcome if you keep dying to the same foes (who magically regenerate all their health when you go right back in by the way!) to at least offer you some guidance what you need to upgrade.

I haven't got time to source external sites for data to study which weapon combinations are better than others for my ships when I game TO RELAX not for endless frustration at doing different things over and over again but getting the same RNG results. It's utter cr@p!

I wanted to like this, I really did, but I just can't recommend it for what I've got out of it... hair-tearing frustration at seeing your ship get destroyed because the RNG loot drops you get after a fight just WON'T give you the weapons that give you a fighting change against enemies you should be obliterating.

This is looter-shooter at it's most banal and I haven't got anymore time to waste without having something more substantial to show for it.

If you ignore this review, then that's your call, just know I don't want you to have anywhere near the frustration I've had when other games are actually ENJOYABLE to play!

This isn't. Not when the risk-reward just is not up to snuff.

After what felt like an endless search, I finally found Adventure Escape Mysteries, a story-driven puzzle game that’s actually free to play! It’s everything I’d been looking for: a mix of compelling stories and clever puzzles that lets you feel like a detective, uncovering secrets and solving mysteries one clue at a time.

The game has a variety of stories, each with its own vibe—murder mysteries, supernatural adventures, you name it. I got so caught up in them; every story brings new characters and settings, which keeps things feeling fresh. The puzzles aren’t just random challenges either—they’re woven into the plot in a way that makes solving them feel rewarding and adds to the story’s momentum.

One of the best parts is that most stories are completely free, which is honestly hard to find in this kind of game. But heads-up: some premium stories do require a purchase to unlock. It can be a bit of a bummer if you’re hoping for everything to be free, but the quality and depth make it feel worth it to me. Plus, there’s so much free content that it doesn’t feel like you’re missing out if you decide not to pay.

Overall, I’d say Adventure Escape Mysteries finally delivers on the promise of a great, free story puzzle game. With its balance of engaging storytelling, cool art, and satisfying puzzles, it’s definitely worth downloading if you’re into mysteries and love solving problems!

review_text:
OPEN LETTER TO THE DEVELOPERS:

A very awesome VR "Left 4 Dead" alike. Changed just enough to make some fresh new mechanics that up play-ability over L4D, IMO. The sad thing is, the difficulty is very, VERY much too hard. I can blow through the entire level on Veteran (normal) difficulty, but when I get to the boss, I get destroyed in very short order. This is in single player, and it doesn't get much better for two players. The higher difficulties are a raging inferno of mass runs of zombies that overwhelm, and bosses that eradicate.

Now here's the BIG problem with all of this: The only way to get the better gear is to play the higher difficulties! I was very excited to farm and play this game, slowly working up to getting better and better gear based on random drop probabilities, but with the "hard" and "hardest" modes being the ONLY way to get most of the good upgrades, you end up stuck at a dead end once you've beaten veteran difficulty a few times! You NEED the better gear to play higher difficulties, and you can't get it without playing them! This chicken and egg dilemma really lowers the replay-ability.

Now, I know, yes I KNOW there will be some people who can stomp through the higher difficulties and have no problem, but you can't make a game for the hardcore players and have it be long-term successful. Tried the free weekend and...The game is 50/50 to me but leaning towards negative because of its technical problems. 
The game can be pretty badass at times but THE SERVERS AND PERFORMANCE ARE MADE FROM EXTRA OLD DOO DOO which is what has me on the fence about purchasing and leaves much to be desired.

-Multiple crashes to desktop whenever I played

-The tutorial does a bad job of explaining what to do in your first few matches which can make you feel so lost at times. 

-Youll have major desync and rubberbanding the entire match if you get a bad server (which is VERY common)

-The bugs are lower resolution at a distance plus their low FPS animations make it look like a stop motion skit. review_text:
the Short - Check this game out at your own risk. It’s not terrible but it is a disappointment considering the director.

the Good - Audio and (most) visuals are top notch, the atmospheric elements are well done, the voice acting is solid, and many areas are interesting in level design. 

the Mid - Background lore and world building has some highs and lows, barring similarities to beloved Dead Space. Exploration is light and a bit cumbersome with back tracking, vent crawling, or mini puzzles. Melee and Gunplay combat could use some tweaks to be more fluid and responsive when dealing with multiple enemies. Often times you’ll be locked into combat with a foe while unable to dodge a ranged attack, other times you’ll take damage from a “simultaneous” hit or from a second opponent with no way to block it.

the Ugly - a bit.

First, the story and pacing. Elias, Dr. Mahler, and the Circle are the exceptions here and actually stand in the good/interesting category. While the protagonists Jacob and Nakamura are terribly written. Jacob has very little personality and is bland and uninspiring at best. You are suppose to sympathize with Nakamura, someone who raids Jacob’s ship causing him to be stuck in this situation while killing the copilot in the process. This seemingly gets hand waved later for “survival sake” along with a magical wonder cure and Jacob’s ending being a forced trope.

Second, The Biophage has some massive plot holes or straight up illogical plot points for “horror sake”. You’ll encounter people in webbing for no reason, nothing causes it. Environmental corruption/terraforming from a [spoiler] body parasite [/spoiler], how/why? The overall life cycle of the [spoiler] parasite and potential hive mind [/spoiler] are as well thought out as a late night B sci-fi flick. I’m not expecting everything to be explained in the first game (if a second game was seemingly planned) BUT at least have a logical explanation or spend some time reading on how parasitic anatomy and biology work before putting a sci-fi spin on it.

Third, there are multiple times throughout the game where considering the spread of the Biophage and general damage to the prison, you may ask yourself “How long was Jacob passed out for after surgery?” or “How could this have spread so far and so fast in such a small amount of time when incubation takes weeks” (per the story).

Fourth, there is some balance issues with the guns especially considering when you acquire them and many of the weapons including the baton look out of place.. as in they just don’t fit the aesthetic that the rest of the game has going for it.

Finally, some technical hiccups. I encountered a save file glitch causing a temporary loss of auto saves and some missing audio during the colony chapter. (fortunately caught it with subtitles on)

**Original Review, additional notes below @ 17 hours**
A shameless cash grab, preying on two groups of people: 1) SAO fans who just wanted a good game to drop to fill their hearts with GGO era vibes(This aint it) and 2) Thirsty whales who want skimpy outfits for children.   Even if you can look beyond that, the game runs terrible even on modern high-end hardware, with stutters and a camera that is tied to the mouse, so if you don't play on controller, get ready to feel like you've got .. a syndrome.  In either event, if this wasn't a gift from a friend I would return it right now.  Instead I'll warn anyone who goes to get it that the devs have taken exactly zero feedback from the open network test, and have in fact made some elements worse.  There are now weird shader elements in cutscenes, the UI in the lobby has even more clunky items to slow you down and keep you looking at their other paid options, because you didn't just pay between $60 and $120? for the game which feels like it's just north of an asset flip but not quite a complete indie game.   There is a battlepass which ironically (so far) seems like the only thing that isn't a cash grab but give it time.  They have DLC bundles for gear and aesthetics, and they have a buggy but built in system for getting RNG boosters to give you more drops, which will undoubtedly be in their bundles.  This is the game that all the youtuber game reviewers warn you not to buy.

**17 hour review notes**
Fractured daydream is an appropriate name for the story since it's what I imagine an AI would think up after reading the wikipedia page for SAO.  There's not really any fundamental lore involved, and 90% of the plot is the characters arguing in an attempt to be cute, 5% of the time is regurgitated plot devices and 5% is actually new/specific to this game lore information.  I could spoil the entire 5 chapters in 2 sentences or less.

The game is abysmal for its inability to properly actuate some skills, like where you hafta mash and hold C/L1 to use your unique skill - i don't know if this is supposed to be a feature so you don't accidentally it, but it's a bad UX.  With the user experience being not worthy of a $19.99 pricetag, the idea that I'm playing on a $100+ version of the game seems about as out of touch with reality as the script writer for this plot.  Graphical bugs, text bugs, and combat bugs galore riddle this game, and there's no where to report problems to, no one to send screenshots and information about them back to.

The problem that's a glaring one though, and the one that will 100% kill this game, is the fact that on top of the pay walls, there's not enough players to even fill a group on mid-tier content in advanced access.  I don't think that full release is going to change that dramatically, so when high-tier raids and co-ops are being matched for they're going to be all NPCs, and the end result is going to be near-impossible to complete. I set out to play through this VR rip-off of Left4Dead solo and then replay it online at harder difficulties once I had learned the basics.

Halfway through (3 of the 5 maps), I felt pretty certain that I would end up giving this short and unpolished game a slightly reserved but positive recommendation.

But here, it seemed to go hand in hand with nasty glitches. Suddenly, the manual gun reload became super unreliable and inconsistent. The weapon model would start to drift out of position and remain there, something I never experience in any other similar VR FPS games.

I have an Intel 8700K CPU (@4.8ghz) and a RTX 3080 GPU. Regardless of the quality preset, this would happen. I double-checked that there was no thermal throttling going on.

There's potential here, but I cannot recommend it in its current state, and I have no intention of spending more time with it.

I'm really glad Adam had a return to form making this game. Gives a lot of the vibes WTTG2 did in a good way, while cutting down on some of the more cryptic and frustrating elements. It's definitely not as hard. 

I have two critiques. The first concerns the decision to make the Noir talk, specifically the lady. Part of what made them so creepy was their total silence. It takes away a lot of the creepiness to hear them. I understand it's to avoid some frustration with her mechanic of getting close, but you should have more faith in your players to do it, or maybe instead of her speaking she could gesture for you to come closer. 

Secondly, I feel as though there needs to be a short grace period after dealing with threats, at least in the non-nightmare modes. Multiple times now I've had to deal with female Noir on the roof, only to get shot by Lucas two seconds later without even realizing the laser was there. 

Good job on the game besides that.

I played this game yeaaaaaaars ago, so this might be outdated as I did not really keep up. I am not even sure this game works on new systems anymore but I will try to write a review from what I remember. 

Being a satan child out to murder all the residents and family was pretty good. This is more of a puzzle game than horror or anything else really. Your main objectives include killing, acting normal, killing, sneaking and snitching, killing, invoking the powers of the devil by directly talking to him, acting normal and killing again. Yeee this game really doesnt have many different quest options. You have chores which are these side quests like clean your room or do this thing but nothing else. If you are here for something more dynamic, then I would say go find something else. 

Now going from the feel lets go to how this actually plays. You are literal offspring of devil whose powers are just awakening. Your daddy comes in and wants you to kill everyone. Since you are still pretty powerless, you are expected to kill silently. You are a hitman essentially, without choking people and throwing them in closets. Most of the kills will look like freak accidents. This game really is just a puzzle game on that aspect. With more murder, comes more power. Eventually, you will be able to even toss fireballs. Its fun, but you are still a midget, so do sneaky burning. 

For visuals, this game doesnt look all that bad, but there are definitely better looking games from that time. 

As for sounds, they are nothing too special. Maybe except the demonic powers. Where the greatness of sound design lies is in the games music. Its great. The chanting during murders is still stuck in my head even till this day. Its great OST.

What I remember, is this game has a lot of bugs. Some items not spawning, getting stuck, AIs pathfinding was sometimes fucked and some other bugs.

Overall? I do recommend this game, pretty cool experience but do be aware of its age.

The game is reasonably priced for what it is, I guess, but I don't think it's worth the time to play it.

The only real critique I have of the game is its price and runtime. The game itself is really only about eight hours give or take (I have a few more hours on the GOG version), which makes it extremely difficult to justify the $60.00 AUD price tag. It is also a shame considering the artbook and soundtrack are also fantastic. Definitely only get this game on a steep discount, especially if you are unsure whether or not you will enjoy this kind of a game.

Scorn also runs perfectly on the Steam Deck. I was playing on the maximum graphics settings with AMD FSR set to performance mode. It both looked fantastic and ran increadibly smooth without any issues or bugs. My only recommendation is to play with some really good headphones, since the audio design should not be missed out on. If you have a Steam Deck, and feel like traumatising the person sitting next to you on the bus, then look no further!

The gameplay itself is very simple. Walking through various scenes and locations broken up between the occasional puzzle and combat encounter. The movements and gunplay are very slow, which might turn a few people off. I did not mind this, but only because I am more adjusted to slower paced shooters anyway.

While on the topic, combat is purposefully cumbersome in this way, and I feel this is where the game loses a lot of people. The majority of players I witnessed seem to have the false impression that they have to kill every single enemy they come across, in the process wasting their scarce resources, and then proceed to complain about ‘forced combat encounters’ when in reality you can theoretically get through most of the game without needing to kill anything. 

Aside from a select few that will encourage combat, the majority of smaller enemies will spawn in on ‘patrol’ and then despawn at the end of their route. If you do not want to waste your valuable health and ammunition, you can simply break line-of-sight and wait for the enemies to move on. If you do decide to engage in combat, get a couple of hits in, run behind cover, let them spit their acid at you, and then repeat. It is dead simple once you get the hang of it.

I do appreciate that there is an animation for almost everything your character does, making the world feel very tactile and real. While I do think part of the intrigue of Giger-esque art is the viewer is only left to speculate what mechanical functions these contraptions have, I think Scorn strikes the perfect balance of intractability with these devices, while still keeping the majority of these machines mysterious. While traditionally gameplay to me is the most important aspect of a video game, I approached this game from the perspective of it being an interactive artbook and was not disappointed in the slightest.

Speaking of which, what can be said about the artstyle that has not been already recited thousands, if not millions of times over? It is gruesomely gorgeous! Wearing the inspirations from both H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński on both its sleeves. Despite the obvious comparisons though, I feel that Scorn does retain its own identity apart from both Giger and Beksiński, and that partially comes from the uniquely strange and esoteric universe the developers have built. In true Giger-esque fashion, you will come across various contraptions, devices, and machines that you can only theorise as to their function. Piles of humanoid and not-so-humanoid bodies clambering up the walls, hinting at some greater struggle, extremely Beksiński-like. In this way, it gives the impression that the developers of Scorn both respect Giger and Beksiński and understand their work, in all its cryptic intrigue.

It is because of this reason, that to me, this is where the real horror of the game is. Naturally, horror is a very subjective concept, what might be scary to me might not phase you in the slightest. This game is a perfect example of this, since to me the true horror comes from the atmosphere, the environment, monolithic structures, and glimpses into atrocity. There is something about the strangely familiar yet completely alien environment that Scorn depicts throughout its runtime that fills me with such a unique feeling of dread and unease, unlike any other horror game has managed to capture before.

While there are a few monster enemies scattered throughout the game, they were not the scary part to me. What was scary was the implications that the world and environmental storytelling convey. The horror that gets to me the most is when there are just enough pieces scattered here and there to get your imagination going and inevitably fill in the blanks between them. An audience’s imagination of what something [i]could[/i] be will always be infinitely more terrifying than any writer, director, or designer could say or show it to be.

This is also true for the story, and the greater lore. There is no dialogue to convey the narrative to the player, no recordings, notes, or documents left behind, which I love. Scorn takes the ‘show, do not tell’ philosophy of storytelling to its most literal, leaving only for speculation into the specifics. This removes the inevitable frustration of bogging down the story with long exposition and endless collectable notes to comb through, and simply just [i]shows[/i] you instead. If you do not understand what you are looking at, good. That is the point! Naturally, this kind of story telling should not be applied to [i]everything[/i], it is perfect for Scorn and the world it depicts.

I only wish we could have seen more of the game, especially the last section of the game that takes place in an entirely new location that is distinctly different from the rest of the architecture prior. One can only pray that an eventual sequel or continuation of Scorn will be greenlit someday. I crave to see more of the horrific lore and witness the rest of this dark world the developers have built.

In summary: Scorn is a short game, so get it on sale. It will not be a game for everyone, but if you are a H.R. Giger or Zdzisław Beksiński fan, you will love it. If you are looking for something completely different, immersive, artsy, and esoteric, you will also love this game. Conversely, you will probably not like this game if you are looking for in-depth combat mechanics, fast-paced gameplay, or an easy-to-understand narrative.

If you are on the fence and buy this game on a discount, simply strap yourself in for the ride and just take your time with it. Look around, drink it all in, absorb the atmosphere and the world around you. I think you will be glad you did!

review_text:
The Callisto Protocol — A Beautiful Horror That Fell Short of Its Promise

Having completed The Callisto Protocol, one can’t help but wonder: why didn’t this game win over the hearts of a wider audience? It certainly boasts stunning visuals and high-quality sound design. As a horror experience, it successfully builds a chilling atmosphere, embracing the essential elements of the genre. And yet, something fundamental seems to be missing.

The root issue appears to be the game’s overall lack of polish and consistency. While certain aspects meet the standards of a AAA title, others feel rushed, generic, or uninspired.

Narrative Shortcomings

The story is one of the weakest links. While serviceable, it feels derivative, especially within the sci-fi horror subgenre. The plot develops in predictable ways that genre veterans will see coming from a distance. The game misses an opportunity to either deliver shocking narrative twists or build emotional depth that would allow players to truly connect with the protagonist. As a result, the storyline feels flat, and the emotional investment simply doesn’t materialize.
Limited Exploration and Interactivity

A hallmark of high-quality games is offering the player multiple paths to enjoy the experience. Whether one prefers fast-paced action or slow-paced exploration, great games reward both. Unfortunately, The Callisto Protocol provides little incentive to deviate from the main path. Exploration feels unrewarding, with very few secrets, surprises, or meaningful world-building elements to discover.

Combat and Gameplay Depth

Combat is initially intense but quickly becomes repetitive. Weapon acquisition is too straightforward — items are simply handed out along the main storyline rather than earned through effort, boss fights, or side quests. The thrill of unlocking powerful gear is absent.

Enemy variety is also lacking. Most encounters boil down to simple shoot-or-bash mechanics, with only one enemy type that invites stealth gameplay. While the game features a telekinesis mechanic, allowing you to throw objects (or enemies) into environmental hazards, it never evolves beyond a gimmick. Additionally, the near-total absence of mini-bosses is a missed opportunity to break up the pacing and introduce tactical variety.

A Rushed Launch and Lost Potential

What’s most frustrating is the sense that The Callisto Protocol could have been so much more — if only it had been given more time in development. There’s a strong impression that the developers envisioned a long-term plan supported by post-launch content and community growth. However, the rocky launch, paired with underwhelming critical reception, likely derailed those ambitions.

Post-launch DLC may have expanded the content, but by then, the damage was done. Players rarely return to games that fail to grip them on the first try.
Technical Problems on PC

The situation was made worse by the troubled PC release, which suffered from serious optimization issues. Clearly developed with modern consoles in mind, the PC port did not receive the technical attention it needed. In today’s gaming environment, a broken PC launch can tank a title’s reputation overnight — and no amount of patching in the days that follow can fully undo the harm.

Conclusion: A Tragic Misfire with Unrealized Ambitions

The Callisto Protocol had the makings of a great game — atmospheric design, strong audio-visual fidelity, and solid horror roots. But its unimaginative storytelling, shallow gameplay, and rushed development cycle prevented it from reaching its full potential. It’s a shame, really. With a bit more time and focus, The Callisto Protocol might have earned itself a much better future.

review_text: The first time I played BioShock, I thought, “Oh cool, an underwater shooter with superpowers and art deco vibes!” By the time I finished it, I was asking everyone “Would you kindly?” and questioning the illusion of free will in my daily life. So, you know, it escalated quickly. Let’s talk about the intro. You crash into the ocean, swim to a mysterious lighthouse, take a bathysphere ride down into the sea, and BAM—Rapture. An underwater city full of philosophical graffiti, broken dreams, and vending machines that scream at you. It’s stunning. It’s terrifying. It’s also completely abandoned except for the homicidal maniacs and giant men in vintage diving suits stomping around with power drills. Vacation destination of the year. The combat? A chaotic ballet of guns, fire hands, and “oh no I accidentally electrocuted myself again.” Plasmids let you do everything from shooting bees out of your arms to mind-controlling enemies, which raises questions that science should never answer. And the Big Daddies? They’re like boss fights combined with emotional damage. You want to fight them. You also kind of want to hug them. (You shouldn't.) But let’s be honest: you're here for the story. The atmosphere. The vibes. This game doesn’t just pull the rug out from under you—it tears out the floorboards, drops you into a moral philosophy class, and then politely hands you a wrench. And just when you think you’re getting the hang of it—BOOM. Plot twist so good it made me question if I was being mind-controlled by my microwave the whole time. Also, shoutout to the audio diaries. I learned more about failed utopias, corporate betrayal, and what happens when you mix unchecked ambition with genetic tampering than I did in any history class.

review_text:
[b]A neat idea, but complicated execution.[/b]

Fractured Daydream brings 20 players into a raid, to take on parts of a dungeon, only to meet up fighting the end boss together. Only to finish what is a confusing conclusion of this game.

This game wants to be co-operative by working together within your groups and other 16 players, so you don't fail a mission together. Rarely this happens as the game teaches you to grind more, get better gear, and be competitive within the missions. These include getting last hit, highest damage, or better party scores to earn that "MVP" end of the game for more rank/stronger characters faster. So if there's a dead player on the ground that needs reviving, or no tower/STM objective being done before the boss, it's probably because the game wants the players to be competitive. 

I'm not sure to call this a PVE MOBA with competitive scores, or an MMO with lots of repeatable grind, or boss raids if everyone can't work together cause of conflicting objective interests.

When you go through parts of the story, or a couple multiplayer matches... you've done the entire game. The only thing different is having stronger gear (if you're lucky or you grinded it) for the same mission with slightly stronger enemies. There is no other variety in the game, for the price of $80 CAD it should be closer to $30-40. 

The flow of the game is to attack small monsters, gain exp throughout, then fight your way to the boss being 'Awakened level 20-25'. You can unlock skills similar to a MOBA when you level up. No other skills per character are different. Once you beat the boss, you get your fancy drops, some exp for the next dungeon or boss and do it again. 
While the grindy game may be a great way to chill and play with friends, there is not a lot for solo or variety combat to enjoy. 



[h1]The Good stuff;[/h1]
- Returning SAO fans will enjoy the story. Referencing previous games/characters and having good dialouge. 
- Environments look well done, models look good, lots of outfits to try on characters. 
- Daily and Monthly objectives for free battle pass rewards to give players incentive to try new roles.
- Crossplay. Didn't have issues playing with others.



[h1]The lots of bad;[/h1]
- Combat is very stiff, feels like this game is better for 2010 era. Using heavy and light attacks, it's not fluid when your attacks or abilities trying to hit targets. You could be swinging in the air for a while, or missing an entire ability, and not because the enemy moved. Most of the time you will be rushing up to the enemies in hopes to stagger them with your attacks before they can damage you. The auto targetting option does help alleviate some issues, but it makes it harder for flying combat or camera adjustments to prepare oncoming attacks for guard/dodges.

- Dungeons are not engaging, not balanced, and are intentionally frustrating. Since you play the same thing over and over to barely get rank exp, you'll be stuck on the same maps for a while. So you will see them 20-30 levels later again just to do the same tile sets.  
5 different groups are split into 5 starting areas, and they are all not fair or balanced. Some starting areas required more travel, or you have to do an escort, or you will have to travel blue boring teleporters, which result less awakening EXP for that match. So the 4 other groups will have a stronger lead on that. 
There's lots of downtime between rooms so most characters with better speeds have yet another advantage. Ontop of traps, bombs, or annoying "watch outs" that don't add value to the grind or complexity. The hitboxes of the shadow blades are extremely big and sometimes not where you think you see them. All they do is add a layer of frustration to players ontop of the hours of repeated dungeons to grind out gear and dailies for.
The pacing is also bad while you're trying to catch up to the other groups so you don't miss out on other objectives and exp for the missions. Adding onto the slow/stiff combat, it just favouring stronger gear so you spend less time on the first areas.

- Hit boxes from enemy indicators are very inconsistent. Seeing a red circle before a big enemy attack should indicate to the player to be ready, but often these attacks are too early, too late, or worst - show the indicator after the enemy has already attacked. Sometimes you can stand inside those red circle indicators and not take damage. While others when you try to dodge or guard correctly, may not register thus taking damage. 

- Net code for monsters and players. Good luck playing Sniper (Sinon/Sterben) for aiming boss weakpoints where there's a lot of visual effects and CHAIN-EXTENDED-DOWN pop ups in your screen. There's an objective to turn other players attacks off, but it's not enough. You can still see other buffs from support characters on you obscuring view. Ontop of if you rush into rooms too quickly in dungeons, the enemies and attacks will not render properly so there are often times you will get hit by bad hitboxes from attacks, or invisible enemies.

- Game is heavily unoptimized. Recommended is a RTX 2060, while my RTX 3070 on medium settings is at full throttle. The anti-aliasing option seems to be the biggest culprit. But the worst offender is the mouse sensitivity options for PC is TIED TO THE FRAME RATE. Playing at 144 FPS tightens your movement while 30 FPS turns your DPI to 999999. While you go into dungeons and loading areas, your mouse sensitivity continues to change and sometimes fixes itself throughout the run. 
Game also crashes a lot. Changing appearances/outfits before a raid can have a high chance of crashing your game, especially after playing for 3+ hours. Some other folks I played with crash randomly whether it be after 1 hour or 2 hours. 

- Currently there are 12 different queues for modes (except free Roam). So if you don't have 20 players game can fill them with bots. While that may be seem positive, it requires players to know ahead of time otherwise they will rush the boss being underleveled and have a much harder time defeating him.  Without a full group, you spend more time on that map farming enemies during the tower/STM objective. Which is unfair for solo groups cause they get matched with 3 bots. Less EXP for them, which means they will have to play the game more and longer to get rewards. Hopefully this gets fixed in the future or some adjustment with a catchup system.

- Roles are a joke. Having a Tank or a Support just have 1 dedicated skill to 'fit their role' which doesn't seem to fit their playstyles of a team. In reality, tanks and support characters often do as much damage as ranged or fighter role characters, ontop of the benefit/support they give to their team. Heathcliff and Yuna are AOE machines that will pretty much top majority of the time. 

- The UI is definitely made for console. Menus could be a lot better for finding stuff you need. The SAO memories for permanent buffs are placed very deep in the menus and is probably very important to level up to have stronger characters. Whilist items to enchant, move sphere effects, inviting friends, changing equipment or appearances, playing with funny stamps, etc. I'm not sure why most games are going horizontal on menus, when something vertical or lists would be effective and simple. 



[h1]Overall;[/h1]
Game is enjoyable to turn your brain off and grind and that's it. Once you ran a couple of dungeons... you've done pretty much the game. The rest is a cookie clicker and RNG fest for stronger equipment to get higher numbers.

For the price, no. This game needed another year of work. With only a couple of bosses, and reskinned dungeons you need to repeat - it's a conflict between co-operative and competitive gameplay, with no end goal or incentive for players.

review_text:
Where Winds Meet implements both tried and true mechanics while also exploring new ideas. 

It took me a while to like the title as I am not a fan of Wuxia films. The flying combat and 1 vs 1000 style of martial arts films don’t really appeal to me, yet they work really well for a video game. Couple that with a high combat difficulty (when playing on harder modes) and you can get a lot of enjoyment from this title.

If combat does not appeal to you, there are other MMO lifeskill-like elements to this game that might pique your interest. For example, you can make friends with a lot of NPC’s. Not all of them, but a fair number of them. To do this requires getting on their good side. How? Through an AI chat bot. Yes, you have to befriend NPC’s by chatting with them and encouraging them to do certain things. Each one is unique and can only discuss what they know. They are not ‘all knowing’ as most modern AI chatbots can be.

If you have a craving for a good MMO, this could be it. You can switch between solo mode and online mode which displays dozens of players at a time in the world. Each mode has their pros and cons and if you want the full experience, you’ll have to play through both modes. 

The only other game I can think of that does something similar is Elite: Dangerous. I’m glad the feature is picking up.

All in all, this game gets a 10/10 - it’s a solid MMO that tries a lot of new things (too much to list), so I suggest you give it a shot. It is free, after all.

For a free game, sure its decent. If you need something to pass the time without spending money its probably up there in top 10 best options. Polished, feels like a finished product, lots of time sink, lots of different things to do in-game. Fantastic vistas and audio and visual immersion. Some funny KFH references, maybe some other stuff I didnt notice. Cinematic/trailer/loading visial seems to bear no relevance that I could discern.

As a game overall it's a waste of time compared to other options. The combat is not engaging at all its just a simple hack and slash with dodge and counter and a few special abilities and poor targetting. You're constantly looting junk off the ground for who-knows-why. The story and quests are goofy in a good way but otherwise pointless and unsatisfying. Graphics and effects are top notch but that doesnt make a good game. I didn't play overly long before getting bored and I can sense the upcoming cash-shop abuse in the not too distant future, probably inventory space, skins, battlepass etc etc. 

The menus and sidequests are ATROCIOUS; While they impressively all work smoothly you need a flight manual to navigate all the different functions and buttons and there just does not need to be so many different forms of gacha and currencies. There's like 5 different areas of the menu for multiple different things. It feels like someone just dumped the contents of a filing cabinet on you and said good luck.

5/10 wont play again just because its too easy, not engaging and the menus are ridiculous. Black Desert was more engaging, better combat, same bs menus and pointless side quests.

review_text:
THINK TWICE BEFORE YOU BUY THIS GAME. DO NOT BE FOOLED BY ITS GREAT FAME. THIS GAME IS NOT FOR EVERYONE.

After 30 hours of playing, i find it hard to say i love this game. Perhaps the demographic this game aims at is those who can find fun and pleasure in an ultra realistic video game in which you are constantly dragged back by all sorts of UNNECESSARY little things. For example, I understand that I cannot sprint when I am overloaded, but why can't I ride a horse? Is it too heavy for the poor horse? In that case, why can I put tons of things on the horseback if they are too heavy for me and i don't wanna discard them? Where is the weight limit now?

Beside that, I simply cannot find any excitement in the map exploring part. The exploration mechanic feels like a combination of The Elder Scrolls and The Witcher 3, by which I mean if somebody mentioned a spot, it is marked on the map, then you can go for it and in every human gathering (villages, tents, towns) there's a chance to find some quests.

Speaking of the quest, the quest design in this game is BORING. No matter it is a main quest or a side quest, they all follow the same structure: Talk to someone, get a quest, and this quest requires you to talk to another one in a village far away (this is absolutely torturing when you are overloaded). When you get that village, that guy says OK I can help you, but I need you to do something for me first. Wanna know more information? Talk to another guy! Then you run to another spot... This stupid cycle runs through all the mission in the first map. I'm not sure if I can make it to the second one. I feel like a errand boy or a clown being played. Apart from that, goals of these quests are BORING as hell. Most of them are about FINDING: find a string, find a document, find lost sheep, find my missing daughter, find a bandit camp, find a lair to kill some wolves... If it is what a real medieval life is, I'd rather quit and play something less realistic. For anyone who thinks I'm overstating this, just check how many 'find's are there in your mission list.

Last but not least, developers are very cunning to prevent gamers from refunding. In the first two hours of playing, the only period when you can actually play this game is about 15 minutes. The remains are all cutscenes. THERE ARE TOO MANY CUTSCENES. That is too say, when I could finally PLAY this game and realised it was not for me. It was too late.

To be fair, there is improvement compared to its predecessor. Graphics are astonishing. Optimization is outstanding. Battle mechanic is unique and engaging. Some of the plot is humorous. Still, I regret spending my money on this game and I hope you won't make the same mistake.

review_text:
As a game: no.
As a work of art: yes.

To elaborate, all the "video game parts" of Scorn are pretty bad. Especially the combat. I think this game would have been far better with zero combat and instead all that dev time could have been focused on the "immersion in an alien world" part of the experience. Most of the puzzles are pretty meh as well. There's really no discernible story as well, which was on purpose? More on that in a moment. 

As a piece of art it's pretty good. It's weird (not weird enough though, in my opinion), and very alien. It's so alien that nothing makes sense and it's almost [i]alienating[/i], which I still can't decide if that is good or bad. Clearly the alien nature of the game is the point, but the alien nature of everything makes it a difficult experience to interact with, and I think they should have leaned into that far more. Ditch the combat and traditional puzzles and have the experience be all about trial and error figuring out how to navigate a totally alien environment. I think that would have made an amazing experience.

Additional thoughts: clearly a lot of effort when into this game. Near the end of the game when you are [spoiler]using the baby crusher to make the red baby juice, and you crush three babies, each crushing animation is unique! That's great! I love that detail.[/spoiler] But in other aspects there was not nearly as much regard, like when you shoot your gun you don't actually pull the trigger! There is no animation for pulling the trigger. And don't tell me the gun is shot via some other interaction like a neural link or whatever, because if that was the case then there should not have been a trigger on the gun in the first place. Just another small example why there should have been zero combat.

Lastly, there is penis in the game one time, and it does involve a penis sucking device. It's great. I love it. H.R. Giger would surely be proud. However! It is only one time. There should have been more. Legit, a lot of panel triggers involve sticking individual fingers into holes to activate elevators and things. Should have just been penis holes triggered by penis insertion. That would have been rad.

review_text:
I regret giving this a negative review because I really fell in love with KCD1. This game is nothing like its predecessor. It is fary too easy even with hardcore mode. Let me tell you (spoiler alert)

After some prologue I started the story nearly naked and was wondering like this trying to get some money and buy basic clothing, that is until an hour later I realized that I have full set of light armor in my backpack. So I lost an hour for nothing instead of just gearing up and moving on (maybe the armor came with DLC, but still, really?).

I was wondering how could I start earning some money, so I went to blacksmith as the main story suggested. He taught me how to make a horseshoe, so I crafted 4 of them and sold them for about 20 Groschen. It took me maybe 20 minutes to do. I was happy with the earned money until I realized that collecting random, widely available herb for 3 minutes will get me 300 Groschen immediately. After that crafting the horseshoes felt like a massive time loss (and crafting is a really fun minigame, REALLY, but why would I do this?! pointless).

The game spams you with massive written tutorial pages, that gives you a headache if you want to read and memorize it all. I played KCD1 so, who cares, I skip it. For the first couple of hours I forgot that I need to spend my experience points (only because there was no challenge at all so why would I wonder how to upgrade anything). So, I had about 20 point to spend, but despite that the game was still way too easy (in hardcore mode).

Fighting 5 wolves with an axe and shield is not a problem at all, whatever your level or if you actually know how to fight. Just click the damn thing. Fighting 3 opponents also not a big deal (in the first hours of gameplay). Parrying and counterattack? Not a problem, the game, also in hardcore, displays a green shield in your face for more than a second, to make sure you won't fail it. In KCD1 a 1v3 fight was nearly impossible to win and this was good, because it was realistic. WTF happened? I won't complain about the bow, because in KCD1 it was too difficult so I get that making it easier makes sense.

From a game in which falling off a staircase forced you to rest for 2 days to a game where your biggest problem is repairing your shoes - unless you quickly figure out that you can sell random weed for a ton of a cash.

Story is not even nearly as engaging as KCD1. I only listen to dialogues because I am Polish and I play the game with Czech audio and it is fun for me, but the game doesn't make me interested in what's being said, so I just listen to words and that gives me a tiny bit of joy from this game.

I loved how fight was difficult in KCD1 and how you had to make every move count. I understand that it felt too difficult for some, but man, did you really had to make it available for a 5 year old? I feel really disappointed, I don't know how this game gets such a good score.

Also, you have 12 (i guess) in-game days to finish the game and I'm really not into the time-limited type of games.

Don't know what I expected since I really don't like Russian classics with its suffering stuff. Good thing I got my refund.

review_text:
It's a pretty serious VR title and I love to see stuff like this being developed for VR, but unfortunately I cannot recommend this game at this moment. 

Good stuff:
 - nice graphics, characters and voice acting
 - okay-ish gunplay (far from Pavlov or H3VR, but it's "fine")
 - lots of comfort options
 - cross-platform play brings playerbase to party with

Bad stuff:
 - poor performance (uncomfortable on my 2060S+Index with low graphics settings, which also makes the graphics quest1-level ugly)
 - very few levels, you can "finish" the game in a few hours, and they are all very similar, because...
 - no variety in enemies or tasks (just walk between checkpoints killing same zombie hordes with occasional large "elite" zombie, press a button or two sometimes)
 - soulless grind for the gun upgrades for no reason, unfun shooting without upgrades (the recoil is pretty insane)
 - no character selection or customization

Still, the game has potential, let's see what it evolves into with updates.

Despot's Game: Dystopian Army Builder is another solid game published by Tinybuild, and developed by Konfa Games who also made Despotism 3k.

In this game you command an army of puny red humans and go from room to room and biome to biome fighting groups of enemies like robots and mutants. As you clear rooms, you earn tokens to buy more humans to replace fallen ones, as well as mutations, weapons, and whatnot. There are also some management parts like your humans needing food sustenance to perform and fight to their optimal ability. As you move around rooms the amount of food is consumed, so more is required to be bought with the tokens earned. Also, more troops mean more food being consumed, and fewer troops mean less fighting power. So, managing your army and tokens is a key part of the game. More people and equipment can be bought and assigned to, like buy a few troops and some shields, rings, and swords etc. The fighting sequences are fun to watch as you arrange them in certain orders manually or have them auto-assigned. When you play the fight button, watch as they charge and fight the enemies which is quite satisfying. Overall, it is quite a tactical game as build your army and fight hordes of enemies.

The pixel art visuals are great to look at as someone who loves pixel art, with colour palette being used well with the dark kind of tone for the background and characters. The vast array of enemies does also keep the game fresh, and it is fun to watch them being taken down. The teeny red humans themselves are cute to observe, especially when there are plenty of them and when the screen is zoomed in for a closer view. Music is another solid point with catchy robotic and groovy tunes playing as you play the game.

Price of the game is rather fair for what it has to offer. It can easily be played for hours are there are several difficulties and classes to choose from when unlocked. Having played it so far, it has been a smooth and fun experience so that is another positive. The game is currently in early access and more content will be added to improve the game throughout the phase. Overall, it is a very enjoyable roguelike game that is most definitely worth taking note of.

review_text:
Some good things about it, the space combat is great at the right times. I really feel immersed in the startrek world when I log on and get into some nice good ol space combat! The space combat really is the magnum opus of the game. Also this game runs on a very good F2P model. 

Now, onto the shitty part of the game. Lets get into the story/lore. This is for the regular starfleet line, where you work with Tuvoc and the old VOY crew for a good portion of the story. The first bit is nice, you fight some romulans, klingons, everythings coherent. Then you get later on, to the iconians. The Iconians really just ruin everything. They are presented as all powerful beings, yet need to use pawn races to get shit done. Why can't they just wave their hand and kill all the leaders. They had a chance to kill the main character, AKA you. When you kill that one Iconion on the flagship, they have a chance to kill you, but they don't, because.... reasons?  On top of that, the Heralds and Iconions don't really seem to be advanced, they seem to just have magic. They literally use staffs that shoot shit at you, and there are these random swirls that show up and explode and it all just looks like magic. I feel like I'm playing some lord of the rings shit mixed in with people with phasers and star trek uniforms. They can also spawn in these Solar gateways, which are just complete bullshit. All of the AI seem to agro on just you, which is annoying and unimmersive. I wish the Iconians, instead of being arbitarily powerful, instead be weak, almost defenseless creatures, that use these other races to do their bidding. Their weapon wouldn't be their bullshit magic. It'd be their brains, so they can manipulate other creatures to fight for them  over the centuries. But no, that would require a good storyline, and good lore. They are just overall really terrible villians. 

This leads into a bigger issue, the ground combat. The ground combat is just ass... it's awful. It's so bad. There are entire portions of the game, that are primarily ground combat. I almost called it quits when I was on the new romulus level. Ground combat could be good! Your away team people use little gadgets, like mobile shields, or healing node things. They can even spawn little turrets. Tac officers have grenades, and other cool abilities. However, this is just negated by the ass gunplay, terrible AI, and buggy gameplay. 

Bugs. The Bugs are not really a bug anymore, but they are features. Triggers fail to activate, so you sometimes have to just restart ENTIRE MISSIONS! I had to spend 2 hours on just 1 fucking mission being something failed to trigger.  This game is a buggy mess. 

In conclusion, this game could be good, but it simply is not. The story is bad, the gameplay is bad, the bugs are everywhere. I get why some startrek fans adore this game, but as a startrek fan myself, this game is awful. It's not worth your time, it's just fucking awful. The plot, gameplay, bugs. All are bad.

It almost was a great game but there’s too no many odd/bad design choices made:

[h2] Gameplay 6/10 [/h2]

Gunplay feels very sluggish (suffers from consolitus) and feels like you’re using marshmallows for ammo…
They tried to make the game a melee centric game then added long segments where melee combat is replaced with stealth killing being the only option making all the points you probably put in melee an absolute waste. The Dodging mechanic is so wonky it just makes said melee a chore.

Upgrades are so expensive you are forced to pick maybe 2 upgrade trees to follow and even then won’t get them filled until the very end of the game. Weapon design was pretty bland too.

[h2] Graphics: 8/10 [/h2]

There is good level design and atmosphere but it only really kicks in at about 5 hours. It’s very bland and generic to start with, like they weren’t sure how they wanted the game to feel/look and just made the first few levels with epic store purchases until they figured it out. Monster design was also pretty boring.

[h2] Sound: 5/10 [/h2]

I didn’t think the sound was that good (definitely not Dead space good). The monsters all sounded the same, your footsteps always sounded the same whether you’re walking on steel or mud. There is very little persistency of sound from the environments which I think is probably the most important part of a horror game, keeping you immersed.

[h2] Story/characters 3/10 [/h2] 

Story is unfortunately dull. It’s the outbreak/teamup/get-out thing we’ve seen a million times and while sticking with what works is fine, making a lesser version of that is not. The characters are not particularly likeable and you won’t really have someone to route for(or hate) which makes any story game a slog to get through. The dynamic between Dani and Jacob is especially very odd: they go from hating one another to being concerned about one another back to hating one another again with no explanations. It just bad character writing. And the main bad guys are Boring As Fk….  

This could have been a great game but something went wrong. Perhaps it was the mistake to try make this a Dead space clone (it could exist in the same universe it’s so similar) and the melee combat was a good idea but fumbled. But the story was very sucky and as a result the characters were sucky too. You can’t have sucky characters in a single player survivor game. Doesn’t work

The Dead Space remake is fantastic. Go play that. You want the best sci fi horror survivor around, that’s the one to try. If you’re bored, try this on sale I guess…

review_text:
+ Strong points:

- A successful and oppressive retro-futuristic atmosphere
- Methodical gameplay
- Inventory and crafting that truly structure the experience
- Good progression
- Mastery of horror tropes: silence, tension, vulnerability
- Outstanding sound design

- Weak points:

- Good ideas but often too formulaic execution
- Unmemorable bosses and sometimes frustrating fights
- No Polish voice acting

Summary: It's no small feat to tackle the theme of time in a work, whether literary, cinematic, or (in this case) video game.
Let's be clear from the start: yes, Cronos is clearly influenced by other works. From Dead Space and Bioshock to Silent Hill and even Resident Evil, the inspirations are obvious.
But the game doesn't rely solely on its predecessors. It's a true melting pot of the best ideas from the genre's masters. Nevertheless, the game manages to forge its own path and offers an interesting perspective.
Cronos certainly doesn't reinvent the wheel, but playing it is truly enjoyable. You want to know what happened to our good old planet, what the real cause of all this mess is, and ultimately understand what we're really doing here.
As you'll have gathered, the story is easy to follow, even if it's sometimes nebulous or even cryptic.
The atmosphere is masterfully crafted: It's oppressively heavy, almost suffocating. The environment, while linear, manages to be quite intricate.
The bestiary maintains constant pressure throughout the adventure and will not forgive any mistakes. This is largely thanks to an old-school, yet no less interesting, inventory system. You'll sometimes have to replay a section several times to complete it optimally.
In short, Cronos: The New Dawn is not a game for everyone. If you enjoy challenging survival horror, where counting your ammo and fleeing from confrontations are central to the experience, then yes, you'll find it to your liking! Otherwise, frustration is likely to set in quickly and leave a bitter taste...
Good luck to the brave souls who dare to try it.

" Such is our calling "

15/20
