review_text:
Honestly... I really tried.
I want to like this game. the beautiful visuals, the expansive list of things to do and to focus on, great character creation and amazing battles... I can describe the game in only one single word... CHAOTIC.

From the 30 difficult to follow menu's, the 60 different materials and currencies, the random reward claims spread everywhere, the terrible texts to follow instructions and tutorials to the buggy and overcomplicated ways of the multiplayer. This game for me is one big mental mess. After every mission or task that I finish, I need 10 min to scour through every menu to claim all random (and kind of insignificant) items for some random objective I completed. Or look through the multiple lists of daily/weekly tasks I still need to complete. Or which currency I have enough of now to use in one of the 20 shops. If you focus on a single mission (especially the main story I really like), it is fine but the moment you look in the open world I'm just bombarded with all that $h!t.

For the typical MMO gamer this is great, they love all the meaningless just do it stuff. I just can't stand it. I do like the Idea of the multiplayer side. I tried to be a support healer. I find it interesting to help other people with their injuries on travel. But when you know EVERYBODY can practically do it, And trying to find/join someone to actually do it (you can request/offer help by list, but both need to be in online mode, Joining sometimes you need to add to friends? and the difficulty is unknown (the mastery is not always correct)) I takes away the good feel it should give you.
And if you joined multiplayer to help people or just interact, You're locked out of all the quests you have because you need to do those in single player. I once had a beggar mission, went to a beggar spot and saw 20 people standing around not knowing what to do and just keep emoting. The multiplayer feels broken.

This game had great potential and I'm sure for a lot of people it is. But I found my self forcing me to like it and I realized I just don't. I don't even want to talk about the pay-walls. Yes it is cosmetic only. But I get bombarded with them constantly reminding me of the things I will never participate in. It just sucks.
It reminds me of those YouTube vids I now see everyday: "This game will change the industry. The AAA industry doesn't want you to play this. This game will change the future of game-making. Where winds meet is a wake up call." NO, it doesn't. I'm always disgusted with these garbage clickbaits. I've seen these over the last years and nothing has changed. It's just more of the same and this game is no exception.

Just git gud? Just throw your money? Stop crying you baby? It will be better after 100 hours? NO! I'm done. I already had my doubts when I saw it was "Free-to-play" Things could be so much better, but to me it just isn't. 5/10

(I have the same fear for ANANTA. If done right it will make it for me the best game I can spend months in just like I thought here. But free-to-play, multiplayer, gacha... I'm afraid).

Good ideas - subpar execution, but considering how very few games in this genre we have - you will still play it.

review_text:
This game has a unique Save game feature. If you die, you are punished by getting a debuff. You can't remove that debuff. If you reload your old save, that save will have that debuff. All of your saves will have that debuff. 

That is amazing and not seen before. However there's some other major issues with the game that prevent people from experiencing that save system and prevent the idea from being added to other games.

There is no Save & Quit. There is no Save & Quit. What is that? There's no harm in adding Save & Quit. It only benefits the experience of the gamer.

You can't quick save. You save at various undisclosed points in the game. You discover these, seemingly randomly, by inspecting every item in every house. 

That's too punishing. No Save & Quit. Going to miss an opportunity to save. I die i get a debuff and have to reload a save from possibly 60 minutes ago.

The save games use GMT to list the time they were saved. Not a big deal
There is no Cloud Saves. THAT is a big deal. Pathologic 1 has cloud saves.

Beyond saving the game. The performance of this game has to be one of the worst I've ever seen in recent years. Even on a 4080 and 7900x. I have to set graphics quality to minimum to stay above 60fps most of the time. The game is poorly made. I don't know why so many 3D games use Unity when Unreal has always been the better of the two for 3D. The small added cost of the engine is worth it and always has been worth it. Heck Unity doesn't even provide customer service or properly support their engine, but Unreal does. You get what you pay for and the product here with Pathologic shows they didn't put the extra work needed as they cut costs on the engine by using Unity and cut costs by not giving enough time to create their engine.

I'm seeing the same stories in this game as found in the first game. Like the burning of the person at the stake, then the people watching. As they walk away they all say 1 by 1 they should've done something to stop it. In Pathologic 1 I murdered all of them for murdering this innocent person. In Pathologic 2 I can't do that as the save system prevents trying it, but more so I have zero rep and can't trade and need to trade to get food to survive. It makes me more passive and a watcher of the story created by the devs.

A unique save system, poorly designed and a badly implemented game. I feel Pathologic 1 is the better game, however graphically Pathologic 1 for sure shows its age and this one is easier to play only for that reason.

This game has zero voice acting. You're reading what everyone says. They do talk, so there is voice acting, but it's random words it seems, so it's just voices, no acting.

Ultimately the lack of Save & Quit is the #1 and only reason I can't recommend this game.
If there's a way to mod Pathologic 1 to make it look modern, I'd for sure recommend that.

I really wanted to try and like this, but I just can't. I don't understand all of the positive reviews on here saying how great the story is, and how fun the combat is. I found myself BEGGING for a skip dialog button, because I cannot STAND how slow the voice acting is. It is intentionally delayed and fragmented into sentences that make me want to rip my ears off. I want to try and enjoy the story, but I end up skipping half of the cutscenes because of the whiny, boring dialog. 

The combat boils down to A A A A A A. . . A A A A A  RB A, A A A A A A , RB A, AAAAAAAAA. I actually fell asleep at one point at my desk. 

The HAND HOLDING! My god. Here's your objective. Better not forget your objective. Go to the marker for the objective. I'll bet I need X of this objective. I should buy X of this item for this objective. 

The pacing is just, bizarre and annoying. You finish a quest, then it forces you to log out of the world to check your mail, only to log back into the world, to do another 15 minute quest. Then you must log back out of the world, so you can check that mail, or forum post, or whatever, then log back in to progress the story. I'm sorry bout after the 15th time of this, I'm over it. 

The world looks like garbage. The landscapes are uninspired. You run copy pastes of the same dungeons and/or fields over and over and over again that consist of the same exact tile sets. I feel like I'm playing a PS1 game. 

Just don't waste your time. Unless you REALLY like the tropey anime stuff with shitty voice acting, boring combat, and mundane, repetitive "quests", find a different game. I know I am.

review_text:
At best I would say the game is disappointing. It was an ok shooter, but there's nothing really special about it. Your morality is decided by whether or not you think killing kids is cool, it lacks any depth. The endings are you being a power hungry psychopath or raising a family. As someone who pretty much hates kids these were both pretty bad endings.

 You also get way more rewards for saving the kids, which is counter intuitive since it acts like you get more from killing, but you quickly find you have more adam than you'll ever need and the saved kids actually give more adam in the end and bullets to boot, which are way more valuable. The weapons are all different from each other, but I thought the starting revolver was the best, which made weapon progression a joke. Also there is 0 penalty for dying so you can just throw your mangled corpse at obstacles over and over again until you finally gun everyone down. I feel like a save and load system would have fit the game better. It's what i did any time I died. I played on the hardest difficulty and I beat the game in 12 hours. I don't expect dark souls, but some challenge would have been nice.

*SPOILER ALERT* 

Andrew Ryan not being the main villain was a good twist, but he never really worked as a villain. He's supposed to be a "evil" capitalist, but I never saw it. He builds a park and charges people admittance in what is an isolationist capitalist utopia these people chose to go to. This is immoral how? He burned down a forrest the government tried to steal from him. Honestly, I feel like this is commendable not evil. It kinda works because he's not the real villain, but since he is who you are fighting for 90% of the game it made me rather unenthused about accomplishing any task.

review_text:
Oof, Lost Ruins is a Game alright.
But in my opinion not a good one.
This Game is kind of a Metroidvania Light with (badly implemented) Souls and "Survival" Elements and it just isn't fun, actually it is a frustrating mess.
I can forgive that a little bit because after seeing the Credits, I think only 2 people really worked on it (disregarding the Localization Teams here) but if a Game is bad, it's bad.

So the first thing you will notice is the extremely annoying sound the "Character Talk Box" makes. This is the first impression. Then you will notice good Pixel Art. It is just that, good, not the best ever but it kinda has it's own chunky style.

The next thing I personally noticed was extremely annoying. I played with a Gamepad, but when I switched to my Keyboard (for opening the Steam Overlay or for going to Desktop) the displayed controls in Game would switch constantly (!) between Gamepad and Keyboard and the only solution is to restart the Game and also: NEVER touch your Keyboard while playing.
Second thing I disliked (I at first thought the Game was buggy) was when an Achievement Notification would pop up but basically it only tells you, that you have fulfilled one step to get the full Achievement. Found it kind of annoying and also useless.

The Music was also kind of meh. More bad than good. More annoying than hooking me. (You see where this is going? There is so much ANNOYING stuff here and that's not all, the worst things I will tell you about next.)

I think this Game does not know what it wants to be, this is a perfect example of an identity crisis. 

- The Game has Souls Elements with slow and "deliberate" combat but it just feels clunky as hell. The Controls don't feel good. Then there are the enemies. Oh boy is this one frustrating Game. Normal enemies can be a pain to kill. I played most of the Game with a Zweihänder (yes, you write it like that) and the enemies are just unfair. The Zweihänder is VERY slow and in the time you attack, most enemies still have longer reach than you and can SPAM their attacks like CRAZY without ever stopping. Of course you are free to use other Weapons/Ranged Weapons/Spells, but everything feels kind of bad here.
Then there are the bosses which are laughably easy. Every Boss has 2-3 Phases (Normal Phase, Big B**b Phase and sometimes a "funny" Phase were you can just kill them easily) and most of them have only 3-4 Attack Patterns which are extremely easy to counter. Also they take a ton of Damage and are down real quick.

- Then there is the Metroidvania Element but the Game fails here as well. There is no real progression (apart from getting a LITTLE more health or getting new Items for new "Builds") here. No Double Jumps, no Dashes, no nothing. The Level Design is also extremely BORING and lazy. There are almost NO secrets to find and no branching paths and backtracking is also rarely if not ever needed. Basically you start on the left side, then go right aaaaall the way, then go up after a boss, go left aaaall the way, go up, go right and so on. This is the basic design here with VERY few variations (sometimes you go down also...).
Platforming when it happens: Also bad. Either you are in a very small space and bump your head or you are outside and jump on a few platforms, it's not really needed here but also not very well implemented.

I read some of the positive and some of the negative reviews on here and I actually agree with most of the negative reviews. 
Another thing: Savepoints and Checkpoints don't restore your health/mana, you have to consume items for that or just play like I did with a ton of regen-Gear.

Storywise it's stupid. So is the dialogue. Just wow, what is that even? Can't and don't want to describe this.
(And what's with all the big b**bs on the bosses?)

Well, my first playthrough took 5.9 hours, only got 12/40 Achievements. In good Games/Metroidvanias/Soulslikes I would want to jump back in to get more Achievements and to see a different ending. Not here. I am just glad it is over. Especially because for some Achievements you have to torture yourself through the whole Game again, grind/farm a lot and/or play different Game Modes.
I literally have 0 interest in that.

So yeah, if you are a REALLY REALLY big fan of Metroidvanias/Souls-Adjacent Games and you need to play everything, MAYBE you will get a kick out of this, for everyone else who just wants a good Game: Stay Away!

review_text: Honestly I was a bit disappointed with this game. It sounded really exciting, a sort of Wuxia themed combination of souls-like combat, RPG elements, MMO elements, and more. For context, I'm someone who loves souls-like games, and I've read Wuxia novels since I was in middle school, so it seemed perfect for me. The skeleton of a good game is definitely present, but I think its muddled by many small issues, which when together, strip a lot of the enjoyability of the game for me. Starting with the translations, while they weren't horrible, at times they definitely felt awkward in some spots of the game, along with some very odd voice acting quality. Some of the characters had good voice acting, some had none, some had extremely obvious AI voices that sounded terrible, sometimes random lines would have no voiceover, while later lines in the same dialogue would have a voiceover. It just feels very messy and rushed. On the topic of AI, some of the NPC's in this game are AI powered, meaning they have AI voiceovers, and you can chat to an AI chatbot acting like the character. Its an interesting idea, but I think the execution in the end is pretty poor. The AI has no integration with the game environment besides attacking you if you're too rude to them, so it can be pretty immersion breaking when they mention taking certain actions which they can't actually do in game. It just ends up feeling lazy to me, like they couldn't be bothered to create dialogue for some of the less important characters around the world or actually voice act them out. Moving on, the menus are quite convoluted in this game. After a while you can mostly understand what to do, but it certainly doesn't make it easy to enjoy the game, with many UI elements and stats having next to no explanation of what they actually do. I think the last straw for me was some of the minigames around the map. For example, Gift of Gab is genuinely one of the most awful things I've seen in a game. It's a debate minigame where you get inspiration, and can then use that inspiration to play cards that "do damage" to the opponents psyche, while they do the same. Each one of the cards do different things, and there are some more mechanics that I won't go in detail about. It sounds nice on the surface, but during the tutorial for it, the game just starts playing in the background, so you can't really read anything, and honestly, you can't even read anything anyway. The game moves so quickly you genuinely cannot even read the cards. Most people I've seen just button mash, spamming cards until they win or lose. Its actually braindead design. In the end, the game just comes off as sloppy to me, which is a shame, because the core aspects of the game are quite good. The combat feels nice, the world is fun to explore, and there are some cool bosses, but ultimately I think whether you'll like this game or not comes down to how much of the small flaws you can tolerate.

review_text:
Play for OG PSO2 if you're at all curious about what happened to the franchise all those years it was kept in Japan. I think OG was better around ep2-3 (although I LOVE summoner, which came with ep4) and although what's left in the wake of NGS feels empty due to there being so few people around and the game being clearly kept alive by a skeleton crew, there's still a lot to enjoy.

As for New Genesis, the new face of PSO2... It's a big meh. The open world did absolutely nothing to improve what PSO started over 20 years ago. In fact, it introduced a plethora of issues, such as skill points being tied to BOTW-esque trials, loot feeling inconsequential, and all classes lacking any identity. The latter might be the worst bit considering how PSO (and even PSU) managed to cultivate the identity of its classes up until later in PSO2's life cycle. And no, the open-world is not even remotely fun to explore. It's fun to traverse, but there's nothing about it that justifies its existence.

All in all, NGS is an absurdly dumbed down game that focuses primarily on cosmetics rather than the loot rush that made this franchise special for 20 years. It's sad that SEGA decided to chase industry trends instead of sticking to what makes PSO what it is, but alas. NGS has its fans exactly because it's a dumbed down game with a sizable, bland open world, and we all know how well those do even though everyone has something negative to say about them. It was fun, Phantasy Star. I'll see you if they decide to remaster the Japan-only PS Nova.

review_text:
Cronos is the ultimate game to hold you over until RE9. This is genuinely an amazing new IP in the survival horror scene. This game borrows a lot of ideas and aesthetics from games like Resident Evil, Dead Space, Silent Hill, SOMA, and more. Despite this, the game absolutely succeeds at feeling fresh and original. I have had my doubts about Bloober Team, as they have mostly worked on "walking sims" in the past. But they really delivered with an amazing remake of Silent Hill 2.

Cronos combines Bloober Team's extensive history making atmospheric walking sims with their newly found ability to create a competent entry in the survival horror pantheon. This is a very impressive and major accomplishment for a AA studio and it should be supported. I absolutely want a sequel.

Biggest criticism: Not enough enemy variety. But this one is more about the story and atmosphere, IMO/

review_text:
This is a very mixed review.

This game has atrocious onboarding and UI.  It loves to break conventions and does a terrible job of making it clear to players what is happening and why.

Despite this, the unique genre combo is quite enjoyable.  City builders can feel aimless, but having to tower defend provides a purpose for expansion.  The introduction of god powers means that you always have some action that you could be taking to improve your game.  The end result is a surprisingly addictive game that's quite fun for ~40 hours if you can get past the initial roadblocks.

Unfortunately, in the late game, the flaws in this unique combo start to show.  Much of the game is structured as a god game where you're not supposed to have insight into hard numbers or mechanics.  This is fine until you realize that enemy difficulty scales infinitely (practically).  When you know you're guaranteed to lose, the only fun is in seeing how far you can get - yet the game doesn't track records and optimizing runs is frustrating when every mechanic is opaque.  The game feels incongruous to me; I think it would be vastly improved if it picked a side between casual god game and deadly tower defense.

Ultimately, if you can accept poor UI and can handle intermittent frustration, this game has a solid amount of fun to offer.  Just don't expect the same amount of depth and replayability as many other city builders.

review_text:
Scorn. 
How did i even get into this?

I never really played any horror games, but i decided to try the genre. I didn't really know what to pick up, then i remembered. If i'm trying out a horror game, let it be the most gruesome i have heard of. Let it be Scorn.

The game was very strange, very alien compared to what i am used to. I didn't know who is was playing with, what i had to do, or why i had to do it. It was strange but very refreshing and rewarding that i figured the stuff out.

Many players say that the combat system is goofy. I would say that it is clumsy, but it makes it immersive. Imagine you had to fight in such conditions with such strange weapons, i came to like it, even though it would have benefited from the devs putting a little more work into it.

The game's atmosphere is the heaviest, darkest that i experienced. I almost drowned in it every time i played. I can only describe it with a Slayer quote: "You wish you were in hell"

Spoilers: [spoiler] Throughout the game i was looking at the keybinds. Nearing the end (i was suspecting it was the end due to the monumental size of the city, and how much time i spent playing the game, having heard that it is quite short.) i only had 3 weapons, and there was room for 4. I suspected a boss fight and i was dreading it, thinking "What kind of monstrosity can they add as a boss into such a game!?". In the end i was able to defeat the guy but i struggled with it. [/spoiler]

I hated the game while playing. Only after completeing it and having time to piece it together in my head did i start to love it.

Spoilers: [spoiler] I absolutely love the the following theory (i read it online but this is my own summary of the theory): The world of Scorn was ruined by war. The game is essentially a test that humans born have to complete to prove themselves. To prove that they have the intelligence to complete the puzzles, can endure such struggles as having their bodies practically ripped apart, not giving up, and that they can manage to ascend at the final portal, to join the rest of the humans in the new world. In the new world, where only the strongest are accepted into. [/spoiler]

I really do recommend the game. It was such a strange experience, that i think i won't really be able to play anything like Scorn again because it was so extremely unique. Some parts of the game may feel a 'little short' and 'feel like wasted potential' due to the developers having some troubles finishing the game. But i think the game as a whole feels 'mostly complete'

So if anyone is thinking about trying it, give it a go. Please don't give up at the first puzzle, it will be worth it to complete, i promise! Also, try to not look up any help online as it may spoil some parts of the game.
Thanks for reading my review!

review_text:
IF you are into realism, and I mean that seriously, then this completely open world recreation of medieval times is for you. NOTE: I mean realism. You want a potion, you have to read the recipe, prep the ingredients, make the potion, then decant it. Craft a sword? OK, first you take a bar of steel and heat it up. So far I am 11 hours into this and I love this game.

All the adorableness of the art of the game is really deceptive for all that this game provides. You can be the grumpy farmer that makes no friends. Want that nice looking fisherman as your husband? He's married? So sad, time to bake his wife a special cake.. aww... sorry to hear of her passing, marry me? Admittedly, I was sad I insulted someone then the next day they died from illness. The gameplay is easy and so relaxing, and they support and encourage the modding community. Right now its only cosmetics but they intend to allow more. 

My *only* gripe of the game is how fast things spoil. I get a quest to catch fish, the quests has a time limit of a week and the fish they want is hard to get.. your fish will spoil before getting all of the requested fish. Crops spoil too fast to get all the ingredients. There *is* an ice box but it costs a lot of metal to get and you have to buy the metal because you can't smelt the small amount of metal you get from mining. There is the option to turn off the spoil time, but I feel like that takes away from the game. What I'd like to see them add is more than just "On/Off" but "Spoil On, Longer Spoil Timer, Off" so there is a middle ground. Right now I turned spoiling off until I can afford to try the ice box. 

Honestly, I am not sure if this game is Early Access or not, it doesn't advertise it on Steam, but it feels like Early Access, but even still, I feel like I am getting a very nice complete gameplay. 

Right now I give the game a 9/10... only because I want more options on the sliding bar. I don't mind the incomplete game because they are still working on it. Other than that, its very different from all my other farming games that I have played, and I have been playing since OG Harvest Moon. I enjoy the idea of crops and food spoiling (just not as fast), I love you don't have to be the cheery helpful farmer, that there is plague and deception. Its fantastic.

review_text:
It's not a bad game, but it could be a much better game.

At it's heart, it's a little town sim, which is cute enough on its own, but to make things a bit more interesting your town gets regularly attacked by monsters. These monsters follow "tower defense" logic where they don't attack walls and take the shortest route to anything else they can break, so your mission is to build a maze of some complexity, plop down some towers, and behind said maze nurture a society that can upgrade and maintain it.

This is a pretty great concept, but for some reason they thought you'd be up for playing the exact same game like 20-something times. Once you've gotten a self-sustaining society behind the maze, and figured out which towers are pointless(bow, phantom dart and any of the bullet ones, really. Why would I ever build a tower that couldn't shoot over walls?), you've won. So really the only challenge is whether you correctly guess the shortest route and defend that within the first few days, and then you've pretty much won.

Hell, half the citizens' basic needs, like social interaction, you don't even notice because just by existing they satisfy those. Things are automated enough that your only real active control of the world is where to put down buildings, but the AI automation isn't interesting enough to cough up any scenarios as a result(your villagers, for instance, have no personalities, specializations, etc. and only two monsters have abilities beyond "walk towards thing, hit thing.").

It feels like an early access game that slipped through and got released early, because there's just a lack of content and depth.

Not to mention pretty goddamn lackluster tutorializing, it took me until my second year(in-game, not real-time) to figure out that what looked like a bit of UI fancy bordering under the available spells was actually a menu allowing access to more spells.

You can complete challenges to unlock stuff, but they're literally all just "have a +% to do thing in game." None of them change up the gameplay experience or open new options.

There are also some weird AI issues, like how you can organize all village constructor tasks in priorities... except for clearing terrain, which they'll always obsessively do first.

Even just some minor things, like being able to waypoint locations or patrol routes for your rangers and defensive golems would have added a bit of stuff to do. Why does the Medic even exist? I don't think I ever had a villager get injured outside of random weather events, but then they just self-bandaged or went to chill at home for a few seconds and were right as rain. You can't manually order villagers to slaughter livestock, so it's up to the vagaries of the AI whether an animal pen generates any food or not. You can't focus on acquiring iron or gold for gear/trading, respectively, since they're all just random drops from mining generic rock. Storage is completely boned, all storage is available in the same amounts, which means that for relatively rare things, like tools and weapons, you'll never need specialized storage because your stock buildings have enough spare storage for all of it. While for super-common things like rocks, wood and food, you'll always be starved for storage and the buildable storage buildings are almost a waste of your time because they don't give *enough* extra space.

Water seems like an afterthought of a feature, terrain-wise, since it's all hip-deep and wadable, being just a movement speed modifier, and you can effortlessly pave it over. So you can't, for instance, spice things up with stuff like a moat.

I can't really recommend this game, because it could be so much better, and it feels like the dev(s) just didn't want to bother going that last stretch.

It was a 7/10 until the final boss, but that solidified this game as a 6, encapsulating everything wrong with the game.

- You basically have zero movement speed and there's no dodge mechanic so you just have to take every melee hit from the boss and he fully knocks you down each time -  you will find yourself clench your fists witnessing this happen over and over with no counterplay.
- zero stagger from boss even on charged shots on a shotgun? and fully upgraded damage..
- teleports everywhere so running is meaningless - most times teleporting in front of your face guaranteeing you get knocked to the dirt.

apart from that here's the rest of the issues

- can't skip majority of cutscenes and the voice acting / animations / lore are just genuinely boring that you'll be in pain watching these. Alt tabbing also pauses the game so you can't ignore it, wtf?
- lore that should be told through INTERESTING cutscenes or in-game events told through a myriad of endless letters and voiceboxes. I literally just interacted with letters and immediately pressed esc it got so old.
- first pistol and shotgun that charge are the best weapons in the game until a final 3 burst carbine, you'll use nothing else as why would you use full auto weapons in a resource management game in which ammo is relatively scarce. Final carbine also can't be upgraded fully if desired as it comes too late - poor foresight by devs. Just a general lack of interesting or diverse weaponry. The other main weapons are just another shotgun and pistol. Very lame. Other weapons not even worth speaking of. 
- Most key items e.g keys will auto discard after use, but the boltcutters you will have for pretty much the entire game as you constantly wonder to yourself if you missed a door earlier in the game as it wont disappear, you'll still be required to use it at the end of the game, and it takes up an inventory spot which is already very limited.
- Cores just aren't ample enough, I think I only fully upgraded inventory slots, got half of the life upgrades and all the torch upgrades, there just needs to be more.
- Bosses we're rather dull, and were even repeated. 
- Enemy variation lacking severely. Like maybe 4-5?? only variations is they have some spikes?? This mechanic also wasn't really ever explained, if they have a spiked head does that mean they are immune to shots on the head completely? just a percentage damage reduction? it's never quite clear.
-female protagonist, don't think I need to elaborate but i will. the majority of us are male, and therefore want to play as one. Just think about the disparity of males that will play this compared to female, why give the majority of your playerbase an inferior experience? From what I saw there was no particular reason to make the player female either, if there was a solid reason then perhaps i'd understand.
-game runs like dirt, but this is bloober team after all, I distinctly remember refunding SH2 because of their ineptitude at performance. Immersion can't exist when you are dropping every 10 seconds. If you purchase this game then understand this will be the experience.
-non charged shots have no purpose, ammo is scarce and charged shots simply deal more damage. Why ever use a non-charged shot? I think I only used non-charged shots on the last boss because the window to hit him is so limited.
-The animation for torch was lame, just give us a molotov or something.
-Pyre was useless and upgrades for it were lame
-Entering a room littered with explosive canisters makes things too predictable.
-I always felt inventory was so limited I was never allowed to carry healing items with me, the only time I did that was for the final two bosses
-The wall crawler enemies that spit green ooze probably have too much health
-frequent enemies smashing through doors that only trigger on your approach, forcing you to take damage with no counter play, bullshit.
-no map
-no fov slider

if combat was more fun with diverse weapons, and your character didn't have glue on her boots maybe I would recommend, but not as is, it's so mid. With that said, there's no little games in 2025 that can meet the minimum bar of looking interesting enough to even consider buying that you'll probably give in like I did.

review_text:
At first glance, Just Cause 4 is stunningly beautiful and undeniably fun. The massive open world, filled with lush landscapes and explosive possibilities, promises endless hours of entertainment. The game's signature over-the-top action and creative use of the grappling hook initially deliver an exhilarating experience.

However, this potential quickly unravels due to one glaring flaw: the puzzles. The sheer volume of puzzles, combined with the lack of meaningful hints or guidance, makes progression a frustrating ordeal. The game often throws you into complex scenarios with no explanation, leaving you to fumble around until something works. This lack of clarity turns what should be a rewarding experience into a tedious chore.

Adding to the frustration is the overwhelming number of key controls. With so many functions mapped to different buttons, the game becomes needlessly complicated, especially for new players. Instead of feeling like a capable action hero, you're left wrestling with the controls in critical moments.

Ultimately, Just Cause 4 sabotages itself. What could have been an enjoyable, action-packed adventure is marred by poor design choices that prioritize complexity over fun. It's a shame, because the game's potential is undeniable—but it’s hard to appreciate when the experience is bogged down by unnecessary frustrations.

review_text:
The first mini boss fight has to be the biggest pile of trash this series has ever produced. And another game with combat that makes no sense at the start.

You're telling me that the guy who has basically been running rampant like a bulldozer can't simply take on two drunk mooks in a bar full of furniture? Oh look they have hyper armour, counter attacks, reblocks, instant grabs in the middle of your combos (good luck trying to grab them if they so much as twitch a pinkie finger). Feels like playing Yakuza 3 again.

For anyone struggling spam grab and heavy attack. About the only thing that really works.

Edit:

After playing through the Saejima chapter, boy does this game sit as a fat mid amongst the rest of the series. Inconsistent plot points, combat that goes from weirdly difficult to oh this is weirdly difficult to oh just spam this set of moves BTW some of them require you to go out of your way to access them. 

Most of the minigames are average at best, and while this is probably an improvement on 3 and 4 (Which set a low god damn bar regardless), it suffers from a consistent issue of troping where a large majority of the problems would be solved if two characters just discussed something for more than 2 seconds of insinuation about something to hold suspense.

The weird mix of minor enjoyment to a jarring snap back to the reality of what this game is leaves a lot to be desired. If one was to read a synopsis of this game they would not be missing much in life.

Edit 2: And it gets more daft after I enter chapter 3.The game takes a note out of Yakuza 4s play book and introduces a plot that makes no sense with characters that exert leverage that they don't have. If playing these in chronological order the experience just seems to be getting worse as time goes on. The plot starts to become the antithesis of what these characters were introduced to be. As a form of growth it just doesn't work in the slightest.

As I understand it the same writer was responsible for Yakuza 0 which probably has the most engaging plot of the games so far, but I personally feel as if the writing for that was restricted by what happens in the subsequent chronological games so it is forced to reign itself in a bit. It isn't often I feel myself compelled to warn people about what they are getting into but this, 3, and 4 all drop the ball that was set up for them.

review_text:
[Gifted by a friend]

No matter what I accomplish in my life, I regret that I cannot say I came up with the single greatest title for a video game ever: "Bomb Rush Cyberfunk."

A triumph! This was my introduction to the gang/graffiti/parkour platformer genre and what a way to start! So no, for reference, I have not played the *Jet Set Radio* games yet, so I can't compare this obvious spiritual successor to those. But man, what a ride!

I've had my eye on Team Reptile since *Lethal League* - a superb unique fighting/sports game. Throw in Hideki Naganuma's music and I had to play this. And yes, even if you only play for the soundtrack it might be worth your time. A compilation of electronic funk songs from an eclectic array of composers that makes the entire game just one solid continuous vibe. Add addictive platforming and tricking gameplay with collectathon elements, a genuinely perfect cel-shaded artstyle, and tight controls and the game really does exceed the sum of its relatively small development team.

If I had to nitpick, there were a few frustrating segments - particularly any time combat is involved. Combat never feels as tight or responsive as the skate controls and bosses are relatively simple and uninspired. That's really all the negatives I have for it, though.

World building and narrative were shockingly...uh...present? I don't know why I wasn't expecting much of a story, but there is one here. It's not the best story ever, but it's solid enough and even tries to pull off some ambitious twists and turns that mostly work. Rival gangs are unique and honestly hilarious. And the game knows exactly how serious it needs to be, striking a perfect balance between cyberpunk absurdity and serious stakes.

Do yourself a favor and play *Bomb Rush Cyberfunk.*

An absolutely fantastic rework of the original Pathologic experience. The gameplay retains the aspect of dispowerement and the game does not hand-hold you. You will learn to appreciate this if you do not from the start. This game is much more available to new-comers and anyone can grasp the mechanics if they persist.

However important role gameplay part plays, the story, dialogues, characters, themes, ideas and questions that the game provides is the real diamond here. A unique and priceless experience, more than saying anything specific, the game ask complex, interesting and pertinent questions, creating an atmosphere convulsive to self-reflection.

You will learn to reject typical game mechanics, you will not try to thrive, you will not expect rewards and punishments for doing 'good' and 'evil' choices. review_text:
I am extremely disappointed in this game. Boneworks is my favorite VR game, and I was looking forward to more of that with some improvements. The physics, environments, and gun selection are all a bit better (yay shotguns!), but that's where the improvements end.

The campaign is pitifully short and is not a cohesive whole like the last game, but is rather a short collection of disconnected mini-game-esque levels. There are only a couple of really good levels, and the rest range from boring and lazy to outright nauseating. The final level, which is the best one, makes it feel like the 'tutorial' is over and the real game is getting started, and then it abruptly ends after less than five minutes. The five hour campaign leaves you wanting much more, and not in a good way.

The also game leans much, MUCH too heavily into the gimmicky body-swapping mechanic. It's a cool improvement, but it's really not the game-changer it's made out to be, and it gets annoying pretty quickly when it's the only thing the game focuses on.

The significantly lacking original content is meant to be made up for with community-made mods, which is a strategy that always frustrates me: developers should make a good game first and then allow the community to add onto it, not rely on them to make the game good. I bought this game for the campaign because I loved Boneworks and I did not get what I wanted, which was a full experience. And for a game relying so heavily on mods, why is there no workshop support??

TL;DR The game is playable, but it's very short and lives up to neither the hype nor the Boneworks legacy.

review_text:
As a foreword, I'd like to point out that despite not recommending this game, that should not imply that it's bad. Before I go any further, I'll say that the biggest reason I'm not recommending this game is because its sequel - Left 4 Dead 2 - is practically a more refined version of the same product, plus more. The second big reason is because this game's community is utterly revolting. I've met my fair share of trolls, griefers, bullies and a couple other words I can't write in this review, and it genuinely defeats one of Left 4 Dead's biggest qualities: the encouragement of cooperative play. When a game designed for four-player action becomes more appealing (and relaxing) when playing offline with the bots, there is a big problem there. I could write a whole review on why I hate L4D's community so much, but I'd rather not go there. 
Let's discuss some good things about Left 4 Dead. 
Set in October 2009, the world has been engulfed by a virus known as the Green Flu, which has turned pretty much everyone into a zombie. And I don't mean the George Romero type zombie that shambles to you at a snail's pace, I mean the rabid, snarling things from 28 Days Later. As you would expect from a game with SPRINTING zombies, Left 4 Dead is a pulse-pounding ride that holds, in my opinion, some of the most addicting game-play I've ever witnessed. It's just pure fun, and extremely gory fun at that. You make your way through abandoned environments throughout Pennsylvania that have become overrun with the infected, from ghostly metropolises, small towns, all the way to the woods of the Allegheny (a real place). Much like Valve's masterpiece game series Half-Life, Left 4 Dead employs a minimalist attitude when it comes to cutscenes and talky-talky bits, making the pace of the game very easy-going, but at the sacrifice of world-building and story-telling. The four-minute introduction that plays at the start of the game is without a doubt one of my all-time favourite game cutscenes, and what's more, it mirrors the intensity of how the game actually plays out once you take control. If that isn't a good sign I don't know what is. 
All D.L.C is completely free, which is great, though I wouldn't say you'd be missing much if you skipped them. The four protagonists are incredibly well-crafted, and have great chemistry and personality. At times they can all be downright funny too, and I still laugh out loud whenever I hear their manic laughter and death-screams. 
The weapon variety is a little bland, but this isn't really a game where it would matter all that much anyway. The special infected (smokers, boomers, hunters, tanks and witches) all unite to create a fearsome opposition for your team, and are so much fun to play as in versus mode. Beware, playing in versus is easily the most toxic aspect of this game. You will most likely be kicked for simply being a better player than the enemy team. There is also a survival mode, but it's really only about as fun and inspired as it sounds. 
As with most Valve games, a very intriguing developer commentary is included, and this is always a very awesome thing that more developers need to take note of. 
So far I have described what most would call a good game, but the big issue here is that Left 4 Dead 2 literally includes all the campaigns in this game (D.L.C included), with even more stuff added on top. For this exact reason, and in the interest of your own money, I cannot recommend Left 4 Dead. If you are curious about this series, and aren't a completionist like me, just go play Left 4 Dead 2. That game isn't perfect, but it's the complete package regardless. All in all, this game is still plenty of fun standing on its own two feet, and if you're fortunate enough to have three friends to join you, (or seven for versus) you're bound to kill some serious hours slaying the undead getting to safety. Definitely play a campaign on expert difficulty for that true survivalist experience. As an experienced player, I prefer advanced over normal difficulty - it's that sweet spot for a challenge. But like I said, go with Left 4 Dead 2. This game is better off left for... ah, never mind.

I think that Kingdom: New Lands has the key to what could make Rise To Ruins shine. The Civilization series can also give some hints. In these games, in a late era of stone castles you no longer even think about basic needs, wooden shacks. IN Kingdom, your experienced peasants skill up to become knights in golden armour. In Rise To Ruins, with your empire sprawling, you still need to waste a population slot for a garbage collector. The *feel* of building from tents to cities just isn't there.

I thought this would be great after the closed betas and the network test, but I'm starting to regret my $140 AUD purchase / hyped buy in. Really, I only have two main issues with the game.

1. The community.
The first issue I have is with the community. It's the most insufferable, horrible anime game community I've ever seen. I've got pretty thick skin living in AUS, but I'm glad that there isn't an in-game chat. I can see many people (with thinner skin) being put off by the many toddlers throwing temper tantrums in-game and on the forums.
Be warned, sharty behaviour is rampant, particularly in-game. People rush through the zones, barely killing anything, and then get shirty with each other over small things, like who does the most DPS on the boss / mission overall. But what really takes the cake is a metric I've been using to judge communities for a while now... Most matches tend to have high amounts of "DBAPM". (Douche Bag Actions Per Second)

2. The lack of content.
Aside from the horrible toddlers that make up the community, there isn't much content in the game. I expected more from Dimps. The story was fine and enjoyable, but the amount of content is a far cry from Xenoverse 2's story at launch.
Despite understanding that the multiplayer live service was the main focus, I can't help but feel like things could've been better. I honestly expected more from a renowned budget (AA) IP dev.

I think the game is fine for what it is, but I doubt I'll stay for the long haul. if I could refund it, I would, without a doubt. Buyers regret is certainly a thing for me in this case. 

Since I'm stuck with it, I'll just dig my heels in and watch the toddlers burn their new toy for myself, just as I did with Overwatch. I'll be lurking, laughing at the SAO toddlers as they destroy their community and new live service toy. With this community, I doubt it'll last more than three months.

review_text: Shadow Tactics is Commandos with ninjas. That’s a good thing, by the way. Very few games swim in the same genre pool as Shadow Tactics. There was the Commandos series, and the Desperados games, and that’s basically it. So all Shadow Tactics has to do is take the “shepherd 2-5 killers during their sneak-and-murder spree across a bunch of maps” to Edo period Japan to feel fresh and original. This means that there is only one question to ask if you want to know if Shadow Tactics is worth your time: Would you like to play more Commandos, or Desperados? For me the answer was “It’s complicated”. I played Commandos way back when. I liked the gameplay at first: Sneaking across the map littered with guards until you find the one unfortunate soul not covered by his colleagues and murder the bejeesus out of him, then moving on the guy whose back he was watching, and so on, pulling on the thread of the guard sweater until only a frayed collar remains… It’s like a beautiful puzzle that drips blood for every piece you set down. But the difficulty spikes were brutal, and at times the precision and speed with which a kill was only possible took so many tries for me to get right that I got frustrated and finally gave up on Commandos. These frustrating moments and difficulty spikes are in here, too, but Shadow Tactics does just enough to mitigate the frustrations that I stuck it out. The excellent quicksave system is one factor: not only does it remind you how long it’s been since your last save, it automatically rotates three slots so that when you save in a situation you don’t yet know is beyond saving, you can revert to an earlier save. The adding of banter between the characters is helpful, too. The story might be kind of rote and have a giant plot hole at the center of it, but the characters are well fleshed out, for the genre, and the dialogue script as well as the voice work elevate the game quite a bit. And yes, it helps that I sneak around ancient japanese fortresses and abduct the son **** from a Sento instead of traipsing around european battefields and assassinating **** commanders, again. Success in Shadow Tactics relies on split second timing at times. That can only work if the controls of the game are excellent, and luckily, they are: Switching between characters and ordering them to do stuff is effortless. The art is serviceable to good: Clearly legible, beautiful at times, but lacking any true wow moments. The sound is sparse but well done, the music unobtrusive and pleasing. The voice work is, as mentioned, well above average for this type of game. This game is for veterans of the genre with a taste for more, spiced with a bit of variation. Complete newcomers interested in the genre might as well start here: They might still bounce off Shadow Tactics, but in a genre with very few members, this is as forgiving as it gets. TLDR: Shadow Tactics is a great stealth real time tactics game. If that’s your jam, it has you covered.

[b] There is no point in playing PSO2:NGS. [/b]

 It's an "MMO" where even a peak hours there's probably a total of 1-2 people you see in 2-3 hours of free roaming, and they tend to ignore you anyways just like you'll eventually do to them. Everyone instead if AFK in hub areas, so getting into this game for the "Multiplayer" aspect will only find it in matchmaking for certain events and activities. 

-Basically, a husk of an MMO with more AFK than playing.

 So how does it play, what if you wanted to play it as a singleplayer game? Well, it gets repetitive really quickly. Pick any playstyle and by the end you'll be mindlessly mashing buttons with a system that has the depth of a kiddie pool. It's like the devs are scared of players having fun with their builds, instead you conform to it because there's barely any variation in your choices. At least the movement is a little entertaining and fun at times, but that's about the only time I had my brain on, it's when I was exploring and not playing the main gameplay loop of beat up enemies while sometimes dodging, casting the same spells, and pressing buttons to win.

-Basically, Early Game is End Game, what you see is what you get.

 You can play dress up in this game. The choices you get are good (if you didn't pick a robot) and you generally have a lot of freedom. That's really good! So good that I see gooners and their eye sore porn addict characters. It's funny at first, but gets old fast. I made a really cool robot girl that actually took a lot of time, and I felt like I stood out like a sore thumb in the wave of big-breasted hookers, questionable characters, and the occasional fetish material. Why is this game so rampant with this?

-Basically, a Gooner's Paradise.

 Is the story worth it? Honestly, I couldn't tell you since I skipped it. 
-Basically, I skipped the boring story after 2 hours. No joke. There is nothing of value even when I didn't skip a cutscene late game, I wish I had. You might even skip this section when skimming over the review, just like how you'll eventually skip the cutscenes too!

 So would I recommend this? No, go play the original PSO2 instead. I'm not kidding, this was the biggest waste of my time and I needed some time to rethink my life choices. I haven't played this game in a bit but I assure you it's guaranteed to be the same even after a year of not playing, trust me. I waited! There won't be content coming to the game unless it's drip-fed additions that all play the same as always, repetitive and boring. Even locations in the game get old fast, and I love exploring! That's such a shame for the potential these spaces had, but there's nothing there except stupid collectable chests! I looked!!

-Basically, an almost empty map and an almost empty experience.

[b] TL;DR: Please either play PSO2 original (which has lots more depth and content, but I don't want this review to be TOO long) or any other singleplayer game, this MMO really does lack content like everyone says unfortunately, I don't see any reason to stick with this when many other games offer a unique and engaging experience that can stick with you for a long time, while this game slides away like grease, becoming a forgotten memory and a lifetime regret of wasted time that's forever linked to your profile. I lost nearly 66 hours of my life, please don't make the same mistake I did. [/b]

review_text:
Where to begin? Man, I could write a whole ass essay about this game, but I'll spare you all and just list some pros and cons! Spoilers below!

Cons:
- God just... The entire ace attorney trial. That was a nightmare. It was so drawn out and kind of pointless? especially since the game doesn't tell you, that you need to keep your items to trade with tagora for the right information. Again, you have no way of knowing this, yet the game scolds you for not doing it right. It's extremely disappointing and frustrating to be chewed out by the game for something you weren't even aware of, let alone able to do anything about. Another point is, that information that is necessary to proceed is held from you and only when the plot calls for it, do characters actually give you the information. Such as one ponit where you're literally just supposed to present wrong evidence (because you don't have any proof) until one of the characters gives you the info you need to continue.
- A general problem my friend and I found while playing, is that at times, you find yourself trying everything on everything, because the game doesn't communictae how you should proceed. We had to look up a walkthrough to get past some of it. Clicking everything randomly kind of takes away from the experience.
- Maybe highlighting the items you can interact with and every character you can talk to would be a good idea? Because it is extremely easy to miss areas, since some of the things you can check aren't that obvious.
- Didn't let us hold Elwurd's hand (my friend was very upset about this)

Now onto the positives!
Pros:
- THE CHARACTERS!! God, this game has some amazing characters, they were what kept us playing through the ace attorney  trial. It's so much fun to go back and talk to the characters, even as you progress further, you really want to get to know them.
- The art!! It's all so well done! I kept stopping and admiring different details in the background and the other background characters, there was so much going on and so much to look at! I'm very pleased with the visual design of this game.
- The music!! Another thing that kept me going during some of the more... "difficult" parts of the game where I had to walk back and forth, the music really helped with the atmosphere, and I will probably be buying the soundtrack.
- The animation! Just... Wow the character animation! Very big fan! :D

So overall, this game is great! I definitely recommend it, if you're willing to sit through the trial part. I've been a fan of hiveswap (ex-homestuck fan here, oof) since the first game came out years ago and I've been excited ever since! I will say, the game does not disappoint, again the biggest criticism is the trial and the persistent issue from the first act, being that you often can get lost in what to do. The final puzzle is a good example of just clicking random shit until something works, this time having the penalty of starting over all the way.
There is definitely some place to improve, but if this sounds like your cup of tea, then I think you should support these creators and buy the game! :)

review_text:
Overall, my experience with this game was very positive. The first story I chose to begin with was the "Trapmaker" series at it appeared to be captivating and interesting based off of the description of the first EP as well as the visual art covers for the 3 separate acts. As expected, it did not let me down and had me on a wild journey that had me glued to the edge of my seat with each puzzle I solved in order to progress the story along. It was a creative take on the who-done-it genera in EP 1. Following that act, it was a complex chase after trapmaker in acts 2 and 3. Many of the puzzles in this story was exciting and thrilling to solve, being very reminiscent of Jigsaw and the "Saw" franchise. The light sprinkles of humor, mixed with the right music in the background made these puzzles very interactive and captivating through and through. The same can be said for the other story I played. The pirate themed story had a great premise and did not rely too heavily on the movie cliches. This story felt like a great mix of various elements from the "Indian of Jones" series and "Pirates of the Caribbean" into one package. This story was not long, but also not too short. The music fit the story very well and helped to further immerse into this world of pirates and scallywags.

Despite this, there are a few huge critiques that makes me feel like this game format was also aimed to copy games that was more focused on revenue instead of overall satisfaction and enjoyment. What I am referring to is the difficulty of many of the puzzles both in the "Trapmaker" and "Pirate Cove" stories. Various of the puzzles from both stories is too complex for someone to just figure out without hints or help. You are given in-game currency to help when you need, but when you run out of this currency you must buy more. This also is the same for unlocking EPs in the game. You have a max of 3 keys over a very long time. Each key to unlock an EP is set at a timer of 2 hours, which in my opinion is way too long of a wait, unless they were thinking that is how long it would take to solve and complete each EP. Although I get the incentive for there being some form of payment in a free-to-play puzzle game, these types of forced payments makes it very difficult to completely defend the enjoyability of the game. A very promising game

I'm sure a lot of people will find this game to be great. I am not one of them for the following reasons

The gameplay is stretched too much (for me) by being grindy. If you enjoy the gameplay loop, know that it's not THAT grindy but it was to me. I had to farm, and farming was done by kill x enemies, clear x areas repeatedly. I'm not a fan of it. I don't mind a little bit, but a big chunk of the gameplay was dedicated to this, which is why I am saying it has great potential but not atm (again, for me).

The lack of content
the repetitive nature of entering the map, clearing map, exfilling, the game pushed me away for a bit. More content would be the solution but as of right now, there isn't enough for me to justify spending more time into the game.

However the game gets a lot of things fantastic.

The gunplay is excellent
Great audio feel, especially on gunshots
Generally good balance of guns
The world is gorgeous (but you get used to it fast due to the repetitive nature)
The difficulty is high, and I love it.
Enemy difficulty is well balanced. They are punishing, but always fair.  I really have to use all of my tools and the game encourages me to.

Some of the things I wish devs would do
Early game ammo issues for some guns clearly make some guns better than others in the start. Why does angelus get 600+ rounds when shotguns get 50+?
That's about it though. the devs are passionate and they listen to community a lot. The project is headed in a very promising direction. Fow now, I will shelf this away and can't wait to get back to it a year later.

review_text:
I don’t know who tested the controls (keyboard/mouse and gamepad), but I haven’t seen anything this buggy and inconsistent in a long time. Want auto-aim because your aim is bad but you still want to play through the story? Sure, here you go. Except in combat it will never actually lock onto enemies — only supply crates, or sometimes enemies, but never their weak spots. For example, the fight in the church against the multi-armed monster: try turning on aim support and beating this boss. You won’t be able to target the weak points (those glowing growths), only the still-invulnerable parts. Okay. Forget the devs’ advice, let’s switch to keyboard and mouse. And right away it’s obvious why the developers push the gamepad. It feels like the input handling was written in Python. It feels like 500–700 ms of delay, though Nvidia overlay shows only 50 ms. I suspect the issue is “object magnetism” and penalty timeouts between actions (animations). But then the question is — why the hell add magnetism/animations for keyboard and mouse if you can’t consistently process my input? On gamepad I can run and reload at the same time. On keyboard/mouse — only if I get lucky and there’s no conflict between the sprint-start and reload animations. You’ll get sprayed with green goo long before the game responds to a basic combo like Shift + turn + W. I get it when edge cases aren’t tested, but skipping testing for core story fights is just shameful. I don’t recommend buying the game until they rework the input handling.

There's a lot of things wrong with this game tbh.

The story is confusing to follow along at the start, the pace is wacky, and I still don't even remember what happened plot-wise. It's just not that impactful. The voice acting is ok I guess.

The gameplay? There's no FEAR involved. When it comes to games like Dead Space and Resident Evil, there's always a fear of running out of resources and having to react in time for any jumpscares or surprises, and when you have to use melee, you need to create opportunities and even then the melee options aren't even that worth it. In this game? Melee is your best option and you don't run out of melee. Your worst option? Guns, and you run out of ammo. How does that make any sense??? The only time guns are useful is for the FINAL BOSS. I feel like because of all of this, any levels of fear is just thrown OUT the window.

The enemies? God I RESTARTED this game to play on the hardest difficulty just to prove a point. When you're using melee, you're safe 90% of the time. The enemies just LINE UP against you one by one. The only time when they gang up on you is when you're close to another enemy. Only ONE enemy is attacking you at a time. The melee attack patterns are so pathetically easy, you just need to remember to move left and right interchangeably, which is a strategy that the game TELLS you to do. And it ALWAYS works until the final boss. There is NO skill involved. 

Now, I rated this game as bad, but maybe this game just isn't for me. Whoever is reading this, you can either trust the reviews, or trust your own judgement. I'd prefer you trust your own judgement and play the game for yourself to see if it's to your liking. Otherwise, I wouldn't even recommend this game to my dog.

review_text:
RCT2 is less of a sequel, and more of a 'remaster' or 'expanded edition' of the first game. 

	Everything is essentially the same, minus a few quality of life and game mechanic changes. And I mean 'few'. The most obvious one is being able to hold the Shift key to adjust height on scenery and rides. Previously you could do this, but only via roundabout ways (such as raising land then lowering it). You also can't adjust ride prices or park entrace fees as before—now it's either one or the other (or neither at all). Which is actually a decent change, since you could always somewhat cheat the scenario objectives by altering prices to increase satisfaction ratings or revenue.

	RCT1 scenarios were typically "Have x amount of guests with a satisfaction rating of Y by G amount of years". RCT2 has many such scenarios, but some measure success on metrics that either weren't used in the first game, or sparesly used. "Have 10 coasters with an excitement rating of at least Y", that sort of thing. I assume the developer realized how much coaster building was the main draw, so a few scenarios give you unlimited cash to build as you please. Which is, like the prices change, a very nice improvement.

	The main draw of RCT2 and the reason for its existence is the editor. You can finally create your own maps, and even fill them with custom rides and objectives without worrying about monetary constraints. There's really not much more to say about it, other than it does its job well and was sorely lacking before. You can forego the scenarios and just make custom dream parks.

	Editor aside, both games play exactly the same. You have a list of premade scenarios (with pre-made maps) that task you with some manner of objective; RCT2 having more variety than 1 in this category. RCT2 features more stalls and scenery options, so you can build up your park with more rides and food vendors than before. The main draw, of course, is the roller coaster building. And RCT2 has far more coaster varieties than the first game, with unique ride carts per scenario. 

	Coasters (and editor) aside, does this replace RCT1 in its entirety? Not entirely; RCT1 still has its own unique scenario maps. I find some of the maps in 2 to be cluttered with a lot of scenery or significant changes in elevation. You still have plenty of flat maps that are easy to build in and around, but the cluttered ones do stick out. I also feel as if the first game gave you more variety in park sizes and the shape of the play area, but a person with more hours in both games can confirm or deny that. Ultimately, people will play favorites with what maps they liked in each game.

	If it was 2002, I might wonder if its a letdown that a sequel 3 years in development feels more like an expansion pack. Goes to show you that reviews and scores change depending on when you review and whether you're comparing it to a predecessor. In 2021, I'm ok with an enhanced follow-up. As such, if RCT1 is a 7, this is an 8 for the minor improvements.

raising land then lowering it ) . you also can ' t adjust ride prices or park entrace fees as before—now it ' s either one or the other ( or neither at all ) . which is actually a decent change , since you could always somewhat cheat the scenario objectives by altering prices to increase satisfaction ratings or revenue . rct1 scenarios were typically have x amount of guests with a satisfaction rating of y by g amount of years . rct2 has many such scenarios , but some measure success on metrics that either weren ' t used in the first game , or sparesly used . have 10 coasters with an excitement rating of at least y , that sort of thing . i assume the developer realized how much coaster building was the main draw , so a few scenarios give you unlimited cash to build as you please . which is , like the prices change , a very nice improvement . the main draw of rct2 and the reason for its existence is the editor . you can finally create your own maps , and even fill them with custom rides and objectives without worrying about monetary constraints . there ' s really not much more to say about it , other than it does its job well and was sorely lacking before . you can forego the scenarios and just make custom dream parks . editor aside , both games play exactly the same . you have a list of premade scenarios ( with pre-made maps ) that task you with some manner of objective rct2 having more variety than 1 in this category . rct2 features more stalls and scenery options , so you can build up your park with more rides and food vendors than before . the main draw , of course , is the roller coaster building . and rct2 has far more coaster varieties than the first game , with unique ride carts per scenario . coasters ( and editor ) aside , does this replace rct1 in its entirety ? not entirely rct1 still has its own unique scenario maps . i find some of the maps in 2 to be cluttered with a lot of scenery or significant changes in elevation . you still have plenty of flat maps that are easy to build in and around , but the cluttered ones do stick out . i also feel as if the first game gave you more variety in park sizes and the shape of the play area , but a person with more hours in both games can confirm or deny that . ultimately , people will play favorites with what maps they liked in each game . if it was 2002 , i might wonder if its a letdown that a sequel 3 years in development feels more like an expansion pack . goes to show you that reviews and scores change depending on when you review and whether you ' re comparing it to a predecessor . in 2021 , i ' m ok with an enhanced follow-up . as such , if rct1 is a 7 , this is an 8 for the minor improvements .

review_text:
Although the story of the game is amazing, I can’t recommend it at its current state. The enemy NPCs are way too easy, to the point where you can take 15 enemies alone. They never dodge, never parry, if they group up against you they fight one by one, it’s boringly easy. Also, if you’re sneaking around, sometimes you’ll literally make eye contact and they still wont see you. 

Overall the NPC AI is not smart at all, like if you get caught by a guard for being somewhere you don’t belong but convince them you’re actually a noble, they’ll let you go only to confront you again. 

Also character progression is way too fast, and you get the best gear in the game almost immediately. This causes the initial side quests not to make any sense at all, in the early beginning of the game I had all the best gear and so much money and most of the early side quests are about working an honest job for like 10 grochens. One of the first swords you get can basically kill anyone with 3 hits, regardless of their armor, once you reforge it once with easy to get materials. Speaking of the blacksmithing in this game which was advertised to be a big feature, it’s literally the most basic minigame, just hit a piece of metal a bunch of times and you have a sword, no need to add a guard or decorate it or anything, it just comes out perfect!

Overall, it really feels like the developers never played this game beginning-to-end, they made sure every part independently makes sense but they never really tested how fast the character progression goes, or how easy it is to fight 20 enemy AIs at once. 

Also, adding gay stuff literally makes no sense with the characters involved, both of which are clearly into women throughout the game and also practising Catholics. It really makes no sense to have either of being gay for either of their characters and for the time period. 

I hope this gets fixed in the future, because this really is a good game

[list]

[/list]

I really cant recommend anyone spend more than $10 on this game.

review_text:
You'll often find yourself losing games because of incredibly frustrating situations like a lone Specter Child slowly destroying your Farm placed far in the back without you noticing due to the lack of any indicators. If you don't have the warnings window open, you genuinely won't know a structure is taking damage without directly looking at it, and the window will simply say "a building is damaged" without even pointing you to it. Later on in the game, when you've got nearly 100 villagers, you will also lose them to random fights for this very same reason. It's difficult to tell if a fight is even happening aside from the occasional combat sounds, and trying to keep track of nearly a 3-figure count of villagers on your own is a feat, to say the least. Also, you can't pause the construction of walls, meaning your Builders will always have it as a priority on their list, even if you don't want those Crylithium Curtain Walls built because your Crystal Harvestry got destroyed by a random Specter last night and you want to spend your remaining Crylithium on charging your Essence Collectors (you can't stop them, and they will spend all of your Crylithium on those walls and you will lose because your towers will have no charge)

As for the tower-defense aspect, it's just a matter of time before you discover that spamming Ice Golems and Ice Bolt towers is the only way to survive the later waves. You can't determine target priority on towers, and Ice is the damage type that no monster in the game resists, as well as dealing bonus damage to Fire Elementals. There isn't any strategy to placing towers beyond the basics (line them up behind walls and make a maze). A couple of towers, especially the Tumbler-based ones, are left in the dust thanks to the lack of a target priority system, while AoE spamming towers remain the most functional. And what do you know - there's an AoE Ice damage tower. Why would you use anything other than it and the Golems?

All in all, it's a fantastic concept, but the game spreads itself thin among its many interacting systems and fails to convey critical information when it should be immediately known. Its cracks will show the more you try to experiment, but even if you're fine with sticking to the meta, you'll still find yourself at the short end of the stick when you eventually fail to notice a lose condition the game doesn't do much to help you keep track of.

review_text:
I bought this game for the aesthetic, but I have regrets.As you can tell by my profile picture, I'm a sucker for anything neon.

This game is _very_ unpolished. The movements feel super jank to me. It also doesn't have native controller support when it seems like there's no practical reason to exclude it. This also means no steam deck support, and no native Linux support. I place a very heavy weight on these things, but I was willing to look the other way.

Sadly, it gets worse... The game starts you in a huge open arena with zero instructions of what to do. There's a question mark that you can walk over. One might expect that walking over it would tell you something useful about the game. One would be wrong. Instead, you're greeted with a passive-aggressive note from the dev basically saying "people keep asking why you start in an empty arena, here's why I do that" and then it goes on to explain his strategy for developing the game that literally nobody cares about. Conspicuously missing is literally anything useful about what to do next to start playing the game.

I explored as much as I could stand, where I was greeted with what appeared to be chests that could be purchased with in-game currency that I could not purchase and no indication as to how currency is earned.

I'm sure the information on how this game is played in there, but I honestly have no patience for a game that doesn't just drop me into the action. People are asking why for a reason, pick up on it. Drop them into a tutorial like every other game, or at least into the first level where they can start killing crap. Very few people care enough about your game to have to read the manual before beginning, this isn't _actually_ 1980.

I'm certain I could have figured out what to do next, but I had no interest in doing so. In its current state, I don't recommend this game even though every part of me wanted to like it.
